comments.quote: And how many of these were computationally reproducible (I think it was in that paper!)

comments.issue: Clinical health still rarely does this, about 17% of studies.
comments.request: Add this comparison with clinical health.
comments.quote: line 211 - Still rarely done in clinical health - ~17% of studies

comments.issue: The suggestion to act lacks a concrete vision, for example leadership by SORTEE.
comments.request: Suggest what action would look like and engage universities and organisations.
comments.quote: What do you suggest this would look like – something for SORTEE to lead on perhaps?

comments.issue: The point at line 255 is good but its importance is not explained.
comments.request: Add a sentence explaining why this point matters.
comments.quote: Maybe not room in this manuscript to explore this but perhaps you could add a sentence here to explain how/why this is important.

comments.issue: The databases accessed in WOS are not listed.
comments.request: List the databases available in the Advanced Search of WOS.
comments.quote: Which databases in particular did you have access to? Please list these – you can find this in the Advanced Search part of WOS.

comments.issue: Trim and Fill has long been questioned; only Nakagawa et al. is cited.
comments.request: Cite additional papers on the problems with Trim and Fill.
comments.quote: Trim and Fill has been considered problematic for a while – perhaps refer to other papers here in addition to Nakagwa et al.

reviews.assessment: Finds the topic important but has substantial concerns about framing, the conceptualisation of research waste and recommendations that may be sub-optimal at scale.
strengths: extensive reporting of methods and data/code availability
brings attention to an important topic
good conceptualisation of research waste in Figure 1

comments.issue: Writing is colloquial and the flow is stop-start, especially the first section.
comments.request: Formalise the language so it reads like serious research.
comments.quote: The writing style seems quite colloquial or conversational in places and I find the flow a little stop-start (particularly the first section of the main text).

comments.issue: The term exploitative waste suggests deliberate wrongdoing and is confusing.
comments.request: Rename it, for example limitation waste, study potential waste or future waste.
comments.quote: However, the term ‘exploitative waste’ is confusing to me – it sounds like people are deliberately causing waste in this way

comments.issue: The paper risks blaming single parties for a systemic problem.
comments.request: Avoid victimising any one party and present waste as a systemic interaction.
comments.quote: I think you need to be very careful throughout this not to victimise or place the blame for research waste on any one party

comments.issue: Randomisation and blinding are presented as the ideal design although ecology differs from medicine and observational studies may be more cost-effective.
comments.request: Account for the cost-effectiveness of different research designs.
comments.quote: I would just be careful about suggesting randomisation and blinding are the ‘ideal’ study design in a field that is very different to medicine in many ways.

comments.issue: Basic metadata (date, location) and cost reporting are aspects of research waste not considered.
comments.request: Include metadata completeness and cost reporting as forms of waste.
comments.quote: Other aspects of research waste to consider are basic things like the date and location studies were conducted (i.e., basic metadata) which can help inform the external validity and relevance of the study to policy and practice.

comments.issue: Publication delay is not considered as a form of research waste.
comments.request: Mention publication delay and its costs for evidence synthesis.
comments.quote: You don’t seem to consider time in your consideration of research waste.

comments.issue: Recommendations may reduce waste locally but create waste at discipline scale; the optimal overall research strategy is not considered.
comments.request: Consider what the optimal discipline-wide research strategy should be.
comments.quote: I would like to see greater consideration of what the overall optimal research strategy should be.

comments.issue: Introducing unused potential while saying it cannot be calculated is contradictory.
comments.request: Resolve the contradiction about the new term.
comments.quote: To me that seems quite a contradiction and confuses me about what you’re trying to achieve here.

comments.issue: Weighting ignores methodological quality; precision is not accuracy.
comments.request: Account for methodological quality or state this as a limitation.
comments.quote: your weighting takes no account of the methodological quality of each meta-study. How you do propose you account for this?

comments.issue: Typos: field is written filed at L150 and though is written thought at L314.
comments.request: Correct these typos.
comments.quote: L314 – should be ‘though’ not ‘thought’.

comments.issue: Blinding is difficult in ecology and medical blinding cannot simply be transferred.
comments.request: Focus on feasible design aspects such as randomisation, controls and pseudoreplication.
comments.quote: blinding is a complex issue in ecology – I think we need to be careful when trying to apply blinding methods from medicine to ecology and expect them to be possible.

comments.issue: Systematic reviews are enormous and time-consuming; always doing them is not cost-effective.
comments.request: Match the scale of synthesis to the costs of misinforming decision-makers.
comments.quote: Systematic review is not a panacea and we need to be much smarter as to how we deploy it as a useful and crucially cost-effective tool to inform policy and practice.

comments.issue: Losing research at L332-333 is misleading; it is research impact that is lost.
comments.request: Use a term such as losing research impact.
comments.quote: L332-333 – this is misleading, we are not losing research, but more like we are losing research impact or similar term.

title: Quantifying research waste in ecology

study.system: Neotropical cloud-forest Viburnum (Oreinotinus); phylogenomic, morphometric and biogeographic analyses

editor_summary: Reviewers find the work of potential interest but raise substantial concerns; the editor cannot accept it, though a revised version addressing the serious concerns would be considered.

reviews.assessment: Enjoyed the detailed study and finds it worth publishing, but wants replicated-radiation claims toned down and syndrome categorization and climate links strengthened.
strengths: detailed plant study rivaling famous animal radiations

comments.issue: Claims that the study establishes a replicated radiation rivaling animals are overstated and ignore similar plant studies.
comments.request: Tone down these statements and cite comparable plant radiation studies.
comments.quote: I would perhaps tone down these and similar statements throughout the text.

comments.issue: It is unclear how the four leaf syndromes were categorized; classification may be subjective rather than statistical.
comments.request: Describe and statistically justify syndrome classification, e.g. with cluster analyses.
comments.quote: However, at the same time, it’s not very clear how this categorization is performed.

comments.issue: Pubescence was not scored as a continuous trait, limiting the morphospace and syndrome categorization.
comments.request: Include pubescence in a mixed-data morphospace (e.g. NMDS) and cluster analysis.
comments.quote: I wonder if it wouldn’t be possible to include this trait in a morphospace analysis that allows mixing

comments.issue: Micro-climate comparison samples only one species per leaf syndrome, so the ecomorph-climate correlation is unreplicated.
comments.request: Compare climatic envelopes and syndromes for every species using CHELSEA and GBIF data.
comments.quote: Only one example from each leaf syndrome is sampled in this comparison, meaning that there is no replication

comments.issue: The ecomorph-micro-climate correlation is unconvincing and the ecological function of traits such as marginal teeth is not discussed.
comments.request: Expand the niche-differentiation discussion and address trait ecological function.
comments.quote: I think not only the correlation between ecomorph and micro-climate is not convincing

comments.issue: The choice of Figure 4 variables is unjustified and appears driven by significance, with 14 CHELSEA variables unreported.
comments.request: Justify the variable selection and report the remaining CHELSEA variables.
comments.quote: It’s not completely clear how the variables shown in Figure 4 were chosen.

comments.issue: The main-text figure lacks a time-calibrated tree, which would show the timing of events.
comments.request: Present the time-calibrated tree in Figure 1.
comments.quote: I would have presented the time calibrated tree in Fig1.

comments.issue: The species count may be wrong because V. tinoides appears to comprise two species.
comments.request: Correct the number of species or clarify delimitation.
comments.quote: Maybe only three species as it looks like V. tinoides is actually two species.

comments.issue: The phrase 'as many Oreinotinus species as possible' is vague about the actual sample size.
comments.request: State how many species were included or rephrase.
comments.quote: “for as many Oreinotinus species as possible” – How many specifically? (or rephrase)

comments.issue: Criteria for identifying hybridization evidence before omitting specimens are not defined.
comments.request: Define what counts as evidence of hybridization.
comments.quote: Specimens showing any evidence of hybridization between species were omitted.

comments.issue: The phrase 'the South American radiation' at L712 is unclear.
comments.request: Specify which radiation is meant.
comments.quote: Line 712: Which is the South American radiation?

comments.issue: A sentence at L712 should not start with a numeral.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence so it does not start with '1000'.
comments.quote: Line 712: Do not start sentence with “1000”

reviews.assessment: Highly positive about the exemplar system and analyses, but asks for a formal test of independent leaf-morph evolution and clearer evolutionary framing.
strengths: much needed exemplar system for plant replicated radiation
lots of data and detailed analyses

comments.issue: The admixture section does not explain that introgression is now typical of recent adaptive radiations.
comments.request: Clarify why introgression was tested and where it fits in the literature.
comments.quote: I think it would be worth clarifying that introgression is now regarded as a more typical feature of many recent adaptive radiations

comments.issue: It is not stated whether the results mean Oreinotinus should now be regarded as an adaptive radiation.
comments.request: State whether Oreinotinus is considered an adaptive radiation.
comments.quote: Also, based on your results, is Oreinotinus now regarded as an adaptive radiation?

comments.issue: Independent evolution of leaf morphs is asserted from a well-supported tree but not tested against a clade-morph alternative.
comments.request: Apply an AU test comparing morph-constrained and clade-constrained trees.
comments.quote: could you constrain the leaf morphs (per morph per analysis) and then apply an AU test

comments.issue: Parallel evolution is used without defining it against convergent evolution.
comments.request: Define parallel versus convergent evolution in the main text.
comments.quote: you use the term parallel evolution (but you may want to define this from convergent evolution) in the main text.

comments.issue: The cited cichlid example does not focus on replicated ecomorph evolution; a more relevant reference is missing.
comments.request: Add the suggested cichlid reference demonstrating convergent evolution.
comments.quote: The ref cited (4) does not really focus on replicated evolution of ecomorphs per se.

reviews.assessment: Impressed by the data but finds the paper under-delivers on trait convergence, niche evolution and ancestral-uncertainty analyses promised by the introduction.

comments.issue: Main-text Figure 1 uses uninformative branch lengths and a single ancestral-range reconstruction instead of the time tree with uncertainty.
comments.request: Show the time-calibrated tree with ancestral-state uncertainty in Figure 1.
comments.quote: Fig. 1 shows a phylogeny with uninformative branch lengths and a single most probable ancestral

comments.issue: Ancestral area estimation ignores phylogenetic uncertainty from low-support nodes.
comments.request: Explore the effect of phylogenetic uncertainty on ancestral area estimation.
comments.quote: some exploration of the effect of phylogenetic uncertainty on ancestral area estimation would belong

comments.issue: No convergence analysis was run; SURFACE or alternatives could handle the mixed discrete-continuous data.
comments.request: Quantify convergence with SURFACE, K, QVI or l1ou using the PCA axes.
comments.quote: Those PC values could be input into SURFACE or other similar programs.

comments.issue: Only discrete leaf types were used, so the analyses show radiation but not convergence directly.
comments.request: Use continuous variation and community-phylogenetic approaches to test convergence.
comments.quote: these analyses reinforce the radiation part but don’t demonstrate convergence (at least not directly).

comments.issue: Niche differences are measured for only three species, so morph-niche association across the clade is unknown.
comments.request: Test whether the same niche differences associate with morphs across the clade using bioclim data.
comments.quote: one would want to see if these same niche differences are associated with the morphs across the clade

comments.issue: Paper focuses on gene flow and peripheral topics rather than the convergence evidence central to its case.
comments.request: Refocus the paper on analyses most central to the replicated-radiation claim.
comments.quote: I would suggest focusing on those that are most central to making the case

comments.issue: The discussion of timing and movement would be clearer with a time-axis tree in Figure 1.
comments.request: Add a time axis to Figure 1.
comments.quote: This discussion of time and movement is one reason that I wished Fig. 1 had a time tree

comments.issue: The stochastic mapping does not report the transition number with credibility interval or account for phylogenetic uncertainty.
comments.request: Report transition estimates with intervals and run realizations across sampled trees.
comments.quote: It would be ideal to fold phylogenetic uncertainty into this analysis by completing realizations across a sample of trees.

title: Replicated radiation of a plant clade along a cloud forest archipelago

study.system: duckweeds Lemna minor and Spirodela polyrhiza; lab competition experiments and Beverton-Holt model

reviews.assessment: Interesting, well-written experimental-theoretical study; interpretation of plasticity effects and invasion estimates needs work, but there are no fundamental flaws.

comments.issue: Fig. 1a is confusing: a single point suggests low-frequency individuals of both species coexist, whereas it shows invasion into a high-frequency resident.
comments.request: Clarify the legend, e.g. invader from low-frequency treatment and resident from high-frequency treatment.
comments.quote: Fig. 1a: I found this figure initially a bit confusing. For example, for a single red point it looks like L. minor from the low-frequency treatment coexists with S. polyrhiza from the low-frequency treatment.

comments.issue: Both treatments are plastic, so the results show the effect of plasticity per se only under an assumed non-plastic high-density type.
comments.request: Discuss this assumption and what it implies for interpreting the results.
comments.quote: One can only interpret the results as effect of plasticity if one assumes a non-plastic type that is adjusted/adapted to a high conspecific density.

comments.issue: The L269-271 assumption may not hold in real life, so real invasion dynamics and coexistence outcomes might differ.
comments.quote: I find this potentially problematic because in real life this might not happen and and the real invasion dynamics and coexistence outcome then might be different.

comments.issue: Full parameter estimates for both plasticity treatments are not reported, limiting interpretation of the results.
comments.request: Provide a supplementary table of lambda values and all intra- and interspecific competition coefficients.
comments.quote: Could you provide a supplementary table with all parameter estimates (the lambda values and all intraspecific and interspecific competition coefficients) for both plasticity treatments?

comments.issue: Invasion into an equilibrium resident relies on interpolation into a population size range with no data, because growth rates stay above one there.
comments.quote: I was a bit concerned that the results on invasion into a resident population at equilibrium are based largely on interpolation into a population size region for which there are no data

comments.issue: A more direct approach, introducing few individuals into a resident population at equilibrium and measuring N(t+1)/N(t), was not used.
comments.request: Explain why the direct invasion experiment was not chosen.
comments.quote: why you didn't choose the more direct approach of introducing a small number of individuals from the high-frequency and low-frequency treatment into a resident population

comments.issue: Frequency dependence is central to the paper but becomes ambiguous when density is not held constant and can vary.
comments.request: Comment on in what sense frequency dependence remains meaningful.
comments.quote: frequency and frequency dependence can be a bit confusing if density is not held constant but can vary as well.

comments.issue: An opposite expectation is plausible: plasticity could increase competition by broadening the range of conditions species tolerate, limiting niche differentiation.
comments.request: Comment on this alternative expectation.
comments.quote: One might also expect that plasticity increases competition because individuals and species can deal with a broader range of environmental factors which limits the opportunity for niche differentiation.

comments.issue: It is unclear what quantity the posterior probabilities at L91-92 refer to.
comments.request: Specify what the posterior probabilities are of.
comments.quote: L91-92: posterior probabilities of what?

comments.issue: Ambiguous whether 'magnitude of plasticity' means the slope of the reaction norm or the magnitude of plastic change.
comments.request: Clarify which quantity is meant.
comments.quote: L112: magnitude of plasticity (i.e. slope of the reaction norm) or magnitude of plastic change?

comments.issue: The order of the L190-195 presentation hinders understanding of the derivation.
comments.request: Present the single-species equilibrium and its equation first, then the invasion growth rate.
comments.quote: The order can be improved to facilitate understanding. First say that you solved for the single-species equilibrium and give its equation

comments.issue: Relevant literature on plastic trait variation and on reversal of competitive dominance is missing.
comments.request: Consider citing Banitz (2019), Pimentel (1965), Pease (1984) and Ayala (1966).
comments.quote: Some additional papers that came to mind as potentially relevant

reviews.assessment: Enjoyable, clearly written paper on an important topic; the logic linking experiments to invasion growth rates needs validation and sensitivity checks.

comments.issue: Predicted coexistence outcomes were never checked against observed long-term outcomes in the experimental tubs.
comments.request: Check for a few replicates whether predictions match long-term outcomes of starting both species at high abundance.
comments.quote: have any of the predicted outcomes been retrospectively experimentally validated? That is, when the model predicts that plasticity ought to result in coexistence

comments.issue: The constant-lambda Beverton-Holt inference assumes no further plastic change during the one-week competition experiment after five weeks of induction.
comments.request: Provide evidence that additional plastic change during the competition experiment is negligible.
comments.quote: is there a good guarantee that populations plastically “adapted” to one environment do not plastically change within the time frame of the competition experiments?

comments.issue: The linear candidate model is not credible, so model selection effectively compares two similar models and is weakly discriminative.
comments.request: Add a more credible population dynamical model to the comparison.
comments.quote: the linear model in the last row of Supplementary Table 1 is not a serious population dynamical model, as it can produce negative population densities.

comments.issue: Sensitivity of the Bayesian parameter estimation to the assumed prior forms was not assessed.
comments.request: Try alternative priors, e.g. uniform distributions in place of Gammas or truncated Gaussians.
comments.quote: it would be good to check the sensitivity of the Bayesian parameter estimation to alterations of some of the underlying assumptions

comments.issue: Results may depend on the artificial fitting 'hack' described in the supplementary methods.
comments.request: Exclude the lowest-abundance experiment, repeat the analysis and check whether Figure 1b outcomes hold.
comments.quote: it would be important to check the sensitivity of the results to this procedure in some way.

comments.issue: The claim that plasticity is independent of traditional coexistence conceptualizations is overstated; the machinery to include plasticity already exists.
comments.request: Rephrase to say plasticity is underappreciated rather than independent of traditional frameworks.
comments.quote: Is this really independent of traditional conceptualizations? Or merely underappreciated? What I mean is that the machinery to deal with the possibility of plasticity is all there

comments.issue: L132 is ambiguous: unclear whether the concepts are unlikely to hold or merely unhelpful unless the coexistence problem is posed broadly.
comments.request: Clarify the wording.
comments.quote: Are these concepts unlikely to hold, or unlikely to be particularly useful without posing the coexistence problem broad enough to allow the inclusion of plastic effects?

comments.issue: Difficulties may simply reflect that the right traits were not measured; traits other than SLA or root-to-shoot ratio may matter.
comments.request: Consider whether other traits are relevant.
comments.quote: Could it be possible that these difficulties are due to simply not having the right traits?

comments.issue: Laboratory simplification of real environments is treated as a shortcoming, although it is natural and possibly a virtue.
comments.request: Rephrase this limitation.
comments.quote: I would say it is quite natural (and possibly a virtue instead of a shortcoming) that a laboratory experiment simplifies the complexity of real environments.

comments.issue: It is unclear how the Gaussian prior was truncated and whether it was renormalized.
comments.request: Describe the truncation procedure.
comments.quote: It is not clear how the Gaussian distribution was truncated. Was the negative region zeroed out and the rest of the curve renormalized to have an area of 1 underneath?

comments.issue: Figure S1 is informative enough to belong in the main text.
comments.request: Move Figure S1 to the main text as the new Figure 1.
comments.quote: This is a nice figure - I would consider moving it to the main text as the new Figure 1.

comments.issue: Panel 1a is redundant with panel 1b and could move to the Supplement with absolute invasion rate distributions.
comments.request: Move panel 1a to the Supplement and add absolute distributions of invasion rates.
comments.quote: I am not sure if panel 1a is needed, because the overall information it conveys is also visible from panel 1b alone.

comments.issue: Shading of the 95% highest-density intervals is unnecessary when the full distributions are visible.
comments.request: Remove the shading and the corresponding text in line 592.
comments.quote: I don't think the shading of the 95% highest-density intervals is necessary, because those are only informative when the full distributions are not visible.

comments.issue: The phrase 'and so are mutually positive' in the line 596 caption is uninformative because the quantities are always positive.
comments.request: Remove 'and so are mutually positive' in line 596.
comments.quote: in line 596, remove “and so are mutually positive” (they always are, even if there is no coexistence)

reviews.assessment: Impressed by this clear, economical study with high impact potential; comments concern how coexistence theory and plasticity are framed, not the results.
strengths: straightforward way to consider plasticity in coexistence studies

comments.issue: Negative frequency dependence is presented as the requirement for coexistence, but coexistence theory is based on density dependence.
comments.request: Reframe the theory presentation around density dependence rather than frequency dependence.
comments.quote: While stable coexistence often implies negative frequency-dependence, it is a not a diagnostic feature. The reason is because the theory of species coexistence is based on density-dependence.

comments.issue: The competitor-density context is hidden until the third introduction paragraph, suggesting plasticity was never part of coexistence research.
comments.request: Clarify early the distinction between plasticity to the physical environment and to competitor presence.
comments.quote: The first two paragraphs are about plasticity, competition, and density-dependence generally. The third paragraph is really about the study system, at which point the environmental context is made clear.

comments.issue: Plasticity is a malleable concept and, under the definition used, storage-effect studies also count as plasticity; the scope of the definition needs justification.
comments.request: Give a clear justification of the plasticity definition and its scope.
comments.quote: Clear justification of the definition here is important for defining the scope of the results both conceptually and experimentally.

comments.issue: Fig. 1b posteriors show no correlation between the species' invasion growth rates despite shared parameters, suggesting parameters were sampled independently.
comments.request: State whether all parameters are estimated jointly with correlations accounted for.
comments.quote: are you estimating all model parameters jointly and accounting for correlations in estimates, or are you estimating each parameter without estimates of the other?

comments.issue: The introduction argues intraspecific competition must be measured, but the methodology does not estimate plasticity in alpha_jj; motivation and methods seem at odds.
comments.request: Explain why plasticity effects on intraspecific competition are not estimated.
comments.quote: However, the methodology presented in the ppaer argues that one does not, in fact, need to estimate plasticity effects on intraspecific competition

comments.issue: Line 54 should specify that the plasticity referred to is a response to a competitor, not to the physical environment.
comments.request: Specify that this is plasticity in response to competitor presence.
comments.quote: This would be a good place to specify that this is plasticity in response to the presence of a competitor, not the physical environment.

comments.issue: Lines 104-111 should state the particular environmental context, competitor identity, as part of the motivation.
comments.request: State the competitor-induced context in the motivation.
comments.quote: This is the particular environmental context that should be stated as part of the motivation.

comments.issue: The term 'competitive differences' is poor terminology because niche overlap also involves competition, so the descriptor misrepresents the quantities.
comments.request: Avoid 'competitive differences' and do not proliferate terminology.
comments.quote: Niche overlap (or niche difference) also includes aspects of competition and so defining one as being related to competitive interactions and the other not seems like poor terminology.

comments.issue: The claim that plasticity invalidates the niche overlap/fitness inequality concepts is unjustified; only the measures derived under specific assumptions need updating.
comments.request: Distinguish concept from measure when revising lines 131-133.
comments.quote: The real issue here is that there is a big difference between a concept and a measure.

comments.issue: The limitation that slow plasticity induction relative to population change may make plasticity unimportant is not discussed.
comments.request: Add this limitation to the discussion.
comments.quote: If plasticity truly takes that long to induce in this species, it’s possible that species may not acclimate sufficiently fast to low-density conditions before they go extinct, and so plasticity may be unimportant.

comments.issue: Alpha is a competition coefficient, not the per-capita effect of one species on another; equating the two confuses readers.
comments.request: Describe the alphas as competition coefficients.
comments.quote: The alphas here are better stated simply as competition coefficients rather than the per-capita effect of one species on another.

comments.issue: The wording suggests parameters were sampled independently by species, which may explain the apparent independence in Fig. 1b.
comments.request: Sample all parameters jointly per draw and clarify the procedure.
comments.quote: The wording here suggests that you independently sampled model parameters by species to get invasion growth rates.

comments.issue: The description of 'improper flat priors' does not specify their scale and bounds.
comments.request: Explain the scale and bounds of the priors.
comments.quote: In general, improper priors are a multiple of a uniform distribution on some unbounded range, on some scale. Can you explain the scale and the bounds?

title: Phenotypic plasticity promotes species coexistence

study.system: rattlesnake species complex; venom gene population genomics

editor_summary: Editor requires conclusive evidence for balancing selection that excludes alternatives, especially collapsed duplications, as explained by Reviewer 2.

reviews.assessment: First-of-its-kind venom study adding important knowledge, well suited to the journal; only minor questions and suggestions.
strengths: first study of its kind in venom research
comprehensive genomic analysis of venom regions
important for venom and broader evolutionary biology
well suited for the journal's readership

comments.issue: The role of C. atrox in the study is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify what C. atrox was used for.
comments.quote: It is not fully clear to me what did you use C. atrox for.

comments.issue: Animals were sacrificed despite blood samples being used for DNA, which is hard to justify given population declines.
comments.request: Justify the sacrifice of animals or explain why it was necessary.
comments.quote: I see that you use blood samples for DNA extractions. Why did you sacrifice the animals then?

comments.issue: Myotoxins, an important venom component especially in C. viridis, were not considered.
comments.request: Explain why myotoxins were excluded or include them.
comments.quote: Why didn’t you consider myotoxins? If I remember correctly, it is an important component of rattlesnake venom, especially in C. viridis.

comments.issue: The results suggest heterozygote advantage but do not exclude frequency-dependent or spatiotemporally variable balancing selection.
comments.request: Explain why other forms of balancing selection are difficult to test.
comments.quote: they do not rule out the influence of other forms of balancing selection, including frequency dependent or spatially and temporally variable processes

comments.issue: The phrase 'to quantify the genomic landscape associated with venom genes' at lines 162-163 is generic and unclear.
comments.request: Reword or remove this sentence.
comments.quote: What do you mean by this? How do you quantify a landscape?

comments.issue: Removing indels at line 191 is questionable because presence/absence of whole venom genes drives composition variation.
comments.request: Justify why indels were removed.
comments.quote: Line 191: Why indels were removed? Isn’t presence/absence of whole genes what drives variation in venom composition?

reviews.assessment: Appealing idea and plausible arguments, but the evidence for balancing selection is not convincing because collapsed duplications remain a parsimonious alternative.
strengths: appealing idea with plausible theoretical arguments
well-written text with arguments easy to follow
PSMC analysis and descriptive results are informative

comments.issue: Collapsed duplications, possibly polymorphic, mimic balancing selection and could explain the patterns; the steps taken were insufficient to exclude paralogous regions.
comments.request: Provide conclusive evidence excluding collapsed duplications and CNV.
comments.quote: The alternative explanation is that the detected patterns resulted from collapsed duplications, which may be polymorphic in each species, resulting in copy number variation (CNV).

comments.issue: CNV-seq assumed fixed copy-number differences between species with C. viridis as reference, ignoring shared duplications and segregating CNV in both species.
comments.request: Account for shared and polymorphic duplications in CNV detection.
comments.quote: This approach, however, doesn’t consider a possibility of duplications shared between species or that CNV polymorphisms are segregating in both species, possibly at different frequencies.

comments.issue: Extreme heterozygosity excess (h > 0.9) implies implausible overdominance coefficients, and the Hardy-Weinberg p < 1e-4 filter cannot exclude it with this sample size.
comments.request: Apply filtering appropriate to the sample size, since even all 17 CO1 individuals heterozygous would pass.
comments.quote: however with the sample size they had for the CO1 population, even if all 17 individuals would be heterozygous, the p-value from Chi2 test would by > 2e-4

comments.issue: Convincing support for balancing selection requires additional evidence that the regions are single-copy.
comments.request: Provide family segregation or phased haplotype (amplicon or HiFi PacBio) evidence.
comments.quote: if no departures from Mendelian expectations occur in offspring in regions with elevated pi, Tajima’s D or beta, that would constitute strong evidence for single-copy nature of these genomic regions

comments.issue: The authors test against positive directional selection but never formally test balancing selection against neutral expectations.
comments.request: Apply formal tests of balancing selection against neutral expectations.
comments.quote: they do not formally test the alternative of balancing selection against neutral expectations

comments.issue: The manuscript is verbose: 870 lines without references and a discussion over 200 lines, with descriptive results reported one by one.
comments.request: Shorten and condense, e.g. the paragraphs at l.74-106, l.143-153 and l.540-567.
comments.quote: The paper is very well written, the arguments are easy to follow, but the text is verbose at places and, as a result, the manuscript without references is 870 lines and discussion alone exceeds 200 lines.

comments.issue: Clustering of known balancing-selection targets with venom genes does not imply balancing selection in the latter, though the wording suggests it.
comments.request: Soften the wording at l.111-112.
comments.quote: the fact that both genes known as targets of balancing selection and venom protein genes occur in clusters does not in any way imply balancing selection in the latter

comments.issue: The reasoning at l.166-168 assumes selection must be involved without testing against neutrality.
comments.request: Test the patterns against neutral expectations.
comments.quote: this assumes that some kind of selection must be involved, while this is not necessarily the case, that's why you need to test against neutral expectations

comments.issue: The procedures to identify and mask CNV regions may not be sufficient.
comments.request: Strengthen CNV masking.
comments.quote: as explained above, the procedures to identify and mask CNV regions may not be sufficient

comments.issue: The PSMC analysis is not incorporated into the inferential procedures.
comments.request: Use simulations conditioned on the inferred Ne trajectory to derive neutral predictions.
comments.quote: PSMC analysis is informative but has not been incorporated into the inferential procedures

comments.issue: The Ne trajectories of the two C. viridis populations do not converge until over 1e6 years ago despite apparently shallow divergence.
comments.request: Explain this inconsistency between Ne trajectories and divergence.
comments.quote: One thing that I found surprising is that the Ne trajectories for two C. viridis populations didn’t converge until > 1e6 years ago, while the divergence between these populations appears much shallower.

comments.issue: The long descriptive part at l.226-267 is difficult for a general reader to follow.
comments.request: Condense this section for general readers.
comments.quote: this long descriptive part is interesting and generally well written, but it may be a bit difficult to follow for a general reader

comments.issue: At l.327-329 only relative outlier status was tested, not an explicit test of balancing selection.
comments.request: Use an explicit test of balancing selection.
comments.quote: you tested for the relative outlier status of these regions, while an explicit test of balancing selection would be more elegant

comments.issue: 'Testing' at l.512-513 is used loosely for looking at patterns and their consistency with expectations.
comments.request: Use more precise wording than 'testing'.
comments.quote: “testing” here is used in a broader sense, as you rather looked at the patterns and their consistency with expectations

comments.issue: It is unclear whether blank parts of the plots at l.570 and Fig. S9 result from masking CNV regions.
comments.request: Indicate CNV masking in the figure legend.
comments.quote: are the blank parts of the plots in this figure also resulting from masking CNV regions? If so, please indicate this in the legend

comments.issue: The effect of collapsed duplications on recombination rate estimation is not discussed or explored.
comments.request: Explore and discuss how duplications could affect recombination rate estimates.
comments.quote: it would be useful to discuss the effect of potential collapsed duplications on the estimation of recombination rate

comments.issue: The claim that new data challenge the rarity of long-term balancing selection is controversial.
comments.request: Temper this claim at l.676-678.
comments.quote: the opinion that new data challenge the rarity of long term balancing selection is controversial – of course new cases appear, but given the amount of research on the subject, they hardly tip the balance

comments.issue: Figure 3 panels do not correspond to the legend (SVMP are a, b, e, f; SVSP are c, d, g, h).
comments.request: Correct the panel-letter correspondence in Figure 3.
comments.quote: The panels in the figure don’t correspond to the legend: SVMP are a, b, e, f, SVSP are c, d, g, h

comments.issue: Boxplot scales in Figure 3 and other figures make groups with means near zero visually indistinguishable.
comments.request: Adjust boxplot scales so group differences can be assessed visually.
comments.quote: boxplots showing df scale should be adjusted so that the differences between groups could be assessed visually – in the current form the mean values that are very close to 0 are not distinguishable visually

title: The roles of balancing selection and recombination in the evolution of rattlesnake venom

study.system: global forests; 1.3 million inventory plots, richness drivers

editor_summary: Editor sees considerable potential interest but substantial concerns; cannot accept but would consider a revised version addressing the serious concerns.

reviews.assessment: Well written with exciting results and impressive data synthesis; concerns are structural, about main-text methods detail and unclear objectives.
strengths: Figures 4 and 5 are very cool results

comments.issue: The main text gives too little detail on the approach; the paper's power is buried in the supplement and risks being overlooked.
comments.request: Bring the methods approach to the front, for example with a flowchart as a main figure.
comments.quote: I get the space constraints but the power in this paper is buried in the supplementary material, which is a real shame.

comments.issue: The methods section lacks structure, so the purpose of each step is hard to follow.
comments.request: Add structure to the methods section clarifying the purpose of each step.
comments.quote: I would also encourage you to add some additional structure to the methods section so that the reader understands the purpose of each step or set of steps.

comments.issue: No justification is given for using upscaled species richness rather than the million empirical plots in the partitioning analyses.
comments.request: Provide a clear rationale for using the upscaled product.
comments.quote: why then was the upscaled data necessary for that step? I never saw a justification and it seems as though the same questions could be asked directly using the empirical data

comments.issue: Research objectives and questions are not clearly stated up front, so analyses cannot be linked to questions.
comments.request: State the research objectives very clearly.
comments.quote: This leads to another major comment which has to do with the lack of clearly stated research objectives/questions.

comments.issue: 'Environmental temperature' is awkward and its meaning is unclear.
comments.request: Use a better recognized term such as mean annual temperature.
comments.quote: the term "environmental temperature" is used here and throughout. I find that term quite awkward and wonder what you mean by it.

comments.issue: The strong LDG pattern in tree richness is presented as a discovery but is already well known.
comments.request: Drop this discovery claim and highlight instead that MTB underestimates the LDG at low latitudes.
comments.quote: The finding of a strong LDG pattern in tree species richness is by no means a discovery.

comments.issue: Publishing tree-level Canadian Forest Inventory plots may violate data sharing policies; the same applies to other governmental datasets.
comments.request: Confirm that data sharing policies permit publication of these plot data.
comments.quote: I am familiar with the data sharing policies associated with the Canadian data and I am wondering whether the publication of those data are allowed?

comments.issue: Figure 1 is beautiful but adds no useful content and seems textbook-like.
comments.request: Replace Figure 1 with the suggested methods diagram.
comments.quote: While it is a beautiful figure, I do not think it provides any useful content for the paper and seems more like something for an ecology textbook.

reviews.assessment: Disappointed: the link between patterns and mechanisms is weak and the co-limitation conclusion is undermined by the African data gap.

comments.issue: The link between observed patterns and potential mechanisms is poor; the discussion only describes patterns and is insufficient for the journal.
comments.request: Discuss the mechanistic links deeply and in relation to previous studies.
comments.quote: there is a rather poor link between observed patterns with the potential mechanisms. Though authors proposed the four processes at the beginning, and other hypotheses related to LDG, they almost had no deep discussion about the mechanistic link.

comments.issue: The co-limitation conclusion is doubtful because Africa has very few data points, and added data would change it.
comments.request: Fill the African data gap or temper the co-limitation conclusion.
comments.quote: I doubt the existence of the co-limitation in low latitudes, as least based on the current analyses. The major uncertainty is from the data gap in Africa

title: Co-limitation towards lower latitudes shapes global forest diversity gradients

study.system: prokaryotes and eukaryotes; algebraic models of cellular energetics

editor_summary: Work of considerable potential interest but with substantial concerns that must be addressed; revision invited although the current version cannot be accepted.

reviews.assessment: Careful re-analysis reveals a methodological flaw that invalidates the eukaryotic-advantage conclusions; major revision needed.
strengths: respiratory deficit results highly relevant to mitochondrial origin
analysis sheds light on membrane surface, cell size and genetic organisation

comments.issue: The model design gives eukaryotes an almost unconditional advantage, which the text understates with soft wording.
comments.request: State the built-in eukaryotic advantage openly and avoid 'may be'.
comments.quote: This unfair advantage of eukaryotes is due to the design of the model.

comments.issue: The relative eukaryotic advantage is always greater than one regardless of genome size.
comments.request: Present parameter cases where prokaryotes gain the advantage.
comments.quote: Fig5B shows that dividing the two functions yields the relative eukaryotic advantage that is *always* greater than 1, regardless of what genome size one uses!

comments.issue: The model compares only modern taxa instead of the early phase of mitochondrial integration.
comments.request: Model early integration with less-evolved partners.
comments.quote: authors should focus on the early phase of mitochondrial integration by a proto-eukaryote, parameterizing the model assuming less-evolved partners

comments.issue: The original results on eukaryotic advantage are unexciting.
comments.request: Strengthen the analysis of eukaryotic advantage.
comments.quote: I find the original results about eukaryotic advantage lacking and dry

comments.issue: Eukaryotic advantage is doubly log-transformed in Figure 5D,E and Figure S4, contradicting Figure 5B.
comments.request: Recheck the double-logarithmized advantage results.
comments.quote: yielding thus a doubly-logarithmized value (Figure 5D,E and FigureS4)

comments.issue: The claimed ~120% third conclusion could not be identified and other results may be compromised.
comments.request: Recheck the ~120% result and affected analyses.
comments.quote: I also failed to identify the ~120% claimed as the third conclusion (P12 L12), and other results might also be compromised by this issue.

comments.issue: The 20% energetic disadvantage at P12 L38 could not be reproduced and its 1.2-fold wording is confusing.
comments.request: Clarify how the 20% disadvantage was calculated.
comments.quote: How did the authors arrive at the 20% energetic disadvantage at P12 L38? I failed to reproduce this particular numerical result.

comments.issue: Initial mitochondrial genome size is four orders of magnitude below a plausible early endosymbiont genome.
comments.request: Justify or revise the initial mitochondrial genome size.
comments.quote: at the onset of the endosymbiosis, mitochondria clearly had almost full genomes, meaning that L_mtDNA_0 (initial mitochondrial genome size) must be comparable to L_prok (as per Figure 4)!

comments.issue: Polyploid endosymbiont and multikaryote host scenarios are not considered.
comments.request: Consider polyploid and multikaryote scenarios.
comments.quote: The captured endosymbiont could also have been polyploid. The host could have been a prokaryote or (as some recent papers envisage it) even a multikaryote

comments.issue: Mitochondria-early versus nucleus-first scenarios are not compared via parameter cases.
comments.request: Model scenarios to polarize nucleus-first versus mitochondria-first.
comments.quote: The authors should investigate parameter cases that comply with the early phases of different eukaryotic origin scenarios (mitochondria early/late), to differentiate between them based on the size of conferred advantage

comments.issue: The volume at which prokaryotes lose their advantage is only visually inspected.
comments.request: Calculate the exact volume where prokaryotes lose the advantage.
comments.quote: Instead of visually inspecting the graphs, authors should calculate the exact cell volume (or genome size) where prokaryotes lose their advantage.

comments.issue: An energetic advantage does not translate into a selective advantage, especially early in the symbiosis.
comments.request: Emphasize that energy advantage is not selective advantage.
comments.quote: while modern eukaryotes seem to have a quantifiable advantage (genetic or energetic) over prokaryotes, that does not mean much in terms of selection, especially early selection of the endosymbiotic pair

comments.issue: The conclusion ignores the early costs of inventions and assumes eukaryotes always had an advantage.
comments.request: Consider early costs of inventions in the model.
comments.quote: I find this conclusion shallow mainly for the reason that it does not at all consider the early costs of any invention

comments.issue: Linear energy demand does not rule out increased eukaryotic energetic capacity.
comments.request: Qualify the linear energy-demand argument.
comments.quote: The observation, that the energy-demand seems to be linear in both domains does not explain away any increased energetic capacity of Eukaryotes.

comments.issue: Word choice at P1 L29.
comments.request: Use 'dependent' rather than 'contingent'.
comments.quote: P1 L29: I think the authors may wanted to use "dependent" and not "contingent".

comments.issue: The P1 L45 sentence wrongly implies origins are explained because a complexity gap exists.
comments.request: Reword the sentence to remove this implication.
comments.quote: imply that authors attempted to explain eukaryotic origins from prokaryotes *because* the complexity gap exists

comments.issue: Complexity is treated as anatomical only, though non-anatomical differences are more relevant.
comments.request: Clarify that complexity includes non-anatomical features.
comments.quote: Complexity is not only anatomical, and as a matter of fact, those differences not being anatomical (gene packing, cell cycle, etc.) are likely more relevant.

comments.issue: Figure 1 assumes linear energy per volume without stating or sourcing this in the caption.
comments.request: State the linear assumption and its source in the caption.
comments.quote: In Figure1, it is assumed that energy/cell volume is linear. This should be made clear in the caption. Where does this assumption stem from?

comments.issue: The 100x eukaryotic energy increase in the figure is unexplained and unreferenced.
comments.request: Justify the 100x increase and its origin.
comments.quote: It should be clearly stated that the image assumes a 100x increase for eukaryotes, and whether this is the assumed value of Lane & Martin, or other literature, or just an ad hoc constant.

comments.issue: The P3 L29 sentence does not make clear that no bacteria were excluded from Fig. 2A.
comments.request: Reword and annotate bacterial giants as outliers.
comments.quote: Reword this sentence to make it clear, that no bacteria were excluded from the analysis (distribution and when calculating median) of Fig2A.

comments.issue: Whether any eukaryotes overlap prokaryotes in volume, genome size and gene number simultaneously is untested.
comments.request: Check whether the overlapping sets intersect in all traits.
comments.quote: It would be even more informative to investigate whether the overlapping sets of eukaryotes and prokaryotes regarding volume/genome-size/gene-number themselves intersect or not?

comments.issue: Figure 1 also suggests an upper limit to prokaryotic gene number.
comments.request: Note the apparent upper limit to prokaryotic gene number.
comments.quote: According to Figure1, data also suggests an upper limit to gene number for prokaryotes.

comments.issue: Length is used where radius should be.
comments.request: Use radius instead of length.
comments.quote: Instead of length, radius should be used.

comments.issue: What metabolic rate means, ATP per hour or per cell division, is unclear.
comments.request: Define metabolic rate consistently.
comments.quote: Make it clear, what the metabolic rate of a cell means: the ATP production per hour (as L36 suggests) or per cell division (as L38 suggests).

comments.issue: Membrane invagination or evagination as an alternative way to increase surface is not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention membrane folding as an alternative.
comments.quote: Another alternative that is worth mentioning is the in(or ex-)vagination of the plasma membrane, i.e. developing external folds or appendages.

comments.issue: Figure 3A legend obscures where lines reach a respiratory deficit of 1.
comments.request: Move the legend so the crossing point is visible.
comments.quote: The legend gets in the way to clearly see the cell volume at which the lines reach a respiratory deficit of 1.

comments.issue: Notation and grammar errors at P9 L13, P10 L14 and P11 L6.
comments.quote: P9 L13: "architecture remain" > "architecture to remain".

comments.issue: Figure 5C,E x-axis is not in Mbp and lacks median genome-size markers.
comments.request: Use Mbp and indicate median genome sizes.
comments.quote: X axis should be in Mbp, to comply with Fig1. It should be indicated where the median genome size of present day (single-celled) eukaryotes and prokaryotes are, as per Fig1.

reviews.assessment: Detailed critique of cost-accounting assumptions and missing justifications; the model needs clarification before its conclusions hold.

comments.issue: The discussion stays within energetic costs of DNA synthesis instead of a broader scope.
comments.request: Broaden the discussion beyond DNA synthesis costs.
comments.quote: A broader scope, at least at the level of a discussion, by going beyond energetic costs of DNA synthesis alone and energetic cost arguments alone, would be interesting additions to this paper.

comments.issue: The universal genomic design claim rests on few references and is not convincing for prokaryotes.
comments.request: Provide stronger evidence for universal genomic design scaling.
comments.quote: I’m not convinced based on the couple of references pertaining to Synechococcus elongatus or Epulopiscium that this genomic design exists universally for prokaryotes

comments.issue: 'Cell cycle' is confusing for prokaryotes.
comments.request: Use 'cell division time' instead.
comments.quote: "Cell cycle" could potentially be confusing when used in the context of estimates made for prokaryotes.

comments.issue: Direct costs are applied to growth but not maintenance, and maintenance processes are undefined.
comments.request: Clarify maintenance costs and whether fd applies.
comments.quote: The authors factor in direct costs only for the growth component and not the maintenance component.

comments.issue: Lynch and Marinov costs are total costs, so applying the fd factor needs justification.
comments.request: Explain why the fd factor is appropriate for total-cost equations.
comments.quote: the energetic costs reported by Marinov and Lynch are total cost estimates (i.e. account for potential ATPs that are not cashed due to the synthesis of molecular building blocks)

comments.issue: Growth conditions and comparability of the cited empirical datasets are not explained.
comments.request: Explain growth conditions and agreement between datasets.
comments.quote: In general, a thorough explanation surrounding empirical data from other studies cited is needed.

comments.issue: Direct and total cost estimates are mixed, e.g. the 101 ATPs per base pair is a total cost.
comments.request: Clarify the use of direct versus total costs.
comments.quote: The 101 ATPs is based on total costs so there is a back and forth between using direct costs and total cost estimates in this manuscript. A clarification needs to be made.

comments.issue: The per-nucleotide cost differs slightly from reference 31.
comments.request: Reconcile the per-nucleotide cost with reference 31.
comments.quote: The version of cost estimate per nucleotide based on reference 31 is slightly smaller than what is used in this paper.

comments.issue: 'Active cytoplasmic volume' is not clearly defined.
comments.request: Define active cytoplasmic volume.
comments.quote: "active cytoplasmic volume" is not very clearly defined

comments.issue: The unit and basis of the Figure 1 y-axis are unclear.
comments.request: State the y-axis unit and whether it is total cost.
comments.quote: What is the unit of the y-axis in Figure 1 (AU)? Is this based on total cost?

comments.issue: The exclusion of multicellular eukaryotes is not noted.
comments.request: Note the exclusion of multicellular eukaryotes.
comments.quote: the exclusion of multicellular eukaryotes from the paper would need to be noted for clarification unless there is additional data from other sources that would support their inclusion

comments.issue: Energy sources other than ATP hydrolysis are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss other cellular energy sources.
comments.quote: A brief discussion on other sources of energy in a cell besides ATP hydrolysis (other types of hydrolysis reactions, for example) would be helpful.

comments.issue: Cell division time is treated as if dictated only by the energy budget.
comments.request: Note other limits on division time.
comments.quote: I think it’s important to note that cell division time is not assumed to be solely dictated by the energy budget.

comments.issue: Other factors behind the genomic complexity divide are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss non-energetic factors behind the complexity divide.
comments.quote: A general discussion about how other factors besides the energy budget could be important to the divide in genomic complexity seen across prokaryotes and eukaryotes would be very topical.

comments.issue: Only DNA synthesis costs are compared, ignoring protein, RNA and lipid synthesis.
comments.request: Compare DNA costs with protein, RNA and lipid costs.
comments.quote: Another point of confusion is why the energetic demand of DNA synthesis is only considered in making comparisons between eukaryotes and prokaryotes?

comments.issue: FECA is not defined.
comments.request: Define FECA.
comments.quote: Minor comment: FECA is not defined in the paper.

reviews.assessment: Likes the paper a lot and encourages publication, with only optional terminology and model-extension suggestions.

comments.issue: 'Genomic design' implies unintended meanings.
comments.request: Consider using 'genomic architectures'.
comments.quote: I dislike the term ‘genomic design’ used throughout and implies things I am sure the authors would not want to imply. ‘Genomic architectures’?

comments.issue: 'Anatomical complexities' at pg 2 line 1 is a poor term.
comments.request: Use 'cytological complexities'.
comments.quote: P.g. 2 line 1. ‘anatomical complexities’ – ‘cytological complexities’ (see also pg 3 line 4’.

comments.issue: The 'gasp for air' metaphor does not help.
comments.request: Remove or replace the metaphor.
comments.quote: P.g. 6 line 19 ‘gasp for air’. I don’t think the metaphor is helping you here.

comments.issue: The source of mitochondrial volume data at pg 11 line 3 is not referenced.
comments.request: Add a reference for mitochondrial volume data.
comments.quote: Pg 11 line 3. Where is mitochondrial volume data coming from? Reference needed?

comments.issue: The source of gene and regulatory sequence numbers at pg 12 line 20 is missing.
comments.request: Provide context and references for these numbers.
comments.quote: Pg 12, line 20. Where are the numbers of genes and regulatory sequence coming from. Context and references needed?

comments.issue: Typo at pg 13 line 12: ')eukaryote a with'.
comments.request: Correct the typo.
comments.quote: Pg 13, line 12. Correction needed ‘)eukaryote a with’

comments.issue: Suggested addition at pg 13 line 12.
comments.request: Add '[back into the mitochondria]'.
comments.quote: Pg 13, line 12. ‘gene products [back into the mitochondria]’. Suggested addition in square brackets.

comments.issue: The model ignores selection over generations and ATP passed to daughter cells.
comments.request: Extend the model to ATP investment in daughter cells.
comments.quote: I would like to see iterations of this model, where the authors consider 10-20-30% ATP resource investment in daughter cells?

title: The role of mitochondrial energetics in the origin and diversification of eukaryotes

study.system: ctenophores, cnidarians and sponges; mass spectrometry and functional assays of neuropeptides

editor_summary: Editor requires reviewer concerns and editorial points to be addressed in a revision before a final decision can be made.

reviews.assessment: Biochemically strong and broadly interesting study, but the criteria for calling cells neural and several figure and wording points need attention.
strengths: broad interest for the origin of neurons debate

comments.issue: The basis for calling peptide-expressing cells neurons is not stated, and processing or secretion machinery does not independently support neural identity.
comments.request: State the criteria for calling a cell neural and separate antibody-validated cells from peptide-only cells.
comments.quote: But beyond the expression of these peptides, what is the basis for assuming that these are neural cells?

comments.issue: It is unclear why Mnemiopsis clusters 27 and 29 are labelled peptidergic neurons when epithelial clusters 18 and 19 look very similar.
comments.request: Justify the neuronal labelling of clusters 27 and 29.
comments.quote: In the same vein: why are Mnemiopsis cl 27 and 29 listed as “Neuron (peptidergic)” in the same Ext Fig 7? Epithelial cluster 18 and 19 seem to be very similar.

comments.issue: The selection of transcription factors is unexplained and broadly expressed TFs could be used to make a different point.
comments.request: Explain TF selection and test how robust the neuron-similarity conclusion is to the choice of TFs.
comments.quote: Since some of these TFs (e.g. sox1, BarHx, six1/2) are rather broadly expressed, I was wondering about the strength of this correlation and whether it would be possible to use different TFs to make a different point

comments.issue: The location of the imaged area in Figure 2d is not clear.
comments.request: Describe the imaged area better or use a cartoon.
comments.quote: for Fig 2d, please describe better or use a cartoon to show where in the animals the imaged area is.

comments.issue: Stereocilia cannot be discerned in Figure 2d, yet the cells are described as sensory.
comments.request: Provide a better image or remove stereocilia and cilia from the text and legend.
comments.quote: I cannot discern stereocilia or any other type of cell protrusion in Fig 2d. This is relevant for describing these cells as sensory in the figure legend.

comments.issue: 'Close' species at Line 175 is subjective and lacks a ctenophore phylogeny reference.
comments.request: Provide a reference for ctenophore phylogeny and justify the closeness.
comments.quote: Line 175: a “close” species: please provide a reference for ctenophore phylogeny. “Close” is very subjective

comments.issue: 'Homogenous distribution' of neuropeptide signal at Line 194 is inaccurate.
comments.request: Use 'broad' instead of homogenous.
comments.quote: Line 194: The labelling indeed seems to be not restricted to typical synaptic puncta. But I don’t think there is homogenous distribution of the neuropeptide signal. “Broad” would be better.

comments.issue: The argument at Lines 201-202 assumes synapses share bilaterian molecular composition, a contentious point.
comments.request: Qualify the assumption about synaptic molecular composition.
comments.quote: Line 201-202: This seems to assume that synapses should have the same molecular composition as those in bilaterians

comments.issue: The generic term 'ctenophore' is used where the species could be named.
comments.request: Indicate the species whenever possible, e.g. at Line 199.
comments.quote: Whenever possible (e.g.. line 199) please avoid using “ctenophore” and indicate the species.

comments.issue: The missing labelling in Figure 2 makes it hard to relate NPW expression to the peptide treatment effect, and the mouth position is not indicated.
comments.request: Indicate the position of the mouth in Figure 2.
comments.quote: Line 231: The lack of labelling in Fig2 makes it a bit difficult to relate the expression of NPW to the observed effect of the peptide treatment. Is it possible to indicate the position of the mouth in Fig 2?

comments.issue: A table comparing Mnemiopsis and Bolinopsis neuropeptides is missing.
comments.request: Add a comparison table of the neuropeptides.
comments.quote: A table for comparing the Mnemiopsis and Bolinopsis neuropeptides would be nice, even though the methods for their identification differ.

comments.issue: The age or stage of Bolinopsis used for mass spectrometry is not stated.
comments.request: State the age or stage used for mass spectrometry.
comments.quote: At what age/stage of Bolinopsis was mass spec performed?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether any antibody controls such as pre-adsorption or Western blots were performed.
comments.request: Report antibody validation controls.
comments.quote: Are there any controls for the antibodies? Like pre-adsorption with antigen? Or Western?

comments.issue: The counterstain used in Extended Data Figure 3 is not stated.
comments.request: State the counterstain used.
comments.quote: What is the counterstain in Ext Fig 3?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether acidic cleavage sites require different proteases and whether this was included in the cluster analysis.
comments.request: Explain whether different proteases are needed and included.
comments.quote: Do the acidic cleavage sites require different proteases? If so, is this included in the analysis of the Mnemiopsis clusters?

comments.issue: The weak peptide conservation raises the question of whether the data really support a common origin of neurons.
comments.request: Reflect on how much support the data provide for a common origin.
comments.quote: The peptides appear to have very little conservation compared to other animals (and even among ctenophores), so I am wondering if we would consider it support for common origin

reviews.assessment: Important new data and elegant functional tests that should be published after the antibody specificity and transcriptome analysis concerns are addressed.
strengths: new data that will attract community attention

comments.issue: The recently reported molecular identity of ctenophore neuron clusters is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the neuron and sensory cell cluster identities from Sachkova et al. 2021.
comments.quote: The molecular identity of ctenophore neurons has been reported recently by Sachkova et al, 2021.

comments.issue: Conservation of neuropeptide expression patterns and neuronal architecture across ctenophore species is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss conservation of expression patterns between B. mikado, V. multiformis and Mnemiopsis.
comments.quote: I think it would be worth to discuss conservation of neuropeptide expression patterns between B. mikado, V. multiformis and Mnemiopsis.

comments.issue: Antibodies raised against 2-3 residue peptides may bind non-specifically, and the choice of short peptides is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the choice of short peptides and validate antibody specificity.
comments.quote: However I have a concern regarding the specificity of antibodies used for Nematostella and NPWa antibody. Peptides used for immunisation are just 2 to 3 residues long, it may result in non-specific binding to several targets.

comments.issue: Summing expression across cell clusters can create artificial hybrid cell types and bias results by cluster number.
comments.request: Explain and justify the rationale for summing expression across clusters.
comments.quote: The rationale behind this approach should be explained better since the logic of summing up gene expression levels across several clusters is not clear.

comments.issue: The digestive neuron hypothesis is not compared with other recent hypotheses on neuron origins.
comments.request: Discuss it against Moroz et al. 2021 and Burkhardt and Jekely 2021.
comments.quote: “Digestive neuron” is an interesting hypothesis. I suggest to discuss it in comparison to other recently proposed hypotheses.

comments.issue: Published evidence for translucent synaptic vesicles and mixed peptidergic and synaptic vesicles contradicts the volume-transmission discussion.
comments.request: Consider these facts when discussing pre- and postsynaptic machinery and glutamate.
comments.quote: Synapses with translucent synaptic vesicles do exist in ctenophores (Hernandez-Nicaise 1973); translucent vesicles are normally filled with small molecule transmitters.

comments.issue: The statement at Line 151 is unclear and wrongly links receptor repertoire complexity to peptide concentration.
comments.request: Clarify and correct the statement about receptor complexity and peptide number.
comments.quote: this statement is not really clear. I think the reduced complexity of peptide receptor repertoire rather correlates with reduced number of peptides, not their concentration.

comments.issue: 'Peptide receptor' is used although peptide binding has not been shown experimentally.
comments.request: Rephrase as 'peptide receptor homologues'.
comments.quote: Additionally, I would suggest to rephrase “peptide receptor” as “peptide receptor homologues” since it has not been shown experimentally that they indeed bind peptides.

comments.issue: The full mass spectrometry search engine output for all organisms is not available, limiting reproducibility.
comments.request: Provide an accessible .csv file with the full search engine output.
comments.quote: full list of proteins identified by mass spectrometry should be made available. An easily accessible .csv file with full search engine output for all the studied organisms (including the sponge) is critical for reproducibility of this research.

comments.issue: The rationale for selecting the longest peptide variant is not explained and it may be a maturation intermediate.
comments.request: Explain why the longest variant was selected.
comments.quote: It would be nice to explain the rationale behind choosing the longest variant.

comments.issue: 'Small molecule fractions' at Line 397 probably should read peptide fractions.
comments.request: Correct the wording at Line 397.
comments.quote: Line 397: «small molecule fractions» - I guess authors meant peptide fractions.

comments.issue: The conserved sponge neuropeptide precursors reported by Yañez-Guerra et al. 2021 are not discussed in light of their absence from the mass spectrometry data.
comments.request: Discuss the Yañez-Guerra et al. preprint and the missing peptides.
comments.quote: Recent preprint by Yañez-Guerra et al, 2021 reported 2 neuropeptide precursors (phoenexin and nesphatin) conserved in sponges. I think it’s worth discussing in connection to the fact that mass spectrometry did not identify these peptides.

reviews.assessment: Impressive and well-performed study, with a few points on possible artifacts, search criteria and the neuron-centric framing of neuropeptide evolution.
strengths: impressive and well performed LC-MS peptidomics

comments.issue: Observed acidic cleavages may partly be artifacts of storing peptides in formic acid.
comments.request: Assess whether acidic cleavages could reflect sample preparation.
comments.quote: Could their observation of acidic cleavages, at least partially, be a sample preparation artifact as they stored their peptides in a formic acid solution?

comments.issue: The search algorithm requires amidation, excluding non-amidated peptides, and it is unclear what fraction was lost and which enzymes are present.
comments.request: Report the fraction of peptides excluded and identify the amidation enzymes.
comments.quote: While amidation is certainly a hallmark of bioactive neuropeptides (and toxins: see below), in most animals, only a fraction of bioactive neuropeptides are amidated; their search algorithm appears to require this.

comments.issue: Statements assume neurotransmitters originate from neurons although these molecules predate neurons and have non-neuronal functions.
comments.request: Modify the statements to reflect non-neuronal functions.
comments.quote: The statements made throughout assume neurotransmitters are from neurons. Perhaps these statements should be modified slightly in terms of their evolutionary wide-spread non-neuronal functions.

comments.issue: Alternative well-conserved functions such as toxins, immunity and developmental signalling qualify the neuron-centric claims about neuropeptide evolution.
comments.request: Qualify the claims linking neuropeptides to the ancestral nervous system.
comments.quote: The citations 14-17 and claims that neuropeptides are related to the ancestral nervous system may need qualification.

title: Mass spectrometry of short peptides reveals common features of metazoan peptidergic neurons

study.system: eukaryotes; rDNA metabarcoding phylogenies and habitat transitions

reviews.assessment: Pioneering study, well written and analysed, with suggestions on reporting, topological uncertainty, undersampling and fungal transition rates.

comments.issue: The first comparative analysis is dismissed as hiding variation and reported too briefly.
comments.request: Report these analyses in more detail, including BayesTraits rate parameters.
comments.quote: I think these analyses should be reported better - even if they do provide give clear-cut evidence, more detailed reporting would make this section easier for readers to assess.

comments.issue: Whether 100 ML topologies sufficiently cover topological uncertainty is untested.
comments.request: Test whether bipartition counts plateau with the number of trees.
comments.quote: Testing whether the 100 ML topologies are sufficient to cover topological uncertainty would be interesting.

comments.issue: Undersampling of some groups may affect rate estimates and ancestral state reconstructions.
comments.request: Discuss potential undersampling and its influence on the results.
comments.quote: In the discussion, it would be interesting to mention if undersampling exists in the dataset and how, if at all this might have influenced rate estimations and ancestral state reconstructions.

comments.issue: Fungal transition rates may be overestimated because spores occur in habitats where fungi cannot live (also line 336).
comments.request: Run a sensitivity analysis or interpret fungal rates cautiously.
comments.quote: I still think there might be an overestimation in fungi, given the ubiquitous occurrence of their spores.

comments.issue: Copy edits: strange phrase at l51 and misspelling rhiziarians at l273.
comments.request: Fix the wording and spelling.
comments.quote: l51 - strange phrase, maybe ‘increasing <number of?> inferences?

comments.issue: It is unknown whether transition rates are asymmetric between qMT and qTM.
comments.request: Report rate parameters from a model with independent qMT and qTM.
comments.quote: at this point it would be interesting to report rate parameters from a model in which qMT and qTM can take independent values (but uniform across the tree). Is there a rate asymmetry?

comments.issue: Rate values from the analyses at lines 161-162 are not reported, nor is any reason they could not be.
comments.request: Report the rate values or explain why the tree is unsuitable.
comments.quote: please report rate values from these analyses. Or, if the global tree proved for some reason unsuitable for analyzing rates, please detail why.

comments.issue: The robustness of the trees at l167 is not reported.
comments.request: Report how robust those trees were.
comments.quote: l167 - how robust were those trees?

comments.issue: BayesTraits rates lack clear parsimony interpretation; per-clade transition counts would be easier to interpret.
comments.request: Report the number of parsimony-inferred transitions for each clade.
comments.quote: I think reporting the number of transitions inferred by parsimony, in each clade, wold make interpretation easier.

comments.issue: How significance was defined at l201 is not indicated.
comments.request: Indicate how significance was defined.
comments.quote: l201 - please indicate how significance was defined.

comments.issue: A marking for the polytomic MRCA of ichthyosporeans and metazoans is missing in Fig. 4b.
comments.request: Clarify whether the missing marking is intentional.
comments.quote: fig4b - a marking is missing for the polytomic mrca of ichtyosporeans and metazoans - on purpose?

comments.issue: The manuscript does not show that the salt barrier per se shaped eukaryotic diversity, only that diversification involved transitions.
comments.request: Temper the claim about the salt barrier shaping diversity.
comments.quote: well, I’m not sure this ms showed that the salt barrier per se shaped euk diversity. It showed that euk diversification involved several transitions across this barrier.

reviews.assessment: Well-written and comprehensive in reporting, but flags methodological biases (extraction kits, habitat pooling, unbalanced datasets, primer bias) that need justification.
strengths: provides all information to redo the experiment and statistics

comments.issue: Different DNA extraction kits across sampling locations can bias community profiles.
comments.request: Assess and discuss the effect of different extraction kits.
comments.quote: The choice of the DNA extraction kit can have an impact on the community profile that you will obtain (Santos et al., 2017).

comments.issue: Combining plankton and sediment as freshwater and freshwater with soils as terrestrial conflates distinct environments.
comments.request: Use no marine instead of terrestrial and justify habitat grouping.
comments.quote: The authors combine plankton and sediment samples under the term “freshwater”. Nevertheless, the community composition between this two environments can be really different

comments.issue: Filtered water volume and mesh size differ between studies and locations, affecting community profiles.
comments.request: Discuss the impact of differing filtration and mesh sizes.
