comments.request: Repeat the analysis without the weighing factor.
comments.quote: use of weighing factor. This makes sense and is often done. Are the results (conclusions) the same without the weighing factor?

comments.issue: Supplement Figure 14 labels ('AMF colonies' vs 'AMF'; 'Bacteria culture medium' vs 'Bacteria') are not explained.
comments.request: Explain these labels in the figure legends.
comments.quote: What is the difference between "AMF colonies" and "AMF"? Similarly what is the difference between "Bacteria culture medium" and "Bacteria".

title: Meta-analysis reveals the effects of microbial inoculants on the biomass and diversity of soil microbial communities

study.system: marine clades; fossil morphometrics across the Permian-Triassic mass extinction

editor_summary: Editor asks for more methods reporting detail (in methods or supplement) so the main text can discuss findings; revisions invited after addressing all reviewer and editorial concerns.

reviews.assessment: Well-written, novel science with a cogent narrative, but the method-versus-science focus and sparse methods reporting need major attention.
strengths: simulation and empirical results interesting and novel

comments.issue: Focus is split between introducing DeepMorph and the empirical results; framing needs clarifying and tightening.
comments.request: Clarify and tighten the framing of the paper.
comments.quote: The focus of the manuscript is split between the introduction of the new DeepMorph method and the empirical results.

comments.issue: Methods lack necessary detail, especially deep learning and landmark extraction, making it impossible to know what was done.
comments.request: Add the missing methodological detail.
comments.quote: The methods are missing a significant amount of necessary detail. This is true even if the authors decide to focus more on the scientific question being asked than on DeepMorph itself.

comments.issue: DeepMorph components are all well-established methods; its novelty is limited.
comments.request: Justify or de-emphasize the novelty of DeepMorph.
comments.quote: the pieces of DeepMorph are all well-established methods by this point (segmentation using deep learning, outline extraction, etc.)

comments.issue: Dataset of 656 images does not demonstrate the scalability and speed advantages of automation.
comments.request: Highlight the scientific application and de-emphasize the method novelty.
comments.quote: The application presented here also does not really demonstrate the main advantage of automated deep learning methods -- that is, scalability and speed.

comments.issue: Initial training and pre-trained weights (dataset, framework) are not described or specified.
comments.request: Clarify the training provenance and name the framework in methods.
comments.quote: Did you do this initial training yourselves? I'm assuming not, since you invoke transfer learning on the next line and it wouldn't make sense to do so.

comments.issue: OpenCV is a library, not a method; specific functions and algorithms are not given.
comments.request: Specify the OpenCV functions/algorithms used.
comments.quote: OpenCV is a library of computer vision methods, not a particular method in and of itself. More details are needed here.

comments.issue: Landmark extraction methodology and interpolation algorithms are unclear, including concave and asymmetric shapes.
comments.request: Describe the landmark and semi-landmark extraction in detail.
comments.quote: There is little detail provided on how the landmarks were extracted, and what detail is provided is a bit unclear.

comments.issue: A word is missing after 'asymmetric' and 'symmetric' at lines 49-50.
comments.request: Add the missing word.
comments.quote: I believe you're missing a word after "asymmetric" and "symmetric" (probably "process"?)

comments.issue: Sentence at lines 57-59 is strangely worded.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence.
comments.quote: This sentence is a bit strangely worded; I think it should be rephrased to something along the lines of "Studies using traditional morphometric descriptions suggest that ammonoid disparity barely decreased during the PTME, with no evidence of morphological selectivity."

comments.issue: Line 64 uses 'Actinopterygian' instead of 'Actinopterygii' or 'actinopterygians'.
comments.request: Correct the taxon name.
comments.quote: Line 64: Should be "Actinopterygii" or "actinopterygians", not "Actinopterygian"

comments.issue: Figure 2 x-axis is not explained and labels are not spelled out.
comments.request: Label the x-axis time period and type, spelling out labels.
comments.quote: Indicate that x-axis is time period (on the left) and type (on the right). I would also recommend spelling out the x-axis labels so that everything is clearer

comments.issue: Morphological disparities are not shown in a figure and organism images are lacking.
comments.request: Add disparity figures and more organism images.
comments.quote: Can these morphological disparities be shown in a figure (probably in the supplement)? I think this would help make the descriptions more concrete.

comments.issue: Figure 3 legend omits explanations of victims/survivors/newborn, the red cross and orange x, distributions and silhouettes.
comments.request: Expand the Figure 3 legend and panel labels.
comments.quote: Also include a legend indicating what the red cross and orange x indicate (instead of only including it in the caption).

comments.issue: Figure 4 caption does not define panels a and b, and the P_SOR vs P_DPOC difference is easy to miss.
comments.request: Explain panels a and b and make the difference clearer.
comments.quote: There's no indication in the caption what panels a and b refer to. The difference (P_SOR vs. P_DPOC) is only in the y-axis in the figure and is small and easy to miss.

comments.issue: Figure 5 selectivity curves are hard to compare across separate panels and selectivity=0 curves do not match.
comments.request: Plot selectivities together and use consistent y-axis ranges.
comments.quote: I think the comparisons would be clearer if all selectivities were plotted together (i.e., collapse d-f and g-i into one figure, respectively).

comments.issue: About seven line-level copy edits suggested (L203, L345-346, L351-353, L362, L369, L395-397, L403).
comments.quote: Line 203: Remove the comma at the end of the line.

reviews.assessment: Innovative and carefully presented study that is appropriate for publication, with points on abstract clarity, unaddressed stress thresholds and several limitations.
strengths: well considered, interesting and very carefully presented

comments.issue: Abstract is vague in reporting results and does not do justice to the findings.
comments.request: Rewrite the abstract results more specifically.
comments.quote: The abstract is a little vague in reporting the results, and doesn't do justice to the findings here.

comments.issue: Environmental tolerance thresholds, the heart of the main result, are not addressed in the Discussion.
comments.request: Elaborate why clades differ in morphological selectivity.
comments.quote: This is an interesting point, which gets to the heart of your main result, but isn't actually addressed in the Discussion

comments.issue: L34 is confusing: morphological diversity is by definition morphological variation in organisms.
comments.request: Clarify this definitional statement.
comments.quote: L34 – this is a bit confusing – surely morphological diversity is "morphological variations in organisms" by definition.

comments.issue: Decoupling of diversity and disparity is described across clades but not across events.
comments.request: Consider whether the decoupling also holds across events.
comments.quote: L45 – "a decoupling of diversity and disparity, a pattern recorded in different clades" – and across different events as well?

comments.issue: Simulations should be reported before selectivity patterns at L176.
comments.request: Reorder the reporting of simulations and selectivity.
comments.quote: L176 – It makes more sense to me to report the simulations before reporting the selectivity patterns.

comments.issue: The method's broader applicability to other questions and timescales is never stated.
comments.request: Mention the broader applicability at L211.
comments.quote: Nowhere in the manuscript is that next step clearly made, that this new methodology has the potential to be applied to other scenarios to address many different questions about the evolution of form over geological timescales.

comments.issue: Only PC1 and PC2 were used, which do not capture all variance; major trends may be missed.
comments.request: Demonstrate that the results capture the major trends.
comments.quote: Your analyses only used PC1 and PC2, which inevitably did not capture all of the variance (as shown in Fig. S1). Are you confident that your results still capture the major trends?

comments.issue: Genus-level analyses ignore variation among species and individuals within genera.
comments.request: Assess how within-genus variation affects the results.
comments.quote: Analyses were conducted at the genus level. How variable are species within a genus in these clades, and could that influence how well your pipeline captures morphological variation?

comments.issue: Robustness of the results to sampling biases is not assessed.
comments.request: Test the sensitivity of results to sampling biases.
comments.quote: How robust do you think your results are to sampling biases?

comments.issue: Conodont fossils are feeding apparatus rather than shells, which may explain their small morphological change.
comments.request: Address this anatomical difference as a possible confound.
comments.quote: Conodont fossils represent feeding apparatus, a small and highly functional part of the animals' anatomy, whereas in all of the other clades, the fossils are shells.

comments.issue: 2D views of hard parts may not represent whole-animal morphology.
comments.request: Discuss whether results hold for whole animals.
comments.quote: Similarly, there are some elements of morphology not captured here, such as through a 2D rather than 3D view, and the focus on hard parts of morphologies. Do you expect your results to hold true for the whole animals?

comments.issue: Dataset coverage (proportion of PBDB genera, clade representation, geographic bias) is not quantified.
comments.request: Add statistics or supplemental figures on dataset coverage.
comments.quote: Could you add some statistics, or even supplemental figures, to demonstrate the coverage of your dataset?

comments.issue: Proportion of genera represented by multiple species is not reported.
comments.request: Report this proportion.
comments.quote: What proportion of the genera were represented by multiple different species?

comments.issue: Calling interval II 'PTME' is confusing since it lies between extinction pulses.
comments.request: Use a clearer label such as 'intermediate fauna'.
comments.quote: Referring to interval II as "PTME" makes the Results a bit confusing to read, as you also describe this as the interval between extinction pulses

comments.issue: L377 does not mention that only PC1 and PC2 were used subsequently.
comments.request: Mention the PC1/PC2 choice at L377.
comments.quote: I think it should be mentioned here that only PC1 and PC2 were used in subsequent analysis.

comments.issue: Key differences between the two metrics and their aims are not described.
comments.request: Add a sentence explaining the two metrics.
comments.quote: An extra sentence describing the key difference(s) between these two metrics, and what they aim to show, would justify this choice.

comments.issue: Selectivity levels read as dimensionless without context at L394.
comments.request: Provide context for the selectivity levels.
comments.quote: These selectivity levels read as dimensionless, providing a little more context here would be useful.

title: Heterogeneous selectivity and morphological evolution of marine clades during the Permian–Triassic mass extinction

study.system: clonal species; somatic genetic clock; eelgrass Zostera marina

editor_summary: Editor invites a revision addressing all reviewer and editorial concerns, with changes highlighted in the manuscript.

reviews.assessment: Promising and valuable clock, but model generality for clonal plants and layered meristem structure needs to be addressed.
strengths: solves age estimation in clonal species
valuable SAM structure and development details

comments.issue: Models assume the somatic cell population is always updating, unlike plants with long-quiescent stem cells whose clock is temporarily off.
comments.request: Explain how quiescent stem cells are treated or incorporate them.
comments.quote: their models seem to always assume that the somatic cell population is forever “updating” (both during growth and homeostasis)

comments.issue: Apical dominance makes proliferation and branching non-random, so clocks may run at different speeds among ramets.
comments.request: Model the competition between stem cell niches.
comments.quote: The apical dominance leads to slower (or even stopped) proliferation rate in axillary meristematic stem cells compared to the apical ones, so the branching process is far from a purely random process.

comments.issue: Re-activation of quiescent niches could reset the clock, limiting the model to cancer-like systems.
comments.request: Explain or extend the model to cover these developmental details.
comments.quote: Re-establishing of clonal population from an earlier quiescent or much slower divided stem cell niche could lead to re-setting of the somatic molecular clock.

comments.issue: In monocots the L2 layer is the regeneration centre and eudicots have three layers, so the eelgrass-based model may be too simple.
comments.request: Address layered structure and founder cell origin in the model.
comments.quote: for monocots, the L2 layer is long considered as the regeneration center, which means most founder stem cells for new ramets are likely derived from L2

comments.issue: The genet is described as sexually produced although it is the asexual product.
comments.request: Correct to 'asexually'.
comments.quote: P2-L43: “the sexually produced offspring (genet)”, do the authors mean “asexually” here?

comments.issue: VRF values are sensitive to stochastic library construction and sequencing events.
comments.request: Assess how VRF50 accuracy affects calibration.
comments.quote: The VRF value derived from NGS can be substantially influenced by stochastic events during library construction and sequencing.

comments.issue: Sequencing coverage differs strongly between time points and recommended depth is not given.
comments.request: Explain the coverage difference and recommend a depth.
comments.quote: The coverage is ~1000x for 4 years but only ~80x for 17 years. Why it varies so great?

comments.issue: Genetic and epigenetic clocks were not compared for robustness to confounding.
comments.request: Compare the two clock types.
comments.quote: Did the authors compare the genetic based and epigenetic based clocks to see which one is possibly more robust to confounding factors?

reviews.assessment: Significant and robust contribution, with questions about mutation rates, model assumptions and bulk sampling.
strengths: novel molecular clock for clonal species
robust methodology combining theory and data

comments.issue: The actual rate of fixed somatic mutation accumulation in eelgrass is not reported.
comments.request: State mutations fixed per year and discuss implications for short timescales.
comments.quote: it was not clear to me from the text what the actual rate was, i.e. how many somatic mutations are fixed per year (or other unit of time) in eelgrass?

comments.issue: Mutation rates may vary within species due to genetic variation or environmental mutagenesis, invalidating the clock.
comments.request: Discuss whether mutational signatures could detect environmentally induced mutations.
comments.quote: variation in somatic mutation rates, caused by genetic variation within a population or environmentally induced mutagenesis could alter mutation rates and impact the validity of the clock

comments.issue: Trinucleotide spectra of detected mutations were not compared with germline SNPs.
comments.request: Run this sanity check against germline spectra.
comments.quote: did the authors look at the trinucleotide spectra of mutations they are detecting? A nice sanity check would be to compare this to the spectra of germline SNPs in the eelgrass population

comments.issue: Human evidence that mutations arise during maintenance rather than division would strengthen the clock's rationale.
comments.request: Mention this in the text.
comments.quote: If this is the case then the model may not be dependent on cell division rates. This may in fact make it even more robust as a linear clock for calculating age.

comments.issue: The choice of cells for bulk sequencing could affect results if parts derive from different stem cell populations.
comments.request: Comment on tissue choice and highlight it in the discussion.
comments.quote: I assume that the choice of cells selected for bulk sequencing in each ramet could impact the results if different parts of the organisms are derived from different stem cell populations.

comments.issue: Spatial growth patterns of eelgrass are not explored using ramet relatedness.
comments.request: Consider a ramet phylogeny and test correlation with spatial proximity.
comments.quote: Did the authors consider exploring if you could create a phylogenetic tree of the different ramets within an eelgrass to gain insights into how an eelgrass has grown over time

comments.issue: Abascal et al. 2021 does not support the claim that fixed mutations accumulate with age.
comments.request: Replace or qualify the reference.
comments.quote: However the Abascal et al. 2021 reference does not show that fixed mutations accumulate with age but rather uses single molecule duplex sequencing to show that cell specific somatic variants accumulate with age, without reaching fixation in a bulk sample.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and impressive study combining modelling with cell morphology; only minor clarifications requested.
strengths: very nice story combining modelling and microscopy

comments.issue: It is unclear how much the method relies on comparing ramets of similar age given slower growth of old ramets.
comments.request: Clarify the consequences of comparing old and young ramets.
comments.quote: what will happen if one uses an old ramet and a young ramet, instead of comparing two ramets of the same life-stage

comments.issue: Whether calibration must be species-specific is unclear.
comments.request: Discuss using calibration from related species.
comments.quote: how important is it that the calibration is done for the target species? Or do the authors consider it possible to use calibration from a related clonal species?

comments.issue: One line-level copy edit ('algae' should be 'macroalgae').
comments.quote: Line 28 - “macroalgae” instead of “algae” (excluding microalgae)

comments.issue: Symmetric versus asymmetric cell division is introduced too late and their frequency is unclear.
comments.request: Explain these division types earlier, including mixed occurrence.
comments.quote: It would be useful to the reader if “symmetric” vs “assymmetric” cell division could be explored a bit more from early in the text

comments.issue: Why stratification is crucial and problematic is not explained.
comments.request: Briefly explain stratification on line 117 and line 130.
comments.quote: it is not clear to me why “stratification” is crucial. Can this be briefly explained here?

comments.issue: Geographic parthenogenesis is a pattern, not a hypothesis.
comments.request: Correct the terminology.
comments.quote: “geographic parthenogenesis” is not a hypothesis, I would rather call this a pattern. But there are many different hypotheses to explain this pattern.

comments.issue: More direct studies of the colonisation hypothesis are not cited.
comments.request: Consult Rafajlovic et al. 2017 and Pereyra et al.
comments.quote: there are two papers that explore the colonisation hypothesis much more directly than the Eckert 2002 paper here used as a referece

comments.issue: The ~1000-year Finnish clone estimate is not compared with the size-based estimate.
comments.request: Compare these age estimates.
comments.quote: This is an interesting conclusion, still the Finnish clone was estimated to be approx 1000 years old (which seem to be a good estimate) from size!?

comments.issue: 'Animal and fungal kingdom' appears to exclude macroalgae.
comments.request: Correct the wording.
comments.quote: Line 246 - “animal and fungal kingdom” excluding macroalgae ?!

reviews.assessment: Beautiful framework but not innovative, practically uncertain and insufficiently validated with data or figures.
strengths: interesting topic with wide application potential

comments.issue: The model needs many usually unknown parameters, making its practical utility uncertain.
comments.request: Demonstrate how these parameters can be obtained in practice.
comments.quote: Although the equations are theoretically beautiful, their practical utility is uncertain.

comments.issue: The statistical model is not innovative and can be inferred logically.
comments.request: Clarify the novel advance.
comments.quote: Although the statistical model product is beautiful, it is not innovative, but something can be inferred from the logical inference.

comments.issue: Accuracy of N and Ne determination is hard to judge from supplementary procedures.
comments.request: Show the experimental parameter estimation with a main figure or admit it is not critical.
comments.quote: the experimental part should be shown more vigorously in the main manuscript with a main figure

comments.issue: Per-sample mutation counts, sequencing depth, mutation call accuracy and structural events are not shown.
comments.request: Report these sequencing data explicitly.
comments.quote: the authors need to explicitly show the sequencing data (the number of mutations) of many samples

comments.issue: Main figures are cartoons, simulations or processed data that do not permit validation.
comments.request: Add figures showing real observations.
comments.quote: many of them are 'cartoons', simulation data, or processed data that do not allow validation of their findings or 'critical reading' of the manuscript

comments.issue: Calibration relies on few samples from only two time points and a crude regression.
comments.request: Add more calibration samples.
comments.quote: Although the authors showed the linear regression model, I think it is too crude, and the authors need more samples (observations).

comments.issue: Number of mutations per known-age sample is not reported.
comments.request: Report mutation counts per sample.
comments.quote: How many mutations were detected from each of the samples with known ages?

comments.issue: Estimated ages of the old samples and the difference between simple and sophisticated models are not reported.
comments.request: Apply the regression to old samples and compare estimates.
comments.quote: If the linear regression model (in Figure 4a) is applied to those samples, what are the estimated ages of the samples?

comments.issue: Impact of absolute mutation rate on age estimation and mutational signatures are not addressed.
comments.request: Report mutation rate effects and signatures.
comments.quote: How does the absolute mutation rate impact the age estimation? What were the mutational signatures (patterns) of the genomic mutations?

comments.issue: Figure 1c wrongly depicts mutation subclonality.
comments.request: Update the figure.
comments.quote: Fig 1c should be updated. The current version seems that the mutation M3 is subclonal to the mutation M2, and the M4 is subclonal to M3.

title: A somatic genetic clock for clonal species

study.system: microbial microcosms on carbon-source complexity; 16S sequencing and consumer-resource models

editor_summary: Editor: all referees positive, but Referee 3 questions whether mechanisms are supported by the data and Referee 1 asks how diversity and divergence relate.

reviews.assessment: Significant contribution; main concern is that divergence metrics may depend on species-vector size, plus several smaller points.
strengths: significant contribution to microbial community theory
compelling model consistent with prior data

comments.issue: Divergence/convergence measures may depend on species-vector size, and handling of zeroes can flip the result.
comments.request: Address how zeroes are treated and how this affects the divergence measure.
comments.quote: whatever degree of divergence or convergence that one measures may be dependent on the size of the species vector (i.e. on diversity)

comments.issue: Unclear whether analyses use the initial species set or a shrinking species vector over time.
comments.request: Clarify how the species vector is defined in the time-series analysis.
comments.quote: Do you do this analysis relative to the initial set of species, or do you shrink the size of the species vector at every time point to include only the union of species that are still present?

comments.issue: Convergence concerns composition only; invoking structure-function conflates composition with potential multi-stability.
comments.request: Clarify that the argument concerns potential multi-stability, not structure-function.
comments.quote: Convergence is in composition only, but for all we know the function landscape could be flat. I think the authors are talking about potential multi-stability, not structure-function.

comments.issue: Work by Maslov and coauthors on resource supply and multi-stability is not considered.
comments.request: Consider citing and discussing the Maslov et al. resource-supply paper.
comments.quote: I suggest the authors consider whether the arguments put forward by Sergei Maslov and coauthors (https://elifesciences.org/articles/49720) on the role of resource supply on multi-stability could be of relevance for their results.

comments.issue: The relevant Enke, Datta, et al. 2019 reference is not included.
comments.request: Include the Enke, Datta, et al. 2019 reference.
comments.quote: I find the model described in Fig 5 very compelling and consistent with what we have previously observed in our data

reviews.assessment: Calls the results a valuable addition but requires extensive contextualization and clarification, including 16S limitations and possible confounders.
strengths: valuable addition to microbial ecosystems biology

comments.issue: 16S data lack strain-level resolution, so functional conclusions need explicit qualification.
comments.request: Qualify conclusions given the limitations of 16S analysis.
comments.quote: The study uses 16S analysis which has many limitations in microbiome analyses especially the lack of resolution required to make functional conclusions.

comments.issue: Metabolic complexity is defined arbitrarily, and treating mixed metabolites differently from single ones is unclear.
comments.request: Define metabolic complexity clearly and justify treatment of mixtures.
comments.quote: The definition of metabolic complexity is rather arbitrary and needs a clear definition. Unclear why the mixed metabolites situations are treated differently than single metabolites

comments.issue: Non-metabolic interactions such as antagonism could confound the specialist/generalist patterns.
comments.request: Test whether specialism reflects sensitivity to antagonistic co-occurring taxa.
comments.quote: whether a taxon survives in a community for any condition is not just dependent on its metabolic compatibility but also on whether it manages to survive passive or active antagonisms with other community members

comments.issue: Ecological and evolutionary change may be entangled through mutation and selection during the experiment.
comments.request: Discuss this possible confounder as a limitation.
comments.quote: Another possible confounder is entanglement between ecological and evolutionary changes as in the experimental time-frame it is possible (perhaps even likely) that genetic mutations and selection takes place.

comments.issue: Setting specialist diversity proportional to resource complexity may make the modelling outcome circular.
comments.request: Address whether this choice determines the modelling results.
comments.quote: would this lead to circularity as the outcome of the modelling results is decided by this choice?

comments.issue: Random resource transformations lack thermodynamic or biological justification.
comments.request: Provide biological context and justification for random resource transformations.
comments.quote: What would be thermodynamic justifications for random resource transformations in models? Trophic structure is more intuitive, so the interpretation of this section could benefit from authors providing biological context/justification of random resource transformations.

comments.issue: Line 45 does not make clear whether resemblance is functional/metabolic or taxonomic.
comments.request: Specify the type and taxonomic level of resemblance.
comments.quote: it was not immediately obvious to me if authors meant functional/metabolic resemblance or taxonomic resemblance

comments.issue: Some samples are missing at several timepoints, contradicting the impression that all samples were sequenced.
comments.request: Mention the missing samples and repeat time-series analyses excluding them.
comments.quote: E.g. from Supplementary table 1, samples HF1P15 and HF1H15 are missing from all the conditions at day 3. The same two samples have missing sequencing for other days.

comments.issue: It is unclear how the single replicate sequenced at earlier timepoints was chosen.
comments.request: Explain how the sequenced replicate was selected.
comments.quote: How was the replicate to be sequenced for the other time points selected?

comments.issue: Unclear whether Fig. 2f slopes use the same carbon-source order as Fig. 2e and how missing data affect them.
comments.request: Clarify the slope calculation and missing-data handling.
comments.quote: Is the slope values for the different time points always calculated using the same order of carbon sources as in figure 2e for single and mixed carbon sources?

comments.issue: The mixed-carbon-source divergence trend appears only at day 33 and may reflect missing earlier data.
comments.request: Assess whether missing information on previous days drives this result.
comments.quote: The trend of increasing divergence relative for mixed carbon sources is detected only when taking into consideration day 33 according to the supplementary figure cited. Could this results from missing information on previous days?

comments.issue: The violin plot in Supplementary Figure 2 is not explained in the caption.
comments.request: Explain the violin plot in the caption.
comments.quote: Supplementary Figure 2 top plots: Explanation of the violin plot on the bottom is missing or unclear from the actual caption.

comments.issue: Supplementary Figure 3 caption should reference figure 2f, and the statistical test used is unspecified.
comments.request: Correct the caption and specify the statistical test.
comments.quote: Supplementary Figure 3: the caption should be “as in figure 2f”, also is the statistical test used the same? Please specify.

comments.issue: Supplementary figure 4 caption lacks detail relative to the figure.
comments.request: Expand the caption.
comments.quote: Supplementary figure 4: the caption could be further expanded to improve the details relative to the figure.

comments.issue: Supplementary figure 5 caption appears wrongly edited and the figure is not cited in the main text.
comments.request: Correct the caption, cite the figure, and show where sampled sites fall.
comments.quote: Supplementary figure 5: it looks like the caption has been wrongly edited, please correct it. Also, this figure is not cited anywhere in the main text.

comments.issue: Figure 3a curves appear mislabelled: text says the slope increases but the caption says the red line decreases.
comments.request: Check and correct the labelling in Figure 3a.
comments.quote: I think the authors may have mislabelled the two curves in figure 3a and the red line would represent the decreasing Shannon diversity as the author point out in the text, is that correct?

comments.issue: The diamond symbol in Figure 4a is not explained.
comments.request: Clarify what the diamond symbol represents.
comments.quote: Figure 4a please clarify what the diamond symbol in the plot represents

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the significant Figure 5f bar is plotted correctly or should be negative and omitted.
comments.request: Clarify the plotting of this bar.
comments.quote: Figure 5f is the condition type “Random resource transformation”/ “trophic consumer preferences” bar that is statistically significative plotted? or it should be having negative values and not plotted there?

comments.issue: The colour scale in Supplementary Figure 6d is unexplained.
comments.request: Specify the colour scale in the caption.
comments.quote: Supplementary Figure 6d what the colour scale on the left is referring to? Please specify that in figure caption.

comments.issue: The CRM methods lack a table of model parameters, meanings and units.
comments.request: Add a parameter table with units.
comments.quote: Methods section of CRM starting in line 370: section might benefit from a table detailing the meaning of model parameters, as well as their units.

comments.issue: The biological relevance of trophic structure sustaining diversity chains is not illustrated with examples.
comments.request: Provide explicit examples and biological contextualisation.
comments.quote: there is also the biological relevance that in certain cases, the trophic structure is necessary for diversity

reviews.assessment: Praises the experiment and analysis but finds novelty relative to related studies unclear and the cross-feeding mechanism unsupported by data or protocol.

comments.issue: The study is not sufficiently demarcated from closely related previous studies such as Goldford et al. and Refs 16 and 18.
comments.request: Explain what is new relative to these related studies.
comments.quote: the authors need to do more to demarcate this study from a suite of previous closely related studies to tell the reader what is new here that was not known before

comments.issue: The proposed cross-feeding mechanisms and the models they motivate are not supported by the data or protocol.
comments.request: Support or revise the proposed mechanisms of cross feeding.
comments.quote: the proposed mechanisms of cross feeding and the modeling formalisms they motivate are not supported by the data or the experimental protocol

comments.issue: The abstract does not explain how metabolic pathway structure produces the diversity-complexity effect.
comments.request: Add the mechanism linking metabolic structure to the effect.
comments.quote: From the abstract it is unclear how the structure of metabolic pathways leads to the diversity-complexity effect. The effect, as stated sounds like it depends on stochasticity, not on metabolic structure.

comments.issue: The statement in lines 52-53 about not depending on the distribution is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify this statement.
comments.quote: I do no understand the statement in lines 52-53

comments.issue: 'Divergence' in Fig. 1D is confusing without labelled comparison.
comments.request: Label the figure so the divergence comparison is clear.
comments.quote: "Divergence" in Fig. 1D is confusing. Divergence between what and what (I can see it now, but can you label this in such a way that it is clear?)

comments.issue: The motivation for manipulating single versus mixed resources is not articulated.
comments.request: Explain the experimental design rationale.
comments.quote: What is the motivation for doing single-resource and mixed resources? My question is -- why design the experiment in this way? I don't see a good motivation articulated here

comments.issue: The metabolic complexity definition rests on an unverified assumption that excretion increases with complexity.
comments.request: Provide experimental evidence beyond Ref 16 that excretions increase with metabolic complexity.
comments.quote: can the authors provide any experimental evidence that excretions actually increase with "metabolic complexity" as they have defined it -- evidence beyond Ref 16?

comments.issue: It is doubtful that lignin degradation yields glucose excretion, and the stronger single-carbon effect needs comment.
comments.request: Comment on the mechanism and on the stronger single-carbon-source effect.
comments.quote: In general, this stronger effect in single carbon sources (blue) than mixed (red) -- warrants more of a comment and is closely related to the results of Ref. 16.

comments.issue: Culture conditions are likely anaerobic, making fermentation rather than the proposed cross-feeding the likely mechanism.
comments.request: Compute the Reynolds number and consider anaerobic fermentation as the mechanism.
comments.quote: Culture conditions are likely effectively anaerobic. 200rpm in a deep well 96-well plate will have a low reynolds number -- please compute it, but I suspect around 100 or so.

comments.issue: A fully aerated repeat experiment would test whether fermentation drives the effect.
comments.request: Consider replicating the experiment with full aeration (Reynolds >10,000).
comments.quote: if the authors redid the experiment (asking for this would be too much, but let me put it out there so the authors can respond) -- with full aeration

comments.issue: It is unclear whether carbon concentration was capped at 50mM carbon atoms or kept equimolar; lignin is a complex mixture.
comments.request: Clarify carbon normalization and comment on lignin's composition.
comments.quote: my hope is that the total carbon atom concentration is kept constant not the molarity of the compounds -- because this will be more comparable in terms of total resources available

comments.issue: Invoking a rugged structure-function landscape is imprecise when only taxonomic diversity is measured.
comments.request: Unpack or revise the rugged landscape language.
comments.quote: Line 116 -- why does this imply a rugged structure-function landscape? this language is very imprecise and i think it would need quite serious unpacking to make sense

comments.issue: The 'diversity begets divergence' statement is vague and its logic is not followed.
comments.request: Clarify the argument and whether stochasticity or interactions are proposed.
comments.quote: diversity begets divergence could happen due to more variation in the abundances of each microbe. This statement is vague and I don't follow.

comments.issue: The increasing specialization with metabolic complexity mirrors Ref. 16.
comments.request: Point out any difference from Ref. 16.
comments.quote: the result of increasing specialization with metabolic complexity is very similar to the result found in Ref. 16. Can the authors point to any difference here?

comments.issue: It is unclear how taxa are defined in the CRM, which has traits but no taxonomy, while Fig. 2 divergence is taxonomic.
comments.request: Explain how taxonomic divergence maps onto the trait-based CRM.
comments.quote: What I am confused about is how the authors define taxa within the CRM framework. The plots in Fig. 2 are computing divergence based on taxonomy, not traits. But the CRM has no notion of taxonomy only traits.

comments.issue: The role of functional redundancy and phylogenetically distributed traits in driving divergence is barely discussed.
comments.request: Discuss functional redundancy and trait phylogenetic distribution.
comments.quote: some traits may be more phylogenetically variable -- meaning more broadly phylogenetically distributed, and this could drive divergence because the chances of getting two different taxa that have the same traits will rise

title: Metabolic complexity drives divergence in microbial communities

study.system: introduced rabbit populations; genomic sequencing across three continents

editor_summary: Revision invited: address all reviewer criticisms and editorial concerns, and highlight changes in the manuscript.

reviews.assessment: An absolute pleasure to read; only the most minor suggestions about terminology and figures.
strengths: interesting question on genomic mechanisms of feralisation

comments.issue: 'back-selected' is not a familiar term and may confuse readers.
comments.request: Replace 'back-selected' with 'selected against'.
comments.quote: ‘back-selected’ is not a term I’m familiar with. Suggest replacing – selected against?

comments.issue: Maladaptive phenotypes are not highlighted in Fig. 4.
comments.request: Highlight the maladaptive phenotypes as relevant in Fig. 4.
comments.quote: The authors could consider highlighting the maladaptive phenotypes as relevant in Fig 4.

comments.issue: Black lines at the top of Fig. 5B are not explained.
comments.request: Indicate what the black lines represent.
comments.quote: In Fig 5B, indicate what the black lines at the top of the panel represent (exons/genes?)

comments.issue: The term 'insights' is over-used in the closing section.
comments.request: Reduce repetition of 'insights' on L469-496.
comments.quote: L469-496: the term ‘insights’ feels a bit over-used here.

reviews.assessment: Comprehensive genomic study with significant contributions to understanding feralization; wholeheartedly recommends publication.
Interesting, well-written study; recommends publication after minor adjustments about terminology and references.

comments.issue: Very low sequencing depth (1.5x) and how it was handled are not discussed.
comments.request: Highlight the cons of low depth and how the authors dealt with it.
comments.quote: the very low depth of sequencing (1.5 x for each animal, on average): it should be better highlighted the cons of this in the manuscript and how the authors delt with this.

comments.issue: Yellow fat may not be a domestication trait.
comments.request: Reconsider classifying yellow fat as a domestication trait.
comments.quote: yellow fat might not be a domestication trait

comments.issue: Angora and rex alleles are rare even in domestic populations, so their presence in feral rabbits is uninformative.
comments.request: Discuss the rarity of these alleles in domestic breeds.
comments.quote: angora and rex alleles are also very rare alleles even in domestic populations: that measn only peculiar breeds have these alleles

comments.issue: In-text citations for coat colour genes do not match the reference list.
comments.request: Correct the mismatched references in the methods paragraph.
comments.quote: the references cited in M&M in paragraph: Inspection of causal variants underlying common breeds, related to coat colour genes do not match with what is reported in the reference list.

comments.issue: Key references on the agouti mutation are missing.
comments.request: Cite additional references for the agouti mutation.
comments.quote: In addition, a few other references, in particular for agouti mutation, should be cited.

title: Selection against domestication alleles in introduced rabbit populations

study.system: tropical to subalpine forest trees; metabolomics and herbivory

editor_summary: Referee #2 positive but wants reframing away from species diversity and clearer chemical/functional diversity metrics; Referee #1 concerned about disentangling drivers, uncontrolled shared ancestry, and the design's ability to address latitudinal interaction change.

reviews.assessment: Impressive dataset and metabolomics approach, but the site design confounds latitude, elevation and diversity, ancestry is uncontrolled, and herbivore classification from leaf damage is questionable.

comments.issue: The introduction shifts between elevation, latitudinal, climatic and diversity gradient framings, so the comparison target is unclear.
comments.request: Frame the study around a single gradient and hypothesis.
comments.quote: Some sections of the introduction talk about elevation gradients, others about latitudinal gradients, others about climatic gradients, and others about contrasting forests with different diversities.

comments.issue: Each site differs in both latitude and elevation, confounding elevation, latitude, climate and diversity effects.
comments.request: Disentangle these factors or acknowledge the confounding in the design.
comments.quote: Given that each site is at a different latitude and elevational range, it is challenging to disentangle the effect that each of these factors (elevation, latitude, climate, and diversity) has on the observed patterns.

comments.issue: Chemical diversity comparisons do not control for common ancestry; clades differ in inherited metabolic pathways.
comments.request: Control for phylogenetic relatedness in the chemical diversity comparisons.
comments.quote: Additionally, I was very surprised by the lack of control for common ancestry for comparing chemical diversity. Different plant clades express distinctive classes of metabolites due to inherited pathways and/or phylogenetic constraints.

comments.issue: Environmental factors such as UV radiation are a plausible alternative driver of metabolite divergence and are barely mentioned.
comments.request: Discuss the role of environmental factors in metabolite evolution.
comments.quote: Also, it is remarkable that the authors have almost no mention of the possible role of environmental factors on the evolution (and divergence) of specialized metabolites.

comments.issue: The possible role of pathogens in the observed patterns is omitted.
comments.request: Consider pathogens as an additional driver of the patterns.
comments.quote: Another important omission is the possibility of the role of pathogens in the observed pattern.

comments.issue: Phylogenetic non-independence is not accounted for in diversity and similarity analyses, though gradients are phylogenetically structured.
comments.request: Account for phylogenetic non-independence in all diversity and similarity analyses.
comments.quote: I strongly recommend accounting for phylogenetic non-independence in all their analyses of diversity and similarity, especially in comparisons between sites/habitats, communities, and chemistry.

comments.issue: How secondary metabolites were classified is unexplained, and some listed groups are primary metabolites.
comments.request: Explain the classification of secondary versus primary metabolites.
comments.quote: Another detail is the lack of explanation of how the authors classify "secondary metabolites". Some of the groups of compounds mentioned are commonly condor primary metabolites (e.g., carbohydrates, amino acids, and fatty acids).

comments.issue: Using leaf-damage patterns to classify herbivore specialization across a wide host phylogeny is unvalidated.
comments.request: Justify or validate damage-based specialization as a proxy.
comments.quote: As far as I know, there is no previous data that shows that classifying herbivores based on leaf damage patterns across such a wide plant host phylogenetic scope will yield data that will represent a good proxy for specialization.

comments.issue: Abundance weighting is applied inconsistently across diversity calculations without explanation, and species abundance is not addressed.
comments.request: Explain the weighting choices and account for species abundances.
comments.quote: In their diversity calculations, the authors sometimes use "abundance weighted" and sometimes not. No explanation of why or what does it mean is one is significant and not the other.

reviews.assessment: One of the most exciting papers in years and a significant advance; asks for reframing toward phytochemical diversity, clearer metric definitions, and several clarifying analyses.
strengths: one of the most exciting papers in recent years

comments.issue: The species-diversity framing is not linked to phytochemical diversity, no species diversity data are shown, and the analyses do not address species diversity questions.
comments.request: Incorporate tree species diversity data or refocus the introduction on phytochemical diversity.
comments.quote: However, the conceptual link between species diversity and phytochemical diversity is not explicit, the authors do not present data on species diversity, and the analyses themselves do not really focus on answering questions surrounding species diversity gradients.

comments.issue: The functional diversity metrics measure distinct chemical functional groups among species, not the diversity of compounds per se, and this is not made clear.
comments.request: Explain exactly what the diversity metrics capture and how they differ from other studies.
comments.quote: So, by these metrics, a community with 6,000 compounds could have the same “phytochemical diversity” as a community with 60 compounds, assuming that the species in those communities are similarly chemically distinct from one another.

comments.issue: Species-level data relevant to selective pressures (compounds per species, damage by species traits) are not analyzed.
comments.request: Answer or follow up on the species-level questions raised.
comments.quote: Mostly, I wanted to know more about the species-level data, which I think is most relevant for answering questions related to the selective pressures that generate phytochemical diversity.

comments.issue: 'Important' at L17 is undefined.
comments.request: Define what important means in this context.
comments.quote: L17: I think it would be helpful to define what you mean by “important” here. Important for what?

comments.issue: The hypotheses behind the two phytochemical diversity predictions are unclear.
comments.request: Explain the predictions and the evolutionary mechanisms behind them.
comments.quote: Here the authors lay out two predictions related to phytochemical diversity, but the hypotheses behind these predictions are not clear. I would suggest explaining this more, and being specific about potential evolutionary mechanisms.

comments.issue: Figure 1d is cited but does not exist.
comments.request: Check the Figure 1 panel references.
comments.quote: L 104: I don’t see a Fig. 1d

comments.issue: Figure 1b shows a different dimension (unique chemical features) than the community-scale functional diversity of the other panels.
comments.request: Reorganize or clearly separate the rarefaction panel.
comments.quote: First, Figure 1b feels out of place for me. Conceptually, it is focused on a very different dimension of chemical diversity (the numbers of unique chemical features detected across samples)

comments.issue: Figure 1b cannot be read as per-species accumulation because its x-axis counts samples, not species.
comments.request: Correct the interpretation or add parallel species-accumulation curves.
comments.quote: I don’t think we can necessarily interpret Fig. 1b as “phytochemical diversity accumulating faster on a species-by-species basis” as stated in the text. This is because the x-axis is number of samples, not number of species.

comments.issue: The number of species per region is not reported.
comments.request: Report basic species numbers per region.
comments.quote: At the very least I think we need some basic numbers of how many species were in each region.

comments.issue: Feature-compound alignment depends on mass tolerance settings and is not documented.
comments.request: Provide information on feature-compound alignment and network settings.
comments.quote: I think it will be important for the authors to provide some more info on the alignment between features and compounds in their network (also see comments in methods).

comments.issue: Phytochemical alpha and beta diversity are applied inconsistently in the literature and need explicit description.
comments.request: Define exactly what each metric measures.
comments.quote: Just saying “phytochemical alpha and beta diversity” is not sufficient because these terms and concepts are applied very inconsistently, especially in the phytochemical diversity literature.

comments.issue: The R code link is not public, so the analyses cannot be checked.
comments.request: Make the R code publicly available.
comments.quote: Without the author’s R code (I tried the link provided but it seems it is not public yet) I cannot be sure exactly what they did

comments.issue: The Figure 2 legend does not state what the measures are or what counts as a replicate.
comments.request: Add metric descriptions and replicate definitions to the Figure 2 legend.
comments.quote: I also think it is essential that the legend for Fig. 2 provide a clear statement of what these measures are (metrics of community-scale functional diversity), and what counts as a “replicate” in each panel

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the dissimilarity matrix was based on CSCS scores or plain chemical composition.
comments.request: Clarify the basis of the dissimilarity matrix.
comments.quote: To be clear, was this the phytochemical dissimilarity matrix based on CSCS scores? I think that is really important to clarify, since one could also calculate a dissimilarity matrix just based on the chemical composition

comments.issue: Beta diversity terminology is ambiguous; explicit metric names would avoid confusion with within-community variation.
comments.request: Use explicit metric descriptions such as community-to-community chemical dissimilarity.
comments.quote: Here and elsewhere, I think it would be helpful to use more explicit descriptions of metrics, e.g. “community-to-community chemical dissimilarity” instead of “community phytochemical beta diversity”

comments.issue: Steeper tropical relationships may reflect greater geographic distances between plots, since only elevational distance was accounted for.
comments.request: Control for or discuss geographic distance effects.
comments.quote: Since it seems only elevational distance was accounted for in these analyses, is it possible that the steeper relationships in the tropical region are due to greater geographic distances between plots?

comments.issue: The biotic interactions hypothesis is not well defined.
comments.request: Define the biotic interactions hypothesis clearly.
comments.quote: L 166: Related to my comments on the intro, I don’t think the “biotic interactions hypothesis” is very well defined.

comments.issue: The claim that phytochemical diversity exceeds expectation given species diversity cannot be assessed without the actual species diversity gradient.
comments.request: Report the underlying species diversity gradient.
comments.quote: I find it very tricky to assess whether the results do really show that phytochemical diversity is “greater than that expected given the underlying species diversity gradient”. It would be very helpful here to know what the actual underlying species diversity gradient is!

comments.issue: With functional groups as units, regional gamma diversity already depends on beta diversity, making the calculation circular.
comments.request: Acknowledge or resolve the gamma-beta dependency in this analysis.
comments.quote: But when the “species” are instead functional groups defined based on chemical similarity, a the “gamma diversity” of a region already depends on its beta diversity!

comments.issue: Phytochemical data alone say little about the importance of biotic interactions.
comments.request: Temper conclusions about biotic interactions.
comments.quote: L206-207: I am not sure the phytochemical data, on their own, tell us much about the importance of biotic interactions.

comments.issue: The damage-type guide was developed for fossil damage and does not justify specialist/generalist classifications.
comments.request: Justify damage-based host specialization with references or data.
comments.quote: I looked at the referenced “guide to damage types”, which was developed for classifying fossil damage, and it does not seem to have any references or data that justify the classifications of particular damage types as specialist, intermediate, or generalist.

comments.issue: Equating features with compounds requires documenting curation and quality control of adducts.
comments.request: Describe dataset curation and feature-compound confidence.
comments.quote: I think we need some more information in this section about how/whether the dataset was curated and quality-controlled to remove adducts, etc.

comments.issue: Multivariate homogeneity of variances, an assumption of PERMANOVA and a beta-diversity metric, was not tested.
comments.request: Run a betadisper test alongside the PERMANOVA.
comments.quote: In addition to conducting this PERMANOVA, it would be great to also do a related test for multivariate homogeneity of variances (the betadisper function in vegan).

comments.issue: Repeated species in the dataset violate PERMANOVA independence, and repeat rates differ among regions.
comments.request: Resample one sample per species and rerun the analysis.
comments.quote: This violates the assumption of the PERMANOVA that each sample is independent, but also the number of potential repeats per species might be higher in the sub-alpine and sub-tropical zones than in the tropical zones.

comments.issue: The rarefaction results may be sensitive to including multiple non-independent samples per species.
comments.request: Test sensitivity to repeated samples, e.g. with constrained rarefaction.
comments.quote: Also, it might be a good idea here (as elsewhere) to examine how sensitive this analysis is to the inclusion of multiple (non-independent) samples per species.

comments.issue: The section at lines 497-511 needs more explanation.
comments.request: Expand the explanation of this section.
comments.quote: L497-511: Related to my comment above, I would love to see more explanation here!

comments.issue: It is unclear how chewers and miners were attributed 75% of damage when piercing, sucking and galling do not remove area.
comments.request: Explain how damage percentages were quantified and whether miners were measured.
comments.quote: the authors state that chewers and miners account for 75% of the observed damage. Is this percentage based on total area removed? Many other types of damage they mention (piecing/sucking, galling) would not have led to area loss

comments.issue: Four line-level word corrections (L181, L195, L379, L469).
comments.quote: L181: significantly L195: abundance

title: Tree phytochemical diversity and herbivory are higher in the tropics

study.system: global drylands; spatial layers, protected areas and vertebrate data

editor_summary: All three referees are generally positive but find the dryland-designations section disconnected and recommend moving it to supplementary; Referee 1 wants validation and Referee 3 wants assessment of systematic data gaps.

reviews.assessment: Values the topic and second section, but the dryland-classification section adds little and the land-use intensity classification needs justification and independent validation.
strengths: well written and enjoyable to read
second part interesting and clearly presented

comments.issue: The premise that dryland definitions are highly debated is overstated, since the UNEP definition is widely accepted.
comments.request: Acknowledge that the UNEP definition is widely accepted and revise the motivation.
comments.quote: To me the UNEP definition is widely used and accepted, both within the scientific and policy communities, and thus is not as debated as suggested.

comments.issue: The dryland-delineation section is disconnected and adds little value to the paper.
comments.request: Remove the section or justify its value, soundness and need.
comments.quote: I was not convinced that the analyses presented in the first part of the paper, while undoubtedly interesting, add anything relevant to the paper.

comments.issue: The Figure 2 caption does not let readers understand what the figure shows.
comments.request: Rewrite the Figure 2 caption.
comments.quote: I had problems to fully understand Fig. 2 based on the information provided in the caption.

comments.issue: The mention of 'Presumed Drylands' at L411-412 is confusing.
comments.request: Rewrite or delete the 'Presumed Drylands' mention.
comments.quote: The mention to “Presumed Drylands” is confusing, either rewrite to clarify or delete it

comments.issue: The methods section is too brief to understand what was done.
comments.request: Provide all methodological explanations and details.
comments.quote: the methodological part of the manuscript is very brief and do not provide all the explanations/details needed to allow readers to fully understand what they did

comments.issue: Land-use intensity does not weight land uses with clearly different ecological impacts, giving untrustworthy results.
comments.request: Fully justify how land-use intensity was defined and weighted.
comments.quote: it is not clear how they weighted the different land uses considered, whose ecological impacts and thus their “intensity” clearly differ

comments.issue: The land-use intensity classification is not validated against independent data.
comments.request: Validate the land-use intensity classification with independent data.
comments.quote: I feel the authors should also validate their land use intensity classification using independent data

reviews.assessment: Finds valuable material in parts but the three components are poorly connected and the threats framing is not convincing.
strengths: protected areas and biodiversity section really interesting
material on pages 11-12 extremely valuable, the strength of the manuscript
uncovered major differences among dryland definitions

comments.issue: Three poorly connected concepts; the dryland-definition analysis is not clearly relevant to a discourse on threats.
comments.request: Connect the analyses explicitly to threats to drylands.
comments.quote: in the context of threats, it is unclear how this particular analysis is relevant to a discourse on threats

comments.issue: The claim that inconsistent mapping is a major obstacle to conservation planning is unjustified.
comments.request: Justify or revise the claim about inconsistent definitions as an obstacle.
comments.quote: The lack of consistent mapping does not appear as a major threat to conservation planning in drylands.

comments.issue: The protected areas section is largely descriptive and does not link protection to conservation or ecology.
comments.request: Make links between protected-area coverage, conservation and ecological processes explicit.
comments.quote: One is left wondering about the links between percent protected areas and conservation.

comments.issue: Statements that protected areas permit multiple land uses and resource extraction are not novel.
comments.request: Clarify exactly what these statements refer to.
comments.quote: statements about protected areas permitting multiple land uses and resource extraction are not particularly novel

comments.issue: The choice of a 50% cut-off is unjustified and inconsistent with the 99% cut-off for endemics.
comments.request: Justify the 50% cut-off or test alternatives such as 90%.
comments.quote: It is not clear how the authors chose 50% cut off. This differs from their 99% cut off for endemic species.

comments.issue: The broad ecological mechanisms underpinning the threats are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the ecological mechanisms behind these threats.
comments.quote: It would have been really good to have had a discussion of some of the broad ecological mechanisms underpinning these threats

reviews.assessment: Welcomes the important, well-written contribution, requesting more depth on layer comparison, a data table, better methods signposting and checks for WDPA data gaps.
strengths: important contribution relevant to a broad audience
falls well within the journal's scope

comments.issue: The comparison of the four dryland layers is superficial and could be deepened with environmental and human factors.
comments.request: Consider an in-depth analysis of what drives differences among layers.
comments.quote: I think the authors are missing an opportunity to do more on their analysis comparing the four layers.

comments.issue: The text describing the four layers would be clearer as a table of source data, resolution and dryland types.
comments.request: Add a table outlining the main aspects of the four layers.
comments.quote: I think the text on the four different layers (ca. lines 74-89) would be much better represented by a table that outlines the main aspects of the four layers.

comments.issue: The results need more signposting of methods and data sources because methods come last.
comments.request: Introduce data sources briefly in the results, e.g. the World Database on Protected Areas.
comments.quote: the results section, more generally, would benefit from these types of small additions that makes it a little less necessary to flip between the methods and results when reading

comments.issue: The Figure 2 legend misleadingly says white represents all IUCN categories I-VI.
comments.request: Correct the description of the white portion in the Figure 2 legend.
comments.quote: the description of the white portion of the graph seems misleading in the figure legend

comments.issue: The arbitrary 10% protection threshold ignores established adequacy measures based on species range size.
comments.request: Use adequacy measures such as Rodrigues et al. instead of the 10% threshold.
comments.quote: The use of thresholds of protection (i.e. 10%) is a bit crude and doesn’t include long established approaches to integrate the total range-size of a species when assessing adequacy of protection.

comments.issue: The WDPA has systematic gaps because some countries, including China and India, do not release their data.
comments.request: Check for systematic WDPA gaps and re-run the protected-area analyses if needed.
comments.quote: the database has some major gaps. Some countries don’t allow for their data to be displayed and downloaded.

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 71-72 is unclear.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence at lines 71-72.
comments.quote: Lines: 71-72: Not sure what this sentence means

comments.issue: The language around the strictness of IUCN categories I-IV versus V-VI needs refinement.
comments.request: Refine the language about IUCN category strictness.
comments.quote: I think the division can be accepted, but the language around it needs to be refined.

comments.issue: The 100% conversion under SSP2-4.5 versus 'most' under SSP5-8.5 wording invites misunderstanding.
comments.request: Rewrite these statements to avoid confusion.
comments.quote: I am a little confused as to how 100% was converted under the less depressing scenario and “only” most was projected to “undergo some degree of conversion”.

comments.issue: The reported 0.002 km2 resolution for a global analysis is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the 0.002 km2 resolution figure.
comments.quote: I just need to be sure, you were working at a 0.002 km2 resolution in a global analysis?

comments.issue: How protected areas without an IUCN category were treated is not described.
comments.request: State how uncategorized protected areas were treated.
comments.quote: its not entirely clear to me from the description here how protected areas that was not categorized as one of the six/seven IUCN categories were treated

title: Habitat amount modulates biodiversity responses to fragmentation

study.system: moa and flightless birds, New Zealand; process-based extinction models

editor_summary: Editor notes two reviewers found the contribution interesting and the approach well done, while one reviewer with system expertise disagrees; wider interest exists but R1's closer knowledge raised important considerations.

reviews.assessment: Strongly critical: argues the study is back-to-front, ignores key literature and data, and draws conclusions the sparse dated record cannot support.

comments.issue: Line-level edits: title 'harbour' spelling, L48 wording, L49 redundant 'genetically distinct', L50 hyperbole, figure legend misspellings, macron usage.
comments.quote: Line 50: “hundreds of thousands” is hyperbolic and superfluous.

comments.issue: The study is back to front: extinct taxa with unsettled biology are used as the basis for understanding extant taxa.
comments.request: Reverse the inferential logic or justify it.
comments.quote: the study seems to me to be back to front. It takes a suite of extinct taxa, whose habitats and biology are still subjects of research

comments.issue: Key papers on moa extinction chronology and geography from the last decade are uncited and partly pre-empt the results.
comments.request: Cite and discuss this prior work.
comments.quote: the lack of citation of papers on the chronology and geography of moa extinction which have been available for nearly 10 years, one of which could be seen as at least partly pre-empting the present results

comments.issue: Earlier lowland extinction should have been no surprise given documented forest loss by fire and habitat loss plus hunting.
comments.quote: In any event the result of an earlier extinction in the lowlands (survival in the mountains) should have been no surprise to the authors.

comments.issue: The identified refugia are simply the only remaining natural habitat, making the finding trivial.
comments.request: Acknowledge this triviality.
comments.quote: a few minutes spent with Google Earth will demonstrate that the “refugia” identified in the MS are the only areas left on the main islands with significant “natural habitat”

comments.issue: Statistical modelling of conjectural biology cannot replace analysis of actual distributional and chronological data.
comments.request: Base conclusions on actual data.
comments.quote: Adding statistical modelling based on conjectural biological characteristics cannot replace analysis of actual data distributional and chronological data.

comments.issue: Fundamental flaw: reliance on latitudinal trends when longitude and altitude drive South Island moa distribution, and climate was not constant.
comments.request: Use longitude and altitude and account for climate change.
comments.quote: There is a fundamental flaw in the analysis, with respect to the reliance on latitudinal trends in moa distribution. In the South Island, the major determinant at that level is longitude, the differences between the eastern lowlands and western mountains.

comments.issue: Actual museum distributions are not used, three key moa taxa are excluded, and sexual dimorphism and skewed sex ratios are ignored.
comments.request: Include museum distributions, missing taxa and sex structure.
comments.quote: The study fails to consider either the actual distributions of the taxa as recorded in museum collections, excludes three key moa taxa, and takes no account of sexual dimorphism, and non-equal sex ratios.

comments.issue: The origin point for modelling human spread is novel but irrelevant to subsequent colonist behaviour.
comments.request: Reconsider this parameter.
comments.quote: The choice of origin for modelling human population spread is novel and does not seem to me to be relevant to what the colonising human populations did from then on.

comments.issue: Abstract reads like a thesis extract with unnecessary statements, hyperbole, and long-canvassed claims.
comments.request: Rewrite the abstract.
comments.quote: This seems to be lifted from a postgraduate thesis. It includes unnecessary statements, hyperbole, and claims results that have been canvassed in the literature over many years.

comments.issue: Simulations cannot reveal ecology and demographics unless based on data from the birds themselves (L52-53).
comments.request: Ground simulations in bird data.
comments.quote: Lines 52-53: can simulations really reveal differences in ecology and demographics? Surely simulations must be based on data from the birds themselves.

comments.issue: Similar range collapse across taxa is unsurprising given identical influences of hunting and habitat destruction (L55-56).
comments.quote: Lines 55-56: Given that all moa taxa were simultaneously subjected to the same influences – hunting and habitat destruction – is it any surprise that the patterns in range collapse were similar?

comments.issue: Claim that lowland species persisted in cold suboptimal mountains is contradicted by records for P. elephantopus (L56-57).
comments.request: Correct this claim.
comments.quote: The “final populations” of lowland species such as Pachyornis elephantopus were never found in “suboptimal habitats in cold, mountainous areas

comments.issue: The refugia result is obvious: high cold places are the only habitat left after destruction; weka and kiwi persist in lowland forest (L58-60).
comments.quote: The high, cold places are the only places where habitat for the others – optimal or suboptimal – persist after waves of destruction that began in earliest Polynesian times.

comments.issue: A co-authored forest-loss paper is used as a reference for Pacific-wide collapses; Hawaii is not mentioned (L85).
comments.request: Cite more appropriate comparative references.
comments.quote: Why is a paper (by co-authors) on birds and forest loss by fire in New Zealand given as a reference for faunal collapses in the Pacific as a whole, especially as the context must be comparative.

comments.issue: Self-referential citation for 'unique flightless species'; more relevant references exist and Ref 18 may be unnecessary (L87).
comments.request: Use more relevant citations.
comments.quote: Line 87: Self-referential (in terms of the present co-authorship) citation for “unique flightless species”.

comments.issue: A same-year Bayesian radiocarbon paper produced identical results and is uncited; the present MS may be redundant.
comments.request: Cite the paper and state the advance beyond it.
comments.quote: In some respects, that paper makes the present MS redundant because the present MS fails to go beyond the conclusions offered then.

comments.issue: Sweeping unreferenced statement ignores recent published progress (L90-93).
comments.request: Add references and nuance.
comments.quote: Lines 90-93: This sweeping and unreferenced statement ignores recent published progress on just these matters.

comments.issue: Fine-scale prediction needs data densities unavailable for moa because deposition and preservation sites are feature-controlled (L94-105).
comments.request: Acknowledge this data limitation.
comments.quote: fine scale prediction depends on densities of basic data that are not available for moa

comments.issue: The method is called 'verified' on the basis of a single reference; one study cannot verify an approach.
comments.request: Temper the validation claim.
comments.quote: They claim, on a single reference, that this method is a “verified” approach.

comments.issue: Big claims about interspecific trait differences rest only on the time and place of radiocarbon-dated remains.
comments.request: Justify with the wider literature and museum collections.
comments.quote: That is a very big claim, based simply on the time and place – however well-established – of their radiocarbon-dated remains.

comments.issue: The two primary questions seem backwards and confused about prehistoric versus historic time.
comments.request: Reframe the questions.
comments.quote: seem rather the wrong way around as well as confused in terms of the matter of time

comments.issue: For lowland moa the periphery of their range was not in the mountains, so the range-collapse narrative is wrong.
comments.request: Correct the range-collapse interpretation.
comments.quote: The key point that the authors seem to be pushing is that the ranges of the moa taxa shrank to the periphery of their original extents. For lowland moa that periphery was not in the mountains.

comments.issue: It is unclear what moa range reduction can add to understanding declines of species that have already declined.
comments.request: Clarify the added value.
comments.quote: what more can an understanding of the pattern of range reduction in moa add to “inform pathways of decline”?

comments.issue: Saying ecology affected the speed of range collapse is trite (L109-111).
comments.quote: It is trite to say that ecology affected the speed of range collapse

comments.issue: More recent analyses of moa nesting behaviour and habitat preferences exist (L328).
comments.request: Cite newer work.
comments.quote: Line 328: There are more recent analyses of the nesting behaviour and habitat preferences of moa.

comments.issue: Ref 16 is outdated; habitat preferences remain poorly known for several taxa (L330-331).
comments.request: Update the references.
comments.quote: Lines 330-331: Ref 16 is out of date for these factors of moa biology. Indeed, moa habitat preferences are still not well defined

comments.issue: Potential ecological niches as mathematical constructs may not reflect reality given Holocene climate and habitat change (L332-336).
comments.request: Validate niches against environmental studies.
comments.quote: Hence the “full potential ecological niches” as mathematical constructs do not necessarily reflect reality.

comments.issue: Lumping P. australis and P. elephantopus is taxonomically wrong; they had the most different ecologies of any species pair.
comments.request: Analyse the two species separately.
comments.quote: For Pachyornis, linking and analysing P. australis and P. elephantopus together is just plain wrong.

comments.issue: Using first arrival rather than earliest settlement as the baseline is inappropriate for a mobile colonising population (L344-353).
comments.request: Use settlement sites instead of arrival points.
comments.quote: The baseline parameter of location of first arrival rather than of first/earliest settlements is certainly novel, and likely completely inappropriate for the purpose used here.

comments.issue: Egg harvesting contributed insignificantly compared with predation on breeding adults (L359).
comments.request: Reconsider the egg-harvest parameterisation.
comments.quote: It should be remembered that taking moa eggs would have contributed insignificantly to the rate of reduction in moa populations relative to predation on breeding adults.

comments.issue: Latitudinal centre is an inappropriate basic parameter; preservation-site locations drive it (L377-382).
comments.request: Replace this parameter.
comments.quote: Why is “latitudinal center (sic) of ‘natural’ (pre-human) distribution” used as a basic parameter in the statistics?

comments.issue: Radiocarbon-dated geographic sampling is far too meagre for credible spatial resolution of range reduction.
comments.request: Acknowledge the sampling limitation.
comments.quote: While the dated individuals can definitely provide statistical predictions for the date of extinction, the geographic sampling is far too meagre to allow credible spatial resolution of range reduction through time.
