comments.quote: It'd be nice if the authors could also look at diversity in their sampled Neandertals to verify that it is indeed low.

title: Ignoring population structure in hominin evolutionary models can lead to the inference of spurious admixture events

study.system: Amazonian and Atlantic Forest trees; 271 plots, trait data

editor_summary: Editor invites revision; reviewers find the work of interest but raise concerns; contacted Reviewer 3 for clarification of unclear expectations but proceeded without a reply.

reviews.assessment: Large and carefully interpreted synthesis with consistent forest-loss effects; asks to better link results to ecological drivers.
strengths: data synthesis large enough to test consistency across a broad region
consistent impacts of forest loss on a trait subset

comments.issue: The discussion does not leverage the detailed results to distinguish which direct ecological drivers explain the winner-loser spectrum.
comments.request: Discuss which ecological drivers (edge effects, fire, disperser loss) the results support.
comments.quote: the authors could make more of the detailed results to help disentangle which ecological drivers (rather than landscape metrics) cause the winner-loser spectrum

comments.issue: Only the upper 95% percentile was considered, although increases in very small-seeded species are equally meaningful.
comments.request: Consider a lower percentile as well.
comments.quote: I’m unsure why only the upper 95% percentile was considered and not a lower percentile as well in this case

comments.issue: The Fig. 3 legend does not explain the (~ A | B) notation or its link to the causal diagram.
comments.request: Explain the notation and causal links in the Fig. 3 legend, as done for Fig. 4.
comments.quote: It would help readers to provide a description of the (~ A | B) notation within the figure legend

comments.issue: Some cited papers are missing from the reference list.
comments.request: Add the missing references.
comments.quote: There are some cited papers missing from the References list.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and potentially important study, but the key terms are not defined correctly and the interpretation needs care.
strengths: can test whether earlier case studies are context-dependent

comments.issue: Forest loss is computed as the inverse of forest cover assuming 100% original cover, so it measures habitat amount, not loss.
comments.request: Use historical maps and calculate loss from changes in forest cover.
comments.quote: the authors used the inverse of forest cover as forest loss and assumed that all forest landscapes have an original cover of 100%, which is not reasonable in this case

comments.issue: Fragmentation is defined as the number of fragments, a dynamic quantity that need not track actual fragmentation processes or extinction debt.
comments.request: Justify the fragmentation metric and consider the time period and extinction debt.
comments.quote: Fragmentation is defined as the number of forest fragments in this study. However, habitat fragmentation is again a dynamic process

comments.issue: Basal-area-based degradation is likely confounded with forest cover, fragmentation and edge density, so the factors are not independent.
comments.request: Check independence and whether basal area can be driven purely by local degradation.
comments.quote: Please check whether these factors are independent from each other, and whether basal area can be driven purely by local degradation.

comments.issue: Results are reported for all spatial scales although they change little, cluttering the main text.
comments.request: Focus on one scale and report the others in the supplement, or discuss scale effects.
comments.quote: To make the results clearer to readers, the authors may consider focusing on only one spatial scale (e.g., 1000 m)

comments.issue: The DBH>10 cm cutoff means results describe large surviving trees and may not hold for young generations or whole communities.
comments.request: Acknowledge that the pattern applies to large remaining trees only.
comments.quote: This needs to be kept in mind that the observed pattern fits for large remaining trees in the fragments, and the effect for the whole community (e.g., trees DBH> 1cm) is different.

comments.issue: Lewis et al. 2015 is cited for the importance of tropical rainforest to biodiversity and ecosystem services, which it does not cover.
comments.request: Cite Pillay et al. 2022 for this point instead.
comments.quote: Lewis et al 2015 mostly discuss the impacts of humans on tropical rainforest, but not on the importance of tropical rainforest to biodiversity and ecosystem services

comments.issue: The period over which the deforestation rate was calculated is not specified.
comments.request: Specify the deforestation period.
comments.quote: please specify which period for this rate of deforestation

comments.issue: Whether the basal-area proxy reliably quantifies disturbance, and how it separates loss, fragmentation, fire and logging, is unclear.
comments.request: Justify the reliability of the disturbance proxy.
comments.quote: quantification of disturbance (using a proxy based on basal area), is this method reliable?

comments.issue: Species niche centroids are undefined and their link to winner and loser species is unclear given no winner/loser data.
comments.request: Define SNC and justify its link to winner and loser species.
comments.quote: what is species niche centroids (SNC) and what it represents?

comments.issue: The time period of forest loss and fragmentation, which are dynamic processes, is not accounted for.
comments.request: Account for the time period of loss and fragmentation.
comments.quote: the time period of forest loss and fragmentation matters. Loss and fragmentation are a dynamic process.

comments.issue: The discussion of winners and losers is weak and does not explain the mechanism behind the dominant role of forest loss.
comments.request: Discuss the mechanisms by which forest loss drives trait changes.
comments.quote: Why forest cover (loss) has a dominant role in driving functional trait changes is still not fully discussed, what is the mechanism?

comments.issue: Vegetation data include only trees >10 cm DBH, so the effects concern large trees, not young generations.
comments.request: State this scope limitation in the methods.
comments.quote: all trees are those > 10 cm in DBH, so this is more of an effect on large trees, not for young generations

comments.issue: Table S1 on plot details and regional land-use histories should be in the main text.
comments.request: Move Table S1 to the main text.
comments.quote: Details about the plot size, number of plots, number of trees in each plot are very important

comments.issue: The number of species with complete trait data is not reported.
comments.request: Report how many species have full trait data.
comments.quote: how many species have full trait data?

comments.issue: The rationale for the 500, 1000 and 2000 m buffer zones is not given.
comments.request: Explain the choice of buffer distances.
comments.quote: the reasons to use 500-, 1000- and 2000 meter as buffer zones need to be told

comments.issue: The definition of winners and losers is unclear and the method's reliability is not justified.
comments.request: Clarify the winner/loser definition and justify the method.
comments.quote: definition of winners and losers, not very clear. Please state why this method is reliable.

reviews.assessment: Reviews only the causal framework; the DAG omits likely common causes, so the causal model needs strengthening.
strengths: causal inference framework is a useful approach for this question

comments.issue: The DAG includes only the analysed drivers and outcome; a complete DAG should include all common causes of variables.
comments.request: Include plausible common causes in the DAG.
comments.quote: My main concern is that the DAG presented in Figure 1 consists only of the analyzed anthropogenic drivers and outcome variable of interest.

comments.issue: DAG-data consistency is not tested, which could support the presented causal structure.
comments.request: Test DAG-data consistency.
comments.quote: It would also be beneficial to test DAG-data consistency, as this can provide additional support to the presented DAG.

title: Winner–loser plant trait replacements in human-modified tropical forests

study.system: dune and non-dune Helianthus petiolaris; population genomics and QTL crosses

reviews.assessment: Fascinating question and comprehensive data, but linkage-disequilibrium concerns and readability issues leave some conclusions in doubt.
strengths: addresses linkage disequilibrium head-on in the discussion

comments.issue: Window-based analyses are biased because inverted regions contain more variants and recombination varies along chromosomes.
comments.request: Repeat some analyses with centimorgan-based windows or neutral expectations accounting for LD variation.
comments.quote: For me these are problematic as you expect higher number of variants in inverted regions (and thus smaller windows there) and that the same number of kb to cover fewer centimorgans.

comments.issue: Information on the evolutionary history of the inversions and populations is missing.
comments.request: Clarify when inversions arose, whether gene flow occurs, and how long populations have been separated.
comments.quote: I was also missing some information about the inversions investigated here. I assume these were segregating in the population before the MON and GSD population split. Is there gene flow between MON and GSD?

comments.issue: The paper is difficult to read because of the sheer number of datasets, inversions, tests and populations.
comments.request: Add an overview figure showing which datasets were used for which tests.
comments.quote: My final major comment is that I did find the paper somewhat difficult to read. This is due to the extensive nature of the data presented and the sheer number of inversions, tests, and populations.

comments.issue: A supplemental table of inversion sizes and genomic locations is missing.
comments.request: Add a supplemental table of inversion sizes and putative locations.
comments.quote: A supplemental table of inversions sizes and putative genomic locations would be nice to have.

comments.issue: It is unknown whether Fig. 2 looks different using window-based associations instead of the inversion as an allele.
comments.request: Add the window-based version of Figure 2 to the supplement.
comments.quote: Figure 2 – Does this figure look different if you use window based associations rather than the inversion as an allele? Would be nice to have that in the supplement.

comments.issue: Figure S11 displays the data better than Table 1 but is only in the supplement.
comments.request: Consider moving figure S11 to the main text.
comments.quote: Line 215 – The authors should consider moving figure S11 to the main text as this displays the data better than Table 1.

comments.issue: The significant overall P-value for MON1 vs. MON2 conflicts with non-significant sub-tests.
comments.request: Explain how the overall test can be significant when the component tests are not.
comments.quote: Table 1 – How can the overall P-value for MON1 vs. MON2 be significant when the within inversions, outside inversions, and within vs. outside inversions tests are not significant?

comments.issue: It is unknown how a PCA of SNP data from each inversion separately would look.
comments.request: Run per-inversion PCAs and report them.
comments.quote: Figure 4 – How does a PCA look when made of SNP data from each inversion separately?

comments.issue: The same pattern could arise if inversions were already present in the ancestral population, so calling it convergence is questionable.
comments.request: Clarify how convergence is distinguished from ancestral polymorphism.
comments.quote: Line 359-36 – How can you know this is convergence? If the inversions were present in the ancestral population before GSD and MON split wouldn’t you find the same pattern?

comments.issue: The discussion does not compare these results with other non-sunflower systems.
comments.request: Add text comparing the results with other systems.
comments.quote: In the discussion it would be nice to have some text comparing the results here to other non-sunflower systems as well.

reviews.assessment: A nice and meaningful contribution supporting the importance of inversions; only small quibbles plus a suggestion to broaden the discussion.
strengths: combines three approaches showing a disproportionate inversion role
interesting discussion of translocations versus inversions

comments.issue: Evidence that seed size is adaptive could be clearer.
comments.request: Strengthen or qualify the evidence that seed size is adaptive.
comments.quote: There are small issues that I could quibble about, such as clearer evidence that seed size is adaptive, but I do not view these as being critical for preventing the publication of this important work.

comments.issue: Systems with few or single inversions are not discussed, limiting the scope of the claims.
comments.request: Discuss examples from other systems to expand the scope and impact.
comments.quote: I would suggest the authors consider some of those examples from other systems and perhaps discuss them more. I think that might help to expand the scope and impact of this work.

reviews.assessment: Not convinced inversions contribute disproportionately, and finds LD non-independence and sweep-scan bias problematic; terminology needs fixing.
strengths: evidence for parallelism for some inversions
results stand out in genome-wide analyses

comments.issue: Counting windows across inversions as independent data points is invalid because LD within inversions is very high.
comments.request: Prune for LD and re-estimate the proportion of independent parallel regions in inversions.
comments.quote: I don’t think it is valid to count individual windows across inversions as independent data points. Given the lack of recombination across an inversion, I would expect LD to be very high.

comments.issue: Sweep scans may mainly detect rearrangements rather than adaptive loci.
comments.request: Run the original CLR approach in addition to check whether inversion signals remain.
comments.quote: We used the same approach and found that the results seemed to represent mainly rearrangements, which we had no reason to believe were adaptive.

comments.issue: 'Convergence' is used when 'parallelism' is meant, and parallelism is not defined.
comments.request: Use parallel evolution terminology and explain what is meant by parallelism in the introduction.
comments.quote: the authors often refer to ‘convergence’ when ‘parallelism’ would fit better. This is because the selected loci are expected to be the same between populations.

comments.issue: No model of parallel evolution emerges from the complex results, and the patterns are not simplified.
comments.request: Present a simplified model of parallel evolution in the discussion.
comments.quote: In the discussion it would be helpful if they could say something about the model of parallel evolution that results from their analysis.

comments.issue: More structuring would help readers understand the main message.
comments.request: Restructure the manuscript to clarify the main messages.
comments.quote: Overall, I thought more structuring of the manuscript could help the reader understand the main message(s).

comments.issue: Figure 4 would be more useful at the start of the Results with the environmental PCA.
comments.request: Move Figure 4 earlier, possibly as panel A.
comments.quote: Figure 4: It would be helpful to see this at the start of the Results. It could be panel A in the figure with the environmental PCA to show the contrast between genetics and environment.

comments.issue: Without knowing the causal loci, the lack of parallelism when inversions are shared is hard to interpret.
comments.request: Acknowledge this interpretive limitation.
comments.quote: without knowing anything about the underlying causal loci it is difficult to know how to interpret the lack of parallelism when inversions are shared

comments.issue: Figure 6 is confusing.
comments.request: Replace diamonds with letters for loci on the chromosome map.
comments.quote: Figure 6: I found this figure confusing. How about skipping the diamonds and instead putting the letters that represent different loci in the chromosome map at the bottom?

comments.issue: Functional variation within inversions is not analysed, so reasons for parallel versus non-parallel associations remain unclear.
comments.request: Add analyses of functional variation in the inversions.
comments.quote: I would really like to see analyses that get at the functional variation in the inversions so that we could better understand why in some cases associations occur in parallel across populations and in others they do not.

comments.issue: The Discussion lacks a clear summary of the take-home message.
comments.request: Add a clear summary of the paper's main message.
comments.quote: I felt like the Discussion missed providing a clear summary of what the take-home message was from the results in this paper.

comments.issue: The discussion does not address why inversions dominate sunflower genomics, a pattern not universal across species.
comments.request: Discuss possible reasons why inversions dominate this system.
comments.quote: I think it could be useful in the Discussion to give some ideas about why this might be the case, especially since it is a pattern that is not universal across species.

comments.issue: Figure S15 is an ineffective display; outlier regions appear to span the genome due to the circos style.
comments.request: Replace the circos plot with a linear plot.
comments.quote: Therefore, I do not think this is an effective way to display the information and would suggest using a linear plot rather that circos plot.

title: Inversions contribute disproportionately to parallel genomic divergence in dune sunflowers

study.system: climate-disease research; simulated infectious disease vignettes

editor_summary: Finds the Perspective of interest but several points need addressing; notes Reviewer 2 suggested reworking or removing two vignettes, which the editor does not require but asks the authors to consider.

reviews.assessment: Calls the paper terrific, important and elegant, offering only relatively minor suggestions and pointers to additional literature.
strengths: elegant approach of simulating and then analyzing epidemics

comments.issue: The point that ecological exposures are invulnerable to confounding by case characteristics is under-recognized and worth making.
comments.request: Make explicit this advantage of ecological exposure data.
comments.quote: the fact that use of ecological exposures makes observational studies invulnerable to confounding by case characteristics

comments.issue: Recent reports that climate models themselves are beginning to fail may warrant mention.
comments.request: Consider mentioning the failure of climate models and cite the Nature news piece.
comments.quote: it has recently been noted that climate models themselves are beginning to fail, presumably as a result of as-yet unrecognized positive feedback loops in climatic systems. This may warrant mention.

comments.issue: Using smoothers to remove nonspecific seasonal oscillation is not mentioned, risking spurious correlations.
comments.request: Discuss using smoothers such as Fourier terms or splines.
comments.quote: an important fix to this, which doesn't seem to be mentioned in the MS, is simply using smoothers (whether fast Fourier terms or cubic splines, or other trend terms) to eliminate nonspecific seasonal oscillation

comments.issue: ENSO-type phenomena can act like randomized exposures or instrumental variables on a DAG.
comments.request: Discuss the use of ENSO as a climate-change-like natural experiment.
comments.quote: on a DAG ENSO might look and awful lot like a randomized exposure or instrumental variable

comments.issue: Distributed nonlinear lag models can address multi-causality in infectious disease research.
comments.request: Point to distributed nonlinear lag models as a solution.
comments.quote: the use of the environmental epidemiology toolbox (e.g., distributed nonlinear lag models) can be really useful

comments.issue: Pseudo-diffusion issues could be addressed with multilevel models treating geographies as fixed or random effects.
comments.request: Suggest multilevel models for the pseudo-diffusion problem.
comments.quote: the issues around “pseudo-diffusion” that the authors flag would be readily addressed using multilevel models that treat geographies as fixed or random effects

reviews.assessment: Doubts the target audience can follow the text and questions the journal fit, while finding no serious errors beyond Vignette 1.
strengths: no serious errors apart from Vignette 1
ideas in the vignettes are conceptually connected under causal inference frameworks

comments.issue: The text never defines the causal inference framework nor explains how readers should use it, so the audience may not follow.
comments.request: Explain the framework and its use, or reduce and revise the vignettes.
comments.quote: the text doesn’t clarify what a “causal inference framework” is and, in all four vignettes, does not explain how readers are supposed to use such a framework to improve their analysis

comments.issue: Vignette 1 and Figure 1 do not reflect the confounding among S_t, I_t and β_t introduced via μ and β.
comments.request: Align text, figure and simulations with the actual confounding structure.
comments.quote: it’s important to align the text, figure, and simulations of Vignette 1 to properly reflect confounding among S_t, I_t, and β_t (or C_(t+1)) that would bias the effect estimators

comments.issue: It is often unclear whether observed or unobserved incidence rate is meant.
comments.request: Distinguish observed and unobserved incidence rates consistently.
comments.quote: It was unclear throughout most of the text whether the authors were referring to the observed incidence rate

comments.issue: Half of Vignette 1 concerns transmission-incidence correlations, not the measurement bias its title emphasizes.
comments.request: Link the vignette's exercises clearly to measurement bias.
comments.quote: half of vignette 1 seems to have nothing to do with “measurement bias,” as emphasized in the vignette title, but instead focuses on correlations between transmission and incidence

comments.issue: Vignette 2 on confounding bias only presents correlations, and switches from Spearman to Pearson without reason.
comments.request: Illustrate how spatial heterogeneity biases effect estimates.
comments.quote: it does not illustrate how spatial heterogeneity may bias the effect estimators, but instead refers exclusively to correlation values (swapping from Spearman’s to Pearson’s correlation in the text for no clear reason)

comments.issue: The Vignette 2 exercise does not tell readers the assumption may be unknowable or how frameworks test its plausibility.
comments.request: Explain how causal frameworks assess assumption plausibility.
comments.quote: it fails to tell the reader that one may not know whether the assumption is correct in real observational data, nor does it tell the reader how causal frameworks may allow one to determine whether the assumption is plausible

comments.issue: The latter half of Vignette 2 removes environmental variables, losing the causal question about weather effects.
comments.request: Reframe this exercise around sticking to a single causal question.
comments.quote: the latter half of vignette 2 (lines 230-242) omits the environmental variables entirely from the model as an exercise, which is perplexing

comments.issue: The introduction does not set up the problem, and some sentences are cryptic.
comments.request: Make the introduction accessible to novices.
comments.quote: The introduction doesn’t do a great job of setting up the problem. Some of the sentences are cryptic and hard to parse even for someone who understands this literature

comments.issue: The references at line 97 do not focus on causal inference.
comments.request: Cite Runge et al. 2019 or 2023 for methods instead.
comments.quote: These two refs don't focus on causal inference, do they? Wouldn't Runge et al. (2019) in Nature Communications, or the more recent Runge et al. (2023) article in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, be better citations for methods?

comments.issue: Bias is called a property of estimates, though it is a property of estimators.
comments.request: Use 'estimate an effect with bias' rather than biased estimates.
comments.quote: Technically, bias is a property of an estimator (a design or estimation procedure) not an estimate.

comments.issue: The phrase 'a risk earlier described' is misleading because the Table 2 fallacy was never discussed earlier.
comments.request: Remove the 'earlier' reference or introduce the fallacy first.
comments.quote: the Table 2 fallacy was never discussed in the main or supplementary text, so “earlier” is misleading

comments.issue: A key sentence about causal inference is buried in a paragraph instead of serving as a topic sentence.
comments.request: Make the sentence a topic sentence and elaborate the issues.
comments.quote: We recommend you make the following sentence a topic sentence rather than bury it in a paragraph

comments.issue: The easier-to-read Discussion text previewing the vignettes should be used earlier.
comments.request: Move the clearer preview text into the introduction.
comments.quote: It may be easier for a reader to understand what is coming in the manuscript if the authors used text from the Discussion that is easier to read

comments.issue: Vignette 2's causal reasoning and what an 'explicit causal model' is remain unclear.
comments.request: Start with confounding and clarify the explicit causal model.
comments.quote: Would it be easier for a reader if one started with a description of confounding and then gave, as an example, the description of spatial heterogeneities?

comments.issue: Vignette 3 is hard to read even for experts, and its contribution is unclear.
comments.request: Rewrite Vignette 3 and clarify its contribution.
comments.quote: Even for someone who is very familiar with natural experiments and instrumental (surrogate) variables, this vignette is hard to read. We can’t imagine a novice being able to read and understand it.

comments.issue: Mathematical modelers and experimentalists are not engaged, and how the three research approaches fit together is not shown.
comments.request: Engage modelers and experimentalists, e.g. via Schlueter et al. 2023.
comments.quote: finding a few ways to engage the latter two groups and help them see how causal inference frameworks can help their work

comments.issue: Simplifications such as observation-interval mismatch are ignored without telling readers how they remove complications.
comments.request: Flag these assumptions and their implications for causal inference.
comments.quote: an author should indicate how those assumptions remove certain complications for making causal inferences that must be handled appropriately in real observational data

comments.issue: Vignettes use inconsistent R_0 and immunity settings without explaining why values change.
comments.request: Use consistent parameter settings across vignettes.
comments.quote: Vignettes 1-4 do not use consistent R_0 and average immunity settings (particularly, settings for Vignette 2 are inconsistent with Vignette 3 and 4)

comments.issue: The manuscript's fit to the journal is questioned; the connection to ecology is mostly implicit.
comments.request: Justify the journal fit and make the ecological connection explicit.
comments.quote: we find it odd that this manuscript was submitted to NEE rather than a climate journal or a public health or infectious disease journal

reviews.assessment: Enjoys the timely manuscript and finds the vignettes clear, asking for clarifications and more pointers on overcoming the issues.
strengths: Vignette 1 clearly elucidates issues with time series regressions

comments.issue: It is unclear how the causal inference framework relates to traditional mechanistic disease modeling.
comments.request: Comment on how the framework supports or contrasts with mechanistic models.
comments.quote: I was wondering if the authors could comment more broadly on how their causal inference framework supports/(or other wise) traditional mechanistic disease modeling approaches?

comments.issue: Whether regression-only approaches are always biased, and whether estimating transmission first avoids bias, is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify when regression approaches remain biased, including Vignette 3 methods.
comments.quote: Are approaches using only regression models always biased (vignette 1)? If we somehow estimate transmission first, then run the regression, does that still lead to bias?

comments.issue: Traveling waves might be mistaken for climate drivers, and the two are hard to distinguish.
comments.request: Explain how to distinguish traveling waves from climate effects.
comments.quote: can traveling waves be mistaken as climate drivers? How might we distinguish between the two in observations?

comments.issue: The manuscript offers few pointers on how to overcome the issues raised.
comments.request: Add practical pointers, e.g. in the discussion or after each vignette.
comments.quote: I would have appreciated a few more pointers throughout the manuscript on how to overcome some of the issues raised.

comments.issue: How results would change under continuous rather than discrete time is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the implications of continuous time.
comments.quote: How might things change in a continuous time world?

title: Causal inference concepts can guide research into the effects of climate on infectious diseases

study.system: pollinator diversity and plant reproductive success; global meta-analysis

editor_summary: Reviewers find the work of considerable potential interest but raise substantial concerns that must be addressed; a revised version would be considered.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and timely meta-analysis, but the methods and several inferences need substantial clarification before publication.
strengths: more realistic scenario than total pollinator loss

comments.issue: Methods lack the detail needed to understand data collection and analysis, and how inferences were made.
comments.request: Expand the methods so that data collection and analysis are fully replicable.
comments.quote: In particular the methods section requires more details to be provided and more clarity.

comments.issue: It is unclear which manipulative study designs were included and what designs observational studies used.
comments.request: Describe the experimental designs of the included manipulative and observational studies.
comments.quote: I did not find it easy to assess what type of manipulative studies were included, what were the experimental designs

comments.issue: Clarity is lacking on the moderators extracted, the choice of models and how non-independence was handled.
comments.request: Explain the moderators, model choices and treatment of study non-independence.
comments.quote: more clarity is needed on the moderators extracted, on the choice of models and how lack of study independence was dealt with

comments.issue: No grey literature or non-English search is reported, which is essential for a global meta-analysis.
comments.request: Report a grey literature search and searches in languages other than English.
comments.quote: include a grey literature search and wherever possible a search in a language other than English

comments.issue: Inclusion criterion 4 requires pollinator diversity differences, but how studies measured these differences is unclear.
comments.request: Describe how pollinator diversity differences were measured (manipulation, observation, both).
comments.quote: how were the differences in pollinator diversity measured in the studies included? Experimental manipulation, observation, both?

comments.issue: Lower and higher pollinator diversity treatments are used for effect sizes before being described.
comments.request: Describe the lower/higher diversity treatments before introducing the effect-size calculation.
comments.quote: these treatments have not been described yet in the manuscript

comments.issue: It is unclear how non-independence of observations was addressed and whether random terms were crossed or nested.
comments.request: Clarify which random factors were crossed or nested and why the final model had no nesting.
comments.quote: It is not entirely clear to me how the non-independence of observations was addresses.

comments.issue: The moderators section is hard to follow; whether moderators were used in analyses, extracted or only observed is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the role of each moderator and list those actually used.
comments.quote: This section is hard to follow. It is not clear if the moderators mentioned in L398-403 were used as moderators in the analysis

comments.issue: Manipulative experiments are introduced too late, and observational study designs and their effect-size comparisons are undescribed.
comments.request: Describe observational study designs and the comparisons used for effect sizes earlier in the methods.
comments.quote: Also, it is necessary do describe what observational studies were included, what the experimental design was for these studies

comments.issue: It is unclear which moderators were used and whether they were the same for each subset.
comments.request: State which moderators were used for each subset of analyses.
comments.quote: needs to clarify what moderators, and are they the same for each subset?

comments.issue: Results analyse climatic zone although this was not among the questions posed at the end of the introduction.
comments.request: Add the climatic-zone question to the introduction or justify the analysis.
comments.quote: The results report analysis on the effect of climatic zone, though this is not mentioned in the original questions at the end of the introduction

comments.issue: The inference that invertebrates suffer more than vertebrates rests on diurnal/nocturnal manipulations and may not hold.
comments.request: Clarify the basis of the inference and whether nocturnal invertebrate pollinators were excluded.
comments.quote: The inference that the negative effect is greater for invertebrates than for vertebrate seems to be based on the diurnal/nocturnal manipulation

comments.issue: What manipulation produced invertebrate exclusion in Fig. 6B is unclear; it may be total exclusion.
comments.request: Clarify the manipulation behind Fig. 6B and whether observational studies are included.
comments.quote: In Fig 6B what manipulation was used for the invertebrate exclusion? Wouldn’t that be total exclusion?

title: Loss of pollinator diversity consistently reduces reproductive success for wild and cultivated plants

study.system: tetrapods; phylogenetic comparative analysis of body size

editor_summary: Editor says two reviewers raised concerns that must be addressed before publication; revision invited, with changes highlighted in Word.

reviews.assessment: Finds the approach very useful and the conclusions thought-provoking, offering one suggestion and his own references.
strengths: consolidates old ideas while proposing original viewpoints
will open new perspectives on SSD evolution

comments.issue: Mechanisms proposed by Slatkin (1984), beyond inter-sexual competition, are not discussed.
comments.request: Review Slatkin's mechanisms and consider the suggested articles.
comments.quote: the authors should review the mechanisms proposed by Slatkin (1984) to explain the evolution of SSD under natural selection.

reviews.assessment: Interested and sees broad appeal, but finds the analyses too unclear to assess and cannot support publication in current form.

comments.issue: Analyses lack clarity, making it very difficult to understand what was actually done.
comments.request: Describe exactly how the statistical tests were carried out.
comments.quote: there is a lack of clarity regarding the analyses which makes it very difficult to understand what exactly the authors have done.

comments.issue: Unclear whether PGLS data are branch-wise, species-level, terminal-branch, or path-wise.
comments.request: Specify the data structure used in the PGLS models.
comments.quote: What is the data here? Is it branch-wise or species-level? If it is species level is this calculated only on the terminal branch leading to the species or is it a path-wise measure?

comments.issue: If only branches meeting the 2 SD criterion were used, sample sizes should be much smaller than Figure 2 suggests.
comments.request: Clarify which branches were included and reconcile sample sizes.
comments.quote: If it only includes branches which fit the two standard deviation criterion, then we’d expect some huge reductions in sample sizes (implied in the extended data tables) which does not seem to be the case in Figure 2.

comments.issue: The binomial tests are equally unclear about which changes were counted and how they were classified.
comments.request: Outline clearly what was counted and how the data were classified.
comments.quote: The binomial tests examining number of positive and negative directional changes also suffer from the same lack of clarity

comments.issue: Unclear what the tests study; they may only be testing whether SSD exists.
comments.request: Explain the rationale of these tests.
comments.quote: Furthermore, it is difficult to know what these tests are studying – is this not just studying whether there is sexual size dimorphism?

comments.issue: Body mass change axes in log units cannot be correct; axes may be standardized but this is not stated.
comments.request: Clarify the units and standardization of the change axes.
comments.quote: The PGLS analyses of SSD against directional change are stated to study change in log units of body mass (e.g., Figure 2) but this cannot be correct.

comments.issue: The simulation procedure adds little; simulated data were apparently not used with the fabric model.
comments.request: Use the simulations to test the fabric model or justify them.
comments.quote: The simulation procedure does not seem to add much in its current state – it might be interesting to see what the simulated data gives in terms of the fabric model

comments.issue: Applying the fabric model is not shown to be a novel approach relative to previous work.
comments.request: Outline how the fabric model advances on prior approaches.
comments.quote: It currently feels a little bit like the authors had a set of analyses that they have quickly re-worked to use the recently published fabric model without a comprehensive understanding of why.

comments.issue: Expectations for the fabric model and post-hoc analyses are not stated.
comments.request: State expected results and predictions for the model analyses.
comments.quote: what are the expectations with regards to this model? What about the post-hoc analyses? How would the authors expect their results to look?

comments.issue: The overall goal is vague and exploratory; the introduction sets out no expectations.
comments.request: State the questions, expected results, and how the analyses address them.
comments.quote: it is also not entirely obvious what the overall goal of the manuscript is. It currently suffers from a vagueness that feels exploratory.

comments.issue: First results paragraph is a dense list of descriptive statistics with no biological interpretation.
comments.request: Remove it or move it to figure captions or discussion.
comments.quote: the first paragraph of the results section is simply a list of descriptive statistics about the data. I don’t think this is necessary at all

title: Evolution of sexual size dimorphism in tetrapods is driven by varying patterns of sex-specific selection on size

study.system: microbial communities; invasion experiments and gLV models

editor_summary: Reviewers find the work of considerable potential interest but raise substantial concerns; the paper cannot be accepted but a revised version addressing these concerns would be considered.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, soundly executed study; comments mainly aim to make the exposition easier to follow.
strengths: timely and relevant exploration of invasions

comments.issue: Apparent contradiction between Fig. 1 and Fig. 2/3 is not explained early.
comments.request: Highlight the apparent contradiction early on.
comments.quote: It is later revealed where this apparent contradiction comes from, but I believe it would be immensely helpful if this contradiction was highlighted early on.

comments.issue: Three terms with opposite meanings describe the probability of successful invasions.
comments.request: Use a single term throughout.
comments.quote: This issue is made more severe by the use of three different terms to describe the probability of successful invasions (invasion probability and invasion resistance, also invasibility)

comments.issue: 'Priority effect' is used in an unorthodox sense.
comments.request: Use a different description or explain the usage.
comments.quote: I am not convinced that this is the sense in which most ecologists tend to use that term

comments.issue: 'Alternative stable states' at l251 is unclear and off-topic.
comments.request: Remove or clarify the term.
comments.quote: Similarly, I find the use of “alternative stable states” (l251) to be unclear since that is not really the subject of this paper.

comments.issue: Comparison baseline for 'lower probability' is unclear.
comments.request: Specify the comparison.
comments.quote: L110: “The lower probability” – compared to what?

comments.issue: Communities may differ in interaction strength despite matched averages.
comments.request: Clarify how interaction strength was controlled.
comments.quote: is it clear that different synthetic communities can be characterized by the same average interaction strength?

comments.issue: Wording at L227.
comments.request: Change 'on' to 'with'.
comments.quote: L227: correlation on -> with

comments.issue: 1:1 correspondence expectation is not explained when introduced.
comments.request: Explain it earlier.
comments.quote: Why should we expect a 1:1 correspondence between survival fraction and invasion probability? This only becomes clear in Fig 4b

comments.issue: Ergodicity is insufficiently explained.
comments.request: Explain ergodicity.
comments.quote: L280: ergodicity likely needs a bit more explanation to be clear

comments.issue: Invasion effect definition is unclear.

comments.quote: L285: definition of invasion effect is slightly unclear. Is this the same definition as in L296?

comments.request: Reconcile the claim with the figure.

comments.issue: Fig. 4a colours are hard to parse.
comments.request: Improve colour distinguishability.
comments.quote: Fig 4a: it is very hard to parse the different colors

reviews.assessment: Interesting questions and appropriate model choice, but experimental decisions, gLV justification and missing statistical tests are substantial concerns.
strengths: appropriate choice to connect experiments with minimal models

comments.issue: Modelling choices (gLV without explicit resources) need more justification.
comments.request: Justify the modelling choices.
comments.quote: At a minimum the authors should provide additional justification for their modelling choices and why they are appropriate for their mode.

comments.issue: Mapping from nutrient/pH manipulation to interaction strength is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain how resource manipulation maps to interaction strength.
comments.quote: it would be difficult for the reader to understand how the manipulation of resource concentration can be modeled as an increase in the strength of competitive interactions in a phenomenological gLV

comments.issue: pH dynamics within a transfer cycle may invalidate the phenomenological gLV.

comments.quote: Since the change in pH within a transfer cycle is on the same timescale of the growth rate, I do not see how a phenomenological gLV can serve as an appropriate model.

comments.issue: 'Fluctuations' (chaotic versus stochastic) are not clearly distinguished.

comments.quote: it would aid the typical reader if the authors clarified what form of fluctuations they are focused on in the Introduction

comments.issue: Necessity of continued migration is not explained.

comments.issue: No comparison with experiments lacking daily migration.

comments.quote: did the authors perform any experiments without daily migration from the regional pool? Contrasting the results of this study with that type of experiment would strengthen their claims

comments.issue: Whether the imposed migration rate induces chaos is not shown.
comments.request: Report this check.
comments.quote: Is the experimentally-imposed migration rate sufficient to induce chaotic dynamics in the context of their gLV model?

comments.issue: Code and raw data are not publicly available.

comments.quote: I would also encourage the authors to make both their code and raw data available on public repositories to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

comments.issue: Extinction threshold value is unjustified.

comments.issue: Mapping of environmental variables onto competition coefficients is not described.

comments.issue: How alternative stable states were determined is unclear.

comments.issue: Biomass decrease in Fig. 1d may reflect experimental details rather than intrinsic dynamics.

comments.issue: Statistical test for Fig. 1g is not reported.

comments.quote: Fig. 1g; lines 380-382: What statistical test was performed here?

comments.issue: Fig. 2f dashed and solid grey lines are unexplained.

comments.issue: Fig. 4c colorbar lacks an axis label.

comments.issue: 'Effect on resident community' in Fig. 4d is vague and its estimation unclear.

comments.issue: Fold-change timepoints and their robustness are unclear.

comments.issue: Serial dilution is not explicitly encoded in the simulations.

comments.issue: Simulation time units are not related to experimental timescales.

comments.issue: CV definition and evidence for bimodal classification are unclear.

comments.issue: Biomass appears on both sides of the Fig. S12c,d correlation.

comments.issue: Alternative analysis of biomass versus relative-abundance CVs is suggested.

comments.issue: Phylogenetic structure of the results is untested.
comments.request: Test for phylogenetic structure.
comments.quote: Does the placement of a species on the phylogeny relative to the phylogenetic composition of a given community determine species invariability?

comments.issue: Timepoints used for Fig. S12 SD are inconsistent with Fig. 1d.

comments.quote: this detail is confusing since the timeseries represented in Fig. 1d ends at day six

comments.issue: Fig. S13 claims are ambiguous and lack statistical tests.

comments.quote: if the claims are about the increase in correlation in one treatment vs. another, then additional statistical analyses are necessary

comments.issue: No test supports claims of composition change in Figs. S15, S16.

comments.issue: Tests for invader-specific composition changes are missing in Figs. S17, S18.

comments.issue: Relationship between invader abundance and resident change is untested.

comments.issue: Correlation coefficients are missing alongside p-values in Figs. S19-S21.
comments.request: Report coefficients and use constrained permutations.
comments.quote: I think the correlation coefficient should be provided along with the non-significant P-value

comments.issue: Passive and active voice are mixed throughout.

comments.issue: Suggested rewording at line 76.

comments.issue: Question wording at lines 85-86 could be more apt.
comments.request: Rephrase the question.
comments.quote: Given the experiment performed, would be more apt to say that the question is whether the dynamics are stationary with respect to deterministic fluctuations?

comments.issue: 'Niches and resources' may be redundant at line 235.
comments.request: Clarify or remove the redundancy.
comments.quote: Is “niches and resources” redundant here? My understanding that the niche is resource niche in the context of this study.

comments.issue: DADA2 parameters and pipeline are not available.
comments.request: Document the parameters and share the pipeline.
comments.quote: Please summarize the DADA2 parameters used in your script and make your DADA2 pipeline available in a public code repository.

comments.issue: raxml code is not available.
comments.request: Share the raxml code.
comments.quote: Please make your raxml code available in a public repository.

comments.issue: Steady-state definition sentence is confusing.
comments.request: Clarify the sentence.
comments.quote: This sentence reads as if steady state is defined as the state where community properties change with time.

comments.issue: Time-window analogy to 24 hours is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the mapping between simulation and experiment.
comments.quote: How is a window of time of 100 units analogous to a timescale of 24 hours in the experiment?

comments.issue: Time-window sensitivity results are not shown.
comments.request: Plot the sensitivity results.
comments.quote: Can you plot the results from varying the choice of time window?

comments.issue: Fig. S1 colour scale is not taxonomy-based.
comments.request: Use shades by phylum.
comments.quote: Would an alternative color scale help the reader? It does not appear that colors are assigned based on taxonomy.

comments.issue: Extinction threshold is not plotted in Figs. S8-S11.
comments.request: Add a dashed threshold line.
comments.quote: Figs. S8-S11: Can you plot the extinction threshold as a dashed/dotted horizontal line?

comments.issue: The 0.05 cutoff is not shown in Fig. S12.
comments.request: Add reference lines to the subplots.
comments.quote: Consider plotting the cutoff of 0.05 as a horizontal dashed line for reference in subplots a and b

comments.issue: Priority effect quantification and y-axis are unclear in Fig. S14.
comments.request: Explain the quantification.
comments.quote: Fig. S14: How were priority effects quantified? What does the y-axis of the priority effect plot represent?

comments.issue: 7 line-level copy edits (grammar and plurals at Lines 192, 304-305, 378-379, 379-380, 389, 437, Supplement 174).
comments.quote: Lines 378-379: Grammar.

reviews.assessment: Valuable and novel contribution integrating model and experiment, but limitations of interaction tuning and invasion-impact measures need explicit discussion.

comments.issue: Only competitive interactions are considered; positive interactions could reverse the result.
comments.request: Run the model with positive interactions included.
comments.quote: Increasing interaction strength in this case could increase community invasibility, which is a possibility not considered by this study.

comments.issue: Fold change in biomass cannot separate resident loss from invader growth.
comments.request: Make this limitation explicit.
comments.quote: It is not possible to distinguish between the change in biomass of the resident community, and the increase in biomass of the successful invader.

comments.issue: Effect size for the composition difference is not reported.
comments.request: Report effect sizes with confidence intervals.
comments.quote: it is important that the authors provide information about the effect size

comments.issue: Functional redundancy could mean no functional change despite composition change.
comments.request: Discuss these limitations explicitly.
comments.quote: though species composition may have changed, the invader could be functionally redundant with the species that were excluded, resulting in no change to community functioning

comments.issue: Key terms (community diversity, rich dynamics, richness) are undefined.
comments.request: Define key terms explicitly.
comments.quote: I strongly recommend including explicit definitions of key terms, which would improve clarity of the manuscript.

comments.issue: Results are not linked to niche theory and resource competition concepts.
comments.request: Embed findings in existing invasion ecology concepts.
comments.quote: The findings of this study could be embedded more explicitly into existing concepts in invasion ecology

comments.issue: Interface between interaction strength, pool size and dynamical regime is unclear.
comments.request: Explain how these features combine.
comments.quote: More explanation about how these features interface is necessary for clarity of the manuscript, since they are not independent.

comments.issue: Dispersion measure is not defined in the text.
comments.request: State the dispersion measure.
comments.quote: parameter estimates are given as mean +/- X, where X is a measure of dispersion, but which measure it is is not defined

comments.issue: Invader selection is not described.
comments.request: State how invaders were chosen.
comments.quote: State how invaders were chosen (line 146) - I assume they were chosen at random?

comments.issue: Invader introduction abundance is not stated.
comments.request: State the relative abundance.
comments.quote: explicitly state at what relative abundance the invader is introduced relative to the community

comments.issue: Invader abundance may influence invasion effect beyond interaction strength.
comments.request: Test this pattern across simulations and experiments.
comments.quote: it would suggest that there is another factor that influences invasion effect aside from interaction strength

comments.issue: Nutrient conditions are not linked to interaction-strength labels.
comments.request: Add (strong/weak interaction) labels throughout.
comments.quote: I would include (strong interaction) or (weak interaction) every time high/low nutrient conditions are mentioned for clarity.

comments.issue: Claim about resident community determining invasion outcome is unsupported.
comments.request: Remove the statement.
comments.quote: Invader properties have not been sufficiently explored in this manuscript to claim they don't play an important role in determining invasion outcome.

title: Collective dynamical regimes predict invasion success and impacts in microbial communities

study.system: boreal forest timber; simulation framework applied to forest plot data

editor_summary: Editor overrules Reviewer 1 on novelty and impact but asks the authors to respond and address technical concerns about wind throw; all reviewers want more discussion of generalizability, ideally a further general application.

reviews.assessment: Thinks the framework is not innovative or robust, the empirical design cannot capture transient dynamics, and the paper may not interest a broad audience.
strengths: useful as a reference paper for such applications

comments.issue: Storyline and main message are hard to follow; no outstanding features identified.
comments.request: Improve the clarity of the main message and storyline.
comments.quote: I needed to read the text really many times to comprehend the main messages and the storyline.

comments.issue: Claimed research gap (limited disturbance-ES studies) is wrong; the field has accelerated.
comments.request: Place the work in the context of existing advances.
comments.quote: The authors repeatedly justified the relevance and timeliness of this work by lacking research on the effects of disturbances on ecosystem services, which I disagree with.

comments.issue: Framework is a standard protocol rather than an innovation.
comments.request: Justify the novelty of the framework.
comments.quote: I had difficulty to see the overall framework innovative. Assessing disturbance impacts on ecosystems, evaluating changes in (forest) ecosystem structure, and the subsequent impacts on ecosystem services and their economic value sounds like a standard protocol.

comments.issue: Doubtful that the design can attract a broad interdisciplinary audience.
comments.quote: I have doubts if such a design can attract a broad interdisciplinary audience

comments.issue: Empirical, non-mechanistic framework cannot capture transient dynamics, tipping points or future changes.
comments.request: Use process-based approaches or justify the empirical design.
comments.quote: I do not consider such an approach suitable for assessing transient ecological and social phenomena

comments.issue: Two stylized disturbance scenarios and two price assumptions are too narrow; inferences are not robust.
comments.request: Evaluate a broader range of assumptions probabilistically.
comments.quote: I cannot consider such inferences robust as this design captures only a fraction of possible variability

comments.issue: Framework is not different from existing carbon-accounting frameworks; not new.
comments.request: Clarify what distinguishes it from existing frameworks.
comments.quote: however, I did not find it different from, for example, frameworks used for carbon accounting based on dynamics model simulations

comments.issue: Research question 1 is poorly formulated and contradicted by the next sentence.
comments.request: Reformulate research question 1.
comments.quote: I do not consider research question 1. “Do response in ecological communities predict changes in ES?” well formulated

comments.issue: Wind/timber case is well-studied; the tight impact-production link is not optimal to show uncertainties.
comments.request: Justify or replace the demonstration case.
comments.quote: I consider this case to be particularly well-studied given its commercial relevance and abundant studies

comments.issue: Claim that wind disturbance increases under climate change lacks evidence in the cited paper.
comments.request: Provide quantitative evidence or temper the claim.
comments.quote: I quickly reviewed the cited paper Frelich and Reich 2010, but I did not find there any quantitative evidence for this statement

comments.issue: Choice of windstorms over climatically sensitive disturbances is not justified; criteria apply to any stand-replacing disturbance.
comments.request: Justify the choice of windstorms.
comments.quote: I found it unclear why the authors decided to use windstorms and not climatically highly sensitive insect outbreaks or wildfires

comments.issue: Unclear how the climate-amplified disturbance distribution was created.
comments.request: Explain the construction of the amplified disturbance regime.
comments.quote: I did not comprehend how the authors created disturbance distribution amplified by climate change

comments.issue: Wind damage is modelled from tree traits only, omitting stand and landscape drivers.
comments.request: Include stand and landscape properties or justify the omission.
comments.quote: I have concerns about simulating wind damage based on tree traits while omitting the effect of stand (canopy complexity, presence of wind-exposed edges, etc.) and landscape properties.

comments.issue: No stand is fully disturbed, which is unexpected for stand-replacing windstorms.
comments.request: Explain why no stands were completely disturbed.
comments.quote: I found it surprising that no forest stand was completely disturbed (Fig. 3, no data point dropped to 0)

comments.issue: Bias conclusion is not supported: price assumptions produce variability, not a one-directional shift.
comments.request: Support or soften the bias conclusion.
comments.quote: the presented analysis does not support the conclusion of “bias”, i.e., a one-directional shift.

comments.issue: Treating tight linear structure-ES relationships as 'desired' and low correlations as problematic is unjustified.
comments.request: Reconsider the interpretation of correlation values.
comments.quote: I did not understand why a tight linear relationship between forest community / biomass resistance and the resistance of ES provision is considered ‘desired’

comments.issue: Predictors (community, biomass) were chosen arbitrarily; other variables may be more relevant.
comments.request: Justify the predictors or test alternatives.
comments.quote: Moreover, the authors arbitrarily selected forest community and biomass as predictors, but other variables (tree identity, tree dimensions, variability of sizes, or even wood assortment structure in a stand) can be more relevant predictors of different ES.

comments.issue: Rationale and message of the resistance-structure section are unclear.
comments.quote: I had difficulty understanding the rationale and message of this section.

comments.issue: Lines 95-96 repeat previous text and do not follow logically.
comments.request: Remove or rewrite the repeated sentence.
comments.quote: The sentence in lines 95-96 repeats the previous text and does not logically follow the previous sentence

comments.issue: Research questions are scattered and the two questions in L98-99 are hard to distinguish.
comments.request: Consolidate and clarify the research questions.
comments.quote: Formally, it would be better to keep them in one place. I had difficulty to understand the difference between the two questions in L 98-99.

comments.issue: Disturbance impacts should be labelled as model predictions, not observations, in captions and text.
comments.request: Label predicted values explicitly as model-based.
comments.quote: The study should indicate explicitly in figure captions and across the text that the disturbance impact is predicted by a model and not observed

comments.issue: Figs 2 and 3 should be combined into one two-panel figure.
comments.request: Combine Figs 2 and 3.
comments.quote: Fig. 2 and 3 would be better to present as a single figure with two panels.

comments.issue: L124-130 is confusing and unnecessary; the L146 label is unclear.
comments.quote: L124-130 I found this part confusing and not really necessary L 146 timber production?

reviews.assessment: Very positive about the topic and novel framework; concerns about generalizability, scale and values are considered addressable.
strengths: practical implications for policymakers and land managers

comments.issue: Framework demonstrated only for a relatively simple boreal forest system; more complex applications untested.
comments.request: Add an application to a more complex system such as coral reefs.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to illustrated how a simplified approach could be applied to a more complex system, such as coral reefs

comments.issue: Example comes from a data-rich region; applicability to data-poor regions is unclear.
comments.request: Discuss applicability in data-poor regions.
comments.quote: Further, the example given is in a data rich region. How might this work in a data poor region?

comments.issue: Spatial scale of the ecological communities and disturbances is not clear.
comments.request: Discuss spatial scale explicitly.
comments.quote: there is much reference to ecological communities, but the spatial scale is often not clear

comments.issue: The 'value' of ecosystem services is not defined as monetary or non-monetary for the general framework.
comments.request: Clarify the value concept and address non-monetary values.
comments.quote: However, for the more general parts of the paper, it is not clear if this is referring to monetary or non-monetary values.

comments.issue: Fig. S1 is helpful but placed in the supplement.
comments.request: Move Fig. S1 to the main text if possible.
comments.quote: Fig s1 is very helpful in understanding the case study and should be included in the main text if possible.

comments.issue: Fig. S3 would better illustrate results if combined with Fig. 3.
comments.request: Combine Fig. S3 with Fig. 3 as a multipanel figure.
comments.quote: Fig s3 could be combined with F3 as a multipaneled figure and would help illustrate results.

comments.issue: Figure S4 is conceptual and does not show the correlations it is cited for.
comments.request: Show the correlations or correct the figure reference.
comments.quote: Figure S4 seems to be a conceptual figure and does not show results or correlations.

comments.issue: The link between Fig. 3 and the wedge argument is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify how Fig. 3 supports this point.
comments.quote: It is not clear how fig 3 relates to this point.

reviews.assessment: Strongly supportive: the topic is important and the main conclusions justified; offers detailed suggestions on novelty, terminology and economic framing.
strengths: addresses an under-researched and important topic

comments.issue: Novelty relative to existing forest economics studies on risk and uncertainty is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the novelty better, perhaps with a broader uncertainty example.
comments.quote: It might thus be helpful to explain the novelty of the study better

comments.issue: Ecosystem services and nature's contributions to people are used interchangeably despite different definitions.
comments.request: Use one term consistently.
comments.quote: Instead of using both terms interchangeably, one could also consider to decide consistently using only one of the terms.

comments.issue: Risk versus uncertainty terminology is used inconsistently given the probabilistic framework.
comments.request: Clarify whether the paper addresses risks or uncertainties.
comments.quote: the caption to the Figure 1 and also the manuscript text does often refer to the term “uncertainty”

comments.issue: Management and decision-making under deep uncertainty are not integrated into the framework.
comments.request: Discuss management integration and deep uncertainty.
comments.quote: One could thus wonder how the management is displayed/integrated in the assessment framework.

comments.issue: It is not clear what is new relative to existing ecological-economic studies.
comments.request: Articulate the new contribution.
comments.quote: Maybe it would be possible for the authors to show better what is the new point with their finding.

comments.issue: The claim that ES assessments ignore disturbances holds mainly for non-market services.
comments.request: Qualify the claim for market-based services.
comments.quote: the ignorance of disturbances mainly holds for non-market-based, not to the same extend to market-based ecosystem service values

comments.issue: Resistance index averages two means, so it does not capture the variability the paper criticises.
comments.request: Use an index that captures variability or uncertainty.
comments.quote: this index consists of two measure both reflecting average conditions, while the critique of ecological studies, which commonly work with average conditions, was one of the justifications of the study

comments.issue: Existing forest economics studies that consider disturbances are not cited.
comments.request: Cite these studies and show how this paper goes beyond them.
comments.quote: there are still some (forest) economics studies which explicitly consider disturbances, including 9, 10, 11, 12, 7, or13

comments.issue: Assumption that timber prices rise after disturbance contradicts observed post-disturbance price declines.
comments.request: Reconsider the price and salvage assumption.
comments.quote: Is the assumption that downed trees cannot be harvested perhaps too strict?

comments.issue: Disturbance regimes may not be empirically justified.
comments.request: Justify the disturbance regimes with empirical data.
comments.quote: Is it possible to justify the disturbance regimes empirically?

comments.issue: The modest correlation between community similarity and service resistance is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the modest correlation.
comments.quote: Is it possible to better explain why there is only a modest correlation between ecological community similarity and the measure of service resistance?

comments.issue: Existing risk-return trade-off studies for forest ecosystem services are not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention these risk-return trade-off studies.
comments.quote: Risk-return trade-offs have already been shown, even for multiple forest ecosystem services, for example by7. This could be mentioned

comments.issue: Utility function and utility discount rate are not reported, though they may drive results.
comments.request: Report and discuss the utility function and discount rate.
comments.quote: The reviewer could not find any information on the type of the utility function used and also not on the utility discount rate.

title: Quantifying disturbance effects on ecosystem services in a changing climate

study.system: boreal forests; kNDVI temporal autocorrelation and forest cover trends

editor_summary: Editor rejects: concerns about the advance over Forzieri et al. (2022), weakly articulated hypotheses, and technical issues including additional resilience indicators and greenness measures.

reviews.assessment: Timely topic but insufficient novelty over Forzieri et al., unclear methods and hypotheses, and unsupported mechanism and management claims.
strengths: focus on linking forest resilience to forest cover change
good context in the resilience literature

comments.issue: The study reproduces Forzieri et al. 2022 with the same methods and datasets, giving limited advance.
comments.request: Demonstrate a clear advance beyond Forzieri et al. 2022.
comments.quote: In essence, Liu et al. reproduce results from (Forzieri et al., 2022), in that they use the same method and datasets in quantifying resilience and in linking resilience to forest cover.

comments.issue: Research questions and objectives are not clearly introduced; questions appear only in the results.
comments.request: State research questions and objectives clearly.
comments.quote: The work suffers from a lack of clearly introduced and phrased research questions and objectives.

comments.issue: Methods lack clarity: TAC equations, forest cover trends, data inclusion and disturbance handling are unexplained.
comments.request: Explain TAC calculation, trends, data inclusion and disturbance handling.
comments.quote: The methods do not allow readers unfamiliar with resilience research to comprehend the approach and calculations.

comments.issue: Splitting results into gain and loss groups adds little over a continuous forest cover gradient.
comments.request: Use the continuous forest cover change gradient.
comments.quote: I am confused as to why the authors separated the results on resilience trends and the sensitivity to forest cover into two major groups of forest gain and loss.

comments.issue: Results are mostly aggregated; pixel-based relationships, regression output and figure explanations are missing.
comments.request: Show pixel-based relationships and explain supplementary figures.
comments.quote: I missed a simple figure that shows the tree cover change on the x-axis and resilience on the y-axis with all points presented in a density map or at least as fitted line.

comments.issue: The distinction between local and regional sensitivity analyses is unclear.
comments.request: Explain local versus regional sensitivity.
comments.quote: the difference between local and regional sensitivity is neither clearly explained nor is the rationale for splitting analyses in such a way clear

comments.issue: Greenness indices mix forest and ground vegetation signals, so resilience increases may not be forest resilience.
comments.request: Discuss greenness-index limitations and mixed signals.
comments.quote: If resilience increases, it remains unclear whether it may come from increased resilience of forests, shrubs or ground vegetation.

comments.issue: The climate-mortality-boreal shift links are asserted too broadly without explanation.
comments.request: Explain the climate-mortality-shift links.
comments.quote: The link between climate change, forest mortality and ‘boreal forest shifts’ is not explained sufficiently despite a long list of recently published results on this topic in support of these linkages

comments.issue: Treating forest cover as a universal resilience determinant conflicts with evidence of tropical tipping points.
comments.request: Qualify the forest cover-resilience generalization.
comments.quote: If forest cover is a universal determinant of resilience, it would be difficult to explain the increasing evidence of tropical forests approaching a tipping point due to resilience loss despite these forest being the densest forests in the world.

comments.issue: Mechanistic connections are claimed without being tested.
comments.request: Label untested links as interpretations.
comments.quote: The authors make several claims about the connection between their results and underlying mechanisms without having tested these connections in their analyses.

comments.issue: Forest-management recommendations are not conclusively supported by the management-type comparison.
comments.request: Temper forest-management recommendations.
comments.quote: their relatively simple comparison of resilience trends between management types is insufficient to make these claims on fundamental approaches in boreal forest management as a whole

reviews.assessment: Builds closely on Forzieri et al.; land cover dataset caveats, missing uncertainty and unclear methods undermine confidence in the claims.
strengths: timely question about forest cover effects on resilience

comments.issue: MODIS land cover data has trend-analysis caveats; findings should be evaluated with the same ESA dataset as Forzieri et al.
comments.request: Repeat analyses with ESA CCI land cover and acknowledge MODIS limitations.
comments.quote: My main comment for the authors is that they evaluate their findings using the same Land Cover dataset used by Forzieri et al so that their findings can be evaluated fully and with more confidence.

comments.issue: Uncertainties in results and analyses are not explicit.
comments.request: Report uncertainties explicitly.
comments.quote: I also encourage the authors to be more explicit about uncertainties in their results and analysis.

comments.issue: Sensitivities are given per 100% forest change while observed ΔFC ranges are far smaller; Table 1 has the same issue.
comments.request: Rescale to 1% ΔFC or caveat the range.
comments.quote: I think it would either be better to present the results as ΔTAC/1% ΔFC or at least explicitly mention the range of ΔFC as a caveat.

comments.issue: 'Resilience' is used where 'change in resilience' is meant; resilience is an intrinsic property.
comments.request: Distinguish resilience from change in resilience.
comments.quote: I think this should be ‘Change in resilience’? Since technically resilience should be an intrinsic property that doesn’t depend on external drivers

comments.issue: The claim that forest density effects were overlooked is wrong; Forzieri et al. found it a top driver.
comments.request: Acknowledge Forzieri et al.'s forest density results.
comments.quote: So, I think it is not fully correct to say that this has not ever been evaluated and I think this should be better acknowledged.

comments.issue: The forest cover-resilience relationship at lines 78-79 is not novel and should cite Forzieri et al.
comments.request: Cite and acknowledge Forzieri et al. here.
comments.quote: This is of course very interesting, but not necessarily novel. Forzieri et al. show this relationship quite clearly in their Extended Data Figure 2c.

comments.issue: Figure 1 caption implies the map evaluates causes of TAC change, which it does not.
comments.request: Rephrase the Figure 1 caption.
comments.quote: I don’t think the second half of this sentence is fully accurate. The figure only shows change in TAC, but does not evaluate causes (e.g., change in FC).

comments.issue: The locations of the East Siberian Taiga and Great Bear Rainforest are not indicated in figures.
comments.request: Add location boxes to the figure.
comments.quote: It would be very helpful for the reader to have some boxes in the figure to know where they should be looking for the “East Siberian Taiga” and “Great Bear Rainforest”.

comments.issue: Sub-plot ordering is inconsistent between Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 1.
comments.request: Make sub-plot ordering consistent.
comments.quote: Not a big deal, but the ordering of sub-plots is not consistent.

comments.issue: Potential reasons for the 27% anomalous regions are not explored.
comments.request: Explore reasons for the anomalous regions.
comments.quote: This is interesting, but the potential reasons are not fully explored.

comments.issue: How seasonality and trends were removed is not explained, though it strongly affects TAC trends.
comments.request: Explain the deseasoning and detrending methods.
comments.quote: The methods by which seasonality and trends were removed is not explained.

comments.issue: The relation between Equations 8 and 9 is unclear and ΔTACres is undefined.
comments.request: Define ΔTACres and clarify the equations.
comments.quote: The relationship between Equation 8 and 9 was not very clearly described. For example, ΔTACres is not defined here.

comments.issue: Supplementary Figure 5 is unclear: one value per forest cover value and misaligned zero lines.
comments.request: Clarify Supp. Fig. 5 and align axes.
comments.quote: This figure is not very clear to me, or at least how it was created. Why is there only one value of ΔFC and ΔTAC for each value of FC.

comments.issue: The difference between ΔTAC and ΔTACres in Supplementary Figure 6 is unclear and the pie chart is unhelpful.
comments.request: Explain Supp. Fig. 6 and reconsider its presentation.
comments.quote: At least for me, the differences between ΔTAC and ΔTACres in the figure is still not very clearly explained here.

comments.issue: Statistical significance of the deciduous forest results is not reported.
comments.request: Report significance.
comments.quote: Are these results statistically significant?

comments.issue: kNDVI still inherits NDVI saturation and performs poorly in needle-leaf forests; claims need caution.
comments.request: Add caution about kNDVI limitations.
comments.quote: At its core NDVI still has saturation issues, so these transformations can maybe at best mitigate this issue slightly. Maybe some more caution or at least careful phrasing is warranted?

comments.issue: Code availability is not stated.
comments.request: State code availability.
comments.quote: No mention is made about whether code is going to be made available or not.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and timely concept, but resilience indicators, deseasoning, time windows, forest classification and figures need clarification.
strengths: nice analysis of the role of forest cover change

comments.issue: TAC alone is an incomplete resilience measure; variance and lag-1 autocorrelation should both be used.
comments.request: Add variance and compare resilience indicators.
comments.quote: The authors rely solely on the TAC to quantify resilience – this is however not a complete picture of resilience changes.

comments.issue: Deseasoning and detrending methods are not described although they strongly affect resilience estimates.
comments.request: Describe and justify the deseasoning method.
