comments.request: Improve size scaling and explain symbol types.
comments.quote: The relative size of the circles is too similar. Why are some points circumferences and others circles?

comments.issue: Figure 1c plot, its axes and the grey square are incomprehensible.
comments.request: Explain the axes and grey square in Figure 1c.
comments.quote: I don’t understand this plot. What is the meaning of the “axes”? What is the “grey square”?

comments.issue: Green reference dots for primary vegetation in natural landscapes are unnecessary in Figure 2, and y-axis labels are cut off.
comments.request: Remove reference dots and fix the axis labels.
comments.quote: I see no need to show the green dots for “Primary vegetation in natural landscapes.”

comments.issue: Dashed red lines in supplementary figures S5-S12 are unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the dashed red lines.
comments.quote: What is the meaning of the dashed red lines in figures S5-S12?

comments.issue: Duplicate supplementary figure numbers (two S5, two S9, two S14).
comments.request: Fix the duplicate figure numbers.
comments.quote: ATTENTION: Some of the figures have the same “number” (two figures S5, two figures S9, and two S14).

reviews.assessment: Important global question and solid biodiversity analysis, but the normative scenario assumptions are unexplained and likely drive the results.
strengths: addresses an important global research question
well written with appropriate data and methods
interesting new findings on intensification effects

comments.issue: The uniform +1% production target per pixel is arbitrary and its choice is not justified.
comments.request: Justify the 1% target or test alternative targets.
comments.quote: both scenarios aim at reaching the same production increase target of +1%. This seems arbitrary to me, and it is not explained why 1% is chosen.

comments.issue: Normative scenario assumptions may largely determine the results and conclusions.
comments.request: Test robustness of the results to changed scenario assumptions.
comments.quote: the assumptions underlying the two land use scenarios are very normative and I am afraid that the assumptions also largely determine the results

comments.issue: No theory explains what drives agricultural expansion or intensification and where it occurs.
comments.request: Provide a theoretical basis for the scenario drivers and locations.
comments.quote: there is no theory behind, what is driving agricultural expansion/intensification and where this is gonna happen

comments.issue: Per-pixel uniform yield increases are less meaningful than a global production target.
comments.request: Consider a global production increase target.
comments.quote: Why e.g. not implementing a global production increase target? Yields are increased uniformly on each pixel by 1%

comments.issue: Yield increases should realistically be stronger where yield gaps are large.
comments.request: Model stronger increases in high-yield-gap regions.
comments.quote: It would also be more realistic to assume that yield increases are stronger in regions with high yield gap

comments.issue: The intensification scenario lacks land sparing (freed land restoration), so conclusions about the sparing/sharing debate are biased.
comments.request: Implement true land sparing or soften the debate conclusions.
comments.quote: linking your approach to the land sparing/land sharing debate is difficult, and therefore, in my opinion, your conclusion is biased in that regard

comments.issue: Methods are hard to follow due to many datasets; an overview is missing.
comments.request: Add a schematic overview figure of data and models.
comments.quote: It is not easy to follow the methodology at first reading due to the many different data sets. I had to read several sections twice. An overview is missing

comments.issue: Scenarios target approximately the year 2000 rather than future projections incorporating climate change.
comments.request: Consider future projections including climate change.
comments.quote: The time period the authors target their scenario is approximately the year 2000 and not a future projection, considering climate change

comments.issue: Observation-based potential yields (Mueller) ignore spatial heterogeneity and future climate impacts.
comments.request: Use crop-model simulated potential yields instead.
comments.quote: Instead of using potential yield estimates by Mueller, that are based on observed yields within AEZs, you could use potential yields, simulated by crop models

comments.issue: The discussion omits that other ecosystem services such as carbon storage and water infiltration must also be considered.
comments.request: Add a sentence on other ecosystem services.
comments.quote: I would additionally expect one sentence saying that also other ecosystem services rather than biodiversity must be considered in an integrative approach

comments.issue: No maximum expansion potential constrains expansion in land-scarce bread basket regions.
comments.request: Consider limits to expansion in land-scarce regions.
comments.quote: I am wondering if you consider any kind of maximum expansion potential, which limits agricultural expansion mainly in bread basket regions

comments.issue: Title should say 'cropland' rather than 'farmland', which includes pasture and rangeland.
comments.request: Replace 'farmland' with 'cropland' in the title.
comments.quote: I suggest to use the term “cropland” instead of “farmland” in the title, because farmland could include pasture areas or rangeland

comments.issue: Abstract gives a quantitative intensification result but only qualitative language for land conversion.
comments.request: Give quantitative results for both aspects in the abstract.
comments.quote: I suggest to give quantitative results for both aspects for comparison, which would improve the significance and informative value of the abstract

comments.issue: Figure titles are used instead of subtitles, which is confusing.
comments.request: Use figure subtitles.
comments.quote: Figure titles are used instead of figure subtitles, which confused me.

comments.issue: Maps are poorly illustrated without a global frame.
comments.request: Use a global frame cut at -60°S.
comments.quote: Maps are not well illustrated. I’d suggest to use a global frame and cut at -60° South

comments.issue: 3 line-level copy edits (Ln 25, 51, 452).
comments.quote: Ln 25: “yield increases also lead to” instead of “yield also lead to

comments.issue: Prior work (Zabel et al. 2019) already addressed this, undermining the stated gap.
comments.request: Cite and position the study relative to this prior work.
comments.quote: Which has already been done by some other studies, e.g. Zabel et al. (2019).

comments.issue: Sustainable intensification is not considered and would substantially change the comparisons and conclusions.
comments.request: Discuss sustainable intensification and its implications.
comments.quote: Nevertheless, sustainable intensification is not considered in your approach, which I assume, would impact on the comparison between expansion and intensification quite drastically

comments.issue: It is unclear what kind of intensification the statistical approach implies in different regions.
comments.request: Explain what the modelled intensification means in different regions.
comments.quote: I would be interested in an explanation, what kind of intensification this data driven statistical approach implies in different regions and how this could impact on biodiversity?

comments.issue: Rainfed rice may also not be used by subsistence farmers, questioning the classification.
comments.request: Check and justify the subsistence/rainfed classification.
comments.quote: At least for rice, I assume that rainfed systems are also not used by subsistence farmers, but honestly I don’t know.

comments.issue: Cash crops may be managed more intensively than assumed, an important unaddressed limitation.
comments.request: Address this limitation.
comments.quote: This is an important limitation of this study, because usually cash crops might be used at much higher intensity level than other crops.

comments.issue: 'Cropping system' may be the wrong term; 'across different crops' may be more accurate.
comments.request: Use a more accurate term.
comments.quote: I was wondering if ‘cropping system’ is the right term here? Maybe, ‘across different crops’ might be more accurate?

comments.issue: Key scenario assumptions (where and by how much yield gaps close) appear too late in the text.
comments.request: Mention the assumptions earlier, at the end of the introduction.
comments.quote: This is an important assumption for understanding the whole study and I have been missing this information while reading the chapters before.

comments.issue: Assuming homogeneous yields within a pixel overestimates yields on expanded land.
comments.request: Address and discuss yield assumptions for expansion.
comments.quote: If you increase the area by 1%, you assume homogeneous yields within a pixel, which may not be correct. I guess this overestimates yields

comments.issue: 'Closing yield gaps' and 'increasing yields uniformly by 1%' are conflated in the text.
comments.request: Clarify which operation the scenarios actually apply.
comments.quote: However, increasing yields uniformly by 1% is s.th. else than closing yield gaps by 1%.

comments.issue: Statistical sensitivity to tiny 1% yield changes in high-gap regions is doubtful.
comments.request: Assess whether the approach can detect such small changes.
comments.quote: the question if the statistical approach is sensitive enough to capture the impacts on biodiversity of such small absolute yield changes?

comments.issue: Unclear whether the section refers to conversion of all primary vegetation or the +1% scenario.
comments.request: Clarify which scenario the results describe.
comments.quote: Does this refer to a land conversion of all primary vegetation or to the +1% production increase scenario?

comments.issue: Figure S23 lacks a source.
comments.request: Provide the source.
comments.quote: Appendix Figure S23. Source missing.

reviews.assessment: Comprehensive global dataset, but novelty is uncertain and the yield-based intensification framing and result interpretation need caution.
strengths: probably the most comprehensive global biodiversity study

comments.issue: Novelty is doubtful: land sharing/sparing and conversion impacts have already been studied extensively.
comments.request: Clarify the conceptual advance over existing studies.
comments.quote: Therefore, I have some doubts regarding the novelty of these results.

comments.issue: Many results in Figure 3 are not described or emphasized in the text.
comments.request: Describe and discuss the full range of results.
comments.quote: However, only a limited number of results were emphasized and described in the paper.

comments.issue: Why some crop-metric relationships appear (soy-RCAR) and others do not (wheat-RCAR) is not explained.
comments.request: Explain these differential relationships.
comments.quote: like why are there many relationships (like for soy and RCAR), while none in others (wheat and RCAR)

comments.issue: Yield is prioritized over fertiliser use, though yield alone does not capture intensification impacts on biodiversity.
comments.request: Justify yield as the intensification metric.
comments.quote: I find it difficult to fully endorse the prioritization of yield over factors such as fertiliser consumption, particularly when the focus is solely on biodiversity benefits

comments.issue: RCAR as biotic homogenisation does not characterise species, since range sizes are themselves shaped by human activities.
comments.request: Discuss the limitations of the RCAR metric.
comments.quote: Biotic homogenisation is a measure of community composition, restricted to spatial context. Note, however, that this not characterise the species in the community

comments.issue: The 1% production target is arbitrary; larger targets would be more realistic.
comments.request: Test or justify other production targets such as 5% or 10%.
comments.quote: Why 1% increase in total production was targeted? 5% or 10% increase would be also interesting.

comments.issue: Model assumptions are not fully met, so results need cautious interpretation.
comments.request: Check model assumptions and temper the interpretation.
comments.quote: In addition, the models not fully fit assumptions. Thus, results need some caution when interpreting.

comments.issue: 'Closing the yield gap' is not defined.
comments.request: Define closing the yield gap.
comments.quote: What is closing the yield gap? Define.

comments.issue: Land sharing/sparing terms appear in the introduction but not the abstract, creating a mismatch.
comments.request: Align the abstract with the introduction's framing.
comments.quote: From this point, the introduction is on land sharing/sparing. However, these terms are ignored from the abstract, making a little bit of mismatch between these sections.

comments.issue: The claim that no global yield-biodiversity assessment exists ignores Martin et al. (2019) at the European scale.
comments.request: Cite and position the study relative to Martin et al. (2019).
comments.quote: it is true but, Martin et al (2019, Ecol Letters) published a large study on yield and landscape at the European scale

comments.issue: Rationale for the 30% and 70% shares is not explained.
comments.request: Explain why 30% and 70% were chosen.
comments.quote: why 30 and 70% are the shares?

comments.issue: Supplementary tables start at S4; Tables S1-S3 are missing.
comments.request: Fix the supplementary table numbering.
comments.quote: where are Table S1-2-3? Not elegant to start with Table S4.

comments.issue: Clustered sites mean biodiversity decline attributed to human modification may be a spatial/biogeographic effect.
comments.request: Separate geography from human-influence variables.
comments.quote: a conclusion that biodiversity decline is due to human ecosystem modifications can also be a spatial effect, that is the "treatments" are in different biogeographic regions. How to separate geography and human influence variables?

comments.issue: Unexplained pale blue circles appear in Figure 1.
comments.request: Explain or remove the pale blue circles.
comments.quote: There are also pale blue circles (in Chile and Argentina, Japan, NE America). Is this a typo, or has some meaning?

comments.issue: Figure 1c is incomprehensible.
comments.request: Explain or redesign Figure 1c.
comments.quote: 1/c figure. I cannot understand it

comments.issue: Figure 2 panels a and b overlap in the y-axis legend.
comments.request: Increase the spacing between panels.
comments.quote: Increase the distance between a) and b), otherwise there is overlap in Y axis legend.

comments.issue: Figure 2 lacks significance indicators for values shown with error bars.
comments.request: Add significance information to Figure 2.
comments.quote: On a figure with values and error bars, the reader will look for significances, which are missing from this figure

comments.issue: Figure 3 is overloaded with information and two panels are empty.
comments.request: Simplify the figure and explain the empty panels.
comments.quote: It has an extreme amount of information, really need time to digest it. Interesting to see that two graphs are empty, while others have a lot relationships plotted.

comments.issue: Similar abundance and RCAR trends in maize and soy may signal invasion risk, which is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the potential invasion threat.
comments.quote: abundance and RCAR show similar trends in maize and soy, indicating more individuals in more homogenised communities

comments.issue: The 70% versus 30% values in Figure 3 differ from the earlier text numbers.
comments.request: Explain why the numbers differ.
comments.quote: This was 70% versus 30% above (line 97-98). Why different numbers?

comments.issue: Only the data-richest relationship is shown per panel; other relationships may be missed.
comments.request: Present the remaining relationships somewhere.
comments.quote: are the other relationships presented somewhere? Did not the reader miss some important results?

comments.issue: 'Most often' overstates the result: it holds for only two of the four crops.
comments.request: Temper this statement.
comments.quote: I would not say most often, as from the four crops it is true for two (missing in soy, and contrasting in rice).

comments.issue: Tropical yield increases show both richness benefits and costs, unlike mostly costs in temperate zones.
comments.request: Acknowledge this tropical/temperate nuance.
comments.quote: increase in yield in the tropical areas has both benefits and costs on richness, while mostly costs in the temperate zone

comments.issue: Landscape-context effects were already published (Batáry et al. 2011).
comments.request: Cite and position the study relative to Batáry et al. (2011).
comments.quote: The role of landscape context was multiple times published see e.g. Batáry et al. (2011, Proc R Soc).

comments.issue: Prior work argues multifunctional landscapes combining sharing and sparing are needed (Grass et al. 2021).
comments.request: Discuss this alternative conclusion.
comments.quote: Others concluded that multifunctional landscapes are needed, a combination of sharing and sparing lands (Grass et al 2021, Adv Ecol Res).

comments.issue: Supplementary tables have conversion problems with misplaced '?' characters.
comments.request: Fix the corrupted characters.
comments.quote: there was probably some converting problem, a few letters were misplaced by

comments.issue: The acronym SR is used without definition.
comments.request: Define SR at first use.
comments.quote: Explain what is SR as this acronym was not used before.

comments.issue: RCAR is renamed 'RCAR 55km' without explanation.
comments.request: Use one consistent name.
comments.quote: RCAR 55km is also new name (it was RCAR before).

comments.issue: Table S7 column width breaks 'abundance' across two lines.
comments.request: Adjust the column width.
comments.quote: Table S7, first column, correct column width to have

comments.issue: Figure S23 scale dimension (%) is unclear.
comments.request: State the scale dimension.
comments.quote: Fig S23: what is the dimension of the scale? %?

title: Geography and availability of natural habitat determine whether cropland intensification or expansion is more detrimental to biodiversity

study.system: ecology and evolution journals; survey of 541 journal websites

editor_summary: Editor agrees with reviewers' requests for concrete examples of disabilities for different file formats, implementation of Universal Design principles, and clarification of terms throughout.

reviews.assessment: Needed article on accessible journal practices; clarifications on Universal Design, terms and concrete examples will make it more impactful.

comments.issue: Universal Design principles are not tied to what they mean for a journal.
comments.request: Explain concretely how Universal Design applies to journals.
comments.quote: In the Introduction when discussing Universal Design principles, it would be useful to tie into what that would look like for a journal and provide context for readers.

comments.issue: Assistive technologies and screen-readers are mentioned without definition or examples.
comments.request: Define assistive technologies and screen-readers with examples.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to define this for the audience who may not be familiar with such technology and provide examples.

comments.issue: Figure 1 alt text describes the graph rather than conveying its major take-aways.
comments.request: Add major take-aways to the Figure 1 alt text.
comments.quote: it is essential that the alt text includes the major take-aways that someone would get from the figure rather than just describing the circular bar graph

comments.issue: Criteria for classifying major versus minor publishers are not given.
comments.request: State the criteria used to classify major versus minor publishers.
comments.quote: some terms should be clarified for the readers (major versus minor publishers- what is the criteria used to classify)

comments.issue: Only statistics are given; the accessible journals themselves are not listed.
comments.request: List the accessible journals in the supplementary material.
comments.quote: For the ease of the readers, listing, perhaps in supplementary section, the accessible journals would be helpful

comments.issue: Specific journals are not named in the text (single journal with guidelines; 13 removed).
comments.request: Name the journals and the 13 removed from analysis.
comments.quote: When possible, list the journal name in the text (such as in the section when referring to only one journal had guidelines on publisher website and perhaps the 13 removed from analysis).

comments.issue: Publishers said to be already acting are not named.
comments.request: Name the publishers already implementing accessibility practices.
comments.quote: in the widespread improvements section, it is said that “some publishers are already doing this” so please provide names of which

comments.issue: The need for continuous learning as accessibility technology advances is not stressed.
comments.request: Add that accessibility requires continuous learning as technology advances.
comments.quote: it is important for the authors to stress that there are often advancements in technology and that it is the responsibility of everyone to continuously learn about accessibility

comments.issue: Peer reviewers may not be trained to ask for accessible practices.
comments.request: Recommend reviewer accessibility checklists and training.
comments.quote: For bottom-up pressures, it is important to note that peer reviewers may not be trained to ask for accessible practices.

comments.issue: Accessibility of archived material is not covered.
comments.request: Add recommendations for making archived material accessible.
comments.quote: One aspect that this article does not cover, but is important to mention is the ability to make archived material accessible.

comments.issue: Supplemental table lacks concrete examples and source links.
comments.request: Add concrete examples and links; encourage reviewers to assess alt text.
comments.quote: Under supplemental table, it would be helpful to provide some concrete examples.

reviews.assessment: Important topic with no major comments; suggests more actionable, better-organized content and a clearer figure and scoring scheme.

comments.issue: Figure 1 is hard to read: groups indistinguishable in black and white, scale confusing.
comments.request: Improve or drop Figure 1 and fix its scale and distinguishability.
comments.quote: I don’t think figure 1 is as clear as it could be. For example, as a reader who printed this in black and white, I couldn’t tell the groups apart

comments.issue: Table S3 sits in the supplement instead of the manuscript body.
comments.request: Move Table S3 into the main manuscript.
comments.quote: I think Table S3 should be part of the manuscript instead of the supplemental material.

comments.issue: Table S3 lacks specific actions for authors and reviewers.
comments.request: Add concrete author and reviewer actions to Table S3.
comments.quote: I would also love to see specific things that I should do as an author or look for as a reviewer

comments.issue: How Universal Design applies to manuscript preparation is not detailed.
comments.request: Detail how Universal Design applies to manuscript preparation.
comments.quote: it would be more useful for the reader if how UD applies to manuscript preparation specifically was detailed

comments.issue: What falls under the 'other' disability category is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the 'other' category with in-text examples.
comments.quote: it would be useful to know what falls under the category of other and how type/text/format/etc of pdfs would be able to target other disabilities

comments.issue: The data compilation and composite scoring are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify what the composite score is and how it was built.
comments.quote: Could the data compilation/composite scoring be clarified? As a reader I didn’t quite understand exactly what that composite score looked like

comments.issue: Coders subjectively judged whether information was required or suggested.
comments.request: Provide standard definitions for required versus suggested.
comments.quote: I was confused by each coder being able to subjectively make a decision about whether the information was required or suggested in the guidelines

comments.issue: Data S1 organization is difficult to follow, with unexplained multiple rows per journal.
comments.request: Reorganize Data S1 by publisher with nested journals and sortable columns.
comments.quote: I found the organization difficult to follow. Why did some journals have multiple row entries?

comments.issue: Open Access only and predatory-list journals are not identified or analysed.
comments.request: Report these journal counts and their influence on accessibility prevalence.
comments.quote: I was curious how many of the journals were Open Access only and how many were on the “predatory” publishers list.

comments.issue: No general checklist of accessibility actions is provided for readers.
comments.request: Add a general accessibility checklist, combined with UD and disability categories.
comments.quote: having at least a general check list of accessibility things that I could do to address major/common disabilities would be incredibly useful

reviews.assessment: Addresses an important topic with thorough methodology; suggests defining Section 508 and Universal Design and covering further workflow steps.

comments.issue: Section 508 standards and Universal Design principles are not clearly defined or supported by literature.
comments.request: Define Section 508 and Universal Design with examples and citations.
comments.quote: This paper would be strengthen by clearly defining the Section 508 compliance standards and universal design principles with examples of each.

comments.issue: Release of an accessible final PDF to authors is not covered in the workflow.
comments.request: Add accessible final PDFs to the workflow recommendations.
comments.quote: A step in the workflow not mentioned is the release of the final PDF to the authors.

comments.issue: Journal establishment year was not recorded, so whether newer journals are more accessible is unknown.
comments.request: Report journal age and test whether newer journals are more accessible.
comments.quote: Did the authors note when the journal was established during their review? I am curious as to whether or not newer journals are more accessible

title: Widespread lack of article accessibility policies among ecology and evolution journals

study.system: freshwater fish; 21-yr Upper Paraná floodplain community and fishery data

editor_summary: Editor says reviewers found the work of interest but raised concerns; responses to the criticisms and a revised manuscript are needed before a publication decision.

reviews.assessment: Finds the analyses sound and the perspective novel, asking for temperature methods clarity and optional interaction analyses.
strengths: novel perspective linking land use, non-native fishes, size spectra and ecosystem services
data collection, processing and analysis steps appropriate
potential for broad generalization to freshwater ecosystems

comments.issue: How temperature was incorporated is unclear; it appears to be instantaneous water temperature at sampling.
comments.request: Explain the temperature variable in the main text methods.
comments.quote: The way temperature was incorporated is unclear to me & this could be explained – from the supplement, I believe its instantaneous water temperature collected at the time of sampling.

comments.issue: Instantaneous temperature may not represent the thermal regime, which could affect the temperature conclusions.
comments.request: Evaluate whether a longer standardized air temperature series gives different results.
comments.quote: Did the authors evaluate whether a more standardized longer time series of air temperature showed different results?

comments.issue: Potential synergistic effects of temperature and land use on native versus non-native size spectra are untested.
comments.request: Optionally test temperature by land-use interactions.
comments.quote: One suggestion could be to investigate potential synergistic effects (or interactions) of temperature and land-use on native vs. non-native size spectrum.

comments.issue: A few line-level copy edits (grammar and phrasing).
comments.quote: L. 80: decreases --> decrease L. 169: whole community did not

reviews.assessment: Finds the data and conclusions robust and significant, with only small clarifications on survey timing and supplementary detail.
strengths: data interpretation and conclusions valid and robust
links community structure to fishery yield for an important fishery

comments.issue: It is unclear when the fisher surveys were conducted relative to the biological sampling.
comments.request: Clarify the timing of fisher and market surveys.
comments.quote: My one question is when the surveys of fisherman were conducted. It was unclear if this occurred every year that the biological information was collected or if this occurred at different times.

comments.issue: The rise in smaller-bodied non-native omnivores is not addressed or explained.
comments.request: Discuss trends in other trophic guilds and whether they reflect introductions and habitat loss.
comments.quote: It appears from the supplementary data that smaller-bodied non-native omnivores also increased. Do the authors speculate this is due to increased introduction and reduced natural habitat (Lines 241-244)?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether all species occurred in all eight water bodies.
comments.request: Add habitat and site-count columns to Table S1.
comments.quote: I’m also curious if all the native and non-native species listed in the supplementary material were found in all eight water bodies.

comments.issue: Comparable findings from other rivers are not mentioned.
comments.request: Include examples of similar findings elsewhere.
comments.quote: The authors could consider including an example or two where similar findings exist in other rivers.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and ambitious study whose causality and metric interpretation need stronger support, including fishing pressure and alternative explanations.
strengths: rich supplementary material with data and scripts

comments.issue: Causality is questionable and alternative explanations for the observed patterns are not sufficiently ruled out.
comments.request: Rule out alternative explanations, including variables merely covarying with time.
comments.quote: My main concern is that I wonder about the causality here, and whether alternative explanations of the observed patterns have been given enough attention.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the size-spectrum exponent is the best predictor of fishery potential.
comments.request: Consider alternatives such as mean size.
comments.quote: I also wonder if the size-spectrum exponent is the best predictor for fishery potential (how about mean size, for instance).

comments.issue: A declining slope alone cannot demonstrate loss of large fish, since it also declines when small fish increase.
comments.request: Support the claim with size-distribution quantiles.
comments.quote: Size spectrum slopes (or exponents) are tricky in this context because it can decline if you have less large fish, but also if small fish increase and you have the same amount of large fish.

comments.issue: The maximum likelihood method estimates the exponent of the individual size distribution, not exactly a size-spectrum slope.
comments.request: Describe the estimated quantity accurately.
comments.quote: since you use the recommended maximum likelihood method developed by Edwards et al., you do not really estimate a size spectrum slope, but rather the exponent of the individual size distribution

comments.issue: Models 1a-1d use a negative binomial family although the data appear continuous.
comments.request: Justify the family or use a gamma family for continuous positive variables.
comments.quote: I’m curious why in models 1a–1d use a negative binomial family when the data seem continuous. I ran your code (great you made that easily available) to verify this is the case and not just a typo.

comments.issue: Several line-level copy edits (grammar, article use and wording).
comments.quote: Line 153: Not sure you need the title “a” for single panel figure.

comments.issue: “Decoupling of biomass flux” is unclear and its link to dominance of small-bodied individuals is not evident.
comments.request: Clarify what decoupling of biomass flux means here.
comments.quote: Line 88: Can you clarify what you mean by the “decoupling of biomass flux” here? I’m not sure I follow how this necessarily leads to a dominance of small-bodied individuals

comments.issue: The pattern could also work in the opposite direction if invaders are smaller.
comments.request: Acknowledge the reverse possibility.
comments.quote: Line 92: Works the other way too, invariable, or even more changed if invaders are smaller!

comments.issue: Calling the parameter a rate is incorrect because the units are not per time.
comments.request: Remove or correct this sentence.
comments.quote: Line 96: I wouldn’t call this parameter a rate, since the units are not “per time”. I think this sentence can be removed.

comments.issue: Invasive species cannot be said to be generally bigger than native species.
comments.request: Qualify the generalisation.
comments.quote: Line 101: same as on line 92, could also work the other way around. I’m not sure one can say that invasive species in general are bigger than native species.

comments.issue: “Exotic species” in Fig. S2b is inconsistent with the term non-native.
comments.request: Use “non-native” consistently.
comments.quote: Line 147: In the supplementary Fig S2b you refer to “exotic species”, best to be consistent and call them non-native.

comments.issue: The significance of the slope change is untested and by-year slopes rely on only eight points.
comments.request: Fit a year by native-slope interaction and report its confidence interval.
comments.quote: Line 155: Is this statistically significant? You could fit an interaction (year*native_slope) and look at the Cis of that coefficient.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the relationship is causal or both variables simply correlate with time.
comments.request: Test whether the relationship is causal or time-driven.
comments.quote: Line 157: Do you think this is a causal relationship or that both correlate with time?

comments.issue: Fishery potential was not plotted against the invasive size-spectrum slope.
comments.request: Add this plot for completeness.
comments.quote: Line 170: For completeness, you could/should also plot fishery potential against the invasive size spectrum slope.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the fishery potential analysis includes only commercial species or all native species.
comments.request: State which species are included in this analysis.
comments.quote: Line 170: In this analysis, do you include only commercially important species or all native species?

comments.issue: Fishing pressure, which strongly affects size structure, is a missing factor.
comments.request: Account for commercial and recreational fishing effects on size structure.
comments.quote: Line 263: Seems like a potentially very important factor is missing. In systems I’m familiar with, both commercial and recreational fishing has the strongest effect on size-structure (and thereby potentially also the exponent).

comments.issue: Fig. 1 does not distinguish lakes from rivers and the y-axis should read biomass density.
comments.request: Clarify habitat types and correct the y-axis title.
comments.quote: Fig. 1: It’s a bit difficult to see what is a lake and what is a river. Also the y-axis title should probably read biomass density, not only biomass.

comments.issue: Sample sizes are not reported although size-spectrum estimates can be sample-size sensitive.
comments.request: Report sample sizes and confidence intervals of the exponents.
comments.quote: Line 296: It’s an impressive data collection program! Could you spell out the sample sizes? I find estimation of size spectrum exponents to be sensitive to sample size sometimes.

title: Human land use and non-native fish species erode ecosystem services by changing community size structure

study.system: 35 boreal bird species; population genomics of seasonal migration

editor_summary: Editor: revise; reviewers flag calling heterozygotes on very low coverage data; strongly encourage deep-sequencing a few species to estimate heterozygosity as Reviewer 3 recommends.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, well-written study with an impressive dataset; minor comments on alternative explanations and low-coverage caveats.
strengths: enjoyable to read with attention to detail
strong contribution on evolutionary consequences of migration

comments.issue: Philopatry is presented as the primary explanation although ecological selection, phylogeny and behavioural mechanisms are not clearly ruled out.
comments.request: Elaborate the comparison of philopatry against alternative explanations.
comments.quote: Based on the evidence provided I’m not sure the support for philopatry is stronger than that of ecological selection (habitat specialization), phylogeny or behavioral mechanisms (other dispersal or territorial behaviors).

comments.issue: The phylogenetic signal in spatial structure residuals could use more elaboration, including possible genes and similar findings elsewhere.
comments.request: Discuss candidate genes and comparable patterns in other taxa.
comments.quote: The authors find a strong phylogenetic signal in the residual variation of spatial structure, suggesting the influence of an unidentified conserved trait.

comments.issue: Validation rests on one high-coverage individual per species, which may not represent population diversity; mean and range should be reported.
comments.request: Report the high-coverage individuals' mean and range and highlight the caveat.
comments.quote: Given that these results are only based on one individual per species, there is potential that heterozygosity of a single individual does not reflect the genetic diversity or structure across populations. The discussion might benefit from highlighting this as a caveat regarding your conclusions.

comments.issue: Heterozygotes are unlikely to be called accurately at ~2.8x coverage, and validation uses only one individual per species.
comments.request: Give a stronger recognition of this limitation in the discussion.
comments.quote: Heterozygotes are unlikely to be called accurately at this low of coverage. I appreciate that the authors have tried to acknowledge this by validating with high coverage individuals, but they only have one representative individual per species.

comments.issue: Some individuals in Dataset S1 lack coverage statistics without explanation.
comments.request: Note whether these samples were removed for low quality.
comments.quote: Dataset S1: There are some individuals missing coverage statistics – do these represent samples that were removed due to low quality? If so, note this in the table?

reviews.assessment: Well-written and convincing; specific comments mainly on the title, WGS novelty framing and additional analyses.
strengths: well-written with clear and convincing arguments
significant contribution to understanding trait-genomic variation

comments.issue: The title phrase 'unexpected population genetic consequences' is vague.
comments.request: Make the title more explicit about the findings.
comments.quote: Title: The “unexpected population genetic consequences” mentioned in the title is somewhat vague. I suggest making it more explicit, reflecting the findings.

comments.issue: The novelty of whole-genome sequencing is unclear when only nucleotide diversity and IBD metrics are used.
comments.request: Clarify the WGS novelty or reduce its emphasis.
comments.quote: What novelty does WGS bring here, considering the authors only rely on metrics like nucleotide diversity and IBD while excluding structural variation or explicitly analyzing demographic changes?

comments.issue: The comparability of boreal and tropical early successional habitats is not well characterized, weakening genetic expectations.
comments.request: Characterize habitat seasonality and use across realms with references.
comments.quote: A better characterization of how comparable boreal and tropical early successional habitats are would help to justify genetic expectations.

comments.issue: Sex-biased dispersal could contribute to the unexplained spatial variation.
comments.request: Consider sex-biased dispersal as an additional explanation.
comments.quote: Could sex-biased dispersal contribute to the unexplained spatial variation observed in this study?

comments.issue: Genetic substructuring is not tested with clustering methods and could bias IBD estimates.
comments.request: Apply clustering programs to assess population groupings.
comments.quote: Was any clustering method (e.g., Structure-like) employed to test the number of populations in species with apparent genetic substructuring

comments.issue: Figure 4 lacks the correlation coefficient and p-value on the panel.
comments.request: Add the correlation coefficient and p-value to Figure 4.
comments.quote: Figure 4: Including the correlation coefficient and p-value directly on the figure (perhaps in the upper left corner) would enhance its clarity.

reviews.assessment: Potentially contributing study, but substantial revisions are needed to data quality, clarity and cautious conclusions.
strengths: large dataset of 1673 genomes from 35 species

comments.issue: Average sequencing coverage is only 2.8x, which is too low to accurately estimate heterozygosity.
comments.request: Deep-sequence a subset of species (e.g., 30x) to determine the optimal depth.
comments.quote: The authors have made efforts in sampling, but the average genome-wide sequencing coverage is only 2.8x. I suggest increasing the sequencing depth (e.g., 30x) for a subset of studied species, to check the optimal depth required to accurately estimate the heterozygosity.

comments.issue: Sampling uniformity and discrete genetic structuring are not evaluated and could overestimate beta-IBD; isolation by environment is also unexamined.
comments.request: Evaluate sampling uniformity and test substructuring and isolation by environment.
comments.quote: Could such patterns influence the estimation of genetic diversity and overestimate the βibd in the model? Furthermore, do some species exhibit isolation by environment?

comments.issue: The introduction does not explain how the hypotheses fill current knowledge gaps or why migration is uniquely positioned to affect genetic outcomes.
comments.request: Deepen the gap statement and the unique role of seasonal migration.
comments.quote: the introduction would benefit from a deeper explanation of how these hypotheses address existing gaps in current knowledge. The manuscript could better highlight why seasonal migration is uniquely positioned to mediate such genetic outcomes

comments.issue: How philopatry interacts with other dispersal behaviours is unclear; the black-backed woodpecker lacks a spatial pattern.
comments.request: Explain the woodpecker exception and the philopatry mechanism.
comments.quote: The results suggest that philopatry in long-distance migrants plays a role in shaping spatial genetic structure. However, how this mechanism interacts with other dispersal behaviors remains unclear.

comments.issue: The hierarchical modelling description is fragmented, trait rationale is not tied to prior work, and HMSC details are excessive in the main text.
comments.request: Summarize the HMSC description and justify trait selection.
comments.quote: The hierarchical modeling approach is described in detail but presented somewhat fragmented, and the rationale for selecting specific traits (e.g., body size and habitat association) could be more explicitly tied to previous studies or theoretical frameworks.

comments.issue: Conclusions extend beyond the data, especially regarding broader evolutionary implications; limitations such as few nonmigratory species need acknowledgment.
comments.request: Frame the conclusions more cautiously.

title: Dominant species predict plant richness and biomass in global grasslands

editor_summary: Reviewers find the work of considerable potential interest and have made a number of comments to improve the paper; a revision is invited for further consideration.

comments.issue: Net wood productivity is not a conventional term and approximates aboveground woody productivity.

comments.issue: Biomass relative to water availability may be biased because big trees contain more heartwood.

comments.issue: Net aboveground productivity is not a conventional term.

no flaws that should prohibit publication

title: Amazon rainforest adjusts to long-term experimental drought

study.system: Japanese forests; tree census growth and mortality data

editor_summary: Reviewers raise concerns that must be addressed; editor stresses adding phylogenetic analyses, reconsidering the human lifespan comparisons, and justifying the size:age proxy before a revision.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, well-written study with generally sound methods; recommends revision but questions human-life comparisons and missing climate and human-activity factors.
strengths: well written with generally sound methods

comments.issue: Human lifespan is repeatedly mentioned although it is irrelevant to tree ecology.
comments.request: Remove or justify the human lifespan comparisons.
comments.quote: This is an ecological study, but sometimes I am lost when human’s life has been intentionally mentioned in the manuscript.

comments.issue: The analysis relies only on mean annual temperature and precipitation; other indices are not tested.
comments.request: Consider additional indices such as natural hazards.
comments.quote: I am curious whether some other indices such as natural hazards can be used in the analysis?

comments.issue: Human activities covary with the climate gradient and could confound the climate-severity effect.
comments.request: Discuss human activity as an alternative explanation.
comments.quote: Another important factor in addition to climate may be human activities. Logically, there are more human activities in regions with milder climate, which co-varies with the climate gradient, I think.

comments.issue: Fig. 1 and Extended Data 3d start with different numbers of trees (10000 versus 100).
comments.request: Unify the starting tree numbers.
comments.quote: Fig. 1: this illustrative diagram starts with 10000 trees at age 0, while the Extended Data 3d shows a start with 100 trees. But I think they should be unified.

comments.issue: Fig. 2 point sizes differ too little to judge the ratio.
comments.request: Use a wider size range for the ratio.
comments.quote: Fig. 2: I suggest using a wider size range to refer to the ratio. It may be slight difficult to notice the size differences of these points in the current figure.

comments.issue: After removing outliers, required tree number appears to decline with optimal AP.
comments.request: Address this potential decreasing relationship.
comments.quote: In my opinion there seems to be a decreasing relationship between the required number of trees and optimal AP when some more outliers are removed.

comments.issue: Wrong figure reference at line 186 (3d should be 4d).
comments.request: Correct the figure citation.
comments.quote: Line 186: Should be Fig. 4d rather than 3d.

comments.issue: Time periods used for MAT and AP are not specified.
comments.request: Clarify the climate periods and consider inventoried-year values.
comments.quote: Lines 278–283: Please clarify the time periods used to calculate MAT and AP. If data are available, MAT and AP of inventoried years may lead to a more straightforward analysis throughout the manuscript.

comments.issue: Extended Data 3c scale is unclear and live-tree points show negative values.
comments.request: Explain the scale and the negative values.
comments.quote: Extended Data 3c: What is the scale for the points for live and dead trees? Why do points for live trees have negative values?

reviews.assessment: Detailed review: finds the ratio analysis compelling but raises major concerns about the PML metric, size-age proxy, optimality measure and the headline result.
strengths: innovative ratio between PML and LE

comments.issue: Page and line numbers are missing, making referencing comments difficult.
comments.request: Add page and line numbers in future versions.
comments.quote: Page and line numbers would be nice in the future for referencing comments and suggestions.

comments.issue: The longevity-trait discussion ignores the trade-off in competition for establishment.
comments.request: Discuss the trade-off between growth, establishment and longevity.
comments.quote: Slower growth and greater investment in structural stability should limit short term competitiveness and potentially survival.

comments.issue: Taking the 99% size quantile for PML creates a self-fulfilling requirement for the number of small trees.
comments.request: Justify or revise the PML quantile approach.
comments.quote: it seems to lead to a self-fulfilling aspect to the number of small trees required to have an ancient tree

comments.issue: A second ratio, PML versus the oldest observed tree, is not examined.
comments.request: Examine the difference between estimated PML and oldest observed individual.
comments.quote: there might be a second ratio which could be examined - the difference between the estimated PML and the oldest observed individual

comments.issue: Variation in the PML:LE ratio and its extreme species are not explored.
comments.request: Explore further trait/phylogenetic relationships and the outlier species.
comments.quote: This is surprising and indicates the complexity and diversity of tree life history strategies and a lot more could be explored here

comments.issue: Fig. 3 does not show each species' PML or its position along the environmental spectrum.
comments.request: Indicate PML of each species in Fig. 3.
comments.quote: In Fig 3, it would be interesting to somehow indicate the PML of each species on these figures.

comments.issue: Optimality is the species mean MAT/PA, ignoring variance and generalist ranges.
comments.request: Account for the variance/range of environmental conditions.
comments.quote: This doesn’t take into consideration of variance around this mean - some species will be more generalist than others and then have a much larger range of variation for these environmental measures.

comments.issue: Size does not uniformly indicate age across species and environmental ranges.
comments.request: Justify the size-age proxy across species distributions.
comments.quote: This would indicate that size would not uniformly indicate age for a species and again this would vary according to the size and nature of the species distribution.

comments.issue: Slower growth in harsh sites would bias LE downward and exaggerate the PML:LE disparity, weakening the headline result.
comments.request: Test or temper the headline result against this bias.
comments.quote: it is possible that the smaller trees will grow more slowly than the larger established trees, meaning that LE would be underestimated in these circumstances, which would exaggerate the PML:LE ratio

comments.issue: No calculation of overall cumulative reproductive effort or its optimum is provided.
comments.request: Consider analysing cumulative reproductive effort.
comments.quote: If you can survive until that point, LE greatly increases and the individual now has centuries of reproductive potential.

comments.issue: The pattern could equally reflect lottery-like survival rather than the proposed mechanism.
comments.request: Discuss the lottery alternative for the LE-climate relationship.
comments.quote: This relationship could also all boil down to the lottery idea - in harsher environmental conditions, the chances of winning the lottery go down and the number of trees that successfully survive drops off proportionally.

comments.issue: Fig. 3c equation says MAT where AP is meant, and the correlation directions confuse the reader.
comments.request: Correct and clarify the Fig. 3c text.
comments.quote: And I don’t quite understand what is going on with Fig 3c - the equation states MAT, which I assume is a simple mistake and should say AP

comments.issue: The key number of required trees for the 5 cm versus 1 cm comparison is missing.
comments.request: Fill in the missing number.
comments.quote: A key number in the discussion seems to be missing

comments.issue: Strong outlier species in Fig. 4 are not explored or explained.
comments.request: Explain these outlier species and their implications.
comments.quote: Fig. 4 - what is up with those outliers? A bit more exploration and explanation about these tree species, already mentioned in the text, is warranted.

reviews.assessment: Finds the method versatile and the results reasonable and worthy of publication, but raises major concerns about diameter-only mortality, missing phylogeny and restoration extrapolation.
strengths: worthy of publication in this journal

comments.issue: Mortality is modelled by diameter only, ignoring light-environment/AGR effects that may bias estimates.
comments.request: Include AGR in the mortality assessment or state the expected bias.
comments.quote: At the very least, the authors should mention the bias in the estimates that is expected to result from not taking into account the effect of AGR on mortality.

comments.issue: Life-history types and phylogenetic relatedness among the 53 species are not analysed.
comments.request: Analyse the influence of tree types and phylogeny.
comments.quote: In particular, I believe that phylogenetic analysis is essential in terms of the generalization of the results.

comments.issue: Results from undisturbed natural forests are extrapolated to restoration and reforestation planning.
comments.request: Rewrite this section with more appropriate restoration scenarios.
comments.quote: Therefore, the results of this study (i.e., an estimate of how many individuals with a diameter of 1 cm were in the background of the maximum life span of a single tree) should not be applied to restoration planning.

comments.issue: No tabulated summary of the estimates is provided.
comments.request: Provide a summary table of the estimates.
comments.quote: L90-92: Provide a tabulated summary of the estimates.

comments.issue: Human life expectancy comparison is not meaningful.
comments.request: Remove the human life expectancy comparison.
comments.quote: L92-92: I don't think there is any meaningful comparison to human life expectancy here.

comments.issue: Fig. 2 lacks uncertainty estimates for the plotted values.
comments.request: Show uncertainty, e.g. in the summary table.
comments.quote: Fig. 2: The authors should indicate how much uncertainty there is in the estimates shown in this figure.

comments.issue: Different LE and PML axis scales in Fig. 3c,d may mislead readers.
comments.request: Use the same axis scale for LE and PML.
comments.quote: Fig 3c & 3d: Make the LE axis scale the same as the PML scale axis. The current diagram may mislead the reader.

comments.issue: Wording at L165 reverses the intended causal direction ('results in' versus 'is mainly offset by').
comments.request: Rephrase L165 as 'results in'.
comments.quote: L165: Shouldn't it be “results in” instead of “is mainly offset by”?

comments.issue: Reforestation discussion ignores nurse-tree practice in harsh environments.
comments.request: Revisit the whole consideration of reforestation of degraded lands.
comments.quote: In reforestation in harsh environments, nurse trees are often planted to milden the environment, followed by planting the target species.

comments.issue: Decisions need individual remaining lifespan (e.g. LE100d), not average lifespan, and planted trees differ from natural forests.
comments.request: Rewrite or delete the over-discussed paragraph.
comments.quote: The information people need to make decisions in this situation is not the AVERAGE life span of the tree, but how long the individual, as seen in Fig. 5, can live from now on (LE100d, for example).

title: Climatic differences among habitats shape the balance between maximum lifespan and life expectancy in Japanese tree species

study.system: ancient Papua New Guinea humans; ancient genomes and archaeology

editor_summary: Reviewers raised a number of concerns that must be addressed before publication; the editor requests responses to criticisms and editorial concerns in a revision.

reviews.assessment: Standard, well-executed methods with no major concerns; asks for a few result clarifications and figure checks.
strengths: extensive experience reflected in study design

comments.issue: The language-barrier explanation for population structure is developed only in a single unsatisfactory paragraph.

comments.quote: I thus think the manuscript would benefit from a more detailed comparison of the history of language evolution in this specific region, beyond the sparse information provided.

comments.issue: Possible ascertainment bias from captured 1240k sites is not ruled out.

comments.issue: Figure 1 colour codes are not explained.

comments.issue: Figure 2 colour codes are not explained.

comments.issue: A circle overlaps the admixture-timing block for ERI007 in Figure 3d.

comments.issue: 2 line-level copy edits

reviews.assessment: Important, high-quality aDNA study; asks mainly for narrative, terminology and archaeological-context improvements.

comments.issue: 'Isolated' is problematic because groups may have exchanged without intermarrying.

comments.issue: The term East Asian is vague and confusable with modern sociopolitical regions.

comments.issue: The relationship between Austronesian dispersals and East Asian ancestry is not introduced early.

comments.issue: Title is vague and the abstract has an awkward transition; both need rewriting around the headline findings.

comments.issue: Shaw and Allen are incorrectly credited for first discussing the Papua Hiccup period.

comments.issue: 'Ancient inhabitants' at line 56 is odd phrasing.

comments.issue: The Aru Islands are not addressed at line 83.

comments.issue: Original papers for the Papuan/Ceramic Hiccup are not cited.

comments.issue: The argument in this part of the introduction is not clear.

comments.issue: 1 line-level copy edit

comments.issue: 'Seafaring probabilities' are not defined.

comments.issue: Bulmer is not cited at line 375.

comments.issue: Genetics is not a holistic analysis of socially constructed family and kin.

comments.issue: The admixture date likely reflects limited sample size and should be caveated.

comments.issue: An alternative explanation at lines 519-521 contradicts the archaeological evidence.

comments.issue: Wrong citations for hiri emergence and the Kula.

comments.issue: A headline result at lines 605-606 is not sufficiently foregrounded.

comments.issue: Alois Kuaso is acknowledged but not offered authorship despite substantial input.

reviews.assessment: Valuable first ancient genomes from the region, well executed; needs better description of data, figures and tables.

comments.issue: The abstract does not report the number of individuals with genomic data.

comments.issue: East Asian admixture results are not ground-breaking given sampling post-dates Austronesian arrival.

comments.issue: Colour-coded fields in supplementary tables are unexplained and not machine-readable.

comments.issue: Unmodelled Philippine ancestry in the Marianas admixture graphs could be constrained with a present-day reference.

title: The impact of human dispersals and local interactions on the genetic diversity of coastal Papua New Guinea over the past 2,500 years
