comments.issue: The sex chromosome section is confusing and the 215 MiY average difference is undefined.
comments.request: Clarify the 215 MiY statistic and how it was computed.
comments.quote: Additionally, the section on sex chromosomes is confusingly written. What does “215 MiY average difference” (line 332) mean?

comments.issue: Whether younger sex chromosome adjacencies are unique is untested; zebrafish pseudogene repeats offer an alternative explanation.
comments.request: Test autosomes and consider alternative explanations.
comments.quote: has each autosome been tested against the genome to confirm whether this younger age of sex chromosome adjacencies is indeed a unique feature of sex chromosomes?

comments.issue: Key statistics for the 1,133 ancestral genomes (genes, contigs, contiguity, hard cases) are missing.
comments.request: Report reconstruction statistics and the method's added value.
comments.quote: I found the lack of information on the 1,133 ancestral genomes disappointing. How many ancestral genes and contigs are reconstructed? What level of contiguity is achieved?

comments.issue: Errors in younger ancestral genomes could propagate into older reconstructions.
comments.request: Discuss error frequency and mitigation strategies.
comments.quote: The method propagates ancestral genomes from younger to older nodes, raising the possibility that errors in younger genomes could be carried into older reconstructions.

comments.issue: S3.X1 and S2.X1 may be inverted in the Figure 1 gene tree.
comments.request: Check and correct the gene tree.
comments.quote: Shouldn’t S3.X1 and S2.X1 be inverted in the central gene tree?

comments.issue: Line 39 misstates Muffato et al.'s 624 ancestral genomes as 98 vertebrate genomes.
comments.request: Correct the citation description.
comments.quote: Muffato et al. reconstructed 624 ancestral genomes, not just 98 vertebrate genomes, as stated.

comments.issue: Line 41 misstates AGORA's complexity as quadratic.
comments.request: Correct the complexity to O(n×log(n)).
comments.quote: AGORA has a time complexity of O(n×log(n)), not quadratic, as stated

comments.issue: Parallelisability, memory usage and computer specifications are not reported.
comments.request: Report memory usage and runtime test hardware.
comments.quote: Is EdgeHOG parallelisable? It would be helpful to provide memory usage information compared to other methods.

comments.issue: 'Varies' and 'varying' appear in the same sentence at line 317.
comments.request: Fix the repetition.
comments.quote: Line 317: “Varies” and “varying” in the same sentence?

comments.issue: Line 335 should read 24.3 MiY.
comments.request: Correct the value.
comments.quote: Line 335: 24.3 MiY.

comments.issue: 'The co-localisation of cluster subunits in one locus' at line 319 is simply a cluster.
comments.request: Simplify the wording.
comments.quote: “The co-localisation of cluster subunits in one locus”—isn’t this simply “a cluster”?

comments.issue: The species tree used and whether LECA has outgroups are not stated.
comments.request: State the species tree and outgroup treatment.
comments.quote: Which species tree is used? Does LECA have outgroups?

comments.issue: Supplementary tables and figures lack legends.
comments.request: Add legends to supplementary tables and figures.
comments.quote: Supplementary tables and figures need a legend.

reviews.assessment: Very interesting tool that supersedes AGORA in speed; suggestions to improve the linearization description and manuscript balance.
strengths: supersedes AGORA in speed and functionality

comments.issue: The linearization phase, especially cumulative edge weights, is confusing in results and methods.
comments.request: Clarify the linearization phase.
comments.quote: All parts of the algorithm are well explained and relatively easy to follow except the ‘linearization phase’.

comments.issue: Figure 2c appears to show a wrong edge score between genes I and J.
comments.request: Check the edge score, add node W and colour the paths.
comments.quote: I believe that Figure 2c has an issue - the edge score between gene I and gene J in the first graph has a value of 3, while in the others a value of 2

comments.issue: Figure results, especially the vertebrate set, are not reported in the main text.
comments.request: Expand lines 211-214 with the figure results.
comments.quote: I would suggest the authors to include in the main text the results reported in the figures, particularly for the vertebrate set (expand lines 211-214)

comments.issue: Whether masked-species selection explains the precision and recall ranges is not discussed.
comments.request: Add this explanation to the text.
comments.quote: does this explain the broad range for both precision and recall depending on the species? It would be beneficial to add this into the text.

comments.issue: Consistency between the 50-species and 156-species reconstructions is not assessed.
comments.request: Compare gene orders reconstructed from both sets.
comments.quote: How consistent are the reconstructions between both sets? Do they reconstruct the same gene order using 50 or 156 species?

comments.issue: The dating application results are interesting but somewhat expected.
comments.request: Strengthen the novelty of the dating results.
comments.quote: This particular feature of the algorithm makes it stand out and the results presented are interesting, although somehow expected.

comments.issue: The discussion reads as future steps with no citations and does not cover all results.
comments.request: Balance the discussion across all results and include citations.
comments.quote: To this reviewer’s view, the discussion can be more balanced, referring to all results presented. As it stands, it reads more as “Future steps”, considering no citations are included.

comments.issue: How EdgeHOG could improve extant genome assemblies is not explained.
comments.request: Expand on this application.
comments.quote: How could this be achieved? Does this point refer to the benchmarking using “masked” genomes? Please expand.

comments.issue: Line 330 uses autogametic instead of homogametic.
comments.request: Change autogametic to homogametic.
comments.quote: Line 330 – change autogametic to homogametic.

comments.issue: The dating gene adjacencies script is in the supplement but not the repository.
comments.request: Add a dating gene adjacencies section to the GitHub page.
comments.quote: I would suggest however, that the authors include a section on "dating gene adjacencies" in their github page.

reviews.assessment: Enthusiastic about this innovative, well-written tree-of-life synteny reconstruction; one concern about organelle genes inflating LECA clusters.
strengths: well written with clear method description
new evidence for co-functional gene clusters in LECA

comments.issue: Organelle-genome genes in nuclear assemblies are scored as LECA adjacencies and may affect the GO enrichment analysis.
comments.request: Systematically exclude organelle-genome genes from cluster detection and enrichment.
comments.quote: I am concerned that gene adjacencies that originated by endosymbiosis are being scored incorrectly as present in LECA

comments.issue: Table S1 provides only GO terms, not sequences, preventing user BLAST searches.
comments.request: Provide sequence access via OMA links or gene names.
comments.quote: it would be very helpful to provide access to the some of the sequences themselves (not just GO terms), so that users could run their own BLAST searches etc.

comments.issue: Contig sizes are hard to see in Figure 5a and the ordering is unclear.
comments.request: Improve the visual representation of contig sizes and order.
comments.quote: It’s too difficult to see the sizes of the contigs. Most of them are only 2 genes long, but they’re drawn so close together that they look larger.

comments.issue: The range of contig sizes is not given in the text at line 246.
comments.request: Indicate the contig size range in the text.
comments.quote: Give an indication of the range of sizes of the contigs in the text.

comments.issue: Line 258 refers to the wrong figure.
comments.request: Reference Figure 5c instead.
comments.quote: Line 258, reference should be to Figure 5c.

comments.issue: Table S3 is labelled 'SuppTable1' on its tab.
comments.request: Fix the table label.
comments.quote: Table S3 is labelled “SuppTable1” on a tab.

title: EdgeHOG: a method for fine-grained ancestral gene order inference at large scale

study.system: cichlid fishes; activity tracking of 60 species

editor_summary: Reviewers find the work of considerable potential interest but raise substantial concerns about temporal niche categorization and behavioural differences between species (R1 suggests experiments and phylogenetic analyses) and genomic data processing (R2).

reviews.assessment: Well-written and strong evidence for temporal partitioning, but the assay's social isolation and the subjective niche categorization need testing.
strengths: strong evidence for temporal niche partitioning
places findings in an ecological and evolutionary context

comments.issue: The single-fish assay may produce patterns that are a product of behavioural isolation rather than natural activity.
comments.request: Test whether patterns persist with multiple fish, using three representative species.
comments.quote: I wonder how the signal may change if there are multiple fish in a tank that can directly interact. I would like the authors to confirm the patterns they are seeing are not a product of behavioural isolation.

comments.issue: How taxa are assigned to diurnal, nocturnal or crepuscular groups, partly via PCA, is not objectively defined.
comments.request: Explain and objectively define the grouping of taxa.
comments.quote: I can’t understand how you ultimately define whether a taxon belongs to the diurnal, nocturnal, or crepuscular behaviour groupings.

comments.issue: The proposed crepuscular bridge between diurnal and nocturnal states is not tested phylogenetically.
comments.request: Test transition rates in a phylogenetic context.
comments.quote: Could the authors test these transition rates in a phylogenetic context (e.g., Price et al. 2014)?

comments.issue: Phylogenetic signal methods for multivariate data are not considered.
comments.request: Consider analyses such as Adams 2014 and Mitteroecker et al. 2024.
comments.quote: Additionally, there are methods to compute phylogenetic signal for multivariate data – see Adams 2014 and Mitteroecker et al. 2024. The authors should consider these analyses as well.

comments.issue: The specific PLS function used for comparing behaviour to ecological features is not mentioned.
comments.request: Name the PLS function used.
comments.quote: Unlike other sections, you do not mention the specific function for the PLS. I’m guessing two.b.pls and/or phylo.integration.

comments.issue: Figure 1g branch lengths are too small to make out groupings.
comments.request: Scale the cluster-analysis branch lengths in Figure 1g.
comments.quote: Figure 1g – Scale the branch lengths of your cluster analysis. The branches are really small, and I can’t make out the groupings.

comments.issue: Figure 2a does not paint the discrete behaviours across the tree.
comments.request: Paint discrete behaviours on Figure 2a as in Figure 1g.
comments.quote: Figure 2a – painting the discrete behaviours here (as you did for Figure 1g) will help a reader visualize the distribution of the behaviours across the tree.

comments.issue: Figure 2g includes non-corrected data despite phylogenetic non-independence of traits.
comments.request: Show only the phylogenetically corrected data in Figure 2g.
comments.quote: Figure 2g – I do not believe there is a good reason to include both the corrected and non-corrected data here given the phylogenetic non-independence of your traits. Just include the corrected.

reviews.assessment: Important contribution with impressive tracking data, but reservations remain about whether the assay captures ecologically relevant temporal activity and supports the radiation claim.
strengths: important contribution to temporal niche diversification

comments.issue: Reservations that the data provide direct evidence that temporal niche partitioning was crucial in the adaptive radiation.
comments.request: Temper the claim or provide stronger direct evidence.
comments.quote: I have however more reservations than those shown by the authors that their data provides direct evidence that temporal niche partitioning was crucial in the adaptive radiation of these fishes.

comments.issue: The tracking design may not capture ecologically relevant temporal activity across light environments, especially given isolation from social activity.
comments.request: Demonstrate that the assay captures natural activity patterns.
comments.quote: The experimental design of the behavioral tracking dataset, while impressive, might unfortunately not be enough to capture ecologically-relevant changes in temporal activity across different light environments.

comments.issue: Uncorrelated activity with morphology may indicate the data capture noise around circadian rhythms, possibly reflecting social responses.
comments.request: Address whether patterns reflect natural rhythms rather than assay noise.
comments.quote: activity patterns across light environments were not correlated with any specific known morphological feature are quite unexpected, and might be indicative that the obtained behavioral data is capturing certain noise

comments.issue: A formal systematic comparison of the categorization with a trait varying across diurnal-nocturnal species is missing.
comments.request: Compare categorization with sensory traits known to differ across activity patterns.
comments.quote: I think a formal systematic comparison of their categorization with a trait known to vary strongly across diurnal-nocturnal species would strengthen the idea that they are capturing natural temporal activity patterns in their setup.

comments.issue: Feeding during behavioural assays is not described; no activity peaks at feeding times were detected.
comments.request: Provide details on feeding during assays.
comments.quote: I think it would be beneficial to provide additional info on how fish were exactly fed during behavioural assays. I am surprised that the analyses did not detect a signal indicating peaks in activity associated with feeding times

comments.issue: Discussion of correlations with physiological measurements and the body-size literature is missing; the lack of a body-size correlation contradicts prior work.
comments.request: Extend the discussion and align it with the body-size literature.
comments.quote: I suggest that the authors extend their discussion on correlations found/not found between behavioral data obtained and physiological measurements.

comments.issue: The movement threshold for total rest may need adjusting to individual body size.
comments.request: Explain or adjust the movement threshold by individual size.
comments.quote: Regarding the methods to capture total rest in tracking data, should the movement threshold not be adjusted based on the size of each individual being tracked?

comments.issue: Body-size correlations use species-level literature values rather than the body size of tracked individuals.
comments.request: Include individual participant body sizes in the models.
comments.quote: I find it somewhat unusual that correlations with body size were calculated using previous data for each species without considering the body size of the individual participants in these experiments within their models.

title: Widespread temporal niche partitioning in an adaptive radiation of cichlid fishes

study.system: global forests; age maps, biomass and CO2 flux data

editor_summary: Editor says reviewers find the work of considerable potential interest but raise substantial concerns that must be addressed; the manuscript cannot be accepted now but a revised version is invited.

reviews.assessment: Important global-scale analysis that may advance the field, but the NEE data behind Figure 3a and the inversion scale mismatch undermine confidence.
strengths: global-scale analysis may be a large step forward
mostly clearly written with good quality figures

comments.issue: It is unclear how the "changes in NEE" data points in Figure 3a were obtained; they are inconsistent with the individual inversion lines.
comments.request: Explain the derivation of the NEE values and their soil carbon component.
comments.quote: Figure 3a shows the key result of your study. However, it is not clear how you obtain the data points in this figure.

comments.issue: The large differences among individual inversion models give low confidence in the averaged relationship.
comments.request: Show how averaging individual inversion models affects the relationship.
comments.quote: the fact that the responses of inverted NEE by individual models to stand replacement differ so greatly gives a very low confidence in the relationship that you established in this figure after some steps of averaging processes

comments.issue: Scale mismatch: atmospheric inversions are unreliable at high resolution and stand-replacing disturbances occur in small patches.
comments.request: Address the scale mismatch between inversions and disturbance patches.
comments.quote: atmospheric inversion is typically unreliable at high spatial resolutions as the reliable ground-based CO2 observations are sparse and/or satellite column observations have large uncertainties and transport errors increases greatly with increasing spatial resolution

comments.issue: Regional literature on forest growth curves and carbon sinks by age is not used to evaluate the findings.
comments.request: Use the cited age-growth literature to strengthen or evaluate the results.
comments.quote: There has been a fair amount of literature on forest growth curves (NPP vs age) and carbon sinks at different ages (NEP vs age) for various regions of the world.

comments.issue: The meanings of the grey and green column pairs in Figure 3c are unclear.
comments.request: Explain what the column pairs represent.
comments.quote: Figure 3c: The meanings of the pairs of grey and green columns are not clear to me.

comments.issue: The "2x2 spatial window" in the Figure S2 caption is ambiguous.
comments.request: Specify whether 2x2 means degrees or pixels.
comments.quote: Figure S2 caption: “within a 2x2 spatial window”. What do you mean by 2x2? In degrees or 2 pixels by 2 pixels?

comments.issue: Figure S3 colour bars are labelled "forest age" instead of "forest age change".
comments.request: Relabel the colour bars.
comments.quote: Figure S3: It would be clearer to label the color bars with “forest age change” rather than “forest age”.

comments.issue: "Stand-replaced mature forests" is ambiguous and used inconsistently across figures and text.
comments.request: Use "young stands replacing mature forests" and harmonise the phrasing throughout.
comments.quote: I guess “stand-replaced mature forests” means mature forests replaced by young stands, but it could also mean replaced stands ageing to mature forests.

comments.issue: Large managed-unmanaged contrast in Figure S8 may stem from data processing or inversion uncertainty.
comments.request: Investigate whether processing or flux uncertainty explains the contrast.
comments.quote: I am concerned by the large contrast between managed and unmanaged forests in terms of the change of NEE due to stand replacement.

comments.issue: Growth rates in different age classes often do not follow typical forest growth curves, raising data quality concerns.
comments.request: Check the data quality behind Figure S11.
comments.quote: in about half the cases in this figure, the annual growth rates in different age classes do not follow the unusual patterns of forest growth curves

comments.issue: Ambiguous phrases such as "stand-replaced old growth" make Figure S12 impossible to interpret.
comments.request: Clarify these phrases and the direction of carbon stock change.
comments.quote: Because I can not understand the phrases like “stand-replaced mature forests”, I could not understand the content of this figure.

reviews.assessment: Interesting age-mapping work with serious reservations about modelling age from biomass; the carbon-flux findings add little new information.
strengths: spatial patterns of modeled forest age are interesting
use of forest structure as a proxy is relevant today
interesting addition even at coarse global scale

comments.issue: The premise of representing a pixel's age distribution by one number modelled from biomass is questionable; age maps resemble biomass maps.
comments.request: Justify or validate modelling forest age from biomass.
comments.quote: I have serious reservations about the premise that something as complex as the age distribution of thousands of trees within a pixel a) could be represented by a single number and b) that number could/should be modeled from biomass

comments.issue: The carbon stocks and fluxes findings seem intuitive and add no new information.
comments.request: Highlight the significance of the second group of findings.
comments.quote: The second group of findings (impact on changes in forest age / disturbances on carbon stocks and fluxes) seems intuitive and to my knowledge does not provide new information in this field.

comments.issue: "Old-growth" is a loaded term; age alone does not justify it and high biomass does not imply old growth.
comments.request: Use "old" rather than "old-growth" throughout.
comments.quote: Please reconsider the term ‘old-growth’, which is a loaded term that usually has additional constraints in addition to the ‘age’ of a forest

comments.issue: The GAMIv2 methods section is difficult to follow; the Hansen subtraction is misdescribed and items 1-3 lack justification.
comments.request: Give a clear, precise description of the GAMIv2 processing steps.
comments.quote: A clearer overview of that product (~line 520 in methods) would be helpful in the interpretation of lines 520-567.

comments.issue: "Gradual ageing" and "rapid transition" conflate growth with ageing, which cannot vary in rate.
comments.request: Distinguish growth rates from ageing rates in the text.
comments.quote: Growth rates and ageing rates seem to be conflated here, or, if this is not the case, then the distinction between the two is not well explained by the authors.

comments.issue: The stand-replaced versus gradually ageing partitioning is not explained well enough to understand the age differences.
comments.request: Explain the partitioning logic and the interpretation of the 1-degree resampling.
comments.quote: The methods section “Partitioning stand-replaced and gradually ageing forests” does not make sense as explained, or at least context is missing.

comments.issue: South America being listed as prevalent for both stand-replaced and gradually ageing forests seems contradictory if fractions sum to one.
comments.request: Check and clarify the regional classification.
comments.quote: South America tropical is listed as a region with “more prevalent” stand replaced forests and gradually aging forests, which seems at least counter intuitive, and potentially incorrect, if these two forests class fractions sum to 1.

reviews.assessment: Timely and challenging analysis, but uncertainties in age, flux partitioning, climate confounding and projections need to be addressed.
strengths: addresses critical and complex carbon cycle topics
efforts to incorporate nine inversion estimates

comments.issue: The definition of forest age, which appears carbon-based, is not made clear.
comments.request: Provide a clear and precise definition of age.
comments.quote: I believe the definition of age in this study appears to be related to carbon, so providing a clear and precise definition is still crucial.

comments.issue: Age validation results are missing and age uncertainty is not accounted for when relating age to NEE.
comments.request: Include age validation and propagate age uncertainty into the analysis.
comments.quote: it is essential to include age validation results and account for this uncertainty when assessing the relationship between age and NEE (e.g., Fig 3)

comments.issue: Results depend heavily on one outlier inversion product with a steeper slope.
comments.request: Test robustness by excluding the outlier inversion product.
comments.quote: Therefore, I recommend testing the robustness of the results by excluding this outlier to ensure the conclusions are not overly dependent on a single product.

comments.issue: It is unclear how the study separates climate variability effects from ageing effects on NEE.
comments.request: Isolate climate variability from ageing when interpreting NEE.
comments.quote: It is unclear how the study isolates the effects of climate variability from ageing on NEE.

comments.issue: The 2050 projection omits major drivers such as CO2 fertilization and warming.
comments.request: Consider these drivers and state whether estimates are optimistic or conservative.
comments.quote: This becomes even more problematic when considering projections for 2050, as major drivers such as CO2 fertilization and warming are not explicitly considered in the projection.

comments.issue: The BAU scenario assumes an unchanged age distribution, contradicting the observed age shifts, and ignores biomass accumulation within age classes.
comments.request: Revisit the BAU assumptions and account for within-class biomass gain.
comments.quote: The manuscript assumes that the age distribution remains unchanged under the BAU scenario and, based on this, concludes that biomass is nearly unchanged. However, this assumption is flawed.

comments.issue: The projection method is not validated against observed biomass changes.
comments.request: Test whether the method reproduces AGB changes using ESA Biomass data.
comments.quote: A simple way to test the validity of the method is to check whether it can accurately reproduce AGB changes using ESA Biomass data.

comments.issue: The negative sign is missing in ">30" in Figure 1 and the meaning of negative values in Figure 1c is unclear.
comments.request: Fix the sign and explain negative values.
comments.quote: In fig 1, the negative sign is missing in “>30”. Additionally, it would be helpful to clarify what the negative values in fig 1c imply.

comments.issue: For Figure 3b it is unclear whether age classes are based on 2011 or 2020 and how NEE by age class was derived.
comments.request: Clarify the age class basis and the NEE partitioning method.
comments.quote: For fig 3b, it is unclear whether the age class is based on 2011 or 2020.

comments.issue: How Figure 3b supports the statement at P4, L55 is unclear.
comments.request: Make the link between the figure and statement explicit.
comments.quote: In P4, L55, it is unclear how Figure 3b supports the statement being made.

comments.issue: The statement about lower net CO2 uptake of younger forests is unclear about whether emissions are legacy or from surrounding forests.
comments.request: Specify which emissions are meant.
comments.quote: the statement “younger forests typically have lower net CO2 uptake because of emissions related to stand-replacement (Fig. 3b)” is unclear

comments.issue: The data source of the unmanaged and managed layers is missing.
comments.request: Report the data sources for these layers.
comments.quote: L9, L277, the data source of unmanaged and managed layers is missing.

comments.issue: The unmanaged-forest effect may reflect higher tree cover rather than diverse age structure.
comments.request: Test the tree cover explanation for the unmanaged forest result.
comments.quote: This suggests that, at the spatial scale of Figure 3a and S8, grids classified as unmanaged forests may simply have higher tree cover, which leads to greater carbon uptake, thereby offsetting losses from stand-replacement and making the slope insignificant.

comments.issue: The link between the stock partitioning and the earlier paragraph at P11, L374-383 is unclear, and stock changes over the interval are missing.
comments.request: Clarify the connection and report stock changes over the interval.
comments.quote: I am not sure how the carbon stocks partition among age classes from L370-383 is related to the former part of this paragraph.

comments.issue: The definition and assumptions of the BAU scenario are unclear.
comments.request: Define the BAU scenario and its key assumptions.
comments.quote: how exactly was the BAU scenario defined? Assuming the current rate of deforestation continues?

comments.issue: What "mean" refers to (time or space) and how the AGB standard deviation was derived are unclear.
comments.request: Define the aggregation and standard deviation calculation.
comments.quote: it is unclear what “mean” refers to. Mean over what (time or space)? Additionally, how is the standard deviation of aboveground biomass (AGB) derived?

comments.issue: How the gain layer was used in age estimation is unclear given it lacks dates.
comments.request: Explain how the gain layer informed age estimation.
comments.quote: it is unclear how the gain layer was used in the age estimation process

comments.issue: The method for estimating forest age from Landsat-based estimates is unclear and may not reflect recovery start.
comments.request: Clarify whether this is the time-since-disturbance layer.
comments.quote: the method for estimating “forest age from Landsat-based estimates” is unclear. Are you referring to the “time since disturbance” layer?

comments.issue: How uncertainty data were incorporated, particularly in Figure 3a, is unclear.
comments.request: Explain how uncertainties were factored into the results.
comments.quote: it is unclear how the uncertainty data were incorporated into the analysis, particularly in Fig 3a

comments.issue: The choice of modelled forest age over Hansen loss and gain layers, and their consistency, is not discussed.
comments.request: Justify the data choice and compare the two approaches.
comments.quote: what was the consideration for not using the Hansen forest loss and gain layers, which are closer to direct observation, and instead opting for modeled forest age? How consistent are these two approaches?

comments.issue: The method for calculating NEE by age class and its relation to the stand-replaced ratio is not clearly explained.
comments.request: Explain how NEE by age class was calculated.
comments.quote: the method for calculating NEE by age class is not clearly explained. How is the “ratio between the fraction of stand-replaced and gradually aging forests” related to the age classes shown in fig 3b?

title: Global covariation of forest age transitions with the net carbon balance

study.system: Vibrio parahaemolyticus pandemic clone; phylogenomics and lab assays

editor_summary: Editor asks for more methodological detail, broader literature on adaptive gene loss, toned-down generalizability and novelty claims, and better interpretation of explosive gene gain and wave succession.

reviews.assessment: Careful, well-executed phylogenomic and functional study; minor clarifications needed on gene-loss precedents, Ne context and methods detail.
strengths: results placed in broader context of pathogen emergence

comments.issue: The authors overlook early Shigella work by Maurelli in which adaptive gene loss also involved a polyamine (cadaverine).
comments.request: Discuss this parallel polyamine-loss example.
comments.quote: Some of the first reports of adaptive gene loss in bacteria were published by Anthony Maurelli (refs 46,47 and much earlier refs) involving lysine decarboxylase loss in Shigella.

comments.issue: Effective population sizes below 100 are called large without any context for judging that claim.
comments.request: Provide context for whether Ne below 100 is large.
comments.quote: Their census sizes are probably huge, but their effective sizes do not seem so huge.

comments.issue: The reference-genome sequencing error in puuC may reflect a homopolymeric tract or other frameshift cause worth flagging.
comments.request: Explain the cause of the puuC frameshift.
comments.quote: Is there a homopolymeric tract or some other biological reason why this gene might be subject to frameshifting?

comments.issue: No PCR cycle cutoff is reported for the allele-frequency fitness assay, which could distort frequencies.
comments.request: Report the PCR cycle cutoff.
comments.quote: I did not see any cutoff in the number of PCR cycles used, which could greatly distort the allele frequencies. This should be mentioned.

comments.issue: Adding chitin to the media may favour biofilm growth and thus the mutant, biasing the fitness assay.
comments.request: Justify the addition of chitin to the media.
comments.quote: Also why was chitin added to the media for this fitness assay? Chitin would seem to favor biofilm growth (for Vibro) and thus the mutant.

comments.issue: The phylogeographic analysis identifying cross-continent transfers lacks software and script details.
comments.request: Provide software details and script links.
comments.quote: The details of the phylogeographic analysis (lines 452-454) identifying the cross-continent transfers are not adequate.

comments.issue: Dashed lines on pre-PC lineages in Figure 1b are unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the dashed lines in the legend.
comments.quote: What are the dashed lines on some of the pre-PC lineages in Fig 1b?

comments.issue: The phrase 'dispersedly distributed' needs refinement.
comments.request: Refine the wording.
comments.quote: Line 121 refine wording “dispersedly distributed”.

comments.issue: Figure 4d does not indicate which strain is light versus dark blue, and colours differ across panels.
comments.request: Label the strains consistently in Figure 4d.
comments.quote: Figure 4d, indicate which strain is light vs dark blue. Different colors and orders of the strains occur in the earlier panels of this figure

comments.issue: Rationale for choosing one E. coli and one V. cholerae strain for the knockout experiment is unclear.
comments.request: Justify the choice of knockout strains.
comments.quote: What was the rationale for choosing the 1 E. coli and 1. V. cholerae strain for the puu knockout experiment?

comments.issue: Puu loss is not universal in other species, since derived E. coli and V. cholerae clades retain the genes.
comments.request: Soften the claim to 'is under selection in some species'.
comments.quote: in E. coli and V. cholerae the most derived clades have not lost these genes, so it is not universal that puu loss is necessarly required to achieve pandemics in other species

comments.issue: Inadequate surveillance could also explain the gap between the first clinical isolate and epidemiological attention.
comments.request: Acknowledge inadequate surveillance as an alternative cause.
comments.quote: inadequate surveillance could also be a cause for the large gap between first clinical isolate known and epidemiological attention

reviews.assessment: Interesting and generally sound, but key claims about explosive gene gain, dating, global wave succession and novelty need stronger support.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the PC/pre-PC phylogeny is recombination-stripped and how recombination affected the relationships.
comments.request: Clarify how recombination was accounted for in the phylogeny.
comments.quote: the authors do not clarify whether the relationship between PC and the pre-PC lineages (shown in Fig. 1) is based on a recombination-stripped phylogeny, or what impact recombination has had on the relationships among PC, pre-PC, and non-PC isolates

comments.issue: Calling gene acquisition 'explosive' is meaningless without a baseline expectation for gene gains on the branch.
comments.request: Provide a baseline or moderate the 'explosive' language.
comments.quote: While the authors define an ‘explosive’ evolution as the acquisition of several genes/islands in a short period this seems meaningless without a baseline for the expectation of the number of gene gains on this branch.

comments.issue: Marker genes in non-PC isolates may have been lost by pre-PC lineages rather than gained by PC; this alternative is not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention the loss-then-gain possibility.
comments.quote: The presence of these markers in non-PC isolates raises the possibility that they were lost by the pre–PC lineages (rather than gained by the PC population).

comments.issue: Figure S2 shows several acquisition patterns, contradicting a single burst on the lineage leading to PC.
comments.request: Reconcile these patterns with the single-burst claim.
comments.quote: the phylogenies shown in Figure S2 suggest several different patterns of acquisition rather than a single burst of acquisition on the lineage leading to PC

comments.issue: The 86 mutations and 80 recombination events on the branch are reported without mutation types or recombination-detection details.
comments.request: Describe the mutation types and recombination detection.
comments.quote: they note that 86 mutations and 80 homologous recombination events occurred along this branch without any reference to the type of mutation or the analysis that identified recombination along this branch

comments.issue: Population growth may bias BactDating dates unless an exponential growth model was used, which is not reported.
comments.request: Report or test dating under an exponential growth model.
comments.quote: I am concerned that this may bias the dating analysis using BactDating unless an exponential growth model was used (which is not mentioned)

comments.issue: Global wave succession rests mainly on China and Figure 2d; sparse sampling elsewhere, and UK waves overlap.
comments.request: Soften the claim about global wave succession.
comments.quote: This pattern of lineage turnover appears clear in China, but sparse sampling in other regions makes it difficult to assess whether similar patterns occur elsewhere.

comments.issue: The 'first evidence' and 'paradigm' claims are overstated; adaptive gene loss is widely reported and the approach is not novel.
comments.request: Moderate the novelty and 'paradigm' claims.
comments.quote: While the evidence of this being an adaptive gene loss appears strong, the approach taken to study this process is not novel, nor is the finding that gene loss can be adaptive in bacterial pathogens.

comments.issue: 'A recent global wave succession event' is unclear and could be rephrased.
comments.request: Rephrase for clarity.
comments.quote: It’s not clear here what is intended by ‘a recent global wave succession event’. Perhaps this could be rephrased for greater clarity.

comments.issue: The geographic origins of the non-PC isolates in the collection are not described.
comments.request: Describe the geographic origins of the isolates.
comments.quote: I can’t find a clear description of the geographic origins of the isolates in your collection (except for those in the PC).

comments.issue: The overall geographic distribution of the dataset is needed to interpret Pre-PC spread.
comments.request: Provide the dataset's geographic distribution.
comments.quote: Context is required to interpret this statement about geographic spread of the Pre-PC subgroups - i.e. what is the overall geographic distribution of the data set.

comments.issue: Significant temporal signal is claimed without reporting the test results.
comments.request: Provide details of the temporal signal test.
comments.quote: The authors mention significant temporal signal but provide no reference to the results of a test for temporal signal.

comments.issue: T3SS2 does not appear in Fig. S6v, and the cited differentiation is weak; likely T6SS2 was meant.
comments.request: Correct the figure reference and differentiation claim.
comments.quote: but T3SS2 doesn’t appear in this figure. I guess that they intended T6SS2 - which does show some differentiation between wave 4 and other waves - but not clear differentiation

comments.issue: Figure 1c omits gene frequencies for non-PC isolates, which are relevant to their origins.
comments.request: Show gene frequencies for non-PC isolates.
comments.quote: Why aren’t the gene frequencies shown for the non-PC isolates? This is surely relevant in terms of understanding the origins of this group.

comments.issue: Supplementary figures lack legends, making them hard to interpret.
comments.request: Provide legends for the supplementary figures.
comments.quote: The supplementary figures lack legends and this makes it difficult to interpret these results

reviews.assessment: Exceptionally interesting and well-written study with strong evidence; only minor comments on overstated generality and missing context.

comments.issue: The claim that puu loss is generally selection-driven is not demonstrated in all the examples given.
comments.request: Limit this statement or provide supporting analyses.
comments.quote: The statement that puu gene loss is generally selection driven has not been demonstrated in all the examples given, so I would limit this statement unless analyses demonstrating it can be provided

comments.issue: T6SS occurs in all vibrios, so it is not an acquired factor specific to the pandemic lineage's success.
comments.request: Remove or qualify the T6SS claim.
comments.quote: T6SS is found in all vibrios, so it is not a factor acquired in the pandemic V. parahaemolyticus lineage contributing to its success

comments.issue: The parallel with cag pathogenicity island loss in H. pylori, the best-known colonization/virulence trade-off, is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss parallels with H. pylori cag loss.
comments.quote: The best known example of gene loss leading to enhanced colonization but reduced virulence is the cag pathogenicity island in Helicobacter pylori.

comments.issue: The role of putrescine in bacterial physiology is barely explained, so readers cannot judge why its loss is adaptive.
comments.request: Add a short description of putrescine physiology.
comments.quote: There is little mention of the role of putrescine in bacterial physiology. A short description would be beneficial for readers to understand why its loss can be adaptive.

title: Wave succession in the pandemic clone of Vibrio parahaemolyticus driven by gene loss

study.system: wild meerkats; MHC and tuberculosis over 20 years

editor_summary: Editor notes reviewers find the work of considerable potential interest but raise substantial concerns that must be addressed; cannot accept but would consider a revision addressing these serious concerns.

reviews.assessment: Values the unique long-term dataset but finds the interpretation over-stated, with major concerns about selection evidence and statistics.
strengths: one of the largest wild studies on MHC variation
excellent long-term data on MHC and TB
cyclical change results unique and solid

comments.issue: NFDS cannot be distinguished from fluctuating selection in a single population, and the cycling alleles are not the rarest.
comments.request: Temper the claim that the results strongly evidence NFDS.
comments.quote: I do not think the authors can theoretically differentiate NFDS from FS in a single population.

comments.issue: Significant terms for both the specific allele and allele number suggest heterozygote advantage and NFDS/FS both operate.
comments.request: Acknowledge that both mechanisms may operate jointly.
comments.quote: if they fit both the specific allele and the number of alleles in the same model and find both terms are significant, it suggests that both HA and NFDS/FS exist in the population

comments.issue: The manuscript text overstates NFDS without acknowledging fluctuating selection and heterozygote advantage.
comments.request: Change the text throughout to reflect that FS and HA also operate.
comments.quote: The authors need to change the text across the manuscript to reflect that FS and HA are also operating in this system.

comments.issue: Lifetime breeding success is not reported, so selection and selection response are not convincingly demonstrated.
comments.request: Analyse associations between MHC alleles/haplotypes and lifetime breeding success.
comments.quote: Given that the pedigree is available in the current study, I think it is feasible and essential to examine the association between MHC alleles/haplotypes and lifetime breeding success (LBS).

comments.issue: The claim that allele frequencies changed beyond drift rests on observation only.
comments.request: Run pedigree-based simulations to test whether changes exceed drift.
comments.quote: I wonder if the authors can run simulations like Huang et al.(refer No. 40) along the pedigree to confirm the MHC allele frequency change is beyond the change under genetic drift.

comments.issue: Results for other alleles and haplotypes are not reported, so it is unknown whether their frequency changes are TB-associated.
comments.request: Demonstrate that other alleles' frequency changes are not associated with TB prevalence.
comments.quote: the results of other alleles and haplotypes are not reported. I think they need to demonstrate that the change of frequency in other alleles/haplotypes is not associated with TB prevalence.

comments.issue: No analysis links allele/haplotype frequency to survival in a given year.
comments.request: Examine correlations between allele/haplotype frequency and yearly survival.
comments.quote: I would suggest the authors examine the correlation between allele/haplotype frequency and survival for a certain year.

comments.issue: No table summarizes raw model results, so exact p-values are unavailable.
comments.request: Report all model results, including non-significant ones, with details.
comments.quote: The authors used many statistical models, but there is no table summarizing the raw results. In this case, we do not know the exact p-value for each model.

comments.issue: Multiple testing across alleles/haplotypes is not addressed.
comments.request: Apply a correction such as Bonferroni.
comments.quote: although they ran models for each allele/haplotype, the multiple testing problem has not been addressed in this study. At least, Bonferroni correction should be used

comments.issue: Colors in Figures 2C and 2D are too similar to track alleles versus haplotypes.
comments.request: Use linetype or linetype plus color.
comments.quote: in Figures 2C and 2D, the color is too similar between alleles and haplotypes; it is nearly impossible to track the change of the alleles/haplotypes

comments.issue: The violin plot colors in Figures 4B and 4D are not explained.
comments.request: Explain the color coding in the figure legend.
comments.quote: For Figures 4B and 4D, we do not know what the color in the violin plot means exactly.

comments.issue: Caveats such as old-fashioned microsatellites and amplicon error reducing power to detect NFDS are not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention the study's caveats in the paper.
comments.quote: Even if those caveats may not necessarily bias the results, they should mention them in the paper.

comments.issue: Basic information about the study system (lifespan, group size, study area, migration) is lacking.
comments.request: Provide supplementary information on the study system.
comments.quote: I found the authors did not include enough information about their study system.

reviews.assessment: Impressive, well-written 20-year study, but the correlational evidence is not sufficient for the claims and several major points remain.

comments.issue: The final frequency increase is presented as NFDS evidence without statistical support that it exceeds typical oscillation.
comments.request: Test whether the change is greater than usual fluctuations, e.g. against neutral markers.
comments.quote: there is no statistical evidence that this change was more than just a fluke or typical oscillation

comments.issue: Other alleles with opposing or protective patterns (DRB*1, DRB*16, haplotype C) are not explained by the NFDS story.
comments.request: Test and discuss whether other alleles follow NFDS expectations.
comments.quote: What about DRB*16 – it shows a reverse trend compared to DRB*13 – changes from being somewhat protective to susceptibility.

comments.issue: The non-functional DRB*4 was excluded from analyses although its haplotype C shows adverse TB association.
comments.request: Re-analyse including non-functional MHC alleles.
comments.quote: given what is seen and described for the haplotype C – a re-analysis would be warranted (perhaps for all non-functional MHC alleles)

comments.issue: The plotted values are allele prevalence, not frequency, and prevalence may not function like frequency under NFDS.
comments.request: Explain the measure clearly and discuss whether it can be equated with frequency.
comments.quote: these are not really frequencies – as the values sum to more than 1. What is presented most likely represents “prevalence” of alleles, rather than frequency

comments.issue: The study is purely correlational and lacks functional or experimental evidence for the mechanism.
comments.request: Recognise this weakness and add functional evidence if possible.
comments.quote: the study is purely correlational, and would be much stronger with some functional/experimental data to back it up

comments.issue: Whether TB affected lifetime reproductive success is not reported, leaving the fitness picture incomplete.
comments.request: Report TB effects on lifetime reproductive success.
comments.quote: no information on whether TB affected (lifetime) reproductive success was provided – and this would be needed for a full picture of the TB effect on fitness

comments.issue: Generation time or number of generations is not given.
comments.request: Provide generation time and number of generations.
comments.quote: Even the number of generations or generation time was not provided for the species.

comments.issue: No selection coefficients or comparable metrics are calculated.
comments.request: Calculate selection coefficients combined with simulations.
comments.quote: calculation of selection coefficients or similar metrics combined with appropriate simulations would strengthen presented findings

comments.issue: The meerkat social and reproductive system may alter allele frequency responses and is not discussed directly.
comments.request: Discuss how the social system modifies expected allele frequency dynamics.
comments.quote: might also alter how the overall allele frequencies change in response to pathogen pressure (compared to what is expected under standard population genetics scenarios) – and this aspect should be discussed more directly

comments.issue: Latent phase length may be a better resilience feature to study than the current measures.
comments.request: Discuss or analyse variation in the latent phase length.
comments.quote: Can the length of the latent phase in TB vary? If so, that might be a better feature to study the resilience of individuals

comments.issue: Long latency and infection-to-symptom lags confound associations between allele frequency and TB.
comments.request: Consider allele frequency at the time of infection instead.
comments.quote: given long latency, and presumably the retention of a TB strain throughout infection –wound not the relationship with frequency of alleles at the time of infection be more informative?

comments.issue: DNA-based genotyping does not show whether alleles are expressed; some may be non-functional despite an ORF.
comments.request: Provide expression data or at least discuss this limitation.
comments.quote: all genotyping is based on DNA analysis, are all (presumably functional = without premature stop codon) alleles expressed by the meerkats?

comments.issue: It is untested whether the allelic diversity association holds when DRB*13 carriers are excluded.
comments.request: Re-run the diversity analysis excluding DRB*13 carriers.
comments.quote: is the relationship with high number of alleles/STs maintained when carriers of DRB*13 allele are entirely excluded from an analysis?

reviews.assessment: Strong, uniquely detailed dataset, but the balancing-selection interpretation is weakly supported and the manuscript should reduce its emphasis.
strengths: longest-term, largest and most genetically detailed immunity dataset
transparency in providing copious data summaries
data, methods and much of the main text are strong

comments.issue: NFDS requires pathogen evolution and functional host-parasite connections, for which the study offers no data.
comments.request: Add pathogen genetic data if available or state the evidence gap.
comments.quote: This study offers no data to support pathogen evolution or direct functional connections between host alleles infections resistance/susceptibility.

comments.issue: Only transitional states 2 and 3 of the four in Fig 1D are captured, and these limitations are not stated.
comments.request: Clearly state these limitations.
comments.quote: of the 4 important transitional states noted in Fig 1D, at best this paper only captures states 2 and 3. These limitations should be clearly stated.

comments.issue: Weak trends may reflect social-group infection dynamics and rarity rather than a functional disease link.
comments.request: Discuss how rarity and group-level dynamics could create false positive associations.
comments.quote: if those alleles reside in a social cluster that got hit hard by TB during those years then it would show an elevated signal of susceptibility driven more by rareness across social groups and stochasticity in infection prevalence than a functional connection to disease

comments.issue: Statistical models omit social cluster identity and within-group infection prevalence as covariates.
comments.request: Add social cluster ID and infection prevalence as covariates.
comments.quote: and think the following would be important covariates to add: -Social cluster ID -Prevalence of infection (i.e., frequency of individuals with signs of infection, not just the presence/absence of infection in a group)

comments.issue: It is unclear how much evolution could occur given the dominance system, and which groups drive the late DRB*13 increase.
comments.request: Identify the social groups driving allele increases and describe what allowed evolution.
comments.quote: I’m particularly concerned that the trend of increased DRB*13 could come from a small number of groups with very low exposure rates late in the study.

comments.issue: Haplotype F contains three alleles, so DRB*13 would be dragged along if selection acts on diversity; this is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss this haplotype confound.
comments.quote: Haplotype F happens to be one of a few that contains three distinct alleles. DRB*13 would thus necessarily be dragged along if selection was simply for diversity. This is not discussed in the paper.

comments.issue: Models are not compared, and the diversity argument rests on a proportion that is not compelling.
comments.request: Compare models with R2 or SEM and restrict tests to groups able to inherit DRB*13.
comments.quote: There should at least be a description of R^2 values of models focusing only on DRB*13 or only on allelic diversity/heterozygosity. Another option might be to apply some kind of SEM/path analysis.

comments.issue: Figure 6 arguments are not fully consistent with NFDS across selection cycles, and the allele versus haplotype disconnect is unexplained.
comments.request: Reconcile Figure 6 with the NFDS cycle and explain allele versus haplotype patterns.
comments.quote: Figure 6 builds on arguments that are not completely in line with negative frequency dependent selection, at least not across cycles of negative vs positive selection.

comments.issue: Supertypes get short shrift although other supertypes switch associations; supertypes may better predict functional similarity.
comments.request: Refocus on supertypes or justify sticking with alleles/haplotypes.
comments.quote: given that supertype is probably a better predictor of functional similarity between alleles, there is an argument to be made for refocusing the paper on supertypes rather than individual alleles or haplotypes

comments.issue: Figures 4 and 5 are discussed only briefly and their connections are not synthesized in the discussion.
comments.request: Synthesize why these metrics matter and how associations differ.
comments.quote: The connections between TB resilience, life expectancy, disease progression and mortality are extremely interesting but not thoroughly synthesized in the discussion section.

title: Twenty years of tuberculosis-driven selection shaped the evolution of the meerkat major histocompatibility complex

study.system: brown algae; comparative genomics of U/V sex chromosomes across nine species

editor_summary: Editor finds the work of considerable potential interest but notes substantial concerns; the manuscript cannot be accepted as is, though a revised version addressing the serious concerns would be considered.

reviews.assessment: Substantial critique: the haploid system limits some questions, and many conclusions, statistical tests and terminology need clarification before they are convincing.
strengths: excellent system for testing over-representation of sex-determination genes in sex-linked regions
interesting questions about sex chromosome evolution
the evolution of U- or V-specific genes is interesting
valuable study of SDR size differences and gene loss

comments.issue: Evidence for the conclusions is not clearly described, and tentative conclusions are not flagged as such.
comments.request: Clearly describe the evidence for each conclusion or mark conclusions as tentative.
comments.quote: most importantly, to clearly describe evidence for the conclusions (or to make clear to readers when these are tentative

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the regions described are all SDRs in the sense of controlling sex determination.
comments.request: Clarify whether each described region actually controls sex determination.
comments.quote: It is not clear whether these are all SDRs, in the sense of controlling sex-determination.

comments.issue: Bull's predictions are cited unclearly and not explained before the relevant data are described.
comments.request: Cite Bull and explain the prediction before presenting the data.
comments.quote: Probably Bull’s predictions should be cited here, and the prediction explained before the data are described, but this work is cited only in a bit of unclear text and not in clear relation to this question.

comments.issue: Many conclusions are not evidently reliable; it is unclear which are speculations, merely consistent with conclusions, or exclude alternatives.
comments.request: Distinguish speculation from supported conclusions and exclude alternative possibilities.
comments.quote: It is often unclear which are speculations, or simply consistent with a conclusion, and, among those, which have excluded alternative possibilities, as only the latter can properly be termed conclusions.

comments.issue: The text uses promotional, emotional language and unnecessary sentences that advertise the findings.
comments.request: Remove promotional language and unnecessary text.
comments.quote: There is no need to use a lot of words with emotional connotations, suggesting that the findings are very interesting.

comments.issue: Coined terms such as gene cradle pattern and gene nurseries are obscure and undefined.
comments.request: Define or avoid non-standard coined terms.
comments.quote: Similarly, terminology such as “gene cradle pattern” is obscure. It may be a term used in the authors’ lab, but outsiders will need clearer words, and definitions.

comments.issue: The word linked is used where genetic linkage is not meant.
comments.request: Use a different word and a statistical test if correlation is meant.
comments.quote: Finally, it is extremely confusing to use the word “linked” when writing about a genetical topic, when one does not mean genetically linked.

comments.issue: The introduction fails to distinguish diploid and haploid-dominant organisms, and diploid-only statements such as heterogametic sex are misapplied.
comments.request: Distinguish diploid and haploid systems and correct diploid-only statements.
comments.quote: The introductory paragraph fails to distinguish between diploid and haploid-dominant organisms, although the study deals with the latter. Several statements (such as “heterogametic sex”) apply only in diploids.

comments.issue: Inversions are claimed to have caused suppressed recombination, but consistency is not evidence; inversions can also spread after suppression.
comments.request: Show that inversions caused suppression, or present the alternative order of events.
comments.quote: Consistency with the idea that inversions may lead to suppressed recombination between sex chromosomes is not evidence that they did indeed do so (as the text states), as inversions are also predicted to arise and spread after recombination becomes suppressed

comments.issue: The claim that size differences coincide with inversions lacks a statistical test.
comments.request: Provide a statistical test that size changes are associated with inversions.
comments.quote: Readers should be told precisely how they can see that size differences of clearly specified regions indeed coincide with inversions, with a statistical test to show that these changes are associated.

comments.issue: It is not stated whether inversions affected the U, the V or both haplotypes.
comments.request: State whether inversions can be inferred to affect U, V or both haplotypes.
comments.quote: then it should be mentioned whether these can be inferred to have affected the U or V, or both haplotypes

comments.issue: Not all models of recombination suppression apply to haploids, and this is not considered.
comments.request: Consider which recombination-suppression models can apply in haploids.
comments.quote: The authors should also consider which of the models can apply in haploids, as not all of them can do so.

comments.issue: The statement that U/V chromosomes arose via an inversion in a locus is unclear about why suppression evolves and about the meaning of locus.
comments.request: Revise the text and clarify the use of locus.
comments.quote: Here readers need to be told why suppressed recombination might evolve in a locus, or maybe the word “locus” needs to be amplified

comments.issue: The phrase evolved after U/V-SDR divergence is ambiguous between duplication and undetectable allelism.
comments.request: Clarify which scenario is meant.
comments.quote: it could either mean that genes duplicated into The U or the V haplotype after recombination ceased, or that U and V sequences of a gametolog pair diverged so much that their allelic nature is no longer detectable

comments.issue: The text appears to contradict itself about whether SDR gene numbers differ or coincide.
comments.request: Clarify the apparent contradiction.
comments.quote: The text reads as if there is a contradiction: “Despite differences in SDR gene numbers” versus “U and V-SDR gene counts coincide in both species”.

comments.issue: The difficulty of detecting strata in U/V systems is explained incorrectly because neither region recombines.
comments.request: Correct the explanation of why strata are hard to detect in U/V systems.
comments.quote: The difficulty in detecting strata in U/V systems is because neither of these fully sex-linked regions recombines. In XY diploid systems, for example, the X recombines, and this largely prevents rearrangements

comments.issue: Ks analysis needs many genes to detect strata, but the species have very few, making four strata in D. herbacea and its expansion optimistic.
comments.request: Reassess the strata and expansion conclusions given the small gene numbers.
comments.quote: Another difficulty arises because Ks analysis requires many genes to detect strata with different Ks values (because the variance of these estimates is large), but in these species the numbers of genes are very small

comments.issue: Larger SDR size could reflect repeat accumulation, boundary changes, reductions or gene loss, which are not distinguished.
comments.request: Distinguish the different causes of SDR size differences.
comments.quote: It is also important to distinguish between larger SDR size due to accumulation of repetitive sequences, and changes in its boundaries so that genes flanking it in some species (meaning PAR genes) are within the SDR in others.

comments.issue: Repeat sequence densities, which test the predicted accumulation in non-recombining regions, are only dealt with sketchily.
comments.request: Describe and analyse repeat density patterns more fully.
comments.quote: it is important/valuable to describe the density patterns of repetitive sequences, to test the prediction that these should accumulate when a genome region ceases to recombine. However, the ms deal with this quite sketchily.

comments.issue: The inference that the ancestral V-SDR carried seven sex-determination genes lacks a statistical test.
comments.request: Add a statistical test for the seven-gene ancestral inference.
comments.quote: This would be a valuable conclusion, but needs a statistical test.

comments.issue: The reasons for conclusions about SDR gene content are unclear, and PAR boundary movement is not distinguished from new genes.
comments.request: Explain how gene-content conclusions were reached and separate boundary movement from new genes.
comments.quote: the reasons for the conclusions are not described clearly enough. Specifically, changes such as movement of the PAR boundaries are not clearly distinguished from the ideas about new genes.

comments.issue: The sexual-dimorphism/SDR-expansion scenario is not clearly worked out and gene-movement statements are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the scenario and avoid implying gene movement where boundaries change.
comments.quote: Statements like “sexually antagonistic selection may drive gene movements into the SDR” are not clear enough (especially if the scenario envisaged does not actually invoke gene movements, but simply changes in the PAR boundaries).

comments.issue: The absence of a correlation between sex-biased expression and sexual dimorphism is surprising and unexplained.
comments.request: Address the missing correlation between sex-biased expression and dimorphism.
comments.quote: the absence of a correlation between levels of sex-biased expression and sexual dimorphism in brown algae is surprising

comments.issue: The sexual dimorphism section repeats arguments made earlier.
comments.request: Shorten this section.
comments.quote: This section can be shortened, as essentially the same argument was already made earlier.

comments.issue: The overall conclusion about SDR gene gains and losses is unclear.
comments.request: State the overall conclusion on gene gains and losses clearly.
comments.quote: The overall conclusion concerning SDR gene gains and losses is not clear.

comments.issue: Citing the moss C. purpureus, whose sex chromosomes carry thousands of genes from fusions, is not helpful.
comments.request: Remove or reframe the C. purpureus comparison.
comments.quote: It is not helpful to cite the case of the moss, C. purpureus, whose sex chromosomes carry thousands of genes, probably due to fusions with at least two autosomes.

comments.issue: It is not explained whether species that lost their UV system still reproduce sexually.
comments.request: Explain whether these species still undergo sexual reproduction.
comments.quote: Here, it should be explained whether those species still undergo sexual reproduction, for instance having gametophytes that produce archegonia and antheridia (or the relevant brown algal terminology).

comments.issue: Retained genes suggest roles in sex development, not sex determination as stated on page 5.
comments.request: Correct the claim that these genes function in sex determination.
comments.quote: it nevertheless suggests that these genes are important for pathways in sex development (though of course not sex determination, as stated on page 5)

comments.issue: It is untested whether SDR regions gained via PAR boundary changes contain genes with unrelated functions and whether they were retained.
comments.request: Test the functions and fate of genes newly included in SDRs.
comments.quote: it may be interesting to test whether any regions that have become part of a lineage’s SDR by changes in the PAR boundary included any genes with functions unrelated to those of the genes just mentioned

comments.issue: The different gene-content results are not integrated into an overall conclusion.
comments.request: Integrate the results into an overall conclusion.
comments.quote: In my opinion, these different results should be better integrated into an overall conclusion.

comments.issue: The correlation between V-SDR size and dimorphism, which validates the ancestral inference, is not mentioned where that inference is described.
comments.request: Mention the correlation when describing the ancestral state inference.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to mention this when describing the ancestral state inference, as it would seem to validate that inference.

comments.issue: The two-event expansion of D. herbacea's SDR is explained only later, not when strata are first described.
comments.request: Explain the expansion events when the strata are first described.
comments.quote: These results would be more helpful if explained when the strata are first described.

comments.issue: Ks values for the young strata are not stated and the Fig. 2 y-axis scale hides them.
comments.request: State the Ks values and rescale Fig. 2 so the young strata are visible.
comments.quote: however, it is not stated in the text how large Ks values are for these strata, and Fig. 2 shows Ks values on a y axis scale that includes the shared, ancient stratum, so one cannot see the relevant information

comments.issue: Two genes on autosomes suggest genes can move off the UV pair, contrary to the authors' conclusions.
comments.request: Reconcile the autosomal location of two genes with the stated conclusions.
comments.quote: while two others are located on this species’ autosomes, which suggests that some genes not involved in male or female functions may move off the UV pair, contrary to the authors’ conclusions

comments.issue: The concept of heteromorphic generations is used without being explained earlier.
comments.request: Explain heteromorphic generations earlier in the manuscript.
comments.quote: and to be lacking in species that lack heteromorphic generations (a concept that needs to be explained earlier)

comments.issue: The conclusion that new genes arise more often in SDRs is not supported by an enrichment test and may need a dedicated study.
comments.request: Provide evidence that new genes appear at an unexpected rate, or soften the claim.
comments.quote: These are interesting speculations, but solid evidence is needed that new genes are actually appearing at an unexpected rate.

comments.issue: The claim that mutation rates in U/Vs are high lacks a reference.
comments.request: Add a reference for high U/V mutation rates.
comments.quote: It then mentions that mutation rates in U/Vs are high (a reference is needed)

comments.issue: The speculative de novo gene birth scenario is flagged only by the word may, which is not clear enough.
comments.request: Make the speculative status of the scenario explicit.
comments.quote: relies completely on the word “may” to tell readers that this is speculative, and I feel that this is not clear enough

comments.issue: The claim that the gene cradle pattern is pervasive across kingdoms is not backed by a comparative analysis or references.
comments.request: Provide the comparative analysis and references for the pervasive pattern.
comments.quote: but no adequate comparative analysis is described, and other U/V systems are stated to show the same pattern

comments.issue: Fig. 3 Circos plots are very hard to read, with unexplained symbols and combined gene and repeat density tracks.
comments.request: Make Fig. 3 readable, explain symbols and separate the density tracks.
comments.quote: The Circos plots in Fig. 3 are extremely difficult to read, and I could not find an explanation of some symbols, such as some microscopic ones near the chromosome names.

comments.issue: Gene ages shown in Fig. 3 Track 1 are not defined.
comments.request: Define what gene ages means in Track 1.
comments.quote: Track 1 shows gene “ages”, which need to be be defined.

comments.issue: Results are not plotted for the UV pair alone, which would support the presence of non-recombining regions.
comments.request: Plot results for the UV pair or for single U or V chromosomes.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to plot results for just the UV pair, or even just U or V chromosomes whose other pair member was not sequenced

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the plotted repeat densities are means for U and V or values from one chromosome.
comments.request: Explain what the plotted density values represent.
comments.quote: It is also unclear if these are mean densities for the U and V, or values (presumably in windows of some size) from just one of these.

comments.issue: It is unclear what Ks is estimated between and what the higher values are higher than.
comments.request: Specify the species pairs and reference values for the Ks estimates.
comments.quote: readers need to be told what Ks is estimated between (mutation rates are mentioned, and this appears to refers to pairwise inter-species divergence between closely related species, but the species pairs are not specified)

comments.issue: The monoicy results cannot be located and the species involved are not named.
comments.request: State where the monoicy results can be seen and name the species.
comments.quote: but readers are not told where these can be seen, or which species this refers to

comments.issue: It is unclear what a U-SDR-derived gene present in both monoicous species means.
comments.request: Clarify what is meant by this phrase.
comments.quote: it is not easy to understand what is meant by “a U-SDR-derived gene present in both monoicous species”

comments.issue: With only two monoicous species, a fundamental role in the female pathway cannot be inferred.
comments.request: Temper claims based on only two monoicous species.
comments.quote: With only 2 monoicous species, it is also unclear whether this suggests its fundamental role in the female developmental pathway.

comments.issue: Clear ideas are needed on how a species expressing both sex functions could re-evolve dioicy.
comments.request: Develop ideas on re-evolution of dioicy from monoicy.
comments.quote: clear ideas about how these things might word are needed, including how a species expressing both sex functions could re-evolve dioicy

comments.issue: An example of sex chromosome loss in brown algae is worth reporting.
comments.request: Report a brown algal example of sex chromosome loss.
comments.quote: An example in brown algae is worth reporting, adding to the cases already described.

comments.issue: The text overstates the findings by claiming genetic networks governing sex determination were rewired, which the results do not describe.
comments.request: Remove or soften the rewiring claim.
comments.quote: the results do not actually describe “genetic networks governing sex determination” being “rewired” during the transitions described

comments.issue: Repeat densities in the retained SDRs and other regions of monoicous species are not described, and Fig. 3 shows only dioicous species.
comments.request: Describe repeat densities in monoicous species and include them in Fig. 3.
comments.quote: It would be valuable to describe repetitive sequence densities in the retained SDRs and the other genome regions of the monoicous species

comments.issue: Calling F. serratus an XX/XY system implies visible sex chromosomes, but none were detected.
comments.request: Clarify what evidence supports genetic sex determination and male heterogamety.
comments.quote: The term XX/XY system gives readers the impression that sex chromosomes have been seen in males and females, but this seems not to be the case

comments.issue: It is not stated whether MIN or nearby sequences in F. serratus were tested for sex linkage.
comments.request: Report whether MIN has been tested for sex linkage in F. serratus.
comments.quote: It is not made clear enough whether the MIN gene, or sequences physically near it in F. serratus, have been tested for sex linkage (a straightforward matter)

comments.issue: The Fucus story, including evidence for a monoicous intermediate, is hard to follow.
comments.request: Explain the Fucus scenario and its evidence more clearly.
comments.quote: I suspect that I have not correctly understood the story about this species, and I feel that it can be explained more clearly, including the evidence for a monoicous intermediate.

comments.issue: It is not explained why a monoicous intermediate is indicated rather than an extension of the diploid stage.
comments.request: Justify the monoicous intermediate scenario over alternatives.
comments.quote: However, it is not explain why a monoicous intermediate is indicated, rather than an extension of the diploid stage, which might have reproduced vegetatively and then evolved a new genetic sex-determining system

comments.issue: The final Discussion sections repeat the findings and could be shortened or integrated earlier.
comments.request: Shorten the discussion and integrate it into earlier sections.
comments.quote: The final Discussion sections appear mainly to repeat the findings and interpretations, and are unnecessary, or could be greatly shortened.

comments.issue: The connection between TE enrichment and sex-linked regions is not explained in a dedicated section.
comments.request: Expand the section on TE accumulation.
comments.quote: The connection with TE enrichment in the Ectocarpales sex-linked regions would be easier to explain in an expanded section on such accumulation.

comments.issue: The phrase have moved into is ambiguous and the mechanism causing gene movement is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify whether genes are now within the SDR and what mechanism is proposed.
comments.quote: does “have moved into” simply mean “are now within”? And what mechanism causes these movements? Is it through rearrangements, of do the PAR boundaries change?

comments.issue: The claim that male genome assemblies are better quality lacks details and references.
comments.request: Provide details and references for male versus female assembly quality.
comments.quote: Genome assemblies are stated to be better quality for males than females, but no details or references are given.

comments.issue: The assumption of parallel U/V-SDR evolution is unclear and unjustified, and may not hold.
comments.request: Explain and justify the parallel U/V-SDR evolution assumption.
comments.quote: the meaning of the statement should be explicitly clear, and the assumption explicitly justified

comments.issue: The aspects of Fig. 2E and F supporting the argument are not pointed out.
