comments.quote: Why did the authors not use a less guided comparison of genomic characteristics (i.e. compare entire genome), to avoid this biased assessment of patterns

comments.issue: No benchmark against non-phytoplankton-associated genomes from bulk seawater.
comments.request: Include non-phytoplankton genomes as a benchmark.
comments.quote: it would have been very useful to compare the genomic characteristics from the dinoflagellate and diatom associates with non-phytoplankton associate genomes taken from the bulk seawater sample at the time of sampling.

comments.issue: Co-occurrence network construction is unclear: whether each strain was a node or groups were pooled.
comments.request: Describe the co-occurrence network construction.
comments.quote: Was each phytoplankton strain a node in the network, or were all diatoms and dinoflagellates binned into one of two groups?

comments.issue: Grammar is patchy and the manuscript needs careful editing.
comments.request: Have the manuscript professionally edited.
comments.quote: Throughout the manuscript the grammar is patchy and indeed pretty rough in several areas, indicating the manuscript needed a more careful editorial process

comments.issue: Dominance of Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria and Flavobacteria is not a new observation.
comments.request: Acknowledge this is not novel.
comments.quote: The observation that Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria and Flavobacteria dominate phytoplankton cultures is not a new observation

comments.issue: Secretion systems are only framed as weapons against bacteria, ignoring possible roles in bacteria-host material transfer.
comments.request: Discuss alternative roles of secretion systems in host interactions.
comments.quote: solely discussed as a weapon in inter-bacterial interactions in the phycosphere, but couldn't these be more important as a means for transfer of material between the bacteria and a phytoplankton host?

title: Taxonomic composition and ecophysiology of resident bacteria associated with marine phytoplankton

study.system: US streams and riparian birds; continental monitoring and eBird data

editor_summary: Reviewers find the work of considerable potential interest but raise a number of concerns to address; the editor asks for responses to them.

reviews.assessment: Finds the study valid, original and robust with no major flaws, suggesting only minor additions and clarifications.
strengths: highly original combination of biodiversity crises and data scale
significant step forward for aquatic-terrestrial linkages
conclusions robust, valid and reliable with well-reported uncertainty

comments.issue: A map showing spatial patterns in the strength of the insect-bird link is missing.
comments.request: Consider a choropleth map of model coefficients at HUC6 or HUC8 level.
comments.quote: I thought there was a missed opportunity to show the spatial patterns of the strength of the link between insects and a subset of species of interest

comments.issue: Credible intervals and confidence intervals are used interchangeably, leaving the statistical framework unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the underlying statistical framework for the models in the Methods.
comments.quote: used the terms posterior distributions and credible interval here (and Fig. 2), confidence interval elsewhere. Are these interchangeable terms in the modeling framework presented here?

comments.issue: How bird diet components were assigned to species is not described.
comments.request: Describe how diet components were assigned by species.
comments.quote: unclear how these diet components were assigned by species – expert opinion, literature, available within eBird basic data set?

comments.issue: The suitability of hurdle models for zero-inflated data is not explained.
comments.request: Add a phrase explaining why hurdle models suit these data.
comments.quote: I'll suggest adding a quick phrase or sentence indicating how hurdle models are suited to the type(s) of data used in this study (i.e., zero-inflated).

comments.issue: Code is public but restricted, so the reviewer could not inspect it.
comments.request: Make the code openly accessible.
comments.quote: The code is available publicly, but restricted to users with access. I was unable to review the code for this reason.

reviews.assessment: Timely and valuable continental-scale synthesis, but the site-matching workflow, buffer justifications and potential confounding of land-use covariates need clarification.
strengths: timely study addressing aquatic subsidies to terrestrial biodiversity
enormous data synthesis and complex analysis effort
Figure 1 clearly explains the site-matching workflow

comments.issue: The introduction contains strong statements that are not supported by equally strong citations.
comments.request: Support strong statements with evidence or flag where evidence is lacking.
comments.quote: there are some strong statements that are not currently supported with equally strong evidence through citations

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the 50m core, 550m riparian clip and 5km buffer are used separately or combined, and whether the 50m zone is used at all.
comments.request: State explicitly how the 50m core zone is used, or remove it.
comments.quote: Are the 50m area of “core emergence”, the 550m clip of riparian area, and 5km circular clip of site buffer used separately, or how are they combined?

comments.issue: The order in which the site-matching decisions are described makes the buffer relationships hard to follow.
comments.request: Revise the order in which the matching decisions are described.
comments.quote: I had to read the methods and Figure 1 caption many times to get to sort out the relationships between the different buffer zones and riparian data.

comments.issue: The zone used to calculate land-use characteristics is unclear and is not stated in figure captions.
comments.request: State which buffer zone is used for land-use variables, including in captions.
comments.quote: I’m also unclear about in which zone the land use characteristics are being calculated – only in the 550m clip of riparian area, or in the entire 5km circular buffer?

comments.issue: The choice of a 5km buffer is not justified in terms of organismal dispersal.
comments.request: Justify the 5km buffer with explanation and citations.
comments.quote: I would also like to see more detailed justification for the 5km buffer; is this choice mainly about organismal dispersal

comments.issue: Land-use covariates affect both EPT richness and birds, so direct and indirect effects on birds cannot be disentangled.
comments.request: Address whether the method handles effects on both predictor and response.
comments.quote: Is the statistical method used here robust to the fact that these covariates affect both the predictor and the response?

comments.issue: The statement about agricultural attenuation and 'EPT taxa prevailed' is hard to interpret after sentences about richness.
comments.request: Rewrite this sentence to clarify what is attenuated and what 'prevailed' means.
comments.quote: this is a bit hard to interpret, what is being attenuated and what is meant by “EPT taxa prevailed”?

comments.issue: 'Co-benefits' is not defined.
comments.request: Define co-benefits or use 'benefits to both terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems'.
comments.quote: L35: define co-benefits, or else “benefits to both terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems” would be more clear.

comments.issue: The claim that insects often dominate secondary production is not supported by the cited paper.
comments.request: Provide much stronger citation evidence or soften the statement.
comments.quote: The Baxter et al. paper cited doesn’t really say this; it cites Jackson & Fisher 1986 which is an example from a desert stream.

comments.issue: The spring emergence statement is too general given biogeographic and food-web nuance.
comments.request: Clarify that the statement applies only to the conterminous United States.
comments.quote: this, also, is likely too general of a statement; there is nuance with biogeography and food web characteristics

comments.issue: The link from individual-level growth and fitness to community composition skips levels of biological organization.
comments.request: Lay out the steps linking individual processes to community composition.
comments.quote: growth, reproduction, and fitness are measured on individuals, but composition is a community-level metric. Lay out the steps linking the two

comments.issue: The cited Statzner & Resh paper reports weak, not necessarily significant, richness-productivity trends.
comments.request: Provide better support or soften the strong correlation statement.
comments.quote: it is strongly correlated” is a strong statement and needs better support than the citation provided.

comments.issue: What 'prevalence' means and which of the weighted or unweighted metrics is presented are unclear.
comments.request: Define prevalence in the main text and state which metric is presented.
comments.quote: in the methods the authors describe calculating both weighted and unweighted prevalence, but the results and figures do not state which metric is being analyzed/presented

comments.issue: The effect size of 0.2 is not translated into a tangible difference.
comments.request: Link the effect size to the percent or x-fold difference.
comments.quote: If possible, make the effect size more tangible – what does an effect size of 0.2 mean?

comments.issue: The important context recovered by the analysis is not mentioned in the abstract.
comments.request: Consider mentioning this context in the abstract.
comments.quote: this seems very important – it is fantastic that the analysis is able to pull this context out. It may even merit a mention in the abstract.

comments.issue: It is not stated that invertebrate surveys sampled benthic communities rather than emerging insects.
comments.request: State this and provide an accessible overview of sampling methods.
comments.quote: Somewhere it should be stated that the freshwater invertebrate surveys were done on benthic communities and not emerging insects.

comments.issue: Invertebrates may have emerged before surveys, potentially biasing richness estimates and the bird link.
comments.request: Address emergence timing relative to invertebrate surveys.
comments.quote: is there a chance that some had emerged before the surveys were conducted, and if so how would this affect richness estimation

comments.issue: 'Continental-scale' overstates coverage, since boreal regions, Canada and Mexico are excluded.
comments.request: Acknowledge that the study does not cover the entire continent.
comments.quote: this is not actually the whole continent, leaving out boreal environments for example, as well as numerous unique ecological settings to the south

reviews.assessment: Appreciates the study design and idea, but doubts that bird prevalence from citizen-science data can support causal inference.
strengths: appreciates the main idea developed by the authors
study is clear and relatively well-designed
hurdle beta mixed models are a good choice for bounded positive responses

comments.issue: Key recent references on aquatic-terrestrial linkages are missing from the introduction.
comments.request: Add the suggested references to the introduction.
comments.quote: I would suggest adding these references in the Introduction section, considering the importance of such a section

comments.issue: Citizen-science bird data bring quality, rigour, bias and standardisation problems for the weighted prevalence metric.
comments.request: Discuss these limitations and provide evidence for the metric's reliability.
comments.quote: I am a little bit sceptical about the use of "weighted bird prevalence" as the main metric

comments.issue: A causal-effect analysis may not be valid when combining in-situ EPT richness with opportunistic bird prevalence data.
comments.request: Justify the causal interpretation or temper causal claims.
comments.quote: I am not sure that a causal-effect analysis like that could be performed using so different sources of information

title: Cross-ecosystem linkages between freshwater insects and riparian birds across the USA

study.system: multicellularity evolution model; Proterozoic ocean water column

editor_summary: Reviewers raise concerns; editor notes Reviewer 1 wants the Proterozoic Ocean part removed while the other two are enthusiastic, and recommends engaging better with recent literature.

reviews.assessment: Convinced by the framework and main conclusion, but wants O2 regimes tied to Proterozoic estimates and the timing question addressed.
strengths: integrates Proterozoic redox environment into modelling
well-written with well-designed equations and figures
discussion of culturing and experimental evolution

comments.issue: Model O2 regimes cannot be compared with current estimates of Proterozoic ocean O2.
comments.request: Relate the modelled O2 levels to Proterozoic O2 estimates.
comments.quote: As currently written, it is difficult to compare the O2 regimes used in the authors’ model to current estimates for the O2 content of the Proterozoic ocean.

comments.issue: The paper does not engage with the timing question of why multicellularity arose only late in the Proterozoic despite persistent O2 gradients.
comments.request: Discuss the timing question in light of the modelling results.
comments.quote: The reason why so many geobiologists explore specific environmental triggers (e.g., rising O2) and various direct benefits (e.g., escape from phagotrophic predation) during the origins of multicellularity is that they want to explain the timing of these transitions

comments.issue: Assumption that transitions occurred among planktonic marine forms is not justified by where and when these groups evolved multicellularity.
comments.request: Discuss the evolutionary setting to justify the model parameters.
comments.quote: This is assuming that these unicellular-multicellular transitions all occurred among (ancestrally) planktonic forms living in the marine water column? Is that the most likely scenario for animals and plants?

comments.issue: Relative phrases like 'oxygen-deprived' and 'lower layers' are confusing and imprecise.
comments.request: Clarify whether anoxic deep oceans or hypoxic shelves are meant.
comments.quote: the use of relative phrases like “oxygen-deprived” and “lower layers” is a bit confusing here (and elsewhere). First of all, even the air-saturated surface waters of the Neoproterozoic ocean were already “oxygen-deprived” by modern standards

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the 'oxygen-deprived lower layer' is anoxic.
comments.request: State whether the lower layer is free of dissolved O2.
comments.quote: is the “oxygen-deprived lower layer” anoxic (that is, free of dissolved O2)?

comments.issue: What 'low', 'moderate' and 'abundant' O2 mean and how they compare with Neoproterozoic estimates is unclear.
comments.request: Define the regimes and compare them to estimated concentrations.
comments.quote: Again, what does “low,” “moderate,” and “abundant” O2 mean? How do these regimes compare to the estimated O2 concentrations for the Neoproterozoic ocean?

comments.issue: Bozdag et al.'s moderate O2 (24-25% PAL) exceeds Proterozoic estimates (1-10% PAL), so comparisons need absolute ranges.
comments.request: Give absolute O2 ranges and compare with Proterozoic atmospheric and marine estimates.
comments.quote: This is why 1) absolute O2 concentration ranges, and 2) comparison with atmospheric and marine O2 estimates for the Proterozoic are required to make meaningful connections here.

reviews.assessment: Enthusiastic and finds the work convincing; offers presentation fixes and questions about boundaries, motility and mixing.

comments.issue: The slash between particles in Fig. 1a is confusing.

comments.quote: Even though it is explained in the text, I would add in the figure caption a note that rates m_{1,AB} and m_{1,BA} are the same for both types.

comments.issue: Definition of life-cycle size at line 254 is unclear; some intermediate cycles appear classified as large in Fig. S2.
comments.request: Explain how life-cycle size classes are defined and the Fig. S2 classification.
comments.quote: I think that it would be useful to comment on the definition of the size of life cycles at line 254. In particular, the size of the small cycles is only determined by N_S

comments.issue: Link between Fig. 4 panels c and d is unclear.
comments.request: Extend horizontal traits between panels and label sinking size on the y axis.
comments.quote: the relation between panels c and d of Fig. 4 might be made clearer by extending two horizontal traits between the final bar of panel c and the first bars of panel d

comments.issue: 'Anaerobic' is used where 'anoxic' is more appropriate.
comments.request: Use 'anoxic' for oxygen-free environments.
comments.quote: I think that anoxic rather than anaerobic would be a more appropriate term for characterizing an environment without oxygen.

comments.issue: Supplementary time-course figures for the regions of Fig. 4d are missing.

comments.issue: Origin and meaning of sharp boundaries in Fig. 2 parameter space are unclear.

comments.issue: Periodic mixing environments and fluid dynamics are not considered.

comments.issue: Whether lineages coexist with unicellular ancestors in nature is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss real examples of coexistence and its environmental basis.
comments.quote: I was wondering if there are examples of lineages that coexist, or not, with their unicellular ancestors, and, in case there are, if one can make sense of why they do/don’t coexist based on the properties of the environment

title: Direct benefits are not necessary for the evolution of multicellularity

comments.issue: Matching is flawed and point estimates vary by model; a DiD/BACI design would better support causality.
comments.request: Use a Difference-in-Differences/BACI design for newer PAs.
comments.quote: As the extent of protected areas has increased since the 2000s, why haven’t we focused on these protected areas and estimated a Difference in Difference / BACI model?

comments.issue: Panel data do not rule out migration bias; attrition differs across treatments.
comments.request: Correct the claim and address differential attrition.
comments.quote: I believe this claim is not correct. Yoi have attrition in your data, and this attrition can be different across treatments.

comments.issue: LSMS sampling weights were not used, biasing results.
comments.request: Apply LSMS sampling weights.
comments.quote: From your methodology, you don’t seem to have used the sampling weights of LSMS, which are necessary to produce unbiased results.

comments.issue: Table 1, said to detail LSMS outcomes, is missing from the manuscript.
comments.request: Provide Table 1.
comments.quote: You mention that you detail your LSMS outcomes in Table 1 but I can’t find the table in the manuscript.

comments.issue: Standard errors are not clustered above the matched-pair level.
comments.request: Cluster standard errors at enumeration-area or administrative level.
comments.quote: you could consider clustering your standard errors at a higher level than the matched pairs

title: Trade-offs between nature and people in Ethiopia’s protected areas demonstrate challenges in translating global conservation targets into national realities

study.system: white-faced capuchin groups; 33-year behavioural and remote-sensing data

editor_summary: Reviewers raise concerns that need addressing before publication; editor stresses that two reviewers could not access the code files, so accessibility of code must be improved.

reviews.assessment: Excited by the long-term dataset and approach, but finds the between-group competition interpretation overreaches the data.
strengths: excellent long-term dataset with broad cross-sectional sampling
novel attempt to disentangle within- and between-group competition

comments.issue: The opening suggests primacy of between-group competition benefits while largely ignoring predation risk as a benefit of group living.
comments.request: Acknowledge predation-sensitive strategies in the framing.
comments.quote: The first sentence suggests primacy of the benefits in between-group competition as a benefit of large group size, disregarding the impact of group size on predation risk.

comments.issue: The '+1' in t+1 is actually variable (up to 8 years), so the timing of group-size shifts and encroachment may not be tightly correlated.
comments.request: Clarify the lag structure and its consequences for interpretation.
comments.quote: it appears that the “+1” component of t+1 is actually variable (might this be better called “t+i”?)

comments.issue: Decreased home range overlap does not necessarily indicate territoriality.
comments.request: Temper the territoriality interpretation.
comments.quote: I’m hesitant about saying that decreased home range overlap suggests territoriality

comments.issue: Spatial separation after encounters need not mean territoriality or higher intergroup costs; avoiding depleted areas is an alternative.
comments.request: Repeat the directional range-shift analysis using the wet-dry season transition.
comments.quote: Again just because frequent encounters lead to spatial separation does not mean that the mechanism is territoriality or increased IGE costs for subordinate groups.

comments.issue: The interpretation is inconsistent with the data: large groups still face lower intake without reduced travel costs, so net energy gain should be lower.
comments.request: Revise the interpretation of between-group versus within-group competition.
comments.quote: Lower intake in large groups is not balanced by reduced travel costs, so one would predict lower average net energy gain in large groups.

comments.issue: The claim exceeds the data because large groups do not do better than small groups in the dry season.
comments.request: Run an additional analysis including dry-season severity.
comments.quote: This last point seems to be exceeding the data, as well.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether line 61 reports percent time or amount consumed.
comments.request: State the basis of the measure.
comments.quote: Line 61: Should provide whether this is percent time or based on amount consumed.

comments.issue: Figure S3b colour key appears based on mean NDVI but the colour-change values are inconsistent with it.
comments.request: Clarify or correct the colour key.
comments.quote: The key to the colors seems to be based on mean NDVI (same as represented in the y-axis), but the y-values where colors change are inconsistent.

comments.issue: The assumption at lines 893-894 conflicts with species that maintain low overlap through frequent border interactions.
comments.request: Reconsider this assumption.
comments.quote: This assumption seems out of keeping with territoriality in some species wherein lower overlap is maintained specifically through frequent interactions at borders.

comments.issue: The data could not be accessed by the reviewer.
comments.request: Make the data and code files accessible.
comments.quote: Attempts to review the data came up with "the requested file is not found".

reviews.assessment: Excellent study with a remarkable dataset, clear writing and robust analyses; critiques are minimal.

comments.issue: The distinction between within-group contest and scramble competition is not addressed explicitly.
comments.request: Clarify the competition types or state the focus on scramble competition.
comments.quote: I wonder if the authors could succinctly address the distinction between within-group contest competition vs. within-group scramble competition.

comments.issue: How group identity is handled after permanent fission or fusion is unclear.
comments.request: Explain which fission product retained the group name and the implications.
comments.quote: my understanding of Figure 1c raises the question of group id following a permanent fission (or fusion)

comments.issue: Proportional overlap may not distinguish encroachment by a neighbour from encroaching into a neighbour's space.
comments.request: Clarify what proportional overlap measures and its limits.
comments.quote: how does proportional overlap provide insight into encroachment by neighbor as opposed to encroaching into a neighbor's space?

reviews.assessment: Beautiful, spectacular case study; asks for better inference criteria and more scrutiny of derived response variables.
strengths: beautiful case study of the Ecological Constraints Model
clear organization and compelling logical structure

comments.issue: 'Demography' is used as a synonym for group size, ignoring relatedness and age/sex composition.
comments.request: Do not call group size demography.
comments.quote: I thought the use of the term “demography” as synonymous with group size throughout the manuscript was a little misleading.

comments.issue: The competition presentation is static; dominance hierarchies and coordination problems are not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention these social dynamics in the introduction and/or discussion.
comments.quote: The presentation of within- and between-group competition felt a little static on occasion

comments.issue: 89% HPDIs are used as arbitrary cut-offs, which is over-generous for claiming effects.
comments.request: Report 50% and 95% HPDIs and the posterior probability supporting each effect.
comments.quote: The most serious ‘minor’ gripe I have with this study, however, is the idiosyncratic use of 89% HPDIs in the presentation of statistical results.

comments.issue: Several response variables are derived modelled estimates rather than empirically observed values.
comments.request: Address the implications of using modelled estimates as responses.
comments.quote: at least 3 of the 7 response variables (daily path length, revisitation rate, and encounter rate) are highly derived, modelled estimates, rather than empirically observed values

comments.issue: The biological information content of the derived metrics is unclear.
comments.request: Expand on what these metrics biologically represent.
comments.quote: to varying degrees, I am unsure of the biological information content of these metrics, so this should be expanded upon

comments.issue: Using modelled estimates as responses risks error propagation, non-independence and double-counting.
comments.request: Explicitly address error propagation, independence and double-counting.
comments.quote: I can see at least 3 methodological caveats with specifying a modelled estimate as the response variable in a subsequent model.

comments.issue: Revisitation rate as a global home range metric lacks biological relevance; it suits depletable resources instead.
comments.request: Justify or reconsider this metric.
comments.quote: I genuinely struggle to see, for example, the biological relevance of revisitation rate, calculated as it is here, as a global home range metric

comments.issue: The encounter rate ignores that animals detect and react to each other, so it reflects a null collision model.
comments.request: Clarify how this measure captures actual encounters and competition.
comments.quote: the ‘ctmm’ algorithm does not take into account that animals detect (and react to) each other’s proximity, well ahead of an encounter

comments.issue: It is unclear whether modelled estimates can be treated as independent; residual independence and a multivariate approach are not reported.
comments.request: Report residual independence and consider a multivariate model.
comments.quote: I’m not even sure to what extent modelled estimates can indeed be viewed as independent values, given that they are a function of the same underlying data and ‘ctmm’ model structure

comments.issue: Secondary models may re-test patterns built into the derived outcomes, double-counting effects and biasing effect sizes.
comments.request: Address this double-counting risk.
comments.quote: thereby double-counting effects. This may result in biased and/or inflated estimates of effect sizes in the Bayesian models.

comments.issue: 'Mediated by additional ecological and social factors' could instead say modulated by local heterogeneity.
comments.request: Consider the alternative wording.
comments.quote: “mediated by additional ecological and social factors” Or, alternatively, modulated by local heterogeneity.

comments.issue: The posterior probability supporting each hypothesis is only reported for one effect.
comments.request: Report the posterior probability for all effects.
comments.quote: Here you actually report the proportion of the posterior probability that supports your hypothesis (PP > 0= 0.94). I would like to see this reported for all effects!

comments.issue: Predicted encounter rates are not validated against observed encounter rates.
comments.request: Empirically validate the derived estimates.
comments.quote: How do these predicted encounter rates relate to observed encounter rates: was there any way to empirically validate these derived estimates?

comments.issue: Group demography is not the same as group size.
comments.request: Use precise terminology.
comments.quote: Line 133 Group demography is not the same as group size!

comments.issue: There is no evidence that smaller groups' home ranges are marginal in terms of lower NDVI.
comments.request: Remove or qualify the claim.
comments.quote: But you didn’t find evidence in your study that home ranges of smaller groups are marginal in terms of lower NDVI values.

comments.issue: The cognitive-abilities passage is overly speculative and unsupported by the data.
comments.request: Temper or remove this speculation.
comments.quote: You certainly can’t say anything about this on the basis of the data you present in this study, so it reads a little overly speculative.

comments.issue: 'These constraints are not fixed' rebuts a claim nobody appears to have made.
comments.request: Remove or rephrase the statement.
comments.quote: “these constraints are not fixed” I’m not aware of anyone ever claiming they were?

comments.issue: Arguing that habitat fragmentation should favour larger groups is speculative.
comments.request: Temper the climate-change/fragmentation claim.
comments.quote: It's rather speculative to argue that, on the basis of your study, habitat fragmentation should favour larger groups.

comments.issue: Only one response variable was validated; similar validations for the others are missing.
comments.request: Validate the other response variables similarly.
comments.quote: Nice that you could validate the soundness of this approach: would have been great to see similar validations of your other response variables.

comments.issue: A single global value per home range may hide very different local scenarios.
comments.request: Justify the use of a single global value.
comments.quote: Are you sure that a similar global value cannot come about through very different local scenario’s within a home range?!

comments.issue: Triadic overlap handling is unclear; dyadic proportional overlaps could sum to over 100%.
comments.request: Explain how triadic overlaps were handled.
comments.quote: How did you handle triadic home range overlap? It seems possible, in theory, for a group to have its different dyadic POs to sum up to over 100% with your current definition.

comments.issue: The number of dyads analysed is not reported.
comments.request: Report the number of dyads.
comments.quote: How many of these dyads were there?

comments.issue: The definition assumes groups are impervious to each other's proximity, which is unrealistic.
comments.request: Reconsider this assumption.
comments.quote: This definition assumes that groups are impervious to each other’s proximity or general whereabouts, a very unrealistic assumption.

comments.issue: Whether the relative overlap values are biologically interpretable at all is questioned.
comments.request: Clarify the biological interpretation.
comments.quote: But, are they even interpretable in a biologically meaningful way at all?

comments.issue: Dependency among the outcome variables should be accounted for, e.g. with a multivariate model.
comments.request: Consider an explicitly multivariate model framework.
comments.quote: I wonder whether the dependency between the different outcomes could/should have been taken into account, in an explicitly multivariate model framework for example.

title: Environmental fluctuations alter the competitive trade-offs of group size in a social primate

study.system: global REDD+ avoided-deforestation carbon projects; quasi-experimental impact evaluation

editor_summary: Three reviewers find considerable potential interest but raise substantial concerns that must be addressed before a revised version can be considered.

reviews.assessment: Questions whether the results could reflect sample selection or outcome definition rather than genuine over-crediting, and asks for clearer methods and definitions.

comments.issue: The sample may suffer selection bias because it is essentially the same as the prior study plus one project.
comments.request: State that the same sample is re-analysed or explain how the sample was selected.
comments.quote: One possible reason is selection bias in the sample of projects

comments.issue: The source of the 71-project list and the criteria for the less-than-80%-evergreen screening are not explained.
comments.request: Explain the source of the project list and the evergreen-forest criteria.
comments.quote: Alternatively, they should explain the source of their list of 71 projects

comments.issue: The matching criteria determining which treated plots could not be matched are not restated.
comments.request: Restate the methods and criteria used to determine matchability.
comments.quote: it would be worth re-stating the methods and criteria used to determine that a plot could not be matched.

comments.issue: How sample characteristics change as the sample is narrowed is not summarised for the reader.
comments.request: Present a summary of sample characteristics at each narrowing step.
comments.quote: present a summary of how sample characteristics (at least project size, country, verifier, etc.) change as they narrow the sample

comments.issue: The deforestation outcome is not clearly defined.
comments.request: Define the deforestation outcome explicitly.
comments.quote: A second possible concern is the definition of the deforestation outcome

comments.issue: Whether and how proximity to previous deforestation, a strong determinant, was matched on is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the matching on proximity to previous deforestation.
comments.quote: whether/how you match on proximity to previous deforestation, which is often one of the strongest determinants of deforestation.

comments.issue: The terms degraded, deforested, disturbed and forest cover lost are used inconsistently.
comments.request: Define these terms and distinguish degraded forest from cleared forest.
comments.quote: I am confused about your use of the terms degraded, deforested, disturbed, and forest cover lost.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether forward stepwise selection pooled data from all countries into one model.
comments.request: Clarify the stepwise selection and pooling of countries.
comments.quote: Clarify if used forward stepwise selection with pooled data from all countries to generate one model.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the half-moon axis symbols in Figure 5 mean statistics exceed the plotted scale.
comments.request: Confirm the meaning of the half-moon symbols.
comments.quote: In Figure 5, it appears that the half moons on the axes means statistics that are too large to portray

comments.issue: Table S1 uses the Figure 4 colour scheme rather than the Figure 1 scheme.
comments.request: Fix the colour scheme used in Table S1.
comments.quote: In Table S1, the color scheme appears to be from Figure 4 (not Figure 1).

comments.issue: The five apparently under-credited projects are not characterised.
comments.request: Comment on their region, forest type and baseline methodology.
comments.quote: What more can be said about the 5 projects that apparently were under-credited?

comments.issue: The Peru 1360 effect estimate differs substantially from the earlier study.
comments.request: Explain the discrepancy in the Peru 1360 estimate.
comments.quote: The estimated effect of project Peru 1360 is very different in this paper than in the previous Guizar-Cutino paper. Why?

comments.issue: The term 'certified avoided deforestation' is undefined.
comments.request: Define whether this means credits generated, registered, sold or retired.
comments.quote: What is meant by “certified avoided deforestation”? Is this carbon credits generated, registered, sold, or retired from the projects?

comments.issue: What selling credits based on ex-post evaluations would require, and whether dynamic baselines suffice, is not discussed.
comments.request: Comment on requirements for ex-post-based credit sales and dynamic baselines.
comments.quote: please comment on what would be required to sell projects based on ex-post evaluations of avoided deforestation. Could this be the “dynamic baselines” now accepted by Verra?

reviews.assessment: Very positive; asks to clarify the introduction's framing and to express over-crediting in terms of issued credits rather than hectares.
strengths: important contribution to carbon market integrity
broad interest to policy and climate finance audiences

comments.issue: The introduction does not make clear how unobservable confounders are addressed via the strongest observable confounder.
comments.request: State this framing up front and move the Fisher anecdote earlier.
comments.quote: the introduction leaves the reader wondering how the authors address unobservable confounders

comments.issue: Over-crediting is expressed in hectares, which vary in carbon content, rather than in issued credits.
comments.request: Express over-crediting in issued credits, e.g. using the Probst et al. achievement ratio.
comments.quote: it would be even more informative to relate this directly to issued credits rather than hectares

reviews.assessment: Values both goals but finds the paper falls short, recommending panel methods and greater emphasis on sensitivity analysis over matching.
strengths: important contribution on the scale of overcrediting
promising demonstration of sensitivity analyses for ecologists

comments.issue: The paper discards panel structure and does not use staggered difference-in-differences, which better isolates causal effects.
comments.request: Use a staggered difference-in-differences panel design.
comments.quote: Why didn’t the authors pursue a staggered difference in differences research design?

comments.issue: Covariates are temporally invariant, but suitable time-varying alternatives are available.
comments.request: Consider gridded population, night lights and price-interaction variables.
comments.quote: it seems like there might be other several other variables that could serve as useful alternatives including: gridded population data, night lights data

comments.issue: Decisions constrained by comparability to the prior study weaken the paper as a stand-alone contribution.
comments.request: Strengthen the paper as a stand-alone contribution rather than maintaining consistency.
comments.quote: I believe the authors could strengthen this paper as a stand-alone contribution if they didn’t feel the need to maintain consistency across these two studies.

comments.issue: Methods emphasise matching while the core sensitivity analysis is minor in space, misaligned with the stated goals.
comments.request: Rebalance the methods to emphasise the sensitivity analysis.
comments.quote: the methods section on “matching” is 1088 words, while the (final) section on the sensitivity analysis that represents the core results presented in the paper is only 171 words.

comments.issue: The literature review and implementation description of sensitivity analysis are too thin.
comments.request: Expand the sensitivity-analysis literature and describe OLS versus matching implementations.
comments.quote: provided a more comprehensive description of the literature on, and the authors’ implementation of the sensitivity analysis

comments.issue: Several line-level copy edits (odd word choice, typos).
comments.quote: Line 52: “unpicking” is an odd word here, maybe “unpacking”?

comments.issue: What counts as an 'independent study' is unclear; some are supported by verification bodies or share authors.
comments.request: Define what is meant by 'independent studies'.
comments.quote: What do the authors mean by “independent studies”? Aren’t some of these supported by REDD+ verification bodies?

comments.issue: The research design is described only vaguely as using 'sophisticated statistical methods'.
comments.request: Name the specific method at that point.
comments.quote: The authors are a bit vague in how they describe their research design as using “sophisticated statistical methods.”

comments.issue: The additional analyses on alternative model structures are not synthesised into conclusions.
comments.request: Summarise what can be concluded from the additional model structures.
comments.quote: You ran lots of additional analyses on different model structures – is there anything useful to conclude based on that?

comments.issue: Crediting performance is assessed only per project, not for the overarching portfolio.
comments.request: Use the sensitivity analysis to make portfolio-level crediting statements.
comments.quote: Can you reflect on your sensitivity analysis to make statements about the crediting performance of the overarching portfolio of projects

comments.issue: Too little intuition is given about how the comparison informs potential confounding.
comments.request: Add an intuitive explanation linking the comparison to confounding.
comments.quote: I think it’d be useful to provide a bit more intuition about how this comparison provides information about potential confounding.

comments.issue: Caveats are limited to sample selection bias, omitting cross-sectional and sensitivity-analysis limitations.
comments.request: Add caveats about cross-sectional analysis, sensitivity analysis and observable confounders.
comments.quote: Are there any other caveats you might want to raise about the broader analysis?

comments.issue: An unfinished placeholder ('avoided XX ha of deforestation') remains in the text.
comments.request: Replace the XX placeholder with the correct number.
comments.quote: Line 181: “avoided XX ha of deforestation”

comments.issue: The order of the figures should be reconsidered.
comments.request: Re-order the figures.
comments.quote: Line 200: May want to re-order figures

comments.issue: The choice of the TMF dataset rather than GFC is not justified given the noted limitation.
comments.request: Justify using TMF rather than GFC.
comments.quote: Given this limitation, why do you use the TMF dataset rather than GFC?

comments.issue: Projects starting before 2000 are dropped even though JRC data go back to 1990.
comments.request: Explain why pre-2000 projects were dropped.
comments.quote: Why did you need to drop projects starting before 2000? Given that you’re using JRC data, you can go back to 1990.

comments.issue: The basis for the cut-off is not explained.
comments.request: Explain how the cut-off was chosen.
comments.quote: Line 233: How did you decide upon this cut-off?

comments.issue: The reason for sub-sampling before matching is unclear.
comments.request: Explain why sub-sampling preceded matching.
comments.quote: Line 235: Why did you do this sub-sampling before matching?

comments.issue: 'Confounders' and 'covariate set' sections use the terms interchangeably.
comments.request: Distinguish theoretical confounders from matching covariates and integrate the sections.
comments.quote: You have sections on both “confounders” and “covariate set” but seem to use these terms somewhat interchangeably.

comments.issue: Observed and unobserved confounders and their treatment in the prior deforestation and REDD+ bias literature are incompletely described.
comments.request: Add a fuller description of these confounders and the prior literature.
comments.quote: I think a more complete description of these confounders, both observed and unobserved, and how they’ve been discussed in the prior literature

comments.issue: The propensity score subclass analysis is motivated by problems with difference-in-differences although DiD is not used.
comments.request: Clarify the motivation for the propensity score subclass analysis.
comments.quote: Here you motivate your propensity score subclass analysis by describing issues with difference in difference estimators, but my understanding is that you’re not using DiD?

comments.issue: The sensitivity analysis could include additional variables such as night lights, population and agricultural suitability.
comments.request: Expand the sensitivity analysis with these additional variables.
comments.quote: Additional variables that might be worth including to expand the sensitivity analysis: Night lights as a proxy for income; gridded population; FAO agricultural suitability or potential yields

title: Unobserved confounders cannot explain over-crediting in avoided deforestation carbon projects

study.system: eukaryotic osmotrophs (fungi, pseudofungi, labyrinthulids, teretosporeans); phylogenomics, dating and HGT analyses

editor_summary: Editor cannot accept but invites revision: Reviewer 1's major reservations about eukaryote phylogeny, limited taxon sampling and HGT inference reliability must all be addressed (echoed by Reviewer 3), with R1 sign-off needed.

reviews.assessment: Sees value in the understudied topic but has major reservations about the controversial tree topology, limited taxon sampling and HGT inference reliability.

comments.issue: Event-order inferences rest on a single controversial tree topology; root and higher taxa are uncertain.
comments.request: Discuss topological uncertainty and temper the inferred order of events.
comments.quote: the inferences about order of events in evolution of osmotrophy are much more uncertain than presented here

comments.issue: Alternative origin of genes via cooption from other metabolisms is excluded.
comments.request: Consider gene cooption from other functions.
comments.quote: This logical framework also excludes the possibility that some genes have been coopted from other metabolisms

comments.issue: Only 86 lineages sampled, likely biasing osmocluster and background-cluster inferences.
comments.request: Expand taxon sampling across eukaryotes.
comments.quote: The study relies on data from only 86 lineages!

comments.issue: Mixotrophic and phototrophic lineages unsampled, weakening power and interpretations of osmotrophy as distinct.
comments.request: Sample key mixotrophic and phototrophic lineages.
comments.quote: Not sampling key lineages will decrease the power of the study, and weaken the interpretations

comments.issue: Molecular clock interpretation is problematic given the limited number of sampled taxa.
comments.request: Strengthen dating or qualify clock-based conclusions.
comments.quote: The interpretation of the clock here is also problematic given the limited number of taxa sampled

comments.issue: Discussion ignores other events and key literature from the 800-1000 Ma focal period.
comments.request: Discuss contemporary events and cite key papers.
comments.quote: the manuscript would be improved with a greater discussion of the other events that likely occurred during the focal time period of 800-1000mya

comments.issue: HGT interpretation ignores gene loss and unstable topologies; caveats and literature are neglected.
comments.request: Explore alternative topologies (e.g. AU tests) and acknowledge uncertainties.
comments.quote: interpretation of single gene trees requires considerable more finesse to account for gene loss and unstable tree topologies

comments.issue: Last sentence of the abstract lacks logical flow.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence.
comments.quote: The logical flow of the last sentence of the abstract could be improved

comments.issue: All osmotrophs are equated with decomposers, but many parasites are osmotrophs.
comments.request: Correct the generalisation.
comments.quote: I am unconvinced that all osmotrophs are decomposers

comments.issue: 'Canonical phagotrophy is absent' claim is circular given the definitions used.
comments.request: Revise the claim.
comments.quote: The claim that 'canonical phagotrophy is also absent' (line 91) in osmotrophs seems a bit circular given definitions here

comments.issue: Coenocytic/syncytial development is not unique to osmotrophs as claimed.
comments.request: Acknowledge its occurrence in other groups.
comments.quote: the association of "​multinucleated coenocytic/syncytial development" with osmotrophy misses that these features are also widespread among photosynthetic 'algae' and in many phagotrophic amoeboid groups

comments.issue: 'Specialisation must require gene content changes' ignores exaptation and simple gene loss.
comments.request: Revise this logic.
comments.quote: this could be an exaptation, or a simple case of gene loss

comments.issue: Quotes from past literature feel forced and unclear.
comments.request: Tone down and clarify quotations.
comments.quote: Perhaps 'tone down' quotes from past literature as at times they feel forced and they may not be widely accessible

comments.issue: Figure images are not easily readable.
comments.request: Improve figure quality.
comments.quote: The quality of figures could be improved to make images more easily readable

comments.issue: Discussion is surprisingly brief; relevant literature is missing.
comments.request: Expand the discussion with more literature.
comments.quote: The brevity of the discussion is surprising, and incorporating more literature (including those linked above) would strengthen the manuscript

reviews.assessment: Very positive; calls the study rigorous and acceptable pending only two minor wording corrections.
strengths: rigorous study of evolutionary origins of osmotrophy
reasonable assessment supported by fossil-record timing

comments.issue: Grammar: 'have received' should be used at abstract L24 and discussion L318.
comments.request: Change to 'have received'.
comments.quote: Abstract Line 24 and Discussion Line 318: I would say "have received"

comments.issue: Describing reticulate evolution as species or branches 'merging' is incorrect and informal.
comments.request: Revise the L46-51 section.
comments.quote: I don't think it's correct at all to state that RE is a process by which species or branches of a phylogeny can "merge" either by endosymbiosis or HGT

reviews.assessment: Values the extensive work but finds the manuscript obscured by conceptual confusion, unclear hypotheses and non-linear structure needing considerable rewriting.
strengths: extensive support for HGT-driven adaptation to osmotrophy

comments.issue: Introduction lacks the specific questions and hypotheses, which appear only later or in the methods.
comments.request: State questions and hypotheses in the introduction.
comments.quote: the introduction discusses some generalities about the importance of endosymbiosis but does not present the specific questions and hypotheses actually addressed in the present research

comments.issue: No thorough comparison with photoautotrophs; shared gene enrichment undermines the 'osmotrophic toolkit' concept.
comments.request: Address the photoautotroph overlap or refocus on the phylogenetic side.
comments.quote: if the same genes are enriched in osmotrophs and photoautotrophs, can these genes be considered an "osmotrophic toolkit"?

comments.issue: Function versus shared phylogeny as drivers of gene enrichment is not disentangled.
comments.request: Add comparative data and tests or discuss this confound.
comments.quote: How can one differentiate between function and phylogeny as drivers of the observed patterns?

comments.issue: 'Osmogroup' is confusing: it loses 'troph' and clashes with 'osmoclusters' and orthogroups.
comments.request: Rename to unambiguous terms such as 'osmotrophic lineages'.
comments.quote: The use of the term "osmogroup" (meaning osmotrophic eukaryotic groups) is extremely confusing and unnecessary

comments.issue: Abstract equates osmotrophs with decomposers, but not all decomposers are osmotrophs.
comments.request: Correct this concept.
comments.quote: in the abstract, osmotrophs are equated with decomposers

comments.issue: Title implying higher trophic complexity of osmotrophy is misleading.
comments.request: Focus the title on osmotrophy.
comments.quote: Even the title of the article is a bit misleading in this sense

comments.issue: Whittaker's outdated evolutionary scheme does not support, and in fact contradicts, the argument.
comments.request: Drop the Whittaker reference.
comments.quote: Whittaker – please, drop the reference to his work

comments.issue: Bacterial gene donors ('non-eukaryotic donors') are unidentified and undiscussed.
comments.request: Identify and discuss the prokaryotic donors.
comments.quote: Which are the bacterial donors? This information is missing or so hidden that it is impossible to retrieve

comments.issue: Dating section would fit better later, close to the discussion.
comments.request: Reorganise the dating section.
comments.quote: potentially this part would rather benefit from being introduced later, close to the discussion

comments.issue: Poorly resolved gene trees make the number of false-positive HGT calls unclear.
comments.request: Discuss and estimate false-positive HGT rates.
comments.quote: many gene trees are poorly resolved. How to discriminate between poor signal and real HGT?

title: Signatures of gene transfer in the parallel evolution of osmotrophic specialization in eukaryotes

study.system: fossil cetacean Kalakocetus; Eocene India, dental and phylogenetic analyses

editor_summary: Reviewers raise concerns to address before publication; respond to criticisms and editorial concerns and highlight all changes.

reviews.assessment: Essential contribution, but the abstract and introduction undermine its importance and several statements need correction.
strengths: thorough analysis based on limited fossil evidence

comments.issue: The abstract and introduction undermine the contribution, use unexplained dental jargon, and lack a broad closing view.

comments.issue: 'Cupid' is not a tooth cusp.

comments.issue: The phrase 'on the setting up' at line 233 is unclear.

comments.quote: Except for minor issues (see below), I’d only have one more substantial recommendation for the authors, namely addressing the fact that raoellids and cetaceans are now known to be components of the same fauna.

comments.issue: What parts of the dentary and symphysis are preserved, including its medial surface, should be specified more explicitly.

comments.issue: A sister-group is referred to as ancestral.

comments.issue: Panel d corresponds to the medial, not lateral, view.

comments.issue: Supplementary Data 3, 4 and 6 are not provided as processed program files.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether Lower and Upper Subathu can be placed on the log in Figure S1.

comments.quote: Fig. S1 Could "Lower Subathu" and "Upper Subathu" be placed on the log?

comments.issue: When discussing loadings, their contribution to the PCs should be described rather than explained variance.

comments.issue: The abstract does not mention the functional results.

comments.issue: Potential food items are only suggested in SI section 4.4, not in the discussion.

comments.issue: No sentence summarizes the function based on all analyses at line 220.
comments.request: Add a summarizing sentence or two.
comments.quote: 3) Line 220: a sentence (or two) summarizing the function based on all analyses would be very welcome.

comments.issue: 'A more carnivorous' diet is vague and used with different meanings across three contexts, really meaning omnivorous.

comments.quote: 4) Lines 218, 240 and 244: what is meant exactly with “a more carnivorous” diet? It is used three times, with slightly different context (“adaptation to”, “initial shift”, “further specialization”). This is all a bit vague; it all means “omnivorous”.

comments.issue: CT scanning metadata are sparse and two different voxel sizes are reported without explanation.

comments.issue: The MorphoMuseuM upload was not accessible so the provided material could not be checked.

comments.issue: No R script is provided for the dental topographic analysis.

comments.issue: Height maps and processing documents for the DMTA are not supplied for reproducibility.

comments.issue: Figure 3 colour and symbol information is in the caption rather than a legend.

comments.issue: Extended Data Figure 4 quality is low in the merged PDF.

comments.issue: Figure 4b axes are labelled Dim1/Dim2 while the title and caption say PC1-PC3, and the data are not PC1-PC2.

comments.issue: The type and size of the ellipses plotted are not reported in the caption.

comments.issue: SI files lack internal titles and are only provided in DOCX, making files hard to identify.
comments.request: Add titles within all SI documents and convert DOCX to PDF.
comments.quote: for the review process, the filenames have been changed but the formats have not. This means that it was actually quite annoying to find the correct file, as the tables don’t have titles in the document.

comments.issue: The SI table of contents lacks hyperlinks.
comments.request: Add hyperlinks to the table of contents.
comments.quote: a. Adding hyperlinks to the table of content is very easy in Word and would be nice for the readers.

comments.issue: Babiacetus is not identified on Figure 3, making the results hard to follow.
comments.request: Identify Babiacetus on Figure 3.
comments.quote: b. Lines 609-619: Babiacetus is not identified on Fig. 3 so it’s difficult to follow these results.

comments.issue: The claim that raoellid diet was diversified is an overstatement based on 7 specimens of 2 species without comparison to other groups.
comments.request: Temper the diet diversification claim and add comparisons.
comments.quote: c. Line 653: I think that “the diet of raoellids was diversified” is an overstatement with 7 specimens belonging to 2 species, even with the small number of specimens being acknowledged at the beginning of the sentence.

comments.issue: The French acronym ACP is used for PCA in Supplementary Data 5 and 6.

comments.request: Provide scripts as .R files and include the input file.

comments.issue: Six typographical errors (comma, capitalisation, missing bracket, italics, plurals).
comments.quote: 18) Line 303: close bracket after “surface texture analysis using ISO parameters60-62”

title: A basal representative of Cetacea from the Eocene of India

study.system: golden jackals, wolves and humans; acoustic monitoring and distribution models across Europe

editor_summary: Reviewers find the work of considerable potential interest; Reviewer 3 raises major concerns about the human-shield framing, unrealistic scenarios and unsupported continent-wide predictions; revision invited.

reviews.assessment: Positive; finds the study well constructed and analyses effective but questions snow-cover confounding and wants a stronger tradeoff discussion.

comments.issue: Snow cover duration may be confounded with unmodelled landscape measures such as elevation or ruggedness.
comments.request: Consider correlated landscape predictors or discuss this limitation.
comments.quote: Do you think snow cover duration is correlated with other landscape measures not included in your models (e.g., elevation, terrain ruggedness) that might better predict jackal occurrence/range expansion

comments.issue: Discussion does not adequately address tradeoffs and benefits, especially wolf-jackal coexistence and conflict.
comments.request: Discuss wolf-jackal tradeoffs at agricultural, exurban and urban interfaces.
comments.quote: I do not find the points highlighted adequately address potential tradeoffs and benefits that would be useful for the reader to draw from this study

comments.issue: Feeding slaughter remains to jackals is unlikely to be an ecosystem service and may cause conflict.
comments.request: Reconsider this claim.
comments.quote: I'm not sure I agree that intentional feeding of slaughter remains (offal) to jackals would constitute an ecosystem service

comments.issue: Statement at L349-351 lacks support without discussion of conflict and coexistence tradeoffs.
comments.request: Justify it with the suggested tradeoff discussion.
comments.quote: This statement would be better justified with the suggested discussion of conflict/coexistence tradeoffs

comments.issue: Concluding sentence is nebulous and raises unanswered questions about ecosystem function.
comments.request: Tie the conclusion back to jackals and their functional role.
comments.quote: The concluding sentence feels overly nebulous, leaving me with questions that the study didn't address

comments.issue: Dashed lines in Fig. 3 showing jackal distribution and sampled area are hard to see.
comments.request: Improve the visibility of these lines.
comments.quote: The dashed lines indicating current jackal distribution/area sampled with bioacoustic sensors is difficult to see

comments.issue: Line-level copy edits: L194-195 awkward sentence, L309 phrase, L758 'prevalence' vs 'occurrence'.
comments.quote: Awkward sentence. Consider a semi-colon or otherwise rewording.

comments.issue: L291-297 sentence would be clearer if the four scenarios were listed.
comments.request: List the four wolf-presence scenarios.
comments.quote: This sentence would be easier to follow if the four scenarios were listed

comments.issue: Unclear whether 'field-recorded' data are acoustic surveys or observations; R version not reported.
comments.request: Clarify the data source and report the R version.
comments.quote: Are you referring to acoustic surveys or observations when mentioning "field-recorded" occurrence data?

reviews.assessment: Very positive; only asks for extra methodological details on playback elicitation, species identification and detection rates, none challenging the results.
strengths: robust statistics with clear data presentation

comments.issue: Details of the elicitation playback experiments and how calls were selected are missing.
comments.request: Fully describe playback methods and call selection.
comments.quote: there are some missing details on how the elicitation playback experiments were performed and how the calls were selected for playback

comments.issue: Usual success rate of this playback method is not reported.
comments.request: Report the typical response rate (e.g. Jaeger et al. 53%).
comments.quote: it is not clear from the current write-up what the usual success rate is for this type of playback

comments.issue: Wolf howls may suppress jackal responses, so jackal presence could be underestimated where wolves occur.
comments.request: Mention this potential detection-rate effect.
comments.quote: jackal presence may be underestimated if wolves are present already

comments.issue: Data collection needs a more detailed description.
comments.request: Add detailed description of how data were collected.
comments.quote: it would be better to include a more detailed description of how the data were collected

comments.issue: Line 680 details missing: repetition, call origin, selection, solo/chorus, duration.
comments.request: Report these playback details.
comments.quote: How often were the howls repeated per night, if no response was heard?

comments.issue: Species identification method (listening, spectrograms, second listener) is not described.
comments.request: Add details on species identification.
comments.quote: Can you add brief details on how the species ID was done? By listening alone, or inspection of spectrograms

comments.issue: Response rate of this study is not confirmed for wolf presence versus absence.
comments.request: Report the response rate with and without wolves.
comments.quote: It would just be good to confirm the response rate here in the presence and absence of wolves

comments.issue: Supplementary Table 1 lacks a column for howl response rate.
comments.request: Add a response-rate column to Supplementary Table 1.
comments.quote: Could you please just add a column for a rate of howl responses?

comments.issue: 'Unrestricted by human pressure' at L343 is unclear and unlikely to occur in Europe.
comments.request: Clarify the intended meaning (e.g. 'relative').
comments.quote: Can you please just clarify what you mean by "unrestricted by human pressure"?

comments.issue: A directly relevant recent paper (Smith et al. 2025) is missing from the literature review.
comments.request: Cite Smith et al. 2025.
comments.quote: I would note that there is one recent paper that the authors might like to add to their literature review

reviews.assessment: Praises the monitoring and analysis but believes the human-shield emphasis and continent-wide predictions are unsupported and misleading.
strengths: impressive study with very high monitoring effort
perfectly executed from an analytical perspective

comments.issue: Manuscript is overly complicated; some analyses seem implemented just because they could be.
comments.request: Remove or revisit the unnecessary analyses.
comments.quote: I also found the manuscript overly complicated and I recommend that the authors remove or revisit a range of the analysis

comments.issue: No-wolf and full-wolf coverage scenarios are unrealistic and their conclusions untenable.
comments.request: Use realistic scenarios or move these to supplementary material.
comments.quote: Neither of these are realistic and the lessons inferred from them and the data produced are untenable

comments.issue: Monitoring mostly outside current wolf distribution biases inference and its continental extrapolation.
comments.request: Assess the sampling bias and its propagation.
comments.quote: most monitoring exists outside wolf distribution. As such, the inference is likely biased and this bias is very likely propagate and explode

comments.issue: Wolf distribution types and prediction uncertainty are not mapped.
comments.request: Add a wolf distribution map and a residuals/CV uncertainty map.
comments.quote: The predictive map Figure would benefit from a residuals, CV or other uncertainty type of map

comments.issue: Strong assertions about wolf role and human shield rest on very uncertain data and assumptions.
comments.request: Temper the assertions.
comments.quote: The authors make very strong assertions based on very uncertain data and HUGE assumptions about wolf functional role and human shield effect

comments.issue: Transposing Eastern European ecological relationships to Western Europe is unsupported.
comments.request: Justify transferability or restrict the predictions.
comments.quote: the assumptions of ecological relations in Eastern Europe being transposed to Western Europe are not supported, from wolf recovery to the human shield

comments.issue: Stray and free-ranging dogs offer an alternative explanation for jackals avoiding settlements.
comments.request: Consider this alternative explanation.
comments.quote: The presence of pack of stray and free ranging dogs alone can be used to explain avoidance of settlements

comments.issue: Areal future-range estimates are unreliable and the many assumptions driving them are untested.
comments.request: Add uncertainty and sensitivity estimates.
comments.quote: the areal estimates of future ranges are very likely unreliable and potentially misleading

comments.issue: Title is misleading: wolf presence, not the human shield, is the main driver.
comments.request: Revise the title to reflect the main finding.
comments.quote: The title is misleading since the human shield, while a very sexy concept, is trumped by wolf presence and is wolves that drive Golden Jackal distribution

comments.issue: Modeling framework should be revisited, including spatially varying specifications across gradients.
comments.request: Refine models (e.g. geographic weighted regression) and validate within the data area.
comments.quote: implement models that weigh variables differently based on geography (geographic weighted regression, spatial factors etc.)

comments.issue: Continental-scale mesocarnivore expansion is not unique; coyote expansion has been studied for decades.
comments.request: Acknowledge prior coyote work and temper the claim.
comments.quote: this is not an unique case (mesocarnivore expansion at continental scale); scientists have been trying to understand drivers of coyote expansion

comments.issue: The highly disturbed study system makes the implied generalizations hard to justify.
comments.request: Clarify the scope of generalization.
comments.quote: this is a unique case of mesocarnivore expansion in a highly disturbed system, thus the generalizations implied in this comment are hard to conceptualize

comments.issue: Carnivore-guild statement applies only to Eastern and Central Europe.
comments.request: Qualify the statement by region.
comments.quote: this truly only applies to Eastern and Central Europe. What carnivore guilds are we talking about?

comments.issue: Temporal context is missing: when wolves disappeared relative to jackal expansion.
comments.request: Provide a timeline.
comments.quote: can the authors place this in a real temporal context? When did wolves disappear from Europe relative to when the jackals started to expand?

comments.issue: Intrinsic species factors such as behavioral change at the invasion front are not considered.
comments.request: Discuss intrinsic dispersal factors.
comments.quote: what about factors intrinsic to the species, such as behavioral change of dispersing animals at the invasion front?

comments.issue: 100+ year lags and simultaneous wolf expansion argue against direct mesopredator release.
comments.request: Reconcile the timeline with the predator-release claim.
comments.quote: time lags between the wolf disappearance from Europe (in some cases 100+ years ago) and the recent population expansion of jackals. This does not make the case for a direct effect of wolf loss

comments.issue: Shielding effect is weak (0.2-0.4) yet presented as a strong pattern.
comments.request: Recast the human-shield emphasis.
comments.quote: This fits with the shielding effect, but it is not a strong pattern, which the rest of the paper makes it out to be

comments.issue: Village land use and stray dogs could keep jackals away regardless of wolves.
comments.request: Test and discuss this alternative explanation.
comments.quote: These are all reasons why jackals would not venture close to villages, whether you have wolves present or not

comments.issue: Interpretations are biased by North American and Western European settings.
comments.request: Reassess whether these relationships hold in Western Europe.
comments.quote: I believe that the authors' interpretations are biased by N American and Western Europe settings

comments.issue: Distribution of surveys across wolf range types is unknown and likely overrepresents non-core areas.
comments.request: Report survey coverage and add a wolf distribution map.
comments.quote: what is the distribution of surveys conducted across the different wolf range types? I would assume that the number of surveys outside the wolf core range is much greater

comments.issue: Independent validation of wolf influences is needed beyond simplified range classifications.
comments.request: Validate using SNAPSHOT Europe camera-trap data.
comments.quote: I suggest using SNAPSHOT Europe camera trap data instead of relying on oversimplification of both wolf and jackal ranges

comments.issue: Forest-loss explanation is implausible; wolves selecting intact forest is an alternative.
comments.request: Discuss the wolf-based alternative and timelines.
comments.quote: Europe has been gaining, not losing forest thanks to those pesky environmental Directives, so this is not a very plausible explanation

comments.issue: L283-285 vague; wolf management, not settlement distance, is the main lever.
comments.request: Clarify and reframe around wolves.
comments.quote: This is quite vague: are the authors referring to the "shielding effect", which was quite marginal?

comments.issue: L322-324 concept pushed without strong support.
comments.request: Temper or substantiate the narrative.
comments.quote: it feels like the authors really want to push this narrative in the absence of strong support

comments.issue: Figure 4 is misleading given its many assumptions and lacks uncertainty estimates.
comments.request: Add uncertainty estimates to the figure.
comments.quote: so many assumptions go into this figure that this is misleading, particularly in the absence of uncertainty estimates

title: Human shielding from wolves facilitates jackal expansion across Europe

study.system: European fauna compensation price lists; 9,971 species across 24 countries

editor_summary: Reviewers find considerable potential interest but raise substantial concerns that must be addressed; the editors cannot accept now but encourage a revised version, and Reviewer 2's PDF is attached.

reviews.assessment: Valid, robust data and interesting, relevant results, but the monetary-valuation terminology, recommendations and title need revision.

comments.issue: "Monetary valuation" conflates economic valuation methods with legally assigned compensation values; the term should be defined and used consistently (L67, L72-73, L97).
comments.request: Define the term at the start and check it throughout the text.
comments.quote: I felt irritated by the fact that you always talk about "monetary valuation" throughout the entire paper.

comments.issue: The recommendations are weaker than the analysis: what should substitute the legally defined compensation values is not explicit.
comments.request: Be more explicit about what is missing and what more balanced schemes would be.
comments.quote: But what about the recommendations? Here the paper seems weaker.

comments.issue: The title and concept "hidden preferences" is questionable, since preferences belong to stakeholders or citizens rather than legal values.
comments.request: Reconsider the title and the preferences framing.
comments.quote: Is the title of the paper correct? Or misleading? Hidden preferences? Again: In my view preferences are those of stakeholders or of cizizens.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and original analysis with correct statistics; major comments ask for more covariates and clearer interpretation of the results.
strengths: vast work across thousands of species
clearly described with very good graphs and tables
results very interesting for policy implications

comments.issue: The first regression omits potentially relevant covariates such as CITES ratification, deforestation, urbanisation and pollution.
comments.request: Re-run with more covariates or discuss theoretically relevant missing variables.
comments.quote: While I consider that some of the covariates used are relevant and conceptually correct, others are missing and could be introduced pending the availability of data.

comments.issue: The counterintuitive government-effectiveness result may reflect omitted indicators and the East/central-east European composition of the sample.
comments.request: Explore omitted variables and the regional adoption pattern.
comments.quote: It seems counterintuitive that countries with "less perceived capacity" to manage the public goods are more likely setting compensation.

comments.issue: Declining or stable populations receive lower values; the reason behind this misalignment with conservation needs is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the counterintuitive population-trend result from the model.
comments.quote: Conversely, population trends show inconsistent behaviour and counterintuitive results, with declining or stable population typically assigned lower monetary values.

comments.issue: The generation-length effect may be a statistical artefact of traits shared by charismatic species rather than a driver of values.
comments.request: Test or discuss whether ecological traits merely identify charismatic species.
comments.quote: While I do not contest the result of the regression model, I think that this result is a statistical effect rather than explaining people values for these traits.

comments.issue: The recommendations need a concrete action and a clear scale (international CBD versus local).
comments.request: Expand the recommendations with a concrete action and scale.
comments.quote: Can you briefly expand the text (according to the space available- maybe just a sentence) suggesting a concrete action? At what scale this collaboration should be more effective?

comments.issue: The log transformation's normality and homoscedasticity assumptions are not demonstrated; a gamma GLM may be needed.
comments.request: Show the diagnostic statistics or use a GLM with an appropriate error distribution.
comments.quote: However, I have not seen the statistics proving this. In case you do not achieve this, you should use a GLM with a different distribution of the error (gamma?).

comments.issue: The introduction's claim about public preferences for birds and mammals lacks references.
comments.request: Add references, including literature already cited in the discussion.
comments.quote: This can be referenced, even using some of the literature already cited in the discussion.

comments.issue: Figure 2 legend does not state the unit of monetary valuation.
comments.request: Add the monetary unit to the legend or caption.
comments.quote: it would be correct to introduce in the legend of the Figure 2 the unit of the monetary valuation. Or at least report it into the caption.

comments.issue: Valuation methods used by countries could be categorised and tested as covariates.
comments.request: Consider coding valuation methods as covariates in the model.
comments.quote: Do you think it is possible to categorise these methods and use them as covariates to assess their impacts on the response variable?

strengths: detailed revisions and responses are adequate

reviews.assessment: Commends the thorough revision, especially added detail on post-mining impacts, and has no further comments.
strengths: added detail on post-mining impacts and biodiversity data uncertainties

reviews.assessment: Considers the manuscript ready for publication after a careful and comprehensive response to the reviews.
strengths: very careful and comprehensive response to comments
improved clarity and depth of the manuscript
