comments.quote: The conceptual link between orientation strategies and habitat preference if far form trivial and I believe it should be better explained upfront.

comments.issue: Habitat, preference, use and selection are used vaguely, obscuring the causal link.
comments.request: Clarify the habitat-selection terminology (see Lele et al. 2013).
comments.quote: I think much of the problem stems from the vagueness around terms such as ‘habitat’, ‘preference’, ‘use’, and ‘selection’

comments.issue: The known association and untested causality between orientation and habitat use should be stated upfront.
comments.request: State the hypothesis-testing aim explicitly from the start.
comments.quote: I would make clear right upfront that a pattern of association between dominant orientation strategy and duelling in an environment that is more or less abundant with visual markers has been empirically demonstrated

comments.issue: Olfactory cues and other orientation mechanisms are neglected in the navigation task.
comments.request: Discuss a broader range of orientation mechanisms, including olfactory cues.
comments.quote: First, the authors neglect to mention olfactory cues and the part those may play in the navigation task.

comments.issue: The two-strategy dichotomy and its measurability are not justified; poor performers may simply be cognitively limited.
comments.request: Convince readers the assay distinguishes the only relevant strategies.
comments.quote: The authors need to do a better job at convincing the reader that egocentric and visual-cue based allocentric navigations are the only two strategies relevant here and that hey could indeed be discerned using the assay performed.

comments.issue: Binary grouping is less powerful and ignores classification error; allocentricity is continuous.
comments.request: Derive a continuous allocentricity measure with error and use it as a predictor.
comments.quote: the authors chose to view the former as a binary grouping predictor. This has two problems. First, it is less statistically powerful, which raises some concerns given the very small sample size.

comments.issue: The sensitivity of conclusions to misclassification of orientation strategy is not assessed.
comments.request: Assess sensitivity to misclassification errors.
comments.quote: At the very least, consider how sensitive would the conclusion be to missclassification errors in orientation-strategy assignments?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether Manly selection ratios or a binomial GLM were used, why both, and why availability was sampled 10,000 times.
comments.request: Clarify the analysis and justify the availability sampling.
comments.quote: However, at the end of the Methods, the use of a Binomial GLM implies the authors are fitting an exponential habitat selection function based on used-available data? Which one is it? If it is both, why?

comments.issue: Habitat classes were analysed independently although their availabilities are not independent.
comments.request: Combine all habitat classes in one analysis.
comments.quote: More importantly, it seems that the analysis was done independently for each of the habitat classes; why? The availability of the different habitat classes is surely not independent; why not combine all in one analysis

comments.issue: Random sampling does not resolve temporal autocorrelation; left-out points could validate the model.
comments.request: Use sub-sampling and validate with k-fold or calibration plots.
comments.quote: As for the used points, I fail to see how randomly sampling the points resolves autocorrelation (which is inherently temporal); that would require sub sampling to increase the temporal gap between points.

comments.issue: The habitat-selection analysis should follow a home-range-based mixed-effects workflow.
comments.request: Adopt the outlined AKDE-based mixed-effects approach or consult an expert.
comments.quote: Fit a population-level exponential habitat selection model using the mixed-effects approach described in Muff et al. (2019; DOI: 10.1111/1365-2656.13087)

comments.issue: The word 'shaped' at line 144 is questionable.

comments.quote: • Figure 3: perhaps show actual (observed) data points

comments.request: Clarify whether the training phase only is meant.

comments.request: Reserve the term for the 3D representation.

comments.issue: Relevant recent literature on synchrony and connectivity in riverine systems is not discussed.
comments.request: Consider discussing Zanon et al., Lopes et al. and Anderson et al.
comments.quote: There’s a bit of very relevant recent literature I want to make sure the authors are aware of

reviews.assessment: Clear and relevant study with qualitative agreement between models and data; asks for justification of transformations and summary tables.
strengths: qualitative agreement between theory and empirical data

comments.issue: The square-root transformation of distances for empirical data, and its difference from the theoretical analysis, is unjustified.
comments.request: Explain and justify the transformation choices.
comments.quote: Clearly explaining why for the empirical data the authors choose the square root of the distances. What supports this choice?

comments.issue: No table summarizes the fits to the empirical data.
comments.request: Add a summary table of the fits.
comments.quote: Adding a table summarizing the results of the fits to the empirical data

comments.issue: How Moran, diffusion and interspecific effects can be disentangled from synchrony is not summarized.
comments.request: Add a summary table or graph, ideally showing Moran-diffusion separation.
comments.quote: Adding a table or graph summarizing how the effects of Moran, diffusion and interspecific interaction can be disentangled from the spatial synchrony.

title: The geography of metapopulation synchrony in dendritic river networks

study.system: leaf litter decomposition; nitrogen fertilisation experiments, global

editor_summary: Analysis has potential, but accessibility, clarity of results and links between approach and conclusions need explicit attention; more than a minor revision.

reviews.assessment: Exceptionally well-written and potentially highly cited, but the results presentation does not clearly connect the model comparisons to the conclusions.
strengths: potential to become a highly-cited paper

comments.issue: The manuscript was resubmitted without revising for previous reviewer feedback.
comments.request: Address previous reviewer comments before resubmission.
comments.quote: I previously reviewed this manuscript for another journal and am disappointed to see that the authors made no effort to revise the manuscript based on previous reviewer feedback before submitting to Ecology Letters.

comments.issue: The results presentation is disconnected from the conclusions and lacks context linking model comparisons to conclusions.
comments.request: Make the results section clearly link the analyses to each conclusion.
comments.quote: there is currently a disconnect between how the data are presented in the results section (including the figures) and the conclusions drawn, making the manuscript less accessible and digestible.

title: Experimental nitrogen fertilisation globally accelerates, then slows decomposition of leaf litter

study.system: Tasmanian devils and DFTD; 35-year survey, capture and incidence data

editor_summary: Editor reports reviewers found an important issue, robust data and good writing, but require clearer modelling description, more attention to host-density effects, and broader ecological context.

reviews.assessment: Fantastic, exemplary integration of spatiotemporal datasets, but wants density effects tested formally, more model comparison, broader context and shared code.
strengths: strong model-based density and spread maps
useful example of integrating spatiotemporal datasets

comments.issue: Effects of density on DFTD spread are not investigated, only compared visually, leaving conclusions vague.
comments.request: Formally analyse the effect of density on DFTD spread.
comments.quote: I wonder why the authors did not take the extra step of investigating effects of density on DFTD spread.

comments.issue: The candidate model set is limited and all models include vegetation, so its importance cannot be assessed.
comments.request: Compare models with and without vegetation.
comments.quote: It seems worth testing whether vegetation is indeed an important driver, but as all models include vegetation there is no way to assess this.

comments.issue: The discussion does not extend the results into the broader context of pathogen spread or disease ecology.
comments.request: Broaden the discussion to other emerging infectious disease systems.
comments.quote: The discussion is great and links the results to devil literature, but does not extend discussion of results into a broader context of pathogen spread.

comments.issue: The paper is meant as a methods example but no code is shared.
comments.request: Add R code for the different steps or key examples.
comments.quote: it would be very helpful if the authors can add R code for the different steps

comments.issue: Movement is described as separate from R0, but movement and contact determine R0; scales should be stated explicitly.
comments.request: Explicitly distinguish local spread from long-distance movement.
comments.quote: R0 is determined by several factors including movement (and contact), and movement can not be seen as separate from R0.

comments.issue: The paragraph's last sentence is confusing and 'other survey data' is unclear.
comments.request: Expand on linking multiple datasets before the next paragraph.
comments.quote: This last sentence of the paragraph confused me, and I wasn't sure what the 'other survey data' referred to

comments.issue: 'Common ecological currencies' is not defined.
comments.request: Define what common ecological currencies are.
comments.quote: It might not be clear to everyone (including me before I read the reference) what "common ecological currencies" are exactly.

comments.issue: The text conflates three datasets with three key study goals, confusing the reader.
comments.request: Clearly list the three datasets and how they serve the three goals.
comments.quote: I got a bit confused here by the fact that there are both 3 datasets and 3 key study goals.

comments.issue: Only five models were chosen and none lack vegetation, so the vegetation association is guaranteed.
comments.request: Include models without vegetation to test its importance.
comments.quote: It leaves me to guess how important the environmental variables are, and whether or not they actually improve the model.

comments.issue: The DFTD spread model description is too terse for readers unfamiliar with spatiotemporal models or INLA.
comments.request: Expand the description and state the two purposes of the maps.
comments.quote: it may be worth expanding it slightly so that this is clear also to people who are not familiar with spatiotemporal models / INLA

comments.issue: It is not explicit that the joint-likelihood model was also fitted with INLA.
comments.request: State explicitly which models were applied where.
comments.quote: I was wondering how the joint-likelihood model was fitted, and it took me a while to realize it was also done using INLA.

comments.issue: The density-spread comparison is reported as an awkward mix of formal inference and exploration.
comments.request: Label it explicitly as visual, or add a formal analysis.
comments.quote: I suggest to either be very explicit about the fact that this is purely a visual comparison and be careful not to over-interpret

comments.issue: It is unclear which findings were already known from previous work and which come from the new results.
comments.request: Separate prior knowledge from new results in this paragraph.
comments.quote: it is not clear from this paragraph (which is a great overview of studied drivers of transmission) what was already known from previous work, and what is based on the new results

comments.issue: The comparison of the pre-DFTD density map and DFTD spread map is not a statistical comparison.
comments.request: State explicitly in text and legend that it is visual only.
comments.quote: I didn't find any statistical comparison, so does this mean that this is meant as a visual comparison only?

comments.issue: Table 1 does not explain the + sign and the 'order fitted' column name is unclear.
comments.request: Define the + sign and rename 'order fitted' to model complexity.
comments.quote: I would suggest changing the column name to something closer to model complexity.

comments.issue: Table S6 does not explain the + signs and repeats the 'order fitted' issue.
comments.request: Define the + signs and rename the column.
comments.quote: Maybe add what the + signs mean (I assume it means that the variable was included in the model, but I had to double check in the main text to make sure).

reviews.assessment: Praises the impressive dataset and robust results but asks for density/frequency-dependence results and better model comparison instead of stepwise selection.

comments.issue: Specific results on whether transmission is frequency- or density-dependent are missing despite the framing.
comments.request: Integrate specific findings on density and frequency dependence into the Results.
comments.quote: I found the manuscript to be lacking in some of the specific results pertaining to the broader ecological questions, such as whether transmission is frequency- or density-dependent.

comments.issue: Backwards selection is problematic and can miss biologically meaningful models.
comments.request: Compare an a priori set of competing models with an information criterion.
comments.quote: stepwise selection has long been acknowledged as a problematic form of model comparison (e.g., Whittingham et al. 2006 JAE). In particular, backwards selection can miss biologically meaningful models

comments.issue: How the environmental covariates relate to devil ecology or behaviour is not explained.
comments.request: Justify covariates ecologically and consider including age structure.
comments.quote: additional information on how the selected environmental covariates relate to devil ecology or behavior would be helpful

comments.issue: A pertinent reference on wildlife pathogen dynamics is missing.
comments.request: Cite Plowright et al. 2019 PhilTransB.
comments.quote: Another pertinent reference on understanding spatial and temporal dynamics of wildlife pathogens is Plowright et al. 2019 PhilTransB

comments.issue: 'Disease transmission' is used where 'pathogen transmission' is meant in general contexts.
comments.request: Use 'pathogen transmission' except when discussing DFTD specifically.
comments.quote: replace “disease transmission” with “pathogen transmission” in general contexts, except when discussing DFTD in particular

comments.issue: The relative sensitivity of histopathology and cell culture for DFTD diagnosis is not stated.
comments.request: Compare the sensitivity of the two diagnostic methods.
comments.quote: Is histopathology more/less sensitive than cell culture for DFTD diagnosis?

comments.issue: Environmental variables are assumed static since 1985, which is questionable.
comments.request: Confirm the assumption or use temporally varying variables.
comments.quote: Can you confirm that these environmental variables have indeed remained static since 1985?

comments.issue: WAIC is used although LOO is more robust to influential observations.
comments.request: Consider using LOO instead of WAIC.
comments.quote: Note that Vehtari et al. suggest using LOO over WAIC in their 2016 manuscript, as the former is more robust to influential observations.

comments.issue: It is unclear how year was integrated and where the extracted quantity came from.
comments.request: Clarify the year variable and its source.
comments.quote: I’m not entirely clear on how year was integrated here. Is this the variable described in L185 (year of detection) or a quantity estimated from one of the previous models?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether backwards selection was also used for the vegetation model.
comments.request: State the model selection procedure used here.
comments.quote: Was backwards selection again used to model the effect of vegetation type?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the 11 models were a priori hypotheses or stepwise products.
comments.request: State the origin of the 11 models.
comments.quote: Were these 11 models based on a priori hypotheses or from a stepwise procedure?

comments.issue: Age structure, a key predictor of transmission, is not included in the spatial spread models.
comments.request: Consider adding site-level age structure as a predictor.
comments.quote: could this information (e.g., % older individuals per site) be included in the models of spatial spread as a biologically important predictor

comments.issue: The structure and coefficients of the final models are not reported, so the covariates behind the forecasts are unclear.
comments.request: Report final model structure and coefficients.
comments.quote: it would help to report some information on the structure and coefficients of the final models, as it is unclear what covariates (and their magnitude) were ultimately used to generate the forecasted population declines and DFTD spatial spread

comments.issue: It is unclear how the conclusion about density and spread was reached without specific results.
comments.request: Support the conclusion with regression coefficients.
comments.quote: It is somewhat unclear how the authors came to this conclusion

reviews.assessment: Impressed by the topic and dataset but finds the modelling unclear and the density-spread link lacking quantitative support.

comments.issue: The analysis provides no quantitative support for how spread is linked to density in different areas.
comments.request: Quantitatively analyse the density-spread relationship.
comments.quote: it seems that the current analysis does not provide quantitative support of how the spread is linked to density in different areas?

comments.issue: The second aim is confirmative rather than novel, being a modification of the model published by Lazenby et al.
comments.request: Clarify the novel contribution beyond Lazenby et al. 2018.
comments.quote: I would consider your second aim to model the effects of DFTD on devil density to be rather confirmative than entirely novel

comments.issue: Many aspects of the modelling remain unclear, so the analysis does not convincingly support the conclusions.
comments.request: Describe the models in sufficient detail.
comments.quote: many aspects of the modelling remained unclear to me to such extent that I found the current analysis not really convincing in providing rigorous support for the conclusions

comments.issue: No assessment of predictive performance is provided to evaluate the accuracy of the estimates.
comments.request: Assess predictive performance of the models.
comments.quote: some assessment of the predictive performance to better evaluate the accuracy of your estimates

comments.issue: The repeated counts over years are ignored; site-level density dependence could be a random effect.
comments.request: Account for site-level repeated measures in the models.
comments.quote: your data consisted of multiple time series of repeated counts over year but this important feature seems to have been largely ignored in your models

comments.issue: It is unclear how survey inconsistencies for the additional sites (172 versus 132) were handled.
comments.request: Explain how survey inconsistencies were accounted for.
comments.quote: How did you account for inconsistencies in survey for additional sites included in your analysis (i.e. you used 172)?

comments.issue: Uneven detection probability, seasonality and other biases in spotlight counts are ignored.
comments.request: Acknowledge this simplifying assumption.
comments.quote: Its seems that you ignore uneven detection probability, seasonality of counts or any other potential bias that are commonly reported for spotlight count data

comments.issue: The crucial step of deriving density estimates from transect counts is not described.
comments.request: Describe how counts are converted to densities.
comments.quote: How is it possible to use transect counts as proxies of animal densities? The crucial step of how density estimates are derived from a transect count is not described.

comments.issue: The text mentions 15 sites while Figure 2B appears to show only 14.
comments.request: Check and reconcile the site count.
comments.quote: you mention 15 sites while there seems to be only 14 sites in Figure 2B?

comments.issue: Only mean detections are plotted; variation is not shown despite known spotlight bias.
comments.request: Plot a measure of variation alongside the mean.
comments.quote: Plotting a measure of variation in addition to the mean number of devil detections within a bioregion is be of much interest given that spotlight data often come with much bias?

comments.issue: Details of the DFTD spatial spread model and its basic assumptions are lacking.
comments.request: Provide the missing model details and assumptions.
comments.quote: Some details for the model of devil density seem to be provided in Table S5. However, I was not able to find any details of the model for the ‘spatial spread of DFTD’.

comments.issue: 'Relative abundance' is used without definition or link to the spotlight counts.
comments.request: Define relative abundance and its derivation.
comments.quote: The term “relative abundance” is used the first time here and it is unclear if this is linked to the relative counts from spotlight survey or something else.

comments.issue: The steps by which the predictive map was inferred are not described for reproducibility.
comments.request: Describe the SDM steps used to infer the predictive map.
comments.quote: I was not able to find all details of how a predictive map was inferred (there are several steps in SDMs involved that need to be described for full reproducibility?).

comments.issue: Predictive accuracy of the spatial projections was not evaluated.
comments.request: Evaluate and report predictive accuracy.
comments.quote: Did you evaluate the predictive accuracy of you spatial projects and if so, how?

comments.issue: It is unclear how 'spotlight detections' are defined.
comments.request: Define what counts as a spotlight detection.
comments.quote: Lines 179: How are “spotlight detections” defined? Unclear.

comments.issue: 'Percentage cover' is not tied to explicit spatial units.
comments.request: Specify the spatial units for percentage cover.
comments.quote: “Percentage cover” of what spatial units? Unclear and in my opinion needs further details to understand/reproduce your study.

comments.issue: The vegetation data source, resolution and survey period are not documented.
comments.request: Provide the TasVeg 3.0 reference, resolution and survey years.
comments.quote: Please check also Table S5, where a reference to TasVeg 3.0 and also information about its spatial resolution should be provided.

comments.issue: 'Referenced locations' is unclear and most model details remain unclear to the reviewer.
comments.request: Define referenced locations and clarify the model details.
comments.quote: “referenced locations” is unclear because this term is used the first time while you described different data types, which are presumably all georeferenced but in different currencies?

comments.issue: How the triangle mesh was built for the one-dimensional SPDE model is not explained.
comments.request: Explain how the SPDE mesh was constructed.
comments.quote: The INLA SPDE model object (as constructed by the function ‘inla.spde2.pcmatern’ mentioned in Table S5) is based on a triangle mesh from point locations. How was this build for you one-dimensional SPDE?

comments.issue: The joint likelihood description is unclear and more model details are needed.
comments.request: Reword the joint likelihood description and add details.
comments.quote: I found your description of the joint likelihood approach somewhat unclear and suggest rewording.

comments.issue: 'Year since DFTD arrival' may be missing from the model scheme in Figure 1B.
comments.request: Check whether this covariate belongs in Figure 1B.
comments.quote: Please check, of whether “year since DFTD arrival” should be also a covariate in the model scheme depicted in Figure 1B?

comments.issue: The derivation of the year 2032 is not explained and no uncertainty measure is given.
comments.request: Explain the 2032 estimate and include uncertainty.
comments.quote: I would be helpful to explain how the year 2032 was concluded as the year DFTD has been present all across Tasmania for ten years. Also, shouldn’t such estimate include some uncertainty measure?

comments.issue: The phrase '20% after population decline' is vague about a continuous demographic process.
comments.request: Reword to reflect continuous demographic shifts.
comments.quote: The wording “20% after population decline” appears to me somewhat vague.

comments.issue: The text says 'devil density' but the Figure 3A legend states 'devils/transect'.
comments.request: Make the text and figure legend consistent.
comments.quote: you mention here “devil density” while the plot legend of figure states “devils/transect”, please check.

comments.issue: Predictive accuracy measures and credible intervals for the density projections are missing.
comments.request: Report predictive accuracy and credible intervals.
comments.quote: I suggest to provide some measures of the predictive accuracy of your best-performing model and also possible credible intervals of your estimates.

comments.issue: The interpretation of graphical patterns of density-dependent spread lacks a proper quantitative analysis.
comments.request: Quantitatively test the graphical patterns.
comments.quote: it seems that a proper quantitative analysis to support your interpretation of graphical patterns is lacking here?

reviews.assessment: Sees an interesting modelling exercise but finds the model hard to understand and questions several modelling and extrapolation choices.

comments.issue: The coupling between host and tumour dynamics in the model could be stronger.
comments.request: Strengthen the coupling between host and tumour.
comments.quote: It is interesting, although the coupling between the host and tumour could be stronger.

comments.issue: The model is difficult to understand because everything is modelled twice without explanation.
comments.request: Explain the three models and how they relate.
comments.quote: At the moment it's really difficult to understand the model. This is partly because everything is modelled twice, without a good explanation for why or a clear explanation of the three models and how they relate to each other.

comments.issue: The modelling should be described as a single model, written in equations or an INLA formula.
comments.request: Write out the model as equations and frame fitting as two-stage.
comments.quote: I think it would help to stick to describing this as a single model, and write it out, either in equations or a simplified INLA formula.

comments.issue: Density- and frequency-dependence are not explained, and density seems unused in the model.
comments.request: Define these concepts or remove the paragraph.
comments.quote: you do not explain what you mean by density- and frequency- dependence, and l255-6 suggest you mean that spread is related to density

comments.issue: Devils have just been re-introduced on the mainland, contrary to the statement in the text.
comments.request: Correct the statement.
comments.quote: Can I be pedantic and point out that they have just been re-introduced on the mainland?

comments.issue: Several emergent infectious diseases of humans exist, and rabbit haemorrhagic disease may count, weakening the rarity claim.
comments.request: Soften or substantiate the rarity claim.
comments.quote: I think I'm being pedantic again (sorry), but there are several emergent infectious diseases of humans.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether standard errors or equivalents were assembled for the data.
comments.request: Report whether standard errors were assembled.
comments.quote: Did you also assemble standard errors (or equivalent)?

comments.issue: The model implies absence data, which may not be meaningful at this location and size.
comments.request: Justify or ignore the absence-data assumption.
comments.quote: This implies that you have absence data. I also wonder, given its location and size, if this really matters.

comments.issue: INLA is mischaracterized: it computes marginal densities, while the model is a GLMM with a GMRF prior.
comments.request: Correct the description of the estimation method.
comments.quote: INLA is a way to compute marginal densities. You actually used a GLMM with a GMRF prior on the parameters.

comments.issue: Year is treated as continuous although spatio-temporal models are available, and a single spatial field may be used.
comments.request: Consider a spatio-temporal model instead of continuous year.
comments.quote: Why treat Year as continuous? INLA has spatio-temporal models you could use.

comments.issue: Two different methods for model selection are used, so which was actually applied is unclear.
comments.request: State which model selection method was used.
comments.quote: You use 2 different methods for model selection. So which did you actually use?

comments.issue: A log-normal observation model would suit the approximately normal estimates better than the current choice.
comments.request: Consider a log-normal observation model.
comments.quote: Why not just use a log-normal? The estimates have an approximately normal distribution (thanks to one central limit or other), so that would make sense as an observation model

comments.issue: The link functions used for the models are not reported.
comments.request: State the link functions used.
comments.quote: Also, what link functions did you use? The canonical link for all of them?

comments.issue: Age effects are extrapolated from one site to the whole island, which may be unnecessary.
comments.request: Consider a qualitative statement about age instead.
comments.quote: you are extrapolating from one site to the whole of the island

comments.issue: There is little or no data from western and south-western Tasmania and estimated abundances are low.
comments.request: Clarify whether this data gap is expected or problematic.
comments.quote: There is little/no data in western and south-western Tasmania, and the estimated abundances are low. Is this a problem, or is that expected?

comments.issue: The density-spread link is described qualitatively rather than with a model parameter.
comments.request: Add a parameter linking density to time of first appearance.
comments.quote: I would have expected something more qualitative than this, i.e. a parameter in the model to link density to time of first appearance.

comments.issue: The conservation argument underplays that the threat is smaller but the species is not saved.
comments.request: Acknowledge that a status downgrade does not mean the species is saved.
comments.quote: This does not mean that the species has been saved (l379), only that the threat is smaller.

title: Quantifying 25 years of disease‐caused declines in Tasmanian devil populations: host density drives spatial pathogen spread

study.system: animals; conceptual framework of accident landscapes

editor_summary: Reviewers liked and were provoked by the paper but see overlap with existing theories (optimal foraging, risk tolerance, safety-food trade-offs); editor asks authors to tie the framework into existing theory and clarify its relation to the landscape of fear.

reviews.assessment: Well-written but overlaps existing optimization and stress theory; asks authors to justify novelty, scope and provide a simple model.
strengths: not too long with the right amount of tables and figures

comments.issue: The introduction must acknowledge the success of optimization theory balancing predation risk and energy acquisition before questioning whether further digging is needed.
comments.request: Acknowledge optimization theory and pose whether further risk subdivision is warranted.
comments.quote: The introduction needs to acknowledge the success of optimization theory with regards to the balance of predation risk and energy acquisition.

comments.issue: Abiotic risks are already subsumed by optimization models and concepts such as the Environmental Stress Model, Consumer Stress Model and behavioural syndromes.
comments.request: Show whether accident landscapes refine or unify these existing concepts.
comments.quote: abiotic risks have mostly been subsumed by optimization models and other community ecology concepts

comments.issue: The concept arbitrarily focuses on mobile organisms although sessile organisms can behave and physiology can lose control.
comments.request: Logically develop why accident landscapes apply only to mobile organisms.
comments.quote: The authors need to logically develop why accident landscapes are only focused on mobile organisms

comments.issue: A simple model is needed to test whether optimization predictions improve when an accident landscape component is included.
comments.request: Develop a model comparing predictions with and without an accident landscape.
comments.quote: I think the study needs some kind of simple model. The model needs to evaluate the effectiveness of optimization methods predicting ecological dynamics with and without an accidental landscape component.

reviews.assessment: Thought-provoking contribution with wide appeal, but optimality and fitness claims need qualification and more testable predictions.
strengths: potential to appeal to a wide readership
gets readers to think from a different perspective

comments.issue: Optimality and fitness arguments are assumed despite sparse empirical support.
comments.request: Take a more agnostic approach regarding optimality and fitness.
comments.quote: I encourage the authors to take more of an agnostic approach regarding optimality and fitness because empirical data are so sparse

comments.issue: The paper leaves readers wondering what to do next.
comments.request: Enhance the generation of testable predictions.
comments.quote: anything the authors could do to enhance the generation of testable predications could also be very helpful

comments.issue: Line 47 implies all decisions affect fitness; many decisions have little fitness effect.
comments.request: Change 'is' to 'can be'.
comments.quote: To accommodate divergent views in this area, why not change “is” to “can be”?

comments.issue: The distinctness of the different landscapes is questionable and the logic behind landscape choices needs clarifying.
comments.request: Reconsider and clarify the distinctness of landscapes.
comments.quote: I encourage the authors to reconsider the importance (or not) of the distinctness of different “landscapes”

comments.issue: A locomotor performance landscape (speed, maneuverability) might subsume some accident consequences.
comments.request: Consider a locomotor performance landscape.
comments.quote: whether it might make sense to have a landscape of locomotor performance including speed, maneuverability that would subsume some of the consequences of accidents?

comments.issue: The use of 'fear' and its relation to predation risk and accidents needs explicit treatment.
comments.request: Deal explicitly with the fear terminology.
comments.quote: I favor the authors somehow dealing with this more explicitly

comments.issue: Counting increased energetic cost as harm makes the energy and accident landscapes non-distinct.
comments.request: Reconsider whether energetic cost counts as harm.
comments.quote: Considering increased energetic cost as a form of “harm” may be ill advised because doing so would result in the energy landscape not being distinct from the accident landscape.

comments.issue: A maximal-speed or passibility landscape may better separate accidents affecting speed from those causing injury or death.
comments.request: Consider redefining the accident landscape around injury and death only.
comments.quote: I wonder whether it may more useful to have one type of landscape that deals separately with factors (including accidents) that affect speed and passibility

comments.issue: Factors are not grouped into mechanical versus shape attributes, and the role of visual information and animal perception is underplayed.
comments.request: Regroup factors and discuss the information available to animals.
comments.quote: I encourage the authors to consider reorganizing and regrouping of some factors so that some patterns are more apparent

comments.issue: Equating currents with the six surface factors is odd; viscosity versus inertia and solid-surface scope need consideration.
comments.request: Reconsider how currents are treated and focus on solid surfaces.
comments.quote: It seemed a bit odd to try to equate the effect of currents (an external force) to the 6 factors listed above.

comments.issue: 'Overbalancing' is undefined at line 142.
comments.request: Define overbalancing.
comments.quote: (line 142) What is “overbalancing”?

comments.issue: 'Small' is undefined at line 143; many lizards and insects are much smaller than primates.
comments.request: Define what 'small' means.
comments.quote: (line 143) What is “small”?

comments.issue: Sloths could serve as another example of moving with the centre of mass beneath the branch.
comments.request: Include sloths as an example.
comments.quote: Perhaps include sloths as another good example of moving with the COM beneath the branch?

comments.issue: The mechanisms animals use to prevent slipping and falling are not specified per example.
comments.request: Specify adherence, claws, balancing and friction strategies for each example.
comments.quote: It might be helpful to indicate some of the major mechanisms that animals use to prevent slipping and falling

comments.issue: 'Toppling' is used loosely; the axis of rotation matters.
comments.request: Specify the axis of rotation when discussing toppling.
comments.quote: For rotational movements specifying the axis of rotation is important because rotations in different directions require different corrections by the animals experiencing them.

comments.issue: Whether the dove toppling was rotational or merely falling off the perch is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the dove example.
comments.quote: Was the toppling of the dove (line 164) indeed a rotational movement or merely falling off the perch?

comments.issue: Sideways toppling (rolling) on narrow cylindrical surfaces is not covered.
comments.request: Add sideways toppling/rolling to the discussion.
comments.quote: For animals moving along the length of narrow cylindrical surface, a major problem is sideways toppling or rotating about the long axis of the surface

comments.issue: Backward toppling (pitching) on steep planar surfaces is not covered.
comments.request: Add backward toppling/pitching to the discussion.
comments.quote: For animals moving on steep planar surfaces backward toppling (rotating within a sagittal plane of the animal = pitching) can be problematic

comments.issue: It should be clarified that friction examples concern effectively flat surfaces.
comments.request: Clarify that examples are for flat surfaces.
comments.quote: I favor the authors clarifying that their examples are for animals that are on effectively flat surfaces

comments.issue: 'Grip' may be the wrong term for pine beetles; friction, claw penetration and surface roughness are conflated.
comments.request: Distinguish friction, claw purchase and roughness.
comments.quote: (line 189) If the pine beetles are on a flat surface, “grip” may not be the best choice of words.

comments.issue: Ants on sand may illustrate shear layers rather than penetrability.
comments.request: Reconsider the penetrability example.
comments.quote: Ants on sand may not be a good example of penetrability.

comments.issue: The incline sentence should state that accident probability increases with steepness.
comments.request: Change the sentence accordingly.
comments.quote: Change the sentence to “Therefore, the probability of an accident increases with increased surface steepness.”

comments.issue: Object size relative to animal size should be discussed explicitly.
comments.request: Mention relative object size.
comments.quote: I favor more explicit mention of the size of objects in the environment relative to the size of the animal.

comments.issue: Environmental clutter and unobstructed travel distance are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss clutter and branch spacing.
comments.quote: it might be useful to explicitly mention how cluttered an environment is

comments.issue: Whether forces at line 298 are normal or tangential to the surface is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify normal versus tangential forces.
comments.quote: The authors should clarify whether they are referring to forces that are normal or tangential to the supporting surface.

comments.issue: Concrete examples linking terminal velocity to fall severity and climb heights are missing.
comments.request: Provide concrete terminal-velocity examples.
comments.quote: I favor providing some concrete examples to clarify the ecological relevance of terminal velocity for the accident severity of different size animals falling.

comments.issue: The relevant fall height is to the nearest object beneath, and canopy clutter matters.
comments.request: Discuss fall height to the nearest object and canopy structure.
comments.quote: The most relevant height is probably that between the animal and the nearest object directly beneath it.

comments.issue: 'Animal Size' would be a better heading than 'Morphology' at line 339.
comments.request: Rename the heading.
comments.quote: (line 339) Animal Size might be a more apt heading than Morphology.

comments.issue: What a 'direct link' between accident and fear landscapes means is unclear.
comments.request: Define whether the link is causal, correlational or interactive.
comments.quote: I struggled to follow the logic behind suggesting that, “there is likely a direct link between accident landscapes and the landscape of fear”

comments.issue: Several accident examples are inconsistent with the accident versus cognitive-error definition in Box 1.
comments.request: Align examples with the Box 1 definitions.
comments.quote: Some example of accidents in the text seem inconsistent with the definition of accidents vs. cognitive errors in Box 1

comments.issue: Getting stuck in mud could be either an accident or a cognitive error.
comments.request: Clarify this example.
comments.quote: (line 219) Perhaps an animal getting stuck in mud could be considered either an accident or a cognitive error

comments.issue: A bird colliding with a structure seems more like a cognitive error than an accident.
comments.request: Reclassify or clarify this example.
comments.quote: (line 407) Isn’t a bird colliding with a structure a better example of cognitive error

comments.issue: Predators pursuing prey may also be prone to accidents on hazardous terrain.
comments.request: Consider accident risk for predators as well.
comments.quote: If landscape features make prey more prone to having accidents as they move, could this also not be the case for predator pursuing them?

comments.issue: The relative importance of accidents across terrestrial, arboreal, aquatic and flying animals is not considered.
comments.request: Offer conjecture on accident importance across habitats.
comments.quote: Would the authors care to offer more conjecture regarding the relative importance of accidents for terrestrial, arboreal, aquatic and flying animals.

comments.issue: Table 1 column heading 'modulate' may not express the intended 'increases' or 'causes'.
comments.request: Change the wording if needed.
comments.quote: (column 3 heading) Rather than “modulate” do the authors actually mean “increases” or “causes”. If so, change the wording.

comments.issue: An asterisk is missing after 'risk' in the Table 1 heading.
comments.request: Add an asterisk after risk.
comments.quote: (column 3 heading) Add an * after risk.

comments.issue: Friction is decreased, not lost, unless normal force disappears.
comments.request: Replace 'loss of' with 'decreased'.
comments.quote: Friction is never lost unless there is no normal force (inverted surface or contact with the surface is lost).

comments.issue: A compliant surface dropping straight down should not affect toppling torque; this needs clarifying.
comments.request: Clarify the compliant-surface effect on toppling torque.
comments.quote: If a compliant surface, such as a thin branch, drops straight down, this should not affect the toppling torque acting on the animal.

comments.issue: Figure 1 caption does not name the species shown, and the lizard image is too low-resolution to identify toepads.
comments.request: Name the species and improve the image.
comments.quote: The caption for figure 1 should provide the names of the species shown.

comments.issue: The meaning of solid versus dashed arrows and arrowhead directions in Figure 2 is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the arrows.
comments.quote: What different information is being conveyed by solid versus dashed arrows and the direction of arrowheads?

comments.issue: An arrow implying the energy landscape affects the accident landscape does not make sense.
comments.request: Reconsider this arrow.
comments.quote: the arrow seems to imply that the energy landscape affects the accident landscape, and that does not make much sense to me

comments.issue: Causal effects of landscape features and animal attributes on travel velocity are missing from Figure 2.
comments.request: Add arrows showing these causal relationships.
comments.quote: Both physical landscape features and attributes of the animal can affect travel velocity, but no arrows or lines are included that show these causal relationships.

comments.issue: The animal morphology box mixes behaviour with morphology and omits behaviour; intrinsic attributes should be regrouped.
comments.request: Create an intrinsic-attributes box with morphology, physiology and behaviour.
comments.quote: Rather than a box for animal morphology, it might be better to make that a box for all intrinsic attributes of the animals

comments.issue: Figure 5 panel B energy-cost assumption is unclear and the sparse stand also seems costly.
comments.request: Clarify the energy-cost assumptions in panel B.
comments.quote: Is the energy cost high in the stand of trees because an assumption that animals move up and down on all surfaces that a present within a prescribed area?

comments.issue: The units of the vertical dimension of the coloured surfaces in panels A-C are unclear, and the accident landscape should combine probability and severity.
comments.request: Clarify the units and the landscape definition.
comments.quote: I favor clarifying the units for the vertical dimension the colored surfaces in panels A-C.

comments.issue: Combining landscapes with different units may be problematic; probabilities could standardise panels.
comments.request: Use frequencies or probabilities across panels.
comments.quote: If the units of panels A-C are all different, then combining landscapes (panels D and E) could be problematic.

comments.issue: Box 2 confuses limb posture changes with gait changes.
comments.request: Distinguish posture from gait.
comments.quote: With different surface widths, lizards do indeed change their limb posture (Spezzano and Jayne, 2004), but that is a different issue than changing gait

comments.issue: Not all speed loss on narrow perches is due to slipping; foot orientation also matters.
comments.request: Acknowledge the foot-orientation effect.
comments.quote: I doubt that all of the decrement in speed associated with narrower perches is a result of slipping

comments.issue: Foraging speed is not distinguished between prey detection and attack movements, and ambush predators are overlooked.
comments.request: Clarify the type of foraging movement and consider ambush foragers.
comments.quote: When authors refer to foraging speed, they should clarify when they are referring to the movements that are needed to detect (encounter) prey (often very slow) and those that are used when attacking the prey (usually quite fast).

comments.issue: 'Energetically expensive' is not defined relative to anything, and the energy-limitation assumption needs justification.
comments.request: Specify what slipping is expensive relative to and whether animals are energy limited.
comments.quote: The author should specify “expensive” relative to what.

comments.issue: Empirical lizard data exist that could replace the marsupial illustration in Box 2.
comments.request: Use the available lizard data, e.g. Mattingly & Jayne (2004).
comments.quote: Some empirical data for lizards do exist for this topic, which may obviate the need to illustrate this example with work on marsupials.

reviews.assessment: Novel idea, but cognitive versus biomechanical errors and the separation from the landscape of fear are hard to justify.
strengths: valuable addition to the literature with further development

comments.issue: Locomotor accidents and cognitive accidents are hard to separate; the choice of which errors to include is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the distinction between cognitive and biomechanical errors.
comments.quote: I find these very hard to separate in my head.

comments.issue: Avoiding accidents may simply be fear of accidents, which would make the accident landscape part of the landscape of fear.
comments.request: Consider expanding the landscape of fear rather than treating accidents as separate.
comments.quote: does this not make the accident landscape part of the landscape of fear

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 64-65 almost debunks the theory because animals do not always pick the safest routes.
comments.request: Reconsider this sentence and explain why.
comments.quote: I would reconsider this sentence, it almost debunks the entire theory

comments.issue: The theory relies on animal cognition yet cognitive errors are excluded.
comments.request: Reconcile the cognition basis with excluding cognitive errors.
comments.quote: Your whole theory is based on animal cognition with regards whether they use cognition to choose landscapes, but you want to disregard cognitive errors from the study?

comments.issue: A reference is missing at line 116.
comments.request: Add the reference.
comments.quote: 116 reference? 143 - 145

comments.issue: The referent of 'This' at lines 143-145 is ambiguous, and why some species cannot hang is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the referent and the brachiation example.
comments.quote: Sentence refers to “This” from the previous sentence, but it is unclear if This refers to small quadrupedal animals not having the option to hang from branches or if This refers to the heightened risk.

comments.issue: 'Cat-sized' should be removed; northern quolls are much smaller than cats.
comments.request: Remove 'cat-sized'.
comments.quote: 147 suggest removing cat-sized, northern quolls are significantly smaller than cats

comments.issue: 'Less able to project' would read better as 'less proficient at projecting'.
comments.request: Revise the wording at line 170.
comments.quote: 170 ‘less proficient at projecting’ rather than ‘less able to project’ ?

comments.issue: Structural failure of substrates, such as branches giving way, is not covered.
comments.request: Add a sentence or two on structural failure.
comments.quote: maybe you should include a sentence or two on the idea of structural failure of substrate eg. Branches giving way completely

comments.issue: Commas are missing at line 189.
comments.request: Add commas.
comments.quote: 189 are less able to grip, and fall frequently from, smooth-barked sections (add commas)

comments.issue: The example at lines 214-216 may illustrate loose surfaces rather than penetrability.
comments.request: Reconsider this example.
comments.quote: 214-216 not sure if this is a good example for penetrability or just loose surfaces.

comments.issue: Hunting-strategy changes in scrub could reflect getting closer to prey rather than accident risk.
comments.request: State this alternative theory.
comments.quote: could that not also be because they can get closer to prey, I think this alternate theory needs to be stated

comments.issue: Broekhuis 2014 reports hunting with and without moons; only moon intensity correlates.
comments.request: Correct the characterisation of Broekhuis 2014.
comments.quote: Broekhuis 2014 states that they hunt and feed during nights with and without moons, there is only a correlation with moon intensity.

comments.issue: Evidence at lines 437-440 may reflect closing the gap to prey rather than accidents.
comments.request: Consider the gap-closing explanation.
comments.quote: Is there evidence for this, again is this a function of being able to close the gap between prey and predator to increase chance of capture

comments.issue: The section at lines 427-440 misinterprets literature; few papers measured accidents, so attributing hunting behaviour to accident risk is a leap.
comments.request: Revise this section and consider cover availability.
comments.quote: I think this section has misinterpreted a lot of the literature.

comments.issue: Morice 2013 shows leaf litter obstructs sensing, not that it causes unstable footing.
comments.request: Correct this citation.
comments.quote: Morice 2013 found that the leaf litter obstructs both prey and predator in terms of sensing each other through “vision and vibration” not the leaf litter causing unstable footing.

comments.issue: Eaton 1970 argues cheetahs in confined habitats are more successful, relating to stalking rather than collisions.
comments.request: Correct this citation.
comments.quote: Eaton 1970 I think this paper argues that cheetahs that hunt in those more confined habitats are more successful

comments.issue: The evidence supports a role for accidents in navigating obstacles, not in limiting habitat use.
comments.request: Reword as willingness to use the landscape rather than how it is used.
comments.quote: Maybe it should be worded more as the ‘willingness of animals to use the landscape’ rather than how they use the landscape?

comments.issue: Australian predator evidence and prey manoeuvrability complicate the hypothesis.
comments.request: Reconcile this counter-evidence with the hypothesis.
comments.quote: This research combined with Australian predators being less successful in complex habitats complicates your hypothesis

comments.issue: The framework assumes habitat choice is not driven by competition for resources, mates and refuges.
comments.request: Provide evidence that accident responses are landscape-wide rather than situational.
comments.quote: I think one of the largest assumptions this paper makes is that species habitat choices are not driven by intraspecific and interspecific competition for habitat use

comments.issue: In the dam-wall example, competition for the valuable resource and accident risk cannot be separated.
comments.request: Discuss how to distinguish competition from accident responses.
comments.quote: So obviously there is a response to the valuable resource on the dam walls, is it competition or the accident landscape?

title: Accidents alter animal fitness landscapes

study.system: LTER field experiments; long-term abundance time series

editor_summary: Editor notes all reviewers liked the paper but had serious concerns: explain methods better, cite earlier similar work, explore short versus long-term trends, and discuss data and analysis limitations.

reviews.assessment: Novel and important results, but the premise is not new and the abstract overstates the spuriousness of short-term studies.
strengths: long-term experiments needed to understand global change responses

comments.issue: The general premise is not new and key historical publications are not credited.
comments.request: Cite Kareiva, Tilman, Magnuson, Likens, Estes et al. and Callahan.
comments.quote: First, the general premise of this research is not new. Far from it. Yet the literature cited in the text would suggest otherwise.

comments.issue: The data were used without contacting the data owners about possible quirks.
comments.request: Consult data generators before interpreting their datasets.
comments.quote: it is dangerous to just use data without getting some insights from those who generated the data in the first place

comments.issue: Very few LTER papers are cited despite the analysis being based on the LTER network.
comments.request: Cite the relevant LTER literature.
comments.quote: this analysis is based on the LTER research network and yet there actually very few LTER papers cited in the text

comments.issue: The message suggests short-term studies often mislead although spurious trends were rare (10-15%).
comments.request: Report the full results objectively in the abstract and discussion.
comments.quote: please objectively report your full results in the abstract and Discission noting the relatively small number of times that short term research would have misled investigators

reviews.assessment: Nice, novel study; serious concerns about methods clarity and chapter structure, with discussion containing results.

comments.issue: Content does not always conform to the section it is presented in.
comments.request: Align content with the appropriate sections.
comments.quote: the content does not always conform to the chapter it is presented in

comments.issue: Methods lack clarity, including the definition of long-term and how the critical threshold is derived in ambiguous cases.
comments.request: Define long-term and explain threshold derivation for unclear cases.
comments.quote: The methods section lacks sufficient clarity to comprehend the full approach taken. I miss a clear definition of what you mean by "long-term".

comments.issue: Model averaging is described although it was never used.
comments.request: Remove methods that were intended but not needed.
comments.quote: you mention that you use a method (model averaging) that then was never used, because it was not needed

comments.issue: Early results sub-chapters are intermediate steps that belong in the methods.
comments.request: Move intermediate analyses to the methods section.
comments.quote: The first few sub-chapter in results are more or less intermediate steps to come to the final results

comments.issue: The discussion repeats results and adds new results and statistical analyses that belong in the results.
comments.request: Move new analyses to the results and condense the repetition.
comments.quote: Most of this chapter also digs deeper in to the original data and thus provides additional results (even additional statistical analyses), which I would see to be much more appropriate in the results chapter

comments.issue: References in the discussion are redundant with the introduction.
comments.request: Trim redundant references in the discussion.
comments.quote: There are also a few references to the work of others, to place this study into context, but they are to some degree redundant to the line of arguments in the introduction

comments.issue: Implications for other measures (richness, composition, functional diversity) and spatial scales are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss implications for other biodiversity measures and scales.
comments.quote: I would appreciate some more discussion on implications of your results (or suggestions for a way forward) with respect to other measures, such as species richness, community composition, functional diversity etc.

comments.issue: The results for press dynamics are not compared with pulse dynamics.
comments.request: Compare press and pulse dynamics.
comments.quote: How can one compare your results on long-term experiments studying press dynamics with those from pulse dynamics (i.e. one time disturbances and recovery)?

comments.issue: The study is not compared with long-term observational studies lacking an experimental focus.
comments.request: Compare with non-experimental long-term observations.
comments.quote: How does you study compare to long-term observations that follow global change effects but which do not have an experimental focus?

comments.issue: How global change could affect control and treatment, and the time to threshold, is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss global change effects on the critical threshold.
comments.quote: How does global change affect your results, i.e. by affecting control and treatment?

comments.issue: The approach is not compared with studies summarising pitfalls of long-term data analysis (Didham et al. 2020).
comments.request: Compare with Didham et al. (2020) and related studies.
comments.quote: How does you approach compare to other studies that summarize difficulties and pitfalls in the analyses of long-term observational data

comments.issue: The conclusions are generic and would be valid without this study.
comments.request: Ground the conclusions more specifically in the results.
comments.quote: The conclusion is well-written but these conclusions are valid even without this study.

reviews.assessment: Interesting question but under-prepared; main concerns about the moving-window approach, trend response choice and spurious-result analysis.

comments.issue: Subsets drawn from anywhere in the time series are not comparable because experiments start in a fixed year.
comments.request: Vary subsets by sequentially cutting the last years from the time series.
comments.quote: I feel it would make more sense to only vary the data subsets by sequentially cutting the last years from the experimental time-series

comments.issue: Using the trend in effect size as the response does not match the experimental focus on effect size itself.
comments.request: Analyse effect size magnitude and its variation instead, e.g. with a GAM plateau model.
comments.quote: I feel like this summary trend statistic doesn’t obviously make sense in the context of an experiment

comments.issue: Percentage of spurious results is analysed with a Gaussian model without justification.
comments.request: Use beta or binomial regression, or justify the Gaussian model.
comments.quote: it is not necessarily appropriate to be analysed as a Gaussian model. Beta regression would be more appropriate for a %, or, more easily, the data could be analyzed as binomial model as the fraction A/B

comments.issue: The definition of spurious results shifts depending on whether long-term trends are apparent.
comments.request: Separate the analyses so the definition is consistent.
comments.quote: The “spurious results” have a shifting definition, depending on whether long-term trends are apparent in the data

comments.issue: Short-term effects are dismissed as spurious although short and long-term effects can both be real.
comments.request: Discuss what short-term effects mean and the overgeneralisation problem.
comments.quote: Difference between short-term and long-term effect do not necessarily mean only the latter is true

comments.issue: The predictions about environmental variability and the choice of a seasonal climate covariate are not justified.
comments.request: Clarify the variability predictions and why seasonality rather than interannual variability.
comments.quote: Why did you focus on seasonal variability? You use data at a yearly resolution, hence it would be more natural to describe variability as interannual change

comments.issue: A stable long-term trend does not invalidate that a short-term change occurred; the issue is extrapolation.
comments.request: Rephrase to focus on extrapolation rather than dismissing short-term change.
comments.quote: The only issue here is that the short-term study was extrapolated. Even if the long-term trend was stable – it doesn’t invalidate the fact that a short-term change happened.

comments.issue: The URL at line 129 needs updating.
comments.request: Update the URL.
comments.quote: Line 129 - this url needs to be updated

comments.issue: The subsetting procedure at line 150 needs more explanation.
comments.request: Explain the subsetting and add a schematic.
comments.quote: Line 150 - the subsetting needs more explaining – a schematic might be nice

comments.issue: Whether the variable at line 203 is scaled or centred is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the scaling of the variable.
comments.quote: Line 203 – scaled (to units of standard deviation) or just centered?

comments.issue: An interaction is examined at line 249 although it was not hypothesised and is absent from the best model.
comments.request: Explain where the interaction comes from and why it is tested.
comments.quote: I don’t recall you mentioning testing or hypothesizing interactions earlier in the paper. Also Table 1, your best model, does not show any interaction? Where did this interaction come from?

comments.issue: Many instances of strange phrasing and odd word choices (L52, L84, L103, L216).
comments.request: Have the language carefully edited.
comments.quote: I found many instances of strange phrasing or odd word choices, which I found very distracting from the main story of the paper.

comments.issue: A highly relevant paper is not cited.
comments.request: Cite the suggested paper.
comments.quote: A highly relevant paper that the authors might cite:

title: How long do population level field experiments need to be? Utilising data from the 40‐year‐old LTER network

study.system: Jurien Bay dune chronosequence; leaf phenols and silicon

editor_summary: Reviewers positive on the question but very critical; rejection based on chronosequence validity (components peak midway); redo analyses; avoid correlations on means (SI only at most); revise strongly as new submission.

reviews.assessment: Novel approach to the resource availability hypothesis, but questions the evidence that Si defends non-grass families and the within-species trade-off logic.
strengths: novel way of addressing resource availability hypothesis predictions
survey of soil and plant tissue along a chronosequence

comments.issue: The claim that Si acts as a defense in families beyond grasses and monocots lacks supporting evidence.
comments.request: Present more evidence and be circumspect about Si's many functions.
comments.quote: While the authors assert that Si is used a defense in more families than grasses and monocots, I would have liked more evidence presented that Si acts as a defense in these other families.

comments.issue: Family-level differences in leaf Si content are relegated to Figure S3.
comments.request: Incorporate Figure S3 into the main text.
comments.quote: In fact, the Si content of leaves is orders of magnitude greater for Poaceae and Cyperaceae than other families. Figure S3 might be incorporated into the main text.

comments.issue: Trade-off evidence relies on abundance-weighted community values; species-mean evidence is not shown.
comments.request: Test the trade-off using species mean values without relative abundance.
comments.quote: What is the evidence for trade-off between Si and phenolics when just species mean values are used, without incorporating relative abundance?

comments.issue: Cross-species correlations are used to support arguments based on within-individual metabolic pathways, an unclear logic.
comments.request: Reconcile the level of evidence with the proposed mechanism.
comments.quote: the arguments that the authors use for why one might find trade-offs are based on metabolic pathways that are occurring within individuals. So the logic there is not so clear.

comments.issue: Soil-based trade-off evidence reflects species turnover rather than within-species trade-offs.
comments.request: Acknowledge that turnover, not within-species trade-offs, drives the pattern.
comments.quote: the evidence for soil-based trade-offs with Si and phenolic compounds is reflected more in species turnover across the gradient than in trade-offs within species

comments.issue: Trade-offs appear mainly at family level; within-family variation is large and phylogenetic non-independence is not addressed.
comments.request: Run phylogenetically adjusted comparisons to look for trade-offs.
comments.quote: Because the trade-offs are found more at the family level than at the within-species level, the authors should consider phylogenetically adjusted comparisons to look for trade-offs.

comments.issue: It is unexplained why nitrogen was not considered in the study.
comments.request: Explain why nitrogen was not considered.
comments.quote: I am curious why nitrogen was not considered at all in this study. Please provide an explanation

comments.issue: Which nutrient limits growth on each soil is largely hypothesized, with a cartoon figure cited as evidence.
comments.request: Cite experimental evidence of nutrient limitation or soften the claims.
comments.quote: The authors make many arguments about which nutrient is limiting in which soil, but much of this appears to be hypothesis. In one case, the authors cite a cartoon figure for evidence.

comments.issue: Mechanisms are speculated without data on how Si affects herbivores.
comments.request: Reduce speculation on the proposed mechanisms.
comments.quote: in the absence of those data here, there should be reduced speculation on many of the mechanisms proposed.

comments.issue: Most defense studies find positive rather than negative correlations among defense types, contrary to the trade-off claim.
comments.request: Discuss this discrepancy with the literature.
comments.quote: Another issue is that at this point, most defense studies find that different types of defenses are more likely to be positively rather than negatively correlated.

comments.issue: Supplement panels draw lines for non-significant relationships.
comments.request: Remove lines for non-significant relationships.
comments.quote: I seem to recall there was a graph in the supplement in which there were many panels with lines drawn for the relationship between Si and phenolics, **but only one was significant**. Please remove lines from non-significant relationships.

reviews.assessment: Well written and mostly appropriate, but the chronosequence is not suited to test RAH predictions and the defense trade-off is not really tested.
strengths: generally very well written and easy to follow

comments.issue: The chronosequence is a complex non-monotonic fertility gradient for which RAH makes no predictions.
comments.request: Use a monotonic gradient or revise the framework accordingly.
comments.quote: The chronosequence represent a complex and non-monotonic soil fertility gradient. N and P peak at stage 2 and decrease towards older sites especially for P. Whereas, Si peaks at stage 4.

comments.issue: Leaf chemistry does not track the fertility peak, and analyses use chronosequence stages rather than actual plot fertility.
comments.request: Regress leaf chemistry on actual plot fertility levels.
comments.quote: A clearer fertility gradient combined with appropriate analysis that regress leaf chemistry on actual plot fertility levels rather than chronosequence stages can be more helpful.

comments.issue: A trade-off in tissue concentrations is shown, but whether it represents a defense trade-off is untested.
comments.request: Test the defense trade-off interpretation or qualify it.
comments.quote: While the authors show a clear trade off between phenolics and Si defenses does it actually represent a defense trade off (shifting type of defense with resource availability) is not tested.

comments.issue: The study may be better suited to a specialist journal unless reframed for a general audience.
comments.request: Develop a more sophisticated framework or target a specialist journal.
comments.quote: I believe the authors can come up with a more sophisticated framework that can well represent the study for a more general audience or the manuscript is better suited for more of a specialist journal

reviews.assessment: Intriguing and potentially broad-scale results, but the analyses need non-independence and confounding addressed.

comments.issue: Whether plots were randomly selected within each chronosequence stage is unconfirmed.
comments.request: Confirm that plot selection was random.
comments.quote: assuming that selection of plots within each chronosequence stage was indeed random (please confirm) I see no problems

comments.issue: Individual-plant analyses ignore non-independence among multiple observations per plot.
comments.request: Add a plot random factor.
comments.quote: for analyses at the individual plant level, you have multiple observations per plant species, which is corrected for by the species random factor, but also multiple non-independent observations per plot, which would call for an additional plot random factor

comments.issue: Pearson correlations of 25 plot values ignore the five-stage chronosequence structure.
comments.request: Correlate stage means and add within-stage correlations.
comments.quote: A more correct approach would be to correlate the 5 chronosequence stage means rather than the 25 plot values, and compare this with 5 correlations, one per chronosequence stage, based on the 5 plots from each stage

comments.issue: Other variables changing along the gradient (pH, nutrients, salt, climate) are not acknowledged as potential confounders.
comments.request: Acknowledge and discuss these confounding variables.
comments.quote: it would be good to at least acknowledge these other possibly confounding variables and discuss their potential for explaining some of the observed results

comments.issue: The statement that natural communities may differ from single-species fertilization studies is self-evident and directionless.
comments.request: State a hypothesis about the direction of these differences.
comments.quote: Saying that what happens in natural plant communities may be different from what happens in a single-species fertilization study is rather self-evident. Do you have a hypothesis regarding the direction of such differences?

comments.issue: 'Continually decrease' is misleading because values plateau in the last two stages.
comments.request: Revise the wording.
comments.quote: “continually decrease” may be a little misleading as it seems to plateau for the two last stages (both at 0.2 g/kg)

comments.issue: The expectation that the gradient holds further north is asserted without argument.
comments.request: Add argumentation for extrapolating the gradient.
comments.quote: Concerning “further south”, it may be good to add some argumentation here as to why you expect the same gradient to hold further north.

comments.issue: The word 'within' misleadingly suggests an extra nesting level; the plot layout is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the layout, possibly with a map or diagram.
comments.quote: At first reading I was quite misled by the word “within” here, as it suggested 5 plots were selected within each of 10 larger plots, suggesting an additional level of nesting in the design.

comments.issue: The number of leaves sampled per plant is not reported.
comments.request: Add how many leaves per plant were sampled.
comments.quote: “as in Zemunik et al. (2016)” is a bit unsatisfactory here. Please add how many leaves per plant.

comments.issue: It is implausible that 10 individual plants made up 57-88% of plot cover; 'individuals' may mean 'species'.
comments.request: Check and correct the sampling description.
comments.quote: It seems difficult to believe that just 10 individual plants made up 57% to 88% of the total plant cover of a 10 by 10-meter plot. Could it be that “individuals” should be “species” here?

comments.issue: Table S1 mixes two sampling procedures.
comments.request: Split Table S1 into two tables, one per procedure.
comments.quote: Was this again one plant per plot for these other species? I would recommend splitting Table S1 into two separate tables, one for each procedure, for clarity.

comments.issue: Two line-level wording fixes (L184 'calculated' not 'estimated'; L348 'P-limiting').
comments.quote: I assume you mean “calculated” rather than “estimated”.

comments.issue: Whether 'plant-available Si' is the average of the three soil samples per plot is unclear.
comments.request: State how plant-available Si was derived.
comments.quote: “plant-available Si” Is this the average of the three soil samples per plot?

comments.issue: The text claims stage 1 differed from stages 2 and 3, but the figure shows no significant difference.
comments.request: Correct the significance statement.
comments.quote: The figure shows that stage 2 and 3 were not significantly different from stage 1.

comments.issue: Significance of per-species changes along the chronosequence is not quantified.
comments.request: Quantify per-species changes, e.g. with an ordered heterogeneity test.
comments.quote: Why was no attempt made to quantify the significance of the changes in Si or phenols along the chronosequence for each species as was done for the community or family level?

comments.issue: The analyses behind Tables S2 and S3 are not described in the Methods.
comments.request: Add descriptions of these analyses to the Methods section.
comments.quote: Table S2. Please add a description of the analyses resulting in this Table to the Methods section.

comments.issue: Causal wording 'effect of' at L247 and L338 overstates the correlative results.
comments.request: Replace with 'relationship between' or 'correlation with'.
comments.quote: I find “effect of” overstated here, suggest replacing with “correlation with”.

comments.issue: Conostylis candicans accumulates high Si but shows no relationship; this exception is not highlighted.
comments.request: Highlight this species as an exception.
comments.quote: It may be worth highlighting that Conostylis candicans did not show this relationship, even though it seems to accumulate rather high concentrations of Si.

comments.issue: The t-test behind Figure S5 is not described in the Methods.
