comments.issue: Discussion is long and rambling; should return to the three research questions.
comments.request: Tighten the discussion around the research questions.
comments.quote: I found the discussion to be quite long and rambling – rather than sticking to a strict return to the three research questions of interest.

comments.issue: Five line-level copy edits (punctuation, hyphenation, word additions, acronym spelling, grammar).
comments.quote: Line 126 – Should likely spell out full name of BACI experiment since the acronym is used, but not explained.

comments.issue: Modulate is vague in this context.
comments.request: Clarify the meaning.
comments.quote: what specifically does ‘modulate’ mean in this context? It is a little vague.

comments.issue: Explicit explanation needed of how nectar feeding scales to ecosystem carbon dynamics.
comments.request: Add this explanation.
comments.quote: it would be good to see a more explicit explanation of how feeding on nectar scales up to affect ecosystem-level carbon dynamics

comments.issue: How many trees a 50 m invasion area covers is unclear.
comments.request: Translate the area into tree numbers.
comments.quote: about how many trees would a 50 m invasion area cover?

comments.issue: Verification of 5-year invasion duration is unclear.
comments.request: Explain how invasion duration was confirmed.
comments.quote: were these 5 year invaded sites confirmed with long-term invasion maps, survey, previous data from the study sites, etc.?

comments.issue: Should specify that measurements apply to BACI and long-term invasion sites.
comments.request: Mark this in the relevant sections.
comments.quote: probably should specify that these measurements are for BACI and longer term invasion sites

comments.issue: Pooling of the two dry-season and two wet-season sample dates should be specified.
comments.request: Clarify the pooling of sampling periods.
comments.quote: for sampling periods, please specify that is pooling data for the two dry season and two wet season sample dates

comments.issue: Whether site was a random effect and how models were compared is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the random-effects and model-selection procedure.
comments.quote: site as a random effect for GLM? Or did you use GLMM and compare the AICc scores to GLM and if so exactly how was that done?

comments.issue: Terminology inconsistent between text and figures (non-native/invasive, browsed/unbrowsed, excluded/removed, changing symbols).
comments.request: Use consistent terminology across text and figures.
comments.quote: Another inconsistency is that in the paper these are called excluded and in the figures they are called removed.

comments.issue: Whether the line 249 value refers to the 5-year invasion sites needs clarification.
comments.request: Clarify which sites the value applies to.
comments.quote: Line 249 – in the 5 year invasion sites?

comments.issue: Decline in control sites may reflect interannual variation rather than resident ants.
comments.request: Distinguish these sources and discuss nectar production data.
comments.quote: how much of the decline in control sites is due to interannual variation in photosynthesis vs. negative impacts of resident ants?

comments.issue: Effect may be because ant elimination also removed herbivores.
comments.request: Consider this alternative explanation.
comments.quote: or because the method of eliminating the ants also eliminated the herbivores?

comments.issue: Figure 1 should indicate whether transition sites were invaded before or after the 2017 sampling.
comments.request: Mark the invasion timing in the figure.
comments.quote: should indicate in the figure whether transition sites (invaded in Dec 2017) was before or after the 2017 sampling so that it is clear to readers just scanning the figure

comments.issue: Whether P. megacephala harvest nectar from EFNs is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the evidence.
comments.quote: Is it clear that P. megacephala do not harvest nectar from the EFNs on the Acacia trees?

title: Mutualism disruption by an invasive ant reduces carbon fixation for a foundational East African ant‐plant

study.system: Swiss Alps alpine plants; transplant experiment with integral projection models

editor_summary: Reviewers raised valuable points on data analysis and interpretation; also asks to specify the limitations of elevation as a climate analogue, particularly in the introduction.

reviews.assessment: Praises the creative design and extinction-time estimates but is concerned that small sample sizes produced unrealistic vital rate models and overconfident intervals.
strengths: creative experimental design separating climate from biotic effects
estimation of extinction times provides a strong test of extinction debt

comments.issue: Fitting models to each species-site-treatment subset prevents borrowing strength and yields biologically unrealistic intercept-only vital rate models.
comments.request: Fit size-dependent models across treatments and test site/treatment effects; report sample sizes.
comments.quote: A potential consequence of this could be limited sample sizes in many cases resulting in only being able to fit biologically unrealistic intercept-only models.

comments.issue: Bootstrap confidence intervals are overconfident for binary vital rates estimated as zero and ignore uncertainty in species-mean rates.
comments.request: Use a parametric bootstrap that resamples coefficients by their statistical uncertainty.
comments.quote: if these 0 estimates are the consequence of low sample sizes, the real uncertainty in the vital rate estimate will not be captured by bootstrapping

comments.issue: The Panetta et al. 2018 study on warming-driven local extinction is not cited at L64.
comments.request: Cite Panetta et al. (2018).
comments.quote: L64: see Panetta, A. M., et al. (2018).

comments.issue: Confidence intervals around regression lines are not shaded in Figure 2 and other figures.
comments.request: Add shading for confidence intervals around regression lines.
comments.quote: Fig. 2 and others: consider including shading to show confidence intervals around regression lines.

comments.issue: Sites differ in more than temperature, so warming may not be the only distinguishing climate variable.
comments.request: Describe other site differences that could affect the results.
comments.quote: Is warming the main climate variable distinguishing these sites? In general, there is quite a bit of site-level variation not captured by temperature.

comments.issue: Calling lower-elevation transplants 'experimental warming' wrongly implies controlled manipulation of temperature.
comments.request: Revise the term 'experimental warming' throughout.
comments.quote: the use of ‘experimental warming’ to me implies that temperature was experimentally manipulated in a way that would control for other environmental factors, which is not the case when using lower elevation sites as a proxy for climate change

comments.issue: The size range of transplanted individuals relative to the population is not reported.
comments.request: Report the size range of transplanted individuals.
comments.quote: L161: What was the size range of transplanted individuals relative to the size distribution of the population?

comments.issue: Variation in turf community composition within and among sites is not described.
comments.request: Report species composition and abundance data for the transplanted turfs.
comments.quote: It would be informative to know how much the community composition of turfs varied within and among sites.

comments.issue: The relationships among turfs, plots and blocks in the design are hard to follow.
comments.request: Add a supplementary figure explaining the design.
comments.quote: I have a hard time understanding how turfs, plots, and blocks are related in this design. Perhaps an additional figure in the SI would help with this.

comments.issue: The soil treatments and how they were analysed statistically are difficult to understand.
comments.request: Integrate the soil treatments better into methods and results.
comments.quote: Here and elsewhere the soil treatments are difficult to understand.

comments.issue: Using vital rates from other species rather than the same species at other sites is not justified.
comments.request: Justify this choice or use same-species rates as a more conservative option.
comments.quote: What is the justification for using vital rates from other species, vs. vital rates for the same species at other sites?

comments.issue: How lambda was calculated is unclear, and the year fixed effect description conflicts with the Table S4 legend.
comments.request: Explain how lambda was computed from the fitted models.
comments.quote: How was λs calculated? The methods say that year was included as a fixed effect when significant (L216), but also that these coefficients weren’t used to create year-specific IPMs (Table S4 legend).

comments.issue: Whether soil treatment was also included at L211 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify whether soil treatment was included.
comments.quote: L211: And also soil treatment?

comments.issue: Relative LTRE contributions are plotted; absolute contributions would be more informative and comparable.
comments.request: Show absolute LTRE contributions or state relative ones in the legends.
comments.quote: Absolute LTRE contributions are more informative, and can be compared across species since they are plotted separately with differing y-axis ranges.

comments.issue: Modelling recruit size as a normal distribution is questionable.
comments.request: Justify the distribution used for recruit size.
comments.quote: SI L8: Recruit size modeled as a normal distribution?

comments.issue: It is unclear why growth could not be modelled and what the coefficients represent.
comments.request: Explain why growth was not modelled and how coefficients were obtained.
comments.quote: It’s not clear to me why growth couldn’t be modeled – because there were too few survivors?

comments.issue: Size-dependence of growth variance was apparently not tested.
comments.request: Test for size-dependence on growth variance.
comments.quote: SI L20: Did you test for size-dependence on the growth variance?

comments.issue: Whether fixed effect coefficients were similar across these models is not reported.
comments.request: Compare the fixed effect coefficients across models.
comments.quote: SI L31-33: Were the fixed effects coefficients similar in these models?

comments.issue: Whether leaf number was treated as an integer in the matrix models is unclear.
comments.request: State how leaf number was treated in the models.
comments.quote: SI L36: Was leaf number treated as an integer in the matrix models?

reviews.assessment: Strong, well-written study with solid design and comprehensive analysis, though the title and hypotheses are overstated and some analyses need clarification.
strengths: well-written paper within a compelling conceptual framework
combination of strong design with demographic modelling

comments.issue: The title is too assertive and narrow, since no local extinctions were observed.
comments.request: Revise the title to reflect decreased population growth rather than extinction.
comments.quote: The research presented in this manuscript does not indicate any local extinction events per se; rather, it provides evidence of decreased population growth of high elevation species under certain experimental conditions.

comments.issue: The abstract and line 52 should say 'local' extinction to avoid implying full species extinction.
comments.request: Add 'local' to these statements about extinction.
comments.quote: since the research here concerns local extinction, not full extinction of species

comments.issue: The introduction does not adequately justify the hypotheses and states them unclearly.
comments.request: Develop brief justifications for each hypothesis and clarify their wording.
comments.quote: the Introduction needs to more fully – if briefly – develop justifications for the hypotheses, and in some cases the way the hypotheses are stated could be more clear

comments.issue: The first hypothesis is unclear and never explains why warming plus novel species should combine to reduce growth more.
comments.request: Clarify the combination hypothesis and add a hypothesis on single effects.
comments.quote: while the Introduction clearly lays out the ideas that both warming and novel species interactions may contribute to local extinction, it does not address exactly why their combination should contribute more

comments.issue: The second hypothesis lacks sufficient justification, with only one cited paper on alpine species.
comments.request: Strengthen the justification for vital-rate-specific responses.
comments.quote: That’s good, but seems not quite sufficient, given that just one of the four papers refers to alpine species and gives the reader no indication of why survival responded to warming and growth rates responded to competition.

comments.issue: The third hypothesis says 'time to extinction' although this was modelled, not observed.
comments.request: Write 'predicted time to extinction' instead.
comments.quote: Since the study did not extend long enough to observe extinctions, and the “time to extinction” was modeled, it would be more accurate to write

comments.issue: The introduction is not explicit enough about the enhancing effect of novel species on warming-driven extinction risk.
comments.request: Make this thrust more explicit in the introduction.
comments.quote: Generally, the thrust of the paper and hypotheses are about the enhancing effect of novel species on the extinction risk posed by warming on alpine plants. The Introduction could be more explicit about this.

comments.issue: The ecological zones represented by the four elevations are not explained.
comments.request: Describe what zones the four elevations represent.
comments.quote: For readers not familiar with the Swiss Alps, it would be useful to understand what zones the four elevations represent.

comments.issue: Pollinator variation among elevations could affect seed production and lambda but is not considered.
comments.request: Discuss pollinator variation as a potential driver of seed production.
comments.quote: And what about variation in pollinators among the various elevations? One of the vital rates measured was seed production, so pollinators could be key to seed production and to lambda in general.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether source collection location was randomized to avoid relatedness effects.
comments.request: State whether collection locations were randomized across plots.
comments.quote: Was an effort made to randomize the source collection location when planting the collected plants into the experimental plots

comments.issue: Results are not explicitly connected to the stated hypotheses.
comments.request: Add explicit statements linking results to each hypothesis.
comments.quote: it would be useful if the authors made explicit statements connecting the results to the Introduction’s stated hypotheses

comments.issue: Three of four temperature by novel species interaction coefficients are positive, which is not reconciled with the hypothesis.
comments.request: Explain how interaction coefficient signs relate to the hypothesis.
comments.quote: for three of the four species the interaction coefficient is positive, while for one it is negative – how does that relate to the hypothesis?

comments.issue: The many pairwise significance tests in Table S6 are not adjusted for multiple testing.
comments.request: Adjust the tests for multiple comparisons or justify not doing so.
comments.quote: Have these significance tests been adjusted for multiple tests? If so, how? If not, why not?

comments.issue: How Table S5 coefficients produce the novel-species lambda declines is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the calculation in the Table S7 caption.
comments.quote: It is not very clear how the model coefficients from Table S5 were used to compute the lambda declines for the effect of novel species at each 1 deg increase of warming.

comments.issue: The discussion refers to local extinction itself rather than the risk or predicted time to extinction.
comments.request: Use 'risk of local extinction' or 'predicted time to local extinction'.
comments.quote: When discussing local extinction be careful to refer to “risk of local extinction” or “predicted time to local extinction” rather than local extinction itself, since that was not actually studied.

comments.issue: Soil chemistry and biota differences are discussed although no such data were collected.
comments.request: Remove or temper the claims about soil chemistry and biota.
comments.quote: Reference is made here to differences in the chemistry and biota of the soil, but the paper does not include any data on soil chemistry or biota – just different soils in general.

comments.issue: The true scenario of a temporally dynamic community assemblage should be stated more clearly.
comments.request: Describe the realistic dynamic assemblage scenario and species differences.
comments.quote: They might more clearly state here that the true scenario is likely to be that higher elevation plants will face a temporally dynamic community assemblage of faster-arriving novel species mixed in with their current neighbors.

reviews.assessment: Very positive about the design, analysis and writing, with minor concerns about transplantation shock and overly general conclusions from four species.
strengths: well written text and clear figures

comments.issue: Low lambda values in controls suggest transplantation shock may have exaggerated the warming effect and affected elasticity analyses.
comments.request: Discuss transplantation shock as a potential artefact in the discussion.
comments.quote: The question hence is whether transplantation has artificially exaggerated the warming effect on lambda?

comments.issue: Four species with similar growth forms are too few to support numerically precise conclusions for the whole alpine flora.
comments.request: Tone down the general conclusions.
comments.quote: I think your sample is too small and narrow to warrant such numerically precise conclusions for all the alpine flora. I suggest toning down a bit.

comments.issue: Information on turf vegetation types, excavation criteria and temperature measurement is missing.
comments.request: Describe turf selection criteria and how site temperatures were measured.
comments.quote: What were the criteria used for selecting the positions of turf excavation and re-burial? Where have the temperatures at the sites been derived from?

comments.issue: The statement at lines 338-339 is too strong, since local extinctions have occurred at many sites.
comments.request: Soften the statement and acknowledge widespread local extinctions (e.g. Wiens 2016).
comments.quote: Maybe a bit too strong a statement. Depends on what you consider “local”.

title: Drivers of local extinction risk in alpine plants under warming climate

study.system: complex computer simulations; dynamic vegetation model case study

editor_summary: Editor notes two reviewers recommend minor revision while Reviewer 3 doubts novelty; to make it a methods paper, annotated R code must be provided on GitHub and referenced in the paper.

reviews.assessment: Important problem and useful insights, but needs a unified framework and more thorough treatment of identifiability.
strengths: addresses an important and often overlooked issue

comments.issue: Title promises a statistical theory but no unified theoretical framework is presented; solutions remain case-by-case.
comments.request: Provide a unified theoretical framework for the solutions.
comments.quote: The title frames a statistical theory, but the manuscript does not appear to have a unified theoretical framework. The problems were identified, yet the solutions appear largely case-by-case.

comments.issue: Effectiveness of the three solutions is tested only in one scenario with combined structural errors.
comments.request: Run experiments varying combinations and magnitudes of structural errors.
comments.quote: Consider conducting multiple sets of experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of the three solutions in different scenarios.

comments.issue: Which equations were altered and which parameters inferred is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the altered equations and inferred parameters.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to clarify the equations being altered and the parameters inferred.

comments.issue: Machine-learning error terms could absorb true process signals, creating an identifiability problem.
comments.request: Explain how priors or initial values avoid this identifiability issue.
comments.quote: I see a potential identifiability issue, i.e., the signals from true processes could also be modeled accurately as errors

comments.issue: Removing trade-off parameters to avoid identifiability issues requires prior knowledge and can cause structural errors.
comments.request: Address identifiability more properly or warn about limited applicability.
comments.quote: However, this simplification of the model requires much prior knowledge, and is often the source of major model structural errors.

comments.issue: Source of benefit from multiple data streams or scales is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the benefit of multiple scales, especially under non-linearity.
comments.quote: I wonder if the benefit comes from using more data, multiple independent data streams with different biases, or data at multiple scales.

comments.issue: "Internal constraints" at lines 120-121 are not stated.
comments.request: State the internal constraints.
comments.quote: Could you briefly state the “internal constraints”?

comments.issue: Structural model errors are only described in the supplementary materials.
comments.request: Introduce the structural model errors in the main text.
comments.quote: I would appreciate it if the “structural model errors” are introduced in the main text rather than only the supplementary materials

comments.issue: Methods for comparing parameter errors and uncertainty estimates need more detail.
comments.request: Explain how parameter errors and uncertainty were compared.
comments.quote: those for comparing parameter errors and uncertainty estimation could use some more detailed explanations

comments.issue: Observational errors or biases imposed on simulated data are not stated.
comments.request: State the observational errors and biases and test solution robustness to them.
comments.quote: Please state the observational errors and/or biases you imposed on the simulated data, if any.

comments.issue: Averaging over the posterior distribution is not visible in equation 1.
comments.request: Make the averaging explicit in equation 1.
comments.quote: I did not see the averaging over “the posterior distribution” in equation 1.

comments.issue: How ESEU should be interpreted is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the interpretation of ESEU.
comments.quote: It would help to explain how ESEU can be interpreted.

comments.issue: Averaging over the posterior and replicates is not reflected in equation 2.
comments.request: Show the averaging in equation 2.
comments.quote: Again, how is averaging over “the posterior distribution and the five replicates” reflected in equation 2?

comments.issue: Sentence at lines 217-219 is redundant.
comments.request: Remove the redundancy.
comments.quote: Lines 217-219: The sentence was redundant.

comments.issue: Performance impact of removing trade-off parameters is not demonstrated.
comments.request: Compare models with and without the simplification and justify unbiased prediction.
comments.quote: Could you provide some supplementary materials to compare the performance of models with and without this simplification?

comments.issue: Section 4 and results for correcting processes rather than outputs could not be found.
comments.request: Add or clearly locate the missing section and results.
comments.quote: I could not find section 4 or results from correcting processes themselves rather than output.

comments.issue: How the second challenge was handled is not described.
comments.request: Explain the handling of the second challenge.
comments.quote: I wonder how you handled the second challenge.

comments.issue: No guidance on diagnosing the dominance of statistical versus structural errors.
comments.request: Provide recommendations for diagnosing error dominance.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to provide some recommendations on diagnosing how dominant statistical and structural errors are.

comments.issue: Figure 1 panels differ in scenarios and purple lines are hard to see.
comments.request: Align the panel scenarios and improve line visibility.
comments.quote: Why does panel a) not have the “not measured” and “partly measured” scenarios similar to panel b)?

comments.issue: Figure 6 lacks quantitative comparison of computational time and complexity.
comments.request: Show computational time and complexity comparisons.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to show some quantitative comparison of computational time and complexity.

comments.issue: Algorithm used to fit the GP model is not stated.
comments.request: State the GP fitting algorithm.
comments.quote: I am curious about what algorithm was used to fit the GP model.

comments.issue: Acronyms SdGP and MeGP are not defined.
comments.request: Define the acronyms.
comments.quote: The acronyms like “SdGP” and “MeGP” were not defined.

comments.issue: Scalability of the method to many state variables and particle choice is not addressed.
comments.request: Comment on performance with large state spaces and particle numbers.
comments.quote: How does this method work on models with large numbers of state variables (e.g., over 100)? Could you comment on how many particles should be used, considering the number of state variables?

reviews.assessment: Clearly written and well structured; asks for more precise communication and consistent terminology.
strengths: of great interest to ecologists using complex simulations

comments.issue: "The model with structural error" implies a single error although several processes were altered.
comments.request: State explicitly that errors were imposed on several processes and explain the choices.
comments.quote: It may come across as there is a single entity that reflects ‘structural error’, when in fact the authors have introduced structural errors on several different model processes

comments.issue: Terms for the erroneous model are inconsistent across the manuscript.
comments.request: Choose one term and use it consistently.
comments.quote: Please choose one term and use it as much as possible consistently.

comments.issue: Why daily data are called balanced and ten-day data unbalanced is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the balanced versus unbalanced terminology.
comments.quote: Consider explaining the reader why the daily observations are termed ‘balanced data’ whereas those with ten-day resolution are called ‘unbalanced data’

reviews.assessment: Important ideas but opaque presentation and unclear novelty; comes across as a review dressed as a methods paper.
strengths: important ideas about systematic model errors

comments.issue: The case study cannot be understood without the supporting material; model structure and calibration are not sketched.
comments.request: Provide a basic sketch of the model structure, calibration and notation in the main text.
comments.quote: I struggled to make sense of the case study without spending a lot of time looking over the supporting material.

comments.issue: The manuscript is a brief survey of established methods with nothing new, falling between review and methods paper.
comments.request: Demonstrate a genuine methodological advance.
comments.quote: There isn’t anything new in here as far as I can tell, which leaves that manuscript trapped a between a formal review and a novel methods paper

comments.issue: The claim that model error is a major problem is not actually demonstrated by the limited example.
comments.request: Broaden the case and strengthen the theoretical considerations.
comments.quote: However, this manuscript doesn’t actually make the case—the example is somewhat limited in scope and the authors brushed over the theoretical considerations very quickly.

comments.issue: The ad-hoc improvement claim at line 469 has no supporting citation.
comments.request: Add a citation supporting the ad-hoc improvement claim.
comments.quote: Where is the citation to support this?

comments.issue: "Multiple scales" is used loosely without definition.
comments.request: Define whether physical scales or biological organisation levels are meant.
comments.quote: The term ‘multiple scales’ is used a lot. This could do with a tighter definition. Do you mean physical scales or levels of biological organisation?

comments.issue: The KOH method argument at line 339 cannot be followed and lacks a citation.
comments.request: Clarify the argument and add a supporting citation.
comments.quote: I really couldn’t follow the argument here (and there is no citation to follow).

comments.issue: The trade-off in fitting different data streams is not identified.
comments.request: State what the trade-off is (information, ease of fitting, etc.).
comments.quote: What is the trade-off in play when fitting the different data streams? Information? Ease of fitting?

comments.issue: Comparison with simple statistical models omits that ccs usually lack closed-form likelihoods.
comments.request: Discuss the absence of closed-form likelihoods in ccs.
comments.quote: It seems odd to me to compare fitting ccs to simple statistical models without mentioning that the former (often) do not have a closed-form likelihood.

comments.issue: Repeated sentence at line 217 and a missing word at line 329.
comments.quote: Line 329: “allows the Kennedy-O’Hagan ” Missing word?

title: Towards robust statistical inference for complex computer models

study.system: Wood Thrush; natal dispersal in forest fragments

editor_summary: Editor notes all reviewers found an important, novel and well-written topic, but two had significant concerns about methods and interpretation; revision must address univariate analysis concerns (R1) and methods clarity and interpretation (all).

reviews.assessment: Exciting novel method, but the response variable, univariate models and a high-leverage plot undermine the conclusions.
strengths: novel combination of stable isotopes and wing length to estimate immigration
addresses a real need to understand drivers of long-distance immigration

comments.issue: The modelled response (probability of being a long-distance immigrant) does not match the predicted immigration rates.
comments.request: Justify using the probability of being a long-distance immigrant instead of immigration rate.
comments.quote: There seems to be a disconnect between your predictions—which are for relationships between immigration rates and patch size, quality, and conspecific density—and what you use as a response variable in your statistical models

comments.issue: Omitting correlated predictors from univariate models can bias effect estimates.
comments.request: Use models that include correlated predictors.
comments.quote: the possibility that omitting a correlated variable from your analysis could result in biased estimates of the effect of a predictor variable on a response

comments.issue: Univariate models do not test the ideal dominance and social cues predictions, which require accounting for conspecific density.
comments.request: Test the predictions after accounting for conspecific density.
comments.quote: your use of univariate models means you did not actually test the predictions from the ideal dominance and social cues hypotheses described in the introduction

comments.issue: The social cues conclusion depends heavily on one high-leverage sample plot.
comments.request: Investigate and discuss the influence of the high-leverage plot.
comments.quote: the conclusion that results support the social cues hypothesis appears to be heavily dependent on the responses of individuals from a single sample plot with high leverage

comments.issue: Examples of the unique costs of long-distance dispersal are missing.
comments.request: Provide examples of the unique costs of long-distance dispersal.
comments.quote: lines 55-56: Please provide examples of the “unique costs” of long-distance dispersal

comments.issue: Line 62 likely should read immigration rate rather than probability of immigration.
comments.request: Change the wording to immigration rate.
comments.quote: line 62: I assume this should be “immigration rate” not “probability of immigration”, given that immigration rate is the focus in the following sentences and in Fig. 1.

comments.issue: The Fahrig 2013 citation does not support the claim that patch size is the most important driver of immigration.
comments.request: Clarify or remove the Fahrig 2013 citation.
comments.quote: line 66: I do not understand the reference to Fahrig 2013 here. This paper argues that it is habitat amount within the surrounding landscape that drives species richness, not the size of a habitat patch.

comments.issue: The expected immigration rate–patch size relationship is only specified in the Figure 1 caption.
comments.request: State the expected relationship in the main text.
comments.quote: line 66: I suggest stating the expected relationship between immigration rate + patch size here in text. Currently, this is only specified in the body of Fig. 1

comments.issue: The ideal free hypothesis description implies a quality-by-density interaction that is never predicted or tested.
comments.request: Predict and test this interaction explicitly.
comments.quote: what you describe here sounds like an interacting effect of habitat quality and conspecific density on immigration

comments.issue: The sentence on lines 100-104 is confusing and needs revision.
comments.request: Revise the sentence for clarity.
comments.quote: I found this particular sentence confusing and had to read it several times to figure out its meaning. Thus I suggest you revise it.

comments.issue: The single conservation-priority sentence in the introduction is not developed and is outside the study focus.
comments.request: Omit the conservation sentence from the introduction.
comments.quote: This is the only mention of conservation priority setting in the introduction, and it is not clear from this one sentence how information from your study could inform conservation.

comments.issue: Line 143 is ambiguous between sample plot size and forest amount within 2 km.
comments.request: Clarify which quantity is meant.
comments.quote: line 143: It is not clear to me whether you actually mean sample plot size here, or forest amount within a 2-km radius of the plot center

comments.issue: It is unclear why point counts and statistical modelling were needed when all adults were located.
comments.request: Clarify why point counts were needed to estimate densities.
comments.quote: Please clarify why you needed to use point counts + statistical modeling to estimate thrush densities, given that in lines 134-135 you state that you were able to locate all adult wood thrush in each plot.

comments.issue: It is inconsistent to predict patch size effects while arguing the relevant relationship is with habitat amount.
comments.request: Reconcile the predictions with the habitat amount rationale.
comments.quote: if you think the relationship you should be looking at is between the habitat amount within the landscape + immigration rate, then why make predictions for a relationship between patch size and immigration in the first place?

comments.issue: The choice of a 2-km radius for measuring forest amount is not justified.
comments.request: Justify the 2-km radius for forest amount measurement.
comments.quote: line 158: Please justify why you chose a 2-km radius as the appropriate extent for measurement of forest amount.

comments.issue: The term density is used for habitat variables, conflicting with conspecific density.
comments.request: Rename forest density to habitat or forest amount and reserve density for conspecifics.
comments.quote: I think it important to reserve use of “density” for cases where you are talking about conspecific density.

comments.issue: The geographic extent and resolution of the isotope and wing length maps are not reported.
comments.request: Report the geographic extent and resolution of the marker maps.
comments.quote: I believe key details relevant to the current work should be included here. In particular, I would like to see information on the geographic extent considered in your study.

comments.issue: Estimating abundance from unevenly distributed BBS routes is problematic and its handling is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain how abundance was estimated for cells with uneven BBS coverage.
comments.quote: This seems like a problematic way to estimate abundances, given the uneven distribution of BBS routes across the study region. Did every grid cell have at least one BBS route?

comments.issue: Uncertainty in dispersal distance estimates, with ~100 km resolution, is not emphasized.
comments.request: Emphasize uncertainty around median dispersal distance estimates.
comments.quote: I think it is important to emphasize the uncertainty in the estimates of dispersal distances referenced here (and the estimates of median dispersal distances given in your results section).

comments.issue: Ways in which the work could prioritize habitats for conservation are not specified.
comments.request: Specify how the work could be used to prioritize habitats.
comments.quote: lines 403-404: Can you specify ways in which your work could be used to prioritize habitats for species conservation?

comments.issue: Extrapolation from the study to songbirds more broadly is not justified.

comments.issue: Several line-level text edits (line 75 'than', line 157 'of', missing word lines 162-163).

comments.issue: Quality of conspecifics in patches may also influence settlement decisions.

comments.issue: How R was calculated with self-recruitment, and whether isotope data were used, is unexplained.

comments.issue: The resolution of the grid cell used is not stated.

comments.issue: The rationale for the north-south designation and the breeding range extent are not explained.

comments.issue: The inclusion of a quadratic term on line 261 is not explained.

comments.issue: The proposed prospecting mechanism seems unfeasible for first-time breeders.

comments.issue: The claim that avian natal dispersal is under-studied ignores many relevant studies.

comments.issue: The number of individual birds with estimated dispersal distances is never stated in the text.

comments.issue: Dispersal patterns by sex and year are not described even for the whole dataset.

comments.issue: No assurance that data will be made available upon publication.

comments.issue: Assignment methods were not validated with recaptured banded birds.

title: Empirical tests of habitat selection theory reveal that conspecific density and patch quality, but not habitat amount, drive long‐distance immigration in a wild bird

study.system: c. 4000 European plant species; GBIF occupancy trends, 65 years

editor_summary: All reviewers find the paper interesting but question robustness given GBIF data quality; editor wants evidence recorder effort and detection bias do not drive geographic trends, plus clearer writing.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, novel study advancing climatic-debt research, but statistical uncertainty handling is unclear and causal language needs more caution.
strengths: pushes climate-debt and range-shift field forward

comments.issue: Error propagation between separately estimated occupancy and SCI trends is not explained.
comments.request: Describe how uncertainty from the two separate estimates was propagated into model fitting.
comments.quote: It appears that the authors estimate occupancy and SCI separately, and then relate them to one another. Was the error from the first separate estimates propagated into the model fitting SCI and occupancy

comments.issue: Uncertainty intervals for trends are preferred over p-values in Supplemental Table 1.
comments.request: Report uncertainty intervals for the trend estimates.
comments.quote: rather than presenting the p-values of trends in the Supplemental Table 1, I would find it more or additional useful if the uncertainty intervals were provided

comments.issue: Correlative trends over time cannot confirm causation; the nitrogen deposition claim overstates the analysis.
comments.request: Soften causal claims and acknowledge collinearity of temporal trends.
comments.quote: the correlative (not causative) nature of these various trends mean that even strong statistical relationships cannot “confirm” causative relationships

comments.issue: Other explanations for the Mediterranean climatic bonus, such as land-use change, are not discussed.
comments.request: Briefly discuss alternative explanations such as land-use change.
comments.quote: I also wonder if there are other possible explanations for the climate “bonus” that could be briefly discussed; for example, land use changes in the region

comments.issue: The debt/bonus measure may also reflect other changes and long-term disequilibria since glacial retreat.
comments.request: Acknowledge other drivers and longer-term disequilibria in the caveats.

comments.issue: Numerous typos and grammar errors plus line-level wording and paragraphing edits throughout.
comments.quote: there are many typos/small grammatical errors (I have tried to point out many, especially in the Discussion

comments.issue: Figure S3 legend uses 'wild' instead of 'native' to contrast with invasive.
comments.request: Change the figure legend label to 'native'.
comments.quote: The legend shows “wild” but I think the authors mean “native” (in contrast to “invasive”)?

reviews.assessment: Important potential contribution, but occupancy trends from biased GBIF data are analysed without accounting for detection, and limitations are not discussed.
strengths: could make an important contribution to large-scale plant change
first paragraph nicely sets the scene

comments.issue: Occupancy trends from biased GBIF data use a simple method without accounting for detection changes.
comments.request: Use occupancy models, or justify why not, to account for detection bias.
comments.quote: This form of data is very biased and I would have expected the use of an occupancy model to analyse it in order to account for changes in detection over time.

comments.issue: Abstract omits the methods and data used.
comments.request: Add information on the methods and data to the abstract.
comments.quote: it would be good to include some information on the methods and data used if space allows

comments.issue: The SCI acronym is unnecessary and makes the paper less accessible.
comments.request: Keep the full term 'species climatic indices' instead of SCI.
comments.quote: Seeing as “species climatic indices” is not that long or confusing, I would recommend keeping the longer format.

comments.issue: Unclear whether 'species temperature index' on L65 refers to SCI.
comments.request: Clarify the terminology on L65.
comments.quote: Line 65: species temperature index – do you mean SCI here?

comments.issue: Sentence on L71 about other climatic variables is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify or shorten the sentence.
comments.quote: It isn’t clear to me what this line is trying to say – perhaps the part after the comma just needs to be removed?

comments.issue: Other factors besides climate change driving plant trends are not specified.
comments.request: Add more detail on the other factors.
comments.quote: Line 73: What other factors beside climate change? Some more detail would be nice here.

comments.issue: Occupancy is framed as a proxy for abundance although abundance is not the focus.
comments.request: Focus on occupancy itself rather than as an abundance proxy.
comments.quote: is it necessary to use occupancy as a proxy for abundance? I think occupancy in itself is a biodiversity metric of interest

comments.issue: 'Other drivers' on L82 are not identified.
comments.request: Name the other drivers at this point.
comments.quote: Line 82: “taking into account other drivers”, it would be nice to have the other drivers noted here.

comments.issue: Introduction never states the data or methods used to test the hypotheses.
comments.request: Describe data and methods in the last intro paragraph.
comments.quote: I have read up to this point and don’t know what data or method you are intending to use to test your hypothesis

comments.issue: Several line-level edits (L96, L387) and incorrect cross-references (Fig S2a, Table S2).
comments.quote: Line 96: should be “observed in at least”

comments.issue: Cell weighting system is unclear (overall versus yearly record counts).
comments.request: Clarify what each weight is based on.
comments.quote: Is each cell weighted based on the number of records overall, or for the year of interest?

comments.issue: Rationale for the second weighting and its effect on SCI trends are not explained.
comments.request: Explain the second weighting and its effect on SCI variation.
comments.quote: It would be good to state why this second form of weighting has been carried out

comments.issue: How cells are classified as unoccupied and how discretising accounts for sampling pressure is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the classification and the role of sampling pressure.
comments.quote: How are cell classed as not occupied: any cell with no record of the focal species or is it no record of any species?

comments.issue: Grid cells with no focal record may simply be unvisited, biasing non-detection assignment.
comments.request: Infer non-detections from records of other taxa, as other studies do.
comments.quote: This concerns me since it is highly likely that these grid cells have just not been visited.

comments.issue: Removing cells with no species records may remove the pseudo-absences needed for detectability.
comments.request: Explain how detectability is determined without these cells.
comments.quote: Are these not your pseudo-absences and so required to determine detectability?

comments.issue: Why recommended occupancy models or Frescalo were not used is not discussed.
comments.request: Justify the method choice and mention it in the introduction and abstract.
comments.quote: Since you are not using the recommended method for this form of data, I would like to see some discussion as to why this is the case

comments.issue: Species list length is first mentioned without saying what it contains.
comments.request: State exactly what the species list consists of.
comments.quote: this is the first mention of the species list length, it would be good to state what this consists of exactly

comments.issue: Trend validation test ignores detectability changes and may not detect known declines.

comments.quote: I’m not sure this is an appropriate test, since there is no accounting for changes in detectability over time

comments.issue: Notation for time switches between k and other symbols across equations.

comments.quote: k represents time in previous equations, I suggest maintaining the same notation throughout

comments.issue: Model sentence implies each species may have multiple lifespan variables.
comments.request: Clarify the lifespan term in the model description.
comments.quote: why is it change in occupancy of species x with lifespan y? This implies that each species may have more than one lifespan variable.

comments.issue: Why the model was weighted is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the weighting and whether it is usual.
comments.quote: Line 225: why was the model weighted? Is this usual?

comments.issue: Paragraph on early versus late periods is hard to follow and its results are never discussed.
comments.request: Clarify the paragraph and discuss these results.
comments.quote: I have found this paragraph difficult to follow. Why does the “early” data end in 1990 if the major changes in temperature occur from 1980? The results don’t seem to be discussed anywhere.

comments.issue: Whether species names were checked for synonyms across datasets is not stated.
comments.request: Describe how nomenclature consistency was ensured.
comments.quote: Was a check of species names from GBIF done to ensure no synonyms?

comments.issue: Text says precipitation SCIs increased on average, but Fig 1 does not show this.
comments.request: Provide a statistic supporting the precipitation SCI increase.
comments.quote: Results state than precipitation SCIs increased on average, this does not look true when looking at Fig 1

comments.issue: Phylogenetic signal and variable correlations are combined in one unclear sentence.

comments.issue: It is unclear what excluding invasive species means in the species-level trend model.

comments.issue: Urban affinity result may reflect more recording near urban areas rather than a true effect.

comments.issue: No discussion of study limitations, model choice, or known data biases.

comments.quote: I would like to see something on why the model choice was taken as opposed to occupancy models as well as more on the limitation on the current method and the known biases of the data.

comments.issue: Regional differences may reflect species' position within their ranges rather than climate effects.

comments.issue: The species range used to determine historical SCI is not stated.

comments.quote: Line 51: What species range was used to determine the historical SCI?

comments.issue: Unclear whether lifespan data came from the R package or elsewhere.
comments.request: Clarify the source of the lifespan information.
comments.quote: it is not clear here whether lifespan information is part of the R package or whether the R package was used to extract data from elsewhere

comments.issue: Habitat affinity from dominant grid-cell habitat may misclassify specialists of small habitats.
comments.request: Consider other data sources such as IUCN for habitat requirements.
comments.quote: I wonder whether this form of habitat affinity determination is less suitable for certain habitat specialists that might be associated with habitat types that are of a small area within a grid cell

comments.issue: Figure S2 legend is unclear, including which sampling-pressure version was used.
comments.request: Explain the two versions and correct the legend.
comments.quote: The legend here is not very clear. How was sampling pressure taken into account for the blue line/points?

reviews.assessment: Well-written, important addition, with mainly minor requests on data selection, figure explanation and climate-variability discussion.

title: European plants lagging behind climate change pay a climatic debt in the North, but are favoured in the South

study.system: butterfly phenology; GBIF occurrence-record reanalysis

editor_summary: Both reviewers agree the issues raised are important but need addressing: make the re-analysis more sophisticated, articulate the re-analysis conclusions vs the original, and tone down the language.

reviews.assessment: Agrees with most scientific facts raised but finds the conclusions and logic unclear and the statistical critique insufficiently detailed.
strengths: agrees with most scientific facts raised
reanalysis phenometrics better than the original paper

comments.issue: It is unclear what scientific conclusions can be drawn given the sparse current data situation.
comments.request: State which scientific conclusions the data can support.
comments.quote: But would you please tell what scientific conclusions can be drawn under current data situation?

comments.issue: The problems with the original paper's statistical methods are not detailed.
comments.request: Explain in detail the problems of their statistical methods.
comments.quote: However, I suggest you put forward in details the problems of their statitical methods.

comments.issue: The conclusion about phenological changes along geographical gradients is not clearly stated.
comments.request: State it clearly and compare it with the original paper's conclusion.
comments.quote: The conclusion relating to the rule of phenological changes along with geographical gradients in the reanalysis manuscript was not very clear.

comments.issue: The logic of the reanalysis correspondence is not clear enough.
comments.request: Modify the manuscript to clarify its logic.
comments.quote: The logic of this reanalysis correspondence was not clear enough, although people may agree with most of the questions they raised about the original paper by Fric et al.

reviews.assessment: Data-quality concerns are valid, but the reanalysis is not impressive and the language, including the title, is overstated.
strengths: residuals-as-data concern is valid practice point

comments.issue: Coefficient differences between analyses cannot be attributed to modelling technique because data and species differ.
comments.request: Compare models on identical data or temper attribution to method.
comments.quote: It is, therefore, difficult to attribute the differences in coefficient estimates to differences in the included species versus modelling technique or error in the data.

comments.issue: Neither analysis is impressive; mixed-effect or Bayesian models propagating error would be more informative.
comments.request: Fit a mixed-effect or Bayesian model with species effects and propagated error.
comments.quote: A more informative approach would be to fit a mixed effect model with species as a random effect. A better approach would be to fit a Bayesian model

comments.issue: Fric et al. should have the opportunity to examine the reanalysis and consider a correction or retraction.
comments.request: Give the original authors the opportunity to examine this.
comments.quote: I am sure that Fric et al. would want to ensure that their conclusions are robust, and they should be given the opportunity to examine this.

comments.issue: The language is too strong and the title overgeneralises.
comments.request: Temper the language and revise the title.
comments.quote: I also suggest Larsen & Shirey temper their language somewhat. The title is an overgeneralisation.

comments.issue: The 'great power' quotation is misleading because collections data often have low power due to weak signal.
comments.request: Remove or qualify the 'great power' claim.
comments.quote: The quotation referencing ‘great power’ (lines 33-34) is misleading given that collections data often has low power due to weak signal, which is perhaps the more fundamental issue.

comments.issue: The 'threshold far below any reasonable standard' statement is not helpful and is inaccurate; small samples can be modelled.
comments.request: Soften the sample-size claim, acknowledging partial pooling.
comments.quote: The reference to ‘a threshold far below any reasonable standard’ (lines 50-51) with respect to limits on sample size is not helpful, and it is alos inaccurate

title: Method matters: pitfalls in analysing phenology from occurrence records

study.system: macrogenetic literature; COI mitochondrial data and land-use effects

editor_summary: Editor notes hesitation about motivation and timeliness; both reviewers say the criticisms apply equally to Miraldo et al. 2016, and a broader comparison across macrogenetic studies would have more impact.

reviews.assessment: Opposes publication: some criticisms are valid but they apply to the whole macrogenetic literature, and a focused response to one paper is not timely.

comments.issue: The sample-size criticism is overstated since SNP information grows slowly with n and pi can be estimated robustly.
comments.quote: one can get robust results about pi even with a moderate sample size

comments.issue: The claim that the geographic scale is inappropriate is unconvincing because dispersal distances can be large over many generations.
comments.quote: The suggestion that the geographic scale is inappropriate because "most species have dispersal capabilities far shorter than the distances separating the sampling locations of the grouped sequences" is also not very convincing.

comments.issue: The criticisms apply to virtually all macrogenetic literature, including Miraldo et al. 2016, which has the same issues and was more influential.
comments.request: Extend the critique to the broader macrogenetic literature.
comments.quote: these concerns apply to virtually all of the (so-called by Paz-Vinas et al.) "macro-genetic" literature

comments.issue: The response is untimely: the same concerns applied to Miraldo et al. 2016 for four years without reaction, whereas Millette et al. 2020 was more cautious.
comments.request: Justify why this specific response is warranted now.
comments.quote: This is why I question a bit the timeliness of the Paz-Vinas et al response.

comments.issue: A critique aimed at one result of one paper is inappropriate; either demonstrate the relationship with novel data or review the whole body of literature.
comments.request: Provide novel analyses or broaden the review to several macrogenetic studies.
comments.quote: they should not address their criticisms to one specific result from one specific paper

comments.issue: The arguments about data and method limitations imply claims should be more tempered.
comments.request: Refrain from strong conclusions and big claims.
comments.quote: one should refrain from strong conclusions and big claims

title: Macrogenetic studies must not ignore limitations of genetic markers and scale

study.system: Indian meal moth larvae; 10-generation experimental evolution

reviews.assessment: Interesting data on an important question, but doubts about confounding with viscosity, missing baseline data, and overinterpreted conclusions.
strengths: addresses an important question in evolutionary biology

comments.issue: The claim about experimental studies is overstated; burying beetle work exists.
comments.request: Cite burying beetle studies and soften the claim.
comments.quote: This is slightly overstated. There is a growing number of experimental studies conducted in social and subsocial insects, which directly explores how selection shape complex social behaviours and outcomes.

comments.issue: The statement that interactions shape individual distributions is too strong.

comments.issue: The relevance of 'infected individuals' in this paragraph is unclear.

comments.issue: The paragraph entangles cooperation and infection, obscuring the intended predictions.
comments.request: Clarify the argument and drop pathogen references.
comments.quote: I find this entire paragraph particularly difficult to follow because it entangles cooperation and infection to formulate predictions on both.

comments.issue: Claiming generality about cooperation is unsupported when only selfish behaviour was studied.

comments.issue: Larval movement is not introduced before it appears in the results.

comments.quote: The introduction focuses on cannibalism, but the results and discussion section starts with measurements of larval movement.

comments.issue: The treatment effect on within-treatment mobility variation is not discussed.

comments.quote: There is also a striking effect on variation in mobility within treatments. This should be discussed.

comments.issue: The reported sign of the cannibalism-dispersal correlation contradicts the other correlations.

comments.issue: Viscosity, not population structure, was manipulated, and it may affect other parameters.

comments.quote: This is not correct. You directly manipulated viscosity, which in turn modified spatial structure (but it may also have modified other parameters).

comments.issue: Methods are too short to replicate the study.
comments.request: Provide much more setup detail.
comments.quote: The methods section is currently way too short, and it would be almost impossible to replicate the study. Please, provide much more details about the setup!

comments.issue: No data show that viscosity altered population structure and density.
comments.request: Present data on population structure and densities.
comments.quote: you present no data about population structure and densities. Individuals can be both highly gregarious and exhibit high levels of mobility

comments.issue: The first experiment lacks sample sizes, independence details and regression slopes.
comments.request: Report sample sizes, origin of individuals and model slopes.
comments.quote: How many individuals have been tested? Where they independent (where did they come from)? What are the slopes of the regression models?

comments.issue: The pilot tested only short-term glycerol effects, so long-term selection effects may be confounded.
comments.request: Test long-term direct glycerol effects on cannibalism.
comments.quote: This is not convincing enough to rule out that the reported long-term effects of selection are only due to population structure (and not due to glycerol densities).

comments.issue: It is unclear whether 'treatments' refers to selection lines or the pilot experiment.
comments.request: Disambiguate the reference to treatments.
comments.quote: Do the treatments refer to the selection lines or the pilot experiment detailed just above?

comments.issue: The source population's origin, genetic diversity and inbreeding are not reported.
comments.request: Describe the source population and its genetic diversity.
comments.quote: Where do these animals come from? What is their level of genetic diversity (and inbreeding)?

comments.issue: No baseline cannibalism data show the selection lines started equivalent.
comments.request: Report baseline cannibalism and address drift.
comments.quote: I do not see any test of the baseline level of cannibalism in the tested population? How likely is it that the reported effects are simply due to the use of cannibal (versus non-cannibal) individual to setup certain lines?

comments.issue: The choice of F2 individuals rather than treatment individuals is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the choice of F2 individuals.
comments.quote: Why using F2 individuals and not the individuals directly from the treatment?

comments.issue: Figure 1 may not be necessary.
comments.request: Consider removing Figure 1.
comments.quote: Figure 1: I am not sure this figure is necessary.

comments.issue: The correlation may depend on the lowest-viscosity populations.
comments.request: Re-run analyses excluding the lowest-viscosity populations.
comments.quote: I wonder whether the results are qualitatively similar without thee low viscosity populations

comments.issue: Low-viscosity populations show much larger variation, so their averages are less representative.
comments.request: Discuss treatment effects on intra-population variation.
comments.quote: the populations maintained under very low viscosity (value = 10) also have individuals exhibiting a much larger variation in the different measurements compared to the other viscosity

reviews.assessment: Neat experimental evolution study, but the theory presentation is too simple: depending on ecology, viscosity models can predict no effect or the opposite.
strengths: commendable attempt to test theory experimentally

comments.issue: The theory predicts different outcomes depending on ecology, so the study is not a simple test.
comments.request: Review the theory and relate the system to its assumptions.
comments.quote: the theory actually suggests that strikingly different outcomes are expected depending on other ecological and demographic factors experienced by the population

comments.issue: Elasticity distinguishes the experiment from models but is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss elasticity and the system's ecology and demography.
comments.quote: Probably the key ingredient that separates the experimental system from the theoretical models cited above is elasticity

comments.issue: Whether the population is elastic is not tested with productivity data.
comments.request: Test whether low-cannibalism locales are more productive.
comments.quote: is there evidence that more cooperative (lower cannibalism) locales within the medium are more productive in terms of larval biomass or some other proxy of fitness

comments.issue: The uniform rearing of assayed descendants is not clear until the methods.
comments.request: Clarify the common-garden design in the introduction.
comments.quote: it wasn’t obvious to me at this point that the assays are done on descendants reared under uniform conditions

comments.issue: 'Low' and 'high' appear to be swapped on page 5.
comments.request: Fix the swapped labels.
comments.quote: Page 5 Lines 2-3, “low” and “high” seem to have been mixed up here.

comments.issue: The importance of kin recognition is unclear; it may not affect overall cannibalism.
comments.request: Justify the point and cite Faria & Gardner 2020.
comments.quote: it’s not clear why this is so important, because it’s not obvious that kin recognition would have any impact on the overall level of cannibalism

title: Experimental evidence that local interactions select against selfish behaviour

study.system: subarctic-alpine forest-heath ecotone; soil profiles and trenching experiment

editor_summary: Editor says the work is of considerable potential interest but substantial concerns remain: more data and analyses on ericoid fungi, why root-associated fungi increased in trenched plots, formatting, and difficult Figures 2-3.

reviews.assessment: Finds the approach rigorous and results clear; asks for clarifications on dissolved organic matter, trenching terminology and EcM specificity.

comments.issue: 'Depends on' is the wrong phrase for the relationship.
comments.request: Use 'is explained by'.
comments.quote: L198: Instead of "depends on," perhaps "is explained by."

comments.issue: Implications of dissolved organic C and N for mycorrhizal activity are unclear.
comments.request: Explain these implications.
comments.quote: I am not clear on the implications of dissolved organic C and N for mycorrhizal activity. More explanation may be necessary.

comments.issue: Expected C-stock responses from the literature are not stated, so results lack context.
comments.request: State expected C-stock responses from the literature.
comments.quote: Can you be more explicit here about what sorts of responses you might have expected from C stocks based on the literature?

comments.issue: The link between root exclusion and 'trenching' is not made clear, confusing the T and Time terms.
comments.request: Clarify or replace the trenching term.
comments.quote: I would suggest either making the connection between tree root exclusion and "trenching" right away, or replacing the term "trenching" with something that more clearly indicates root exclusion.

comments.issue: Root exclusion removed only EcM fungi, not other root-associated fungi, which is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the selective effect of trenching.
comments.quote: Are you able to explain why root exclusion only removed EcM fungi and not other root-associated fungi?

comments.issue: How ericoid and non-ericoid root-derived inputs were separated is not explained.
comments.request: Explain how root inputs were separated.
comments.quote: how are you able to separate the ericoid root derived inputs from non-ericoid root-derived inputs?

reviews.assessment: Very positive: well organized, well written and compelling, with only minor suggestions on terminology, error bars and data sharing.
strengths: well organized, well written and compelling
novel explanation for C stock differences across the tree line

comments.issue: 'Field vegetation' is not defined as excluding trees.
comments.request: Define field vegetation explicitly.
comments.quote: I would explain explicitly that “field vegetation” excludes the trees. I found this term a bit confusing since it wasn’t clearly defined here.

comments.issue: 'Highest coverage' is ambiguous: which coverage, which sites?
comments.request: Clarify what highest coverage refers to.
comments.quote: It’s not clear what “highest coverage” is referring to. Is this coverage of ectomycorrhizal species, or total plant coverage?

comments.issue: Vegetation composition is hard to visualize because trees and field vegetation use different units.
comments.request: Improve the visualization, e.g. with site photos.
comments.quote: I found the composition of the forest and non-forest vegetation difficult to visualize because the units for trees and field vegetation were different.

comments.issue: Fungal biomass is inferred from ergosterol, which is not the same measure.
comments.request: Call it ergosterol or justify the biomass proxy.
comments.quote: The text here refers to fungal biomass, but the data that was measured and shown is ergosterol, which isn’t strictly the same.

comments.issue: Phosphorus limitation as an alternative factor is not considered.
comments.request: Consider whether P limitation matters.
comments.quote: Line 303: Is it possible that P limitation is a factor?

comments.issue: The birch species is called mountain birch and downy birch in different places.
comments.request: Use one name consistently.
comments.quote: Line 334, 336, 77: The trees are referred to as mountain birch here, and as downy birch in other places

comments.issue: The correspondence between sample and species plots in Figs 2-3 is unclear.
comments.request: Use shapes to indicate sample types.
comments.quote: I think it would help with the interpretation if the points in the species plots had different shapes indicating which sample type (forest, heath, etc) they were collected from.

comments.issue: Error bars in Figs 4 and 5 are undefined.
comments.request: Define the error bars.
comments.quote: Figures 4 and 5: What do the error bars indicate? Standard deviation, or standard error, or something else?

comments.issue: Soil profile measurements, including layer thicknesses, are not available.
comments.request: Share the soil profile measurements.
comments.quote: I would suggest including a spreadsheet of the soil profile measurements underlying the analysis (including layer thicknesses) either in a public repository or supplemental material.

reviews.assessment: Likes the trait-based link but questions the role of ericoid fungi and argues a faster-cycling pool is an equally plausible explanation.

comments.issue: The role of ericoid fungi is confusing: their lab-documented N-mining ability conflicts with the framing that they are unimportant decomposers.
comments.request: Clarify the functional role of ericoid fungi.
comments.quote: I am a bit confused on the role of the ericoid fungi in this system.

comments.issue: Amounts and C:N of tree versus ericaceous shrub litter inputs are not presented.
comments.request: Present the litter input amounts and C:N.
comments.quote: I think it would be important to present more specific information on both the relative amounts and C:N of the different plant litter inputs.

comments.issue: Lower C:N tree litter priming decomposition is an equally plausible explanation for lower forest C stocks.
comments.request: Test the faster-cycling alternative.
comments.quote: it seems that simply a faster cycling pool (due to lower C:N inputs) is an equally plausible explanation for the lower C stocks in the forest soil organic layer as ectomycorrhizal N mining

comments.issue: The N-mining mechanism would predict higher litter C:N in trenched plots, but this is not tested.
comments.request: Compare litter C:N in trenched versus control plots.
comments.quote: If N mining by ectomycorrhizal fungi is key to organic matter decomposition, then the C:N ratio of remaining litter in the trenched plots should be higher than the C:N ratio of the remaining litter in the control plots.

comments.issue: Other fungal functional types are binned coarsely; finer taxonomic analyses could bolster the argument.
comments.request: Analyze other fungal groups at finer taxonomy.
comments.quote: if the authors can show that the other functional types of soil fungi do not have the same kinds of taxonomic shifts in composition as the ectomycorrhizal fungi, that would bolster their argument

comments.issue: Which EcM fungi remain in trenched plots, and whether they are short-distance types, is unknown.
comments.request: Show the exploration types of remaining EcM fungi.
comments.quote: Can the authors add some information (maybe in an appendix) showing that those remaining ectomycorrhizal fungi are just short-distance type?

comments.issue: Deslippe et al. studies on EcM host trees and soil C at the ecotone are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the Deslippe et al. studies.
comments.quote: it seems like these studies need discussion here in the introduction

comments.issue: Work on EM fungi priming decomposition is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the priming work.
comments.quote: This result is consistent with some of the work by Eddie Brzostek and Rich Phillips, which suggested that EM fungi may prime decomposition.

title: A tipping point in carbon storage when forest expands into tundra is related to mycorrhizal recycling of nitrogen

study.system: plant phenolic metabolites; bioassays with 4 insect herbivores and 4 fungal pathogens

editor_summary: All reviewers see merit and praise the elaborate experiment, but all raise substantial concerns about data treatment and statistics, unreported parameters (nutrient content, pH) and compound choice for the synergy hypothesis; major revision needed.

reviews.assessment: Impressive scope and analysis, but biochemical documentation (diet composition, pH, concentrations) and the synergy-hypothesis test need strengthening.
strengths: careful analysis of insect and fungal data

comments.issue: Artificial diet constituents are not listed and nutrient content (especially nitrogen forms and iron) is not documented.
comments.request: List diet constituents and report nutrient contents, especially N and Fe.
comments.quote: The constituents of the artificial diet should be listed so the results can be better evaluated and in the future repeated.

comments.issue: Diet pH is not reported or compared with herbivore gut pH, although pH changes phenolic mode of action.
comments.request: Report diet pH and compare it with gut pH values.
comments.quote: For all these reasons, the authors should give the diet pH (whether available from the manufacturer or measured directly) and compare it with the pH values of the herbivore guts

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the tested phenolic concentrations (~1% dry weight) are comparable to natural plant tissue.
comments.request: Compare tested concentrations with values typical of plant material.
comments.quote: It would be good to know that this experiment has been carried out in a way that the results could be applied to herbivores and pathogens attacking real plant tissue.

comments.issue: Compounds chosen for the synergy test are chemically too diverse (six skeletal types, sizes, polarities), unlike the closely related compounds of the original synergy concept.
comments.request: Comment on how chemically related compounds might change the synergy results.
comments.quote: The authors chose compounds that to my opinion seem chemically so diverse that they go against the sense of the original ideas underlying the synergy hypothesis.

reviews.assessment: Novel, elegant and well-written study; concerns that varying statistical power between metrics could influence hypothesis testing.

comments.issue: For predictions 1d and 1e, error propagation through model coefficients into derived variables and final models is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify or quantify error propagation in the derived variables.
comments.quote: you use model coefficients to calculate derived variables, and it's not currently clear how error or variance propagate through this approach to affect the outcome of the final models

comments.issue: Interpreting significance from any one of three herbivore models may inflate false-positive detection relative to fungi.
comments.request: Use null models and acknowledge this multiple-model issue in the text.
comments.quote: with herbivores you interpret a significant result from any one of three models to determine whether a consumer is affected by phenolics, and it is unclear whether this makes you three times more likely to detect a signal by chance

comments.issue: Discrepancies between 24 individual models and a single large model likely reflect statistical power, weakening the lack of support for predictions 1a/1b.
comments.request: Add null models to show the lack of support is not a power artifact.
comments.quote: in Table S4 there are some significant interactive effects of these variables when considered in a single large model (particularly for fungal growth)

comments.issue: Marginally significant results are reported and discussed (L278-281, L293-297), which is misleading given the many models.
comments.request: Remove the marginally significant results.
comments.quote: There are a number of occasions where you report/discuss marginally significant results (see line comments, below). I think this is misleading and undermines your message, so my preference would be for you to lose them all.

comments.issue: Line-level copy edits: add "in" or "of" at L62 and write "October" at L182.
comments.quote: L62: Add an "in" or "of" before "untangling".

comments.issue: Pupal mass units are missing at L189.
comments.request: Add units to pupal mass.
comments.quote: L189: add units to pupal mass.

comments.issue: Strong richness and SD interaction effects on fungal growth (Table S4) are glossed over, and the decision to use separate models is not convincing.
comments.request: Acknowledge and interpret the interaction effects on fungal growth.
comments.quote: you glaze over some fairly strong interaction effects of richness and SD on fungal growth (Table S4)

comments.issue: Whether repeated treatments influenced the statistics is not established.
comments.request: Test or discuss the influence of repeated treatments.
comments.quote: can you be certain that the repetition of some treatments had no influence over the outcome of your statistics?

reviews.assessment: Elaborate, clearly communicated experiment with a novel diversity metric, but molarity was ignored, complicating interpretation and synergy assessment.
strengths: great respect for the elaborate experiment
clear communication of the chemical diversity manipulation
novel use of the Tanimoto coefficient
four herbivores and four fungi broaden the ecological context

comments.issue: The vast number of tables and figures makes it hard for readers to follow the line of reasoning.
comments.request: Reduce or streamline the presented tables and figures.
comments.quote: I found it a considerable challenge to scrutinize the vast numbers of tables and figures while keeping in touch with the line of reasoning

comments.issue: Aromatic acids are not strictly phenolics, which affects the compound classification.
comments.request: Address the classification of aromatic acids as phenolics.
