strengths: key arguments of broad conceptual interest

comments.issue: Model comparison may be biased by numerical problems; robustness diagnostics are needed.
comments.request: Provide diagnostics showing the estimates are robust.
comments.quote: It is stated that the Weibull is more problematic to fit. Does this mean that the model comparison results are biased by numerical issues?

comments.issue: Whether present-day truncation biases results needs simulation evidence.
comments.request: Simulate artificial datasets with known properties.
comments.quote: To be convinced in practice, I would like to see simulation results. I recommend you develop artificial datasets with known properties and see if you can recover the correct results

comments.issue: Life-history comparisons (trees/shrubs versus perennials) add little insight.
comments.request: Clarify what is learned from life histories.
comments.quote: The discussion of trees/shrubs versus perennials, etc. is not terribly revealing. It seems fairly logical that different life histories will influence time to naturalization

comments.issue: The verbal argument for declining SD of lag times is unclear; a formal model is needed.
comments.request: Develop a formal model.
comments.quote: it is not clear to me why the standard deviation should decrease. I think the paper might benefit from a formal model

comments.issue: The paper does not make a general case for why naturalisation matters to a broad ecology audience.
comments.request: Add a broader discussion of invasion debt for general readers.
comments.quote: EL is a general ecology journal, so I feel the author really needs to make the case beyond the narrow interest in invasive plants

comments.issue: Extinction-probability literature (Lande et al. 2003) could inform life-history arguments.
comments.request: Cite and use this literature.
comments.quote: when making arguments about life-histories in invasion debts, the authors could tap into the extinction probability literature

reviews.assessment: Very nice, elegant and novel study that anticipated and addressed her concerns; only a few minor clarifications requested.

comments.issue: Increased recent detection effort could shorten apparent lag times and should be mentioned.
comments.request: Mention this potential bias.
comments.quote: there might be more effort in recent years to detect first records of alien species in the wild. This should at least be mentioned

comments.issue: Pysek et al. 2020 warnings paper should be cited.
comments.request: Add this reference.
comments.quote: Page 3, line 16: Another good reference would be the recent ‘warnings’ paper by Pysek et al. (2020) in Biological Reviews.

comments.issue: Two line-level wording edits (insert 'also'; 'our' to 'the').
comments.quote: Page 3, line 58: I would insert “also” after “around the world, but”.

comments.issue: Maurel et al. 2016 should be cited.
comments.request: Add this reference.
comments.quote: Page 4, line 47: Another good reference: Maurel et al. (2016) Global Ecology and Biogeography.

comments.issue: 'Total planting effort' is ambiguous (per species or across all species).
comments.request: Clarify the meaning.
comments.quote: It was not clear to me whether “total planting effort” refers to planting effort of a given species or the planting effort across all species in cultivation

comments.issue: The meaning of 'the hazard function steepens' should be clarified with reference to Fig 1.
comments.request: Add the clarifying bracket.
comments.quote: I therefore suggest to add in brackets behind “the hazard function steepens”: “the differently colored lines in Fig. 1”.

comments.issue: A model allowing variance to differ among life forms could be useful.
comments.request: Consider adding this model.
comments.quote: I was, however, wondering whether it would be useful to also include a model in which also the variance differs for the 3 life forms

comments.issue: Why anthropogenic climate change cannot explain the sustained decline needs clarification.
comments.request: Add a clarifying sentence.
comments.quote: It is not clear to me why anthropogenic climate change cannot account for the sustained decline in the mean and variance of the lag-time distribution. Please, add a clarifying sentence

comments.issue: Figure y-axis labels should be horizontal.
comments.request: Rotate the y-axis labels 90 degrees.
comments.quote: The figures are very nice, but I would turn the y-axis labels by 90 degrees, so that they are horizontal.

title: Time lags and the invasion debt in plant naturalisations

study.system: bryophyte species in springs; C:N:P stoichiometry and elementomes

editor_summary: Editor notes all reviewers found the paper well-written and novel; asks special attention to Reviewer 3's requests for explicit hypotheses and discussion of homeostasis, and methods clarifications.

reviews.assessment: Interesting link between stoichiometry and niche differentiation; two minor comments plus a question on the other elements.
strengths: interesting paper linking stoichiometry to niche differentiation

comments.issue: The role of the other measured elements (K, Na, Mg, Ca, S, Fe) is not explained.
comments.request: Explain whether these elements only affect Euclidean distances.
comments.quote: What I lack is information of how the elements other than C,N, P that were measured ((K, Na, Mg, Ca, S, Fe) play a role. Are they just affecting the Euclidian distances in the elementomes?

comments.issue: How standardization was done is not defined.
comments.request: Define the standardization procedure.
comments.quote: Define how the standardization was done.

comments.issue: Meaning of a higher C:N:P ratio is ambiguous; ratios involve two variables.
comments.request: Clarify what a higher C:N:P ratio means.
comments.quote: It is not clear what a higher C:N:P ratio means. Such a statement can only refer to a ratio of two variables.

reviews.assessment: Enthusiastic about the study but several major points on homeostasis, hypotheses and methodology need addressing.
strengths: novel and promising results on biogeochemical niches

comments.issue: Homeostasis is treated as the single factor shaping elemental composition, ignoring intraspecific differences.
comments.request: Discuss additional non-homeostatic drivers of elemental content.
comments.quote: Elemental content in living organisms can also be shaped by differences associated to intraspecific differences due to e.g., size, developmental stage, etc., differences that are independent from elemental homeostasis.

comments.issue: Elements differ in their degree of homeostatic regulation, which is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss element-specific homeostasis and its relevance for niches.
comments.quote: This differential degree of homeostatic regulation among elements might be key to our ability to define a biogeochemical niche and its relevance on species coexistence. I think these two points deserve further discussion.

comments.issue: Clear hypotheses are missing for the study's goals; only goal (iii) has a prediction.
comments.request: Develop hypotheses and predictions for each goal.
comments.quote: You study addresses three goals, and clear working hypotheses can be developed for each one of these, but you only provided a prediction for goal (iii).

comments.issue: Number and type of models run are not stated.
comments.request: State how many models were run and whether they were multivariate.
comments.quote: How many models did you run in total? Were these 3 models for the ratios, 4 models for the main macronutrients and five models for the micronutrients?

comments.issue: Models were not compared to a null model.
comments.request: Compare the models to a null model.
comments.quote: Did you compare your models to a null model?

comments.issue: Whether selected species were present in all springs and the number of communities studied is unclear.
comments.request: Report species presence across springs and the number of communities.
comments.quote: were the species selected present in all spring samples? If not, how many actual springs/communities did you study?

comments.issue: Purpose of the two elementome analyses is not explicitly stated.
comments.request: Explain the exact purpose of the first and second analyses.
comments.quote: it would help if you explicitly tell the reader the exact purpose of the first (elementome-environmental distance) and second (elementome-frequency of coexistence) analyses

comments.issue: Correlations among ratio measures are partially spurious.
comments.request: Interpret these correlations with caution.
comments.quote: Correlations among ratio with common measures (e.g., C:P, N:P) are partially spurious, and the interpretation of these correlations should be taken with caution.

comments.issue: Niche volume was not estimated or tested for contraction with coexistence.
comments.request: Estimate niche size and test contraction or expansion with coexistence.
comments.quote: I wonder whether is it possible to estimate the size (volume) of the niche and test whether species niches contract of expand depending on the frequency of coexistence.

comments.issue: Mechanism behind the tight N-P correlation is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss possible mechanisms for the N-P correlation.
comments.quote: What mechanism(s) might explain the tight correlation between N and P?

comments.issue: Homeostatic regulation cannot be inferred from observational data.
comments.request: Temper conclusions about the degree of elemental regulation.
comments.quote: Homeostatic regulation should not be inferred from observational studies (see Halvorson & Small 2016 for a good perspective on this issue).

comments.issue: Conclusions at lines 397-398 cannot be drawn from these data and analyses.
comments.request: Tone down the conclusion about homeostatic regulation and niche diversification.
comments.quote: Some of your conclusions (e.g., Lines 397-398) cannot be drawn from your data/analyses.

comments.issue: "Climatic water availability" at line 301 is undefined.

title: Bryophyte C:N:P stoichiometry, biogeochemical niches and elementome plasticity driven by environment and coexistence

study.system: fleshy-fruited plants; fruit colour syndromes, dispersers, environment

editor_summary: Editor: all reviewers were enthusiastic about this interesting, timely study with an impressive dataset; authors must explain how fruit colour is defined and justify the taxonomic over the phylogenetic model and the bird frugivory measure.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, timely and meticulous study that deserves publication, but the two main variables are crude and may render the results unreliable.

comments.issue: The two main variables, bird frugivory and fruit colour, are crude and questionable at the global scale.
comments.request: Acknowledge and address the crudeness of the main variables.
comments.quote: the two main variables used (bird frugivory, fruit color), are both crude and questionable

comments.issue: Fruit colours are classified using Janson's Neotropical 'bird colours', which may not apply globally.
comments.request: Reconsider the global imposition of the Neotropical colour classification.
comments.quote: this classification is based on the situation in the Neotropics, in which bird diversity is high and the main mammalian disperser has inferior color vision capacities

comments.issue: The bird frugivory index ignores biomass and seed dispersal effectiveness, overestimating birds in mammal-rich regions.
comments.request: Account for biomass and seed dispersal effectiveness.
comments.quote: it ignores critical variables like biomass, and basically the entire Seed Dispersal Effectiveness framework

comments.issue: The similar Valenta et al. 2018 study is only mentioned once in the discussion.
comments.request: Acknowledge Valenta et al. 2018 more fully in the introduction.
comments.quote: given the similarity, I’d expect this earlier work to be better acknowledged in the introduction, and not only be mentioned once in the discussion

comments.issue: The cruder taxonomic model is chosen over the more robust phylogenetic model without justification.
comments.request: Justify the taxonomic model or use the phylogenetic model.
comments.quote: Yet the authors chose to focus on the cruder taxonomic model. I fail to understand why.

comments.issue: L73 statement ignores the diversity among birds such as tanagers versus hornbills.
comments.request: Acknowledge variation among bird species.
comments.quote: L73 - birds are also pretty diverse. There’s a huge difference between a small understory tanager and, for example, hornbills.

comments.issue: L77 ignores the geographic separation of overlapping disperser groups; syndromes are local.
comments.request: Discuss local versus global syndrome patterns.
comments.quote: the entire paragraph ignores geographic separation of these so-called overlapping groups

comments.issue: The L81 conundrum is not real; a syndrome comprises multiple traits, so overlap in one dimension is expected.
comments.request: Reconsider the argument that overlap undermines syndromes.
comments.quote: By definition, a syndrome is an accumulation of multiple traits, so overlap in one dimension doesn’t imply no separation along others

comments.issue: Valenta et al. 2018a already tested UV reflectance in leaves and fruits and should be cited at L83.
comments.request: Cite Valenta et al. 2018a here.
comments.quote: Valenta et al. 2018a suggested just that and tested whether UV reflectance in leaves predicts UV reflectance in fruits

comments.issue: Two key citations on honest signals for nutrient content are missing on L107.
comments.request: Add Schaefer et al. 2014 and Albrecht et al. 2018.
comments.quote: I’m missing two important citations here (Schaefer et al. 2014 Proc R Soc B; Albrecht et al. 2018 Nat Comm)

comments.issue: The L109 paragraph lacks the approach and the main hypothesis is not numbered.
comments.request: Edit the paragraph to clearly convey hypotheses, approach and results.
comments.quote: the organization of the hypotheses tested is a bit confusing because the main hypothesis (DSH) is not numbered

comments.issue: Bird-dependency hotspots in northern Africa and Arabia are not mentioned on L250.
comments.request: Mention these bird-dependent regions.
comments.quote: according to Fig2a the most bird-dependent regions are in the northern half of Africa and the Arabian peninsula

comments.issue: The sentence on L261 is broken and two words are swapped.
comments.quote: these regions should be mentioned here. L261 - sentence broken; swap “also” and “colors”

comments.issue: The term 'bird color' is based on unique Neotropical natural history, not global patterns.
comments.request: Reconsider the term 'bird color'.
comments.quote: this means that the term “bird color” is problematic because it is based on the somewhat unique natural history of the Neotropics, not on global patterns

comments.issue: Species richness is not equivalent to biomass, seed removal or dispersal services.
comments.request: Account for biomass and seed removal in the argument.
comments.quote: Species richness in a broad region such as Amazonia does not necessarily translate into higher biomass, seed removal, and seed dispersal services

comments.issue: The L371 point may not be based on the study's data and lacks a citation.
comments.request: Add a citation or support the point.
comments.quote: is this point based on your own data? If not, please add citation

comments.issue: Fig. 1 and 2 captions do not explain the colour coding.
comments.request: Explain the colour coding in the captions.
comments.quote: the captions do not explain the color coding. One can quite easily guess, but why not make it easier to understand?

comments.issue: The red-green gradient is unfriendly to colourblind readers.
comments.request: Use a colourblind-friendly scheme.
comments.quote: red-green gradient is very unfriendly to people who suffer from the most common forms of color blindness

comments.issue: Figures and captions should be placed within the text.
comments.request: Place figures and captions in the text.
comments.quote: Please always place figures and captions in the text

reviews.assessment: Impressive, thorough global analysis providing new insights on fruit colour evolution, with terminology and framing points to address.
strengths: new insights on a longstanding question
compelling evidence that temperature constrains fruit colour

comments.issue: 'Bird colours' terminology conflates the description of fruit colours with the hypothesis being tested.
comments.request: Use objective criteria such as luminance contrast instead.
comments.quote: the terminology used unnecessarily conflates a description of fruit colors with the hypothesis being tested

comments.issue: 'Bird frugivory' terminology is misleading since only relative species richness is measured.
comments.request: Rename it 'relative richness of frugivorous birds' and similarly for mammals.
comments.quote: The category “bird frugivory” (e.g. line 247 and many other places) should more appropriately be called “relative richness of frugivorous birds”

comments.issue: Why models operate at both species and grid-cell level, and the framework behind this, is vague.
comments.request: State the theoretical justification for the two-level analysis in the introduction.
comments.quote: It is vague at present why the models look both at species level and grid-cell level

comments.issue: The paedomorphic hypothesis as presented is uncompelling and may be a straw man.
comments.request: Remove it or introduce it more robustly.
comments.quote: Is this a straw man? If so, I think it can be removed and just mentioned in the discussion as another nail in the coffin

comments.issue: No justification is given for using taxonomy models rather than phylogenetic models; Family nesting in Order is unconfirmed.
comments.request: Justify the model choice and confirm Family is nested within Order.
comments.quote: What is the justification for focusing on taxonomy models over phylogenetic?

comments.issue: Why lemurs are split from other primates while other mammalian taxa are grouped is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain or remove the lemur split.
comments.quote: Why are lemurs split from other primates when other mammalian taxa are separated

comments.issue: 'These dispersers' on Line 81 is ambiguous and the food preference wording is inaccurate.
comments.request: Reword for clarity.
comments.quote: which does “these dispersers” refer to? Reword for clarity

comments.issue: Line-level edits: wording on L93 and unnecessary parentheses on L268 and L291.
comments.quote: L 268- remove parentheses around “plus their main effects”

comments.issue: The latitudinal examples on L239-242 are confusing, treating cold as equivalent to high latitude.
comments.request: Rework the section.
comments.quote: As written the examples about latitudinal differences are confusing. Please rework this section

comments.issue: The 'different evol. histories' thread on L380-386 is poorly developed.
comments.request: Clarify how mammal evolutionary histories explain fruit traits.
comments.quote: What is specifically meant about “different evol. Histories” of frugivorous mammals and how do they explain fruit traits?

comments.issue: The claim that the region is more shaded than African tropical forests is unsubstantiated.
comments.request: Provide data or soften the claim.
comments.quote: Do the authors have data that this region is more shaded than in tropical forests of Africa?

comments.issue: The 20% cut-off for high and low bird frugivory is not justified and its sensitivity untested.
comments.request: Justify the cut-off and test sensitivity.
comments.quote: What justification is there for the 20% cut off for high and low “bird frugivory”

reviews.assessment: Sound analysis of an impressive dataset and an important contribution, with only minor wording, definition and framing suggestions.
strengths: sound analysis of an impressive dataset
important contribution to the fruit syndrome hypothesis
geography of frugivory results is amazing

comments.issue: The Line 82 claim about colour-specific syndromes is overstated and distracting.
comments.request: Remove or tweak the last sentence.
comments.quote: The number of fruit colors that have been attributed to mammal, primate, or bat fruit syndromes is pretty much every color except for purple

comments.issue: 'Paedomorphic' on Line 99 is unexplained and its link to growing season is unclear.
comments.request: Define paedomorphic and clarify the link.
comments.quote: What the heck does paedomorphic mean? It seems like the authors are referring to variation stemming from developmental changes in fruit, but it’s a bit unclear

comments.issue: 'Darker' fruits are central to the predictions but darkness is never defined or measured.
comments.request: Define and explain how darkness was measured.
comments.quote: I may have missed this, but it’s clear to me how you assigned fruits to a bird-dispersal category, but not how you defined or measured darkness

comments.issue: The source and scoring of UV data on Line 185 are not explained.
comments.request: Explain how UV reflectance was obtained and scored.
comments.quote: Where’d you get UV, and how was it scored. Just UV reflectance yes/no?

comments.issue: Predictions hinge on fruit darkness but no results for darkness are presented.
comments.request: Present results for darkness or align predictions and results.
comments.quote: all of the predictions seem to hinge on fruit darkness as that last paragraph of the Intro reads currently. But there are no results for darkness, only colors associated with dispersal syndromes

comments.issue: Fish as important Amazonian seed dispersers are not considered.
comments.request: Consider fish as dispersers in the Amazon.
comments.quote: what about fish? I believe recent analyses have shown that fish actually may be super important dispersers, particularly in the Amazon

title: Dispersers and environment drive global variation in fruit colour syndromes

study.system: hard and soft selection concepts; literature review and synthesis

editor_summary: Editor: all three reviews positive about the topic but with very important concerns; the soft-selection definition is too narrow and clarity and definitions need improving.

reviews.assessment: Positive and compelling overall, but the writing and figures make the paper a slog; arguments need to be more accessible.
strengths: compelling practical applications to conservation and management

comments.issue: The way arguments are presented makes the paper very hard to read; almost every paragraph is cryptic.
comments.request: Rewrite paragraphs and figures for accessibility, with concrete examples.
comments.quote: I also found this paper a slog to read because of the way arguments are presented.

comments.issue: All figures except Figure 1 are inscrutable.
comments.request: Redesign the figures to be understandable.
comments.quote: I found the figures, other than figure 1, to be inscrutable.

comments.issue: The phrase 'relentless demographic costs' is confusing because costs should diminish over time.
comments.request: Restate the point more clearly.
comments.quote: My first reaction is that hard selection will relentlessly diminish the difference between the actual population mean trait and the optimal mean trait which means the costs will diminish with time

comments.issue: The treatment of interacting species as biotic agents of hard selection is cryptic.
comments.request: Explain the direct and indirect interspecific consequences more clearly.
comments.quote: Again, I was able to reason through what was said here, but the way it was said was cryptic and made me have to stop and think it through.

comments.issue: The claim about Darwin misrepresents his emphasis on biotic interactions over intraspecific competition.
comments.request: Correct the Darwin statement using the Origin, ch. 3.
comments.quote: Darwin emphasized biotic interactions, not intraspecific competition.

comments.issue: The definition at lines 506-508 is hard to defend and contradicts definitions used in the body.
comments.request: Reconcile the definition with the rest of the paper.
comments.quote: Your definition here is hard to defend and contradicts implied definitions in the body of the paper (e.g., Line 284).

reviews.assessment: Well-researched and clearly argued, but the soft-selection definition is too narrow and the inbreeding depression section mischaracterises selection.
strengths: cogent review useful for students and researchers

comments.issue: Defining soft selection as emanating only from intraspecific competition is too narrow; density- and frequency-dependent interspecific interactions also qualify.
comments.request: Adopt a broader definition throughout.
comments.quote: I feel that the definition of soft selection as only emanating from intraspecific competition is too narrow for modern usage

comments.issue: Global change feels forced as the motivation for the review rather than its importance for eco-evolution generally.
comments.request: Reconsider the framing of the review's impetus.
comments.quote: It’s unclear why global change should be the impetus for the review rather than, say, the importance for eco-evolution, more generally.

comments.issue: Discussion of outcomes and dynamics, including trait thresholds above which soft selection operates, is missing.
comments.request: Add discussion of these mixed threshold cases.
comments.quote: I’d like to see more discussion of both soft and hard selection on outcomes and dynamics, such as when a trait threshold exists, but above that soft selection operates.

comments.issue: Inbreeding depression is an absolute fitness decline and cannot result from soft selection; it is caused by close mating, not selection.
comments.request: Correct the inbreeding depression section.
comments.quote: I think inbreeding depression is an absolute decline in fitness and thus cannot result from soft selection.

comments.issue: Using HS and SS acronyms forces readers to remember codes unnecessarily.
comments.request: Avoid the acronyms.
comments.quote: I find it distracting to find that soft selection and hard selection need to become acronyms.

comments.issue: The logic that discrete traits are more relevant for eco-evolutionary dynamics is unclear and doubtful.
comments.request: Clarify or drop the discrete-trait argument.
comments.quote: I have no idea for the logic that discrete traits are more relevant for eco-evolutionary dynamics. I doubt it’s true.

comments.issue: The statement about ecological models generating soft selection ignores that those models lack phenotypic variation.
comments.request: Add 'models with phenotypic variation'.
comments.quote: this sounds like purely ecological models can generate soft selection, but those models ignore phenotypic variation.

comments.issue: The claim that interacting species induce hard but not soft selection is unsupported and follows from the narrow definition.
comments.request: Revisit this claim under a broader definition.
comments.quote: that interacting species typically induce hard selection and not soft selection does not seem to be supported by the data

comments.issue: Predation examples are not truly hard selection because predators are often frequency-dependent.
comments.request: Reconsider whether these are hard selection examples.
comments.quote: in practice, I believe that predators often will be frequency-dependent, hunting the camouflaged hares when no uncamouflaged ones can be found because they simply need to eat

comments.issue: The review is too dismissive of landmark papers such as Christiansen and Levene.
comments.request: Give these landmark papers fairer treatment.
comments.quote: In my mind this review is too dismissive of landmark papers like Christiansen and Levene even if they didn’t exactly follow Wallace.

comments.issue: Figure 2 y-axis may need to be density rather than frequency; S is undefined and should be called weak/strong.
comments.request: Define S and reconsider the y-axis.
comments.quote: Shouldn’t the y-axis be density and not frequency? Define S. Call S weak and strong?

reviews.assessment: Mostly clear and mistake-free, but presentation needs substantial improvement: unclear criteria for examples, undefined selection terms, and figure problems.
strengths: mostly clear and good to read

comments.issue: The distinction between panmictic and spatially structured populations is not made explicit up front.
comments.request: Clarify and discuss this difference early on.
comments.quote: I suggest that this difference (pop. with and without spatial structure) should be made clearer and discussed more up front.

comments.issue: Terms such as selection coefficient and relative fitness are used differently across contexts without clarification.
comments.request: Clarify the different usages.
comments.quote: An old problem in discussions of SS and HS is that terms are used that are used differently in different contexts.

comments.issue: Selection coefficient and relative fitness are not properly defined and change meaning across examples and the glossary.
comments.request: Define s and Ws precisely and track their meaning.
comments.quote: The selection coefficient (s) and relative fitness (Ws) are not properly defined in the context of this paper.

comments.issue: Empirical examples are classified as hard or soft selection without clear criteria; density dependence was not investigated in several cases.
comments.request: Present explicit classification criteria up front.
comments.quote: How did you decide what is an example for HS and SS? It reads as if cases of a rather fast response to selection (or visible selection) are considered to be likely HS.

comments.issue: Hard and soft selection are presented as mutually exclusive, though mixtures may be common.
comments.request: Address mixed cases and how to identify them.
comments.quote: The HS and SS distinction if largely presented as a one or the other scenario. Only at some places the text makes statements that indicate that a “mixture” between the two may act.

comments.issue: Implications of hard and soft selection for genomic signatures are not covered.
comments.request: Add a section on genomic signatures.
comments.quote: It would be good to include a section addressing what implication SS and HS have for the genomic signatures produced by natural selection.

comments.issue: The title is misleading; 'Wallace' suggests Alfred Russel Wallace and the choice of hero is unexplained.
comments.request: Reconsider the title.
comments.quote: I find the title somewhat miss leading. When thinking about “evoluton” and reading the name “Wallace”, I think about Alfred Russel Wallace

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 71-74 is hard to understand without more introduction.
comments.request: Add introductory explanation.
comments.quote: The sentence is hard to understand at this place. Without more introduction to the topic the sentence will only be understood by specialists.

comments.issue: Resource availability is itself dynamic and density-dependent, which the treatment does not acknowledge.
comments.request: Acknowledge the dynamic nature of resource availability.
comments.quote: Resource availability is often a function of past and current density and thus itself highly dynamic.

comments.issue: 'More complex' at line 200 lacks a comparison baseline.
comments.request: Specify more complex than what.
comments.quote: The demographic consequences of SS are more complex during exploitative competition

comments.issue: It is unclear what decreases in the inbreeding depression sentence; 'purging' may be clearer.
comments.request: Clarify what decreases and consider 'purging'.
comments.quote: This is unclear. What is actually decreasing: the mean inbreeding coefficient in the population, the mean effect of inbreeding depression

comments.issue: 'Maladapted' is a problematic term in evolutionary biology and implies a better alternative.
comments.request: Avoid the term.
comments.quote: The term “maladapted” is a strange term in evolutionary biology. I would not use it.

comments.issue: The glossary is incomplete and imprecise, missing terms such as selection coefficient and absolute fitness.
comments.request: Extend and sharpen the glossary.
comments.quote: The Glossary is helpful, but incomplete and not very precise.

comments.issue: Figure references do not point to sub-panels.
comments.request: Refer to sub-panels (e.g., Fig. 2A).
comments.quote: For better explanation of the figures it would be useful to refer to figure sub-panel, e.g. Fig.2A, Fig.1B,

comments.issue: Figure layouts and colours are inconsistent across figures.
comments.request: Standardise layout and colour scheme.
comments.quote: For better illustration, I suggest to make the layout of the figures consistent. E.g. always HS on top and SS on the bottom

comments.issue: Figure 2 is hard to interpret; the y-axis label frequency is misleading and counts may be clearer.
comments.request: Clarify and relabel the y-axis.
comments.quote: It would help to make clear what does the Y-axis show? It is labelled frequency, but I guess most people would assume that this would add to 1

comments.issue: Figure 3 is not well explained; axis, peaks and colour meanings are unclear.
comments.request: Integrate and explain Figure 3 better.
comments.quote: The figure is not well explained. It could be better integrated into the main text and the terminology used in a consistent way to make the figure clear.

title: The ecological causes and consequences of hard and soft selection

study.system: plant-microbe interactions; conceptual framework

editor_summary: Editor says three excellent reviews; general agreement on usefulness of a conceptual framework and good writing, but divergence on conceptual novelty (recent special issue must be differentiated); revision encouraged.

reviews.assessment: Very supportive of the goals and topic but asks for important clarifications on symbiont focus, terms, theory and experimental recommendations.

comments.issue: Most examples are symbiont-based; the distinction from free-living microbes and its implications are not highlighted.
comments.request: Highlight the symbiont versus free-living distinction.
comments.quote: the majority of examples that are described are based on symbionts (leaf or root symbionts). This distinction seems important and should be better highlighted since free-living microorganisms may or may not have the same function

comments.issue: Recommendations for designing studies (e.g. replicated genotypes) are missing from the future directions.
comments.request: Recommend replicated genotypes/populations in Box 1 and future directions.
comments.quote: A big missing piece of the ‘future directions’ section is to make some recommendations for how to undertake these studies to enhance the chances of seeing these patterns.

comments.issue: Heritability of microbial communities is not well described.
comments.request: Describe the heritability of microbial communities better.
comments.quote: Heritability of microbial communities could also be better described.

comments.issue: The proposed design and interpretations test only the feedback phase and do not address the conditioning phase or plant versus site confounds.
comments.request: Address conditioning and separate plant effects from site/climate effects, citing Van Nuland and Ware.
comments.quote: The experimental design and statistical interpretations only seem to test the “feedback” phase as it does not, as currently written, strongly address the “conditioning” phase

comments.issue: New terms are unnecessary; microbe-facing and environment-facing traits map onto existing conditioning and feedback language.
comments.request: Reuse existing terminology instead of new terms.
comments.quote: As intimated above, I don’t see the need for new terms.

comments.issue: How microbe-mediated local adaptation and adaptive plasticity are not mutually exclusive is underdescribed.
comments.request: Describe when the two mechanisms overlap or matter together.
comments.quote: More is needed to describe how microbe-mediated local adaptation and microbe-mediated adaptive plasticity are not mutually exclusive.

comments.issue: Thompson's Geographic Mosaic of Co-Evolution theory and Hoeksema's work are missing from the discussion.
comments.request: Add this missing body of theory and relevant work.
comments.quote: A missing body of theory here is Thompson’s Geographic Mosaic of Co-Evolution, which is highly relevant to the discussion as it is not just about antagonistic interactions (as cited).

comments.issue: The opening paragraph could be expanded with more (plant-focused) examples of evolutionary innovations.
comments.request: Expand the introduction's examples.
comments.quote: Love the first paragraph of the Introduction describing major evolutionary innovations across the tree of life, but this could be expanded a bit to provide more examples

comments.issue: Microbial 'form' at line 66 is a vague term; community composition may be meant.
comments.request: Replace the vague term with precise language.
comments.quote: Line 66. Is microbial ‘form’ community composition? Vague term

comments.issue: 'Locally important' microbes are undefined and 'enrich' wrongly implies positive-only interactions.
comments.request: Define how importance is decided and use more precise language.
comments.quote: Line 40 also suggests “locally important” microbes. How is importance decided (presence/absence of symbionts, positive functions, diverse community composition?)?

comments.issue: Figure 1A does not show the complex interplay or the conditioning and feedback phases; Figure 1B is unclear about single-generation inference.
comments.request: Redesign Figure 1 with clearer phases, arrows and environment.
comments.quote: Fig. 1A does not indicate to me “complex interplay between host genotype, microbial community composition and the environment” – it shows the experimental design that is often employed but misses the nuances of where/when selection can take place.

comments.issue: A bolded section heading is missing at line 127 and section language does not match the stated goals.
comments.request: Add the heading and align terminology across sections.
comments.quote: Line 127 – missing bolded section heading “patterns and processes of microbe-mediated adaptation” before starting the sub-sections

comments.issue: Box 2 needs visuals, a less colloquial title, and concrete examples of the three mechanisms.
comments.request: Improve Box 2 with examples and visuals.
comments.quote: Box 2 could use more visuals to help makes the points. Title is also too colloquial, even if true!

comments.issue: 'Habitat' is undefined in the experimental approaches and is confounded with 'Microbial source'.
comments.request: Explain what habitat represents and disentangle it from microbial source.
comments.quote: I don’t know what habitat is meant to represent in the ‘experimental approaches’ section – climate alone? In many ways ‘Habitat’ and “Microbial source” are confounded and should be better explained.

comments.issue: Table 1 omits the sterilization factor, which tests a key part of the interaction.
comments.request: Add sterilization factors to Table 1.
comments.quote: Table 1 defines the statistical interpretations of a fully reciprocal experiment (although the sterilization factors need to be added here since that is testing a key part of the interaction).

comments.issue: Other random effects and statistical approaches, notably a Bayesian approach, are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss additional random effects and Bayesian approaches.
comments.quote: What other approaches or factors could/should be included as random effects? Are there other approaches that could be important? It seems that a Bayesian approach might be important to at least mention.

comments.issue: The implications section covers too much ground and should focus on examples linked to the main points and research directions.
comments.request: Trim the implications and merge Box 3 with Fig. 4 aspects.
comments.quote: The implications section describes fantastic and interesting examples but covers a lot of ground. It might be helpful to choose a few of these specific examples that better link to the main points of the paper

reviews.assessment: Praises the helpful framework but requests clarifications on scope, Table 1, microbial biogeography and the new terminology.

comments.issue: The beneficial-microbe focus is stated only once and not reflected in figures, tables or the title.
comments.request: Remind readers of this focus and consider changing the title.
comments.quote: The focus of this paper is how beneficial microbes (not pathogens) impact plant local adaptation. I believe this is stated just once, line 112. But it would be helpful to remind readers of this, especially in figures and tables.

comments.issue: Table 1's interpretations are oversimplified and omit maladaptation, plasticity variation and microbial adaptation; the legend lacks the response variable.
comments.request: Expand the table and its legend.
comments.quote: I find Table 1 “Interpretations” to be oversimplified, which may cause confusion. Is each interpretation meant to be just one possible outcome?

comments.issue: The unstated belowground focus limits integration of aboveground beneficial microbes.
comments.request: State the focus/bias and integrate aboveground microbes.
comments.quote: There is an unstated focus on belowground microbes. I suggest stating this focus/bias, and/or integrating more on aboveground plant-associated beneficial microbes.

comments.issue: The locally important microbe discussion ignores the rich microbial biogeography literature.
comments.request: Develop this with microbial biogeography literature.
comments.quote: The authors only briefly discuss how “locally important microbes” (line 205) may contribute to local adaptation. But there is a rich literature on microbial biogeography that would improve this discussion.

comments.issue: The consequences of field vs greenhouse settings for microbial control and interpretation are not discussed.
comments.request: Expand Box 3 on field-greenhouse differences.
comments.quote: I suggest a more detailed discussion of the key differences between field and greenhouse studies, especially with respect to ability to control microbes and how this impacts interpretations.

comments.issue: The relationship to the recent Philosophical Transactions special issue on microbiomes and host evolution is not addressed.
comments.request: Differentiate this paper from the special issue papers.
comments.quote: There is a recent special issue in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B on the role of microbiomes in host evolution (including a paper by Lau). How does this paper relate to the review/idea papers in that issue?

comments.issue: Figure 1A arrows are confusing and hard to interpret.
comments.request: Clarify the arrows in Figure 1A.
comments.quote: Fig 1A: Arrows are confusing. It is not clear how I am meant to interpret them.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the sterilization effect is a fixed effect and how it relates to Table 1 and the microbial source effect.
comments.request: Clarify the sterilization effect's role.
comments.quote: Line 288 – Please clarify the sterilization effect? If it is a fixed effect why is it not included in Table 1? Or is it part of the microbial source effect?

comments.issue: Introducing 'microbe facing traits' and 'environment facing traits' adds confusion rather than clarity.
comments.request: Drop the new terms and use existing language.

title: Microbe‐mediated adaptation in plants

study.system: moth population dynamics; 34-year census and precipitation time series

editor_summary: Both reviewers admire the ambition; one questions sampling intensity and duration, the other model selection in MCMC; tone down bold conclusions and discuss model-selection shortcomings.

reviews.assessment: Interesting temporal analyses, but identifiability and model-selection issues may call the conclusions into question.
strengths: very interesting suite of temporal analyses
simulation analysis is a great idea

comments.issue: It is unclear why the change-point and state-space analyses are separate; identifiability may stem from too little data.
comments.request: Discuss the identifiability issue or use a single model.
comments.quote: It is unclear to me why the change-point analysis and the state-space model are separate?

comments.issue: Simulations use point estimates; propagating MCMC posterior uncertainty would make dissimilarity comparisons robust.
comments.request: Run each simulation using the full posterior distribution.
comments.quote: I suggest that each simulation is run using the full MCMC posterior distribution. This would then allow the dissimilarity matrix (d) to also have a posterior distribution.

comments.issue: Models in Table S2 are virtually identical (deltaWAIC at most 1.76, CIs overlapping zero), undermining model-selection conclusions.
comments.request: Acknowledge this and discuss implications for the conclusions.
comments.quote: close inspection of Table S2 reveals that the models are all virtually identical, with deltaWAIC equal to 1.76 at most and many parameter estimates with CIs that overalp zero

comments.issue: Identifiability of two density-dependence terms is doubtful; posterior predictive checks are missing.
comments.request: Perform and report posterior predictive checks, parameter correlations and MCMC traces.
comments.quote: I recommend the authors perform and report posterior predictive checks of their model including correlation of parameters and MCMC traces.

comments.issue: Statistical models are poorly described: y and X undefined, and the standard-deviation prior is implausible.
comments.request: Follow best practices for reporting statistical models.
comments.quote: The statistical models are not adequately described. Parameters and inputs (y and X) are not defined at all.

comments.issue: No figure shows the simulation results for the different scenarios.
comments.request: Add a figure of simulation results per scenario.
comments.quote: Please consider a figure showing the simulation results for the different scenarios.

reviews.assessment: Interesting findings from an unusual 34-year dataset, but data adequacy and overstated statistical support temper enthusiasm.
strengths: potential to make a major contribution

comments.issue: Sampling is limited to 10 bushes in one patch; timing, bush selection and representativeness are unclear.
comments.request: Report sampling protocol details and data representativeness.
comments.quote: the annual sampling is limited to caterpillar counts on 10 lupine bushes ‘in the same patch’ at the study site

comments.issue: Only 16-18 data points are used to estimate models with up to four parameters.
comments.request: Address the limited sample size for the model complexity.
comments.quote: there are only 16-18 data points used to estimate models that involve up to 4 parameters

comments.issue: The paper overstates statistical support for the cycle shift and density-dependence results.
comments.request: Indicate the level of support for each conclusion, including in the abstract.
comments.quote: I do think the paper overstates the level of statistical support for some the conclusions.

comments.issue: Model presentation is not reader-friendly: X and Y undefined, delay order and simulation rationale unstated.
comments.request: Define terms and state the rationale for the delay and simulations.
comments.quote: I think the presentation of the model could be more reader-friendly. X and Y are not defined (presumably X is caterpillar density and Y is caterpillar number).

comments.issue: Diapause and overwintering instars, and their effect on sampling, are not described.
comments.request: Explain diapause and overwintering biology and its sampling implications.
comments.quote: Does this species diapause? What is the range of instars in which overwintering occurs? How might this affect sampling?

comments.issue: Fig. 3 is discussed before Figs. 1 and 2.
comments.request: Reorder the figures.
comments.quote: Why is Fig 3 discussed in the Methods and Results before Figs 1 or 2? Reorder these.

comments.issue: It is unclear how caterpillars and precipitation were scaled.
comments.request: Explain the scaling of both variables.
comments.quote: line 113. How were caterpillars and precipitation scaled? Why?

comments.issue: It is not explained why area is included in Y but not X.
comments.request: Explain the treatment of area in the model.
comments.quote: line 130. indicate why area is in Y but not in X (presumably to shift from density to count).

comments.issue: Previous work at lines 225-230 is not introduced early enough to motivate the model.
comments.request: Mention this previous work in the Introduction.
comments.quote: lines 225-230. Briefly mentioning this previous work in the Introduction would help in better motivating the model.

comments.quote: The description of Fig 2 in the Results section is lacking, and it provides no explanation of the different regions on the plane

title: Altered precipitation dynamics lead to a shift in herbivore dynamical regime

study.system: host-symbiont cophylogeny; 212 studies; ~10,000 species

editor_summary: Reviewers agree the goal is important but raise concerns about the statistical analyses, their validity and interpretations; rewriting and additional analyses are needed, including discussion of recent methods.

reviews.assessment: Interesting topic, but the study is descriptive, its novelty limited and the statistical implementation flawed.
strengths: overall idea of the study is appealing
meta-analysis approach to cophylogeny is valuable and can inspire further studies

comments.issue: The study only describes general congruence patterns and does not link them to mechanisms.
comments.request: Strengthen the mechanistic contribution and highlight it in the manuscript.
comments.quote: I am not convinced that the study contributes significantly to fill this knowledge gap

comments.issue: The vertical transmission result was advanced before and is not a major breakthrough.
comments.request: Better position the advance relative to prior work.
comments.quote: This is valuable but I am not convinced that it represents a major breakthrough in our understanding of the evolution of symbiotic associations

comments.issue: Congruence is conflated with symbiont tracking, though vicariance, coevolution and preferential switching produce the same pattern.
comments.request: Separate congruence from tracking throughout.
comments.quote: it is often assumed in the manuscript that phylogenetic congruence between hosts and symbionts indicates symbiont tracking of the host phylogeny, when it is not necessarily so

comments.issue: ParaFit is symmetric, so a significant p-value supports congruence, not tracking.
comments.request: Correct the interpretation of the test.
comments.quote: strictly speaking a significant p value does not support phylogenetic tracking, but just phylogenetic congruence

comments.issue: The choice of TreeMap and ParaFit is not justified and recent alternatives are not considered.

comments.issue: Commensal associations are introduced but excluded without justification.
comments.request: Justify excluding commensalism.

comments.quote: I cannot see why N (sample size) is taken as the sum of the numbers of host and symbiont species included in a randomisation test

comments.issue: Working hypotheses are scattered through Results and Discussion instead of being declared in the introduction.

comments.issue: The discussion lacks depth and wider context of interorganismal associations.

comments.quote: an analysis the results in a wider context of interorganismal associations (e.g., commensalism, pollination)

reviews.assessment: Well-conducted, well-written study with no major flaws; only minor comments on interpretation and presentation.

informative figures and rich supplementary material

comments.issue: Biological relevance and implications of the congruence patterns are not discussed in enough detail.

comments.issue: It is unclear how the results quantify co-divergence versus host shifts, as posed in the abstract.

comments.issue: Whether the prediction applies to mutualisms is not addressed.

comments.issue: 'Distantly' related is imprecise and 'Maybre' is a typo.

comments.issue: What a broad versus narrow interpretation of the rule means is unclear.

comments.issue: The strong effect for microbial hosts and other taxonomic effects are barely discussed.

comments.quote: Do you think it could be interesting to provide some discussion/speculations on why the effect for microbial hosts seem so strong?

comments.issue: An important result at lines 208-210 is described too briefly.
comments.request: Describe and explain this result in more detail.
comments.quote: That seems to be a pretty important result that could be described/explained in a little bit more details.

comments.issue: The conclusion does not link the effect size back to the motivating question.

comments.quote: Maybe you could describe what are the pro and cons of both approaches? For example, are they complementary?

comments.issue: The presentation of the conclusion in the supplement is not straightforward.

comments.issue: Lines in Figure 2 (L496-497, L501) are not dashed as stated.

comments.quote: it could be useful to add a legend for the schematic representation of host (in grey) and their symbiont (in back)

comments.issue: Valuable methodological recommendations are buried in the supplementary material.

comments.issue: Sentences describing variables in Extended Table 2 lack final punctuation.

comments.issue: The univariate regression section has a missing word and unclear rationale.

comments.issue: Supplementary table estimates are hard to compare across sensitivity analyses.

reviews.assessment: Fascinating topic and original approach, but the meta-analysis validity and biological conclusions raise serious concerns.

comments.issue: Statistical sections are not accessible, and essential explanations sit only in the supplements.
comments.request: Rewrite for a general audience and move essential explanations to the main text.
comments.quote: many explanations are only provided in the Supplementary extended documents, whereas they are essential for the understanding of the manuscript

comments.issue: The Student-distribution approximation of permutation distributions and the p-to-r conversion are untested.

comments.issue: Supplementary Table 2 is hard to read in its current format.

title: A broadscale analysis of host‐symbiont cophylogeny reveals the drivers of phylogenetic congruence

study.system: terrestrial non-volant mammals; range size and niche breadth

editor_summary: Editor sees potential in the manuscript and approaches, but both reviewers requested significant changes; clarity and communication need major revision before a second review round.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and well-executed, but clarification is needed; the extinction-risk interpretation is unconvincing and terminology imprecise.
strengths: complex and disparate analyses handled well
partial support for the niche-breadth range-size hypothesis
thoughtful supplementary treatment of bats and human impacts

comments.issue: Key findings are not distilled and highlighted for the reader.
comments.request: Better summarise the main messages.
comments.quote: I think that the key findings from these analyses could be distilled and better highlighted/summarized.

comments.issue: Extinction-risk claim in the abstract is unsupported because extinction risk was not analysed.
comments.request: Remove this claim from the abstract and discuss it cautiously.
comments.quote: I do not believe it should be in the Abstract, especially as there is no direct analysis of extinction risk.

comments.issue: The niche-specialisation trade-off, the paper's crux, is not the highlighted interpretation.
comments.request: Communicate this trade-off in the abstract and conclusions.
comments.quote: I think this could be the key interpretation that needs to better communicated in the Abstract and concluding sentences.

comments.issue: The term 'scale' is used without specifying spatial versus taxonomic scale or grain versus extent.
comments.request: Clarify each use of the term scale.
comments.quote: I would like each use of the term scale to be as clear as possible to what it refers to (e.g., spatial scale, taxonomic scale, etc.)

comments.issue: 'Scale dependency', a major implication, is not clearly described.
comments.request: Explain what type of scale dependency is meant.
comments.quote: This is also true for ‘scale dependency’, which is a major implication of this manuscript, yet is not clearly described.

comments.issue: Niche terms are imprecise: fundamental versus realized niches and niche breadth versus niche space.
comments.request: Define and use niche terms consistently.
comments.quote: Another term that likely needs more precision is ‘niche’, are we talking about fundamental or realized niches; plus ‘niche breadth’ vs ‘niche space’ have different interpretations and implications

comments.issue: 'Dispersals' and 'movements' are used without description or consistent distinction.
comments.request: Describe and use these terms consistently.
comments.quote: Also, ‘dispersals’ vs ‘movements’ - I think these need short descriptions and consistent use

comments.issue: The coarsest niche breadth representation (counts) was used for the main analysis.

comments.quote: I don’t see a clear reason why the coarsest representation of niche breadth (i.e., counts) were used for the main analysis.

comments.issue: The surprising absence of phylogenetic bias may reflect a coding error and should be rechecked.
comments.request: Rerun the phylogenetic diversity analysis to verify it.
comments.quote: I am surprised that the phylogenetic diversity of the 545 focal species is not different from expected from a random subset of the same number of species, suggesting no apparent phylogenetic bias.

comments.issue: Results should not be generalised to all terrestrial mammals because bats are missing and behave differently.
comments.request: Restrict statements to terrestrial non-volant mammals.
comments.quote: Thus, I would suggest referring to terrestrial non-volant mammals in the text where applicable, rather than terrestrial mammals.

comments.issue: The human-impact supplementary analysis uses non-endangered species, a non-random subset that introduces bias.

comments.quote: Non-endangered species are a strongly non-random subset of species (Fig. S7 and S8), thus while trying to remove the effect of human influence, this approach introduces a different bias.

reviews.assessment: Exciting and useful goal, but vague terminology, unarticulated assumptions, hard-to-follow hypotheses and logic leaps require major revision.
strengths: evaluates niche axes across biological scales
considers implications for conservation and management

comments.issue: Scale dependency is undefined and the word scale is used inconsistently.

title: General statistical scaling laws for stability in ecological systems

comments.issue: Line 78 should use transience rather than dispersal.
