comments.issue: Three line-level presentation edits: 'framework' is overstated (L32), 'indispensable' (L370), and the growth-rate symbol mismatch in Table S1.
comments.quote: L32: 'framework' is perhaps a bit overstated? it's a model, not a new framework. Suggest you rephrase.

comments.issue: Emergent Allee effects are defined as internal feedbacks, but the perturbation pushing between states need not be internal.
comments.request: Reword the sentence on emergent Allee effects.
comments.quote: emergent Allee effects is a mechanism of positively reinforcing feedbacks ('internal' to the system) ensuring the persistence of two alternative stable states in a community

comments.issue: With vB growth, asymptotic size and growth rate are not independent, so k being intake-independent does not make growth intake-independent.
comments.request: Explain the dependence between asymptotic size and growth rate.
comments.quote: may be good to explain that with vB-growth, asymptotic size and growth rate are not independent

comments.issue: Predation risk depends on absolute rather than relative size, but actual body sizes of small consumers are not reported.
comments.request: Complement beta details with a measure of actual body size.
comments.quote: predation risk is a result of absolute and not relative size, so it'd be good to complement your details on beta with information on some measure of actual body size of such small consumers

comments.issue: Methods state indiscriminate predation below a size, but the results imply the size specificity was varied.
comments.request: Clarify whether the vulnerable size threshold was varied or fixed.
comments.quote: So was the size below which prey was vulnerable to predation varied? Or was it kept fixed for the predator and their prey size is just a consequence of the size-difference imposed on the consumers?

comments.issue: 'Total effective productivity' is not defined or distinguished from the sum of the two productivities.
comments.request: Define total effective productivity and its relation to the sum.
comments.quote: please clarify what you mean by total effective productivity (as opposed to just total productivity), and why it isn't the same as the sum of the two productivities

comments.issue: The green and brown colours in Figure 1 may be hard for colour-blind readers to distinguish.
comments.request: Change the pelagic colour to blue.
comments.quote: I suggest you change the pelagic colour code to blue instead of green (colour blinds will likely have a difficulty distinguishing the green and brown colours used)

comments.issue: Axis labels in Figures 3-5 are hard for non-modellers to understand.
comments.request: Use more informative axis labels such as 'resource productivity'.
comments.quote: suggest you use a more informative x-axis label (in 3A & 3B, and 4-5) and y-axis label (in 3B) that is easier to understand also for non-modellers, e.g. "resource productivity"

comments.issue: The difference between Figure 4 panels A, B and C is unclear.
comments.request: Add an arrow indicating benthic resource productivity across panels.
comments.quote: it is unclear from just looking at the figure what the difference is between A, B and C. Suggest you insert an arrow above all subplots from left to right with the text "benthic resource productivity"

comments.issue: The purposes of the three proportionality constants in Table S1 are unspecified.
comments.request: Specify what each proportionality constant is used for.
comments.quote: please specify what the different proportionality constants are used for (you now list 3 proportionality constants)

title: Community structure and collapses in multichannel food webs: Role of consumer body sizes and mesohabitat productivities

study.system: Anolis and Draco lizards; field displays, robot playbacks, comparative analysis

editor_summary: Editor notes mixed reviewer assessments and a range of concerns; concrete evidence is needed that Anolis-Draco similarities are convergence rather than retained ancestry, and jargon and terminology must be defined and used consistently.

reviews.assessment: Sees the idea as interesting but finds the manuscript flawed in concept definitions, model testing, data documentation and taxon sampling, and cannot recommend publication.
strengths: liked the general idea of comparing Anolis and Draco

comments.issue: The claim that communication convergence is rare lacks primary support; cited reviews concern repeated evolution and do not correct for sample size.
comments.request: Support the claim with primary literature.
comments.quote: First, there is no primary research paper cited to support this claim.

comments.issue: Convergence, convergent, parallel and repeated evolution are used interchangeably though they are different concepts.
comments.request: Define and distinguish these concepts.
comments.quote: the authors are very sloppy in their use of the terms convergence/convergent evolution/parallel evolution/repeated evolution

comments.issue: Only a single OU model is used; alternative trait-evolution models are not compared.
comments.request: Compare alternative trait-evolution models.
comments.quote: It appears essential to me that the authors evaluate model fit of different models of trait evolution, in particular the white-noise and Brownian motion model as a potential baseline

comments.issue: Data collection is not described well enough to be reproduced.
comments.request: Describe the data collection procedure.
comments.quote: it was absolutely not clear to me (based on the available information) how this data was collected

comments.issue: Raw video material and analysis scripts are not available.
comments.request: Make videos and scripts publicly available.
comments.quote: The raw video material needs to be made publicly available (and to reviewers beforehand), just as the scripts used.

comments.issue: Taxon sampling is marginal (11 and 12 species) and its representativeness is unclear.
comments.request: Justify the taxon sampling.
comments.quote: I found that the taxon sampling was marginal for such a study (11 and 12 species, respectively)

reviews.assessment: Nice, broadly interesting paper, but jargon, poorly explained variables and vague model descriptions make the findings hard to judge.
strengths: nice paper combining ecology, evolution and behavior

comments.issue: Territory holding is contested in Anolis, so extrapolating the behavioural system to Draco is tenuous.
comments.request: Remove or avoid the territory framing.
comments.quote: it seems tenuous to extrapolate a behavioral system (territory holding) from Anolis to Draco

comments.issue: Questions and the data needed to answer them are not clearly defined.
comments.request: Add a table mapping questions to data.
comments.quote: the questions and the data needed to answer them are not clearly defined in the methods or the introduction

comments.issue: 'Contextual reaction norms' is unexplained jargon introduced only in the analysis.
comments.request: Define and explain the term.
comments.quote: This phrase is first used in the analysis section. It reads as unexplained jargon.

comments.issue: Model descriptions are inconsistent and vague; interactions and components are unclear.
comments.request: Write out the models explicitly.
comments.quote: Here and in other model descriptions, the wording is inconsistent (e.g., within taxon vs. radiation history?) and the description vague

comments.issue: The identification analysis appears without motivation in the introduction.
comments.request: Motivate this section in the introduction.
comments.quote: This comes out of nowhere. Motivate in the introduction.

comments.issue: How the ecology differs, making the comparison not apples-to-apples, is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the ecological differences.
comments.quote: It’d be nice to know how the ecology is different.

comments.issue: Ord et al. 2020 may not support the statement that Draco are the only gliding lizards.
comments.request: Check the citation.
comments.quote: Is Ord et al. 2020 an appropriate citation for noting that Draco are the only lizards that glide?

comments.issue: The study risks cherry-picking a likely case of deep-time convergence; the comparison needs justification.
comments.request: Justify the comparison and list shared traits.
comments.quote: make the case that anolis and draco are a fair, apples to apples comparison

comments.issue: Section introduction confuses convergence with animal movement as the question.
comments.request: Reframe the section introduction.
comments.quote: reveals a bit of confusion over what the question is in this paper

comments.issue: 'Motion environments' is jargon without definition.
comments.request: Define the term.
comments.quote: “motion environments”. Jargon. What is a motion environment?

comments.issue: The predictions from communication theory are not specified.
comments.request: State the predictions.
comments.quote: Line 133: which “predictions from communication theory”?

comments.issue: 'Adapting' is ambiguous between plasticity and evolutionary fine-tuning.
comments.request: Clarify the meaning of adapting.
comments.quote: Is this about real-time plasticity at the individual level or evolutionary fine tuning at the population/species level?

comments.issue: The role of robot playbacks in testing convergence is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the robots' role.
comments.quote: It’s unclear to me where robots play a role in the test of deep time convergence.

comments.issue: The description of taxa is hard to parse.
comments.request: Rewrite the taxa description.
comments.quote: The description of taxa is tough to parse.

comments.issue: Whether the Puerto Rico and Jamaica data were previously published is unclear.
comments.request: State the data provenance.
comments.quote: Were the data from Puerto Rico and Jamaica previously published? If so, where?

comments.issue: The superlative about the world's most complex motion-based communication systems is hyperbolic.
comments.request: Support or remove the superlative.
comments.quote: By what criterion are these the “world’s most complex motion-based communication systems”?

comments.issue: Ambient light measured only at the end of 30-minute observations may not represent the session.
comments.request: Address the light measurement timing.
comments.quote: Does it matter that ambient light was measured at the end of the observation?

comments.issue: Unclear whether the reanalysis results are from Klomp et al. 2017 or produced here.
comments.request: Clarify the reanalysis provenance.
comments.quote: It’s ambiguous from the text whether the results of the reanalysis are in Klomp et al 2017 or whether Klomp et al. 2017 merely provide the data reanalyzed here.

comments.issue: The choice of an OU model is not justified among many alternatives.
comments.request: Justify the OU model.
comments.quote: Why OU? There are many different evolutionary models.

comments.issue: 'Taxon mean display values' are not explained.
comments.request: Explain what these values are.
comments.quote: “taxon mean display values”. It’s unclear to me what these are.

comments.issue: 'Non-contextually plastic macroevolutionary relationship' is unexplained jargon.
comments.request: Explain the term.
comments.quote: what is a “non-contextually plastic macroevolutionary relationship”?

comments.issue: Only Jamaica is mentioned where Puerto Rico also matters.
comments.request: Include Puerto Rico.
comments.quote: Line 324: “Jamaican”. What about Puerto Rico?

comments.issue: 'Various combinations' is vague and probably means all possible model combinations.
comments.request: Describe the model combinations precisely.
comments.quote: Again, model description is vague. I’m guessing it’s not various combinations but rather all possible model combinations.

comments.issue: Sentence on visual and vibration displays is hard to parse.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence.
comments.quote: I think that I’ve mis-parsed this sentence. Are visual and vibration displays convergent?

comments.issue: 'Random regression models' is an unfamiliar term.
comments.request: Explain the term.
comments.quote: I’m not familiar with the term “random regression models”.

comments.issue: The slope does not measure momentary changes in display, contrary to the text's implication.
comments.request: Correct the slope interpretation.
comments.quote: my understanding is that the slope doesn’t measure momentary changes in display

comments.issue: The meaning of 'identical' is unclear.
comments.request: State the measure of identity.
comments.quote: Line 390: “identical” by what measure. Statistically identical?

comments.issue: Whether 'adaptive' is justified is questioned.
comments.request: Justify the adaptive claim.
comments.quote: Line 446: Is the use of “adaptive” justified?

comments.issue: Table 1 is not discussed in the results.
comments.request: Discuss Table 1.
comments.quote: Line 458: Table 1 should be discussed in the results.

comments.issue: 'Diverse and often similar' reads as self-contradictory.
comments.request: Rephrase the phrase.
comments.quote: “diverse and often similar” seems to contradict itself.

comments.issue: Figure 2 elements are unexplained and panels are too small.
comments.request: Clarify figure elements and split panels.
comments.quote: More generally, I recommend breaking up the panels to increase font sizes and make it possible for the caption to be on the same page as the figure.

title: Deep‐time convergent evolution in animal communication presented by shared adaptations for coping with noise in lizards and other animals

study.system: boreal Lepidoptera in Finland; two-decade monitoring data

editor_summary: Both reviews largely positive; editor needs to see how authors deal with Reviewer 2's concerns and criticisms before deciding.

reviews.assessment: Highly positive; novel combination and sound methods, but causal direction and either-or strategy need clarification.

comments.issue: Reasoning for the 'either-or' strategy is too short; trade-offs of investing in one response are not explained.
comments.request: Explain trade-offs and link the either-or strategy to evolutionary processes.
comments.quote: The authors should better explain why species should rely on only one of both responses in terms of trade-offs for investment, e.g. into growth, and thus generate a link to potential evolutionary processes.

comments.issue: Phylogenetic signal itself is interesting but only used to handle non-independence.
comments.request: Expand on phylogenetic signal and its evolutionary interpretation.
comments.quote: the phylogenetic signal itself seems interesting in terms of evolutionary strategies and the authors should expand a bit more on this

comments.issue: Causal links are unclear: population trend may enable range expansion rather than the reverse, and feedback to phenology is questionable.
comments.request: Describe the causal links and mechanistic feedbacks clearly.
comments.quote: A clear description of causal links is needed here, since the authors use population trend as response and range shift as explanatory, which is likely the other way round at the first sight

comments.issue: Earlier phenology may cause mismatches with vegetation; simple advance may not capture phenological matching.
comments.request: Relate advance to vegetation phenology using NDVI-based measures.
comments.quote: advance should be related to actual shift in the phenology of the vegetation, e.g. using NDVI-based measures of start or peak of the vegetation period

comments.issue: 2 line-level copy edits: wording at L50 and L251.
comments.quote: L50 Please change to “population trends were observed”

comments.issue: The Fig. 1 citation is misplaced and Fig. 1 does not address life-history traits.
comments.request: Move the Fig. 1 citation and correct the statement.
comments.quote: L115 Move “(Fig. 1)” to the first part of the sentence. Life-history traits are not addressed in Fig. 1.

comments.issue: Using residuals as response variables overestimates degrees of freedom.
comments.request: Correct for this or use change in prevalence as a covariate.
comments.quote: Any further analyses using these residuals as response variable will overestimate the degrees of freedom.

comments.issue: The explanation of the correction is placed too late in the text.
comments.request: Move the explanation upwards so the rationale is clear from the start.
comments.quote: upwards (e.g. to L188) to make clear from the beginning why you are doing this.

comments.issue: Transforming categorical traits into dummy variables is unnecessary for the statistical analyses.
comments.request: Explain or remove the dummy-variable transformation.
comments.quote: L252 Why did you transform the categorical traits into dummy variables? It is not necessary for statistical analyses

reviews.assessment: Very positive; topical, well-written, state-of-the-art study; only minor clarifications requested.
strengths: well-suited system with solid monitoring data

comments.issue: Altitudinal responses are not considered alongside latitudinal shifts.
comments.request: Clarify how the potential altitudinal response was dealt with.
comments.quote: The paper only discusses latitudinal shifts, whereas an altitudinal response might also play a role (as acknowledged on p.5).

comments.issue: Phylogenetic signals are only mentioned briefly in the supplement.
comments.request: Discuss phylogenetic signals in more detail in the main text.
comments.quote: I would appreciate if the authors would discuss phylogenetic signals in more detail.

comments.issue: No supplementary table provides species-level results (prevalences, shifts, hypothesis outcomes).
comments.request: Add a supplementary table with species names grouped by family and their results.
comments.quote: I consider it an absolute must to include a supplementary table with the species names (grouped by family) and at least the following information

comments.issue: Reference at l.460-462 is incomplete and over-capitalised.
comments.request: Complete and correct the reference.
comments.quote: l.460-462: reference is incomplete and not all words should be in capitals

comments.issue: Panel (a) of Fig. S5 is not described.
comments.request: Describe what panel (a) shows.
comments.quote: Fig. S5: please describe what is shown in panel (a).

title: Combining range and phenology shifts offers a winning strategy for boreal Lepidoptera

study.system: ecological ODE models; biodiversity-ecosystem functioning theory

editor_summary: Editor wants the literature survey and main results strengthened, more explicit analysis of one example, math moved to appendix, and a clearer title.

reviews.assessment: Values the scale-invariance test but finds the method hard to adopt and the literature analysis and key results underdeveloped.
strengths: worthwhile and useful extension of existing concepts
clear mathematical criteria for richness invariance

comments.issue: As a Methods paper the approach is hard to operationalise, boiling down to a manual equation-matching check with no code or symbolic library.
comments.request: Make the method more readily transferable, for example with symbolic-mathematics support.
comments.quote: actually operationalising the authors' approach is highly nontrivial and largely boils down to "the equation matching check must be performed"

comments.issue: The authors' own worked example contains an error: the beta term in Eq (5) leaves an extraneous beta*P1*P2 term.
comments.request: Correct the derivation of Eq (5).
comments.quote: they themselves have made an error when adding Eqs (2) and (3) and simplifying it into the expression for P-dot in Eq (5)

comments.issue: How the 26 models were identified is not described, so the literature survey is not reproducible.
comments.request: Describe how the surveyed models were identified and selected.
comments.quote: I would like to know much more about how the authors identified the models they examined. Was this literature systematic (and reproducible?) in some way

comments.issue: Table 1 does not indicate which scale-invariance criterion each surveyed model failed.
comments.request: Add columns showing which criteria each model failed.
comments.quote: it would seem much more useful for the authors to include columns indicating which criteria or criterion the model failed

comments.issue: The full analytical work behind the 26 model assessments is not provided, so others cannot check it.
comments.request: Write up the full analyses in the Supplementary Material.
comments.quote: it would seem prudent---and possibly essential---that the authors write up their full analyses as part of the Supplementary Material so that others can check and refer to them in the future

comments.issue: The literature analysis reads as an afterthought and should receive the space it deserves, possibly changing the article type.
comments.request: Give the literature analysis the space it deserves or drop it to a separate contribution.
comments.quote: every mention of the analysis of pre-existing models gave the impression that it was an afterthought rather than an important facet of this contribution

comments.issue: Richness is referred to by many interchangeable terms throughout the manuscript.
comments.request: Use one consistent term for richness.
comments.quote: they interchange between richness, number of species, raw number of species, number of species per se, raw species numbers, plain species richness

comments.issue: Richness and diversity are not explicitly defined or distinguished as the authors use them.
comments.request: Define richness and distinguish it from diversity.
comments.quote: it would instead seem opportune for them to explicitly define richness (as they intend to use it) and then distinguish between it and diversity (as they intend to use it)

comments.issue: Functional diversity may not capture the paper's key concept, and functional equivalence is defined contrary to convention.
comments.request: Clarify the concept and the definition of functional equivalence.
comments.quote: I'm also not certain that functional diversity really captures their key concept, possibly the authors' explanation of what renders two species equivalent is somewhat contrary to convention

comments.issue: The phrases 'ecological network models' and 'eco-evolutionary network models' mislead about the class of models covered.
comments.request: Use terminology that matches the models actually analysed.
comments.quote: I found myself expecting a very different class of mathematical models upon reading the phrases "ecological network models" and "eco-evolutionary network models"

comments.issue: The key results are too brief and cursorily treated to make an impact, e.g. the Thébault & Fontaine scale-invariant comparison.
comments.request: Expand and properly present the key results.
comments.quote: I feel like the key "results" are too brief to make a meaningful impact and treated so cursorily that they will swiftly be forgotten

comments.issue: 6 line-level copy edits: word substitutions such as 'plays' to 'play', 'said models' to 'models' and 'form' to 'from'.
comments.quote: of these research lines -> of this research relies (page 3, line 23)

comments.issue: The history component of the introduction's first paragraph could be cut without losing anything.
comments.request: Cut the historical opening of the introduction.
comments.quote: the authors could probably cut the history component of the first paragraph of the introduction (up to around line 33) without losing anything of obvious consequence

comments.issue: Introductory text about the literature survey is interpretation and belongs in the Discussion.
comments.request: Move the literature-survey text to the Discussion.
comments.quote: The text in the intro about the literature survey (page 4, lines 35-44) is really Discussion rather than Introduction since it hinges on the interpretation of the authors' analyses.

comments.issue: It is unclear why the study requires multiple trophic levels to be applicable.
comments.request: Explain the multiple-trophic-level requirement.
comments.quote: Why must there be multiple trophic levels for the authors' study to be applicable? (page 5, line 19)

comments.issue: The text on page 6, lines 27-34 is very difficult to follow.
comments.request: Rewrite this passage for clarity.
comments.quote: I found the text on page 6, lines 27-34, very difficult to follow.

comments.issue: P-dot notation is unusual and should be defined as the rate of change upon first introduction.
comments.request: Define P-dot at first use.
comments.quote: Many readers will be more accustomed to dP/dt rather than P-dot. Therefore please define P-dot as the rate of change of P upon first introduction.

comments.issue: Functional equivalence of P1 and P2 also appears to require epsilon1 and epsilon2 to be equal.
comments.request: Address the missing epsilon equality in the definition.
comments.quote: doesn't functional equivalence of P1 and P2 also require that epsilon1 and epsilon2 are equal? (page 7, line 26)

comments.issue: The inline definition of functional equivalence would fit better where artificial splitting is discussed.
comments.request: Move the definition next to the splitting discussion.
comments.quote: the inline definition of functional equivalent found after Eq 5 (page 7, line 45) would fit much better immediately after the authors talk about artificially splitting the prey species P into two new species that are functionally identical

comments.issue: What 'the dynamics are forced' means is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the phrase 'the dynamics are forced'.
comments.quote: It is unclear what is meant by "the dynamics are forced" on page 7, line 47.

comments.issue: The expression for P-dot in Eq (6) is also incorrect.
comments.request: Correct Eq (6).
comments.quote: For similar reasons to the error I outlined previously, the expression for P-dot in Eq. (6) is incorrect.

comments.issue: The term Lipschitzian is used without definition.
comments.request: Define Lipschitzian.
comments.quote: Please define Lipschitzian.

comments.issue: Qualifiers such as 'for all species i' are missing in some equations and could be misread.
comments.request: Include the qualifiers in all equation instances.
comments.quote: it would seem prudent to include these in all instances (e.g., Eqs. 11 or 14) lest their omission be interpreted incorrectly

comments.issue: The section ends without prescriptive guidance on choosing among the equivalent scale-invariance tests.
comments.request: Provide prescriptive guidance based on the 26 models analysed.
comments.quote: Surely they can provide some prescriptive guidance to the reader in this regard based on their own learned experience analysing 26 different models?

comments.issue: Scale invariance may hold for some network structures but not others, so it may be context dependent rather than a pure model property.
comments.request: Discuss whether scale invariance depends on the network structure and what to recommend.
comments.quote: A population dynamics model may not be scale invariant in general but may be for some underlying network structures to which it is applied?

comments.issue: Many x's in Eq (18) are missing the tilde.
comments.request: Add the missing tildes in Eq (18).
comments.quote: Shouldn't all x's in Eq. (18) be adorned with "~"? Many appear to be missing this.

comments.issue: The discrete-time models section appears out of place and is relegated to an appendix.
comments.request: Move it immediately after the continuous-time criteria, ideally into the main text.
comments.quote: The mention of application to discrete-time models seems very out of place (page 14, line 29). Shouldn't it appear immediately after the criteria for continuous-time models are introduced?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether rebranding scale invariance as 'addability' has any benefit.
comments.request: Justify the new term or keep scale invariance.
comments.quote: Is there an obvious benefit to rebranding scale invariance as "addability"?

comments.issue: The non-normalized and normalized systems sections are redundant and their condition order should mirror the non-adaptive case.
comments.request: Streamline the two sections and align the order of conditions.
comments.quote: The sections about non-normalized and normalized systems are extremely redundant. Surely this can be better streamlined to save space for more relevant main text material.

comments.issue: f_ij is missing the tilde on page 16, line 42 and page 18, line 52.
comments.request: Add the missing tildes to f_ij.
comments.quote: Shouldn't f_ij be adorned with "~" on page 16, line 42 and page 18, line 52?

comments.issue: The paragraph about model transients is off topic and could be cut.
comments.request: Cut the model transients paragraph.
comments.quote: it struck me that the paragraph about model transients could be cut to make room for more relevant material as it veers rather off topic

comments.issue: The statement 'We found a scale-invariant version...' is ambiguous for a Method others should adopt.
comments.request: Make the statement more specific.
comments.quote: is very ambiguous, particularly for something being described as a Method others could adopt

comments.issue: Mentioning the 'more complex models' is not useful because nothing is done with them.
comments.request: Remove the mention or do something with those models.
comments.quote: Since nothing is done here with the "more complex models", it doesn't seem very useful to mention here that they exist.

reviews.assessment: Disagrees that non-scale-invariant models yield artifacts, but finds the testing procedure novel and worth reframing.
strengths: raises an overlooked question in BEF literature
points out model features relevant for interpreting BEF results
extends the procedure to a large number of models

comments.issue: Manuscript formatting and line numbering made reviewing more complicated.
comments.request: Pay more attention to manuscript formatting when submitting.
comments.quote: I would ask the authors to pay a little more attention to the formatting of their manuscript when submitting

comments.issue: The question is not presented as such; the paper asserts that only BEF relationships depending on functional diversity are valid, which the reviewer disputes.
comments.request: Present the question neutrally and reconsider this assertion.
comments.quote: the authors consider that only BEF relationships that depend on functional diversity are valid. I disagree with this assertion.

comments.issue: Dismissing non-scale-invariant models as artifacts ignores ecological redundancy and the role of diversity per se.
comments.request: Acknowledge that BEF depends on both functional diversity and diversity per se and revise the artifact claims.
comments.quote: It is thus presumptuous to affirm that the results of the models that are not scale invariant are "artifacts" (p4, l. 42) and should be "discarded"

comments.issue: Models without interspecific competition may legitimately fail scale invariance because biology, not theoretical convenience, should drive assumptions.
comments.request: Reconsider whether scale invariance should override biologically realistic assumptions.
comments.quote: I am convinced that it is the biology that should govern the modelling assumptions, rather than the desired theoretical properties imposing the biology of the system

comments.issue: The testing procedure and its implications need to be reframed to interest the BEF field, requiring major rewriting of the introduction and discussion.
comments.request: Reframe how the test and its implications are presented and rewrite the introduction and discussion.
comments.quote: This would imply a change of paradigm in the way the test is presented, significant rewriting of the introduction, and more importantly of the discussion section.

comments.issue: The assumptions used to grow networks when duplicating species are not documented per model, making the literature analysis non-transparent.
comments.request: State the assumptions and equations used to add species for each model.
comments.quote: These assumptions should be clearly stated somewhere (in an appendix for instance that could give, for each model investigated, the equation used to "artificially" add a species, at least when there is ambiguity).

comments.issue: Qualitative differences between original and scale-invariant models are mentioned but never specified.
comments.request: Explicitly describe the qualitative differences and refer to Appendix 3.
comments.quote: here in the discussion or in Appendix 3, the authors should explicit the qualitative differences they are talking about

comments.issue: The equality between epsilons is missing from the functional equivalence definition.
comments.request: Add the epsilon equality to the definition.
comments.quote: Page 7 line 27: the equality between epsilons is missing

comments.issue: Splitting a species in a system without interspecific competition changes the biology by reducing intra-competition.
comments.request: Reframe Eq (5) as a formal proof that splitting changes the biology.
comments.quote: I suggest to directly say that "artificially" splitting one species in such a system corresponds biologically to reducing the intra-competition in P1+P2

comments.issue: The alphas should be retained in Eq (5) for comparison with Eq (1).
comments.request: Leave the alphas in Eq (5) for comparison.
comments.quote: I think it is better to leave the alphas for comparison purpose with equation (1)

comments.issue: The reduction from (2)(3)(4) to (5) assumes P1=P2 at equilibrium, which is not stated.
comments.request: Make the equilibrium assumption explicit.
comments.quote: the reduction from (2)(3)(4) to (5) relies on P1=P2 at equilibrium. It should be made explicit.

comments.issue: 5 line-level copy edits: word substitutions, plus 'x̃0 y x̃1' to 'x0 and x1' and 'such is the case' to 'for'.
comments.quote: P23 line 19 "a more involved scale-invariance test"  evolved

comments.issue: The definition of adding a species to a network is not clear.
comments.request: Reformulate the definition.
comments.quote: already in the network." Not clear, needs reformulation

comments.issue: The definition of sum-dependence is unclear because relationship (11) displays no xi.
comments.request: Clarify the sum-dependence definition.
comments.quote: Not clear for me as relationship (11) does not display any xi.

comments.issue: The xi on the right side of Eq (18) is missing a tilde.
comments.request: Add the tilde in Eq (18).
comments.quote: Equation (18), 3rd relationship: the xi on the right side should have a ~ on top

comments.issue: The non-normalized and normalized addability sections are redundant and should be merged.
comments.request: Merge the two addability sections.
comments.quote: These two sections should be merged into one section as the only difference is the "reasonable rule" you propose for preserving the normalization when "artificially" splitting a species in two.

comments.issue: The discussion changes ideas without starting new paragraphs, making it hard to follow.
comments.request: Start new paragraphs when the idea changes.
comments.quote: The discussion is hard to follow mainly because you sometimes change the idea without starting a new paragraph

comments.issue: Disagrees that evaluating BEF relationships through mathematical models introduces artifacts.

comments.issue: Supp Fig 1: the X-axis 'value' and its common scale across six variables are unclear, including negative values.
comments.request: Explain the axis and scaling.
comments.quote: What is the “value” on X-axis? How could these 6 variables come to a common scale (and how would they have negative values, e.g. percentage of uniques< 0)?

reviews.assessment: Clear, logical and useful, but the compilation is abstract, not connected to organism biology, and several analytical choices need clarification.

comments.issue: Results are useful but the compilation is abstract and yields little insight into organism ecology.
comments.request: Connect results more to organism biology.
comments.quote: In terms of the significance of the results, I think researchers in this field will find these results useful, though I do not feel that I have learned much about the ecology of the organisms from the results.

comments.issue: Handling of missing data is unclear: whether pairwise distances use different trait sets per species pair.
comments.request: Clarify how Gower's distance treats missing values.
comments.quote: The handling of missing data is not clearly explained. The authors state on line 203 that Gower’s distance is less sensitive to missing data than other methods.

comments.issue: Variance explained by PCoA axes is not reported; how many axes explain 50% of variation is not asked.
comments.request: Report variance explained by the PCoA axes.
comments.quote: I don’t understand why the authors have not also presented information on the variance explained by the PCoA axes.

comments.issue: Theoretical basis of the AUC elbow method is not described and the elbow position may be noisy.
comments.request: Describe the basis and robustness of the elbow method.
comments.quote: Can the authors briefly describe the theoretical basis for this method? I have seen it used before, but it has always seemed a bit arbitrary and potentially noisy (i.e., the position of the elbow may not be very robust).

comments.issue: No null model comparison for the dimensionality results.
comments.request: Compare with a null model of random uncorrelated traits.
comments.quote: It would be very helpful to compare the results on the compiled datasets to some kind of null model.

title: The dimensionality and structure of species trait spaces

study.system: Pieris napi butterfly; lab and field cage development, microclimate data

editor_summary: Editor encourages resubmission but stresses three concerns: the temperature ranges used to fit versus predict, the validity of the degree-day contrast, and whether the result only shows TPCs beat degree-days.

reviews.assessment: Calls the study a simple but strong demonstration that will spark debate; requests clarifications and one sensitivity analysis.
strengths: nice thermal performance curves for Pieris napi

comments.issue: The TPC lacks data between Topt and CTmax, so high-temperature predictions rely on extrapolation that should be acknowledged.
comments.request: Acknowledge the extrapolation in the paper.
comments.quote: it is incomplete with points lacking on the right-side of the curve (between Topt and the said CTmax). The choice of the nonlinear function is therefore critical

comments.issue: The consequences of the extrapolated TPC shape for the Jensen inequality are untested.
comments.request: Add a sensitivity analysis on the position of Tmax.
comments.quote: perhaps an additional sensitivity analysis on the position of Tmax may reinforce the conclusion by showing that this does not matter directly

comments.issue: Mortality rates in the different cages are not reported.
comments.request: Report mortality rates per cage, possibly in the supplement.
comments.quote: the paper should also report more details on mortality rates in the different cages (probably can go in the supplemental materials)

comments.issue: The different microhabitats are not described in enough detail.
comments.request: Describe the microhabitats more thoroughly in the supplement.
comments.quote: I wish the different microhabitats were more thoroughly described in the supplemental material for example so I can understand why these thermal environments differed that much

comments.issue: Logger temperatures may reflect sun-exposed logger body temperature rather than air temperature inside cages.
comments.request: Assess and discuss what the loggers actually measured.
comments.quote: I fear that these temperatures correspond to the 'body' temperature of the logger when exposed to the sun (although the net may have blocked some radiations), and therefore do not represent the air temperature inside the cage.

comments.issue: Processes other than the Jensen inequality (acclimation, carry-over, covariation) that could cause deviations are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss processes unrelated to Jensen's inequality in the discussion.
comments.quote: discuss more on which processes unrelated to the Jensen inequality are responsible for potential deviations between constant and fluctuating regimes (acclimation, carry over effects, covariance of temperature and nutrition or other multifactorial processes etc.)

comments.issue: The meaning of 'per se' and 'inherent' is unclear in the key paragraph.
comments.request: Rephrase, for example as eco-physiological effects.
comments.quote: even after reading 4-5 times this paragraph, I was unsure about the meaning of "per se" and "inherent"

comments.issue: The line 44 statement does not specify what is modelled or predicted.
comments.request: Be more precise about what is modelled and predicted.
comments.quote: Line 44: need to be more precise: model of what and predictions of what? One can argue that many empirical studies have compared trait response to constant vs fluctuating thermal regimes.

comments.issue: The temperature of the ambient condition (likely 15C) is not reported; it is the egg acclimation temperature.
comments.request: Provide the ambient temperature of this condition.
comments.quote: Line 158: important to provide the temperature of this ambient condition (I suspect 15C?): this is the acclimation temperature of the eggs with possible consequences for interpreting the results for larvae.

comments.issue: The claim that generalism increases with multi-year data requires overlap among years for treatments.
comments.request: Remove or qualify this sentence.
comments.quote: generalism increases with data from multiple years, but only if there is at least partial overlap among year for certain temperature treatments, no? This sentence can probably be omitted.

comments.issue: The portion of individuals still larvae at the ending date is not reported.
comments.request: Report what portion of the sampling this concerns.
comments.quote: Line 209: what portion of individuals were still larvae at that ending date? Provide the info so the reader can realize what portion of the sampling is concerned.

comments.issue: The horizontal cutoff above 30C in the degree-day model is unexplained and atypical for such models.
comments.request: Explain and justify the cutoff choice.
comments.quote: Line 221: At this point of the paper, it is not clear why this horizontal cutoff? this is never done in typical degree day models

comments.issue: The choice of the uncommon Ratkowsky function is not argued in the main text.
comments.request: Argue the choice of nonlinear function in the main text.
comments.quote: Line 223: Given the questions related to the shape of the non linear regression of the TPC, I think that this choice of the Ratkowsky function (not so common) should be argued more carefully in the main text.

comments.issue: The main text is confusing about how published data were collected and how models were built from them.
comments.request: Clarify the published-data methodology in the main text.
comments.quote: Line 273: the main text is indeed confusing on the methodology used to collect published data, while the supplemental material is very detailed

reviews.assessment: A nice, convincing set of experiments and analyses; asks for more discussion of high-temperature effects and minor clarifications.
strengths: combines lab, field transplants and published data

comments.issue: The abstract's last line can be misread as saying temperature changes do not affect performance.
comments.request: Rephrase to refer to effects of fluctuations independent of direct temperature effects.
comments.quote: I understand what you’re trying to say, but this phrasing could be misinterpreted to mean ‘changes in temperature don’t result in changes in performance rate.’

comments.issue: High-temperature effects are poorly understood: short exposures may have delayed consequences and field temperatures exceed the fitted TPC range.
comments.request: Discuss what is known about Topt, CTmax and upper lethal temperatures in Pieris.
comments.quote: these highest temperatures are where the duration of exposure is likeliest to have the largest effects; i.e., maybe individuals can survive 36 C+ no problem if exposures are only a few hours but cannot survive them over the long term

comments.issue: The phrase 'external temperatures' is conceptually wrong; body temperature drives rate processes.
comments.request: Use internal or body temperature terminology.
comments.quote: It’s not ‘external temperature’ that drives rates processes in organisms but rather internal (or body) temperature.

comments.issue: It is unclear how the authors knew field-collected females were not previously mated.
comments.request: Explain how female mating status was ensured.
comments.quote: Line 177, how do you know that the field-collected females weren’t previously mated?

comments.issue: Details of the temperature loggers (lead type, internal sensors, sun heating) are missing.
comments.request: Describe the loggers and how closely they measure cage air temperature.
comments.quote: need a few more details about the temperature data loggers – did they have separate leads and what were they? (thermocouples, thermistors?) Or are they internal?

comments.issue: It is unclear what watering a plant 'continuously' means and what 'synchronous pupation' refers to.
comments.request: Clarify these methodological descriptions.
comments.quote: Line 204 I don’t understand what it means to water a plant ‘continuously.’ And ‘synchronous pupation’?

comments.issue: Several line-level copy edits (split infinitive, odd phrase, verb agreement, stray punctuation).
comments.quote: Line 88 ‘methodological scrutiny’ is an odd phrase.

reviews.assessment: Finds the main argument neither novel nor surprising and identifies conceptual errors and an invalid linear-model comparison.

comments.issue: The claim that linear degree-day models are used extensively is incorrect and the TPC literature is poorly described.
comments.request: Correct the literature description and discuss relevant work such as Dowd et al. 2015.
comments.quote: the description of the TPC literature in general, and its impact on fluctuating temperatures in particular, is extremely poor and neglects some crucial discussions on the subject

comments.issue: The 'linear model' is unrealistic and cannot be a decent comparison baseline for the nonlinear model.
comments.request: Use a biologically realistic comparison model.
comments.quote: The so-called ‘linear model’ (a function cannot possibly be linear if it includes thresholds) is unrealistic and does not provide a minimally decent standard of comparison, so it is not surprising that the non-linear model performs better.

comments.issue: The linear model predicts performance outside the empirical range under incorrect assumptions.
comments.request: Avoid or justify predictions outside the empirical temperature range.
comments.quote: for the linear model the authors predict performance at temperatures outside the empirical range and rely in assumptions that are simply incorrect

comments.issue: Showing that a model with collapsing performance beats one with stable performance is trivial because TPCs have included this for decades.
comments.request: Clarify what is genuinely new in this comparison.
comments.quote: A drop in performance is an explicit component of TPCs, which have been proposed over three decades ago, so what exactly is new?

comments.issue: The simulated-versus-real data comparison is not surprising given the typical shape of developmental-rate TPCs.
comments.request: Clarify the novelty of the simulated data comparison.
comments.quote: I fail to see what is new in the comparison between simulated and real data in the last figure

comments.issue: Developmental rates are analysed over whole ontogeny for day-degree models but split into eggs and larvae for nonlinear models.
comments.request: Explain or align the data used for the competing models.
comments.quote: it is unclear why the authors decide to analyze developmental rates throughout the whole ontogeny for the day degree analyses and separate into eggs and larvae for the non-linear models

comments.issue: The abstract conclusion is counterintuitive and seems to claim fluctuations do not influence development.
comments.request: Rewrite the conclusion to avoid this implication.
comments.quote: This conclusion is counterintuitive considering the whole rationale described in the Abstract (or the title of the study), and seem to imply that the authors ultimately argue that temperature fluctuations do not inherently influence insect developmental rates.

comments.issue: Rezende et al. 2020 demonstrates the paper's claim but is only cited at the end.
comments.request: Discuss Rezende et al. 2020 in the Introduction.
comments.quote: it clearly demonstrates that ‘models parameterized under constant temperatures [can] yield correct predictions when applied to naturally variable conditions’ and should be appropriately discussed in the Introduction

comments.issue: Line 46 phrasing is awkward; mechanisms are made the subject that cannot differentiate.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence.
comments.quote: Line 46: Awkward phrasing, mechanisms cannot differentiate anything (i.e., ‘mechanisms’ is the subject of this sentence).

comments.issue: The statement that linear models are used extensively and that degree days assume linearity is generic, incorrect and unreferenced.
comments.request: Provide references and correct the statements about degree-day models.
comments.quote: This is a generic and uninformative statement, not to mention that it is incorrect depending on how degree days are defined.

comments.issue: The statement implies parts of the TPC are linear, which is conceptually incorrect.
comments.request: Correct the statement about linear regions of the TPC.
comments.quote: Line 62: This statement implies that some parts of the TPC are linear, which is incorrect.

comments.issue: Maintenance conditions are confounded with measurement conditions, pooling acute and acclimation responses.
comments.request: Distinguish maintenance from measurement conditions and discuss the consequences.
comments.quote: the authors here confound ‘maintenance conditions’ with ‘measurement conditions’, which are not necessarily the same thing

comments.issue: It is unclear which 'linear region' of the TPC is being referred to.
comments.request: Define or avoid the 'linear region' terminology.
comments.quote: Lines 75 – 77: Again, not really sure what ‘linear region’ of the TPC the authors are talking about.

comments.issue: The assertion that prediction improves when x is known more accurately is trivial.
comments.request: Remove or reframe this trivial assertion.
comments.quote: This is a trivial assertion, essentially the authors are arguing that f(x) can be estimated more accurately when x is known more accurately.

comments.issue: It is unclear how 'care was taken to minimize between-year variation'.
comments.request: Explain how between-year variation was minimized.
comments.quote: Line 226: ‘Care was taken to minimize between-year variation’. How?

comments.issue: It is unclear why the typical TPC is separated into two different regions in Figure 1.
comments.request: Justify or revise the two-region depiction.
comments.quote: First, it is not clear why the authors separate the typical TPC into two different regions.

comments.issue: The Fig. 1 caption's overestimation/underestimation claim is wrong because the authors interpolate rather than average.
comments.request: Correct the convex/concave statement in the caption.
comments.quote: is incorrect because the authors are not averaging anything (instead, they are interpolating performance at the mean temperature, which is not the same as averaging extreme values of a nonlinear response)

comments.issue: The Jensen inequality illustration is not novel; an adequate treatment already exists in Dowd et al. (2015).
comments.request: Cite and build on Dowd et al. (2015) instead of repeating it.
comments.quote: Third, this is not novel: an appropriate description of this problem with adequate TPC and sound mathematics is already provided in Fig. 3 of Dowd et al. (2015).

comments.issue: It is unclear how the fitted nonlinear model drops to zero near 35C without empirical data; the model may force it.
comments.request: Explain whether developmental rate was set to zero at 35C and on what basis.
comments.quote: In Fig. 2b it is unclear how the fitted non-linear model drops to zero around 35 ºC in the absence of empirical data. Did the authors include developmental rates = 0 at 35º C?

title: Thermal performance under constant temperatures can accurately predict insect development times across naturally variable microclimates

study.system: consumer–resource models; thermal dependence of biological rates

editor_summary: All three reviewers found the study interesting and novel; many points concern the models, parameters and application to real-world data, and a revision is expected.

reviews.assessment: Covers past work well and finds some results exciting, but the sensitivity analysis assumptions, the interpretation of aggregate parameters and the constant-temperature scope raise concerns.

comments.issue: Sensitivity analysis assumes varied parameters are independent, but biological traits are strongly correlated.
comments.request: Justify or account for correlations among biological parameters.
comments.quote: This analysis assume that the parameters that are being varied are independent of one another. Yet we know that there are strong correlation among these biological traits

comments.issue: Sensitivity results may be trivial: everything matters except r, which is absent from the expressions, and epsilon, assumed temperature-independent.
comments.request: Clarify what the sensitivity analysis adds beyond obvious parameter dependence.
comments.quote: Other than than everything matters except for population growth rate, which is obvious from the fact that r does not even appear in the analytical expressions

comments.issue: Whether the aggregate-parameter analysis is separate from the sensitivity analysis, or could be folded into it, is unclear.
comments.request: Explain why the two analyses are distinct and where the line is drawn.
comments.quote: So is the aggregate parameter analysis really separate from the sensitivity analysis? Could they be folded into the same thing? If not, why not and where is the line drawn

comments.issue: The novel contribution is the phase-space trajectories of aggregate parameters, which should be the paper’s centerpiece.
comments.request: Make the phase-space trajectory analysis the centerpiece of the paper.
comments.quote: I think the author’s real contribution here is to look at the phase space of these two parameters and plot out temperature trajectories within them.

comments.issue: Aggregate parameters are presented as equal in measurability and predictability to base parameters, though they are model outputs, making mechanistic use potentially circular.
comments.request: Clarify that aggregate parameters are outcomes rather than mechanistic predictors.
comments.quote: The biological interpretation of the aggregate parameters are presented as being on the same footing—in terms of measurability and predictability—as the other parameters considered, but I don’t think this is the case.

comments.issue: Aggregate parameters are not easier to measure; they require elaborate experiments and their interpretation as mechanism is unclear.
comments.request: Temper the claim that aggregate parameters are easier to measure.
comments.quote: I also don’t see how the aggregate parameters are easier to measure. Things like population growth rate and morality rate can be measure in isolation in the lab.

comments.issue: Conversion efficiency is assumed temperature-independent although data suggest weak temperature dependence.
comments.request: Consider weak temperature dependence of conversion efficiency and cite the data.
comments.quote: I know it is often assumed that conversion efficiency does not vary with temperature, but I have seen data in talks that challenges this idea. Might be worth considering some weak temperature dependence here.

comments.issue: A single temperature response for attack rate may be wrong; it is unspecified whether temperature refers to consumer, resource, or both.
comments.request: Specify whose temperature is used and consider asymmetric responses and foraging strategy.
comments.quote: This paper seems to consider environmental temperature but never explains if that is assumed to be the temperature of the consumer or the resource or both.

comments.issue: Using dy/d ln(x) alongside the standard elasticity is nonstandard and unjustified.
comments.request: Justify the choice of dy/d ln(x) as a sensitivity measure.
comments.quote: In doing the sensitivity analysis, the authors consider d ln(y)/d ln(x), which is the standard definition of elasticity, and also consider dy/ d ln(x), which is nonstandard.

comments.issue: Colored regions in figures lack biological interpretation and the inequality lists are hard to parse.
comments.request: Add biological interpretations of the regions to the figure captions.
comments.quote: In the figures, biological interpretations for the colored regions should be provided. I see the long list of inequalities in the key, but that is a lot to parse

comments.issue: All results concern constant temperatures; variable temperature regimes in the field are not addressed.
comments.request: Investigate variable temperatures or acknowledge and discuss this limitation.
comments.quote: although I understand if it’s beyond the scope of this paper, the results all seem to be for constant temperatures. In the field, almost always the species will be experiencing variable temperature

reviews.assessment: Liked the manuscript and found no methodological issues; suggestions concern the form, discussion of the aggregate parameters and how to estimate them.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether changes in resource growth rate r affect system behaviour, since the aggregate parameters and stability criteria omit r.
comments.request: Clarify the role of resource growth rate when describing the aggregate parameters.
comments.quote: The aggregate parameters p and k, as well as the stability criteria, are, in their formulation, independent of the resource growth rate (r).

comments.issue: The rationale for choosing k and the formula at L246 is not explained.
comments.request: Explain what led to these two metrics and the formula.
comments.quote: It is unclear how you chose your aggregate parameters. The choice of p is somehow explained L254-260, but things are less clear for k.

comments.issue: The discussion lacks pros and cons of aggregate versus model parameters, which differ in their ability to handle complex food webs.
comments.request: Add a short discussion of the pros and cons of aggregate parameters.
comments.quote: model parameters allow tackling the response of complex food webs to warming, which seems to be not possible with the aggregate parameters presented

comments.issue: How the aggregate parameters p and k can be estimated is not discussed, despite sensitivity to the parametrization.
comments.request: Discuss how p and k can be estimated.
comments.quote: I think it would be beneficial to discuss somewhere how can p and k be estimated

comments.issue: The manuscript could be shortened; the key message is sometimes lost.
comments.request: Consider shortening the manuscript to keep the key message clear.
comments.quote: Even though the manuscript is well written, I believe it could be shortened a bit. Sometimes the key message is a bit lost.

comments.issue: Figures 4 and 7 could be moved to SI to simplify the results section.
comments.request: Move figures 4 and 7 to SI and discuss them in the discussion.
comments.quote: Maybe move fig. 4 and 7 to SI? I understand that they are important as they present the “real world” parameters, but they are more an illustration of the main message.

comments.issue: Equations 3–7 are derivation steps, not part of the final framework, and could be moved to SI.
comments.request: Move equations 3 to 7 to SI.
comments.quote: equations 3 to 7 are essential to understand the derivation of k and p. However, they are not part of the final framework. Maybe it is possible to move that to SI as well?

comments.issue: Section L692-712 should be merged with the Conclusions.
comments.request: Merge L692-712 with the Conclusions.
comments.quote: - L692-712: Should be merged with the Conclusions

comments.issue: The discussion does not remind readers of the results supporting each prediction.
comments.request: Add a short reminder of corresponding results for each prediction.
comments.quote: In the discussion, it would help the reader if, for each prediction, you could make a short reminder of the corresponding results.

comments.issue: Derivations of eq. 8 and the expressions in table 1 are not shown.
comments.request: Show the derivations of eq. 8 and Table 1 expressions.
comments.quote: How did you derive eq. 8? I can’t see any demonstration/explanation for it. Similarly, how did you found expressions presented in table 1?

comments.issue: Two line-level copy edits: double period after “findings” (L134) and a missing space in SI3.
comments.quote: SI3: ‘Thus, S=0at the Hopf’ => a space is missing between 0 and at

comments.issue: The term “dominant eigenvalue” is used without a clear referent.
comments.request: Replace or clarify the term “dominant eigenvalue”.
comments.quote: L146: I’d avoid using the term “dominant eigenvalue” here, as what it refers to is unclear.

comments.issue: The statement at L617 may hold only for the unimodal parametrization.
comments.request: Clarify the scope of the statement at L617.
comments.quote: L617: Only for the unimodal parametrization, right?

comments.issue: Figure captions do not state what the black line represents.
comments.request: State explicitly in the caption what the black line is.
comments.quote: Figures: state more explicitly in the caption what the black line is

reviews.assessment: Very high quality, well written and exhaustively described; supportive of the framework, with minor suggestions on generality, functional responses, figures and measurement claims.
strengths: exhaustively described results and theoretical analyses
fulfills the promise of its title

comments.issue: Prediction #3 depends on functional response type and temperature dependencies; a consumer with a broader thermal range could be stabilized by warming.
comments.request: Discuss how general prediction #3 is across functional responses and thermal ranges.
comments.quote: I think that such prediction strongly depends on model assumptions on functional response type (see my next comment) and on temperature dependencies of parameters.

comments.issue: Consumer extinction through high-amplitude limit cycles is not incorporated into the framework.
comments.request: Consider incorporating a biomass-density extinction threshold into the framework.
comments.quote: I believe many studies set a certain biomass density limit below which a species is considered extinct, even if mathematically its densities are strictly > 0.

comments.issue: Type III functional responses could drastically change the stability predictions.
comments.request: Mention that type III responses may change stability predictions.
comments.quote: It might be worth mentioning, as a type III response has a potential to drastically change model predictions on stability vs. warming.

comments.issue: The stated direction of the metabolic-versus-ingestion rate effect at lines 105-106 is reversed.
comments.request: Correct the direction of the metabolic-versus-ingestion rate effect.
comments.quote: I think it should be the opposite - warming would destabilize a system if metabolic rate increases SLOWER than ingestion rate with warming.

comments.issue: The shapes of monotonic and unimodal parameterizations are not stated explicitly.
comments.request: State explicitly which parameters are increasing, decreasing, hump- or U-shaped.
comments.quote: I think it would be a good idea to write explicitly, for monotonic parameters, which ones are monotonically increasing (e.g. m) and which ones decreasing (e.g., K)

comments.issue: The claim that aggregate parameters are easier to measure than model parameters is questionable.
comments.request: Be more careful and note that advantages depend on the empirical system.
comments.quote: I am not fully convinced that empiricists would agree that measuring these two compound parameters does indeed make their life easier.

comments.issue: Figures may be hard to read if resolution and label visibility are poor.
comments.request: Ensure high-resolution figures with well-visible labels.
comments.quote: make sure that your figures are of high resolution, and all labels are well visible

comments.issue: The symbols CT and Topt in Fig. 1 are not defined in the text.
comments.request: Define CT and Topt in Fig. 1.
comments.quote: in Fig. 1 you use symbols such as CT and Topt. Thermal ecologists probably know what it means, but as these terms are not defined elsewhere in the text

title: Theory of temperature‐dependent consumer–resource interactions

study.system: island plants; drift simulation compared with empirical size data

editor_summary: Editor argues the pattern is regression to the mean, says the model includes selection and is too simple, and asks the authors to reframe it properly as a null model.

reviews.assessment: Supports the study and notes most concerns addressed, but wants clearer drift framing and better presentation of the new model.
strengths: interesting contribution to island biogeography and Ecology Letters
addressed most of the previous concerns

comments.issue: The introduction still does not explain evolutionary drift or why it would differ between mainland and islands.
comments.request: Add a paragraph on drift and explain why the mainland is not expected to show the same pattern.
comments.quote: it still does not introduce evolutionary drift and why this would lead to differences among mainland and islands

comments.issue: Trait boundaries imply selection; the no-selection assumption cannot stand and the origin of boundaries needs discussion.
comments.request: Reframe the fifth assumption as boundaries being under selection and discuss boundary origins.
comments.quote: I think your fifth assumption of your models should actually not be that “insular size changes are not under natural selection” but something like “insular size changes are not under natural selection within given boundaries but these boundaries are under selection”.

comments.issue: The body-size range of the mainland species and how a step of 1 relates to actual body sizes are unclear, biasing toward boundary effects.
comments.request: Explain the parameter ranges and step size relative to real body sizes.
comments.quote: What is the range of values for the body sizes of the 100 related species on the mainland within which the island species can drift?

comments.issue: It is untested what happens if species may exceed the boundaries of their relatives.
comments.request: Run the model allowing species to exceed the boundary to some degree.
comments.quote: what would the results look like if you would allow the species to exceed the boundaries of their 100 relatives to a certain degree?

comments.issue: The generation-based model results are not prominently related to the simpler model, with quantitative comparisons and a Figure 1c-style plot missing.
comments.request: Present the new-model results prominently and give quantitative comparisons.
comments.quote: Mention how the results from the new model (simulated over generations) relate to the results of the simpler model more prominently in the results and discussion texts.

comments.issue: The new model results are not compared with the empirical data.
comments.request: Show the comparison to empirical data for the new model in a supplement.
comments.quote: It would also be consequent if you would show the comparisons of the model results to the empirical data for the new model (in a supplementary file).

comments.issue: The abstract wording is too definite about the island rule resulting from drift.
comments.request: Use less definite wording such as “might result from evolutionary drift”.
comments.quote: Line5: I also think wording should be less definite here: “Here we show that the island rule in plants might result from evolutionary drift”

comments.issue: It is unclear whether “it” refers to evolutionary drift or the island rule.
comments.request: Clarify the referent of “it”.
comments.quote: Line 12: It is not really clear what “it” refers to in this sentence: evolutionary drift or the island rule?

comments.issue: A suggested wording change to “may arise passively”.
comments.request: Reword accordingly.
comments.quote: Line 46: “may arise passively”

comments.issue: Comments on line 52 of the previous manuscript appear not to have been addressed.
comments.request: Explain what happened to these comments.
comments.quote: Line 72: My 2 comments to Line 52 of the previous manuscript have supposedly been addressed but I can’t find any new information. What happened here?

comments.issue: Tidyverse package citations are unnecessary.
comments.request: Cite only the stats packages.
comments.quote: 128-131 I am not sure you need to cite the tidyverse packages here. It is nice that they were used but it doesn’t really matter. I would only cite the stats packages.

comments.issue: The existing hypotheses about relaxed selection on islands are not used to explain why drift should dominate there.
comments.request: Use this line of argumentation, including secondary woodiness hypotheses.
comments.quote: I think you could use this line of argumentation to better explain how drift should become more important than selection on islands and how this might lead to the island rule pattern.

comments.issue: References are missing for the claims about fleshy fruits and wind-dispersed forbs.
comments.request: Add references for these ideas.
comments.quote: 244-247. Give references for the ideas that fleshy fruits are more common in woody species and that forbs are more often wind dispersed

reviews.assessment: Finds the empirical patterns fascinating but struggled with the models and wants code scrutiny, stronger framing and more cautious causal claims.
strengths: empirical patterns are fascinating and worthy of publication
paper would merit space in a top journal if the findings are robust to scrutiny

comments.issue: The simulation code has not been reviewed by someone with coding expertise.
comments.request: Have an expert review how the code works before any acceptance decision.
comments.quote: I think it important that someone who does have appropriate expertise reviews how the code is working on behalf of the journal prior to a decision on acceptance

comments.issue: The abstract claims the island rule results from drift, but generating a consistent pattern does not demonstrate that empirical patterns are caused by drift.
comments.request: Make more cautious statements about causation.
comments.quote: You may show that you can generate patterns consistent with the island rule from a model based on drift but that is not a demonstration that the empirical patterns reported on by previous authors is shown to be a product of drift.

comments.issue: “The island rule” is a misnomer originating from vertebrate ecology.
comments.request: Use a more accurate name such as “island vertebrate body size rule” and be wary of extending mechanisms to plants.
comments.quote: A better name would be the ‘island vertebrate body size rule.’

comments.issue: Plant size shifts may be phenotypic plasticity rather than genetically controlled evolution.
comments.request: Assess how many cases have data distinguishing genetic from phenotypic change.
comments.quote: In how many of the cases in your data set have we got the data (e.g. reciprocal transplant experiments or similar) to determine that this is genetically controlled rather than merely phenotypic?

comments.issue: Framing a single hypothesis as the goal is a straw man; Lomolino et al. argue for a body of theory.
comments.request: Revisit and reframe the introduction's hypotheses and fix the Lomolino reference.
comments.quote: In my view the notion of a single hypothesis “to explain the diverse range of size changes observed in island life” is a straw man.

comments.issue: The claim that mid-domain richness peaks arise passively is disputed; gaps in species ranges and coarse grids undermine it.
comments.request: Qualify the mid-domain effect claims instead of stating them unequivocally.
comments.quote: I don’t actually agree with this claim. The mid-domain effect arises in simulations that assume species ranges must be coherent, without gaps in the range.

comments.issue: The contentious history of Diamond's assembly-rule null models is instructive and not acknowledged.
comments.request: Soften unequivocal statements to avoid opening the paper to criticism.
comments.quote: This is I think instructive. By constructing your arguments and statements in rather unequivocal terms, you open yourselves to criticism.

comments.issue: Asking whether drift generates the island rule seeks too much certainty about causation from a simulation.
comments.request: Rephrase the question as whether the pattern might arise from drift.
comments.quote: If the rule is an empirical pattern (as you claim) then can you prove the causation of that pattern by means of a specific simulation model? I would say not.

comments.issue: The second research question is oddly phrased and largely duplicates the first.
comments.request: Rewrite the second question so it is distinct from the first.
comments.quote: Your second question is very oddly phrased. If drift does not occur (the final five words of your second question) then by definition it cannot explain anything.

comments.issue: The research questions need more careful crafting overall.
comments.request: Put more work into crafting the questions.
comments.quote: Overall, I think more work is needed in crafting the questions.

comments.issue: The bounded-domain simulation inevitably converges on intermediate size and remains an inappropriate null model.
comments.request: Address how the model escapes the bounded-domain critique.
comments.quote: The reviewers first time around argued that your bounded domain simulation was inevitably going to generate convergence on intermediate body size and was thus not so much evidence of drift as a function of an inappropriate null model.

comments.issue: It is unclear why insular conditions should produce drift when the source pool population is also drifting.
comments.request: Explain what is different about insular conditions relative to the source pool.
comments.quote: what is it about the insular conditions that is different from the conditions in the source pool population?

comments.issue: Simultaneous immigration of all species is unrealistic and richness constraints are unclear.
comments.request: Justify or revise the immigration assumption and richness limits.
comments.quote: The first is simultaneous immigration of all species to the island. Presumably the richness per island must be constrained in some way? Otherwise you would simply load up the island with the entire flora of the source pool.

comments.issue: Drift should apply equally to mainland species, yet the model only lets the island flora drift.
comments.request: Explain why only the island flora experiences drift.
comments.quote: So why does the island flora experience drift in body size but the mainland flora doesn’t?

comments.issue: The model assumes the mainland trait distribution is static, contradicting the no-selection, no-change assumptions.
comments.request: Explain how the mainland trait distribution arises and stays fixed.
comments.quote: So, how does the trait distribution get to be as it is in the mainland pool and why does it stay as it is during the period that the island flora is undergoing drift?

comments.issue: Reduced island richness could reflect increased interspecific competition after release from browsing and grazing, an alternative mechanism.
comments.request: Consider this alternative mechanism in the discussion.
comments.quote: in the absence of the usual array of browsing and grazing vertebrates, it may be that one reason for reduced plant richness values on islands is increased interspecific competition

comments.issue: The reference list contains missing initials and an Endnote artefact.
comments.request: Correct the reference list errors.
comments.quote: I happened to notice that in reference 3 you miss of the second initial from Burns. I suspect there may be other cases (ref 7 for example) in the list of missing initials.

reviews.assessment: Argues the bounded random-walk models contain strong selection and that the text wrongly presents them as pure drift.
strengths: novel and important application of the drift explanation to the island rule

comments.issue: The bounded-drift explanation is long established in the Cope's rule literature, which is not cited.
comments.request: Include Cope's rule literature and its methodological advances.
comments.quote: The novel aspect of your paper is that it introduces the explanation explicitly to the island rule. I find this very important but would suggest to include the large body of literature on Cope’s rule as well as its methodological advances into the manuscript.

comments.issue: Both simulation models force species within bounded trait domains, so the changes are not random but strongly selected.
comments.request: Correct the claims that the direction of change is entirely independent/random.
comments.quote: Both statements are wrong and also wrongly communicated in the manuscript text. Your models imply strong selection by forcing your species to remain in bounded trait domains (trait limits are caused by natural selection).

comments.issue: The manuscript must state that bounded domains imply a strong selective mechanism.
comments.request: Rewrite the text to communicate the selection implied by boundaries.
comments.quote: I do not want you to change the simulation but the manuscript text needs to clearly communicate that bounded domains imply a strong selective process/mechanism.

comments.issue: Arguing why the pattern should not hold for mammals is misplaced, since size limits are probably more relevant for animals.
comments.request: Remove lines 155-166 and 187-193.
comments.quote: I thus find those parts of the discussion were you highlight why the pattern should not hold for mammals misplaced and distracting from the main point of the manuscript.

title: A simple null model predicts the island rule
