title: The multidimensional nutritional niche of fungus‐cultivar provisioning in free‐ranging colonies of a neotropical leafcutter ant

study.system: ringed seal prey fish in Hudson Bay; bioclimatic envelope model 1950-2100

editor_summary: Reviewers were generally enthusiastic about the broad topic but raised issues; editor recommends rejection with the possibility of resubmitting a new paper addressing all comments.

reviews.assessment: Modelling approach is reasonable, but the biomass start points are unconvincing and abundance and biomass claims lack empirical support.

comments.issue: The origin of the biomass start points for Hudson Bay is glossed over, leaving their reliability unconvincing.
comments.request: Provide the missing information on where biomass start points came from.
comments.quote: Either I am missing some important information on the start points for biomass estimation pertinent to Hudson Bay or the authors have glossed over where the biomass start points came from

comments.issue: Abundance and biomass changes require much more empirical support than provided.
comments.request: Strengthen the empirical support for abundance and biomass changes.
comments.quote: changes in abundance / biomass require much more consideration, and support, of empirical data that this paper is lacking

comments.issue: The bibliography stops at #50, so most discussion citations are missing.
comments.request: Complete the reference list.
comments.quote: The citation list in the bibliography stops at #50, so most of the citations in the discussion are missing

comments.issue: The literature cited is mostly US- and Hudson Bay-focused, missing the wider ringed seal literature.
comments.request: Broaden the literature beyond Hudson Bay studies.
comments.quote: a lot of the earlier citations are US-only and Hudson Bay-only and while relevant, there is a large body of ringed seal related literature that exists outside HB

comments.issue: Optimal Foraging Theory is characterised with broad, unsupported sweeping statements.
comments.request: Correct the characterisation of optimal foraging theory.
comments.quote: there are some broad sweeping statements on Optimal Foraging Theory and what it "states"

comments.issue: The claim that species select habitat with highest population growth potential confuses species-level selection with individual habitat choice.
comments.request: Correct the statement: individuals, not species, choose habitat.
comments.quote: Species dont select habitat, individuals do, and they optimise their choice of habitat balancing between food, reproduction and predation.

comments.issue: There is no discussion of ringed seal foraging and diving ecology in relation to prey distribution, nor of harp seals and belugas.
comments.request: Add ringed seal foraging ecology and discuss other predators.
comments.quote: There appears to be no discussion on how ringed seals make a living

comments.issue: The paper is framed around ringed seal trophic ecology but lacks ecological linkages between prey and predators.
comments.request: Strengthen prey-predator ecological linkages.
comments.quote: more ecological information and linkages need to be made between prey and predators

comments.issue: Model input data, parameterisation and uncertainties are not described and justified in enough detail.
comments.request: Describe and justify model inputs, parameters and uncertainty.
comments.quote: it would also require a lot more detailed description and justification of some of the model input data, parameterisation and uncertainties

comments.issue: The choice of 1950 as the hindcasting start point is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain why 1950 was chosen as the start point.
comments.quote: why 1950 as a start point for hindcasting?

reviews.assessment: Important and well-presented topic, but the ecological mechanisms are unclear and the abstract does not do the paper justice.
strengths: important topic for understanding Arctic marine ecosystems
use of a well-studied predator to anchor the paper

comments.issue: The ecological mechanism being studied is unclear and no hypotheses are presented.
comments.request: State explicit hypotheses and the mechanisms examined.
comments.quote: What is the ecological mechanism being studied by this modeling?

comments.issue: Only two GHG scenarios are used; more IPCC scenarios could reveal relationships such as linearity of body-size decline.
comments.request: Run models under additional emission scenarios.
comments.quote: Why not run models under more than 2 scenarios (I think IPCC has 4 or 5 scenarios)?

comments.issue: Predator implications are largely speculative and not assessed by other models.
comments.request: Acknowledge that predator implications are speculative.
comments.quote: Although well written and rationalized it is largely speculative and not assessed by other models

comments.issue: The stated goal of modelling forage fish populations is inconsistent with the abstract and discussion.
comments.request: Clarify the paper's goal in the final introduction paragraph.
comments.quote: the main goal of the paper as presented in the last paragraph of the introduction is to model the changes in forage fish “populations”, which is bit inconsistent with the abstract or how the discussion is writing

comments.issue: Forage fish results are only discussed in terms of predator implications.
comments.request: Discuss the forage fish results directly, outside the predator context.
comments.quote: I also think more specific discussion about the forage fish results not in the context of what it means for the predators, would be useful and interesting.

comments.issue: The abstract reports a single set of outcomes although two emission scenarios were run.
comments.request: Clarify which scenario the outcomes refer to and report scenario differences.
comments.quote: The abstract talks of two scenarios of GHG emissions but gives a single set of outcomes

comments.issue: 'Drastic' and 'mild' scenario changes are undefined and the differences are not discussed.
comments.request: Define these terms and discuss the scenario differences.
comments.quote: were the changes under RCP 8.5 are “drastic” and RCP 2.6 are “mild” but these terms are not defined (and not specific)

comments.issue: What direct and indirect effects refer to is never explained.
comments.request: Define direct and indirect effects.
comments.quote: This is also used in the first paragraph of the discussion and abstract but never explained, what is direct and indirect referring too?

comments.issue: The abstract omits spatial distribution and species differences, and does not do the paper justice.
comments.request: Revise the abstract to reflect the spatial and species-specific results.
comments.quote: I guess what I am saying is the abstract does not do the paper justice (see comment 4) and, in some ways, I think confused me about what was done.

comments.issue: It is not mentioned that the forage fish include native and recently invaded species.
comments.request: Mention the native and invaded species.
comments.quote: Should it be mentioned that the forage fish examined include native and recently invaded species?

comments.issue: Scenario wording and the phrase 'at the bottom' need adjustment.
comments.request: Say low and high scenarios and replace 'at the bottom'.
comments.quote: Should the GHG emission scenarios say low and high? 9) Line 48: “at the bottom” is a tad confusing, maybe “under surface”?

comments.issue: 'Regime shift' is used repeatedly but never defined.
comments.request: Define regime shift in the introduction.
comments.quote: “regime shift” is used a few times in the introduction and here in the first sentence of the discussion. What does regime shift mean?

comments.issue: Terminology at line 182 should say fish prey species or consistently use forage fish; ringed seal is not mentioned there.
comments.request: Clarify the terminology in the first discussion paragraph.
comments.quote: Should probably say fish prey species, or maybe stick with “forage fish”.

comments.issue: The 'canary' statement at line 195 is too general and unspecific for this paper.
comments.request: Replace the general statement with something more specific.
comments.quote: I guess but don’t we need something more specific in this paper than a general statement

comments.issue: The paragraph at lines 199-211 is speculative and lacks specific outcomes.
comments.request: Use the sea lion example to give specific outcomes such as reproduction or offspring health.
comments.quote: is pretty speculative, although no doubt correct, but does not give anything very specific

comments.issue: 'Borealization' is not defined.
comments.request: Define borealization specifically.
comments.quote: Line 234: Should “borealization” be defined specifically?

comments.issue: Whether Arctic cod are classified as benthic is questioned.
comments.request: Check and justify the classification of Arctic cod as benthic.
comments.quote: are arctic cod benthic? Feeding around ice is important for sure but have they been classified as benthic?

title: Predicting how climate change threatens the prey base of Arctic marine predators

study.system: tidepool copepod Tigriopus californicus; ABM and selection experiment

editor_summary: Original and important topic, potentially suitable, but all three reviewers found major problems that the editor shares; also fix l.37 wording, the lambda claim (Tuljapurkar), remove 'significantly' twice, and use 'allocations'.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, well-written simulation-experiment study with revealing results, but several methods details and realism assumptions need attention.

comments.issue: 'Periodicity' may be the wrong term because the disturbances occur at stable intervals rather than as sine-like cycles.
comments.request: Reconsider the term periodicity or justify its use.
comments.quote: I believe that using the term “periodicity” to describe the processes you are measuring might not be the most appropriate

comments.issue: The index n is used both for genotypes and as a summation index, causing confusion.
comments.request: Use a separate index such as j = 1, ..., n.
comments.quote: I am a bit confused here by the use of the indices. You use n as an index, but you’ve already said that it refers to the number of genotypes.

comments.issue: The notation for the random normal draw is odd.
comments.request: State simply that values are sampled from normal distributions with the given variances.
comments.quote: your notation for the random normal draw seems a bit odd. It’s sufficient that you state that you are sampling randomly from a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 0.01 mu-bar for maturation or 0.01 f-bar for reproduction.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the assumed variability range matches observed population variability.
comments.request: Justify that the variability assumption is realistic.
comments.quote: Related to the previous point, is this the range of variability that you’ve observed in the population? In other words, is it a realistic assumption?

comments.issue: The density-dependent mortality function is missing and n is reused for population size.
comments.request: Provide the mortality function and use N_t for population size.
comments.quote: it’ll be helpful if you provide a function for the density dependent mortality, second, here you use “n” seemingly in reference to the population size at a given time

comments.issue: Randomly choosing which individuals die assumes no genotype differences in coping with density dependence.
comments.request: Clarify or justify this density-dependent mortality assumption.
comments.quote: you say that you randomly chose who dies due to density dependence, so I guess the assumption is that there are no genotypes that cope better with density dependence

comments.issue: The equation does not make N_t - D(N_t) asymptote to K, so K = 250000 may not represent carrying capacity.
comments.request: Fix or explain the density-dependent mortality equation.
comments.quote: based on the equation you provide, I don’t see how the value of K = 250000 individuals really reflects the carrying capacity

comments.issue: Equal numbers of stochastic and periodic disturbances may be unrealistic since stochasticity acts continuously.
comments.request: Simulate a more realistic scenario with higher stochastic disturbance frequency.
comments.quote: if stochastic disturbances naturally occur with much higher frequency than periodic ones, then even if individually the stochastic ones have relatively less impact, as a whole they will most likely play a much more important role than the periodic ones

comments.issue: 100 realizations may be too few for generalizing given the model's complexity.
comments.request: Justify or increase the number of realizations.
comments.quote: Are 100 realizations really enough to make generalizations? It seems like a bit too low for the complexity of what you are modelling.

comments.issue: Welch's t-test on log-transformed variances assumes normality, which was not verified.
comments.request: Verify the normality assumption for the Welch's t-test.
comments.quote: you used Welch’s t-test for the log-transformed variances, but this implies that you need to assume normality. Is that really the case? Did you verify it?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the variance going to zero in the fast scenario means one phenotype remains or all individuals died.
comments.request: Explain the cause of the zero variance in section 3.4 and Figure 5.
comments.quote: Here you show that after 150 time steps the variance in mu for the fast scenario goes to 0. Is this because only one phenotype remains, or because all individuals died?

comments.issue: The study organism has a simple life cycle, so generalization to longer-lived species with demographic buffering is unclear.
comments.request: Discuss whether results generalize to longer-lived species.
comments.quote: do you expect these results can be generalized to, say, longer lived species, where for instance there could be demographic buffering?

reviews.assessment: Interesting and relevant study with mutually supporting simulations and experiments, but the framework, unexplored density dependence and generality issues need work.
strengths: relevant question beyond the study system
combines simulations and experiments with mutually supporting results

comments.issue: The framework suits fixed genetic change rather than plasticity, and the chosen traits give no leverage for plasticity evolution.
comments.request: Reframe the study around plasticity evolution or justify the current framework.
comments.quote: By defining the life history traits only as the maturation rate and the fecundity, there is not really any leverage for the evolution of plasticity.

comments.issue: The interaction of density dependence with selection on optimal growth rates is not explored, though it should shape buffering effects.
comments.request: Explore density dependence and selection, drawing on experimental evolution studies.
comments.quote: The interaction with density dependence and the force of selection for differences on optimal growth rates is not well explored.

comments.issue: The delayed evolutionary change and the differing variance among simulations versus experiments (Fig. 4C&D vs 4E&F) suggest different selective forces.
comments.request: Expand on the delayed response and the simulation-experiment discrepancy.
comments.quote: I was also puzzled by the fairly constant behavior up to time ~55, only thereafter evolutionary changes seem to kick in, this seems not intuitive to me, could you expand on this.

comments.issue: More analytical quantities such as the damping ratio and generation time are not estimated.
comments.request: Estimate the damping ratio and generation time evolution alongside the ABM.
comments.quote: it might be insightful to estimate a number of more analytical values along, such as the damping ration, the evolution of the (average) damping ratio, as well as the evolution of the generation time

comments.issue: The conclusion that stochasticity matters less than periodicity may only apply to these settings, especially given amplitude differences.
comments.request: Qualify the generality of the stochasticity conclusion.
comments.quote: your somewhat general statement that stochasticity is less important than periodicity might only apply to your settings

comments.issue: The stochasticity statement should specify environmental rather than demographic stochasticity.
comments.request: Clarify that the statement concerns environmental stochasticity.
comments.quote: I would also suggest that you clarify that your statement on the effect of stochasticity relates to environmental stochasticity, and not demographic stochasticity (heterogeneity among individuals)

comments.issue: How generation time is estimated (demographic definition versus time to reproduction) is unclear.
comments.request: State how generation time is estimated.
comments.quote: It was not clear to me how you estimate generation time, as in demography (i.e. the average age at which the expected number of offspring has been produced) or as the time to reproduction, as frequently used in other fields.

comments.issue: The introduction discusses findings in detail before readers can understand the study.
comments.request: Shorten that part of the introduction.
comments.quote: I found the structure of the manuscript not very easy, as in the intro you discuss findings in some more detail without the reader really having the opportunity to understand what you did.

comments.issue: Terms such as state, stage, individual life history, genotype and population are used without clear definitions.
comments.request: Define state versus stage and the life-history terms early.
comments.quote: At various instances you seem to jump between terms, and it becomes sometimes confusing to me what exactly you refer to.

comments.issue: It is unclear why a newborn stage 0 is defined when the model only has juvenile, adult and death stages.
comments.request: Clarify the stage structure and any time delay.
comments.quote: For stage definitions, I don’t understand why you define a new born stage 0, where your model only accounts for J (stage 1) and A stage 2 and an absorbing death stage (3).

reviews.assessment: Likes the novel theory-experiment combination, but the main concern is that fitness comparisons across environments with different cycle periods are invalid.
strengths: combination of theory with a corresponding experiment is a rare delight
enjoyed reviewing and learned a great deal

comments.issue: Comparing absolute fitness (dominant eigenvalue of A) across cycle periods of different length compares growth over different projection intervals and is invalid; the normalization compounds this.
comments.request: Clarify the time scaling, or reframe the paper to compare selection on i-state composition rather than fitness.
comments.quote: comparisons of your absolute fitness (eigenvalue of A) ‘across’ cycle periods (e.g., your Fig. 1C) are nonsensical. It is a comparison of apples and oranges.

comments.issue: The model cannot be followed without referring to Park (2019).
comments.request: Include the critical model elements from Park (2019) in this paper.
comments.quote: The reader should be able to follow the logic and fundamental parts of your model without referring to Park (2019).

comments.issue: Placing a cycle-periodicity axis beside life-history and fitness axes in Figure 1B confuses readers and implies a nonsensical comparison.
comments.request: Rework Figure 1B so the response axes are not conflated.
comments.quote: when placing an axis for cycle periodicity in the same figure as one with axes for life history traits and fitness (e.g., Fig. 1B here), the reader can easily become confused

comments.issue: The introduction never explains how fitness would be measured and compared in stochastic environments or against periodic ones.
comments.request: Explain fitness measurement and comparison for stochastic environments.
comments.quote: When presenting your concepts in the Introduction you never mention how fitness would be measured and compared for stochastic environments, nor how they would be compared to deterministically periodic environments.

comments.issue: How stochastic fluctuation regimes are implemented 'deterministically' is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the deterministic implementation of stochastic regimes.
comments.quote: On line 117, how does one ‘deterministically’ implement ‘stochastic’ fluctuation regimes?

comments.issue: ABM and IBM terminology differs across fields and may not reach the intended audience.
comments.request: Acknowledge the normative terminology (individual-based model).
comments.quote: I know that to many in ecology, and ABM is a synonym for an IBM. I just point this out to acknowledge normative terminology in the field, such that the work is receptive to the appropriate audience

comments.issue: i-state configuration is used without explanation.
comments.request: Add a brief description of what an i-state configuration is.
comments.quote: L117: The reader could use a brief description of what an i-state configuration is.

comments.issue: Parameter notation for the number of offspring is missing.
comments.request: Add notation for the number of offspring.
comments.quote: L139: You need parameter notation to denote the ‘number of offspring’.

comments.issue: With sexual reproduction but no males modelled, inheritance error should reflect offspring similarity to the mother and recombination.
comments.request: Justify the inheritance error size given recombination.
comments.quote: Since the males are not being modeled, but there is sexual reproduction, shouldn’t the inheritance measure the offspring similarity to the mother, and therefore shouldn’t the error be much larger relative to the mean trait (considering recombination during meiosis)?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the number of stochastic draws equaled the number of disturbance events.
comments.request: Confirm the matching of stochastic draws to disturbance events.
comments.quote: So the ‘number’ of stochastic draws equaled the number of disturbance events in the respective deterministically periodic environments, correct?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether experimental variance reflects natural selection or individual stochasticity (drift).
comments.request: Develop a null expectation to separate selection from drift, following Tuljapurkar 2020.
comments.quote: I do wonder how your resulting measures of variance in life-history phenotypes within the population were affected by evolution by natural selection versus individual stochasticity (drift)?

comments.issue: Six minor line edits are suggested (L18, L20, L68, L90, L142, L173).
comments.quote: L90: replace heterogeneity with fluctuations (to be consistent with language used elsewhere)

title: Slower environmental cycles maintain greater life‐history variation within populations

study.system: tetrapod genera; phylogenies and IUCN extinction risk

editor_summary: Editor requires a major overhaul, especially the statistics-on-statistics problem: analyse species number and crown age directly or propagate estimation error; questions the crown/stem ratio argument and constant-rate model; asks to introduce hypotheses first.

reviews.assessment: The best paper on this subject: impressive, well-written analyses with clear figures; only minor clarifications plus a species-level follow-up suggested.

comments.issue: A species-level analysis would better link diversification to extinction risk.
comments.request: Run a species-level analysis with species age and range size.
comments.quote: A way of remedying this would be to conduct an analysis at the species level (binary response), allowing the species age and range size variables to apply to the relevant species and the other predictors to be replicated across the genus

comments.issue: The lineage age hypothesis is confusing; species age has clearer predictions but was not tested.
comments.request: Explain why lineage age was tested instead of species age.
comments.quote: Why test this hypothesis rather than the effect of species age for which the predictions are much more likely and clearer?

comments.issue: Text and legend concern average species extinction while Fig 1 y-axis shows genus extinction risk.
comments.request: Relabel the y-axis 'species extinction risk'.
comments.quote: I suggest relabeling of the y axis to “species extinction risk”.

comments.issue: Lineage age is ambiguous between species age and genus age (L29).
comments.request: Clarify the term.
comments.quote: On first reading I took lineage age to mean the age of the species, but from fig 1 this appears not to be that instead you mean the age of the genus

comments.issue: Young species may also suffer migration load, less genetic purging and smaller populations (L34).
comments.request: Consider these additional mechanisms.
comments.quote: I would have thought that young species may also be subject to greater migration load and have had less time for genetic purging. Also young species will tend to have smaller population sizes.

comments.issue: No reason adaptation should be slower in older species; the Ho et al. citation concerns neutral variation (L38).
comments.request: Reconsider this mechanism or the citation.
comments.quote: I can’t see any reason why adaption would be slower in older species. The Ho et al. paper cited seems to be referring primarily to neutral genetic variation, which is not relevant in this context.

comments.issue: Recent evidence (Hagen et al. 2018) points to younger species being at greater risk (L40).
comments.request: Cite and discuss this contrasting evidence.
comments.quote: Though recent evidence seems to point to younger species being at greater risk of extinction, contrary to Van Valen’s hypothesis: Hagen, O., Andermann, T., Quental, T.B., Antonelli, A. and Silvestro, D., 2018.

comments.issue: Prediction 3.1 should be linked back to prediction 1.1 and the turnover hypothesis (L71).
comments.request: Make these links explicit.
comments.quote: I think this prediction 3.1 could be related back to prediction 1.1 (as well as the turnover hypothesis) to help the reader see the links.

comments.issue: Pigot et al. 2012 on range size change under a null model is not cited (L105).
comments.request: Cite Pigot et al. 2012.
comments.quote: This is a nice paper on the subject of range size changes under a simple null model: Pigot, A.L., Owens, I.P. and Orme, C.D.L., 2012.

comments.issue: Why a negative binomial rather than a binomial formulation is not justified (L196).
comments.request: Justify the negative binomial choice.
comments.quote: I was puzzled why was the negative binomial preferred to a more straightforward binomial formulation. I think including some brief justification would help.

comments.issue: L297 uses 'principle' where 'principal' is meant.
comments.request: Correct the word.
comments.quote: Line 297. principle -> principal

reviews.assessment: Clearly written, careful analysis extending prior findings across tetrapods; wants additional tests (richness, timing metrics, single-model interactions) and resolution of contradictory results.
strengths: general relationship across a large tetrapod dataset is interesting

comments.issue: The association between imperilment/range size and genus richness was not tested, yet richness may predict as well as diversification rate.
comments.request: Test genus richness as a predictor.
comments.quote: do large genera contain a disproportionate number of threatened species regardless of whether they diversified rapidly or slowly?

comments.issue: Metrics capturing the timing of speciation (slowdowns or speedups) could explain variation among clades with equal diversification rates.
comments.request: Test timing-based metrics.
comments.quote: metrics that capture more information about timing (e.g. whether clades show slow downs or speed ups in diversification) could also help in explaining the substantial variation in range size and imperilment

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the results of the extinction-fraction sensitivity analysis are reported.
comments.request: Report how results depend on the extinction fraction.
comments.quote: The authors mention that they examine how their results depend on the assumed extinction fraction when calculating diversification rates. Are these results reported?

comments.issue: Averaging across 100 trees and using mean values discards phylogenetic uncertainty.
comments.request: Repeat analyses across trees and propagate uncertainty into parameters.
comments.quote: Why not repeat the analysis across each of the 100 phylogenetic trees and then incorporate the phylogenetic uncertainty into the parameter estimates?

comments.issue: Separate models per taxonomic group preclude testing slope differences; a single model with clade interactions is needed (L232, L270).
comments.request: Fit one model with clade interactions.
comments.quote: Rather than fitting a separate model for each taxonomic group (L232), why not fit a single model and test for an interaction between each evolutionary metric and clade?

comments.issue: Contradictory species-level results and the two proposed explanations are never resolved in the Discussion.
comments.request: Add discussion resolving the species-level contradiction.
comments.quote: I think addressing these contradictory results would be an important advance and so at least a paragraph or two in the Discussion is needed to address discuss this.

comments.issue: The stochastic-variation explanation is inconsistent: genus-level diversification rate is also a stochastic descriptor.
comments.request: Reconsider this explanation.
comments.quote: However, the metric of diversification rate that the authors use is also simply a statistical descriptor and so will vary stochastically among genera even if they are all governed by the same rate.

comments.issue: The peripatric-speciation explanation needs clearer detail and references (Ezard et al. 2012; Pigot et al. 2012).
comments.request: Spell out the mechanism and cite these papers.
comments.quote: I think this explanation makes much more sense. However, I think the details of this mechanism could be spelt out more clearly.

comments.issue: 'Litany' at L16 may be the wrong word.
comments.request: Check the word choice.
comments.quote: L16 is ‘litany’ the correct term?

comments.issue: The range-size explanation focuses on peripatric speciation; the same logic should apply under vicariance (L100-112).
comments.request: Discuss the vicariance case.
comments.quote: when explaining why range sizes should be smaller in clades under faster diversification, the authors focus on the peripatric speciation model, but wouldn’t the same logic also apply under a vicariance model?

comments.issue: The number of threatened species per clade is not provided (L176).
comments.request: Provide threatened species counts per clade.
comments.quote: L176: please provide number of species per clade that are threatened

reviews.assessment: Several methodological and conceptual concerns: unclear genus-level risk metric, survivorship bias, non-identifiability, modern ranges, and unwarranted links between natural diversification and anthropogenic threats.

comments.issue: Genus-level extinction risk (fraction of threatened species) is unclear: no link between genus threat and number of extinctions, and the extinction unit is ambiguous.
comments.request: Define and justify the extinction-risk metric.
comments.quote: The extinction risk, which is at the basis of the analyses presented here, is computed at genus level as the fraction of IUCN assessed species within each genus that are threatened. This definition makes the meaning of extinction risk unclear.

comments.issue: Robustness to unevaluated species and biased assessment prioritisation is unknown.
comments.request: Assess the impact of unevaluated species.
comments.quote: How robust is this approach when a high proportion of species in a genus have not yet been evaluated by IUCN?

comments.issue: Why the 5-6 IUCN threat levels were lumped into two categories is not explained.
comments.request: Use the higher-resolution IUCN categories or justify lumping.
comments.quote: In addition, it is not clear why the 5-6 levels of threat from IUCN were lumped into 2 categories. Why not using the higher resolution provided by IUCN to measure extinction risk?

comments.issue: Linking natural speciation/extinction theory to modern, anthropogenically driven risk is unwarranted (Lines 329-335).
comments.request: Separate anthropogenic threats from evolutionary legacy claims.
comments.quote: Thus, I do not see how patterns in modern extinction risks might lend support to theories of natural speciation and extinction.

comments.issue: Excluding species already driven extinct leaves a biased subset of survivors, affecting the results.
comments.request: Address the survivorship bias.
comments.quote: the sample of threatened species today is a biased subset of species that have not gone extinct yet. How does this affect the results presented in this paper?

comments.issue: Simple rate estimators are used despite Louca and Pennell's non-identifiability result; constant-rate models are preferred without justification over BAMM/RPANDA/Castor/TreePar.
comments.request: Use identifiable, more realistic diversification models.
comments.quote: It is not clear why a simpler method would manage to tease apart a process that is hardly identifiable with mathematically sophisticated methods.

comments.issue: Analyses use modern ranges that are altered by human activity rather than natural ranges.
comments.request: Incorporate natural species ranges or assess the bias.
comments.quote: For many (most?) vertebrate species the geographic ranges have been be significantly altered by human activity and their modern ranges no longer reflect their natural ranges.

comments.issue: Statement in lines 230-231 is misleading: species are not driven extinct by longevity or range size, only correlated with status.
comments.request: Reword the claim.
comments.quote: Contemporary extinction risk is shaped by anthropogenic pressure, overexploitation, climate change and probably several other factors. Species are not going extinct because of their longevity or range size even though these traits might correlate with their conservation status.

comments.issue: Accurate molecular ages depend on fossil dating rather than taxon sampling (Lines 162-165).
comments.request: Correct this statement.
comments.quote: accurate ages in molecular phylogenies are mostly a function of how well the fossil data can be used to date them, rather than a function of taxon sampling.

comments.issue: Simulations constraining both tip number and root age sample from a weirdly constrained process and tails of the distribution.
comments.request: Avoid this constrained simulation design.
comments.quote: Simulations of birth-death processes while constraining both number of tips and root age should be avoided because they sample from a weirdly constrained birth-death process

comments.issue: Rapid diversification is orders of magnitude slower than anthropogenic change; low diversification rates do not confer high susceptibility to exploitation (lines 347-351).
comments.request: Acknowledge the timescale mismatch.
comments.quote: The attempts to link speciation rates with the dynamics of the Anthropocene (e.g. lines 347-351) should acknowledge the fact that even rapid diversification is likely orders of magnitude slower than anthropogenic changes to environment, climate, range and population sizes.

comments.issue: Traits and functional/ecological redundancy would strengthen the argument at lines 400-401.
comments.request: Consider trait and redundancy analyses.
comments.quote: Perhaps looking at traits and functional and ecological redundancy would make a stronger argument for this point.

title: Evolutionary legacies in contemporary tetrapod imperilment

study.system: multispecies communities; graph-based priority effects framework

editor_summary: All find conceptual ideas interesting and novel; methods/concepts insufficiently developed; more tangible connections to examples suggested (simulation case study; sampling approach); substantial revision feasible.

reviews.assessment: Enthusiastic; conceptually excellent and well-presented, but the neural network and real-world application need clearer explanation.
strengths: fundamentally shifted thinking about priority effects

comments.issue: What the neural network predicts, its inputs and outputs, and why its predictability range differs from the observed range are unclear.
comments.request: Explain what exactly is predicted and how the network was trained.
comments.quote: First, I struggled to tease apart exactly what was being done with the neural network. As far as I can tell, it's predicting how predictive the scenario is, but not actually making predictions about the outcomes?

comments.issue: The framework's real-world application is not demonstrated prescriptively.
comments.request: Elaborate with simulations, empirical data or conceptual examples, including Appendix E.
comments.quote: I would push the authors to try to elaborate a bit---either via simulations, empirical data, or conceptual means---to better highlight how exactly one can apply this in real world settings.

comments.issue: The Fig. 2 example uses identical probabilities and predictabilities, making the concepts look tautological.
comments.request: Provide a more illustrative example with unequal probabilities.
comments.quote: Perhaps an example where the probabilities are not each 0.5, and the predictability are not identically 0.37 would help?

comments.issue: Invasion number is a lynchpin but unmeasurable in real communities; ways to overcome this are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss back-solving invasion intensity or aggregating across communities.
comments.quote: In reality, we never really know how many invasions a natural community/ecosystem experiences. And so this creates a bit of a challenge in application

comments.issue: The VI description at L21 is ambiguous between single invasion and composition cycles.
comments.request: Clarify the VI definition at first use.
comments.quote: Here you describe VI as "the species that arrives late survives", which at first I thought was indicative simply of a single iteration, and once established it cannot be displaced again.

comments.issue: The colour coding and graph conventions in Fig. 1 are not explained with examples.
comments.request: Add a concrete example to the text or legend.
comments.quote: I would suggest giving an example in the text or legend that clearly explains why a graph is written the way it is.

comments.issue: Typo at L146 ("seques").
comments.request: Fix the typo.
comments.quote: L 146. "seques" -- typo?

comments.issue: Whether Fig. 3b distributions converge to 1.0 or to a humped limit is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the convergence behaviour.
comments.quote: It's stated that the distribution converges with increasing invasion, but does this mean it tends towards 1.0, with the mass function continuing to pile up at the right extreme?

comments.issue: Dashed lines in Fig. 4 are not explained as final compositions.
comments.request: Describe how to interpret the dashed lines.
comments.quote: I would reiterate that the dashed lines represent the final compositions. This is also the first time you put dashed lines around trajectories

comments.issue: The temporal process in Fig. 4A (community vs invasion) is hard to follow.
comments.request: Use colour, boxing or size differences to clarify.
comments.quote: I would suggest some sort of coloring, or boxing, or differences in size to make it clear that this is a temporal process.

comments.issue: Whether the importance of stable states vs transient paths holds generally or is system-specific is unclear.
comments.request: State whether these are general guiding principles.
comments.quote: Are these results about the importance of stable states, vs transient paths, etc supposed to be results that hold in general across systems, or are they intended to be system specific?

reviews.assessment: Mixed; conceptually stimulating, but dense writing, undefined terms and an unclear take-home message make it hard to unpack.
strengths: important conclusions with implications for experimental design

comments.issue: Central technical terms, including predictability, are not defined.
comments.request: Define technical terms clearly in introduction, methods and results.
comments.quote: many technical terms lack clear definition or explanation, some of which are the basis of key findings of the paper

comments.issue: The Discussion lacks a clear take-home message and links to the existing framework.
comments.request: Add a summary of important messages and contributions.
comments.quote: Discussion lacks a clear takehome message, which is especially important because the methods-results section is already leaving me with many loose ends.

comments.issue: The empirical outlook discusses feasibility but not specific experimental design.
comments.request: Address relative population frequencies and number of invasions.
comments.quote: The current version only talks about feasibility but should focus more on specific experimental design, such as the effect of relative population frequencies and number of invasions.

comments.issue: Predictability at line 34 may mean reaching a stable state, but no general definition is given.
comments.request: Define predictability in a general sense.
comments.quote: does predictability here mean reaching a stable state given an initial composition?

comments.issue: The statement at line 94 cannot be justified without a proper definition of predictability.
comments.request: Define predictability before this statement.
comments.quote: the fact that predictability is not properly defined makes it hard for me to justify this statement

comments.issue: What multiple invasions look like on a deterministic assembly graph is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the effect of repeated invasions on the graph.
comments.quote: If the assembly graph is deterministic, i.e. B will always fail to invade A, does it matter if B invade multiple times?

comments.issue: The link between temporal uncertainty and final-composition uncertainty is not explained.
comments.request: Clarify any mechanistic association between the two measures.
comments.quote: does it necessarily correlate with the uncertainty of final composition, as mentioned in line 128, or is this relationship deducted from simulations like Figure 3A?

comments.issue: The definition of alternative transient states conflicts with Fukami (2015).
comments.request: Reconcile the definition with Fukami (2015).
comments.quote: Interestingly, this definition of alternative transient states seems to be contrary to Fukami (2015), which shows them as transient paths to a single stable state

comments.issue: The phrase "this possibility to escape can equally" at L165 is incomplete.
comments.request: Complete the sentence.
comments.quote: this possibility to escape can equally

comments.issue: Appendix C lacks method detail, and the number of hidden layers differs between text and appendix.
comments.request: Walk through the classification and network steps and fix the discrepancy.
comments.quote: Even Appendix C does not contain enough information of the method. Are you classifying all assembly graphs by their calculated predictability?

comments.issue: Why predictability increases with more invasions is not mechanistically explained.
comments.request: Explain the mechanism behind the invasion effect.
comments.quote: Is it because more invasions decrease the number of transient states and results in more convergence of final community composition

comments.issue: "Explanatory power" at line 173 is not defined.
comments.request: Define classified predictability/explanatory power.
comments.quote: the “explanatory power” here is a bit confusing.

comments.issue: Main text says "interactions between cycles and stable states" while Fig. 5D says "escapes from cycles to stable states".
comments.request: Clarify the direction and terminology.
comments.quote: Is it possible to have it from the other way, i.e. from stable state back to composition cycles?

comments.issue: It is unclear what the empirical analysis adds and what evidence is still needed (line 195).
comments.request: State what was learned and what remains open.
comments.quote: “little additional evidence” what do you learn from the analysis of empirical data and what evidence do we still need?

comments.issue: The experiment type implied by "a minimum of S+1 experiments" is not specified.
comments.request: Describe the proposed experimental design.
comments.quote: what kind of experiment? Would that be top-down experiments of all possible combination or bottom-up experiments of species invasions?

comments.issue: "Bottom-up assembly" is not defined at line 212.
comments.request: Reiterate its definition from Serván and Allesina (2021).
comments.quote: it seems that the term “bottom-up assembly” has a specific meaning from Serván and Allesina (2021), so it might be better to reiterate its definition here.

comments.issue: Fitting short empirical time series to computational models risks finding dynamics that never existed.
comments.request: Acknowledge this difficulty at L217-219.
comments.quote: fitting empirical interaction data (from only a few generations) to computational models risks finding dynamics that would have never existed

comments.issue: Assembly graphs carry no population density or frequency information, limiting comparability.
comments.request: Discuss the limitation of density-independent graphs.
comments.quote: the assembly graph does not seem to carry any information of population density/frequency, which in many cases could determine competition outcome

comments.issue: Links to the current theoretical and empirical literature are insufficient (line 245).
comments.request: Add more connections to the priority effects literature.
comments.quote: More connections with the current body of theoretical and empirical literature, like in paragraph one of introduction, could be helpful.

comments.issue: "Medications" at line 507 should probably be "meditation".
comments.request: Correct the word.
comments.quote: do you mean meditation?

comments.issue: Appendix D bottom panels say 4 species but should say 5.
comments.request: Correct the Appendix D labels.
comments.quote: Appendix D: bottom panels say 4 species but should be 5.

reviews.assessment: Positive; novel framework and relevant results, but presentation, scalability and invasion-frequency robustness need work.
strengths: novel approach to disentangle priority effects

comments.issue: The synthetic writing makes the Perspective hard to understand; technical details and supplement need expansion.
comments.request: Expand the manuscript and supplementary material.
comments.quote: I struggled to understand some parts of the manuscript because of the synthetic way the manuscript is written.

comments.issue: Complete enumeration limits the approach to few species; sampling large graph ensembles and expectations for large pools are unresolved.
comments.request: Discuss sampling approaches and expectations for large communities.
comments.quote: Is there an effective way to effectively sample the ensemble of assembly graphs for larger communities, without enumerating all possible cases?

comments.issue: The uniform visitation assumption is unrealistic and the effect of non-uniform invasion frequencies is untested.
comments.request: Illustrate non-uniform invasion distributions and test robustness.
comments.quote: I think that they could illustrate how the distribution of invasion events with an example, to assess the robustness of their results

comments.issue: 6 line-level corrections (L31 number; L66 figure ref; L146 typo; L215 90%; L507 word; Fig. S5 label).
comments.quote: L215. According to Fig. S1, it is 90% (not 99%) of assembly dynamics that contain unreachable combinations.

comments.issue: The point at L106 is not illustrated.
comments.request: Add an example in the main text or Appendix B.
comments.quote: L106. Illustrate with an example, either in the main text or in Appendix B.

comments.issue: The rightmost box in Fig. 2B has the wrong label.
comments.request: Relabel as "Predictability on temporal composition".
comments.quote: Fig. 2B. The rightmost box should read ‘Predictability on temporal composition’

comments.issue: No three-species example distinguishes temporal-composition from state predictability.
comments.request: Provide a three-species example.
comments.quote: Could the authors provide an example with three species, to illustrate a situation in which predictability on temporal composition differs from predictability on the states?

comments.issue: Appendix A formula (S5) is missing a log(S!) term and the sentence at L488 is unfinished.
comments.request: Fix the formula and complete the sentence.
comments.quote: Appendix A, formula (S5): a log(S!) is missing. Also, please finish the sentence in L488.

comments.issue: Appendices B, D and F need expansion.
comments.request: Expand the appendices.
comments.quote: As I already mentioned, appendices should be expanded, especially Appendix B, D and F.

title: Untangling the complexity of priority effects in multispecies communities

study.system: sudden oak death in California forests; tree diversity and disease data

editor_summary: Editor asks the authors to be clearer about hypothesized mechanisms and predictions (a table may help), justify how community competence is used, and make the data-selection criteria transparent; both reviewers' substantial suggestions should be addressed.

reviews.assessment: Very well written and appropriate analysis, but the plot-selection criteria might bias the diversity-disease results.
strengths: data and code made publicly accessible

comments.issue: Only 151 of 280 plots were retained; excluding low-diversity, low-disease plots could bias community competence and prevalence.
comments.request: Reanalyse the data to test robustness to plot exclusions.
comments.quote: I am concerned that omitting these plots could bias the results by removing low-diversity, low disease plots from the dataset.

comments.issue: Commonly versus rarely symptomatic hosts are never operationally defined, and infection is conflated with disease.
comments.request: Define symptomatic host categories and distinguish infection from disease in the introduction.
comments.quote: The idea of commonly symptomatic hosts vs. rarely symptomatic hosts is central to the manuscript but never operationally defined.

comments.issue: Rarely symptomatic, high-competence hosts are absent from Figure 1 though they may matter for transmission.
comments.request: Include or explain these hosts in Figure 1.
comments.quote: As an aside, why were rarely symptomatic, high competence hosts not included in Figure 1?

comments.issue: The results are not placed in the context of prior experimental work on plant diversity-disease relationships.
comments.request: Discuss findings relative to experiments such as Hantsch et al. 2013.
comments.quote: I was somewhat surprised that this manuscript did not do a better job of placing these results in the context of prior work on diversity-disease relationships, particularly experimental work in plant systems.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the diversity gradient reflects community disassembly after disturbance, which affects predictions.
comments.request: Clarify the ecological processes driving diversity variation among plots.
comments.quote: But it is unclear to me whether the gradient in this study would be associated with community disassembly.

comments.issue: Models using infection severity instead of prevalence were not explored, although experiments often use severity.
comments.request: Consider rerunning models with infection severity as the response.
comments.quote: I'm curious about how these results would change if models included a measure of infection severity rather than infection prevalence, though I recognize that this might be outside of the scope of this paper.

comments.issue: The Mitchell et al. 2002 citation comes from a purely experimental manipulation and seems out of place.
comments.request: Cite studies measuring community assembly processes instead.
comments.quote: Line 56: The Mitchell et al 2002 citation seems somewhat out of place here, since it comes from a purely experimental biodiversity manipulation.

comments.issue: "Infection density" is undefined and inconsistent with usual prevalence, incidence and severity endpoints.
comments.request: Define or replace the term.
comments.quote: Line 71: I'm not sure what is meant by “infection density”.

comments.issue: "Disease-diversity" is used inconsistently with the earlier "diversity-disease".
comments.request: Use diversity-disease throughout.
comments.quote: Line 78: Earlier paragraphs in this section referred to this as the “diversity-disease” relationship, which I prefer over “disease-diversity”.

comments.issue: The study measures disease prevalence, not infection prevalence, since asymptomatic infections are undetectable.
comments.request: Make the disease versus infection distinction explicit.
comments.quote: Line 118: Based on this definition, this seems to be a study of disease prevalence, not infection prevalence, as there is no way of detecting asymptomatic infections

comments.issue: The proportion of plots with symptomatic hosts but no cultured P. ramorum is unknown, which affects prevalence reliability.
comments.request: Report how often symptoms were caused by other pathogens.
comments.quote: Line 119: I'm curious about the proportion of plots that had symptomatic hosts, but did not contain any P. ramorum based on culturing.

comments.issue: Host count and the prevalence denominator may be the same quantity under different names.
comments.request: Use the same term for both to avoid confusion.
comments.quote: Line 130: is “number of individual hosts in each plot” the same as the denominator in infection prevalence (Total no. of hosts)? If so, consider using the same term for both to avoid confusion.

comments.issue: The competence measurement may depend on total basal area and could need standardisation.
comments.request: Test whether dividing the measure by total basal area changes results.
comments.quote: Line 148: How sensitive is this measurement to the total basal area of plants in a plot?

comments.issue: "Sporulation potential" may be the same as "sporulation" used earlier.
comments.request: Clarify whether the two terms are the same.
comments.quote: Line 150: What is meant by “sporulation potential”? Is that the same as “sporulation” at Line 145?

comments.issue: Line-level copy edits at L155, L211, L215 and L372 (phrasing, rephrasing, grammar).
comments.quote: Line 155: change to “previously observed dilution effect”.

comments.issue: The specific R packages used are not cited.
comments.request: Cite the R packages used for analysis.
comments.quote: I recommend that the authors cite the specific r packages that they used for analysis.

comments.issue: Sensitivity to collinearity is not assessed and covariate correlations are not shown.
comments.request: Add a covariate correlation table to the supplement.
comments.quote: How sensitive were these models to collinearity in the data? And to what extent were different covariates in the models correlated with one another?

comments.issue: The term transmission is used although transmission was not measured.
comments.request: Replace with "disease prevalence" or similar.
comments.quote: Line 287: This study did not measure transmission, replace with “Disease prevalence” or similar.

comments.issue: The rationale at line 349 is hard to follow given bay laurel is the most competent host.
comments.request: Clarify the reasoning.
comments.quote: Line 349: I don't follow the rationale here. Bay laurel is the most competent host species, is it not?

comments.issue: The spatial-scale discussion misses relevant syntheses, and the 2015 frequency argument does not aid interpretation.
comments.request: Discuss results against community- versus individual-level diversity-disease studies and scale syntheses.
comments.quote: How does the frequency with which studies evaluated spatial scale prior to 2015 affect the interpretation of the results from this study?

comments.issue: Figure 1 legend lacks a take-home message.
comments.request: Add one or two sentences explaining the key message.
comments.quote: Figure 1 This figure could be improved substantially with one or two sentences in the legend explaining the key take-home message.

comments.issue: Figure 3 lacks raw-data panels relating richness and competence to infection.
comments.request: Add panels showing the raw data.
comments.quote: Figure 3: I suggest that the authors include panels showing the raw data relating host richness and community competence to the proportion of hosts/plots infected.

comments.issue: "Community competency" is used instead of "community competence" in figure labels.
comments.request: Use "community competence" in Figures 5 and 6.
comments.quote: Figures 5 & 6: I suggest “community competence” instead of “community competency”

reviews.assessment: Impressive synthesis with a compelling nestedness result, but the dilution framing, literature synthesis and amplification statistics need major work.
strengths: important study system of general interest
combination of field survey, laboratory experiment and synthesis
confirms a core requirement for dilution effects

comments.issue: The richness-community prevalence relationship does not qualify as a dilution effect; the concept is misapplied at community level.
comments.request: Reframe the community-level result and clarify the dilution-effect concept.
comments.quote: My largest critique is that I would not classify the negative relationship between richness and community-level prevalence as a “dilution effect.”

comments.issue: Dilution mechanisms per Keesing et al. 2006 (host regulation, encounter reduction) are barely engaged and conflated with measurement levels.
comments.request: Integrate dilution mechanisms and the density-diversity literature.
comments.quote: To me, dilution mechanisms are ways that diluters can interfere with disease transmission, as outlined in Keesing et al. 2006. You only briefly touch on these ideas in the discussion

comments.issue: The discussion of scale diverges from how scale is treated in the diversity-disease literature.
comments.request: Engage with the scale literature (Randolph & Dobson, Wood & Lafferty, Halliday & Rohr).
comments.quote: The way scales are discussed is also quite different from the way issues of scale are discussed in the literature.

comments.issue: The amplification result in Figure 6 is not convincing: it sits near one, depends on unshown terms, and lacks a mechanism.
comments.request: Strengthen the evidence and explanation for the amplification result.
comments.quote: My skepticism stems from 1) the fact that the result is really close to the boundary of 1, even with 90% credible intervals

comments.issue: The abstract calls these mechanisms, which conflicts with how the term is used in the literature.
comments.request: Align the use of "mechanism" with established definitions.
comments.quote: 33: Are these mechanisms? At least, not in the way outlined by Keesing et al. 2006 and others.

comments.issue: "Individual level" in the abstract is confusing.
comments.request: Clarify what is meant at line 36.
comments.quote: 36: “Individual level” is confusing here. Are you just saying that the more susceptible host species were more likely to be infected?

comments.issue: The claim about rarefaction at line 67 appears incorrect.
comments.request: Correct or justify the statement.
comments.quote: 67: Is this true? Whole idea of rarefaction is that more things = more diversity.

comments.issue: "Diversity" is used inconsistently across citations (richness versus evenness).
comments.request: Specify which diversity metric each citation refers to.
comments.quote: 88: Here and elsewhere: what is ‘diversity’ in this citation? Richness? Evenness?

comments.issue: It is unknown whether results hold when the excluded plots are included.

comments.quote: 123 – I would be curious to see whether the results hold if including plots that were excluded because common symptomatic species were absent.

comments.issue: Basal area is a carbon-based density measure, unlike the individual-based density familiar to animal ecologists.

comments.issue: What Figure 4 shows as the community competence contribution is not described anywhere.
comments.request: Describe the plotted quantity (e.g., p_i / P).
comments.quote: 152 – What is shown in figure 4 as community competence contribution? Is it p_i / P?

comments.issue: Permutation replication seems low and the method lacks detail.
comments.request: Use more permutations (e.g., 10,000) and describe the method.
comments.quote: 170 – replication on permutations seems low. 10,000 would be more standard? Some more details about this method would be appreciated.

comments.issue: No mechanism explains how symptomatic hosts might alter infection prevalence, such as a spore barrier.

comments.quote: 175 – how might symptomatic hosts alter infection prevalence of the commonly symptomatic hosts? (This is what I would call a mechanism. Is it by acting as a spore barrier? Something else?)

comments.issue: p_j is used without being defined; only capital P is defined.

comments.quote: 179 – this seems pretty confusing but I don’t think it needs to be. What is p_j? I don’t think it was defined; only capital P is defined above.

comments.issue: Variables may be correlated or conflated.
comments.request: Check correlations among variables.
comments.quote: 186 – any of these variables correlated? Could be conflated.

comments.issue: Using 90% credible intervals for parameters near one is not justified without evidence that sample sizes are too low.

comments.issue: "After controlling for these variables" may mean residual analysis, which is unclear.

comments.issue: The signs of the reported effects may be misstated.

comments.quote: 244 – These are all positive effects, not negative, right?

comments.issue: "Across scales" is misleading; the study remains at plot scale with different denominators.

comments.quote: 271 – “across scales” seems misleading. You are looking at the plot scale

comments.issue: Bay laurel basal area is part of community competence, so their separate effects are correlated and hard to distinguish.
comments.request: Account for the correlation between these predictors.
comments.quote: 275 – Fig 5A seems to show that community competency does have a strong positive effect on infection prevalence, right?

comments.issue: The explanation of the model at line 289 is confusing.
comments.request: Clarify the model explanation.
comments.quote: 289 – confusing explanation of this model

comments.issue: The bay laurel basal area effect is described as slightly higher although it may not be significant.
comments.request: Check the significance claims against the posteriors.
comments.quote: I thought this effect was not significant, ie, posterior did not exclude 0?

comments.issue: The analysis "accounting for species composition" is not identified.
comments.request: Point to where this analysis is described.
comments.quote: 318 – What analysis did this “accounting for species composition?” Sorry, I missed it.

comments.issue: Community-level patterns are not consistent with the definition of dilution effects despite the stated lack of distinction.
comments.request: Reconcile the discussion with the definition of dilution.
comments.quote: it is because the community level patterns are not consistent with how dilution effects are defined

comments.issue: For humans, the number of infected mosquitoes matters more than seroprevalence, as with the tick example.
comments.request: Refine the density-versus-prevalence argument.
comments.quote: 363 – for humans, seroprevalence of mosquitoes is probably less important than number of infected mosquitoes

comments.issue: The claim that Strauss et al. 2015 does not track infections in both host types is incorrect.

comments.quote: 365 – actually Strauss et al. 2015 does track infections in both focal host and diluter.

comments.issue: It is unclear which species "individual-level infection risk" in Figure 1 refers to.

comments.issue: The definition of clonal stems is unclear.

comments.issue: The phrase 'density increase' on line 254 is unclear.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether persistent gaps are dominated by small diameter stems.

title: Local canopy disturbance as an explanation for long‐term increases in liana abundance

reviews.assessment: Completely agrees with the non-linearity argument but warns correlative results are model-dependent and need experimental confirmation.

agrees plant C input was an overlooked factor

comments.issue: Results can differ substantially depending on the structural model or relationship type used.

comments.issue: Correlative results cannot be solidly interpreted without manipulative experiments directly assessing factor effects.

comments.issue: Non-linear relationship may be an artefact of the correlative approach and site selection.
comments.request: Test whether the nonlinearity is an artefact and pursue experimental investigation.
comments.quote: Could this non-linear relationship be an artefact of the correlative approach and site selection?

reviews.assessment: Important and satisfactory response that addresses the main points of Wu et al.; only minor wording edits requested.
strengths: carefully considered responses regarding their original analysis

comments.issue: 2 line-level wording edits.

reviews.assessment: Two substantial concerns: discrepant model fit indices and unexplained log transformation of plant C input.

comments.issue: Model fit indices differ from Wu et al. despite identical formulation; unclear whether the full dataset was used.

comments.issue: Log transformation of plant C input is applied without rationale while other variables are untransformed.
