title: Early queen infection shapes developmental dynamics and induces long‐term disease protection in incipient ant colonies

study.system: 4510 tree pests and 981 host genera; global occurrence data

editor_summary: Impressive dataset, but sharpen the conceptual framework and hypotheses by putting more biology in; biggest concern is mixing taxa with very different biologies; discuss taxon-specific differences and possible undersampling.

reviews.assessment: Very nice dataset but the conceptual framework is missing, several conclusions are trivial and taxon-specific reporting differences are not addressed.

comments.issue: The study lacks a conceptual framework and clear hypotheses derived from the existing literature.
comments.request: Screen the literature and derive testable hypotheses about hosts and pests.
comments.quote: Much has already been published on the topic of hosts and tree colonizing species, which would have made it possible to place the study in a general framework and formulate clear hypotheses for the relationship between hosts and pest species.

comments.issue: Treating huge countries such as the US, China or Russia as single data points makes the minor role of climate questionable.
comments.request: Account for the unequal size and heterogeneity of countries.
comments.quote: However, this is questionable if countries such as the US, China or Russia are considered as one data point.

comments.issue: Host diversity should be separated into a pure diversity and a phylogenetic diversity component.
comments.request: Separate pure and phylogenetic diversity components.
comments.quote: With the diversity of hosts, it would be appropriate to separate into a component of pure diversity and a phylogenetic component of diversity.

comments.issue: Several conclusions are rather trivial, e.g. that pest composition is driven by host phylogenetic composition.
comments.request: Go beyond trivial conclusions or reframe the contribution.
comments.quote: A number of conclusions are rather trivial: e.g. “We show the composition of tree pests is primarily driven by the phylogenetic composition of host trees, whereas effects of climate and geography are minor”.

comments.issue: Hypotheses about the main drivers should be formulated separately for different species groups.
comments.request: Formulate driver hypotheses by species group (e.g. insects vs fungi).
comments.quote: I think the manuscript would gain a lot if the hypotheses on the importance of the main drivers were formulated in dependence of the different species groups.

comments.issue: Taxon-specific reporting differences (e.g. viruses are harder to record than insects) and unseen links in the network analyses are not addressed.
comments.request: Discuss taxon-specific reporting biases and consider unseen links.
comments.quote: Viruses are much more difficult to report than insects for instance, which has to be addressed in the discussion at least.

comments.issue: The general prediction about pests with large host breadths is not validated.
comments.request: Test the prediction using recent expanding pest species.
comments.quote: This should be tested afterward by e.g. the last 30 important pest species with range expansion to validate the prediction.

comments.issue: A reference is missing at line 61.
comments.request: Add the missing reference.
comments.quote: Line 61: a reference is missing here

comments.issue: Host availability is also most important within native ranges, which is not acknowledged.
comments.request: Acknowledge this pattern and cite Brandle & Brandl 2001.
comments.quote: Line 87 host availability is also in native ranges most important see (Brändle & Brandl 2001 J Anim Ecol) also within the native range.

comments.issue: The statement that there is an equilibrium is incorrect; Red Queen dynamics imply none.
comments.request: Correct the equilibrium statement.
comments.quote: Line 95: There is never an equlibirum there, see the Red queen Hypothesis.

comments.issue: What counts as a host is unclear; many trees exist that are colonized by only a small subset of species.
comments.request: Define host status considering bark thickness, chemistry and other determinants.
comments.quote: here the question is when is a host a host?

comments.issue: The passage at lines 265-267 belongs in the discussion.
comments.request: Move it to the discussion.
comments.quote: 265-267: Move to discussion

comments.issue: Figure 3 shows dissimilarity, not diversity, so the sentence is inaccurate.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence.
comments.quote: Line 276: Note that Fig 3 shows dissimilarity not diversity so rephrase the sentence.

comments.issue: The result is common, as in 95% of all turnover studies.
comments.request: Acknowledge that the finding is not novel.
comments.quote: Line 283: a finding as in 95% of all turnover studies

comments.issue: Separate Mantel tests cannot show partial effects; multiple regression on matrices would be better.
comments.request: Use MRMs to estimate partial effects in one analysis.
comments.quote: Line 288: instead of separated Mantel Tests MRMs could show the partical effects of phylogenetic, biogeographic, climatic dissimilarity in one analyses.

comments.issue: Some species may simply not be recorded as pests in their native range.
comments.request: Consider this recording bias.
comments.quote: Line 310: isn’t there the option that those species are simply not recorded as pests in their native range?

comments.issue: The passage at line 311 should be moved to the discussion.
comments.request: Move it to the discussion.
comments.quote: Line 311 remove to discussion

comments.issue: The implication at lines 323-325 is trivial and confirmed by new pest species arriving constantly.
comments.request: Remove or reframe the trivial implication.
comments.quote: This is a trivial implication, which is confirmed by new pest species in new area all the time.

comments.issue: Figure 1 panels are difficult to read, with insufficient phylogeny information and similar colours.
comments.request: Improve readability, phylogeny information and colours.
comments.quote: Figure 1 a: This is difficult to read. I recommend an improvement adding more information on the phylogeny and using much better colorus, at the moment it seems to have all with similar colors.

comments.issue: Figure 2 has a typo ('counties') and unhelpful black dots.
comments.request: Fix the label and remove or improve the dots.
comments.quote: Figure 2: counties – countries, the black dots in the graphs are less helpful

reviews.assessment: Admirable use of a messy global dataset and new analyses, but not fully convinced by range-fill estimates and worried about missing-data biases.
strengths: admirable use of a messy global dataset

comments.issue: Range-fill estimates may be biased because pest geography is poorly represented and host breadth is measured at genus level.
comments.request: Use additional data sources or high-detection pests to assess missing-data biases.
comments.quote: I am skeptical of the measures of range fill (i.e. Fig 5). This is because there is good evidence, even within this study, that the geography of pests is often poorly represented in the dataset.

comments.issue: The 'pest' scope needs more attention because today's pests would not have met that definition before their introduction elsewhere.
comments.request: Define the pest scope more clearly.
comments.quote: The dataset used concerns ‘pest’ species, and I think this scope could use some greater attention

comments.issue: Exact numbers should be given at line 26.
comments.request: Give the exact numbers.
comments.quote: L26 maybe just give the exact numbers

comments.issue: The sentence at L69 mixes similarity and dissimilarity and is confusing.
comments.request: Simplify the wording.
comments.quote: L69: confusingly written, as have of the sentence is about similarity ‘share similar pest communities’, and half is about dissimilarity ‘decay in pest similarity’.

comments.issue: Gilbert and Webb concerns only pathogens; a citation on phylogenetic host breadth of herbivores is missing.
comments.request: Add a herbivore host-breadth citation (e.g. Gilbert et al. 2012).
comments.quote: Gilbert and Webb is really only about pathogens. Maybe add one citation about phylogenetic host breadth of herbivores

comments.issue: The pest scope likely overrepresents generalists and introduced species and implicitly excludes herbivores that could become pests.
comments.request: Define the scope explicitly and discuss this omission.
comments.quote: So, the scope of this paper and dataset is ‘pest’ species that are presumably defined in part based in parts on their ability to invade other places or cause noticeable or economic damage to plants.

comments.issue: Lumping all animals as 'metazoa' may be inappropriate; nematodes and arthropods may differ in responses and sampling biases.
comments.request: Treat or at least discuss these animal groups differently.
comments.quote: L121: are most of the ‘metazoa’ arthropods? I presume there are some nematodes as well, and it might make sense to treat those groups differently

comments.issue: Biogeographic realms are defined only by data source; what they are and why they matter is not stated.
comments.request: Explain the realms and their importance.
comments.quote: Biogeographic realms are defined in terms of their data source “using a polygon based on Olson et al”, but it is not stated what they are or why they are important.

comments.issue: The logic for excluding other portions of a pest's introduced range is unclear.
comments.request: Explain how introduced ranges are treated.
comments.quote: L191: Why? Are other portions of the introduced range of a pest excluded

comments.issue: Host breadth is counted as genera or species even though a host phylogeny exists; a continuous phylogenetic measure could be used.
comments.request: Consider representing host breadth as phylogenetic breadth.
comments.quote: I’m not sure why defining host breadth in terms of number of genera, or species is done when you have the phylogeny of the hosts.

comments.issue: For ~16% of pests the extreme scenario indicates poor completeness of host and biogeographic records, so percent-fill estimates may be off and sampling bias may affect other results.
comments.request: Assess and discuss the completeness and bias of the records.
comments.quote: The fact that this extreme scenario was the case for ~16% of pests certainly suggests that the ‘completeness’ of both host records and biogeographic records is rather poor.

comments.issue: The Fig. 1 network diagrams are hard to interpret, with unclear clustering versus randomness.
comments.request: Improve the caption or display, possibly as a bipartite network.
comments.quote: Personally, the network diagrams in Fig 1 do not do much for me.

comments.issue: Missing data and sampling biases may determine the absolute values of range fill in Fig. 5.
comments.request: Quantify the role of missing data in range fill.
comments.quote: I like the display of Fig 5, though I would question the role of missing data and sampling biases in determining the absolute values of range fill.

comments.issue: Table 2 values are much higher than Figure 5 medians; percent versus proportion is not made explicit.
comments.request: Use consistent units and cross-reference Figure 5.
comments.quote: I wonder why the values of host fill in table 2 are so much higher than median values in Figure 5.

comments.issue: The lack of explanatory power of geography and climate seems superficially at odds with low host geographic fill and needs differentiation.
comments.request: Explain what geographic distance and climate mean here and why this differs from host fill.
comments.quote: It might be worthwhile to differentiate this lack of explanatory power of ‘geographic distance’ and ‘climate’ with the notion of low geographic fill of host distribution because the two results seem superficially at odds.

comments.issue: The logic at L318-320 is hard to follow, especially the pest-host evolutionary relationships clause.
comments.request: Clarify the reasoning.
comments.quote: I do not follow this logic. I think it is the pest-host evolutionary relationships clause that confuses me as to what it means exactly.

comments.issue: The lines at L320-325 seem at odds with L317 and the disparity is not explained.
comments.request: Explain this disparity.
comments.quote: these are the lines that seem at odds with L317, and this disparity requires further explanation.

comments.issue: A discussion of macro-scale consequences of the patterns, such as invasion hotspots and pesticide use, is missing.
comments.request: Add a paragraph on macro-scale consequences.
comments.quote: I think I’d find it useful to have a paragraph somewhere in the discussion that considers macro-scale consequences of the patterns described here

title: Host phylogenetic diversity predicts the global extent and composition of tree pests

study.system: flower-visitor networks; global elevational and latitudinal gradients

editor_summary: Editor: split reviews; the elevational-specialization prediction is unsupported and the introduction must be rewritten from scratch; missing references; asymmetry and specificity measures need justification; nearly complete rewrite needed.

reviews.assessment: Timely question, but the dataset cannot test elevation gradients and the specialization indices are inadequate, making the conclusions unconvincing.

comments.issue: Data come from different sites at different elevations, so real differences across elevation gradients cannot be tested and noise dominates the models.
comments.request: Use data suitable for testing continuous elevation gradients.
comments.quote: my main concern on the study and interpretation of results is that the analyzed data do not allow testing for real differences across elevation gradients, as data come from different sites at different elevations, which certainly introduces much ‘noise’ into the models.

comments.issue: H2' measures selectiveness and asymmetry does not necessarily reflect interdependence, so neither adequately measures trophic specialization.
comments.request: Use normalized degree as a standardized niche-width estimate.
comments.quote: Moreover, I am not convinced that two of the three variables chosen (H2’, network asymmetry) are the most adequate to measure trophic specialization.

comments.issue: Important studies on distributional patterns of mutualistic networks are not cited.
comments.request: Search and cite the relevant elevational and latitudinal network literature.
comments.quote: Several important references of studies that have investigated distributional patterns of mutualistic networks are not cited, which is rather surprising in a review like this.

comments.issue: The expectation of high temperature overlap in temperate mountains lacks a rationale and relies only on Janzen 1967.
comments.request: Justify the expectation and cite newer studies.
comments.quote: You say that a “high overlap in temperature regimes between two adjacent habitats is expected in temperate mountain regions but not in the tropics”. What is the rationale of this expectation?

comments.issue: The mechanism linking higher climatic stability to lower specialization is unclear, and the reviewer would expect the opposite.
comments.request: Specify the mechanism clearly.
comments.quote: I think you should more clearly specify here which is the mechanism whereby a higher climatic stability is expected to result into a lower trophic specialization.

comments.issue: A large gap in cited evidence between 1967 and 2019 suggests relevant studies are missing.
comments.request: Cite intermediate studies on environmental conditions across elevations.
comments.quote: Again, I see a huge gap of information between 1967 and 2019. Are you sure there are no other studies in between that provide data on current and/or historical environmental conditions that vary differently across elevations?

comments.issue: The sentence at page 6, lines 35-40 is too complex.
comments.request: Simplify the sentence.
comments.quote: Page 6. Lines 35-40. Please simplify this sentence.

comments.issue: What fraction of networks found in the search the database represents is not stated.
comments.request: Report the database coverage fraction.
comments.quote: Page 7. Line 26. What fraction of networks does your database represent out of all those you found in your search?

comments.issue: Line numbering is difficult to follow and 'partners' is meant instead of 'patterns' (p.10 L18).
comments.quote: Page 10. Line 18. Do you mean interaction ‘partners’ instead of ‘patterns’?

comments.issue: Why network asymmetry is higher in temperate than tropical regions is not explained.
comments.request: Explain this asymmetry pattern.
comments.quote: Page 13. Line 27. Why do you think network asymmetry is higher in the temperate than in the tropical regions?

comments.issue: The title is misleading because the key index of niche overlap shows no pattern.
comments.request: Reconsider the title.
comments.quote: I actually think the title of the ms is misleading given this finding of ‘no pattern’.

comments.issue: The sentence at page 14, lines 16-23 is hard to understand.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence.
comments.quote: This sentence is hard to understand. I suggest rephrasing it.

comments.issue: The paragraph at page 15 repeats results without interpreting them or citing prior findings.
comments.request: Interpret the results and cite comparable studies.
comments.quote: This paragraph is actually a repetition of results with no discussion of them and no references of previous findings.

comments.issue: A more informative title could be extracted from the page 15 sentence.
comments.request: Consider a more informative title.
comments.quote: Page º5. Lines 16-20. From this sentence I think you could extract a more informative title for the ms than the current one.

comments.issue: Page 15, lines 23-28 are redundant with page 14 and the references appear too late.
comments.request: Remove the redundancy and move the references earlier.
comments.quote: Page 15. Lines 23-28. This is redundant with the sentence in lines 49-52 in page 14. The refs of Schleuning and Dalsgaard should have been mentioned earlier, contrasting to MacArthur’ findings.

comments.issue: The explanation for why H2 decreases with elevation only in the tropics is unconvincing and lacks references.
comments.request: Support the tropical-versus-nontropical migration argument with references.
comments.quote: The explanation you give for why H2 decreases with elevation only in the tropics is not sufficiently convincing, in my opinion.

comments.issue: Classen's study is tropical (Kilimanjaro) while Lara-Romero's is non-tropical (Canary Islands), so the comparison is incorrect.
comments.request: Correct the tropical/non-tropical attribution.
comments.quote: Page 15. Line 56. The study by Classen is performed in Kilimanjaro which is the tropics, but that of Lara-Romero is from the Canary islands, which is the non-tropics, so you need to correct this.

comments.issue: How results might change with only continuous elevation gradients is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the consequences of using continuous elevation gradients.
comments.quote: Page 16. Lines 18-23. This is precisely the main problem I mentioned before. I would thus like to see further discussion on how results might have changed if you had considered only studies performed at continuous elevation gradients.

comments.issue: Page 17, lines 9-14 are redundant.
comments.request: Avoid repeating results.
comments.quote: Page 17. Lines 9-14. Redundant sentences. Try to avoid repetition of results.

comments.issue: The claim that conditions predicting specialization can be identified is not supported; the dataset is too noisy.
comments.request: Temper the claim of predictability.
comments.quote: I think I disagree that your results ‘make it clear that it is possible to predict under what conditions we could find highly or poorly specialized plant-floral visitor interaction networks over environmental gradient. You have too much noise in your dataset, I am afraid.

comments.issue: References supporting the climatic stability statement are missing, including Pauw and Stanway 2015.
comments.request: Add supporting references.
comments.quote: Page 19. Lines 4-9. Where are the references to support this statement. At least one study (Pauw & Stanway 2015) claimed that higher climatic stability might allow ‘phenotypic and functional specialization to manifest and persist’.

comments.issue: Page 19, lines 14-23 are redundant.
comments.request: Remove the redundancy.
comments.quote: Page 19, Lines 14-23. Redundant sentences.

comments.issue: Disagrees that the approach can provide novel information on how environmental conditions influence species interactions.
comments.request: Soften or support this conclusion.
comments.quote: I am afraid I disagree with this conclusion from your study. To me, the approach is not adequate enough to provide ‘novel information’ on how environmental conditions influence species interactions.

reviews.assessment: Globally positive, but the core elevational prediction is not followed and the indices and writing need clarification.

comments.issue: The core prediction of tropical specialization decreasing with elevation is not derivable from the preceding text; Table 1 predictions are the opposite of a priori expectations.
comments.request: Clarify the hypotheses and note where opposite predictions exist.
comments.quote: I’m not following the core prediction that in the tropics, specialization will decrease toward high elevations, and in the temperate zone specialization won’t change with elevation (Intro last paragraph).

comments.issue: Only the animal side is relevant to trophic specialization, yet three indices including plant specialization and niche overlap are used without justification.
comments.request: Specify what each index measures and why plant-side measures are included.
comments.quote: The paper is about trophic specialization and uses networks between flowering plants and their floral visitors, but only one side of that relationship (animals specializing on plants) is relevant to trophic specialization (flowers are not eating animals).

comments.issue: The abstract implies latitude is continuous while it is treated as binary, confusing readers.
comments.request: State early that latitude is treated as categorical zones.
comments.quote: Abstract implies that paper is looking at latitude as continuous, (eg first sentence ‘across latitudes’). This created confusion for me (and skepticism that there would be enough geographic coverage) reading the intro until I figured out that authors treat latitude as binary variable.

comments.issue: The writing is hard to read; sentences need simplifying and paragraphs shortening.

comments.issue: The opening sentence at L7 is dense.

comments.issue: L14 is confusing about whether empirical support for MacArthur's hypothesis is mixed.

comments.issue: Coevolution would seem to require narrow trophic breadths, which is unclear at L28.

comments.issue: L30-32 assumes a pattern exists whereas the paragraph's first sentence proposes one.

comments.issue: 'Adjacent' at Pg5 L4 is ambiguous.

comments.issue: 'Specialised with elevation' at L39 is unclear.

comments.quote: L39 – what does ‘specialised with elevation’ mean? Toward higher elevations?

comments.issue: 'Plant-floral visitor networks' is awkward and the hyphen is misleading.

comments.quote: Is ‘plant-floral visitor networks’ is awkward, as the hyphen makes it seem like ‘plant-floral’ is one thing. Maybe just ‘plant-visitor networks’ or ‘flower-visitor networks’?

comments.issue: The change from 'temperate' to 'non-tropical' at Pg6 L28 is unexplained and less specific.

comments.issue: The intro sentences are hard to parse.
comments.request: Simplify the sentences.
comments.quote: Maybe I’m tired but I’m finding the sentences hard to parse in the Intro

comments.issue: Which previous hypotheses about NPP are meant at L40-44 is unclear.
comments.request: Specify the NPP hypotheses.
comments.quote: L40-44 – which previous hypotheses about NPP?

comments.issue: 'Community wide' is undefined.

comments.issue: Elevational ranges and means are more informative than the SD at L44.

comments.issue: 'Location' at Pg11 L39 is unclear, including how networks are assigned to the same site.

reviews.assessment: Supports the idea and hypotheses; only a few comments, made directly in the PDF.
strengths: idea supported by the presented hypotheses and theories
good work compiling, analyzing and summarizing the findings

title: Global trends in the trophic specialisation of flower‐visitor networks are explained by current and historical climate

study.system: woolly mammoth; process-explicit population models with fossil and ancient DNA data

editor_summary: Clearly strong reviewer support, no major changes required; a very nice piece of work the editor looks forward to seeing published.

reviews.assessment: Impressed by the impressive combination of state-of-the-art models and data; suggestions mainly to explain the workflow better.
strengths: impressive combination of state-of-the-art population modelling and diverse data

comments.issue: Abstract and introduction oversell process-explicit modelling and pattern-oriented validation; all models are calibrated somehow.
comments.request: Reduce emphasis on process-explicit modelling and validation terminology.
comments.quote: I would “sell” these technical modelling aspects (processes, pattern-oriented validation) a bit less and focus more on other aspects and the results.

comments.issue: Simulated mammoth population densities through time are not shown.
comments.request: Show simulated densities through time, perhaps as a supplementary animation.
comments.quote: Not only extinctions were simulated but also mammoth population densities, would be exciting to also show these through time, maybe with an animation as supplement.

comments.issue: Relationship to the closely related Fordham and Brown 2020 bioRxiv paper is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the relationship to the earlier bioRxiv paper.
comments.quote: I am confused about the relationship between it and the manuscript here. I think that should be clarified.

comments.issue: Model description lacks a parameter table with fitted values, priors, and sources.
comments.request: Add a parameter table with fitted values, priors, and sources.
comments.quote: It would be nice to include a table with the parameter list and fitted parameter values, maybe also prior values and sources for these

comments.issue: Niche concept unclear; what a potential realized niche is, and whether merged time slices approximate the fundamental niche.

comments.issue: Supplementary niche figure shows only standardized values, not absolute numbers.

comments.issue: Sentence on upper mammoth abundance and a rate of four animals lacks units and a time frame.

reviews.assessment: Very nice modelling paper; only minor concern about flat posterior distributions and correlated parameters in the ABC approach.

novel demonstration that human effects are older than thought

comments.issue: Posterior distributions in Fig. 1 are flat, indicating wide uncertainty over parameter values that fit the patterns.

comments.issue: Correlated parameters within the selected set could yield equally good fits with different ecological interpretations.

title: Process‐explicit models reveal pathway to extinction for woolly mammoth using pattern‐oriented validation

study.system: Pseudomonas communities; in vitro invasion and supernatant assays

editor_summary: Both reviewers find the problem interesting but request clarifications; editor agrees the term 'public bad' sounds unnatural and says the manuscript needs more work.

reviews.assessment: Novel and enjoyable study, but several results are interpreted as public good activity without direct support, raising doubts about the interpretation.
strengths: novel idea not experimentally tested before
of interest to microbiologists and ecologists

comments.issue: Positive Fig 3A relationship is called public goods although resident pyoverdines did not promote invader growth.
comments.request: Clarify why this pattern is interpreted as public good activity.
comments.quote: strictly speaking resident pyoverdines did not promote invader growth as growth was typically lower in co-cultures versus mono-cultures

comments.issue: Cases with invader success above 1 may be noise; models used medians/means without replication of clones or communities.
comments.request: Include replication of individual clones/communities in the models.
comments.quote: in the few cases where invader success > 1, this could be due to noise as the authors did not include replication of individual clones/communities in the models

comments.issue: Net interference is claimed under iron limitation although invaders invade better there (Fig 4B).
comments.request: Reconcile the net interference reasoning with the invasion results.
comments.quote: Another concern is the authors' reasoning that there is net interference against invaders under iron-limited conditions compared to iron-rich condition, yet the invader invades better under iron-limited conditions

comments.issue: No direct support for interference competition; patterns could equally result from resource competition.
comments.request: Acknowledge resource competition and simplify the introduction accordingly.
comments.quote: the data do not provide any direct support for such interference competition. In other words, the observed patterns could equally likely result from resource competition

comments.issue: Invader success might increase if the probability of matching pyoverdines rises with diversity.
comments.request: Consider this additional expectation in the introduction.
comments.quote: In theory, one might also expect invader success to increase if the probability of matching pyoverdines increases with diversity?

comments.issue: Lines 105-106 phrasing is awkward and overstates promotion of invader growth.
comments.request: Rephrase this passage.
comments.quote: This phrasing is a little awkward – resident pyoverdines did not actually promote invader growth as it is typically lower in co- versus monoculture.

comments.issue: Plate setup and number of isolates per community are not fully described.
comments.request: Clarify replication and how isolates were grouped on plates.
comments.quote: Please clarify that growth and pyoverdine was measured for ALL 160 isolates in four-fold replication, but that isolates were grouped on plates depending on their community origin.

comments.issue: Replicate number for the control is not specified.
comments.request: Specify the control replicate number.
comments.quote: Line 152 – Please specify replicate number for the control.

comments.issue: It is unclear why medians rather than all data were used and how variable replicates were.
comments.request: Explain the use of medians and replicate variation.
comments.quote: Throughout the manuscript, why were medians used and not all data in subsequent analyses? Was there a lot of variation between replicates?

comments.issue: Definition at line 159 differs from the Figure 2 legend.
comments.request: Make the definition consistent.
comments.quote: This definition differ from that given in the legend of Figure 2. Please clarify.

comments.issue: Assembly of the second 10-resident group is not explained.
comments.request: Clarify how the second set of residents was assembled.
comments.quote: Please clarify how the second set of the 10-resident group was assembled for each community (when presumably there were 20 isolates per community to start of with).

comments.issue: Whether OD600 includes invader cells and how this was corrected is unclear.
comments.request: Explain whether and how invader cells were corrected for.
comments.quote: I presume the OD600 includes invader cells. It is not clear from the current description whether /how this was corrected for?

comments.issue: Type of sums of squares used in Anova() is not specified; default type II ignores interactions.
comments.request: Specify the sums of squares type used.
comments.quote: please specify which type of sums of squares were used when determining the significance of explanatory variables using Anova()

comments.issue: Multiple testing correction for post-hoc comparisons is not clarified.
comments.request: State whether post-hoc comparisons correct for multiple testing.
comments.quote: Does the summary function correct for multiple testing when performing post-hoc comparisons between levels of significant treatments with more than two categories?

comments.issue: Response variable for LMM 2 is not stated in the statistics section.
comments.request: Add the LMM 2 response variable.
comments.quote: The statistics section would benefit from adding which response variable is used in LMM 2 (e.g. GE treatment).

comments.issue: Unclear whether line 221 refers to total pyoverdine production.
comments.request: Clarify whether this is total pyoverdine.
comments.quote: Line 221: Is this total pyoverdine production?

comments.issue: No mention of diagnostic plots; figures suggest heteroscedasticity may violate assumptions.
comments.request: Report model diagnostics and address heteroscedasticity.
comments.quote: Were diagnostics plots used to check residual behaviour in each of the fitted models. Looking at the distribution of data in the Figures, there is the potential for heteroscedasticity, which would violate model assumption?

comments.issue: Main effects are stated although interactions are significant and effects vary across levels.
comments.request: Be cautious about interpreting main effects with significant interactions.
comments.quote: I would be a bit cautious stating something about the main effect when interactions are significant, as the effect varies across levels of other explanatory variables

comments.issue: Iron-limited focus is only mentioned later; it should be stated at the start of the section.
comments.request: State at the start that these data are iron-limited.
comments.quote: Please state that these data focus on iron-limited conditions (it is mentioned later but it would be beneficial to state this as the start of this section).

comments.issue: Unclear whether line 306 refers to total pyoverdine.
comments.request: Clarify whether this is total pyoverdine.
comments.quote: Lines 306: is this total pyoverdine?

comments.issue: Resident number effect differs between analyses and is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the discrepancy between the two analyses.
comments.quote: I was wondering why resident number has an effect on invasion success (when there are no significant interactions between resident number and other explanatory variables), but not when analysing the relationship between invasion success and GEnet in iron-limited conditions?

comments.issue: Different analyses on the same dataset give different resident number findings, unexplained.
comments.request: Clarify why the analyses differ.
comments.quote: Different analyses on the same dataset show different findings in terms of how resident number affects invasion success, and it is not immediately clear why this is.

comments.issue: Text seems inconsistent with Figure 3, which shows negative and non-significant effects.
comments.request: Clarify the discrepancy with Figure 3.
comments.quote: This is slightly confusing as Figure 3 shows a negative effect of invader pyoverdine on resident growth for individual clones and a non-significant effect for communities??

comments.issue: Key additional analyses are hidden in the supplement, and the model description is confusing.
comments.request: Move these analyses into the main text.
comments.quote: Rather than being hidden away in the supplementary material, why not show these additional analyses in the main text?

comments.issue: Description of the supplementary model's non-linear decrease is ambiguous.
comments.request: Clarify what the non-linear decrease means.
comments.quote: Does this mean that 'the effect of resident pyoverdines decreases' or that 'higher producers have a stronger negative effect' on invaders?

comments.issue: Table legends lack model descriptions; random effect structure after simplification is unclear.
comments.request: Describe the models and random effects in the table legends.
comments.quote: The table legends would benefit from a brief description of the models used. It is also not clear whether these models still have a random effect structure following model simplification.

comments.issue: Unclear whether figures show means/medians per strain or community.
comments.request: State what the plotted values represent.
comments.quote: I presume that in each of the figures the means/median for each strain/community is given?

comments.issue: Text gives a slightly different calculation for the net effect than Figure 2.
comments.request: Check and align the net effect calculation.
comments.quote: Figure 2. Please check why text gives slightly different calculation for net effect (-1).

comments.issue: Figure 3 panel A-B labels may be reversed relative to panels C-D.
comments.request: Check the panel labels.
comments.quote: Is there a type in the labels of the panels (should effect of invader versus resident be reversed as show in panels C-D).

comments.issue: Figure 4 caption repeats descriptions of lines and shaded areas that do not match.
comments.request: Fix the repeated, inconsistent caption text.
comments.quote: Figure 4. Lines 637-641: Description of lines and shaded areas repeated and not the same.

reviews.assessment: Interesting study making a compelling case for siderophores' key role, but the public good/bad duality conclusion and some patterns need clarification.
strengths: compelling case that siderophores play a key role
clear rationale for supernatant and media combinations

comments.issue: Concluding that siderophores act as both public goods and public bads is not supported.
comments.request: Temper or better support the dual-role conclusion.
comments.quote: I don't think that it is correct to conclude that your results show siderophores can be both public goods and public bads, depending on the specific gxg interaction.

comments.issue: No analyses on replicate measures show supernatant effects differ from neutral.
comments.request: Test supernatant effects against neutral using replicate measures.
comments.quote: There does not appear to be any analyses on replicate measures of a given isolate to show that the effects of supernatant are different from neutral.

comments.issue: Fig 2A variances differ strongly between treatments even after transformation.
comments.request: Explain how unequal variances are handled in the linear model.
comments.quote: Variances are very different between the key treatments (iron-limited vs others), even after transformation. Please briefly explain how this is taken into account in your linear model.

comments.issue: Positive growth-pyoverdine correlation in rich media for soil isolates is surprising and unexplained.
comments.request: Explain this pattern and reconcile it with the narrative.
comments.quote: Any thoughts about why growth is positively correlated with pyoverdine levels in rich media for soil isolates?

comments.issue: Easier invasion under iron limitation despite inhibitory siderophores contradicts the main conclusion.
comments.request: Explain this contradiction with the main conclusion.
comments.quote: why it is easier to invade under iron-limited condition (Fig 4), despite, based on the supernatant assays, siderophores having an inhibitory effect on invaders (Fig 2)?

comments.issue: Rationale for supernatant and media combinations belongs in the methods.
comments.request: Include this rationale in the methods.
comments.quote: You explain the rationale behind the use of the different combinations of supernatant and media in fig 2 really clearly. Could you include this in the methods, please?

comments.issue: New supplementary results introduced in the discussion make it hard to follow.
comments.request: Include all results in the results section.
comments.quote: Lots of new SI results are introduced in discussion. This made it quite hard to follow the discussion in places. Please include all results in the results section.

comments.issue: 'Resident number' is ambiguous and could mean density; 'resident diversity' is preferable.
comments.request: Use 'resident diversity' instead of 'resident number'.
comments.quote: Stick with resident diversity and not resident number. The latter is ambiguous, and could mean density.

title: Siderophores drive invasion dynamics in bacterial communities through their dual role as public good versus public bad

study.system: Arid-region sociable weavers; 7-year nest predator-exclusion experiment

editor_summary: Editor reports positive reviews but flags concerns about the presentation of the statistics, the climatic window, the conclusions and the novelty of certain aspects.

reviews.assessment: An excellent, rigorous long-term study; questions the breeding timing, a clutch exclusion and several literature connections.
strengths: separates direct and indirect temperature effects

comments.issue: Most nests are active at temperatures above peak success, and the seasonal timing of breeding is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain why birds breed at adverse temperatures, e.g., food abundance.
comments.quote: Why do they wait to breed during such temperatures given the high failure?

comments.issue: The prediction of no nest predation effect contradicts the earlier argument that groups may reduce predation.
comments.request: Reconcile the prediction with the introduction's argument.
comments.quote: the prediction of no nest predation effect here seems counter to this earlier argument.

comments.issue: It is unclear why nests losing full clutches of eggs were excluded from the predation analysis.
comments.request: Justify the exclusion of full-clutch disappearances.
comments.quote: I don’t understand why disappearance of full clutches of eggs were excluded? Isn’t this nest predation and contribute to understanding temperature effects on predation probability?

comments.issue: The age of predated nests may show that the relevant Tmax window is simply nest initiation.
comments.request: Report the average age of predated nests.
comments.quote: I wonder what is the average age of nests that are predated? If average age of predation is around 16-18 days, then this again suggests temperature at the start of nesting is key.

comments.issue: The statement that snakes are the main nest predators overgeneralizes across systems.
comments.request: Write this statement more circumspectly.
comments.quote: Write this with a little more circumspect. Snakes are the main predators in SOME systems, but not in many systems.

comments.issue: Drought, which can be confounded with temperature, has been found to increase nest predation and is not cited.
comments.request: Add these references to set up the similar result.
comments.quote: it might be worth pointing out here that drought conditions, which can be confounded with temperature, have been found to increase nest predation

comments.issue: The Cunningham citation is missing at Lines 361-362.
comments.request: Add the Cunningham citation.
comments.quote: Line 361,362 – also the Cunningham citation.

comments.issue: The fledging-probability decline matches the Cunningham et al. heat threshold, which is not noted.
comments.request: Note the similar threshold temperature.
comments.quote: they found 33C to be a threshold for fiscal shrikes (although 35.5 for babblers) where detrimental heat effects started most strongly

reviews.assessment: Finds the results hard to follow and the climate-window justification unclear, and questions the missed literature and whether effects are fully separated.

comments.issue: The climate windows are not justified clearly and the results lose the biological trends.
comments.request: Clarify the window justification and ground results in biology.
comments.quote: Justification of the climate windows needs to be clearer: it is difficult to compare between the results and ground them in biological reality as currently written

comments.issue: Key recent literature on group size and climate is missed, weakening the novelty claims.
comments.request: Cite Bourne et al. 2020, Guindre-Parker and Rubenstein 2019 and meerkat papers.
comments.quote: there is a 2020 paper in this journal, Ecology Letters, that shows that group size does not mediate the climate effects on a species that is experiencing a similar climate to the sociable weavers

comments.issue: The claim that physiological effects are hard to separate from nest predation is questionable given measurable physiology.
comments.request: Reconsider this statement.
comments.quote: I don’t quite understand this statement that it is hard to separate physiological effects on individuals from nest predation.

comments.issue: The expectation of weaker predation effects in larger groups contradicts the earlier argument that large groups attract predators.
comments.request: Reconcile this prediction with the introduction.
comments.quote: why do the authors expect a less marked effect of predation in larger groups? As stated earlier in the introduction, large groups may actually attract more predators due to greater activity at the nest/burrow etc.

comments.issue: 'Windows' is not defined at L130.
comments.request: Define what windows means here.
comments.quote: what is meant by ‘windows’ here?

comments.issue: How predation reduction in the group-size subset was measured is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain how predation reduction was measured and nest checking frequency.
comments.quote: I’m not sure what it means by predation being reduced in the subset with information about group size? How was the predation reduction measured?

comments.issue: 'Prospecting visit' is not defined.
comments.request: Define prospecting visit.
comments.quote: what is a prospecting visit?

comments.issue: Only two possible fates for protected colonies is inconsistent with predation not being eliminated.
comments.request: Explain how predation is handled as a fate.
comments.quote: You have stated above the predation was reduced, but not eliminated at protected colonies. Therefore predation is still a potential outcome for these colonies.

comments.issue: It is unclear how modifying the model enables studying the group-size effect.
comments.request: Explain this modelling step.
comments.quote: unclear how doing this to the model allows you to study the effect of group size?

comments.issue: The statistical methods lack detail on correlated terms, model selection and random terms.
comments.request: Provide full statistical model details.
comments.quote: More details are needed for the statistical analysis: how were correlated terms dealt with? Are analyses conducted via model selection? Are there random terms?

comments.issue: 'Used nest' is not defined.
comments.request: Define used nest.
comments.quote: what is a used nest?

comments.issue: The climate-window selection may force a significant window and must be shown to be robust for the group-size result.
comments.request: Demonstrate the robustness of window selection.
comments.quote: As in, it forces a significant window period to be considered even if this window is not more important statistically than other potential climate windows?

comments.issue: 'Scaled' is not explained at L208.
comments.request: Explain how variables were scaled.
comments.quote: L208: scaled in what way?

comments.issue: The relevance of the interaction at L212 to the question is unclear.
comments.request: Make the relevance of this interaction clearer.
comments.quote: it’s unclear how this interaction is related to the current question though? Perhaps make this clearer

comments.issue: It is unclear why ejection is a good measure of the group-size effect.
comments.request: Justify ejection as a measure.
comments.quote: ejection has been mentioned several times, and here it is used as a measure of the group size effect on reproductive success. Why is ejection a good measure of this?

comments.issue: Group ID was not included as a random term despite repeated breeding attempts.
comments.request: Justify the random-effects structure.
comments.quote: why was group ID not a random term? Where there no pairs/groups that occurred over more than one breeding attempt?

comments.issue: How rain and Tmax were measured or averaged over the window is not stated.
comments.request: Describe the climatic variable measurements clearly.
comments.quote: How were rain and Tmax measured? Averaged over the each chosen time window? I don’t find this clearly stated in the methods.

comments.issue: The main take-home message of the paragraph at L222-226 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the message of this paragraph.
comments.quote: it’s unclear what the main take-home message of this paragraph is.

comments.issue: Results paragraphs do not refer to the tables showing the main results.
comments.request: Cite the relevant tables in all results paragraphs.
comments.quote: Please refer to the tables that show the main results stated

comments.issue: Opening and closing days relative to the fate date are not explained.
comments.request: Explain the fate date and window notation.
comments.quote: what does opening 39 and closing 2 days before the fate date mean? When is the fate date? Is it always the same?

comments.issue: Linear and quadratic models give non-overlapping windows; which reflects biological reality is unclear.
comments.request: State which window is most biologically plausible.
comments.quote: Linear and quadratic models predicted non-overlapping windows that impacted offspring survival the most – which one is most likely to reflect biological reality?

comments.issue: 'Found window' is not defined.
comments.request: Define found window.
comments.quote: what is a ‘found window’?

comments.issue: A statement at L283 lacks a statistic.
comments.request: Provide a statistic for this statement.
comments.quote: please provide a stat for this statement.

comments.issue: 'Statistically clearer' is undefined at L291.
comments.request: Explain what statistically clearer means.
comments.quote: L291: what does ‘statistically clearer’ mean?

comments.issue: The claim that direct and indirect effects are separated is not convincing.
comments.request: Strengthen or qualify the separation of effects.
comments.quote: I’m not convinced that these effects have been fully separated

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the conclusion at L332 holds specifically under high predation or overall.
comments.request: Clarify the scope of this conclusion.
comments.quote: I’m not sure you can conclude this from the analysis: are you saying that specifically under high predation pressure, you observe this effect? Or overall?

comments.issue: Recent papers on heat effects on arid-zone bird physiology are not cited.
comments.request: Cite Cooper et al. 2020 and Moagi et al. 2021.
comments.quote: see also Cooper et al 2020 and Moagi et al 2021 for detrimental effects of heat on physiology in arid-zone birds

comments.issue: Table outputs omit confidence intervals and standardized effect sizes.
comments.request: Report CIs and standardized effect sizes in the tables.
comments.quote: the confidence intervals and the standardized effect sizes are not given, so the reader cannot see if these intersect zero or not.

reviews.assessment: Enthusiastic; found the results interesting conceptually and for conservation, the effects large and the time-window analysis sophisticated.
strengths: very interesting conceptually and for conservation

title: Disentangling climatic and nest predator impact on reproductive output reveals adverse high‐temperature effects regardless of helper number in an arid‐region cooperative bird

study.system: agricultural landscapes; spatially explicit social-ecological model

editor_summary: Three referees found much to like but had several suggestions and criticisms to address carefully.

reviews.assessment: Interesting model with clear writing, but key assumptions need justification and the presentation needs better guidance.
strengths: interesting results from the modeling effort

comments.issue: Major assumptions about socio-ecological systems, including landscape-wide decision-making and perception-based rather than profit-based choices, are not acknowledged or justified.
comments.request: Justify these assumptions with empirical evidence and reconsider them.
comments.quote: there are some major assumptions about socio-ecological systems built into the model that need to be better acknowledged and justified

comments.issue: The model goals appear only at the end of the Methods and the specific scenarios are never spelled out, making the Results hard to interpret.
comments.request: Lead with the goals and describe the scenarios explicitly.
comments.quote: goals of the model are not described until the end of the Methods (p.6, lines 16-20) and there is no explicit mention of the specific scenarios of interest

comments.issue: Foundational landscape-ecology work on percolation thresholds and aggregation is ignored, obscuring what is actually novel.
comments.request: Acknowledge prior work and highlight the novel societal feedbacks.
comments.quote: It would be useful to be clear how some elements shown in the model have long been known (e.g., percolation thresholds and aggregation), which will better highlight what is novel here

comments.issue: The assumption that ecosystem service magnitude scales with area needs justification.
comments.request: Provide evidence or justify the scaling.
comments.quote: it would be useful to better justify why the magnitude of ecosystem services would scale with area. Is there any evidence to support this claim?

comments.issue: The closest-neighbor assumption is critical for the percolation results but is only briefly justified.
comments.request: Add justification for this formulation.
comments.quote: This assumption about closest neighbors is critical as it is the underlying mechanism

comments.issue: Equation 1 appears to sum over all natural cells despite the closest-neighbor rule; the main-text description is inaccurate.
comments.request: Correct the equation description in the main text.
comments.quote: Without referencing the Appendix, this equation appears off to me as the summation implies adding across all natural cells N although the sentence previous to the equation states that only closest neighbors are considered

comments.issue: Equation 3 uses total resource production as carrying capacity, whose units are individuals, without clarifying in the main text.
comments.request: Clarify the carrying capacity term briefly.
comments.quote: This equation appears to use the total resource production as a carrying capacity term, yet carrying capacity is typically in units of individuals

comments.issue: Whether the assumption at p.5, lines 44-46 happens empirically and over what timescale is unclear.
comments.request: Provide empirical support and timescales.
comments.quote: This assumption appears reasonable but is there any evidence empirically that this actually happens and if so, across what time scale

comments.issue: The percolation transition is first mentioned without explanation for a general audience.
comments.request: Describe what a percolation transition is.
comments.quote: I believe this is the first mention of a ‘percolation transition’. The authors need to better describe what this is for a general audience.

comments.issue: The percolation transition is likely sensitive to the habitat aggregation assumption and the scale of ecosystem service provision.
comments.request: Discuss this sensitivity.
comments.quote: I would imagine that this transition is very sensitive to not only the assumption about habitat aggregation but also about the scale of ecosystem service provision (eq 1).

comments.issue: Land-sharing versus sparing is not simply intensification versus extensification and clustering; crop yields and biodiversity are not modeled.
comments.request: Develop this discussion more fully.
comments.quote: Land-sharing v sparing is not simply intensification v extensification and clustering.

comments.issue: The Discussion is too long and could be shortened to make room for methods and scenarios.
comments.request: Shorten the Discussion and cut redundant paragraphs.
comments.quote: Overall, the Discussion is too long. It would be better to shorten and use some of this word count to better explain the Methods/scenarios

comments.issue: The result at p.8, lines 26-27 is a direct outcome of model structure rather than an emergent effect.
comments.request: Acknowledge the model-structure origin of the result.
comments.quote: This result appears to be a direct outcome of the model structure rather than any sort of emergent effect.

comments.issue: The percolation effects depend on the assumed scale of connectivity in the model.
comments.request: Mention this scale dependence.
comments.quote: I would imagine that the potential for the observed percolation effects will largely depend on the assumed scale at which connectivity plays out in this model.

comments.issue: Other studies, such as Finch et al. (2021), have shown similar aggregation results.
comments.request: Cite the related studies.
comments.quote: There have been other studies that show similar results regarding aggregation. See, e.g., Finch et al. (2021, J. Appl. Ecol.).

comments.issue: Two line-level wording suggestions (p.2 line 38 'lower'; p.4 line 11 'how they flow').
comments.quote: p.2, line 38. Consider changing ‘smaller’ to ‘lower’.

reviews.assessment: Interesting model but the novelty of the percolation application is misrepresented and the paper does not target the journal's readership.
strengths: interesting topic of intensive vs extensive agriculture

comments.issue: The paper implies that applying percolation theory to ecology is new while decades of prior ecological percolation work is uncited.
comments.request: Cite the foundational percolation-in-ecology literature.
comments.quote: By not citing these and other papers on percolation theory applied to ecology, the authors are very deceptive.

comments.issue: The conceptual framework is not accessible to a general ecology audience and the paper seems directed elsewhere.
comments.request: Refocus the introduction and discussion on core ecological concepts and fragmentation, citing Fahrig 2019.
comments.quote: the manuscript would require significant clarification of the conceptual framework of the study to be accessible to a general ecology audience

comments.issue: The assumptions in the Methods are made without citations or clarification, and results would change under different assumptions.
comments.request: Justify and cite each assumption.
comments.quote: it is not clear to me how or why did they make all the assumptions in the Methods section without giving citations or clarification

comments.issue: A schematic or conceptual figure of the model is missing.
comments.request: Add a conceptual model figure.
comments.quote: A schematic figure of the model or conceptual description of the model would help audiences to understand their model better.

comments.issue: The discussion is difficult to follow and crams too much material together.
comments.request: Divide it into sections and add a part for a general audience.
comments.quote: I generally find the discussion difficult to follow and they tried to put so many materials there.

comments.issue: Why human demography is important is not explained before its introduction.
comments.request: Explain its importance earlier.
comments.quote: Why is human demography important? It is not explained in previous paragraphs.

comments.issue: How each land-use type was defined is not explained.
comments.request: Define the land-use types.
comments.quote: Page 3 line 57: How did you define each type of land use?

comments.issue: The choice of 0.6 as a threshold is not justified.
comments.request: Justify the threshold.
comments.quote: I may miss some information, but why chose 0.6 as a threshold?

comments.issue: The parameter values in Table 1 are not justified.
comments.request: Provide a brief justification for the parameter values.
comments.quote: I would appreciate a brief justification for the parameter values that are chosen.

comments.issue: Figure labels are too small.
comments.request: Increase the figure label size.
comments.quote: Figure labels are quite too small.

reviews.assessment: Interesting coupled model; asks for more clarity and justification in the main text.
strengths: interesting model of coupled land-use and population dynamics
demonstrates effects of intensification and clustering

comments.issue: The power-law function with exponent below 1 needs more background and justification.
comments.request: Justify the power-law form and reference the appendix.
comments.quote: why a power-law function with z < 1. Please provide some more background and justification

comments.issue: Equation 1 requires more information, including the missing index subscript.
comments.request: Add the missing notation and explanation.
comments.quote: Although referred to details in Appendix 1, equation 1 requires some more information.

comments.issue: A conceptual figure summarizing cover-type dynamics and dependencies is missing.
comments.request: Add a conceptual figure.
comments.quote: The model description would benefit from a conceptual figure

comments.issue: Details on the clustering are missing from the main text.
comments.request: Describe the clustering in the main text.
comments.quote: Please provide more details on the clustering already in the main text as this is fundamental for understanding your results.

comments.issue: Starting values, simulation time and sensitivity analysis details are not provided.
comments.request: Report these simulation details.
comments.quote: More information on starting values of your simulations (with reference to Appendix 2, Table 1), simulation time and sensitivity analysis (specifically steps sizes when varying α, σ and ω) should be provided.

comments.issue: The choice of a 40 x 40 grid and how grid size affects results is not justified.
comments.request: Justify the grid size and test its effect.

comments.issue: Replicate numbers differ greatly across figures (10-100) without explanation.
