title: Habitat percolation transition undermines sustainability in social‐ecological agricultural systems

study.system: Yellowstone aspen; long-term browsing and regeneration surveys

editor_summary: Editor: important paper, but the conclusions need to be less vague (cascade weaker, patchier and slower) and the introduction framed more neutrally; notes risk of a technical comment.

reviews.assessment: Appropriate and impressively large study; recommends rebalancing the abstract and developing the authors' own results more, including whether a cascade still occurs.

comments.issue: The Abstract focuses on problems with earlier work and says little about the authors' approach and findings.
comments.request: Rebalance the abstract towards methods and key findings.
comments.quote: The Abstract focuses on problems with earlier work, and presents little about the authors’ approach and major findings.

comments.issue: Lines 17-22 ignore the large literature on aquatic trophic cascades, which occur at large scales with vertebrate predators.
comments.request: Acknowledge this literature.
comments.quote: This text does disservice (ignores) the large body of literature on trophic cascades in aquatic systems

comments.issue: 'Tree-size' at line 125 is undefined.
comments.request: Define tree-size.
comments.quote: Line 125. Define “tree-size”

comments.issue: The discussion of stand genetic uniqueness says nothing about genetic variation within stands or clonal structure.
comments.request: Report whether stands are single or multiple clones.
comments.quote: But what about genetic variation within stands? Are stands single or multiple clones?

comments.issue: The recruitment threshold at line 158 is given as '200-cm or 300-cm', which is confusing about which value was used when.
comments.request: Clarify the BEH threshold used.
comments.quote: about a stem being considered recruited if it exceeded a BEH of “200-cm or 300-cm” is confusing

comments.issue: Fig. 2 shows three shades but the colour key gives only two.
comments.request: Fix the colour key.
comments.quote: What do the three different shades/colors indicate? The color key shows only two. This is confusing!

comments.issue: The paper refutes existing dogma but does not develop the results and implications of its own datasets.
comments.request: Develop the authors' own findings more fully.
comments.quote: I would have appreciated, however, more development of the results and implications of their own datasets

comments.issue: It remains unclear whether aspen recruitment is happening at all and whether a slower cascade exists.
comments.request: Clarify whether evidence supports a weaker trophic cascade.
comments.quote: what remains a bit unclear is whether it is happening at all

comments.issue: The parallel willow-beaver-elk cascade in the park is not discussed.
comments.request: Comment on whether that cascade may also be overestimated.
comments.quote: I would appreciate the authors’comments on what is happening with another trophic cascade occurring in the park

reviews.assessment: Striking, accurate results that must be published; only minor writing and clarification requests.
strengths: first rigorous test of the 5 tallest stems approach

comments.issue: Paragraph 2 would be more effective if it first introduced published results before raising bias concerns.
comments.request: Open with what published results report, then identify issues.
comments.quote: Paragraph 2 would be more effective if there was an introduction to the results from various studies before voicing concern about bias.

comments.issue: The wording at L26 is clunky.
comments.request: Use 'the hypothesis states' or 'speculates'.
comments.quote: You could say the hypothesis states, or speculates

comments.issue: Moose and bison are also important browsers, and moose browse higher than 2 m.
comments.request: Mention moose and bison alongside elk.
comments.quote: you might mention that moose are also now important browsers, and bison has always been important browsers

comments.issue: The 5 tallest stems are a tiny tail of the distribution and may be inaccessible in deadfall tangles.
comments.request: Acknowledge that 5T stems do not represent the majority of plants.
comments.quote: the 5 tallest likely will not represent the majority of plants in a stand and form a tiny tail on a long distribution of short plants

comments.issue: 'Customary' is inappropriate and 'principled sampling' is unclear.
comments.request: Use a term such as 'objective sampling'.
comments.quote: I suggest not using the world customary, because plant ecologists do not collect or analyze data in such a manner.

comments.issue: The description at L121-123 confusingly mixes plots, transects and stands.
comments.request: Simplify the sampling description.
comments.quote: this is a bit confusing - you have plots, transects and stands

comments.issue: What was measured for browsing (browsed or unbrowsed) at L133 is unclear.
comments.request: State exactly what browsing measurement was taken.
comments.quote: Not sure what you mean we measured browsing (browsed or unbrowsed). What did you measure?

comments.issue: The terms at L146 are not defined.
comments.request: Define these terms.
comments.quote: L146 it might be useful to define these terms,

comments.issue: The statement at L211 attributes inference to random stems rather than to the stand.
comments.request: Say stems were more characteristic of 5T stems than the stand.
comments.quote: Since the random stems provide inference to the stand

comments.issue: Willows and other browsed woody plants tell a nearly identical story but are not highlighted.
comments.request: Highlight findings for willows (Marshall et al. 2013) and other woody plants.
comments.quote: it might be useful to highlight what has been found with willows (Marshall et al. 2013) and other woody plants

comments.issue: The bottom right panel of Figure 1 would be easier to interpret with a photo base.
comments.request: Add a photo base to Figure 1.
comments.quote: A photo base would help improve the interpretation of figure 1, bottom right panel.

comments.issue: Figure 2 panels lack the years 2007 and 2017, so the A-C and B-D differences are hard to interpret.
comments.request: Add the years to the panels or caption.
comments.quote: Might consider adding the years, 2007 and 2017 to the panels as its not easy to interpret from the panels themselves

reviews.assessment: Well-written and important contribution; wants a stronger, more direct conclusion about whether wolves caused a trophic cascade.
strengths: contributes important insights to a central discussion

comments.issue: The paper does not directly answer whether wolves caused a trophic cascade, which is what will draw readers.
comments.request: Tell readers more directly why or why not this question can be answered.
comments.quote: The question that will draw many readers to this study is whether wolves did or did nor cause a trophic cascade in Yellowstone.

comments.issue: The longstanding debate at line 23 is not explained soon enough.
comments.request: State what the debate centres on right after mentioning it.
comments.quote: what is the longstanding debate? Authors should get there soon (like the next line) after declaring there is a debate

comments.issue: The assumption discussed at line 35 is too specific without broader context.
comments.request: Broaden it to non-random sampling as a field measure of browsing pressure.
comments.quote: there were a number of assumptions in the Yellowstone debate, and this one is very specific without further context

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the time series follows the same individual stems or newly sampled ones at each step.
comments.request: Clarify the sampling design of the time series.
comments.quote: its not clear, as written, that the time series data that the authors are referring to are for the same individual tree stems, or randomly re-sampled at each step in the time series

comments.issue: The implications of the sampling misrepresentation for understanding wolf effects need a more specific argument.
comments.request: Explain specifically how the bias changes the apparent wolf effect.
comments.quote: can the authors more clearly describe here what the implications of the misrepresentation are for understanding the effects of wolves on aspen

comments.issue: Temporal autocorrelation at line 159 is not addressed, so the response is not independent across years.
comments.request: Address temporal autocorrelation.
comments.quote: how was temporal autocorrelation addressed here? If year is the predictor, the response variable is not independent in year t and year t+1

comments.issue: The findings' relation to the introduction's debate (weaker but still present cascade) is not stated.
comments.request: Clarify which side the findings support.
comments.quote: the authors are simply claiming that the effect size is weaker than previously reported, say nothing directly about whether their findings support one side or the other in the debate

comments.issue: The paragraph at line 325 is very difficult to follow.
comments.request: Rephrase for clarity.
comments.quote: I really struggled to follow this paragraph and don’t have suggestions to improve it

comments.issue: The claim that principled sampling equals random sampling and that 5T is not principled needs citations.
comments.request: Bolster the claim with citations.
comments.quote: it is worth bolstering the claim (with citations etc) that principled sampling is the same as ‘random sampling’ and that 5T sampling is NOT principled

title: Sampling bias exaggerates a textbook example of a trophic cascade

study.system: Brachypodium distachyon rhizosphere microbiota; 10-generation selection experiment

editor_summary: Considerable enthusiasm; all four reviewers see a good fit for Ecology Letters and the editor asks the authors to address every point raised.

reviews.assessment: Praises the rigor and writing, but doubts the data conclusively prove selection affected host fitness.
strengths: topic of great scientific and translational interest
very high standards of replication and analytical rigor

comments.issue: Fig. S1 does not justify treating leaf greenness as a proxy for plant nutritional and health status.
comments.request: Add caution and evidence linking greenness to nutritional status under the experimental conditions.
comments.quote: It is not clear to me whether the data shown in Fig. S1 is sufficient evidence to claim that leaf greenness can be used as a “proxy for plant nutritional and health status”.

comments.issue: Generation explains far more variation than selection; why lineage is in the model and how much variance generation and its interactions explain are unclear.
comments.request: Report variance explained and justify the lineage term.
comments.quote: The effect of the generation appears to be the strongest source of variation in the data, and it is in any case much higher than the effect of selection regime.

comments.issue: Whether high and low selection regimes differ is unclear, and the generation-by-selection interaction is not appraised.
comments.request: Test high versus low directly and assess the interaction.
comments.quote: It is not clear whether ‘high’ and ‘low’ are significantly different when compared to one another, since the data is split into separate figures (Fig. 1A and 1B)

comments.issue: Axenic controls are missing, so heritable selection effects on plant health are not conclusively demonstrated.
comments.request: Add axenic control treatments.
comments.quote: To convincingly prove that heritable selective variation is having an impact on plant health, axenic controls would perhaps provide convincing data, particularly in light of the strong variation along the duration of the experiment.

comments.issue: Causal heritable variation is not proven; isolation and re-inoculation could link effects to specific microbes.
comments.request: Isolate bacteria from contrasting regimes and re-inoculate axenic plants.
comments.quote: Isolation of rhizosphere bacteria from the contrasting selection regimes and re-inoculation of axenic plants might help the authors convincingly prove the existence of causal heritable variation

reviews.assessment: Positive about the congruence between traits and microbiota, but wants species interactions and several analyses added.
strengths: remarkable congruence between plant traits and microbiota structures
distinct sub-communities steered by directional selection

comments.issue: Species interactions (bacteria-bacteria, fungi-fungi, bacteria-fungi) that underpin community stability are ignored.
comments.request: Analyse microbial interactions to supplement the stability argument.
comments.quote: across whole formation process of stable rhizosphere microbiome, the authors ignore the interaction between species, such as bacteria and bacteria, fungi and fungi, and bacteria and fungi that are cornerstone and result of community stability.

comments.issue: Generation plus residuals explain about 90% of variance, so the importance of selection is not well supported.
comments.request: Report ANOVA results for selection, generation and lineage and initial greenness values.
comments.quote: as shown in Table S1, the variance of Generation+ Residuals was as high as 90%. This data is hard to evident the selection importance.

comments.issue: Large G01-G05 differences may conceal G06-G10 group differences.
comments.request: Analyse the first five and last five generations separately.
comments.quote: The large differences in the G01-G05 will conceal the differences between the groups in the G06-G10, thus the authors should analyze the data of the first five generations and the next five generations separately

comments.issue: Composition of dominant microbial species across generations is not analysed.
comments.request: Add an analysis of dominant taxa across phases.
comments.quote: The authors should provide an analysis related to composition of the dominate microbial species across the different generations of phases.

comments.issue: Figure legends lack details such as sample numbers per group.
comments.request: Add sample sizes and details to figure legends.
comments.quote: The authors should provide detailed data information in figure legends, such as the sample numbers of each group.

comments.issue: Neutral model fits are missing.
comments.request: Fit neutral models separately for the two phases.
comments.quote: We suggest that the authors can use the microbial data to fit the neutral model in two phases, respectively.

comments.issue: Line 777 does not match the figure.
comments.request: Fix the mismatch.
comments.quote: (6) Line 777: Not match the figure.

reviews.assessment: Calls the paper original and creative but doubts that selecting leaf greenness is meaningful and wants a traditional format.

comments.issue: Selecting leaf greenness lacks a strong rationale; greener plants may be deleteriously conspicuous and the microbiome findings may not be relevant.
comments.request: Provide a strong reason for selecting leaf greenness.
comments.quote: Plants do not necessarily want to become “more green” as this will attract unnecessary attention from insects and pathogens. In fact, this could a deleterious trait that plants might avoid in nature.

comments.issue: How leaf greenness could relate to microbial activity is not discussed; direct microbial effects on photosynthesis are unknown.
comments.request: Discuss mechanisms with examples of microbes and activities affecting photosynthesis.
comments.quote: I do not know of any example in which a beneficial microbe could directly contribute to photosynthesis. There could be indirect contributions such as promoting root growth, hormone sharing, etc.

comments.issue: The dataset description is too superficial.
comments.request: Describe the dataset in more detail.
comments.quote: The description of the data set is too superficial.

comments.issue: Short Nature-style format is insufficient.
comments.request: Rewrite in Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion format.
comments.quote: Finally, I think this article should be re-written in a traditional format (Introduction, MM, Results and Discussion). The short format is not enough to communicate all this information in a way that is meaningful.

comments.issue: No rationale for using Ecotron soil.
comments.request: Explain the choice of Ecotron soil.
comments.quote: The authors should provide a strong rationale for using the soil from Ecotron.

comments.issue: Unclear whether rhizosphere samples came from individual plants or microcosms.
comments.request: Clarify the sampling unit.
comments.quote: I am uncertain if the rhizosphere samples were collected from individual plants or from microcosms.

comments.issue: Why soil was autoclaved before each generation is not explained.
comments.request: Specify the reason for autoclaving.
comments.quote: It is not clear why the soil was autoclaved prior to each generation. This should be specified.

comments.issue: Number of plants pooled per generation is not reported.
comments.request: Report how many plants were pooled.
comments.quote: How many plants per generation were selected for pooling?

reviews.assessment: Super impressive study with fascinating results; asks many clarifications, figure improvements and format changes.

comments.issue: Manuscript retains Nature format.
comments.request: Move material and methods into the main text and use standard sections.
comments.quote: This paper was originally submitted to Nature, and still with Nature format, it needs a bit modification to move material and method part into main text.

comments.issue: Stabilisation could reflect plant-driven selection rather than selection acting on microbiota; cause and consequence are ambiguous.
comments.request: Clarify the direction of cause and effect.
comments.quote: then the plant selection effect become stronger after several generations, then the rhizosphere microbiota composition become stable. Which is the cause and which is the consequence?

comments.issue: Within-group variation in leaf greenness across phases is not shown.
comments.request: Report greenness variation within selection groups during oscillations and stabilisation.
comments.quote: Since there were strong oscillations in microbial community composition during the first 5 generations, were there also big variations among leaf greenness inside each selection groups?

comments.issue: End-of-experiment microbiota differences among the three groups are not highlighted.
comments.request: Highlight group differences at generation 10.
comments.quote: It will be better authors can highlight the microbiota composition differences among three selection groups at the end of the 10th generation offspring plant rhizosphere.

comments.issue: 'Stable rhizosphere microbiota' is not defined, though all groups cluster.
comments.request: Define what a stable microbiota means here.
comments.quote: Stable rhizosphere microbiota: how to define a stable rhizosphere microbiota? In all selection groups, the microbiota become clustered as authors showing in Fig.2.

comments.issue: The expected strong G10 greenness difference between high and low selection groups is not evident.
comments.request: Clarify the high-versus-low contrast at generation 10.
comments.quote: I expected that after 10 generations, the leaf greenness of offspring plants at generation 10 from high selection group is much higher than the values of offspring plants at generation 10 from low selection group.

comments.issue: Heritability analysis pools high, low and control groups.
comments.request: Separate the selection groups or remove the control.
comments.quote: For heritability calculation, it’s very cool to see Fig. 3B, but authors mixed all high, low and control groups. Did author try to separate three selection groups, or at least remove the control group?

comments.issue: Figure 1 does not show all data points or combine groups in one panel.
comments.request: Use box plots with all points and combine groups in panels A, B, D.
comments.quote: I would suggest authors to use box plots with all the points for leaf greenness of each individual plant, and put three groups together in one panel (panel A, B and D)

comments.issue: Panels C and E hide the many replicates.
comments.request: Use box plots showing all points for panels C and E.
comments.quote: For panel C and E, there are 591-596 replicates, I did not feel that many replicates in current figures, suggest authors to use box plots with all the points.

comments.issue: Bray-Curtis dissimilarity is computed against all ancestral pools rather than parent pools.
comments.request: Explain or use parent-to-offspring dissimilarities.
comments.quote: which was calculated as Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between rhizosphere microbiota in generation 10 to all previous ancestral pools, e.g., G10-G09, G10-G08, G10-G07? Why not calculate Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between each offspring rhizosphere microbiota to their parent pools?

comments.issue: Figure S9 y-axis labels with log10 and zeros are confusing.
comments.request: Improve the y-axis labelling.
comments.quote: Figure.S9, the title of y-axis is a bit confusing with log10 and so many zero in the y-axis.

comments.issue: Selection and trait measurement are not separated; a final common-garden trait assay is suggested.
comments.request: Consider a final experiment inoculating the 90 selected communities.
comments.quote: I suggest authors to separate the rhizosphere microbiota selection process and the plant trait measuring, during the 10 generation only select rhizosphere microbiota, in total 90 rhizosphere microbiota were selected.

comments.issue: Endophytic microbiota changes across selection groups are not addressed.
comments.request: Consider endophytic community responses.
comments.quote: What does endophytic microbiota change inside plants in different selection groups? The inoculated microbiota is the pool for the new plants to associate in their roots, different microbiota pool will lead to the different endophytic microbiota of plants as well.

title: Artificial selection of stable rhizosphere microbiota leads to heritable plant phenotype changes

study.system: species interactions along stress gradients; meta-analysis of >1600 studies

editor_summary: Editor notes reviewers appreciated the question but raised numerous serious concerns about the overarching questions and definitions, the meta-analysis description, publication bias and small sample sizes.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and broad meta-analysis, but stress definitions, scope rationale, minimal analyses, biodiversity inclusion and observational studies raise major limitations.

comments.issue: Working definition of stress is not stated early despite debate arising from different definitions.
comments.request: State the working definition of stress early.
comments.quote: it would be good that already early on, the authors mention their working definition

comments.issue: The broadened scope (pollination, decomposition, trophic interactions) lacks rationale and theoretical background.
comments.request: Explain the theoretical background and develop context-specific hypotheses.
comments.quote: I would have appreciated some stronger rationale for this in the introduction

comments.issue: Analyses of moderator subsets ignore combinations and collinearity, risking type I and type II errors.
comments.request: Analyse Hedges' g* with moderators and their interactions, with model selection.
comments.quote: this analysis is rather minimal for two reasons: 1) it does not give insights on combinations of mediating factors, and 2) due to collinearity, there is the increased risk of both type I and type II errors

comments.issue: Whether studies were directly inspired by the SGH may drive publication bias; this is untested.
comments.request: Test whether SGH inspiration predicts effect strength or direction.
comments.quote: it would also be beneficial to analyze whether the strength/direction of Hedges’g* depends on whether the study was also directly inspired by the SGH

comments.issue: Biodiversity responses do not fit the SGH; no rationale is given for including them.
comments.request: Justify or omit the biodiversity studies.
comments.quote: the SGH is not about biodiversity, and I don’t see good straightforward theoretical arguments on why it should apply to biodiversity

comments.issue: Observational studies cannot reliably infer interaction strength or direction; co-occurrence may reflect environmental responses.
comments.request: Discuss this limitation and only include studies with reliable interaction measures.
comments.quote: It is extremely difficult to assess the strength (or even direction) of intra- or interspecific interactions based on observations only

comments.issue: The third question is open-ended and the hypothesis is unclear.
comments.request: State the hypothesis more clearly.
comments.quote: the third question is very open-ended, it is unclear whether, and what, the authors were hypothesizing

comments.issue: Why this should reduce bias is unclear; whether publication bias is meant is not stated.
comments.request: Clarify the statement.
comments.quote: it is not very clear why this should reduce bias. Do the authors mean publication bias?

comments.issue: Omitting all search terms from the main text is too extreme.
comments.request: Mention the main search terms.
comments.quote: while it may not be feasible to list all search terms, omitting all in the main test is a bit too extreme, so I suggest the mention the main terms

comments.issue: Statement about forests is wrong; many forests are nutrient limited.
comments.quote: Line 246: actually, many forests are quite nutrient limited

comments.issue: Lines 256-260 reasoning cannot be followed.
comments.request: Rephrase to make the argument clearer.
comments.quote: I can’t really follow this reasoning, and I would suggest rephrasing to make the line of argumentation clearer

comments.issue: Figure 1 grey shades are almost indistinguishable.
comments.request: Use real colours or different patterns.
comments.quote: the different shades of grey in this figure are almost impossible to distinguish, so I suggest to replace them by real colors, or different patterns

reviews.assessment: Ambitious and generally interesting, but effect-size reliability is obscured by incomplete methods and unavailable data, and the discussion needs richer links to prior work.

comments.issue: Incomplete methodological description obscures the reliability of effect sizes and inferences.
comments.request: Describe the methods fully (see detailed comments).
comments.quote: the reliability of the effect sizes and the inferences drawn from this study are obscured due to incomplete methodological description

comments.issue: The data set used for the analyses is not available.
comments.request: Make the data set available.
comments.quote: as well as lack of availability of the data set used for the analyses

comments.issue: Discussion should compare the results with previous meta-analyses and theoretical works.
comments.request: Expand the discussion to include prior meta-analyses and theory.
comments.quote: I believe that the discussion should be expanded and enriched to include how these results coincide or not with the results of previous meta-analysis and theoretical works

comments.issue: Title does not reflect the broader scope of the work.
comments.request: Change the title.
comments.quote: Since the work encompasses much more than the response of intraspecific and intraspecific interactions to stress, I suggest changing the title.

comments.issue: Key references are missing (Bruno et al. 2003; Bronstein 2001; Brooker et al. 2008).
comments.request: Cite these key references.
comments.quote: The authors also appear to have missed some key reference that could have been included here

comments.issue: Smit et al. (2009) showed that consumers alter SGH outcomes; this is not incorporated.
comments.request: Cite and discuss Smit et al. (2009).
comments.quote: Smit et al (2009) pointed out that consumers strongly alter the outcome of species interactions predicted by the SGH

comments.issue: Established quality criteria for ecological meta-analyses are not followed.
comments.request: Adhere to meta-analysis quality criteria (Borenstein et al. 2009; Koricheva and Gurevitch 2014).
comments.quote: I suggest following the quality criteria developed for meta‐analyses in ecology

comments.issue: Full bibliographic details of the primary studies are not provided.
comments.request: Provide the list of included studies.
comments.quote: Please provide a full bibliographic detail of primary studies included in a meta‐analysis.

comments.issue: Data extraction procedures, handling of multiple observations and unreplicated studies are unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the extraction and handling of these cases.
comments.quote: Please explain how you extracted data from papers (text, tables, figures, appendices, etc), the criteria used to manage data from multiple observations per study

comments.issue: How sample sizes, standard deviations and means were extracted from observational data is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the extraction for observational data.
comments.quote: How did you extracted sample sizes, standard deviations, and means for control and manipulated treatments from observational data? Please explain.

comments.issue: Appendix 1 is not attached; the data set with effect sizes and moderators is missing.
comments.request: Provide the full data set including effect sizes and moderators.
comments.quote: Appendix 1 is not attached nor in supplementary files. Please provide the data set used for the meta-analysis including effect sizes and variances/sample sizes

comments.issue: A PRISMA-style flow diagram would clarify the search and selection process.
comments.request: Add a PRISMA flow diagram.
comments.quote: I wonder if a flow graphic diagram (like a PRISMA flow diagram) would apply here and can better guide readers to understand the whole process of literature search and selection

comments.issue: How stress was defined for selection and how stress gradients were accounted for is unclear.
comments.request: Describe and cite the stress definitions used.
comments.quote: How abiotic or biotic stress was defined for the selection criteria? How gradient lengths or contrasts of stress were accounted? Please describe and cite references.

comments.issue: Rationale for the 8 interaction categories and who classified interactions is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the classification scheme and its origin.
comments.quote: What is the point of classifying the interactions in the 8 categories, then? please explain.

comments.issue: Search terms such as facilitation and positive/negative interactions were later classified into categories; the process is unclear.
comments.request: Explain how the search results were classified.
comments.quote: However, in the search list you included also facilitation, positive interactions and negative interactions (Appendix table S1). How those results were classified later into the categories of species interactions?

comments.issue: Decomposition does not meet the definition of a positive biological interaction; inclusion criteria are unclear.
comments.request: Explain the criteria for treating decomposition as a positive interaction.
comments.quote: Please explain the criteria met to include decomposition studies here as a positive interaction.

comments.issue: Control and treatment groups for the Hedges' g calculations are not described.
comments.request: Describe the control and treatment groups.
comments.quote: Please describe which were the “control” and “treatments” groups for the Hedges “g” calculations.

comments.issue: How publication bias was guarded against is not explained.
comments.request: Describe publication-bias checks.
comments.quote: Publication bias is an ongoing issue affecting meta-analyses, leading to bias via the selective publication of statistically significant results. How you guard against this issue? Please explain.

comments.issue: Temporal changes in effect sizes across the 1900-2019 span are not tested.
comments.request: Test for temporal trends in effect sizes.
comments.quote: Since this meta‐analysis combines studies published since 1900 to 2019, have possible temporal changes in effect sizes been tested?

comments.issue: Line 128 statement lacks a reference.
comments.request: Add a reference.
comments.quote: Lines 128. Needs a reference here, after this sentence

comments.issue: The direct vs indirect pressure categorization in Fig. 4 is not mentioned or defined in the text.
comments.request: Explain the criterion and reference it in the text.
comments.quote: No reference to this in the text (introduction, nor methods) was found. Did they mean direct vs. indirect interactions

comments.issue: Whether all interspecific versus intraspecific interactions were considered is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the scope of interactions compared.
comments.quote: did you consider all interspecific interactions (trophic and non-trophic) vs intraspecific (same trophic level)? Please explain

comments.issue: Figure 4 does not show how trophic versus non-trophic interactions change along stress gradients.
comments.request: Show these patterns.
comments.quote: Figure 4. How non-trophic vs trophic positive and negative interactions change along stress gradients?

comments.issue: Short versus longer term effects of facilitation are not discussed.
comments.request: Expand the discussion with Maestre et al. 2009 and Malkinson and Tielbörger 2010.
comments.quote: So,it would be interesting to expand the discussion including at least these two works.

comments.issue: Results are not related to the resource versus non-resource stress framework.
comments.request: Link the results to this framework.
comments.quote: It would be really interesting if you could relate your results with this framework since these predictions have only rarely been tested

comments.issue: Combined abiotic and biotic stress results are not discussed.
comments.request: Add a discussion following Smit, Rietkerk and Wassen (2009).
comments.quote: Since you have abiotic stresses combined with biotic stress it would be interesting to include a discussion of those results following Smit, Rietkerk, & Wassen (2009)

reviews.assessment: Ambitious and valuable meta-analysis, but intraspecific inclusion, small-sample evaluation, confounding among conditions and the underdeveloped discussion need work.

reviews.assessment: Exciting and timely study with a clear approach; asks for clearer strain origins, stage structure and prey-data caveats.

comments.issue: The origin and history of variation among ciliate populations is unclear, including prior prey experience and generation numbers.
comments.request: Describe the source of variation in the ciliate populations.
comments.quote: Authors could make the source of variation in different ciliate populations clearer besides the reference given.

comments.issue: Predator developmental stages and age structure are not considered, though they may cause lagged dynamics.
comments.request: Discuss how stage structure might affect the predictions.
comments.quote: Another less clear issue is the developmental stages/age structures at predator level.

comments.issue: The number and role of carbon sources in competitive ability and their relevance to the media are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the carbon sources and their role in the experiment.
comments.quote: Does the mummer of carbon sources also determine competitive ability?

comments.issue: "Isogenic" is used without explanation.
comments.request: Define what isogenic means here.
comments.quote: Authors could explain what isogenic mean.

comments.issue: Model behaviour with very low densities of the inferior competitor and undetectable abundances is unclear.
comments.request: Address how undetectable abundances are treated.
comments.quote: How would the model perform with very low densities of the inferior competitor when undetectable abundances are not treated as true zeros?

comments.issue: Prey size may be an important niche-difference parameter for filter-feeding ciliates.
comments.request: Consider prey size in niche differences.
comments.quote: Considering ciliates are filter feeders, would prey size be an important parameter for niche differences?

comments.issue: The explanation for slower diversity decline lacks examples from predator-prey literature.
comments.request: Add a couple of literature examples.
comments.quote: Authors could give a couple of examples from predator-prey literature.

comments.issue: Net positive interactions or apparent facilitation could explain the pattern.
comments.request: Consider this alternative explanation.
comments.quote: could this pattern be net positive interactions/apparent facilitation?

comments.issue: Higher-order prey interactions or cascading effects after prey extinction could explain the patterns.
comments.request: Consider these alternative explanations.
comments.quote: Could higher-order interactions among prey, or cascading effects after extinction of a prey explain these patterns?

comments.issue: The relevance of the number of carbon sources and whether it measures functional diversity is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the carbon-source measure and its relevance.
comments.quote: What is the relevance of number of carbon sources used? Was it measured as functional diversity?

comments.issue: Trait redundancy at lower levels may reduce trait overlap and species-identity effects.
comments.request: Discuss the effects of trait redundancy.
comments.quote: Would the traits overlap at lower levels due to redundancy?

comments.issue: Whether media and temperature support all prey species, and possible dissolved-carbon uptake and bottom-up effects, are not addressed.
comments.request: Discuss these aspects and possible bottom-up effects.
comments.quote: Do the media and temperature sport all the prey species? It might alter the carrying capacity of prey species and might be worth to mention.

comments.issue: Treating sequencing data as absolute abundances is controversial and PCR bias is not acknowledged.
comments.request: Acknowledge these methodological caveats for the prey data.
comments.quote: there is still a controversy around treating sequencing data as absolute abundances in latest literature

comments.issue: Syntax error at line 418.
comments.request: Fix the syntax.
comments.quote: Line 418: Something went wrong with the syntax.

title: Effects of phenotypic variation on consumer coexistence and prey community structure

study.system: C. elegans microcosms; 3-patch competition and movement models

editor_summary: Editor notes both reviewers appreciated the approach but differed on recommendation; both saw much needed improvement, especially linking theory and empirics; R1 wants more transparent modelling; R2 more critical of model-data connections.

reviews.assessment: Enjoyable and significant, tightly coupling theory and experiment, but the theory needs greater generality and the results more robustness checks.
strengths: significant contribution of interest to a broad audience
tight coupling of theory and experiment

comments.issue: Theory is shown only for a 3-patch model; generality beyond this configuration is untested.
comments.request: Extend the model from 3 patches to n patches.
comments.quote: I would like to see the theory modified to increase its generality and show that it holds beyond the system presented here. In particular, do the results hold if extended from a 3-patch to an n-patch model?

comments.issue: No sensitivity analysis of how results depend on parameterization choices.
comments.request: Add a sensitivity analysis across parameterizations.
comments.quote: I would like to see a sensitivity analysis showing how general the results are to parameterization choices.

comments.issue: Parameter values not taken from the experiment (r, k, gamma, m, g) are not justified.
comments.request: Justify these parameter values.
comments.quote: I would appreciate a brief justification for the parameter values that are chosen that aren’t directly from the experiment (e.g. r, k, gamma, m, g in Table S1)

comments.issue: Claim that strains are effectively neutral is foundational but lacks single-species experiments.
comments.request: Add supplemental single-species experiments demonstrating neutrality.
comments.quote: I argue this statement needs supplemental single species experiments to show this point, given how foundational it is for the results and framing of this manuscript.

comments.issue: Misidentification rate of the Matlab tracking algorithm and robustness to this error are not reported.
comments.request: Report the misidentification rate and test result robustness.
comments.quote: what is the misidentification rate for the Matlab algorithm used (ln 272-273)? Are the experimental results robust to this observational error rate?

comments.issue: Fig 3 D-F are difficult to interpret and do not show dependence on initial values.
comments.request: Modify the graph, e.g. colour points by initial condition or draw trajectories.
comments.quote: I found these panels difficult to interpret (but nicely described in the text). It was not clear to me that this variation depends on the initial values.

comments.issue: Discussion lacks a broader-audience section with empirical examples and connections.
comments.request: Add broader context and empirical examples to the Discussion or Introduction.
comments.quote: I think the Discussion would benefit from a section written for a more general audience, given the broad readership of Ecology Letters.

comments.issue: Relevant citations on non-random dispersal and movement-mediated coexistence are missing.
comments.request: Cite Amarasekare 2010 and Schlägel et al. 2020.
comments.quote: There are a few citations I noticed might be nice to include, if you agree they add to the manuscript

comments.issue: Ln 179 does not link the appendix equations to the main-text equations per patch.
comments.request: Refer to the equations above and describe their per-patch use.
comments.quote: Ln 179: I suggest this refers to the eqns above in the main text and briefly describes how it uses these eqns to specific for each patch in the appendix.

comments.issue: Appendix B first paragraph contains a duplicated phrase typo.
comments.request: Fix the duplication.
comments.quote: Appendix B: first paragraph has a typo

reviews.assessment: The foraging-with-error model is interesting, but the experiment is incongruent with it and cannot support the validation and coexistence claims.

comments.issue: Model is not connected to optimal foraging and ideal free distribution literature.
comments.request: Discuss optimal foraging and ideal free distribution in the introduction.
comments.quote: It is an interesting model and could be better supported with some discussion of, for instance, optimal foraging and ideal free distribution in the introduction.

comments.issue: Experiment does not mimic the model: uniform homogeneous treatment, single-patch heterogeneous treatment with bare agar called habitat.
comments.request: Change the experimental design and/or model for congruence.
comments.quote: Here, the experiment failed completely to mimic the model, having again only one patch and claiming that bare agar is a habitat.

comments.issue: Six even-aged founders over-stabilize a neutral system and make results sensitive to bias, with identities known during data collection.
comments.request: Increase the effective population size.
comments.quote: The use of 6 even-aged individuals to start each generation provides too much stabilization to a neutral system and simultaneously introduces enormous sensitivity to any unintended bias

comments.issue: Summary statistics of the results are absent.
comments.request: Report summary statistics.
comments.quote: I also think publication requires, at a minimum, summary statistics of the results.

comments.issue: Abstract second sentence needs improvement.
comments.request: Improve the abstract wording.
comments.quote: Abstract. Second sentence could be improved.

comments.issue: Presentation of Wilson and Abrams does not separate assumptions from the finding; coexistence is driven by environmental architecture, not dispersal per se.
comments.request: Articulate the assumptions alongside the finding.
comments.quote: Presentation of Wilson and Abrams should clearly articulate the assumptions alongside the finding. It really isn't dispersal that maintains coexistence so much as all the particulars of the environmental architecture.

comments.issue: More fundamental research should precede the prior paragraph at L106.
comments.request: Reorder these paragraphs.
comments.quote: Just a suggestion that this more fundamental body of research be presented before the prior paragraph.

comments.issue: Dispersal is conflated with movement at perceptible scales; taxis belongs to foraging or habitat selection.
comments.request: Define dispersal and directed movement consistently.
comments.quote: I would strongly argue that dispersal refers to movement at scales that exceed the organism's ability to perceive and compare habitat quality.

comments.issue: Last sentence at L133 belongs with the next paragraph.
comments.request: Move the sentence.
comments.quote: L. 133: Seems like this last sentence goes with the next paragraph.

comments.issue: 'Rigorous' should not be self-ascribed at L142.
comments.request: Delete 'rigorous'.
comments.quote: Delete “rigorous.” Not knocking your experiment. It’s for the authors to demonstrate, not state.

comments.issue: Sentence at L154 is confusing about resource exploitation feedbacks.
comments.request: Clarify the sentence.
comments.quote: I am confused by this sentence. The model has resource exploitation, which clearly feeds back to consumer movement and population growth.

comments.issue: 'Nutrient' should be replaced by 'resource' throughout.
comments.request: Use 'resource' consistently.
comments.quote: I vote for using “resource” throughout. “Nutrient” limits the imagination to primary producers.

comments.issue: Equations at L163-69 are unclear: density-dependent mortality, subscripting, undefined Theta, unnecessary Michaelis-Menten responses.
comments.request: Simplify and clean up the equation presentation.
comments.quote: The equations are a mess. Is density-dependent mortality supposed to be (U + V)V in both Eqs. 1a and b? The choice of subscripting is annoying because i-1, i+1 only works for the central patch.

comments.issue: Eqs 1d,e assume perfect knowledge of the environment; local-state knowledge might suffice.
comments.request: Test dynamics based only on local environmental state.
comments.quote: Eqs. 1d,e suggest perfect knowledge of the environment. Would be very interesting to see if a similar dynamic could be achieved simply through knowledge of the local environmental state

comments.issue: L181 on n=3 and simulating the experimental system is confusing before the experiment is described.
comments.request: Explain the three patches and describe the experiment first.
comments.quote: Something went wrong here. What are the three patches in the experiment?

comments.issue: 'Subpopulations in populations' at L199 is odd language.
comments.request: Use 'strains' or 'species'.
comments.quote: Subpopulations in populations is odd language. Could you go with strains (like the experiment) or species?

comments.issue: L210 wording is unclear about the level of directed movement.
comments.request: Clarify the wording.
comments.quote: Unclear wording. The level of directed movement in the experimental system was unknown? At this point in the text, not important.

comments.issue: Beta is omitted from the denominator at L216.
comments.request: Correct the equation.
comments.quote: L. 216: Omitting Beta from denominator.

comments.issue: Food taxis depends strongly on the mutant; chemotaxis ability varies and relies on external data (Flavell et al.).
comments.request: Measure the behaviour of these strains in this setup.
comments.quote: Food taxis is going to REALLY depend on the mutant. Some mutants lack neurons responsible for chemotaxis, for instance.

comments.issue: Males are not explained for the uninitiated at L236.
comments.request: Explain male frequency and culture management.
comments.quote: L. 236: For the uninitiated: Males occur at low frequency and can become prevalent if cultures are not carefully managed.

comments.issue: Strain details at L240 would interest readers.
comments.request: Add strain descriptions.
comments.quote: L. 240: Some detail on your strains that readers might find interesting:

comments.issue: The simulated dynamic has no analog in the experimental system; simulations may all start in Patch 1.
comments.request: Align the simulation with the experimental design.
comments.quote: Regardless, the explanation for the dynamic given here has no analog in the experimental system. This is the crux of the problem with the paper.

comments.issue: External data are presented as if they were this study's result; measurements on the actual plates are missing.
comments.request: Measure the percentage on bare agar per strain on your plates.
comments.quote: L. 329: Placing this info here makes it seem like your result. I would like to see results like this measured on your plates.

comments.issue: No rigorous demonstration that heterogeneous treatments differed from homogeneous ones.
comments.request: Test the difference statistically.
comments.quote: This sentence is hard to understand. More is needed. I know the data look very convincing, but show me in some rigorous way that the heterogeneous treatments differed from the homogeneous ones.

comments.issue: Wording at L341 needs improvement.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence.
comments.quote: L. 341: Improve wording. Random movement reduces fitness when patches differ in quality.

comments.issue: The simulation-experiment mismatch prevents claiming validation.
comments.request: Remove or qualify the validation claim.
comments.quote: L. 345: The mismatch in simulation/experimental design prevents you from claiming validation here.

comments.issue: Unclear what the delayed-feedback model captures beyond implicit resource dynamics of logistic maps.
comments.request: Explain the added value over logistic-map resource dynamics.
comments.quote: The delayed feedback idea is interesting but please expand clearly on what it is your model captures that the implicit resource dynamics of logistic maps do not.

comments.issue: The experiment did not test whether intermediate directed movement fosters coexistence.
comments.request: Use chemotaxis-defective mutants varying in movement rate.
comments.quote: Your experiment (even if it had two patches) absolutely did not test whether an intermediate level of directed movement fosters coexistence.

comments.issue: 3 line-level copy edits (L180 sentence, L235 wording, L357 exploitable/exhaustible).
comments.quote: L. 357 Replace exploitable with exhaustible

title: Directed movement changes coexistence outcomes in heterogeneous environments

study.system: vertebrate assemblages; global land-use and functional diversity database

editor_summary: Editor rejects without resubmission: methodological concerns are too substantial and scientific impact not high enough; advises a friendlier abstract, wider implications and clearer novelty for a specialist journal.

reviews.assessment: Well-written and of broad interest, but the analysis is dominated by birds and suffers from imbalance and several methodological issues.
strengths: results interesting to a broad readership

comments.issue: Birds are severely over-represented, so the claimed across-class analysis is largely driven by bird trends.
comments.request: Focus on bird assemblages, complemented by smaller analyses of other classes.
comments.quote: it seems that birds are severely over-represented, which makes me wonder how ‘across-class’ this analysis really is

comments.issue: There are about five times more reference sites than other site types and the effect of this imbalance was not tested.
comments.request: Test the influence of the imbalance, e.g. by subsampling reference sites.
comments.quote: there are about five times more reference (primary vegetation) sites than any other type of site. There is no information on how this imbalance influenced the analyses.

comments.issue: 'Resilience' is used loosely; it should be reserved for local stability or Holling-type resilience.
comments.request: Use the more general term 'stability' instead.
comments.quote: I think we should reserve the term ‘resilience’ for what it is (local stability or Holling-type resilience) and advice the use of the more general term ‘stability’ instead

comments.issue: The explanation on lines 52-56 is not clear.
comments.request: Clarify the explanation on lines 52-56.
comments.quote: L52-56: This explanation was not clear to me.

comments.issue: Referring to 'space for time' is unnecessary and ventures into temporal prognoses.
comments.request: Remove the 'space for time' framing.
comments.quote: I don’t think it’s needed to refer to ‘space for time’ here. There is merit in trying to discover community response along gradients of environmental change

comments.issue: The rationale for expected effects on dispersion is missing although H1 covers functional diversity generally.
comments.request: Explain the expected dispersion effects in H1.
comments.quote: The rationale for the hypothesized effects on functional richness is explained, but not for the expected effects on dispersion

comments.issue: The wording on line 79 should be 'simulations with a null model'.
comments.request: Reword line 79 as 'simulations with a null model'.
comments.quote: L79: Rather, “simulations with a null model”?

comments.issue: H3 would also imply a sharper drop in functional richness in tropical zones.
comments.request: Reconcile H3 with the tropical richness expectation.
comments.quote: L81: H3: Wouldn’t this imply a sharper drop in functional richness in tropical zones as well then?

comments.issue: Lower functional diversity without functional loss sounds strange and needs clarification.
comments.request: Add a cartoon in the style of Fig. S1 to clarify.
comments.quote: I think I get what is meant, but still it sounds strange that lower functional diversity would be possible without functional loss

comments.issue: Using a trait database implicitly assumes no environmental effects on traits, which is not stated.
comments.request: State this assumption in the manuscript.
comments.quote: The use of a trait database implicitly assumes no environmental effects on the traits, which should be stated somewhere.

comments.issue: Missing trait values are a weak point and the imputation strategy's adequacy is unclear.
comments.request: Repeat the analyses on sites with matched trait data and compare results.
comments.quote: I’d like to see the analyses for a subset of the sites for which trait data can be matched. Do the results look qualitatively similar?

comments.issue: 'Problematic' on line 130 is undefined.
comments.request: Define what is meant by 'problematic'.
comments.quote: L130: Please define what is ‘problematic’.

comments.issue: Zone (tropical vs. temperate) was not formally included in the model.
comments.request: Include zone as a formal predictor in the model.
comments.quote: L153-154: Why wasn’t zone (tropical vs. temperate) formally included in the model?

comments.issue: It is not explained why a function throws an error, reducing confidence in the analyses.
comments.request: Report and explain the function error.
comments.quote: It is always useful to know why a function is throwing an error, as it increases confidence in the analytical methods

comments.issue: The results text is too redundant with the figures.
comments.request: Focus on main trends needed to support the conclusions.
comments.quote: Some of the text of the results section is too redundant with the figures

comments.issue: The ranking of land-use types by disturbance is not justified; cropland could be as disturbed as urban.
comments.request: Justify the land-use ranking and disturbance classification.
comments.quote: What is the justification for the ranking of land use types? It is clear that urban is more impacted than primary vegetation, but cropland could be just as disturbed as urban

comments.issue: It is unclear whether 'a given class' on line 287 refers to birds.
comments.request: Specify what 'a given class' refers to.
comments.quote: L287: ‘a given class’: are these birds?

comments.issue: The paragraph on line 310 is not really 'another explanation' but a restatement of the general mechanism.
comments.request: Clarify how this explanation differs from the general mechanism.
comments.quote: I don’t see how this paragraph is ‘another explanation’. To me, it seems like an incarnation of the general mechanism.

comments.issue: Calling assemblages 'communities' implies species interactions that may not exist.
comments.request: Justify the term or describe how classes interact.
comments.quote: Referring to the assemblages as “communities” implies species interact. Is this the case?

comments.issue: Shared space S is fully determined by functional gain and loss, so analysing all three is redundant.
comments.request: Justify why all three variables were analysed.
comments.quote: S is fully defined by G and L, so what was the reason to run analyses on all three variables?

comments.issue: The rationale for the functional gain formula is unclear and its interpretation is uncertain.
comments.request: Justify or revise the G formula, or present only G and S.
comments.quote: I don’t understand the rationale for the formula of G. To me, it would seem more logical to compute G = (V_2-V_inter) / (V_1)

reviews.assessment: Well-written and sound overall, but the tropical-temperate comparison is overstated and sample imbalance, imputation and time since conversion are not adequately addressed.
strengths: discussion largely based on the results

comments.issue: The tropical-temperate difference is overstated and the comparison may not be straightforward.
comments.request: Temper the regional comparison and its claims.
comments.quote: my major comments are about the fact that the results of difference between tropical and temperate areas seem overstated

comments.issue: The unbalanced sample (taxa and regions) is not dealt with although regional comparisons are made.
comments.request: Account for the sample imbalance in the comparisons.
comments.quote: The authors state the study is not balance (between taxa but also between tropical and temperate regions), however, the authors do not seem to had dealt with this

comments.issue: Comparing eight imputations shows variation among imputed datasets but not differences from the original data.
comments.request: Compare analyses with original versus imputed trait data.
comments.quote: this only tells something about the variation found between imputed trait dataset but does not tell anything about the differences obtained with the original data

comments.issue: Time since conversion or disturbance is not accounted for, although recently and long-converted sites may differ.
comments.request: Account for time since conversion in the models.
comments.quote: This time since 'conversion' or 'disturbance' may greatly affect the outcome of the overall analysis and the interpretation of results and it would be great of the authors cold account for it in their models.

comments.issue: Temperate regions have fewer species; it is unclear how this is standardised.
comments.request: Explain how species richness differences are accounted for.
comments.quote: l12 - But also temperate regions have less species, how is this taken into account? or standardised?

comments.issue: It is unclear what 'a class' on line 49 refers to.
comments.request: Specify the class referred to on line 49.
comments.quote: l49 - Specify a class of what exactly?

comments.issue: Distinct initial conditions may produce the same FD scores; it is unclear how this is handled.
comments.request: Explain how identical outcomes from distinct initial conditions are handled.
comments.quote: l57-58 But distinct initial conditions may lead to the same outcome, for instance of FD scores, how do the authors deal with this in their analysis?

comments.issue: The intermediate disturbance hypothesis offers an alternative explanation that is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss whether intermediate disturbance could raise diversity.
comments.quote: What about the intermediate disturbance hypothesis? it may be that intermediate disturbed areas could actually have higher diversity than pristine and highly disturbed locations

comments.issue: The pattern may simply reflect the greater species richness of the tropics; the reference is also missing.
comments.request: Add the reference and discuss this alternative explanation.
comments.quote: l81-82 Please add the reference, and may this be simply because there are more specie sin the tropics than in temperate areas?

comments.issue: Traits reflecting energy and matter transfer were chosen rather than traits known to affect responses to land-use change.
comments.request: Justify the trait selection or include response traits such as body size or dispersal.
comments.quote: why to select traits that have an impact on energy and matter transfer and not traits that have been show/or are hypothesized to have an effect on how species respond to land use change

comments.issue: Trait data are incomplete for almost half the traits, especially amphibians, raising doubts about imputed values.
comments.request: Show trait value ranges before and after imputation.
comments.quote: For almost half of the traits, and specially for amphibians, the trait data is quite incomplete (<50% available), I wonder to what extent the trait values obtained with the imputation process make sense?

comments.issue: 'Small' differences on line 127 are not quantified.
comments.request: Quantify what 'small' means.
comments.quote: l127 The authors should specify what 'small' mean, could the authors please quantify small?

comments.issue: How 'not problematically high' was determined is not specified.
comments.request: Explain the criterion for 'not problematically high'.
comments.quote: l130 Please specify how the authors determined the 'not problematically high'

comments.issue: It is unclear whether transformation and z-scoring occurred before or after imputation.
comments.request: Specify the order of transformation and imputation.
comments.quote: l131 Please specify if the transformation and z-scores were carried out before or after the imputation process

comments.issue: Functional diversity could also be greater than the null expectation; only 'smaller than' is considered.
comments.request: Explain why larger-than-null results are not reported.
comments.quote: The FDis and FR could be greater than expected by chance. Could the authors please explain why they only refer to 'smaller than' and not 'larger than'?

comments.issue: The R code behind the reported changes is not available in the SI.
comments.request: Include the R code in the SI.
comments.quote: It would be great if the authors include this R code as well in the SI as to follow the changes made.

comments.issue: Confidence intervals for urban are surprisingly large, indicating great variation and overstated results.
comments.request: Temper the results given this variation.
comments.quote: the confidence intervals, at least for the urban class are surprisingly large, so there is a tremendous variation in the FR response from this LULC class in comparison to the baseline conditions

comments.issue: Removing the ISV makes tropical and temperate patterns look similar.
comments.request: Reconsider the regional difference without the ISV.
comments.quote: l245 seems similar for tropical and temperate regions taking away the ISV

comments.issue: Gains look similar between tropical and temperate regions for most classes, e.g. PV-PA around 20%.
comments.request: Temper the claim of stronger tropical gains.
comments.quote: l257 From the figure it seems the gains are similar for most of those classes between tropical and temperate, for instance PV-PA in temperate seem to be close to 20% and the same for the tropics

comments.issue: Tropical areas may not be more sensitive; they simply have more species to lose, which is a different argument.
comments.request: Reframe the discussion around species richness rather than sensitivity.
comments.quote: Thus, this would indicate that tropical areas may not really be more sensitive to the different land use classes, but it would say they have many more species to lose

comments.issue: Figure 4 shows fairly similar losses in temperate and tropical areas, so the statement on line 332 seems overstated.
comments.request: Temper the claim about regional loss differences.
comments.quote: l332 This seems overstated by looking at figure 4. The two sub-figures of loss in temperate and tropical areas seem fairly similar with major differences between PA and UR only.

reviews.assessment: Broadly appealing global synthesis, but land-use classification, sampling and trait choices raise major issues that compromise confidence in the results.
strengths: explicit treatment of functional loss and gains

comments.issue: It is unclear which land uses count as disturbed or undisturbed and whether different land uses represent equivalent disturbances.
comments.request: Define the disturbance classes and their coverage and scale criteria.
comments.quote: Unclear what land uses are classified as disturbed or undisturbed - are cropland agricultural fields like grassland; what are pasture; are plantation forest, pasture, cropland, and urban are equivalent disturbances

comments.issue: Secondary vegetation has finer resolution than other categories while urban is homogenised, although cities differ in green space and infrastructure.
comments.request: Account for differences among cities and category resolution.
comments.quote: Secondary vegetation has greater resolution than other land-use categories, while urban is homogenized

comments.issue: Dataset sufficiency is not justified given the dominance of birds; taxonomic comparisons are results and need power and null analyses.
comments.request: Justify sample size and investigate taxonomic differences explicitly.
comments.quote: Sample justification – is this dataset sufficient for the questions explored, especially given disproportionate representation of birds? Power analysis required.

comments.issue: Traits relating to geography (home range, geographic range) and mobility (dispersal, locomotion) are omitted.
comments.request: Include geography and mobility traits.
comments.quote: Given the spatial nature of this work, gross omission of traits relating to geography (e.g., home-range or geographic range) and mobility (e.g., dispersal ability and locomotion) is extremely problematic

comments.issue: The abstract's 'most disturbed land-types' is too vague.
comments.request: Specify which land types are most disturbed.
comments.quote: Abstract : revise “most disturbed land-types” to actually specify which ones, at present too vague and not compelling

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the subset represents all vertebrate studies and what the inclusion criteria were.
comments.request: State the inclusion criteria for the subset.
comments.quote: Line 96-98 – unclear if subset of data represents all vertebrate studies and the criteria for inclusion given entire dataset not used

comments.issue: Relevant studies are mentioned without describing their findings to place the new study in context.
comments.request: Describe findings of the cited studies, e.g. Le Provost et al. 2020.
comments.quote: Introduction includes mention of several relevant studies investigating function diversity, but no description of their finding presented to place in context of goals for present study

comments.issue: The tropical versus temperate comparison is not justified.
comments.request: Justify the tropical-temperate comparison.
comments.quote: no justification for the tropical vs temperate comparison

comments.issue: Functional clustering and dispersion are used inconsistently for the same concept.
comments.request: Use terminology consistently.
comments.quote: Be consistent with terminology with stating function clustering and dispersion in referring to the same concept

comments.issue: Treating artificial habitat as a biological trait is odd.
comments.request: Justify the use of artificial habitat as a trait.
comments.quote: The use of artificial habitat as a biological trait is odd and requires justification

comments.issue: Reporting that differences 'were small' is insufficient.
comments.request: Provide means and standard errors or a statistical test.
comments.quote: is insufficient, provide mean and se or statistical test

comments.issue: Flow and structure need improvement; results are mixed into methods and the order does not follow the hypotheses.
comments.request: Reorganise methods and results to follow the hypothesis flow.
comments.quote: Flow and structure needs improvement. For example, mix of results in methods (Line 136-137)

comments.issue: The study is cast as global but the dataset description gives no coverage.
comments.request: Describe the dataset's geographic coverage.
comments.quote: Casted as a global analysis, but no coverage in dataset description 144-146

comments.issue: It is unclear how the dataset went from 180 to 135 studies for functional loss and gain.
comments.request: Explain the filtering from 180 to 135 studies.
comments.quote: How did authors go from 180 studies to 135 studies for functional loss and gain

comments.issue: The criteria for designating sites as tropical or temperate are unclear.
comments.request: State the tropical-temperate designation criteria.
comments.quote: Criteria for designating tropical vs temperate unclear

comments.issue: Figure 1c shows two assemblages but four disturbed and two reference points.
comments.request: Clarify Figure 1c.
comments.quote: Figure 1c unclear – two assemblages but 4 disturbed and 2 reference points

comments.issue: Points are connected in Figure 4 without explanation.
comments.request: Explain or remove the connecting lines in Figure 4.
comments.quote: Figure 4 – why are points connected?

comments.issue: Sol et al. 2020 on urban bird functional diversity is not reviewed.
comments.request: Review Sol et al. 2020.
comments.quote: Review Sol et al. 2020 Ecol Letters urban on bird functional diversity

comments.issue: Results are presented elementarily with percentages and lack rigour.
comments.request: Strengthen the presentation of results.
comments.quote: Elementary presentations of results with percentages, definitely missed opportunity and needs rigor

comments.issue: The use of 'resilience' on line 287 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify or replace 'resilience' on line 287.
comments.quote: Line 287 – use of resilience unclear

comments.issue: It is unclear how variation in sampling effort and survey season was controlled by site.
comments.request: Explain how sampling effort and season were controlled.
comments.quote: Unclear how variation in sampling effort and survey season were controlled by site

comments.issue: Writing style varies between Introduction/Methods and Results/Discussion.
comments.request: Make the writing style consistent throughout.
comments.quote: Writing change varied from Introduction and Methods to Results and Discussion

comments.issue: Several line-level copy edits (grammar on Line 79, capitalization of 'Young', missing reference details).
comments.quote: “Young” should not be capitalized throughout results

title: Intensive human land uses negatively affect vertebrate functional diversity

study.system: global vertebrate populations; Living Planet Database time series

editor_summary: Reviewers found the work potentially interesting but raised clear issues; in particular the definition of resilience for data lacking evident perturbations must be resolved, likely requiring a different paper and re-review.

reviews.assessment: Intrigued by the approach and its potential impact, but unclear how the resilience metrics connect to the disturbance-based concept and how the analyses were performed.

comments.issue: Demographic resilience requires a disturbance, but the analysis applies the concept to time series without identified perturbations.
comments.request: Explain thoroughly how the analyses link to the demographic resilience framework.
comments.quote: The main conceptual challenge I am trying to wrap my head around is that the resilience concept relies on a system being subjected to a disturbance

comments.issue: Changes in r may reflect intrinsic dynamics, density feedbacks or random fluctuations rather than disturbance-driven recovery.
comments.request: Distinguish disturbance-driven from intrinsic change and address the critique of abundance trends.
comments.quote: how can one distinguish to what extent r is changing due to a disturbance vs. intrinsic factors such as dispersal or strong density feedbacks?

comments.issue: Life-history differences among taxa, especially marine reproduction, offer an alternative explanation for declining recovery.
comments.request: Consider life-history-driven compensation as an alternative explanation for recovery declines.
comments.quote: could it be that populations actually increase after disturbances (compensation via reproduction), and then recover towards a stable population structure, with r decreasing less as the population gets closer to its stable state.

comments.issue: Readers cannot see what the underlying abundance time series look like, so the analyses are hard to follow.
comments.request: Add example species time series as a visual guide to the analyses.
comments.quote: provide a visual guide to their analyses (at least for some example species), so that readers can actually see what the abundance time series look like

comments.issue: It is unclear whether resistance and recovery analyses use the same sample size per time series; smaller samples could explain null resistance trends.
comments.request: Report and compare sample sizes for resistance and recovery analyses.
comments.quote: the authors show in the supporting material how many species they had for the resistance/recovery analyses, but not whether they had the same sample size of recovery vs. resistance data for each time series

comments.issue: R scripts and plots of the underlying time series were not provided at submission.
comments.request: Add R scripts of the analyses and additional plots of the time series.
comments.quote: Most of my concerns can be addressed by the authors adding R scripts of their analyses and additional plots of the underlying time series

comments.issue: Threat start and end times are ignored; populations perturbed early versus late would show different recovery patterns.
comments.request: Characterise threat timing and discuss this limitation more thoroughly.
comments.quote: I would think it’s important to also characterise when threats started and ended. For instance, a population that was exposed to a threat at the beginning of abundance measurements

comments.issue: Whether a decrease in r also alters demographic structure is not assessed, so resistance may not capture disturbance to structure.
comments.request: Clarify how resistance accounts for changes in demographic structure.
comments.quote: isn’t it as important to understand whether a decrease in r also substantially alters demographic structure? If r decreases but the demographic structure is not perturbed substantially, would that be considered resistance?

comments.issue: Phylogenetic effects and other life-history parameters such as generation time are not accounted for.
comments.request: Account for phylogeny and life-history parameters when explaining differences among taxa.
comments.quote: The authors accounted for mass, but why not account for phylogenetic effects? Or other important life-history parameters (like generation time).

comments.issue: It is unclear how recovery declines, unchanged resistance and unchanged abundance can coexist.
comments.request: Demonstrate this combination with example time series.
comments.quote: The presence of multiple threats does not explain, at least not to me, how one can have declines in recovery, no changes in resistance, but also no changes in abundance.

comments.issue: The unexpected finding that protected-area populations show stronger recovery declines is not discussed.
comments.request: Explain why protected populations are more prone to recovery decline.
comments.quote: It looks like populations in protected areas are more prone to recovery decline -and I would have expected the opposite.

comments.issue: The equation presents species as a fixed effect; specifying it as random requires a hyperprior.
comments.request: Add the hyperprior specification for the species random effect.
comments.quote: From this equation, it appears as though species is a fixed effect. To specify that it is a random effect, a hyperprior is needed

comments.issue: The term “warm up” is used instead of the conventional “burn-in”.
comments.request: Use the standard term “burn-in”.
comments.quote: I am not familiar with the expression “warm up”; typically “burn-in” is used.

comments.issue: A sentence contradicts the preceding one.
comments.request: Clarify or remove the contradictory sentence.
comments.quote: Doesn’t this sentence contradict the previous one?

reviews.assessment: The abundance-based measures do not capture perturbation-relative resilience, and the stressor-count analysis is not meaningful, so results may merely echo known trends.

comments.issue: Resistance and recovery are defined relative to a perturbation and reference state, which the abundance-based measures ignore.
comments.request: Revise the metrics or their interpretation to respect perturbation-relative definitions.
comments.quote: This is not taken into account (I understand that it is very hard to do in the given dataset) so it makes the interpretation of population increases and decreases into recovery and resistance problematic.

comments.issue: Growth rates are used as resilience components, but negative growth is not resistance; the measures just count abundance changes.
comments.request: Justify why growth-rate direction measures resistance rather than abundance change.
comments.quote: So why would a negative growth rate indicate resistance? It is rather the relative growth of a population. Said in a different way, the authors are basically measuring how often the abundance of a population declined or increased.

comments.issue: Because of how resilience is measured, the findings may merely reflect population trend analyses published elsewhere.
comments.request: Show that the results are not simply known abundance trends.
