comments.quote: inbreeding effects on mating success will more likely capture a male bias in condition-dependent effects

comments.issue: The material on lines 576-578 should come before the previous paragraph.
comments.request: Reorder the paragraphs.
comments.quote: I would discuss this before the previous paragraph.

comments.issue: The statement on line 587 that females invest more in reproduction is imprecise.

comments.issue: Punctuation edits at L70, L71, L80, L442, L579 and L581.

title: Sex‐specific inbreeding depression: A meta‐analysis

study.system: birds; global phylogeny and morphological trait data

editor_summary: Editor finds the paper unfocused, asks to reconsider the claim that analyses are order-independent, suggests intersecting nodes of diversification and disparification, and notes overlap with prior published results.

reviews.assessment: Well-written and important contribution, but the adaptive-radiation framing needs to be clarified and aligned with the results.
strengths: important contribution to recent macroevolution work
thorough evaluation of phylogenetic data problems

comments.issue: It is unclear what the paper claims about adaptive radiation theory; intro and abstract framing do not match the results.
comments.request: Align the intro and abstract framing with the actual results.
comments.quote: the paper could use a close read by the authors to forge some congruence between the intro/abstract framing and actual results

comments.issue: Assumption-heavy methods (BAMM) are not validated with an alternative diversification method.
comments.request: Validate with an alternative diversification method.
comments.quote: given strong opinions out there on the use of diversification methods I think the manuscript could be strengthened by the use of an alternative method

comments.issue: The paper is biased towards bird literature and misses important non-bird studies.
comments.request: Cite relevant non-bird studies.
comments.quote: The paper is throughout biased towards bird literature although a greater number of important topical papers have been published in other taxonomic groups.

reviews.assessment: Useful contribution but not paleo-aware; rate scaling confounds time comparisons and the adaptive-radiation concept should be dropped.
strengths: addresses a worthwhile question about detectability of ancient radiations

comments.issue: The paper ignores fossil-record literature showing the answer is already clear.
comments.request: Engage with the fossil-record literature.
comments.quote: There is a lot of literature on avian morphological evolution that would suggest, from the start, that the answer to the question posed here is clear and in the affirmative.

comments.issue: Rate scaling over widely different timescales confounds comparisons of rate shifts.
comments.request: Address time-dependency and rate-scaling confounds.
comments.quote: There are severe issues with rate scaling that would confound comparisons that span widely-disparate stretches of time.

comments.issue: Estimating the rate correlation as a function of time would avoid relying on discrete ancient shifts.
comments.request: Estimate the rate correlation as a function of time depth.
comments.quote: Would it be more profitable overall to simply estimate the correlation between rates of speciation and phenotypic evolution as a function of time at which the correlation is estimated?

comments.issue: The results are not compared with Cooney and Thomas (2020), which appear to differ.
comments.request: Compare with Cooney and Thomas 2020.
comments.quote: The manuscript should address how the results differ from those of Cooney and Thomas (2020, Nature E&E;).

comments.issue: The adaptive-radiation concept distracts and its definition is unsatisfactory.
comments.request: Reframe results without the adaptive-radiation concept.
comments.quote: all of the results here can be framed in terms of “how well can we detect concurrent shifts of speciation and morphological evolution” (or equivalent) without getting into issues what is and is not an adaptive radiation

comments.issue: The adaptive-radiation concept predates Simpson 1953.
comments.request: Correct the historical attribution.
comments.quote: L70 The concept of adaptive radiation predates Simpson 1953, if that is what is intended here

comments.issue: Fossil-record-only radiations are not acknowledged.
comments.request: Acknowledge fossil-record-only radiations.
comments.quote: for every such example there are probably dozens more that have only left a trace in the fossil record

comments.issue: The rate-based definition of adaptive radiation is problematic in some contexts.
comments.request: Reconsider the rate-based definition.
comments.quote: I would disagree with this definition. This is a useful operational definition in some contexts, but problematic in others.

comments.issue: The paper switches confusingly between whether adaptive radiation occurred and whether it is detectable.
comments.request: Separate the two questions.
comments.quote: This points to a more general confusing switch between foci of the paper, which is: (1) did adaptive radiation occur, versus (2) is it detectable using extant data.

comments.issue: The model at L141-144 and its assumptions need more detail.
comments.request: Describe the model and assumptions.
comments.quote: L141-144: A little more detail on this model and its assumptions needed here.

reviews.assessment: Descriptive paper with unclear hypotheses, uncertain rates and no striking contribution; unlikely to interest the journal's readers.

comments.issue: The paper lacks clear hypotheses of general interest and no striking contribution emerges.
comments.request: Articulate a clear, general-interest contribution.
comments.quote: No really striking results emerge and I found it difficult to summarize the paper’s ultimate contribution.

comments.issue: Both rates are estimated with great and increasing uncertainty; recent results (Louca & Pennell) cast doubt on the model.
comments.request: Address rate uncertainty and Louca & Pennell.
comments.quote: It compares two rates (speciation and morphological evolution) on the tree that are each estimated with a great deal of uncertainty which only gets worse as one goes further back in time

comments.issue: Older adaptive-radiation examples are not mentioned.
comments.request: Add older adaptive-radiation examples.
comments.quote: Line 75: perhaps mention some older ones too, like Lake Tanganyika cichlids (10my?), Caribbean Anolis (40+ my), Hawaiian Drosophila (50 my?).

comments.issue: The rate-shift model is simplistic and its reasonableness under Louca & Pennell is unclear.
comments.request: Justify the rate-shift model and node likelihoods.
comments.quote: Line 128: This is a fairly simplistic model of speciation rate shift. How reasonable is it in light of Louca and Pennell?

comments.issue: Line 137 has unclear meaning.
comments.request: Clarify line 137.
comments.quote: line 137: unclear meaning.

comments.issue: The probability model and how deep-time rates are estimated from tips are not explained.
comments.request: Specify the probability model and estimation.
comments.quote: Line 141: What probability model is assumed? Brownian motion? How is a rate deep in time estimated from only the tips?

comments.issue: The before-after comparison assumes the shifted node is known and its noise is unquantified.
comments.request: Quantify noise in the before-after comparison.
comments.quote: Line 157: This comparison seems to assume that the node with the rate shift is known. How noisy is the before-after comparison likely to be even if the node is known?

title: The causes and ecological context of rapid morphological evolution in birds

study.system: reindeer; logistic population models with density-dependent stochasticity

editor_summary: Both reviewers echo the editor's misgivings about the structural model assumptions and lack of generality; resubmission only if the results are shown robust to the assumed density dependence and how stochasticity enters.

reviews.assessment: Disagrees with how stochastic perturbations and seasonality are modelled and with the realism of proportional harvesting; wants the Hydra Effect context and key references added.

comments.issue: Stochastic perturbations are modelled without seasonality; seasonally varying K rather than r should be used.
comments.request: Rethink how environmental stochasticity and seasonality enter the model (see Xu et al. 2005).
comments.quote: I do not agree with the manner of modelling stochastic perturbations in this ms, especially in context of seasonality.

comments.issue: Proportional harvesting requires abundance estimates that are seldom available; quota harvesting is more typical.
comments.request: Consider quota harvesting rather than a proportional strategy.
comments.quote: implementing a proportional harvesting strategy requires estimates of abundance which are seldom available—pie in the sky. Quota harvesting is more typical, e.g., issuing a set number of licenses.

comments.issue: A difference equation captures none of the nuances of seasonality.
comments.request: Model seasonal dynamics rather than a difference equation.
comments.quote: But using a difference equation none of the nuances of seasonality are captured.

comments.issue: The paper is not placed in the context of the Hydra Effect (Abrams 2007).
comments.request: Add the Hydra Effect context and cite Abrams (2007).
comments.quote: This paper must be placed in context of the Hydra Effect (Abrams 2007).

title: Harvesting can stabilise population fluctuations and buffer the impacts of extreme climatic events

study.system: birds; phylogenetic comparative analyses and flight simulations

editor_summary: Editor: paper is thought-provoking; wants stronger MRCA reconstruction, sister-clade comparisons, HWI recast as efficiency, more support that spurs are costly, more speculation on flight's constraints on sexual selection, and a toned-down introduction.

reviews.assessment: Strong, well-suited study; wants clearer weapon definitions, HWI terminology and phylogenetic sensitivity analyses.
strengths: spur index is a nice innovation

comments.issue: The folksy introduction works overall but the first paragraph is too chatty.
comments.request: Edit the first paragraph to tone it down.
comments.quote: The first paragraph probably needs a little editing so as not to come across too chatty

comments.issue: Calling bony spurs the only specialised avian weapon is unclear, as it excludes other fighting traits such as casques and hummingbird bills.
comments.request: Clarify the definition and explain why these traits are excluded.
comments.quote: the text isn’t clear enough that this definition excludes quite a few other avain morphological traits adapted for fighting

comments.issue: Several line-level edits: wording fixes at lines 57/62, 104, 178 and 433, the ambiguous term at line 349, and updating the HBW Alive citation.
comments.quote: Line 57 “single mention to birds” should be “mention of birds” (same change needed in line 62)

comments.issue: The claim that the 9,993 Jetz tree species are all extant birds is incorrect; Jetz et al. is not a taxonomy.
comments.request: Describe the species as those included in the global birdtree.
comments.quote: Jetz et al is not a taxonomy and the 9993 species contained therein are not all extant species of birds.

comments.issue: HWI is labelled "flight frequency" although evidence links it to flight efficiency and dispersal.
comments.request: Call HWI flight ability or efficiency and rephrase the frequency claim.
comments.quote: I would not call the variable “flight frequency”. Evidence that HWI reflects frequency of flight is not yet published and analysed

comments.issue: Body mass data are not always high-confidence, as many values were inferred from crude models.
comments.request: Limit the statement to "comprehensive" and avoid quality claims.
comments.quote: Data on body mass used by the authors is not always “high-confidence” since hundreds of measures were inferred from crude models by Wilman et al.

comments.issue: The Jetz trees place a third of species algorithmically, which is risky for evolutionary rate models.
comments.request: Run sensitivity analyses using only the molecular tips.
comments.quote: sensitivity analyses are required focusing solely on the ‘molecular tips’

comments.issue: Similar pervasive effects of flight adaptation, such as egg shape, are not mentioned.
comments.request: Add this comparison and the Stoddard et al. 2017 citation.
comments.quote: the authors could mention that their finding is perhaps similar to other findings that adaptation to frequent flight can can have pervasive evolutionary effects

comments.issue: The long paragraph beginning at line 363 needs reorganising and splitting.
comments.request: Break it into two better-organised paragraphs.
comments.quote: Long paragraph beginning line 363: some good information and speculatin in here, but it perhaps needs better organising and breaking into 2 paragraphs.

comments.issue: The point that spur costs can explain lighter alternative weapons in aerial species is not made.
comments.request: Add this point, using hummingbird beak/tooth weapons as examples.
comments.quote: The point could be made that cost of spurs can explain the evolution of alternative (non-specialised) weapons that weigh less in aerial species

comments.issue: The implication that weapon loss drove the evolution of avian visual and vocal signals could be developed further.
comments.request: Refine this message to improve its impact.
comments.quote: the authors could perhaps make a bit more of the fact that their findings might explain why flight adaptation has driven the evolution of classic avian signalling traits

reviews.assessment: Enjoyed the paper and the introduction style; wants more evidence for combat function, cost context, and sister-clade comparisons.
strengths: appreciated the writing and introduction style
novel perspective on weaponry in birds

comments.issue: The claim that bony spurs are primarily used for combat is asserted without evidence.
comments.request: Provide direct or indirect evidence of combat use across spur types.
comments.quote: I would like to see more evidence provided that bony spurs are primarily used for combat in birds.

comments.issue: Tracking devices heavier than spurs are widely tolerated, creating an incongruity with the claimed cost of spurs.
comments.request: Compare spur costs with tracking-device effects and weapon masses in crabs and beetles.
comments.quote: there is still an incongruity here, where the tracking community is mostly (as far as I can tell) ok with putting on devices that weigh a couple percentage points of a birds’ mass

comments.issue: Ancestral-state methods rely on assumptions about deep nodes; simple sister-clade comparisons are missing.
comments.request: Add sister-clade comparisons that do not rely on ancestral-state assumptions.
comments.quote: Is it possible to also include simple sister clade comparisons that do not rely on such assumptions?

comments.issue: The idea could be extended to bats and gliding vertebrates and to sexual dimorphism predictions.
comments.request: Comment on other flying/gliding taxa and dimorphism.
comments.quote: The authors could perhaps also comment on bats and gliding vertebrates (squirrels, colugo, snakes, frogs, lizards).

comments.issue: The Fig. 1 silhouette is placed behind the phylogeny and resembles a bird head.
comments.request: Move the silhouette outside the phylogeny and adjust its orientation.
comments.quote: On Figure 1 I suggest moving the silhouette showing the location of spurs outside of the phylogeny rather than behind the phylogeny.

comments.issue: Fig. 3 shows 80, 90 and 95% intervals.
comments.request: Show only the 95% confidence intervals.
comments.quote: For Figure 3, I would prefer simply showing the 95% confidence intervals (rather than the 80,90, and 95%)

reviews.assessment: Well-justified and interesting, but major concerns about the HWI proxy, ancestral-state estimation, and the unusual introduction.
strengths: liked combining simulations with phylogenetic models

comments.issue: HWI is used as a proxy for flight frequency although it is established as a proxy for efficiency and dispersal.
comments.request: Replace frequency with efficiency when describing HWI.
comments.quote: I found it surprising that HWI is being used here as a proxy for flight frequency specifically

comments.issue: The SIMMAP ancestral reconstruction lacks model-fit testing, alternative programs, and confidence intervals.
comments.request: Test model fit and validate the MRCA reconstruction.
comments.quote: When creating the SIMMAP, which model was used (ER, SYM, ARD) (sounds like ARD from the supplementary materials?), and did you test its fit against other models?

comments.issue: The unusual first paragraph of the introduction risks distracting readers.
comments.request: Reconsider the costs and benefits of this opening style.
comments.quote: I wish to flag that the first paragraph of the introduction is highly unusual.

comments.issue: The hypothetical researcher is specified as female.
comments.request: Use the gender-neutral "they".
comments.quote: I would highly recommend the gender-neutral “they” rather than specifying that this hypothetical researcher is female.

comments.issue: It is odd to describe the hypothetical researcher as not diligent.
comments.request: Revise this characterization.
comments.quote: Why, exactly, is this hypothetical research not particularly diligent?

comments.issue: The citation structure at L60-61 suggests two articles about bird weapons.
comments.request: Clarify the citation structure.
comments.quote: The way the citations are structured in this sentence makes it look like there are two articles about bird weapons

comments.issue: The passage at L61-63 is needlessly combative.
comments.request: Rephrase this passage.
comments.quote: I find this needlessly combative. There are plenty of other aspects of animal biology research that are absent in birds for entirely innocuous reasons

comments.issue: Taxonomic sampling bias is dismissed too quickly as an explanation.
comments.request: Acknowledge this possibility.
comments.quote: Why is taxonomic sampling bias such an outlandishly impossible explanation?

comments.issue: Stating that a literature review is impossible while citing 171 examples is contradictory.
comments.request: Resolve this contradiction precisely.
comments.quote: The fact that you’d just said a literature review of this topic is impossible (i.e. only turns up one article) and are now stating that you’ve found in the literature 171 examples of this trait seems contradictory.

comments.issue: The switch from within-species selection to a macroevolutionary perspective at L82-84 is abrupt.
comments.request: Clarify the relevance of this transition.
comments.quote: why the sudden switch from selection acting within a species to a more macroevolutionary perspective?

comments.issue: The L85 sentence overstates the uniqueness of locomotion for birds.
comments.request: Start the argument with the high energetic costs of powered flight.
comments.quote: I’d suggest just beginning this argument with the high energetic costs of powered flight; the rest of this paragraph is very compelling.

comments.issue: The modelling aspect is not mentioned in the L108-114 paragraph.
comments.request: Mention the modelling in this paragraph.
comments.quote: I’d suggest mentioning the modelling aspect of the paper in this paragraph, and it’s an important aspect of your argument.

comments.issue: Why only 38 of 41 species were used is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the reduction in species number.
comments.quote: Why 38 out of 41? Were they just absent on the Jetz tree?

comments.issue: Permission to scrape HBW Alive and the browsing method used are unclear.
comments.request: Confirm permissions and describe the scraping method.
comments.quote: Scraping the HBW Alive used to be against their terms of service

comments.issue: What was done at L193-218 after the equations is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify this section.
comments.quote: It is unclear to me what was actually done in this section after the equations were established.

comments.issue: The statement at L270-271 about possible transitions is incorrect.
comments.request: Correct the number of possible transitions.
comments.quote: This is false. For two binary characters, there are 8 possible transitions, as transitions between (0,0) and (1,1) are prohibited

comments.issue: The simulation steps and the body mass x HWI interaction are not explained.
comments.request: Add simulation details and explain the interaction.
comments.quote: It is unclear from this text alone what was actually done in the simulations

comments.issue: Which BayesTraits model best fitted the data is not stated or quantified.
comments.request: State the best-fitting model with a Bayes factor or likelihood test.
comments.quote: Which of the four models tested in BayesTraits was the best fit?

comments.issue: The actual transition rates (q values) are not reported.
comments.request: Report the q values.
comments.quote: The actual values of q would be helpful here.

comments.issue: The bills-efficiency sentence at L367-368 is contentious and imprecise.
comments.request: Cite the relevant literature and be more precise.
comments.quote: The underlying argument about specialisation is a good one, just be more precise!

comments.issue: A kiwi, which never flies, is used for the "occasional" flier in Fig. 4.
comments.request: Replace the kiwi image with a flying species.
comments.quote: I find the use of a kiwi image to represent an “occasional” flier to be distracting, as kiwis never fly.

comments.issue: The double silhouette in Fig. 1 is uninformative and hinders readability.
comments.request: Simplify the silhouette.
comments.quote: I find the double silhouette of the bird wing and – reconstructed extinct bird? – to be uninformative and to hinder the readability of this figure.

comments.issue: The small numbers of spur losses and gains are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the number of transitions and whether the sample is adequate.
comments.quote: Some discussion of the minimum numbers of losses and gains of these traits would help the reader to parse your results

comments.issue: The Fig. 2 colour scheme is hard to interpret for colour-blind readers.
comments.request: Choose a colour-blind-friendly palette.
comments.quote: This colour scheme is very hard to interpret for those with the most common form of colour-blindness.

comments.issue: Some Fig. 4 parameter distributions are very wide or non-normal.
comments.request: Discuss the wide and non-normal parameter distributions.
comments.quote: Are you at all concerned that some of these parameter distributions are so wide (e.g. for frequent fliers, spur to no spur?), or so non-normal

comments.issue: The sampling scheme at supplement L690-692 (EqualTrees? sample size) is unclear and possibly excessive.
comments.request: Specify the method and justify the sample size.
comments.quote: I assume this was using the EqualTrees method? One could perhaps specify that.

title: Flight hampers the evolution of weapons in birds

study.system: bacteriophage lambda and E. coli; experimental coevolution, phenotypes and genomes

editor_summary: Editor agrees with R1 and R2 that evidence cannot rule out ARD or prove leapfrog; flags overgeneralization from a single replicate, the neutral-hitchhiker wording, runner-up data, and missing Gandon discussion.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and important analysis of genetic diversity, but not convinced leapfrog is a new dynamic and the single replicate limits scope.
strengths: digs deeply into the origins of genetic diversity
important point about genetic diversity driving arms race dynamics

comments.issue: Leapfrog is not clearly a qualitatively different dynamic and is not placed in the context of past work.
comments.request: Reframe as origins of genetic variation and better contextualize against past work.
comments.quote: it’s not clear to me this is best described as a different kind of dynamic, instead of an effect or process concerning the origins of genetic variation driving arms race (or other) dynamics

comments.issue: Data come from a single replicate, which should be discussed as a limitation.
comments.request: Discuss the single-replicate scope alongside the leapfrog discussion.
comments.quote: The data come from a single replicate of an earlier evolution experiment. They are still rich and interesting, but I would expect this to be discussed somewhere.

comments.issue: The handling of phage-isolation bias is only explained later, not where the method is introduced.
comments.request: Flag at the methods point that this bias is accounted for below.
comments.quote: the possible biases caused by isolating phages on the ancestral bacteria are dealt with later on extremely well, but it would help to already indicate here in the methods that this is accounted for below

comments.issue: Wording at page 7 line 12 is ambiguous about whether variation in EOP values was non-significant.
comments.request: Check and clarify the wording.
comments.quote: Check the wording here - is it that *variation* of EOP values across time was not significant?

comments.issue: Tree patterns look more like single-trajectory evolution than the abstract and discussion imply.
comments.request: Revise the interpretation to reflect the balance of processes in the trees.
comments.quote: statements like that in the abstract about whole genome analyses not fitting the ARD model (p2 L10), and in the discussion about it fitting FSD (p9 L23) don’t seem quite accurate

comments.issue: Day-37 mutations appear in earlier clones, conflicting with the early-arising pool interpretation; mutation counts are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the mutation counts and reconcile Figure 3 with the trees.
comments.quote: it seems the five mutations in the day 37 bacteria were all detected in clones from preceding time points, contrasting with the interpretation they are drawn from an early-arising pool of independent genotypes

comments.issue: Figure 3 genomes and mutation gaps are hard to distinguish at normal zoom.
comments.request: Separate the rings and use a more noticeable mutation indicator.
comments.quote: With a normal level of zoom, I found it hard to distinguish the different genomes and to spot the white gaps for mutations.

reviews.assessment: Interesting phenotype-genotype comparison, but the new-dynamics claim rests on a straw-man version of arms race dynamics and misses relevant studies.
strengths: interesting test of phenotypic and genetic variation correspondence

comments.issue: The hardline single-lineage ARD contrasted against is a straw man; clonal interference and coexisting lineages are expected.
comments.request: Rewrite to acknowledge clonal interference and coexisting lineages.
comments.quote: This seems like a straw man: we know that very large microbial populations that replicate clonally do not evolve like that

comments.issue: The LFD-ARD distinction seems trivial and driven by population genetics and demography rather than a fundamental difference.
comments.request: Temper the language and interpretation accordingly.
comments.quote: the difference seems rather more trivial than is argued in the paper and dependent upon the population geneitics / demography of the system, rather than anything more fundamental of the coevolutionary interaction

comments.issue: Relevant Pseudomonas-phi2 studies (Scanlan et al.; Paterson et al.) are not cited.
comments.request: Cite and discuss these studies.
comments.quote: A couple of studies using the Pseudomonas-phi2 system seem relevant but are not cited

reviews.assessment: Well-written and potentially strong contribution, but the evidence does not conclusively prove ARD versus FSD or a new dynamic.
strengths: potential to make a strong contribution

comments.issue: Nestedness of infection patterns shows gene-for-gene/range interactions, not definitive evidence of ARD.
comments.request: Rely on the time-shift analysis rather than nestedness as ARD evidence.
comments.quote: However, all this actually proves is that the infection patterns are of a range/gene-for-gene nature, and while they commonly produce ARD they can also produce FSD and static coexistence. It is not definitive proof of ARD

comments.issue: Static coexistence of strains on the phylogeny is claimed as FSD evidence without justification.
comments.request: Justify why coexistence implies FSD.
comments.quote: it is stated that static coexistence of strains on the phylogenetic tree is evidence of FSD, but I feel I need to be persuaded of this

comments.issue: Page 2 line 37 implies arms races are the only possible outcome.
comments.request: Acknowledge FSD, branching and ESS alternatives.
comments.quote: This implies Arms Races are the only possible outcome but fluctuating selection (FSD), static polymorphism ('branching') or stable investment at intermediate level (ESS) could also occur.

comments.issue: No reference supports FSD promoting diversification and multi-branch phylogenies; FSD gives temporal, not static, diversity.
comments.request: Provide a reference or revise the claim.
comments.quote: Do you have a reference for FSD promoting diversification and a phylogenic tree with multiple branches?

comments.issue: The discussion neglects ESS/adaptive dynamics models and Agrawal and Lively 2002 as the natural reference.
comments.request: Cite Agrawal and Lively 2002 and engage ESS/adaptive dynamics models.
comments.quote: I'd have said Agrawal and Lively (2002) was the natural reference for models between ARD (Gene for Gene) and FSD (Matching Allele)?

comments.issue: Transient coexistence of multiple good mutants may just be realistic stochastic ARD, not a new dynamic.
comments.request: Clarify the evidence that coexistence is not ordinary ARD.
comments.quote: Couldn't multiple mutations appear that are all better than the current resident strain and so all increase in density for a while, until one eventually takes over?

comments.issue: Why the widely resistant mutant stayed at low density is unexplained; a cost is suggested but not established.
comments.request: Test or discuss the cost hypothesis for the resistant mutant.
comments.quote: A key question is why this widely-resistant mutant did not become dominant as soon as it appeared. Is it carrying a cost that keeps it at low densities until there are multiple (or just more infectious) phage around?

comments.issue: If ecology controls the dynamics, a model with explicit ecological dynamics is not explored.
comments.request: Consider a model with explicit ecological dynamics.
comments.quote: If a key conclusion is that ecology is controlling the dynamics, perhaps a model with explicit ecological dynamics would be worth investigating?

title: Leapfrog dynamics in phage‐bacteria coevolution revealed by joint analysis of cross‐infection phenotypes and whole genome sequencing

study.system: European vertebrates; trait-based food web prediction models

editor_summary: All positive about goals and quality; overselling in title and abstract; remove non-central content and describe methods in far more detail; discuss recent network inference work and end with a stronger 'so what'.

reviews.assessment: Enjoyed the paper; convincing prediction with sparse data, with minor questions on phylogeny, training sets and figures.
strengths: convincing evidence that interactions can be predicted from a small fraction of data

comments.issue: Phylogenetic relatedness is ignored, so trait distributions are not independent and pseudo-replication may inflate results.
comments.request: Address phylogenetic non-independence in the models.
comments.quote: there is pseudo-replication because trait distribution is not independent from phylogeny

comments.issue: Whether non-interactions were used in all training sets is unclear.
comments.request: State how non-interactions were handled in training.
comments.quote: It wasn’t clear to me whether non-interactions were used in all training sets.

comments.issue: Appendix 3 is never referenced in the manuscript.
comments.request: Add a reference to Appendix 3.
comments.quote: I couldn’t find any reference to Appendix 3 in the manuscript.

comments.issue: Figure S3.1 legend states 200-100000 absences, but points below 200 appear.
comments.request: Clarify the legend or the plotted values.
comments.quote: The legend says the number of absences varies from 200 to 100000 but there are points in the graph for number of absences < 200.

comments.issue: Figure S6 x-axis text overlaps and is hard to read.
comments.request: Rotate the x-axis text (e.g., angle = 270).
comments.quote: it would be easier to read the text in the x-axis if it didn’t overlap

reviews.assessment: Great and timely paper with fair analyses; asks for clarification of validation metrics and broader discussion of specialisation.

comments.issue: AUC is used without clarifying how true positive and negative rates and any threshold were determined; sensitivity/specificity/TSS may be more adequate.
comments.request: Clarify the validation framework and metrics.
comments.quote: But your assessment of assessing true positive and negative rates led me to think whether a framework based on sensitivity, specificity and TSS would be more adequate

comments.issue: Specialists are easier to predict, but applicability to other interaction types and the apparent-versus-real specialisation issue are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss how this result generalises to other networks.
comments.quote: I wonder the extent to which this is applicable to other networks, and you do not discuss neither such issue, nor the result I mentioned

comments.issue: Metabolic-rate-based trophic interaction models (e.g., Rall et al. 2012) are not mentioned as future improvements.
comments.request: Mention these modelling approaches.
comments.quote: In the discussion of future improvements to network models I miss some mention to more developed models of trophic interactions based on metabolic rates

comments.issue: The limited coverage of GLOBI (291 of 71,500 interactions) deserves more emphasis.
comments.request: Highlight the sparsity of available interaction data.
comments.quote: I would highlight a bit more in the discussion that data in GLOBI is quite limited (compare the 291 interactions you found there with the 71,500 potential interactions in your metaweb)

comments.issue: Lines 52-53 call the Eltonian shortfall the biggest, which is not supported by the cited review.
comments.request: Call it a critical issue rather than the biggest shortfall.
comments.quote: I checked our Ann Rev paper, and we do not say that the Eltonian is the biggest of all shortfalls anywhere.

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 192-193 does not convey the section's aim; bracketed text should be made explicit.
comments.request: Rewrite to state explicitly what was done.
comments.quote: I think that the sentence in lines 192-193 does not cover exactly what you want to make in this section (which is evident in the title)

comments.issue: Number concordance problems throughout the text (e.g., l.184, l.299).
comments.request: Correct the grammar.
comments.quote: I think there are several problems with number concordance throughout the text

title: Addressing the Eltonian shortfall with trait‐based interaction models

study.system: woody forest plants; common-garden traits of 76 species, phylogenetics

editor_summary: Editor notes only one review was obtained; suggests summarizing the unique functional syndrome in a Crane/Chapin-style diagram, but does not insist.

reviews.assessment: Important, exemplary study with strong praise, but several discussion points and arguments need substantial revision.
strengths: wide range of species and traits
numerous congener pairs for statistical power
exemplary data collection, analysis and statistical techniques

comments.issue: Readers may suspect the study species were cherry-picked based on traits; the pool of species fitting the sampling criteria is unknown.
comments.request: Report how many species would fit the sampling criteria.
comments.quote: more information is needed to settle any doubts by the readers that either the natives or exotics were cherry-picked based on their traits

comments.issue: The utility of long photosynthetic seasons in deciduous forest understories is not developed, and key phenology references are missing.
comments.request: Add the suggested context and citations at line 104 (and 'thus' before the next sentence).
comments.quote: The authors need to provide additional detail re the utility of long photosynthetic seasons (early bud break, late leaf drop) in deciduous forest understories.

comments.issue: 'Jack of all trades phenotype' is too general and insufficiently evocative as the signature label.
comments.request: Rename the phenotype 'rapidly growing but shade-tolerant'.
comments.quote: is, in my opinion, a far too general and insufficiently evocative label

comments.issue: There is no tie back to the rationale for early leafing and late leaf shedding.
comments.request: Insert the suggested rationale and references at line 336.
comments.quote: There is no tie back to the rationale for early leafing/late leaf shedding.

comments.issue: The three arguments at line 352 would read better in a different order.
comments.request: Reshuffle the arguments from 1, 2, 3 to 2, 3, 1, with natural enemies last.
comments.quote: I recommend that the authors reshuffle the order of these arguments from 1, 2, 3 to 2, 3, 1

comments.issue: Climate predictability is not the only difference between Eurasian and eastern North American climates; maritime warming and cooling patterns also matter.
comments.request: Broaden the climatic argument beyond predictability.
comments.quote: predictability is not the only difference between the Eurasian (nw Europe, e Asia) and eastern North American climates

comments.issue: The natural-enemies argument is unfounded: there is no evidence invaders evolved early leafing or late shedding, and the cited evidence against enemy release is misread or weak.
comments.request: Heavily revise or abandon the natural-enemies argument.
comments.quote: The natural-enemies argument is fraught and must be heavily revised or abandoned.

comments.issue: The sentence at line 361 is misleading because it ignores the higher leaf N concentration of invasive species and why phenolics are the focus.
comments.request: Revise the sentence and address the phenolics-to-N ratio.
comments.quote: the sentence beginning on line 361 is extremely misleading because it ignore the much higher N concentration in the leaves of invasive vs. native species

title: Fast but steady: An integrated leaf‐stem‐root trait syndrome for woody forest invaders

study.system: European Alps grasslands; productivity, traits and key species

editor_summary: All reviewers acknowledge novelty and importance but raise suggestions to address; the editor also found it hard to understand how productivity was quantified and asks for evidence on this point.

reviews.assessment: High-interest question and accurate methodology, but SAVI may measure biomass rather than productivity and key-species definitions and figures need work.

comments.issue: SAVI likely measures biomass or production, not productivity, and its use is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain SAVI and use a genuine productivity metric or retitle.
comments.quote: The SAVI index is not explained at all and seems to be mainly an index of biomass or production ? but not of productivity

comments.issue: The soil fertility proxy is not specified.
comments.request: Describe how soil fertility was quantified.
comments.quote: the authors say that they used a measurement of soil fertility without precising the proxy used ?

comments.issue: The Discussion interprets results as productivity despite a likely biomass measurement.
comments.request: Reinterpret or relabel the results accordingly.
comments.quote: Everywhere in the discussion results are discussed like if the authors have really measured productivity whereas they very likely have measured biomass or production.

comments.issue: How key(stone) species were defined is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the key and keystone species definitions.
comments.quote: I had also important problems to understand how were defined key(stone) species.

comments.issue: Figures use very small symbols with very similar colours.
comments.request: Improve symbol size and colour contrast.
comments.quote: Figures have very small symbols with very similar colours.

comments.issue: SAVI at L121 is not explained or referenced and may be a biomass proxy.
comments.request: Explain SAVI and give a reference.
comments.quote: explain more what is SAVI, give a reference. I guess this is a proxy of standing biomass or eventually production but not of productivity ?

comments.issue: Term 'terrain' at L123 is unclear.

comments.quote: what is terrain ? Topography ?

comments.issue: How soil fertility was quantified is not explained at L126.

comments.issue: Height relates to biomass rather than primary productivity.

comments.quote: height is not related to primary productivity but to biomass.

comments.issue: Reasoning is circular if key(stone) species are defined by their correlation with M0.
comments.request: Clarify the circularity and the key-keystone distinction.
comments.quote: It seems to me that the reasoning was quite circular for the calculation of the effect of key(stone) species on SAVI if they are defined by their correlation with M0 ?

comments.issue: Fig. 2 symbols are too small and hard to distinguish.
comments.request: Enlarge and differentiate the symbols.
comments.quote: Fig. 2 : symbols are too small and difficult to distinguish between them.

comments.issue: The K letters suggest moderately warm rather than moderately cool conditions.
comments.request: Clarify the description of the conditions.
comments.quote: it seems to be rather moderately warm than moderately cool considering that the K letters are positionned at intermediate positions along the X rather than Y axis ?

comments.issue: The statement about sedges in warm and dry conditions is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify this statement.
comments.quote: and sedges in warm and dry conditions ?

comments.issue: Fig. 4 increasing and concave curves are both blue despite a purple legend.
comments.request: Use distinguishable colours.
comments.quote: This is impossible to distinguish increasing and concave + curves since both are blue (and not purple as indicated in the legend) !

comments.issue: Negative productivity-LNC relationship suggests SAVI measures biomass.
comments.request: Reconsider the productivity interpretation.
comments.quote: how can productivity be negatively related to CWM of LNC ? This strongly suggests that SAVI is certainly not an index of productivity but of biomass

comments.issue: Fig. 5 symbol colours are hard to distinguish.
comments.request: Use more distinguishable colours.
comments.quote: same than with previous figures the colours of symbols are not easily to distinguish.

comments.issue: Growth rate and competitive ability should be inverted at lines 377-379.
comments.request: Swap the terms and place 'respectively' at the end.
comments.quote: I will rather invert growth rate and competitive ability and say respectively at the end.

comments.issue: Sentence at lines 380-382 is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the sentence more clearly.
comments.quote: sentence not clear, needs more explanation.

reviews.assessment: Wonderful and useful paper; main concern is circularity between species cover and productivity, which a presence/absence analysis can address.

comments.issue: Predicting productivity from species cover is circular because species were selected by cover-productivity association.

comments.issue: A presence/absence supplementary analysis would test whether the cover results are circular.

comments.issue: Species-level trait values are not used as predictors.

comments.issue: Relative explanatory power of environment versus composition is not compared.
comments.request: Fit comparable models to compare explanatory power.
comments.quote: I found myself wondering how the relative explanatory power of environmental vs. compositional differed for your system.

comments.issue: It is unclear which deviances are meant at lines 49-60.
comments.request: State explicitly what the deviances refer to.
comments.quote: Deviances of what (productivity, I assume)? I would say it explicitly in this sentence.

comments.issue: Relevance of the key species traits statement at lines 50-51 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify its relevance.

comments.issue: 'Non-environmental predictors' at line 52 is undefined.
comments.request: Define the term.
comments.quote: “Non-environmental predictors”: Are these traits? Species identities? Or something else?

comments.issue: Key and keystone species are not defined at line 77.

comments.quote: Can you briefly define the difference between key and keystone?

comments.issue: Where species were measured relative to the plots is unclear.

comments.quote: Can you include a bit more information here about where the species were measured, relative to where the plots are for which you are analysing data?

comments.issue: Why data were split into subsets rather than using continuous covariates is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the subsetting approach.
comments.quote: Can you briefly explain why you broke the data into subsets, rather than fitting a model with continuous covariates across the full dataset?

comments.issue: Negative-coefficient species appear to be treated as adding no explanatory power.
comments.request: Explain or revise this treatment.
comments.quote: It seems here like you treated species with negative coefficients as though they added no explanatory power to the model – is that correct?

study.system: North American birds; body size and brain size, 40-year specimens

editor_summary: Editor says R1 questions whether brain size matters if size changes are plastic rather than selected, R2 raises data and analysis issues; rejection with option to resubmit after thorough revision.

reviews.assessment: Interesting question and well-written, but data comparability and analytical choices raise serious doubts.

comments.issue: The data do not allow the question to be addressed in a solid manner.
comments.request: Use data adequate to the question.
comments.quote: I think the work is generally well written, however I am not convinced the data presented in the ms allows the authors to tackle the question in a solid manner.

comments.issue: Body size from many specimens is compared with brain size from few individuals; allometry makes the datasets incomparable.
comments.request: Address comparability of brain and body size data.
comments.quote: It is questionable whether these data are actually comparable, as given the very strong allometric relationship between brain and body size in birds, body size variation is certain to be associated with variation in brain size.

comments.issue: Whether brain size tracks body size reductions, and how quickly, is unknown.
comments.request: Measure brain and body size on the same individuals.
comments.quote: These questions highlight the importance of combining body size measures with the estimates of brain volumes for those same individuals to robustly address the question at hand.

comments.issue: The known migration distance-brain size relationship (Sol et al 2010, Vincze 2016) is not considered for these migrants.
comments.request: Cite and account for the migration distance-brain size relationship.
comments.quote: I am surprised that the authors do not refer to the well known relationship between migration distance and brain size in birds (see Sol et al 2010, Vincze 2016), which can obviously influence their results given they are working with North American migrants.

comments.issue: Highly saturated model followed by criticized backward stepwise selection; residual control for allometry also criticized.
comments.request: Avoid stepwise selection and residual-based allometry control.
comments.quote: The authors begin with a highly saturated model (the number of predictors is about 1/2 the total number of species included in the analyses) and then employ a backward stepwise approach to "simplify" the model, something which has been criticized

comments.issue: Longevity estimates combine captive and wild individuals, which are not comparable.
comments.request: Use comparable wild longevity estimates.
comments.quote: Longevity data combine estimates from captive and wild individuals, but these are not really comparable, as longevity from captive individuals includes solely intrinsic mortality, and is most likely to be quite higher than that estimated in the wild.

comments.issue: Functioning of the complex Bayesian model is not described in enough detail.
comments.request: Give more details of the Bayesian model.
comments.quote: I think more details regarding the functioning of the Bayesian model would be welcome, as it is somewhat complex given your response variable has many entries per singe value of most of the predictors.

comments.issue: Mechanisms proposed for warming-driven size reduction are not discussed or evidenced.
comments.request: Discuss alternative mechanisms such as resource availability and adult mortality.
comments.quote: I would have thought it important to include more discussion regarding the proposed mechanisms responsible for the documented size-reduction attributed to climate change.

reviews.assessment: Wonderful, important paper with solid analyses, but the plasticity-versus-selection justification for the framing needs compelling clarification.

comments.quote: The authors state that it does not matter whether the underlying warming-driven changes in size are the result of plasticity or selection, but I’m not sure I followed their reasoning, and remain unconvinced.

comments.request: Use generation length estimates such as those of Bird et al. 2020.
comments.quote: It seems to me that the authors should use actual estimates of generation length rather than just maximum lifespan.

comments.quote: however, I do think if they want to say the changes in size are small, that statement needs to be justified by the addition of context, showing that a 3% decline is actually small relative to other relevant processes/patterns

title: Sexual dimorphism in immune function and oxidative physiology across birds: The role of sexual selection

study.system: longleaf pine forest; field experiment with drought, invasion, fire

editor_summary: Move species details from Introduction to Methods, broaden the Introduction's scope, and add predictions on whether combined stressor effects exceed the sum of their parts.

reviews.assessment: Sees compelling evidence for invasion effects but finds drought effects unclear, fire-behaviour methods substandard, and global implications exaggerated.
strengths: compelling evidence for invasive species effects on tree mortality
useful results for management of an important tree species

comments.issue: Paper claims to be mechanistic but cannot determine the mechanisms of tree mortality, only associations.

comments.quote: Although the study makes claims to being mechanistic, a limitation of the study was the inability to determine mechanisms of tree mortality

comments.issue: Global implications exaggerated; longleaf pine and cogongrass traits are unusual, and broad inference is not argued.

comments.quote: How general are these traits of tree species and invasive species globally?

comments.issue: Grouping experiments as 'global change model', 'mechanistic model' and 'management model' was distracting.

new angle on a classic puzzle

comments.issue: The individual-level motivation and contribution are buried in the population-versus-individual distinction.

comments.quote: A primary motivation and contribution of this study is understated, in my opinion.

comments.issue: The writing is vague yet inordinately complicated, and the title's 'predation' should be 'predation risk'.

comments.quote: Throughout, the writing style needs a very thorough edit, in that much of the wording is both vague yet inordinately complicated.

comments.issue: 'Unexplained multiplicative effects' is oblique and undefined.

comments.issue: The link between delayed density dependence theory and food or predation drivers is not explained.

comments.issue: 'Low condition' is not defined and could be replaced by a more intuitive term.

comments.quote: if “low condition” = “poor nutritional condition” or “poor body condition”, please use one of these more intuitive terms.

comments.issue: 'Individual-based' and 'population-level' food supplementation are not explicitly defined.
comments.request: Define both terms when first used.
comments.quote: Throughout, the authors distinguish between ‘individual-based’ and ‘population-level’ food supplementation. I think I’m intuiting the difference here, but it would be good to explicitly define each when first they are used.

comments.issue: The confound in past population-level experiments is not made explicit as a key motivation.

comments.quote: I would make this more explicit by identifying it as a potential weakness of past studies (and thus a key motivation for the current study)

comments.issue: 'In these parameters' is vague and does not specify which parameters.

comments.quote: “in these parameters”. Please be specific here—what parameters? Mortality due to predation and mortality due to food limitation?

comments.issue: 'Snow conditions' is undefined, and the related speculation belongs in the Discussion.
comments.request: Define or delete the term and move speculation to the Discussion.
comments.quote: please define or delete “snow conditions”. The speculation here is fine, but likely belongs in a forthcoming Discussion section.

comments.issue: 'Foraging value' is undefined.
comments.request: Define or delete 'foraging value'.
comments.quote: P10 L36: please define or delete “foraging value”.

comments.issue: 'Mortality signal' is unclear and may just be a double pulse.
comments.request: Clarify what the mortality signal represents.
comments.quote: I’m guessing “mortality signal” was simply a double pulse, correct?

comments.issue: The paper does not state that most hare mortality was due to predation.
comments.request: State that the majority of mortality was predation.
comments.quote: I might’ve missed this, but if not, it would be good to state that the majority of hare mortality was due to predation.

comments.issue: Standard errors are used in Figure 2 while other figures use confidence intervals.

comments.quote: Why are SE’s used in Fig 2, but CI’s are used in other figures?

comments.issue: Several sentences are awkward, wordy or contain tense errors (P4 L15, P5 L19-22, P5 L41, P6 L8, P7 L4, P9 L24).
comments.quote: P5 L19-22: the last phrase in this sentence is awkward.

reviews.assessment: Congratulates the authors on an exceptionally interesting, clearly presented study and asks for more specificity on links to past work and feeder allocation.

clearly presented with state-of-the-art data analysis

comments.issue: The connection to the stress hypothesis is left hanging.

comments.issue: Details on how the food supplementation treatment was allocated and used are missing.

reviews.assessment: Very well-written and convincing study, with the only weakness being a too-short discussion that should connect to vole cycle research.

strengths: very well made conceptual diagrams and figures
could be a very important paper with more work

reviews.assessment: Supports the piece and its importance, but asks for clearer definitions and stronger citational evidence throughout.

comments.issue: Training aspects at lines 60-64 lack references for their context.

comments.issue: The 'U' in LGBTQUIA+ at line 250 may be a typo.

comments.issue: No examples of trials or pilot studies of the EFL review are given.

title: An intersectionality lens is needed to establish a global view of equity, diversity and inclusion

study.system: diverse multispecies communities; Bayesian sparse interaction models

editor_summary: All reviewers call for more complete simulations and clarity; need a careful guide for applications, identifiability, alternatives, limitations, credible-interval interpretation, and simulation environmental conditions.

reviews.assessment: Clear, broadly interesting method, but simulations, application guidance and study-design recommendations need strengthening.
strengths: addresses a major challenge in multispecies communities
of interest to a broad audience

comments.issue: All simulations assume mostly generic interactions; performance under different interaction structures is untested.
comments.request: Simulate varying numbers and structures of non-generic interactions.
comments.quote: I think it would be useful to see how the model performs as the number of non-generic interactions varies or when interactions follow a different structure

comments.issue: The role of shrinkage parameter tau and CI-width tuning in model complexity is not demonstrated in the simulations.
comments.request: Explore prediction error with fixed tau and tuned CI widths.
comments.quote: I would also be interested in how the improvements in prediction error with more data (as in Fig. 2c) would change if tau were fixed

comments.issue: Results are not compared with completely generic or completely specific interaction approaches.
comments.request: Compare against alternative modelling approaches.
comments.quote: I wonder if the authors might make a more convincing point if they were able to compare the results to those from different approaches (e.g. completely generic or completely specific interactions).

comments.issue: It is unknown whether fitted coefficients predict community biomass, coexistence or network properties.
comments.request: Test downstream applications or warn readers where the method is unsuited.
comments.quote: Would the simulated coefficients, for instance, correctly predict community-level biomass, community structure (coexistence), or properties of the interaction network (e.g. intransitivity)

comments.issue: No guidance on designing experiments or collecting data for applying the approach.
comments.request: Provide study-design and sampling recommendations.
comments.quote: How should readers interested in applying this approach go about designing experiments or collecting data?

comments.issue: L7 implies the paper addresses nonlinearity and higher-order interactions, which it does not.
comments.request: Correct this implication.
comments.quote: I would argue that nonlinearity is not necessarily specific to diverse systems.

comments.issue: Coefficient notation at L248 does not match the figure labels.
comments.request: Relabel the figure or align the notation.
comments.quote: The coefficients mentioned in this line (generic interspecific competition, e.g. \bar{a}\_{0,i}) don't correspond to the notation in the figure

comments.issue: The number of terms actually present in the model is not reported at L253.
comments.request: Report the number of model terms.
comments.quote: Here it would be useful context to know how many terms were actually present in the model (14, I believe?).

comments.issue: Which theoretical insights are meant at L373 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify this sentence.
comments.quote: I’m not sure I understand which theoretical insights are referred to here, could the sentence be clarified?

reviews.assessment: Interesting, well-situated approach with no major concerns; suggests more realistic simulations and discussion of identifiability and alternatives.

comments.issue: Simulations use the statistical model's own equations with Gaussian noise, giving unrealistic noise structure.
comments.request: Consider more realistic simulation scenarios.
comments.quote: the authors consider only a scenario in which the equations of the statistical model (1-4) are used directly to simulate the data

comments.issue: Performance across sparseness values, data richness and non-Beverton-Holt generative processes is not tested.
comments.request: Simulate a wider range of sparseness, data richness and dynamics.
comments.quote: It would have been nice to see how the approach performs across a range of sparseness values and a range of data richness, to get a better sense of how much data is needed.

comments.issue: Statistical non-identifiability, a core problem for parameter-rich interaction models, is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss non-identifiability and its implications.
comments.quote: In a non-identifiable model, no amount of data can identify the correct model parameters

comments.issue: Non-parametric Bayesian alternatives such as Gaussian and Dirichlet processes are not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention non-parametric Bayesian alternatives.
comments.quote: There is also no mention of non-parametric Bayesian methods, which provide an alternative approach to representing a large range of possible dynamics with far fewer parameters.

comments.issue: The method is not assumption-free, and sparsity-prior influence on results with growing data is not noted.
comments.request: Note the influence of the sparsity prior as data accumulate.
comments.quote: the approach is not assumption-free, it is only relaxing typical assumptions by a degree, not dispensing with them entirely

reviews.assessment: Compelling and substantial contribution, but the simulation exercise needs replication before the results can support the claims.
strengths: good job establishing flexibility and usefulness

comments.issue: Only one model fit per data size, so estimation bias versus imprecision cannot be assessed.
comments.request: Repeat model fits across many simulated datasets.
comments.quote: you're really only simulating a single dataset (composed of many communities) and fitting it 3 different ways, and each parameter is only estimated 3 times in total

comments.issue: Simulation methodology for model fitting in Section 3.3 is unclear.
comments.request: Describe the fitting procedure more clearly.
comments.quote: I recommend being clearer about the simulation methodology with regards to model fitting (not just dataset generation) in Section 3.3

comments.issue: The origins of limitations in community dynamics models are not discussed in the introduction.
comments.request: Discuss where these limitations come from.
comments.quote: In the intro I'd appreciate more discussion on how limitations to community dynamics models arise.

comments.issue: Discussion lacks concrete recommendations on when to use this model versus other approaches.
comments.request: State the method's limitations and appropriate use cases.
comments.quote: I'd like to see more concrete recommendations for when to use this model relative to other approaches

comments.issue: Sentences at lines 19-23 are hard to follow; the point only becomes clear at line 25.
comments.request: Rewrite these sentences.
comments.quote: These sentences are hard to follow; I didn't understand the point

comments.issue: Sentence at lines 57-58 is ambiguous about whether it argues against JSDMs.
comments.request: Make the argument explicit.
comments.quote: This sentence is ambiguous to me. If this is an argument against the use of JSDMs for inference on interactions, please make that more explicit

comments.issue: Line 69's reference to 'these' methodological developments is unclear.
comments.request: Specify which developments are meant.
comments.quote: Which methodological developments are “these”? More than 2 have been discussed

comments.issue: A 75% rate of CIs including the true parameter is called highly accurate, but should be ~95%.
comments.request: Clarify whether this reflects bias or inaccurate CIs.
comments.quote: I would not call a 75% rate of 95% CIs including the true parameter “highly accurate.”

comments.issue: Tension between large datasets improving performance and the method being designed for data-limited contexts.

comments.quote: There seems to be a tension in this paragraph between the idea that large datasets make the model perform better in the simulation, and the fact that this method is designed for data-limited contexts.

comments.issue: Figure 3 omits CIs for intraspecific and species-specific gradient effects.

comments.quote: Is there a reason CIs have been excluded for the intraspecific and species-specific gradient effects?

study.system: complex food webs; predator-prey metacommunity models

editor_summary: Concepts such as evolution and mutation are unclear and misleading, model decisions lack biological justification, the explanatory power is not convincingly demonstrated, and overall merit is below the journal's level.

reviews.assessment: Well-written and fascinating modelling paper, but the evolution and mutation language is misleading and the model notation and interpretation need clarification.
strengths: very well written and pleasant to read
introduction makes a great opening to a fascinating topic
results are very interesting and the paper is solid

comments.issue: The model formulation is convoluted: symbols such as B^{R,C} are hard to read and parameter symbols are used inconsistently.
comments.request: Simplify and standardize the notation and explain it more fully.
comments.quote: I kept on tripping over while reading the model formulation, not because the model is incorrect, but because the explanations and symbols used are at times convoluted

comments.issue: Calling the resampling of new species mutations is misleading, and the implied speciation rate would be implausible.
comments.request: Drop the mutation wording and describe new species arriving with new traits.
comments.quote: To call “mutations” the resampling of new species whose attack rates differ from those of already occurring species is misleading, if not wrong.

comments.issue: Terms such as evolution, mutation and inheritance are used although traits are not inherited and the model is not about organic evolution.
comments.request: Explain how the model should be interpreted and remove misleading evolutionary terms.
comments.quote: Adding words like “evolution”, “mutation”, “inheritance” and the likes, when this model clearly isn’t about organic evolution, as evolutionary biologists understand it, just muddles the waters.

comments.issue: The model tracks species turnover and trait optimization, not evolution of attack rates as claimed.
comments.request: Revise the claim that the model tracks evolution of attack rates.
comments.quote: However, it cannot possibly be argued that this model actually keeps track of evolution in attack rates, as the paper claims.

comments.issue: The establishment step (exploitative competition) in Table 1 is not explained and its origin is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the establishment condition in the text.
comments.quote: Table 1: establishment step (exploitative competition) should be explained in the text. Where is this condition coming from?

comments.issue: L-23 should read 'the arguments invoked then' without 'blunt'.
comments.request: Remove the word blunt.
comments.quote: L-23: “the arguments invoked then”, instead of “the blunt arguments invoked then”

comments.issue: Theory is used as a synonym for hypothesis or mathematical modelling throughout.
comments.request: Rephrase theory where it means hypothesis or model.
comments.quote: The paper uses “theory” as synonymous with hypothesis (although sometimes also as synonymous with other things like mathematical modeling) throughout.

comments.issue: A mathematical model cannot demonstrate what occurs in nature, and theoretical papers are cited as proof.
comments.request: Rephrase the demonstration claims and citations accordingly.
comments.quote: I think that for something to be properly demonstrated in biology, it has to be done using data.

comments.issue: Lines 53-54 are unnecessary.
comments.request: Remove lines 53-54.
comments.quote: as proof that something has been shown to occur in the wild. L-53,54: Unnecessary.

comments.issue: Invasibility is misspelled as invadibility on L-73.
comments.request: Correct the spelling.
comments.quote: L-73: Invasibility instead of invadibility?

comments.issue: The point that unconstrained attack rates evolve towards resource and then predator extinction is only implicit on L-114-128.
comments.request: Make this point explicit and cite the relevant studies.
comments.quote: I think the important point that needs to be made here but isn’t, is that in the absence of constraints on attack rates, they often evolve towards values that lead to the extinction of the resource, and subsequent extinction of the predator

comments.issue: It is unclear whether L-148 refers to food webs with two trophic levels.
comments.request: Clarify the meaning of this statement.
comments.quote: L-148: Do you mean food webs with two trophic levels?

comments.issue: The questions on L-150-153 are set out awkwardly.
comments.request: Fold the questions into the paragraph.
comments.quote: L-150 to 153 I think these questions need not be written like this, and can be folded into the paragraph.

comments.issue: Biomasses written as B^{R,C} are needlessly hard to read.
comments.request: Use R_k and C_k notation instead.
comments.quote: Why are biomasses written as ^B{^R, C}, when they can be written as R and C? State variables in this model are excruciatingly but needlessly hard to read.

comments.issue: Parameter s in Eqs 2a,b is never explained and is easily confused with capital S.
comments.request: Explain or rename the parameter s.
comments.quote: What is parameter “s” for? It shows up out of the blue during non-dimensionalization but is never explained.

comments.issue: Why the expression on L-178,179 is constrained by prudence is not explained.
comments.request: Explain this constraint in detail immediately.
comments.quote: Why is this particular expression constrained by prudence? This being crucial, it needs to be explained in detail and right away.

comments.issue: The R quantity on L 180 reuses a letter already used for resources.
comments.request: Rename the quantity to avoid confusion, e.g. lambda.
comments.quote: Where is this R quantity coming from? Why use a letter that already is being used to allude to resources?

comments.issue: The equal-body-mass assumption behind the L 183 analogy is implausible and the naming is not needed.
comments.request: Drop the analogy and relabel the quantity.
comments.quote: assuming that all species have the same body mass would make no sense whatsoever. I don’t see why this is relevant to even be mentioned.

comments.issue: L-193 does not specify that species, not individuals, are sampled.

comments.quote: While obvious by context, it would be nice to specify that consumer *species*, not individuals, are being sampled here.

comments.issue: Parameter names such as r conflict with ecological conventions and will confuse ecologist readers.
comments.request: Rename parameters to match ecological conventions.

title: Evolution of prudent predation in complex food webs

study.system: wetland plant communities, New Zealand; trait-based abundance models

editor_summary: All referees recognize the study's novelty; R3 and the editor raise methodological concerns about the Gaussian assumption, the explanation of equation 5, hyper-dimensional trait space and unclear passages.

reviews.assessment: Novel and broadly applicable framework, but the Gaussian competition assumption, interpretability of K and documentation need attention.
strengths: addresses a central question in community ecology
of interest to the journal's readership
potential to integrate biotic interactions at larger scales

comments.issue: The standardized carrying capacity K_ij is hard to interpret; a value of 0.5 seems to imply half the ground would be bare.
comments.request: Clarify the interpretation of the standardization.
comments.quote: I found myself confused by the end of the Step 1 section (L126-128) by the standardizing step that converts the carrying capacities K\_ij to a number between 0 and 1

comments.issue: It is unclear which parts belong to the original Traitspace framework and which are new in this study.
comments.request: Distinguish clearly what is new versus previously published.
comments.quote: it is unclear what parts are included under the original description of Traitspace, and what is new here

comments.issue: The Traitspace carrying capacity is not related to Chesson's view that K is the inverse of the intraspecific competition coefficient.

comments.issue: The choice of two aboveground traits for the biotic component rather than one above- and one belowground trait is not justified.

comments.issue: The number of assembly models (twelve versus sixteen) is inconsistent.

comments.issue: Detailed competition experiments in other systems are not cited.

comments.issue: The constant C should be written out at first use.

comments.issue: Line-level copy edits (verb form 'Followed' to 'follows'; 'Competitive' to 'competing').

comments.issue: Figure S1 belongs in the main text; the paragraph is hard to follow without it.

comments.issue: Model numbers are absent from Table 1 and the bracketed ranges are not defined.

comments.quote: I would suggest the authors include these numbers in Table 1 and also use these numbers to describe the results here.

comments.issue: The comparison 'performed better' at L294 lacks an explicit baseline.

comments.issue: Total sample size per model is not reported.

editor_summary: All three reviewers are positive about the paper’s potential but raise serious issues regarding the statistical analysis, the fungicide data and other aspects that must be addressed in revision.

reviews.assessment: Novel approach and phenomena, but NDVI–biomass interpretation, overyielding details and fungicide specificity raise concerns.

comments.issue: The Cedar Creek plot settings, species composition, sown versus realized richness and missing species are not described.
comments.request: Provide plot and species details in the supplement.

comments.issue: Overyielding type, value ranges and error-bar definitions are unclear, and monoculture variance may violate homoscedasticity.

comments.issue: How SEM and the reliability parameter were calculated is not explained.

comments.issue: The null soil fungicide effect may reflect killing of mycorrhizal symbionts rather than unimportant soil pathogens.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and publishable results, but plants, fungi and insects are not black boxes; fungicide treatments and consumer labels need more specificity and information.

comments.issue: Results are likely highly species- and functional-group specific and environment dependent, as plants, fungi and insects are not black boxes.
comments.request: Disentangle the black boxes and acknowledge context dependence.
comments.quote: it is important to emphasize that neither plants, fungi nor insects are black boxes and results are probably highly species/functional group specific and depends on environmental conditions

comments.issue: The plant species used in diversity treatments and their functional groups are not listed.
comments.request: Add a species and functional-group table to the supplement.
comments.quote: it would be useful to add a table with plant species used in diversity treatments into Supplementary data and add information on their functional groups

comments.issue: Foliar fungicide affects many fungal groups, so the treated organisms cannot simply be called consumers or fungal pathogens.
comments.request: Define foliar fungi and report which fungal species the fungicide reduces.
comments.quote: Without more knowledge on the foliar fungicide effect, these group cannot be called “consumers” or “fungal pathogens”.

comments.issue: The claim of a fungal super generalist affecting all plant species equally lacks evidence.
comments.request: Provide data that the observed effect is not species dependent.
comments.quote: Could you provide data, that the observed effect is not species dependent?

comments.issue: Mefenoxam targets oomycetes rather than fungi, and other soil fungi are unaffected, so the soil fungicide treatment label is inaccurate.
comments.request: Specify which organism groups the soil fungicide is expected to reduce.
comments.quote: So your treatments are probably not foliar x soil fungi, but some fungi (with stronger effect on fungi living on/in leaves, because they are most exposed to fungicide) and some Oomycetes.

comments.issue: The limits of pesticide-based studies are not described.
comments.request: Briefly describe the limitations of pesticide-based approaches.
comments.quote: Generally, I would appreciate to describe briefly limits of pesticide-based studies.

comments.issue: The claim at lines 96-98 is not straightforward and relevant references are missing.
comments.request: Support the lines 96-98 statement with the suggested references.
comments.quote: l. 96-98 It is not so straightforward.

comments.issue: Lines 115-118 are difficult to understand.
comments.request: Clarify the lines 115-118 passage.
comments.quote: l. 115-118 Difficult to understand

comments.issue: The claimed contrast between seasonal plant-diversity knowledge and consumer phenology knowledge is not supported by a few old references.
comments.request: Support or soften the lines 125-134 statement.
comments.quote: I do not think that our limited knowledge on effect of plant diversity on plant production during season are in contrast to our knowledge on consumer phenology.

comments.issue: Community composition and phylogenetic relationships may be the key drivers at lines 135-137.

comments.quote: Maybe the key is a plant species community composition and their phylogenetic relationships

comments.quote: I am not so sure about it; different species have different importance for ecosystem functioning.

comments.issue: Generalization about fungal effects is difficult without identifying the affected fungi.

comments.quote: There is no proof that fungal pathogens were affected, only some unknown fungi sensitive to “foliar fungicide”

comments.quote: It should be mentioned that fungicides can directly affect plant physiology, so maybe not only removal of some fungi.

reviews.assessment: Novel, valuable study with large effects; asks for more methodological explanation, mechanistic discussion and uncertainty in spline and slope estimates.

comments.issue: The consumer removal setup, species pool, monoculture selection and mixture design are not described in enough detail.

comments.issue: The null soil fungi effect is never discussed, and whether the soil fungicide actually reduces pathogens is untested.

comments.issue: 2 line-level copy edits (incomplete L48 sentence; L330 wording).
