comments.issue: Only underestimation of diversity effects is mentioned, though infrequent sampling may also overestimate them.
comments.request: Acknowledge that infrequent sampling may also overestimate diversity effects.
comments.quote: Biodiversity-productivity relationships measured only one or two times per season, may presumably also overestimate diversity effects.

comments.issue: Faster emergence after overwintering is an alternative explanation for arthropod effects at L336.

comments.quote: L336: Arthropods could also emerge faster after overwintering.

comments.issue: Pathogen spillover in diverse communities could increase pathogen incidence and severity, an alternative to dilution.
comments.request: Discuss pathogen spillover in diverse communities at lines 345-364.

comments.issue: Diversity was not included as a continuous variable in the models.

comments.quote: Why was diversity not included as a continuous variable in the models?

comments.issue: Supplementary table descriptions do not link results to figures.
comments.request: Link supplementary tables to the relevant figures.
comments.quote: It would be good to mention in the supplementary table descriptions, which figure the results are linked to.

title: PERFICT: A Re‐imagined foundation for predictive ecology

study.system: lake and forest soil communities; food-web structure and assembly models

editor_summary: Editor: rejecting, based on R2: links inferred from co-occurrence rather than observed, making results circular; if authors can show the data are appropriate, resubmission possible; R1's comments attached.

reviews.assessment: Novel and essential investigation of spatial variability in food webs; the minimalistic meta food-web model has excellent potential.
strengths: niche assumption performed better, matching niche models

comments.issue: Methods explanations are hard to follow; more detail is needed on model simulation, behavior and analyses (majors and minors attached as PDFs).
comments.request: Expand the methods explanations for clarity.
comments.quote: I had some difficulties following methods explanations, and more details are necessary for full clarity regarding model simulation and behavior, and analyses employed.

reviews.assessment: Loves the premise but serious methodological concerns about inferred interactions mean the conclusions cannot be supported.

comments.issue: Species lists converted to food webs using metaweb co-occurrence cannot capture local trait changes or altered interaction ability, so the data cannot test the hypotheses.
comments.request: Use actual local food-web data or demonstrate the inferred data are adequate.
comments.quote: The datasets for this study, if I understand correctly, are species lists from each individual lake or forest, rather than food webs. To turn the species list into a food web, interactions from the metaweb are assigned whenever the consumer and resource species co-occur.

comments.issue: Assigning all metaweb interactions to co-occurring species forces zero structural dissimilarity at zero species dissimilarity and removes realised-interaction variation, biasing results.
comments.request: Account for this artefact and the underestimated error variance.
comments.quote: This could generate two artefacts: first, it sets the intercept (in Fig. 2e) to zero, because zero species dissimilarity must equal zero structural dissimilarity, and increasing differences in species composition can produce a greater range of possible differences in web structure.

comments.issue: Pairwise distances are non-independent and the predictor is measured with error, violating regression assumptions.
comments.request: Use a major axis regression that accounts for paired non-independence.
comments.quote: Since these distances are pairwise, doesn’t this non-independence violate the assumption of these regressions and correlations? Moreover, in Fig. 2e, the predictor variable is sampled in local webs, and therefore subject to error

comments.issue: Hypotheses H2 and H3 are difficult to falsify because partial correlation and index-dependent relationships must hold.
comments.request: Reframe hypotheses around which indices should respond and why.
comments.quote: The framing of H1 is fine, but H2 and H3 are difficult to falsify. “Only partly correlated” (H2) pretty much has to be the case; unless food web structure and species composition are the same thing they won’t be fully correlated

comments.issue: H1 restates the already demonstrated insensitivity of network structure to species turnover; the novelty is not captured by the stated hypotheses.
comments.request: Frame the hypotheses to capture the actual novelty.
comments.quote: Even putting aside this framing, H1 is essentially a restatement of the idea that structure is relatively insensitive to changing species composition along gradients, which has been demonstrated across a variety of networks

comments.issue: The L.71 sentence about community assembly and meta-food-web structures is unclear.
comments.request: Split the sentence and define meta-food-web structures.
comments.quote: made sense up until the comma, but I couldn’t understand how the second conclusion about meta-food-web structures arose from the first part.

comments.issue: The Fricke and Svenning paper on distance decay in species and interactions is not cited.
comments.request: Cite Fricke and Svenning.
comments.quote: Although it focused on plant-frugivore networks rather than food webs, and network beta diversity rather than structural turnover, it may be worth citing the recent paper by Fricke and Svenning

comments.issue: The choice of network structure metrics is not defended.
comments.request: Justify the choice of metrics, probably in the supplement.
comments.quote: Using metrics of network structure always invites the criticism of “why didn't you use my favourite metrics”? I would therefore defend (probably in the supplement) the choice of metrics used.

comments.issue: The sentence at L.297 appears incomplete.
comments.request: Complete or rephrase the sentence.
comments.quote: The sentence (L.297) beginning

comments.issue: The L.320 statement is not a result: the model fixes the number of links and assigns them randomly.
comments.request: Remove or reframe the claim as a model property.
comments.quote: Didn’t the models fix the number of links (L.195) but assign them to species at random? In other words, this isn’t a result – it was hard wired into your model.

title: Biotic filtering by species’ interactions constrains food‐web variability across spatial and abiotic gradients

study.system: temperate forest trees; 40+ years survival/growth data across 23 stands

editor_summary: Two reviewers raise serious concerns about analyses and methodology; the editor cannot recommend publication even with major revision but a completely rethought version might be considered; the third review was too negative to be very useful.

reviews.assessment: Finds little novelty, fatal methodological flaws and conclusions inconsistent with theory; recommends a specialty journal.

comments.issue: The study addresses biotic factors only and ignores climate, space and evolutionary history as alternative hypotheses.
comments.request: Consider the other classes of drivers of elevational diversity.
comments.quote: The present study addresses the biotic factors and ignores the others as alternative hypotheses.

comments.issue: The significant results are inconsistent between growth and survival with no mechanistic explanation.
comments.request: Explain why CNDD appears in different vital rates for different size classes.
comments.quote: The significant results are inconsistent because CNDD is present in small trees for survival but not for growth, and vice versa for large trees.

comments.issue: Fig. 4 shows no general pattern, with the three altitude classes showing the same trends and intersecting.
comments.request: Provide explanation or mechanism for the Fig. 4 patterns.
comments.quote: from this figure, no general pattern emerges. There are no consistent differences among the three altitude classes.

comments.issue: Major hypotheses for elevational diversity gradients, such as Rapoport's rule and the mid-domain effect, are not considered.
comments.request: Address the traditional hypotheses.
comments.quote: The current study does not consider the major drivers and hypotheses that have been proposed for explaining diversity gradient, for example, the Rapoport’s rule and the mid-domain effect.

comments.issue: Longitudinal data do not make the study mechanistic; competition and pathogens are not distinguished.
comments.request: Remove mechanistic claims or identify actual mechanisms.
comments.quote: the study does not identify any mechanisms behind the patterns presented

comments.issue: Alternative explanations are unaddressed; growth varies with altitude and neighborhood structure confounds CNDD detection.
comments.request: Address these confounders.
comments.quote: Consequently, the structure and composition of fundamentally different neighborhoods across plots act as a confounding factor for detecting CNDD.

comments.issue: The study joins a long line of correlative CNDD work, including uncited prior elevation studies, and has little novelty.
comments.request: Consider a specialty journal or substantially reframe.
comments.quote: Given the long line of correlative work, and especially the papers by He & Duncan and Xu & Yu's there is little novelty in this paper, and it is probably better suited for a specialty journal.

comments.issue: An irrelevant null-model document on recruitment was uploaded for review.
comments.request: Remove irrelevant review documents.
comments.quote: However, the current document does not focus on recruitment. Why then upload irrelevant documents for review?

comments.issue: The null-model test acknowledges bias but then interprets biased estimates; unbiased methods such as SIMEX exist.
comments.request: Use methods that yield unbiased estimates.
comments.quote: it is therefore okay to interpret and build conclusions on these biased results as if they were not biased. This is obviously more than one step too far.

comments.issue: The paper is poorly positioned in the previous elevation-gradient literature and cites mostly the authors' own work.
comments.request: Engage with the broader literature.
comments.quote: The paper places itself poorly within the context of previous work done on elevation gradients.

comments.issue: The paper has tunnel vision on CNDD and ignores other factors maintaining elevational diversity.
comments.request: Discuss other diversity-maintaining factors fairly.
comments.quote: The paper also suffers from tunnel vision on CNDD (a point made by Hulsman and Hartig 2018).

comments.issue: The claim about rare versus common species CNDD relies on a selective literature list while more evidence opposes it.
comments.request: Cite and discuss the opposing evidence.
comments.quote: Currently, there may, in fact, be more evidence against the hypothesis that rare species suffer stronger CNDD than studies in favor of the hypothesis

comments.issue: Results contradict Song et al.'s meta-analysis of no latitude trends, which is not mentioned.
comments.request: Discuss this contradiction.
comments.quote: Yet they contradict a number of other studies, why are these not mentioned?

comments.issue: The authors claim to have compared different functional forms but used only one model known to be biased.
comments.request: Use or test genuinely different functional forms.
comments.quote: This statement is incorrect, the authors are using only 1 functional form

comments.issue: The line 170 sentence misleadingly claims the work is mechanistic.
comments.request: Remove or correct the claim.
comments.quote: This sentence is misleading, it appears to claim that the work is somehow mechanistic.

comments.issue: The work is correlative and phenomenological, with no evidence that pathogens, herbivores or enemies generate the patterns.
comments.request: Present the study as correlative.
comments.quote: It is correlative work, which is fine, but it cannot be presented as a mechanistic study.

comments.issue: The study should be reframed as observational and placed in the context of others' work rather than the authors' own.
comments.request: Reframe and reposition the study.
comments.quote: My advice would be to reframe the study as observational and place the current piece of work within the context of the large body of work done by others

comments.issue: About 1000 words are spent on a standard random relabeling model, plus an additional document.
comments.request: Condense this material to a few sentences.
comments.quote: I estimated ~1000 words are spent on this (SI + main text), while there is nothing novel or exciting about this very standard approach.

comments.issue: Correlative neighborhood models underestimate heterospecific competition and fail to predict removal experiments.
comments.request: Address the 'ghost of competition past' problem.
comments.quote: multiple papers have now shown that correlative work such as done in this paper, heavily underestimates heterospecific competition

comments.issue: The conclusions are inconsistent with theory because strong CNDD at low latitudes should reduce rather than enhance diversity.
comments.request: Reconcile the findings with coexistence theory.
comments.quote: The displayed strength and variation in CNDD at lower latitudes actually undermines the ability of species to persist, and should lead to lower diversity (Stump and Comita, 2018).

comments.issue: The Lotka-Volterra alpha_ii parameter is equated with stabilization, which is not claimed in coexistence theory.
comments.request: Correct the terminology.
comments.quote: Nowhere in modern coexistence theory is it claimed that the alpha\_ii parameters represent stabilization

comments.issue: Yenni et al.'s stabilization is a compound metric, not CNDD alone, so the persistence claims misrepresent it.
comments.request: Correct the representation of Yenni et al.
comments.quote: Stabilization in Yenni's equation is a compound metric of multiple parameters - of which only one is CNDD.

comments.issue: Yenni et al. and Hulsmann et al. do not advocate the difference-based CNDD metric, which is problematic in multi-species systems.
comments.request: Stop citing them as support for this comparison.
comments.quote: Both Yenni et al. 2017 and Hülsmann et al. 2020 do not advocate this

comments.issue: Random intercepts do not account for pseudoreplication of individual trees, inflating significance.
comments.request: Use survival analysis with one replicate per individual.
comments.quote: Random intercepts do not account for pseudo-replication of individuals, which can lead to an inflated significance

comments.issue: The consistency of ratio and difference results follows from algebra and is not evidence of robustness.
comments.request: Do not present this as robustness.
comments.quote: their consistency follows simply by algebraic considerations

comments.issue: There is confusion about overfitting, and AIC is used despite the concern; Bayesian refitting would reveal the problems.
comments.request: Refit problematic models with Bayesian methods and inspect diagnostics.
comments.quote: It appears there is some confusion on what an overfit model is.

comments.issue: Plot sizes vary from 0.25 to 4 ha but confidence intervals do not reflect this, and plot size may bias trends with altitude.
comments.request: Account for plot size and check for size-altitude bias.
comments.quote: A 0.25 ha plot is much more limited for computing spatial interactions than a 4 ha plot, considering a 10 m buffer zone necessary to minimize edge effects.

comments.issue: The Fig. 4 description is poor and no specific panel is referenced.
comments.request: Describe and reference the panels properly.
comments.quote: Fig. 4 displays eight panels, but there is no reference to any specific panel in the text.

comments.issue: The paragraph at pp. 12, lines 31-47 is conjectural and unsupported by the analyses.
comments.request: Remove or support the conjectures.
comments.quote: All this paragraph is conjectural and not supported by the analyses.

comments.issue: The sentence at pp. 13, line 29 is circular.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence.
comments.quote: This sentence is circular. It claims that CNDD, on top of maitainig species diversity, also acts as a stabilization factor.

comments.issue: The paragraph at pp. 14, lines 21-40 does not explain the inconsistency across life stages.
comments.request: Explain the life-stage inconsistency.
comments.quote: This paragraph does not elucidate the inconsistency across life stages.

comments.issue: The argument at pp. 15, lines 40-45 makes little sense without further explanation.
comments.request: Explain the argument further.
comments.quote: This argument makes little sense or at least should be explained further.

comments.issue: The statement at pp. 15, lines 47-50 implicitly admits the study is not mechanistic.
comments.request: Clarify the mechanistic status of the study.
comments.quote: Does it implicitly assume that the current study is not mechanistic?

reviews.assessment: Important question and approach, but no confidence in the results due to framing, null-model and random-effects problems.
strengths: potentially more reliable approach based on vital rates
links to a central forest ecology hypothesis

comments.issue: The code must be provided with the review materials, and some results exist only in the code.
comments.request: Make the code available for review.
comments.quote: I would ask the authors to provide the code already in the review materials. It is not sufficient to make this available upon acceptance.

comments.issue: CNDD is treated as if any form increases diversity, but CNDD is not a direct measure of stabilization and causation cannot be deduced.
comments.request: Separate CNDD from stabilization and discuss the limitations.
comments.quote: So even if CNDD correlates with diversity one cannot deduce that this is a causal relationship.

comments.issue: Alternative explanations for diversity gradients are dismissed with weak arguments and the limitations of the reasoning are not stated.
comments.request: Discuss CNDD in the context of alternative explanations and soften the abstract.
comments.quote: The authors mention these alternatives briefly in the introduction but seem to exclude them as a potential explanation based on – in my opinion – somewhat weak arguments.

comments.issue: Randomization null models bias other predictors, so the key CNDD-by-elevation interaction test is likely incorrect.
comments.request: Trust parametric tests and report standard errors.
comments.quote: the Null model significance test for the interaction term between CNDD and elevation – the key finding of the publication – should not be interpreted as it is most likely incorrect!

comments.issue: The standardized effect sizes used for the spatial-extent claim are z-values, not effect sizes.
comments.request: Report real effect sizes instead of z-values.
comments.quote: they do not measure the "strength" of an effect but its "significance". They are z-values!

comments.issue: AIC selection on the random slopes of interest, with random slopes for only one of con- or heterospecific density, is problematic.
comments.request: Prioritise random species-by-plot slopes for CNDD rather than AIC selection.
comments.quote: I would however avoid AIC selection on the random slopes of interest (i.e., con- and heterospecific densities).

comments.issue: Shrinkage of species-level random effects is stronger for rare species and may explain the CNDD-abundance relationship.
comments.request: Account for shrinkage in the abundance analysis.
comments.quote: The result is that shrinkage is on average stronger for rare species than for common species.

comments.issue: Species-level random slopes are not tested for mortality models.
comments.request: Explain or add species-level random slopes for mortality.
comments.quote: I was wondering why random slopes for con- and heterospecific densities at the species level are not tested for mortality models

comments.issue: The mechanisms behind the predictions, including directions of temperature and moisture effects and distance dependence, are not described.
comments.request: Describe the mechanisms and their environmental dependence.
comments.quote: What I am missing here, is a detailed description of the mechanisms that are responsible for these predictions.

comments.issue: The title should say 'Tree diversity' to avoid unnecessary generalizations.
comments.request: Rephrase the title.
comments.quote: I would rephrase to “Tree diversity

comments.issue: The correlative approach cannot test whether CNDD contributes to diversity change with elevation.
comments.request: Phrase this hypothesis more cautiously.
comments.quote: With the correlative approach used in this study, “the hypothesis that differences in CNDD contribute to changes in species diversity with elevation” cannot be tested.

comments.issue: What 'relative to other species' refers to is unclear.
comments.request: Specify which effects were compared.
comments.quote: It does not become entirely clear to what “relative to other species” relates here

comments.issue: Numerous line-level edits (repetitions, terminology, notation and wording at L44, L160, L164-165, L174, L182, L189, L199, L204, L281-282, L326, L338, L505, L508-510, P5 and P37).
comments.quote: L 164-165: This information is already in L 157-158. The sentence can be removed.

comments.issue: The statement about macroclimate and microclimate correlation is vague and not linked to hypotheses or biogeography.
comments.request: Strengthen the link to the hypotheses and alternative ideas.
comments.quote: Stating that “Macroclimate and microclimate, particularly temperature and moisture, are strongly correlated [with diversity]” is rather vague.

comments.issue: The motivation should emphasize that even the existence of an elevational CNDD gradient is unknown.
comments.request: Motivate the study differently.
comments.quote: I suggest motivating the study differently, because the study itself is also not suited to provide anything else than “suggestive associations”.

comments.issue: The cited references concern trees, yet the text speaks of general biodiversity; a bird reference is not directly transferable.
comments.request: Align the claims with the taxonomic scope of the references.
comments.quote: These references are all on trees. I wonder if it is misleading to mention "trees and forest diversity" in L 96 only and to speak of general biodiversity until then.

comments.issue: The claim that CNDD maintains diversity should be softened to 'may' and contrary opinions cited.
comments.request: Replace 'is' with 'may be' and cite contrary opinions.
comments.quote: Replace “is” with “may be” and refer to contrary opinions.

comments.issue: The CNDD-abundance relationship is not established and the evidence is more variable than presented.
comments.request: Present the variability of this relationship.
comments.quote: I think the exact relationship between CNDD and abundance has not yet been established. Evidence is more variable than presented here.

comments.issue: More independent citations are needed and it is unclear why the relationship would differ in temperate forests.
comments.request: Cite additional work and explain the temperate difference.
comments.quote: Why should the relationship be different in temperate forests?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether 'changes in climate' refers to temporal change or spatial variability.
comments.request: Clarify the wording.
comments.quote: do the authors refer to real “changes in climate” or to spatial variability?

comments.issue: 'Fitness metrics' is not the correct term; vital rates are only proxies for fitness.
comments.request: Use correct terminology.
comments.quote: “Fitness metrics” is not the correct term here. Vital rates are proxies only

comments.issue: The statement at L135-136 is an overinterpretation that the data cannot prove.
comments.request: Express it as a conjecture.
comments.quote: This is an overinterpretation. It is not possible to prove this with the data

comments.issue: How temperature and precipitation change along elevation and whether this is relevant for pathogens is not discussed.
comments.request: Comment on the elevational climate differences.
comments.quote: How is temperature and precipitation changing along elevation?

comments.issue: The variability in census interval length is not reported.
comments.request: Report the variability in census intervals.
comments.quote: How large is the variability in census interval length?

comments.issue: It is unclear why species-alone random slopes are omitted while plot-species slopes are used, despite Table S2 showing species slopes.
comments.request: Clarify the random-slope structure.
comments.quote: Why is there no random slope for conspecific and heterospecific density effects for “species” alone but for the plot-species combination only?

comments.issue: No CNDD means conspecific and heterospecific effects are equal, not that neither affects survival; a different randomization is suggested.
comments.request: Reconsider the null model logic.
comments.quote: no CNDD means that effects of conspecifics and heterospecifics are the same, not that both don't affect survival

comments.issue: Classic test statistics and post-hoc comparisons of con- and heterospecific effects are not reported.
comments.request: Report mixed-model statistics and post-hoc tests.
comments.quote: The authors should (also) report classic test statistics from the mixed models including post-hoc tests

comments.issue: How local densities are standardized for band-wise analyses, and whether estimates are comparable across bands, is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the standardization and comparability.
comments.quote: How are local densities standardized for band-wise analyses? Within band? Within the entire dataset?

comments.issue: CNDD slopes may be incomparable between size classes when mortality rates differ.
comments.request: Account for differences in mortality rates.
comments.quote: the strength of CNDD (assessed as a slope from a glm) between small and large trees may be incomparable when small and large trees have different mortality rates

comments.issue: The increase in CNDD strength at 5-10 m is not clearly visible and the slope is not significant.
comments.request: Temper this claim.
comments.quote: I don't think that the slope (increasing strength with distance) is significant.

comments.issue: A change in CNDD in 2 of 4 vital rates is not strong evidence.
comments.request: Soften the evidence claim.
comments.quote: Not sure if a significant change in CNDD along elevation in 2 out of 4 vital rates is really “strong evidence”.

comments.issue: The sentence at L276-278 is unfortunate given the critiques, and why the results are consistent is unclear.
comments.request: Rewrite and explain the consistency.
comments.quote: Given the critiques of these approaches, I think this sentence is somewhat unfortunate.

comments.issue: Conspecific density effects are not significantly positive at higher elevations.
comments.request: Correct the statement.
comments.quote: I don't think that conspecific density effects are really positive at higher elevations.

comments.issue: The passage at L291-294 adds little and blurs stabilization and species maintenance.
comments.request: Remove or clarify the passage.
comments.quote: I am not sure what this adds to the sentences before.

comments.issue: Whether the same mechanisms drive high CNDD in tropical and low-elevation forests is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss this mechanistic question.
comments.quote: Do the authors think that the same mechanisms are responsible for higher CNDD in tropical and low elevation forests?

comments.issue: The statement about studying CNDD's contribution to coexistence is problematic because coexistence is an emerging property.
comments.request: Soften or reframe the statement.
comments.quote: Coexistence is an emerging property (so far, it cannot be inferred from simple competition measures).

comments.issue: LaManna et al. 2017b is misrepresented as defining CNDD as the difference between con- and heterospecific effects.
comments.request: Correct the citation.
comments.quote: I don’t think that in LaManna et al. 2017b CNDD is defined as the difference between con- and heterospecific effects.

comments.issue: Figure colours are almost indistinguishable and significance levels for slopes are missing.
comments.request: Use better colours, symbols, transparency and add significance levels.
comments.quote: The colors are almost indistinguishable. A better choice of colors (maybe with symbols) is needed.

comments.issue: It is unclear why fewer iterations are used in one analysis than the 500 used elsewhere.
comments.request: Explain the choice of iterations.
comments.quote: Why not again 500 iterations?

comments.issue: Loess splines are not suitable for testing whether CNDD strength changes significantly with distance.
comments.request: Use an appropriate statistical test.
comments.quote: Loess splines are not very helpful for testing if CNDD becomes significantly weaker or stronger with distance.

comments.issue: The correlation between temperature and precipitation and the role of moisture are not examined.
comments.request: Address the moisture effect.
comments.quote: I had the impression that the authors conclude that T is responsible for CNDD differences between low and high elevation. How about the effect of moisture?

comments.issue: How scaling with exponents below 1 is carried out and in which order transformations occur is unclear.
comments.request: Describe the transformation order.
comments.quote: But how does this go together with exponents < 1? In which order are these data transformations carried out?

comments.issue: Multiplying mortality estimates by -1 to obtain survival effects is questionable given the asymmetric cloglog link.
comments.request: Reconsider the sign conversion.
comments.quote: Because the cloglog link function is not symmetric, I am not sure if it is correct to multiply the estimates from the mortality model with -1 to obtain the effect on survival

comments.issue: How a better fit was defined and whether residuals were checked are not reported.
comments.request: Report the fit comparison and residual plots.
comments.quote: How was a better “fit” defined for comparing cloglog and logistic exposure models?

comments.issue: Repeated observations per tree are not independent; random effects are more appropriate than aggregating years or the null model.
comments.request: Account for dependencies with random effects.
comments.quote: p-values depend on the number of total observations which are replicated per individual tree!

comments.issue: The ecological rationale for comparing functional forms, distance decay and the nine beta values is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the functional-form comparison and beta values.
comments.quote: It should be explained why different functional forms were compared (ecological explanations).

comments.issue: How the abundance-elevation-CNDD relationship was analyzed is unclear, and parametric tests would be more reliable.
comments.request: Clarify the analysis and report parametric tests.
comments.quote: It is not entirely clear how the relationship between abundance, elevation and CNDD was analyzed.

comments.issue: Large-tree mortality patterns could be described as less facilitation by conspecifics than heterospecifics.
comments.request: Consider this alternative description.
comments.quote: For large tree mortality one could say that there is less facilitation by conspecifics than by heterospecifics and this creates CNDD

comments.issue: The null model does not include the same random-effects structure as the original model.
comments.request: Match the random-effects structure in the null model.
comments.quote: I would expect that the null model includes the same random effects structure than the original model.

title: Tree species diversity increases with conspecific negative density dependence across an elevation gradient

study.system: oceanic island mammals worldwide; phylogenies, traits, late-Quaternary occurrences

editor_summary: Generally supportive reviews requiring extensive revision: clarify the writing and why the work matters, specify which results are mammal-specific, and replace distance-to-centroid isolation with distance to the nearest coast.

reviews.assessment: Supportive of the global island biogeography study; wants the mammal focus justified and the isolation, climate and competition analyses reconsidered.
strengths: excellent and comprehensive work on an interesting topic
fits the scope of Ecology Letters
language and figures easy to understand

comments.issue: Introduction never justifies why mammals were chosen over birds, reptiles or other vertebrates.
comments.request: Add background explaining the choice of mammals.
comments.quote: I recommend the authors use several simple sentences to add some basic background information why they choose mammals as the study material, why not birds or reptiles or other animals.

comments.issue: Terrestrial non-volant mammals cannot disperse to oceanic islands, so isolation may be meaningless for them.
comments.request: Analyse bats and non-volant mammals separately.
comments.quote: Most of the terrestrial non-volant mammals do not have the ability to dispersal to the islands. The higher or lower isolation means the same isolation for these mammals.

comments.issue: Excluding islands smaller than 100 km2 is poorly justified and may change the results.
comments.request: Justify the exclusion and assess how it affects the results.
comments.quote: More convincible explanations are needed here. The more islands included in this study, the more solid the conclusions are.

comments.issue: Isolation measured from the island centroid to the mainland coast is controversial and ignores island shape.
comments.request: Use the shortest distance to the nearest mainland coast instead.
comments.quote: The calculation of Isolation is also controversial. Here it was calculated by distance from an island’s mass centroid to the nearest mainland coast.

comments.issue: Excluding Antarctica as a source mainland ignores its role in mammal dispersal history.
comments.request: Justify or reconsider excluding Antarctica.
comments.quote: The other concern I have here is that the excluding Antarctica as the mainland.

comments.issue: Title omits that the study covers only terrestrial mammals.
comments.request: Add terrestrial to the title.
comments.quote: Considering that this studies only focused on the terrestrial mammals, I suggest the authors adding terrestrial in the title.

comments.issue: Testing climatic factors is unnecessary because island mammal assemblages are not sensitive to temperature or precipitation.
comments.request: Remove or downplay the climatic analyses.
comments.quote: As for the testing of climatic factors in this global island study, I think this is not necessary.

comments.issue: Discussion of competition is not supported; the study cannot test competition's role.
comments.request: Rewrite this part or remove it.
comments.quote: I do not think this study could test the role of competition on the assemblages for the island mammals.

comments.issue: Null isolation result may be caused by including terrestrial non-volant mammals.
comments.request: Reconsider the isolation result separately for bats and non-volant mammals.
comments.quote: The authors did not observe a consistent trend in mammal community structure with island isolation may be caused by the terrestrial mammals itself.

reviews.assessment: Timely, interesting and valuable global dataset, but the isolation measurement, paleoconfiguration and species-pool definition need attention.
strengths: timely and interesting for a broad readership

comments.issue: How isolation is measured is questioned and needs to be addressed.
comments.request: Address how isolation is measured.
comments.quote: there are some issues that I do think that the authors need to address: a) how isolation is measured

comments.issue: Potential effect of the islands' paleoconfiguration on the presented patterns is not addressed.
comments.request: Assess the potential effect of paleoconfiguration.
comments.quote: b) the potential effect of the islands’ paleoconfiguration on the patterns presented

comments.issue: How the species pool is defined is questioned and needs to be addressed.
comments.request: Clarify and justify the species-pool definition.
comments.quote: c) how the species pool is defined; please do find my recommendations in the attached file

reviews.assessment: Impressed by the dataset but finds the framing and writing too disorganized and unclear to evaluate, and the species pool potentially biased.
strengths: results interesting and accord with theoretical predictions
with improved framing and writing this could be a great paper

comments.issue: Abstract's opening claim that island biogeography is a fundamental challenge is not meaningful.
comments.request: Replace it with something specific, or start the abstract with the second sentence.
comments.quote: I think that many ecologists would say that island biogeography IS the study of how ecological and evolutionary processes structure island assemblages

comments.issue: Several line-level copy edits (tense, grammar, plurals, unusual wording).
comments.quote: Replace “examined” with “examine”. In general, try to write the abstract in the present tense.

comments.issue: Abstract sentence implies a single island was studied and doubts the extinct-species dataset.
comments.request: Correct this sentence and attend to detail in the abstract.
comments.quote: You examined the species assemblage of a single island? Did you really use a global dataset to evaluate the diversity of a single island?

comments.issue: 'Functional clustering' is used in the abstract without any definition.
comments.request: Briefly define or explain functional clustering.
comments.quote: I have some experience in this field (probably a bit more than the average reader), but do not know what “functional clustering” means.

comments.issue: 'Classic' theory is undefined; the 1963 book and metapopulation ecology are missing.
comments.request: Define or remove 'classic', cite MacArthur & Wilson 1963, mention metapopulation ecology.
comments.quote: Remove “classic” as this is just unneeded. Or define exactly what you mean by classic theory

comments.issue: First paragraph is unclear and claims integration with equilibrium theory that the study does not test.
comments.request: State the questions precisely and remove unsupported equilibrium-theory claims.
comments.quote: But is this what your paper really did? I don’t think you addressed equilibria between immigration and extinction rates (as per the theory of island biogeography) at all.

comments.issue: Competing hypotheses are not tied into a framework; basic framing sentences are missing.
comments.request: Add framing sentences contrasting island biogeography with competition and filtering.
comments.quote: Up until this point, the intro just reads like a list of theories/hypotheses/random notes that aren’t tied into a meaningful framework or comparison that builds tension.

comments.issue: Functional and phylogenetic dissimilarity are never explicitly defined, so the questions are unclear.
comments.request: Explicitly define functional and phylogenetic dissimilarity.
comments.quote: I think you need to explicitly define what “functional” and “phylogenetic” dissimilarity are so that the readers have some idea

comments.issue: Paragraph reads as an unorganized list; hypotheses and their predictions are not structured.
comments.request: Reorganize into a framework stating which hypotheses complement or conflict.
comments.quote: I suggest the authors try to organize these hypotheses into an overall framework. Are they mutually complementary hypotheses or competing hypotheses?

comments.issue: Ecological versus evolutionary timescale dichotomy is invalid and should not frame the paper.
comments.request: Reconsider and revise the timescale distinction.
comments.quote: I think this sort of distinction is meaningless. Upon close examination of ecological and evolutionary processes, it is clear that one is not broader/longer than the other.

comments.issue: Two paragraphs of predictions force back-and-forth reading and should be combined.
comments.request: Combine into one paragraph with predictions clearly contrasted.
comments.quote: I don’t like that this is split into two paragraphs. I found myself having to bounce back-and-forth between them to resolve exactly how the two predictions were different.

comments.issue: Attributing end-Pleistocene extinctions to anthropogenic activities is contentious and indefensible here.
comments.request: Revise or justify the anthropogenic-extinction statement.
comments.quote: To say that the extinction of many species at the end of the Pleistocene was due to anthropogenic activities is very contentious.

comments.issue: Functional clustering and the null models used to identify clustering remain undefined.
comments.request: Define functional clustering and the null models clearly.
comments.quote: After reading the intro, I still have no idea what functional clustering really means, or what null models/concepts were used to identify clustering

comments.issue: Doubts that every island in the stated size range with at least two mammals was included.
comments.request: Clarify and verify the island inclusion.
comments.quote: Did you really include every single island on the plant between 100.65 and 5.91 ×105 km2 with at least two mammals? If so, impressive. But I don’t think this is true.

comments.issue: The order and criteria for excluding islands below 100 km2 are unclear and contradictory.
comments.request: Explain the exclusion criteria in a clear order.
comments.quote: What do you mean you excluded islands less than 100 km2? I thought that your dataset only included islands greater than 100.65 km2?

comments.issue: Paragraph logic is unclear and the stated 212-island count appears false.
comments.request: Rewrite the paragraph and correct the island count.
comments.quote: Considering the entire planet, are there really only 212 islands in the world between 100.65 and 5.91 ×105 km2 with more than two mammals on them?

comments.issue: Calling log-transformed island area simply 'area' is inaccurate and unclear.
comments.request: State clearly that area was log-transformed for modelling.
comments.quote: If you log-transform an islands area, the resulting number is not the area of the island.

comments.issue: Independence of area and isolation is asserted without reporting correlation statistics.
comments.request: Report correlation coefficients and p-values.
comments.quote: Please report back with actual correlation coefficients and p-values.

comments.issue: Unnecessary definitions of crepuscular and cathermal interrupt the text.
comments.request: Remove or shorten these definitions.
comments.quote: No need to define crepuscular or cathermal; readers should know those terms.

comments.issue: Claim that traits directly relate to ecological processes is too vague to be meaningful.
comments.request: Tighten the logic and writing.
comments.quote: Statements like this are so vague they are basically meaningless.

comments.issue: Derivation of the phylogenies and their use in the analyses are not explained.
comments.request: Add a primer on how phylogenies were derived and used.
comments.quote: How you derived phylogenies and how they will be directly included in your analyses wasn’t clear at all; you just dive right into the details without meaningful framing.

comments.issue: Metrics are introduced before explaining what they measure or why they are needed.
comments.request: Explain each metric before using it.
comments.quote: Again, the authors begin writing about a specific metric before they present what the metric actually measures or why it is needed.

comments.issue: 'Community structure' is never defined; its working definition and chosen dimension are unclear.
comments.request: Define community structure and justify this dimension.
comments.quote: Can you please point out where you define what community structure actually is? (You haven’t up to this point.) What is your working definition of community structure?

comments.issue: Tip-level clustering is defined vaguely and only after it is first used.
comments.request: Define tip-level clustering clearly before using it.
comments.quote: You vaguely, but in my opinion inadequately, define what tip-level clustering is here.

comments.issue: Species-pool rationale is repetitive and could be condensed.
comments.request: Condense and prune the redundant writing.
comments.quote: This writing is repetitive and could be easily condensed to increase clarity.

comments.issue: Dispersion-field species pool includes species occurring nowhere near the island, biasing phylogenetic clustering.
comments.request: Revise the species-pool definition and test whether the bias drives clustering.
comments.quote: If you are including species that occur nowhere near an island in the potential species pool (what you call a dispersion field), of course those species will not actually occur on that island.

comments.issue: Acronyms reduce readability and should be removed.
comments.request: Remove the acronyms.
comments.quote: I suggest doing away with all acronyms. In my opinion, they only decrease readability here.

comments.issue: Relevance of this result to the study's general question is unclear; it seems misplaced.
comments.request: Justify its relevance or move or remove it.
comments.quote: Why is this important to the general question your study is addressing? Seems random and misplaced.

comments.issue: 'Classic' island biogeography is used repeatedly without definition or examples.
comments.request: Define it and cite specific examples.
comments.quote: The authors keep using the term “classic” to describe island biogeography theory or studies. What does this actually mean?

comments.issue: Extinct species were likely driven by climate or other non-human events; the human-driven claim needs justification.
comments.request: Justify or temper the human-driven extinction statement.
comments.quote: Many of the species extinct species you include in your analyses were likely driven to extinction by climate change or other events that were not directly related to human activities.

comments.issue: 'Diversification rates' are invoked but were not measured; the term is misused.
comments.request: Write more carefully about what was actually measured.
comments.quote: When did you measure diversification rates? This is a very specific term, and I do not think you measured it

comments.issue: Claim that MacArthur & Wilson integrated diversification rates is not supported by the book.
comments.request: Support or correct the claim about MacArthur & Wilson.
comments.quote: Can you point out exactly where MacArthur & Wilson (1967) integrate diversification rates into their equilibrium theory of island biogeography?

comments.issue: The ecological/evolutionary process dichotomy is introduced only in the discussion.
comments.request: Introduce and justify this dichotomy early in the introduction.
comments.quote: This is the first place you clearly delimit what you have been calling ecological and evolutionary processes. If you really think this dichotomy is valid, it should be expanded on and included early in the introduction

comments.issue: Possible that the traits on which environmental filtering operates were not measured; caveat missing.
comments.request: Include and explain this possibility.
comments.quote: It is entirely possible (and even likely) that the traits on which environmental filtering operate were not measured. You should really include and explain this possibility.

comments.issue: Stating 'the rationale' presents a hypothesis as more established than it is.
comments.request: Call it one hypothesis instead.
comments.quote: Replace “The rational” with “One hypothesis”, as this is clearly just a hypothesis.

comments.issue: Suggests all recent extinctions are human-caused, ignoring climate-driven extinctions in the literature.
comments.request: Qualify the claim and cite relevant literature.
comments.quote: Again, are you saying that all recent extinctions are directly due to human activities? Since the Pleistocene, many are not

title: Phylogenetic and functional clustering illustrate the roles of adaptive radiation and dispersal filtering in jointly shaping late‐Quaternary mammal assemblages on oceanic islands

study.system: songbirds; 3,175 species, nest architecture and traits

editor_summary: All three reviewers recommend acceptable with revision; editor highlights the nest-building duration analysis needing work, situating the paper in the literature with stronger motivation, and insufficient exploration of extreme-habitat and niche dimensions.

reviews.assessment: Reasonable arguments linking nest evolution to avian evolution, with comments on interpretation and data collection.
strengths: contribution linking nest evolution with avian evolution

comments.issue: Domed nests may allow breeding in extreme habitats, but niche variation and outliers are not examined.
comments.request: Test whether domed or open nesters have higher variation in ecological niches.
comments.quote: the authors may also want to examine whether domed-nesters or open-nesters have higher variation in ecological niches (or tend to have more outliers)

comments.issue: How the nest-building duration data were collected is not described, although they underpin a main conclusion.
comments.request: Describe the nest-building time data collection and reliability.
comments.quote: I cannot find the details about how the author collected such data, which is critical to this paper and may interest many ornithologists

comments.issue: It is unclear which of the three nest-categorisation datasets was used for which tests.
comments.request: Justify the dataset choice or apply all tests to all three datasets.
comments.quote: I think the authors need to do a better job in justifying the choice of different datasets across this study

comments.issue: The source of the percentages of families and species using open nests is not cited on line 68.
comments.request: Cite the source or note that it comes from this study.
comments.quote: Is the information regarding the percentages of families and species using open nests from any published literature?

comments.issue: The sentence on lines 98-100 reaches the opposite conclusion from the argument on lines 95-98.
comments.request: Reverse the conclusion of this sentence.
comments.quote: I feel that this sentence should be changed to have an opposite conclusion, if increased availability of milder habitats can have released linages from the costs of domed nest-building

comments.issue: This may not be the first study on the topic, and the topic itself is unclear on lines 106-108.
comments.request: Clarify the topic and acknowledge earlier studies.
comments.quote: This may not be the first study to examine the relevant topic. In addition, it is not clear what exactly the topic described here is.

comments.issue: The definition of urban area or city bird is missing on lines 133-135.
comments.request: Define what counts as an urban area and a city bird.
comments.quote: You did not provide a clear definition of what is urban area or what is not in this study?

comments.issue: The source of the nest-building time data is unclear on line 137.
comments.request: State the data sources for nest-building times.
comments.quote: It is not clear from what resources you obtained the data of the time bird spend building nests?

comments.issue: Cavity is treated as a nest site in one dataset and a structure in others, changing the criteria across tests.
comments.request: Use consistent nest-character definitions across datasets.
comments.quote: I do not see a good reason to change the major criteria for defining nest characters across different tests in the same study

comments.issue: It is unclear whether all three datasets were used for every test, as the results do not show this.
comments.request: Show the results for each dataset or explain the robustness checks.
comments.quote: Do you mean that, for every test, you used all of the tree datasets of different nest categorization? I do not see such results shown in the Results section.

comments.issue: Secondary cavity nesters do not build their own nests and should not be included in a study of nest building.
comments.request: Remove or reclassify secondary cavity nesters.
comments.quote: secondary cavity nesters should be removed from this study (or refined as open or domed nesters) because they do not build (dig) their own nests

comments.issue: It is doubtful whether reliable data exist on cup or domed nests placed in cavities.
comments.request: Justify the reliability of the cavity nest-type data.
comments.quote: Did you have reliable data resources to show whether bird put a cup or domed nests in cavities?

comments.issue: Fig. 2 shows male builders with open nests spending more time than domed builders, contradicting the text.
comments.request: Reconcile this result with the nest-building conclusion.
comments.quote: But the results showed that male builders with open nests spent more time building their nests than those with domed nests (in Figure 2).

comments.issue: The sentence on lines 285-286 about pair-built nests is confusing.
comments.request: Clarify whether pair-built nests take more time.
comments.quote: Do you mean that nests built by both members of mating pairs take more time to complete than nests built solely by male or female birds?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether domed nesters have smaller ranges than open nesters, cavity nesters or both.
comments.request: Make the range-size result clearer.
comments.quote: Did species with domed nests have smaller geographic ranges than those of open nests, cavity nests or both? You should make the result clearer.

comments.issue: The text cites Figure S3 for a result that Figure S3 does not show.
comments.request: Correct the figure reference, likely Figure S4.
comments.quote: Figure S3 does not show such results. Do you mean Figure S4?

comments.issue: The extinction-rate comparison on lines 309-310 is unclear about which nest types are compared.
comments.request: State the comparison explicitly.
comments.quote: Species with domed nests had higher average extinction rates [than did species with open nests]? Is it correct?

comments.issue: Results may depend on which species have genetic data.
comments.request: Repeat the analyses using only species with genetic data in the supplement.
comments.quote: You may want to show the results based only on species with genetic data in the Supplementary information.

comments.issue: Species such as barn swallows reuse nests, so building fewer nests need not reduce fecundity.
comments.request: Consider nest reuse when interpreting fecundity costs.
comments.quote: Some bird species may reuse their nests for multiple clutches in one breeding season such as barn swallows. In such condition, building fewer nests may not necessarily lead to lower fecundity.

comments.issue: Urban environments are not necessarily shadier than natural environments.
comments.request: Reconsider the shade argument on lines 417-419.
comments.quote: Urban environment may not necessarily have more places with shade than natural environment. For example, forests could even more places of shade than cities.

reviews.assessment: Well executed and potentially significant, but it does not yet make a compelling case for what it adds beyond previous domed-nest studies.
strengths: likely significant contribution to nest morphology evolution

comments.issue: The paper does not explain how it adds beyond Price, Griffith and Hall et al., who also addressed domed-to-open nest transitions.
comments.request: Explain what this study adds beyond previous analyses.
comments.quote: What the authors have not yet done with this paper is provide a compelling argument as to why this analysis would substantially add to the previous analyses on the evolution of domed nests

comments.issue: “Comprehensive macroevolutionary framework” is not defined in the introduction.
comments.request: Clarify what the framework means.
comments.quote: In the Introduction, clarify what is meant by a ‘comprehensive macroevolutionary framework’.

comments.issue: Icteridae is mislabelled as a species on line 120.
comments.request: Correct it to family.
comments.quote: Icteridae are a family not a species

comments.issue: Sample sizes and the reason for increasing them are not explained on line 124.
comments.request: Report sample sizes at each point and why they increased.
comments.quote: Explain, at each point, what the sample sizes are, and why they needed to be increased.

comments.issue: Why only the middle of the range is used on line 140 is unclear.
comments.request: Justify using the middle of the range.
comments.quote: Why use just the middle of the range?

comments.issue: The 19 variables are not listed and their relation to the analyses is unclear.
comments.request: List the 19 variables and reconcile them with the supplement.
comments.quote: Provide the list of 19 variables, although it looks from the results that only temperature and precipitation were actually used in the analyses?

comments.issue: How range size was measured and how migrants were treated is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the range size measure and migrant handling.
comments.quote: How was range size measured? What was done with migrants?

comments.issue: It is unclear why breeding range is not the relevant range on line 151.
comments.request: Justify the choice of range.
comments.quote: Is breeding range not the particularly important range?

comments.issue: What the algorithm on line 154 provides is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the algorithm's purpose.
comments.quote: Not prediction, but explains? Actually, it’s not really clear what this algorithm provides

comments.issue: It is unclear whether only standard deviation is used on line 156.
comments.request: Clarify the variation measure used.
comments.quote: Just the standard deviation?

comments.issue: The comparison with breeding range is not shown on line 173.
comments.request: Provide outputs using breeding range.
comments.quote: Please provide the outputs with breeding range so that this comparison is clear.

comments.issue: The “for simplicity” categorisation of pouch nests and mixed builders as open is unjustified.
comments.request: Justify the categorisation or test alternative classifications.
comments.quote: It is also far from clear why pouch nest or birds that build both domed and open nest should be included as ‘open’.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether cavity nesting functionally results in a dome, and what “dome” refers to.
comments.request: Define what “dome” means functionally or structurally.
comments.quote: Is not building in a cavity functionally resulting in a dome?

comments.issue: The study measures structural morphology, not nest-building behaviour as stated on lines 242-244.
comments.request: Correct the description of what is measured.
comments.quote: You aren’t looking at nest building behaviour, you’re looking at structural morphology.

comments.issue: Sample sizes are not given with each analysis, and “different nest types” is ambiguous.
comments.request: Report sample sizes and define the nest categories used in each analysis.
comments.quote: From line 283 and for the rest of the Results, provide the sample sizes with each analysis.

comments.issue: Line 331 raises a nest versus no-nest question that is not addressed.
comments.request: Clarify the scope of this question.
comments.quote: Is this not a nest-no-nest question, which you don’t actually address here (but could be done with other bird species).

comments.issue: The direction of the statement on lines 345-346 may be reversed.
comments.request: Check and correct the direction.
comments.quote: Is this the correct way around?

comments.issue: “Higher flexibility in construction” on line 416 is undefined.
comments.request: Define the phrase.
comments.quote: What do you mean by ‘have a higher flexibility in construction’?

comments.issue: Urban environments are in fact warmer, contrary to the statement on line 418.
comments.request: Correct the temperature statement.
comments.quote: Are urban environments not warmer?

comments.issue: The passage on lines 423-425 is too vague.
comments.request: Be more explicit.
comments.quote: Can you be more explicit than this?

comments.issue: The argument on lines 433-435 does not make sense.
comments.request: Revise the argument.
comments.quote: Not sure this makes sense.

comments.issue: Figure 4B transition lines suggest limited transitions, and figure legends lack sample sizes.
comments.request: Discuss transition probabilities and add sample sizes to legends.
comments.quote: do the transition lines suggest that species are not very likely to transition between open and domed? Sample sizes in all figure legends would be useful.

reviews.assessment: Valuable paper with important results, but climate, elevation and nest-building analyses are unclear or confounded and need rework.

comments.issue: The climate variation data are unclear: timing within the year, annual variation and the 19 variables are not explained.
comments.request: Explain when climate was measured and list the 19 variables.
comments.quote: I found the climate variation data to be unclear. When in the year was it based on – it seems to include annual variation, which is odd.

comments.issue: Elevation is not considered despite its large effects on temperature, precipitation and range limits.
comments.request: Include elevation in climate estimates and as a covariate.
comments.quote: I don’t see consideration of elevation anywhere. Elevation has a huge effect on both temperature and precipitation, as well as their variation

comments.issue: Nest type should be modelled as the dependent variable to examine how range size, climate, latitude, elevation and body size interact to shape nest evolution.
comments.request: Analyse nest type as a function of these predictors.
comments.quote: it seems to me that there should also be an analysis of nest type as the dependent variable as a function range size, climate variation, latitude, elevation, and body size

comments.issue: Latitude is missing from the nest-building analysis; tropical species may simply build more slowly over longer seasons.
comments.request: Include latitude and consider the tropical bias in interpretation.
comments.quote: why wasn’t latitude included in this analysis? It is a critical element

comments.issue: The quality of the nest-building time data is unclear, including sample sizes per species and within-species variation.
comments.request: Report data quality, sample sizes and variation.
comments.quote: no details on the quality of these data are provided. What are the sample sizes per species for these data?

comments.issue: Longer building times when both members build suggest lower per-individual cost, opposite to the authors' assumption.
comments.request: Reconsider the cost interpretation of longer building times.
comments.quote: The longer time when both members build again suggests the possibility of lower cost (net energy spent) than higher, as assumed by the authors.

comments.issue: Species identities and locations are not shown for the nest-building data.
comments.request: Show species identities and locations in a table or phylogenetic figure.
comments.quote: The species identities and locations need to be shown in a table or phylogenetic figure to aid interpretation.

comments.issue: Absolute latitude is used, although southern temperate species resemble tropical species more than northern ones.
comments.request: Repeat the analyses using real latitude.
comments.quote: I wonder why latitude is analyzed as absolute rather than real latitude?

comments.issue: Figures 2 and 3 do not account for latitude, elevation and body size.
comments.request: Correct the figures for these confounds, e.g. using PGLS means and variation.
comments.quote: I find figures 2 and 3 to be problematic related to the above – they need to account for latitude, elevation, and body size.

comments.issue: The speciation/extinction models omit body size and latitude, so narrow niches may reflect tropical distribution rather than nest type.
comments.request: Include body size and latitude or split the analyses to test them.
comments.quote: I’m wondering why body size and latitude are not included? Again, I worry that narrow niches might reflect tropical distribution rather than nest type

comments.issue: The speculation beginning on line 369 is strongly north-temperate biased.
comments.request: Remove this paragraph.
comments.quote: The speculation for the paragraph starting on line 369 should be removed. It is highly north temperate biased, which is not a good representation of domed nest associations.

comments.issue: The logic on line 93 about “now scarce specific habitats” is unclear and habitat loss is not addressed.
comments.request: Clarify the argument about reduced domed nests.
comments.quote: I don’t understand the logic here – why is it ‘now scarce specific habitats’?

comments.issue: An alternative explanation is that domed nesters have narrower thermal tolerances.
comments.request: Consider this alternative on lines 94-95.
comments.quote: the alternative is simply that species that build domed nests have narrower thermal tolerances and require the more stable temperature of domed nests

comments.issue: Domed nests are treated only as a cost although they may provide predation and thermal benefits.
comments.request: Acknowledge the benefits of domed nests.
comments.quote: this is stated as domed nests reflecting a cost, but they can provide benefits – possibly for nest predation and thermal environment

comments.issue: The sentence on lines 95-98 is unclear and lacks evidence for milder-habitat availability.
comments.request: Clarify the sentence and provide evidence.
comments.quote: this sentence is not clear. Has there been an ‘increased availability of milder habitats’ – where is the evidence?

comments.issue: The year is missing from the Jetz et al. citation on lines 113-114.
comments.request: Add the year.
comments.quote: need year for Jetz et al

comments.issue: The use of tertiary data (Wilman via Dunning) is not made explicit on lines 130-131.
comments.request: State the provenance chain of the data.
comments.quote: the authors should be explicit that they are using tertiary data, as Wilman took much of their data from Dunning, who took it from original sources

comments.issue: Elevation is again missing from the latitude measure on line 131.
comments.request: Include elevation in the analyses.
comments.quote: mean latitude, but what about elevation?

comments.issue: The link between body size and nest predation risk is not cited on line 188.
comments.request: Cite Unzeta et al. 2020.
comments.quote: body size also related to nest predation risk shown recently – Unzeta et al 2020 Am Nat

comments.issue: An extra “a” is present on line 209.
comments.quote: Line 209 – an extra ‘a’ present

comments.issue: The claim that open nests are better hidden contradicts classic work showing higher predation in open nests.
comments.request: Reconcile with Nice, Lack and related work.
comments.quote: open nests better hidden from predators is opposite to Nice, Lack, etc. that show higher predation in open nests

comments.issue: Extinction is not integrated as an additional process in the paragraph starting on line 351.
comments.request: Integrate the role of extinction into this section.
comments.quote: You might integrate the role of extinction as an important additional process, as considered in more detail starting on line 387.

title: Nest architecture is linked with ecological success in songbirds

study.system: plants and animals; global richness, phylogenies, habitat transitions

editor_summary: Editor: scope and interest high but methods coarse; R2's critique (circularity of richness versus diversification, flawed diversification estimator) is convincing; R3 shares concerns, R1 forgiving; substantial revision needed.

reviews.assessment: Strongly supportive of the broad-brush approach; the acknowledged uncertainties are unlikely to affect the results.
strengths: refreshingly focused discussion on big questions

comments.issue: The broad-brush approach rests on many assumptions about phylogenies, dating, species counts and family-level habitat assignments.
comments.quote: All these steps involve huge assumptions in terms of uncertainties about phylogenetic assignments, phylogenetic topologies, geological dating, species counts, validity of families, validity of habitat assignments, and habitat generalization to one assignment per family.

comments.issue: Likelihood-based ancestral state reconstruction has been criticized, but standard models were used and alternatives would likely not change the results.
comments.quote: Likewise, there has been criticism of the fundamentals of likelihood-based ancestral state reconstruction, as used here to infer the most likely ancestral habitat at each node back down the tree

reviews.assessment: Ambitious and broadly interesting, but coarse-grained methods and misleading claims about transitions need clearer communication.
strengths: broad scope of interest to a general readership

comments.issue: The coarse-grained approach is not made clear in the main text; the phylum-level tree with 28 tips is described as encompassing over 1.5 million species.
comments.request: State in the introduction that higher-level taxa, not species, are analyzed and that these taxa are arbitrary.
comments.quote: I find it misleading, for instance, to state that the phylum-level animal phylogeny encompasses nearly 1,515,954 described species (line 121).

comments.issue: Diversification rate estimates change systematically with clade age, so the habitat rate differences may be artefacts of average clade age.
comments.request: Respond to this clade-age artefact argument.
comments.quote: it seems possible that the relative diversification rates reported here – marine taxa diversify the slowest, freshwater taxa diversify quicker, and terrestrial taxa the quickest – are artefacts of average clade age rather than reflections of a biological reality

comments.issue: Figure 4 legend claims to show transition events between habitats, but transitions among higher taxa are estimated and many species-level transitions are missed.
comments.request: Correct the legend and note the missed transitions.
comments.quote: A vast, vast number of habitat transitions are being missed with this course-grained approach. Yet the figure 4 legend reads “We show the estimated numbers of transition events between each pair of habitats”. That’s incorrect and misleading.

comments.issue: The word 'patterns' in the first abstract sentences is unclear.
comments.request: Reword the opening abstract sentences, e.g. mentioning the unequal distribution of diversity.
comments.quote: I think it could help to re-word the first couple sentences of the abstract. It’s just a bit unclear by what is meant by “patterns” in the first and second sentences.

comments.issue: The data and time calibration used to build the animal phylogenies are not described.
comments.request: Provide more information on phylogeny building and calibration.
comments.quote: There could be more information on phylogeny building. For instance, it wasn’t clear what data were used to make the animal phylogenies or how they were time calibrated.

comments.issue: 'Related topics' at line 66 is vague.
comments.request: Specify the related topics.
comments.quote: Line 66: what related topics? No need to be vague here.

comments.issue: Equivalence between the sampled tree and a fully resolved species-level phylogeny is assumed without justification.
comments.request: Delete the sentence or support the assumption.
comments.quote: To assume that this tree would yield equivalent results as a fully resolved and dated species-level phylogeny is not credible.

comments.issue: 'Both groups' at line 164 is not identified.
comments.request: State explicitly that plants and animals are meant.
comments.quote: Line 164: by “both groups” do you mean plants and animals? Might just say that.

comments.issue: Clade age is not included as a predictor alongside diversification rate in the regressions.
comments.request: Include clade age as an additional predictor.
comments.quote: since the two competing hypotheses for differences in diversity among habitats are time and diversification rate, would it be possible to include time (i.e. clade age) as an additional predictor in these regression models

comments.issue: The reason for using this metric rather than comparing actual r-squared values is not explained.
comments.request: Clarify why this metric was necessary.
comments.quote: Line 217-219: Some clarification here would be nice – why was it necessary to use this metric? What’s wrong with just comparing the actual r-squared values?

reviews.assessment: Finds the findings not novel, the core richness-diversification analysis circular and the scholarship incomplete.

comments.issue: Findings are not novel; prior literature on the origins of species-rich terrestrial groups and richness variation among environments is overlooked.
comments.request: Acknowledge and engage with this prior literature.
comments.quote: However, I do not feel that the findings are novel. In particular, the paper overlooks substantial prior literature on the origins of some of the most species rich terrestrial groups

comments.issue: Asking whether richness correlates with diversification rate is mathematically circular because the rate is computed from richness.
comments.request: Replace this circular analysis with a valid test.
comments.quote: These include, in particular, mathematical circularity in asking the question of whether variation in species richness correlates with diversification rates (given the way the diversification rates are calculated, they -must- correlate).

comments.issue: The diversification rate estimator is not mathematically identifiable and has been recently criticized.
comments.request: Use an identifiable estimator or address the criticism.
comments.quote: The study also makes use of a diversification rate estimator that is not mathematically identifiable and has been recently criticised (explained below).

comments.issue: The large terrestrialisation literature on insects, land plants and tetrapods is ignored.
comments.request: Cite and discuss this literature.
comments.quote: However, a large literature on terrestrialisation is ignored. Topics such as the origin of insects (and other events in arthropod terrestrialisation), origin of land plants, and the origin of tetrapods (/amniotes) have received a great deal of attention

comments.issue: Transition counts from ancestral reconstruction should instead be estimated as frequencies in statistical models.
comments.request: Estimate transition frequencies from statistical models.
comments.quote: But these intrinsic frequencies (per lineage million years) should be estimated from statistical models rather than reporting the count of transitions based on ancestral state reconstruction as currently done.

comments.issue: Literature on the ancestry of the species-rich groups, from fossils and phylogenies, is not meaningfully referenced.
comments.request: Reference this literature meaningfully.
comments.quote: The extensive literature on this topic, including insights both from fossils and from phylogenies, is not really referenced at all in a meaningful way.

comments.issue: MS estimator assumptions (constant rate, a priori extinction fraction) are not addressed despite known failings.
comments.request: Address the core issues raised for MS estimators.
comments.quote: However, the MS estimator assumes essentially a constant diversification rate through time. The authors argue that their method is robust to variation in rate or mode of diversification through time, citing various simulation studies.

comments.issue: The appendix substantially misrepresents the Rabosky and Benson paper it discusses.
comments.request: Correct the representation and seriously address the core issues.
comments.quote: The authors discuss this paper (Rabosky & Benson 2021) in their appendix. However, their discussion substantially mis-represents what was said in that paper, and does not include a serious attempt to address the core issues.

comments.issue: The pattern may be specific to exceptionally species-rich groups; environment effects are not separated from clade identity.
comments.request: Quantify environment versus clade identity and show rate distributions.
comments.quote: You could think of it this way, from a statistical perspective - to what extent are these difference among environments explained by environment itself rather than by clade identity

comments.issue: Species richness differences among environments are common knowledge, yet are presented as novel and not linked back to earlier papers.
comments.request: Refer back to the earlier papers and temper novelty claims.
comments.quote: The authors do cite some of the papers that examined this topic, in their introduction. But they also simultaneously present their findings as novel, ad they do not refer back to those papers later on.

comments.issue: No process-based reason is given for expecting low total area to predict phylogenetic diversity.
comments.request: Explain the theoretical basis for this prediction.
comments.quote: It's not really clear that low total area makes a specific prediction about phylogenetic diversity - not from a mechanistic point of view at least.

comments.issue: The quoted observation about area and richness is not cited at that point although the authors are cited elsewhere.
comments.request: Add the relevant citations there.
comments.quote: Other authors have noted this and are cited elsewhere in the ms, but not here.

comments.issue: The claim that freshwater origins are far less clear overstates the knowledge gap.
comments.request: Phrase this more circumspectly.
comments.quote: It sees obvious that most species in freshwater ecosystems come from a few groups that certainly had terrestrial ancestors: insects, vascular plants, etc.

comments.issue: The description that tips are families sampled in proportion to richness of phyla is confusing because families cannot contain phyla.
comments.request: Clarify the sampling procedure.
comments.quote: I don't follow what was done here. The text suggests that tips are families, and that they were sampled in proportion to the richness of phyla within them. But families can't contain phyla.
