study.system: alpine grassland plants; turf transplants and community dynamics simulations

editor_summary: Editor asks the authors to address all comments, provide enough methods in the main text for readers to evaluate the modelling approach, and trim the supplementary material so it is functionally useful.

reviews.assessment: Strongly positive: calls it well written and thoughtful with no major concerns, only asking for a broader caveats paragraph in the Discussion.
strengths: excellent study embedding single-species dynamics in the community context

comments.issue: Short observation period: annual weather peculiarities may add noise or bias to model parameters.
comments.request: Add this caveat to the Discussion.
comments.quote: peculiarities of annual weather (e.g. winters poor in snow, unusually warm, dry or cold seasons etc.), for example, might have introduced noise or even bias into model parameters.

comments.issue: Longer warming could trigger soil processes not visible after three years.
comments.request: Discuss this limitation.
comments.quote: A longer phase of warming may trigger soil processes that have repercussions on community dynamics not visible after three years

comments.issue: More frequent and longer droughts and Alchemilla drought sensitivity are not assessable from the observations.
comments.request: Discuss this caveat.
comments.quote: A likely future climate scenario involves increasing frequency and length of drought periods with potentially massive, though different effects on demography of all species not assessable from the observations.

comments.issue: Only 11 of 34 species were modelled and they are probably a biased, more frequent subset, limiting community-level conclusions.
comments.request: Discuss the representativeness of the modelled species.
comments.quote: these are only 11 of 34, and they probably do not represent an unbiased sample (probably the more frequent ones)

reviews.assessment: Sees an interesting insight but cannot fully evaluate the methods, which are buried in a huge supplement, and worries the IBM loses diversity during burn-in.
strengths: interesting insight into community dynamics under climate change
relevant to biodiversity predictions and warming experiment design

comments.issue: Key methods and equations are absent from the main text and buried in a 200-page supplement.
comments.request: Include model and analysis details in the main text.
comments.quote: the main text does not include a single equation or sufficient other details to fully understand the model fitting and simulation process

comments.issue: Unclear whether the IBM maintains coexistence; diversity lost during burn-in could confound the no-lag scenarios.
comments.request: Show diversity retained during burn-in and quasi-equilibrium runs.
comments.quote: I am curious about the IBM's ability to capture the observed patterns of co-occurrence/coexistence in these communities.

comments.issue: Weeding out lower-elevation recruits removes the influence of lower-elevation species, questioning the use of turf transplants.
comments.request: Justify the transplant design versus warming chambers.
comments.quote: wouldn't the influence of lower elevation species be key to understanding how these communities might fare under climate change?

comments.issue: Interactions appear to affect only recruitment to unoccupied quadrants, not survival or growth.
comments.request: Explain why interactions do not affect survival or growth.
comments.quote: both intra- and interspecific interactions only seem to influence recruitment to unoccupied quadrants. Is there a reason to think that such interactions wouldn't also influence survival or growth in this system?

comments.issue: Figure 1: predicted and observed Shannon diversity diverge through time with unclear implications.
comments.request: Discuss the implications of this divergence.
comments.quote: it looks like predicted and observed Shannon diversity increasingly diverge through time. What is the implication of this for the predictions decades into the future?

comments.issue: Figure 3 legend colours do not match the plotted colours.
comments.request: Fix the legend colours.
comments.quote: The colors mentioned in the legend don't seem to match what is shown in the version of Figure 3 in my pdf.

reviews.assessment: Calls the study outstanding and novel but finds the lag terminology imprecise, the main-text methods too sparse, and the demographic unit confusing.
strengths: outstanding example of combining models and experiments
novel application and first clear demonstration that abrupt change differs from gradual
important implications for interpreting climate experiments

comments.issue: 'Demographic lags' is imprecise: interactions and longevity cause lags, demography is not itself a lag.
comments.request: Use more precise wording throughout.
comments.quote: this language, used in multiple places in the manuscript, seems fairly imprecise

comments.issue: The causal role of interspecific interactions in producing lags is inferred rather than demonstrated.
comments.request: Quantify lags with and without interspecific interactions.
comments.quote: could the role of interspecific interactions in causing these lags be quantified by eliminating interspecific interactions in the models?

comments.issue: Main-text model description is inaccurate, wrongly implying no competition and asymmetric recruitment effects.
comments.request: Improve and correct the model description.
comments.quote: My initial reading led to the impression that growth was modeled only as a function of temperature and soil moisture, with no competitive (or facilitative) effects

comments.issue: Main text does not make clear that community survey data are the source of the demographic data.
comments.request: State this clearly in the methods.
comments.quote: the methods in the main text should be much clearer that the community survey data is the source of the demographic data

comments.issue: 'Ramet' is used for an area-based demographic unit, conflicting with its technical meaning.
comments.request: Use a more descriptive term.
comments.quote: the use of the term "ramet", which has a quite clear technical meaning in the literature, to describe this area-based demographic unit is quite confusing

comments.issue: The 2000 m site is not compared with the home site, which was not used as a 0-degree transplant site.
comments.request: Explain why the home site was not included.
comments.quote: Is the 2000m site similar in vegetation to the home site? Why wasn't the home site used as one of the transplant sites

comments.issue: Unclear whether models use annual variation in conditions or site means.
comments.request: State which climate inputs were used.
comments.quote: Did the models use the annual variation in conditions to have more data points for defining environmental dependence of demography? Or simply the means for each site?

comments.issue: Lush growth at one site is hard to explain given transplanted soil and root barriers.
comments.request: Explain this unexpected response.
comments.quote: it is hard to understand why the transplants should have responded so drastically to soil conditions at the new site. Is something else going on there

comments.issue: Lines 243-245: the taxa inclusion criterion remains unclear.
comments.request: Explain the criterion and its rationale.
comments.quote: After several rereadings, I'm still not sure what this criterion for including taxa for the final simulations means and why it was used.

comments.issue: Figure 2C symbols are hard to follow as time trajectories.
comments.request: Connect time points or add smoothed curves.
comments.quote: Could Figure 2C show actual time trajectories, by connecting the different time points as in Fig. 4A?

comments.issue: Lines 321-3: the description of time trajectories understates movement on the second axis.
comments.request: Correct the trajectory description.
comments.quote: the description of the time trajectories (lines 321-3) doesn't seem quite accurate: there is very considerable movement over time on the second axis (circles to triangles)

comments.issue: The origin of the 80% figure is not explained.
comments.request: State where the 80% figure comes from.
comments.quote: Where does the 80% figure come from?

comments.issue: Several minor lapses in English usage.
comments.request: Review the English usage.
comments.quote: The manuscript could also use some review for minor lapses in proper English usage.

title: Ecological lags govern the pace and outcome of plant community responses to 21st‐century climate change

study.system: plants and animals; meta-analysis of dispersal-range size studies

editor_summary: Editor says all three referees found merit but identified major problems: R1 on statistical presentation and the unclear phylogenetic correction, R2 on vague criteria for dispersal-related traits, R3 on linking studies to dispersal stages; plus PRISMA exclusion reasons.

reviews.assessment: Enjoyed the discussion, but the statistical analyses are hard to follow and insufficiently explained to evaluate the meta-analysis.
strengths: good job reporting and summarizing the studies in the field

comments.issue: Vote-counting analyses are presented even though vote counting misrepresents reality and the authors later discard those results.
comments.request: Remove vote-counting results and present only the dataset structure.
comments.quote: I did not understand why the authors are presenting vote-counting analyses. It is known that vote counting can misrepresent the reality and that is the reason why meta-analyses were designed.

comments.issue: Using raw correlation coefficients rather than Fisher Zr, and the effect size choice, are not explained.
comments.request: Justify the effect size and consider transforming r to Fisher Zr.
comments.quote: First why did the authors use correlation coefficient for the analysis and did not transform it into any other effect size (in most meta-analysis r coefficients are transformed into Fisher Zr to normalize the data and to easily get the sampling variance).

comments.issue: The extraction and transformation procedure for non-correlation studies is not described.
comments.request: Detail the extraction procedure and transformations used.
comments.quote: can the authors detail a little bit more on the extraction procedure when the relationship was not presented as the correlation coefficient (what kind of other data did the authors encountered and which transformation procedure did they use).

comments.issue: The type of phylogenetic correction is never described in the methods or supplement, yet effect sizes are not phylogenetically independent.
comments.request: Describe the phylogenetic correction in the methods.
comments.quote: I did not understand which type of phylogenetic correction did the authors use for the meta-analysis. There is only one part about that in the results but no mention of that at all in the methods or in the supplementary materials.

comments.issue: Publication bias analyses are only in the supplement and never mentioned or described in the main paper.
comments.request: Mention the absence of publication bias in the main text and describe the analyses precisely.
comments.quote: the first time I read the manuscript I did not see any mention of publication bias analysis, later I saw that this analysis was performed but only presented in the supplementary without any referencing to those results in the main paper.

comments.issue: Body size correlates with many life history traits, so a positive relationship does not establish that dispersal drives range size.
comments.request: Discuss whether body size is still an appropriate dispersal proxy.
comments.quote: even if there is a positive relationship, we can’t say for sure that it is dispersal which matters here for range size

reviews.assessment: Reads nicely and synthesises the literature well, but the link to dispersal phases and parts of the methods need clarifying.
strengths: reads nicely and synthesises existing literature well
topic of well-established relevance for macroecology
mechanistic view via dispersal phases is helpful

comments.issue: The link between collected data and the three dispersal phases is unclear and the phase framework appears speculative.
comments.request: Argue the link between data variation and dispersal phases clearly throughout.
comments.quote: My main issue is the link between the collected data and the phases. I see that Table 1 tries to establish this link but the text remains unclear in my opinion.

comments.issue: The search algorithm, field tags and search period are not given, so the search cannot be reproduced.
comments.request: Provide the search algorithm, terms and search period.
comments.quote: I would have greatly appreciated having the search algorithm in the methods or the supplement. Search terms are given in lines 157-159, but WoS has a large number of categories (field tags) and I was not able to recover the search spontaneously.

comments.issue: Whether and how studies were weighted in the meta-analysis is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the weighting procedure explicitly.
comments.quote: One further, rather central, aspect is unclear to me which relates to the weighting of the studies for the metaanalysis. Weighting is mentioned on page 8 but not on page 7 which made me wonder whether weighting was generally done or not.

comments.issue: The explanation for the vote-counting versus meta-analysis discrepancy is not backed by a table of evidence.
comments.request: Show sample sizes of neutral and negative studies in a table.
comments.quote: The authors explain the discrepancy between their vote-counting results and the metaanalysis (line 337-339), but fail to show this in a table.

comments.issue: 'Mechanisms' is too strong a word for the factors discussed at line 66.
comments.request: Use 'factors' or a similar term.
comments.quote: line 66: “mechanisms”. Not everything seems to be a mechanism here. Maybe use “factors” or similar?

comments.issue: The claim that dispersal promotes local adaptation ignores maladapted allele influx.
comments.request: Reformulate the statement about local adaptation.
comments.quote: Line 77: dispersal may not always promote local adaptation due to the influx of maladapted alleles. Maybe reformulate?

comments.issue: The reason for splitting the data into four realm subsets is unclear; realm could be an explanatory variable.
comments.request: Explain or reconsider the subsetting of the data.
comments.quote: Line 215: 4 subsets. Why subsetting the data? Marine, terrestrial etc. could be an explanatory variable? Maybe I am misunderstanding this.

reviews.assessment: Pleasant and well-written synthesis, but several conceptual arguments and the dispersal proxies need better justification.

comments.issue: The introduction omits key theoretical models on how dispersal affects range size through evolutionary consequences.
comments.request: Cite and discuss models of dispersal, gene swamping and niche evolution in the introduction.
comments.quote: I found that the introduction failed to give a complete picture of how dispersal may affect range size through its evolutionary consequences.

comments.issue: Several Table 2 proxies are life history traits that may predict spread rates rather than dispersal, blurring what dispersal-range size means.
comments.request: Clarify criteria for calling traits dispersal proxies and stop treating all life history traits as dispersal.
comments.quote: as it is unclear whether some life history traits there are included because they were shown indeed to be predictors of dispersal (correlated to dispersal rates and distances, or predictive of movements of individuals), or because they are predictors of spread rates

comments.issue: Finding effects more often in studies with many traits could be a chance result of multiplying variables.
comments.request: Address the multiple-variable chance-finding issue.
comments.quote: is there not a basic statistical issue there in that by multiplying variables you may by chance find one with a relationship with range size?

comments.issue: Body size may relate to range size for other reasons, e.g. Rapoport's rule, not through dispersal.
comments.request: Reconsider how strongly body size results support the dispersal hypothesis.
comments.quote: body size could be positively related to range size for reasons other than dispersal so I am unsure such a relationship (which contributes quite a lot to the present data set) is supporting strongly the hypothesis made here

comments.issue: The rationale for the Table 3 predictions, especially the endothermy/ectothermy direction and region size, is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the rationale behind the Table 3 predictions.
comments.quote: I failed to follow part of the rationale for some predictions in table 3, in particular that related to endothermy/ectothermy

comments.issue: The results do not show a sharp contrast between traits assigned to different dispersal phases, and many traits are hard to classify.
comments.request: Reconsider the phase classification and the claimed contrasts.
comments.quote: I am not sure that I see a sharp contrast in the results between traits that have been classified in one or another category and some are hard to classify anyway

comments.issue: Reid's paradox may now be explained by microrefugia rather than the stated mechanism.
comments.request: Consider the microrefugia explanation.
comments.quote: Line 127: Is Reid’s paradox increasingly explained by the existence of microrefugia instead?

comments.issue: Two line-level copy edits (number formatting, Table 3 wording).
comments.quote: Line 196: start sentence by Thirteen instead of 13

comments.issue: The broad phylogenetic scale explanation contradicts the finding that phylogeny matters at finer scales.
comments.request: Reconcile the conflicting phylogenetic scale statements.
comments.quote: indeed the too broad phylogenetic scale is likely to be responsible here for the lack of signal, which seems to contradict your finding otherwise at a finer scale that phyogeny is important to consider to detect dispersal limitation

comments.issue: If a trait is not a dispersal proxy, its relationship with range size is not a dispersal-range size relation.
comments.request: Clarify which relations count as dispersal effects.
comments.quote: Line 380: but then if the trait is not a proxy for dispersal this is not a relation between dispersal and range size?

title: Understanding the relationship between dispersal and range size

study.system: interference competition; eco-evolutionary agent-based model of territorial birds

editor_summary: Both experts recognized the importance; discussion brief and model development/verification aspects missing; contextualize the model with data in the discussion and add context on interference competition in the Introduction.

reviews.assessment: Exciting direction for coexistence theory, but the model description needs clarifications (detailed comments in attachment).
strengths: incorporating interference competition into coexistence theory is exciting
work can help push the theory forward

comments.issue: Concerns about the model description and several places needing clarification; details are in the attached document.
comments.request: Clarify the model description (see attachment).
comments.quote: I have concerns about their model description and there are several places where clarifications are needed

reviews.assessment: Refreshing, empirically grounded model with non-intuitive insights; wants deeper discussion and validation of parameter assumptions.
strengths: interesting non-intuitive insights into competitor recognition
dynamic simulation of secondary contact with realistic parameters

comments.issue: The two-paragraph discussion does not explore the significance of the results or relate them to previous work.
comments.request: Expand the discussion of the results and their context.
comments.quote: The two-paragraph Discussion doesn't sufficiently explore the significance of the results and how they relate to previous work.

comments.issue: Linked, pleiotropic effects of body size on asymmetry, refuges and dietary overlap are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss how body-size pleiotropy constrains the parameter space.
comments.quote: These pleiotropic or linked effects mediated by body size can constrain parameter space and lead to repeated outcomes for coexistence according to Fig. 1 - worth including in the Discussion.

comments.issue: Birds may learn to recognise competitors rather than evolving species-specific recognition, an alternative mechanism the model ignores.
comments.request: Mention learning-based recognition and consider parameterizing it.
comments.quote: This broader competitive-recognition mechanism should at least be mentioned in the Discussion

comments.issue: How the model approximates real Ficedula ecologies (nest sites, predation) is unclear.
comments.request: Explain how the model matches realistic situations.
comments.quote: I would like to know how the model approximates realistic situations in nature (Ficedula, or otherwise)

comments.issue: Pooling within- and among-species interactions for recognition evolution may drive the outcomes.
comments.request: Test a model where males always recognise their own species.
comments.quote: I'm a little concerned about the pooling of within and among species interactions for the evolution of competitor recognition during territory settlement.

comments.issue: The claim that interference competition is theoretically incompatible with coexistence is too strong and ignores prior theory.
comments.request: Cite previous theoretical work such as Case and Gilpin 1974.
comments.quote: This seems too strong a statement given that theoretical work has shown evidence for coexistence with interference competition (e.g., Case and Gilpin 1974, PNAS).

comments.issue: Using many pairs of the same species on one territory is unrealistic given within-species territoriality.
comments.request: Consider starting from within-species territoriality.
comments.quote: Given that Ficedula males are territorial within species (like many passerine birds), why not use within-species territoriality as a starting point?

comments.issue: Long-term stasis could arise from evolutionary trade-offs rather than a Red-Queen process.
comments.request: Consider the trade-off explanation with ecological refuges.
comments.quote: I'm not convinced that a Red-Queen-like evolutionary model is necessary to explain long term persistence of (interference) competitors

comments.issue: Typo in SI Model Description line 161.
comments.quote: SI Model Description line 161: “ the offspring inherit a from each parent a haplotype” typo

comments.issue: How autosomal loci model male-only recognition traits (z) is unclear; whether females carry unexpressed values is unstated.
comments.request: Clarify the genetics of recognition traits.
comments.quote: I didn't entirely understand how evolution was modelled for competitor recognition traits given that these are expressed only in the males (e.g., z), but the values are modelled by autosomal loci.

comments.issue: Why species 2 should evolve recognition of a superior interference competitor is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the constraints and realism of this evolution.
comments.quote: Why should species 2 ever evolve the ability to recognize species 1 as a competitor, given that species 1 has an advantage in interference competition?

title: Eco‐evolutionary dynamics of interference competition

study.system: angiosperms; comparative analysis of flower sex allocation and herbivore richness

editor_summary: Editor: novel study, but reviewers question the outcrossing and herbivory proxies and ask to tone down conclusions; pathogens and flower-visibility bias may confound.

reviews.assessment: Very creative and exciting with robust results; suggests testing one additional prediction and lists minor typos.
strengths: exciting robust results with wide impact

comments.issue: The prediction that other outcrossing-enhancing traits also increase with herbivores is supported only from the literature.
comments.request: Test this prediction with the study's own data set.
comments.quote: They provided support from the literature, but I wondered why they didn’t test this with their own data set.

comments.issue: 8 minor typos
comments.quote: Line 350 ‘ According to (the) theory,’ of ‘Theoretically,’

reviews.assessment: Not sold on the conclusion because the outcrossing and herbivory proxies are far from the factors of interest and prior work is not fairly credited.

comments.issue: Both outcrossing rate and herbivore pressure are measured by proxies divorced from the factors of interest.
comments.request: Validate the proxies or temper conclusions based on them.
comments.quote: both factors which are meant to be correlated – outcrossing rate and herbivore pressure – are measured by proxies (% allocation to male function, number of herbivore species) which are sufficiently divorced from the factors of real interest

comments.issue: The claim that flower evolution is governed by natural enemies as well as pollinators is too bold.
comments.request: Tone down this claim.
comments.quote: I am made somewhat uncomfortable therefore by the authors’ bold claim (beginning of discussion) that “flower evolution is not only governed by pollinators but also by the plant’s natural enemies”

comments.issue: Prior work on mating systems and herbivore/pathogen pressure is not fairly credited.
comments.request: Acknowledge this literature and its more complex picture.
comments.quote: I also don’t believe the authors give sufficient credit to other work (see below) that has examined the relationship between plant mating system and herbivore/pathogen pressure, some of which paints a more complex picture than presented by Fonseca et al.

comments.issue: Sampling 10 plants from one population per species may not capture outcrossing variation.
comments.request: Broaden or justify the sampling of male function allocation.
comments.quote: sampling 10 plants from a single population of each species may not adequately assess male function allocation or outcrossing rate

comments.issue: The correlation between male allocation and actual outcrossing rate is untested.
comments.request: Cross-reference the species with existing outcrossing-rate databases.
comments.quote: is there anyway of cross-referencing species included in this study and in these databases to see what the correlation is between average outcrossing rate for a species vs. % biomass allocation to male function.

comments.issue: Herbivore species richness may not reflect herbivore pressure or tissue consumption.
comments.request: Validate the link between herbivore richness and pressure.
comments.quote: it is also not clear how tight the correlation is. Herbivore species richness may have little to do with the amount of tissue consumed by herbivores.

comments.issue: Selection acts at population rather than geographic range level, mismatching the herbivore data scale.
comments.request: Address the scale mismatch between herbivore records and selection.
comments.quote: Selection on plant defense will occur at the population level (or metapopulation level), not at the geographic range level.

comments.issue: A simple count of herbivore species ignores specialization.
comments.request: Account for specialist versus generalist herbivores.
comments.quote: a simple count of all herbivore species, regardless of specialization may not be meaningful.

comments.issue: Tests of the Levin (1975) hypothesis by Busch, Johnson and Campbell & Kessler are not given fair credit.
comments.request: Discuss these prior tests and their implications.
comments.quote: Fonseca et al. cite other tests of the hypothesis (or underlying assumptions of the hypothesis), first proposed by Levin (1975) that herbivore (or pathogen) pressure favors outcrossing in plants, but I’m not sure they give the work fair credit.

comments.issue: The inclusion of specific leaf area as a covariate is not justified.
comments.request: Explain the relevance of specific leaf area.
comments.quote: I fail to see the relevance of specific leaf area and the authors provide none.

comments.issue: The Hamilton-Zuk good-genes parallel is unsupported and should not lead the discussion.
comments.request: Remove or substantially qualify this parallel.
comments.quote: I really don’t think there is any evidence of the type of good genes hypothesis invoked by Hamilton and Zuk, and I don’t see why this parallel is the lead off to the discussion.

reviews.assessment: Constructive comments on a central assumption and on the direction of causality, asking that correlative conclusions be toned down.

comments.issue: 2 line-level copy edits
comments.quote: Line 13. Substitute “Since” for “Because”. (Since is generally used to denote temporality)

comments.issue: The assumption that more herbivore species means stronger selection is not justified.
comments.request: Justify the assumption, noting specialists can inflict more damage.
comments.quote: It makes sense that more herbivore species should impose stronger selection pressures, but not necessarily, as few specialist herbivore species (even a single one) can inflict greater damage than several generalist species.

comments.issue: Feedback between mating systems and herbivory, and the reverse causal direction, are not acknowledged.
comments.request: Discuss the feedback and the alternative hypothesis that herbivores prefer less-defended male-biased plants.
comments.quote: there is a feedback between mating systems and herbivory that can influence the evolution of both, maleness (or outcrossing) and defenses against herbivory

comments.issue: Biogeographic range position could affect inbreeding and herbivore escape but is not controlled.
comments.request: Consider controlling for biogeographical ranges.
comments.quote: Controlling for biogeographical ranges may be also relevant because populations in the edges of a species range may tend to increase inbreeding, due to pollinators and/or mate limitation, and they are also likely to “escape” from some herbivore species.

comments.issue: Multiple forces shaping flower and reproductive evolution are not acknowledged in the introduction.
comments.request: Acknowledge these additional forces in the introduction.
comments.quote: I think that the multiple forces affecting flower and reproductive system evolution should be better acknowledged in the introduction as well.

comments.issue: The statement at line 274 is too strong given the correlative evidence.
comments.request: Weaken the statement, e.g. sexual selection is likely influenced by herbivore resistance genes.
comments.quote: Maybe a less strong statement (given the correlative nature of the evidence presented) could be “sexual selection in plants is likely to be influenced by herbivore resistance genes”

comments.issue: The causality and evidence behind the statement at lines 276-277 are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the causal claim and its evidence.
comments.quote: It is not clear to me the causality/evidence of this statement. Could you please clarify?

comments.issue: An alternative explanation is that male-biased plants produce fewer defenses and are preferred by herbivores.
comments.request: Consider and discuss this reverse mechanism.
comments.quote: Or alternatively, male-biased individuals produce less defenses (due to resource allocation costs between growth, reproduction and defenses), and are preferred by herbivores?

comments.issue: The statement at lines 287-288 is too strong for correlative data.
comments.request: Down-tune the statement to a non-conclusive possibility.
comments.quote: I think this is a too strong statement given the correlative nature of the data presented. Down-tune this statement would be convenient, maybe as a (non-conclusive) possibility?

comments.issue: 'Partially explain' and 'pollination strategies' need clarification.
comments.request: Define pollination strategies and qualify the claim.
comments.quote: “partially explain” (because there are many other selective forces influencing reproductive systems in Angiosperms). What do you mean by “pollination strategies”?

comments.issue: Other adaptive advantages may also have promoted bird and bat pollination.
comments.request: Consider alternative advantages unrelated to natural enemies.
comments.quote: Maybe other adaptive advantages (unrelated to natural enemies) have also promoted the evolution of bird and bat pollination?

comments.issue: The link between herbivore species number, damage and actual plant defense investment needs more investigation.
comments.request: Further investigate damage and defense investment to support the explanation.
comments.quote: The relationship between the number of herbivore species and the damage they produce in plants, as well as the real investment in plant defenses also deserves to be further investigated

title: Insect herbivores drive sex allocation in angiosperm flowers

study.system: aquatic invertebrate ectotherms (Daphnia, copepod, dinoflagellate, crab); lab thermal experiments

editor_summary: Editor asks for a clearer conceptual framework with hypotheses and mechanisms, stronger justification that TER estimates are not artefacts, more ecological context in the discussion, and tempered 'universal' claims.

reviews.assessment: Likes the work and sees it as a nice extension of previous studies, but wants the overblown 'universal' framing toned down and the two experimental parts better integrated and validated.
strengths: nice extension of Ruiz et al. 2020
Figure 6 is a nice conceptual presentation

comments.issue: The title and several claims announce a universal response for all ectotherms from only four planktonic invertebrate species.
comments.request: Tone down the title and general claims, emphasising more specific conclusions.
comments.quote: the title which is, I believe, to general, announcing a “universal” response for ectotherms while working on 4 species of planktonic invertebrates is somewhat enthusiast

comments.issue: The discussion focuses on TER thermal variation and lacks ecological implications for food webs and nutrient cycles.
comments.request: Enrich the discussion with ecological implications and perspectives.
comments.quote: I felt that the discussion mainly focused on the explanation of TER thermal variations and lack of some ecological implications and/or perspectives

comments.issue: The two experimental parts use different methods, but their different or complementary information is never discussed.
comments.request: Discuss how the two methods provide complementary information on the overall response.
comments.quote: I think that it may be interesting to discuss at some point how the use of the different methods may bring different/complementary information of the overall response

comments.issue: Modelled TERs for the three marine species are never compared with directly measured growth or TER.

comments.issue: The title is too enthusiastic in claiming a universal response.

comments.issue: 'such as' at L61 implies more study species than were actually used.

comments.issue: 'Universality' at L66 is too absolute a term for the results.

comments.issue: 5 line-level copy edits (word choice, grammar, sentence length).

comments.issue: It is unclear why TER was modelled rather than directly measured for the copepod, dinoflagellate and crab larvae.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether lateral area is tightly correlated with body mass, especially when food quality varies.

comments.issue: Possible maternal effects on the results are not addressed.

comments.issue: The section at L337-346 contains redundancy and could be shortened.
comments.request: Shorten this section without losing information.
comments.quote: There is some redundancy in this section, I believe that it can be shortened without losing information

comments.issue: The assumption at L387 about warming magnitudes lacks references and clarification, and the large thermal range should not be downplayed.

reviews.assessment: Well-written and carefully performed, but the two experiment sets are not integrated and TER estimation for the marine species rests on potentially critical assumptions.
strengths: both experiments exciting on their own with a clear focus

comments.issue: The two experiments read as two separate studies patched together, with no rationale for combining them or for the species selection.
comments.request: Highlight the rationale for combining both experiments and the choice of species.
comments.quote: I strongly advise the authors to better highlight the rationale of bringing both experiments together, with different methods, and indicate why multiple marine species, but only one freshwater species was used

comments.issue: The Daphnia clones come from different geographical regions, but how clone origin influenced the TERs is not addressed.
comments.request: Discuss how the geographical origin of the clones may have influenced TERs.
comments.quote: the first set of experiments with Daphnia clones show clear differences between a clone isolated from different geographical regions. How may this have influenced the TERs?

comments.issue: At the highest temperature TERs are lower while growth is similar or higher, so focusing only on TER may mislead.
comments.request: Consider growth rates alongside TER when interpreting the results.
comments.quote: In the same experiment, the TERs for the highest temperature are lower compared to the others, however, growth is not very much different or even higher. Only focusing on the TER may thus seem possibly misleading here.

comments.issue: TER calculations use body C:X ratios and autocorrelated terms; body elemental contents may cancel so TER largely reflects ingestion-rate ratios.
comments.request: Clarify which variables drive TER and whether the body C:P/TER contrast follows from the calculation.
comments.quote: the body elemental contents seem to rule out each other in the equation, and the ratio between ingestion rates for C and P strongly determine the TER

comments.issue: P ingestion rates and body C and P contents underlying the TER calculations are not shown.
comments.request: Provide P ingestion rates and body C and P contents in the supplement.
comments.quote: it would be helpful to see data (e.g. in the supplementary) on the P ingestion rates, and also the data on body C and P contents

comments.issue: Mechanisms that shift TERs are not explained, and it is unclear how hump-shaped and earlier U-shaped responses relate.
comments.request: Discuss processes that could flatten or convert hump- and U-shaped thermal responses.
comments.quote: There might be processes that flatten either hump or U-shape, but might there be processes that could turn a hump-shape into a U-shape?

comments.issue: The TER increase at high temperature in the Helgoland crab larvae might reflect a shift in population structure.
comments.request: Assess whether population structure or the short duration explains this increase.
comments.quote: might this have been caused by a shift in the population structure? Though, perhaps the duration of the experiment was too short?

comments.issue: The hypotheses tested by the various experiments are never stated.
comments.request: State the hypotheses for each experiment.
comments.quote: L16-118: What were the hypotheses for these various experiments?

comments.issue: Handling stress may have influenced the findings, perhaps differently across species and temperatures.
comments.request: Check or discuss the influence of handling stress on the results.
comments.quote: The handling seems to induce some stress on the animals? Might this have influenced the findings?

comments.issue: It is unclear how gut content was dealt with or corrected for.
comments.request: Explain how gut content was accounted for.
comments.quote: How was dealt with the gut content? Or is that negligible for these animals? Or was this somehow corrected for?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether growth measured as change in body C and P is really a change in organism size.
comments.request: Clarify what the growth measure represents and how C and P changes relate to size.
comments.quote: Would this technically not be (change in) organism size? How did the changes in C and P correspond to organism size?

comments.issue: Food was provided by cell counts, not biovolume, and cell aggregation could have altered the amount of food given.
comments.request: Report whether cells aggregated and how food quantity was standardised.
comments.quote: Did all algal cells remain as single cell, or was there also cell aggregation? When food provision is only based on cell counts, not biovolume

comments.issue: The feeding measurements may capture net removal rather than feeding rate, and correction for algal growth is unexplained.
comments.request: Clarify the protocol, correction for algal growth and how much removed material was ingested.
comments.quote: it seems to me that they do not really target feeding rate but rather net removal? How was corrected for algal growth in course of the feeding period?

comments.issue: The general conclusion ignores actual growth rates, although growth could increase even at high C:P ratios.
comments.request: Consider growth rates alongside TER in the general conclusion.
comments.quote: Maybe the TER shifts, but if overall growth increases even at high C:P ratios, then the message would be different?

reviews.assessment: Timely, well-written study with a striking unimodal pattern, but the results are not mechanistically explained and may be artefacts of how TER was calculated.
strengths: unimodal TER response found across diverse taxa

comments.issue: The unimodal TER responses are neither mechanistically explained nor formally confronted with theoretical predictions.
comments.request: Provide mechanistic explanations and confront the results with theory.
comments.quote: it is rather unsatisfactory that these responses cannot be mechanistically explained or formally confronted with predictions from theory

comments.issue: The claimed universality of the unimodal pattern is not corroborated by the temperature responses of the underlying variables.
comments.quote: the apparent universality of the unimodal pattern is not corroborated by responses to temperature of the underlying variables (gross growth efficiencies of C and P and their component variables)

comments.issue: The observed TER patterns may be artefacts of the way TER was calculated.
comments.quote: I wonder to what extent the observed patterns in TER could not be an artefact from the way how TER was calculated

comments.issue: The introduction lacks a theoretical framework for mechanisms driving the temperature and food-quality interaction.
comments.request: Introduce expected mechanisms from metabolic theory, ecological stoichiometry and the growth rate hypothesis.
comments.quote: I miss a theoretical framework introducing the mechanisms that could potentially drive the interactions between temperature and food quality

comments.issue: Despite presenting itself as a standardisation effort, the study compiles heterogeneous methods, so cross-species comparisons are not straightforward.
comments.request: Justify or reconcile the differing methods across species for comparability.
comments.quote: Unfortunately, their work itself is based on a compilation of data that have been collected under widely different circumstances

comments.issue: GGEP is presented as the determining factor based on an unconvincing visual reading of Fig. 4 that does not hold for all species.
comments.request: Support the GGEP claim with quantitative analysis across species.
comments.quote: Instead the Gross Growth Efficiency for P (GGEP) is emphasized to be the determining factor, however, this is based on a not so convincing visual interpretation of Fig. 4

comments.issue: TER mirrors body C:P almost exactly, possibly an artefact of Eqn 2 assuming strict homeostasis and of deriving TER from a single C:P estimate.
comments.request: Test whether the TER pattern is an artefact of the homeostatic assumption.
comments.quote: An artefact resulting from the fact that TER is estimated from a very simple model (Eqn 2) that e.g. assumes that organisms are strictly homeostatic when confronted to variable food C:P?

comments.issue: The theoretical considerations mentioned at L100 are not explained.
comments.request: Explain the theoretical considerations.
comments.quote: L100: based on theoretical considerations: please, explain!

comments.issue: It is unclear how the thermal histories of the Daphnia clones differed and how this affects interpretation.
comments.request: Explain the thermal histories and their consequences.
comments.quote: however, from reading throughout the paper it is not clear to me how these histories differed and what consequences it had for the interpretation of the results

comments.issue: The motivation for applying different methods to D. magna and the other species is missing.
comments.request: Motivate the use of different methods across species.
comments.quote: clearly, there is the need for a motivation why different methods were applied for D. magna and the other species

comments.issue: The explanation at L161-165 is confusing; the per-temperature Gaussian fitting of growth versus C:P is not clear.
comments.request: Explain clearly that a Gaussian was fitted per temperature to GR versus C:P.
comments.quote: It would help to explain more clearly that for each temperature level separately a Gaussian function was fitted to the relationship between GR and C:P from which estimates for TER were derived

comments.issue: The Gaussian functional form has no theoretical justification and assumes weaker growth responses at extreme food C:P, contrary to expectation.
comments.request: Justify the Gaussian curve theoretically.
comments.quote: According to such a function, responses of growth rates to changes in food C:P are assumed to become less pronounced towards the extreme food quality levels, whereas one would expect the strongest responses there

comments.issue: Food concentration and C:P values at L216 are not reported.
comments.request: Provide details on food concentration and C:P.
comments.quote: L216: “a known amount and quality”: please provide details on food concentration and C:P

comments.issue: A control was used for O. marina and A. tonsa but not for C. maenas.
comments.request: Explain or add the missing control for C. maenas.
comments.quote: L220: “relative to a control”: why for O. marina and A. tonsa and not for C. maenas?

comments.issue: Gaussian fit statistics are not reported, and the flat D. magna response at 15°C may not justify deriving a TER.
comments.request: Report R2, P and AIC values and contrast with a linear regression.
comments.quote: could you summarize somewhere the results of the Gaussian fit? R2-values and P-values? Or AIC-values and contrast with e.g. a linear regression?

comments.issue: 'with different thermal history' at L307 is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the thermal history if relevant, otherwise omit it.
comments.quote: L307: ‘with different thermal history’: if relevant explain, if not relevant omit.

comments.issue: The reconciliation with Ruiz et al. is speculative because high temperatures were not studied and only one species conforms.
comments.request: Soften or further support the reconciliation with Ruiz et al.
comments.quote: Unfortunately, current study did not consider high temperatures and only one of the four species (and only one of the two populations) conform to this pattern in the highest temperature treatment

comments.issue: The text claims the model of Ruiz et al. was extended, but no such results are shown.
comments.request: Show the results of the model extension or remove the claim.
comments.quote: L321-323: “when we extended the model by Ruiz et al. (2020): Did you do that? Where are the results?

comments.issue: The claim that maximum-TER temperatures match the species' thermal environment is not supported by evidence.
comments.request: Provide evidence, such as field data, that these temperatures match the thermal niche.
comments.quote: Do you have field data that may support this statement? Is there a way to convincingly demonstrate that the temperatures that correspond with maximum TER really do correspond to the species’ thermal environment?

comments.issue: Growth rates peak at the highest temperatures, which contradicts intermediate temperatures being optimal.
comments.request: Reconcile this statement with the observed growth rate pattern.
comments.quote: Species reach maximum growth rates at the highest temperatures in the gradient? Wouldn’t that mean that the intermediate temperatures do not correspond to optimum temperatures for these species?

comments.issue: The claim that low-P effects are weakest at intermediate temperatures contradicts the Daphnia growth data in Fig. 1.
comments.request: Reconcile the statement with the Daphnia growth data.
comments.quote: is that not in contradiction to the data you obtained for Daphnia. According to Fig 1 the difference in growth rate at TER and more extreme food C:P ratios is more pronounced for the intermediate than low temperature treatments

title: A common temperature dependence of nutritional demands in ectotherms

editor_summary: Editor: enjoyed the clear exposition; asks how the regional species pool is constrained and whether specialized natural enemies (frequency dependence) could be included; examples should tie to empirical predictions.

comments.issue: The framework lacks empirical tests.

comments.issue: Assuming g_i=0 implies a strong non-cyclical attractor without acknowledgement.

comments.issue: The approximation at line 131 is not explained.

comments.issue: The migration-selection balance links to population genetics are not discussed.

comments.issue: Equations 2a/2b imply lognormal convergence that is not noted.

comments.issue: Using regional abundance as a parameter is unsatisfying and under-discussed.

comments.request: Engage with these references.

reviews.assessment: Enjoyed the manuscript and its clear hypotheses, but it fails to bridge theory and empirical application for non-theoreticians.

great discussion of the big ecological picture

comments.issue: The paper is not useful for non-theoreticians because it lacks an empirical translation of the theory.
comments.request: Add explicit empirical links, e.g. a case study or box.

comments.issue: The last examples are too specific and less generally interesting than the main ideas.

comments.issue: Terms, functions and per-example assumptions are hard to navigate.

comments.issue: The origin of the m_i term in eq. 2c is unexplained.

comments.issue: Figure 1 does not show where the local TAD comes from.

comments.issue: The right-side asymptote of Preston-plot SADs appears spurious and is not discussed.

comments.issue: The sentence at L220-222 is incomprehensible.

comments.issue: Simulation code is not shared.

comments.quote: I encourage the authors to share the code that generated their results, in order to improve reproducibility and understand the details of the simulations.

reviews.assessment: Well written and promising, but needs clearer scale definitions, discussion of trait-environment limitations, and empirical illustrations.

comments.issue: The local and regional scales of the analyses are not defined.
comments.request: Define the scales and tabulate the simulation parameters.
comments.quote: You should be clearer about the scale of your analyses.

comments.issue: The assumption that demographic rates depend only on traits ignores spatial context, and its limitations are not discussed.

comments.issue: No illustration with real data or reproducible example supports the predictions.

comments.issue: Predictions about SAD gaps and satellite persistence are not discussed within the trait-based framework.

comments.issue: Paragraph transitions are abrupt and some discussion paragraphs are too general.
comments.request: Improve transitions and add examples to L398-401 and L402-407.
comments.quote: you may pay more attention to the transition between some paragraphs

title: A general framework for species‐abundance distributions: Linking traits and dispersal to explain commonness and rarity

study.system: sea ice algal bloom model; uncertainty quantification with polynomial chaos

editor_summary: Editor found the manuscript interesting and highlights Reviewer 1's epistemic-uncertainty versus heterogeneity distinction and Fig. 5c; suggests adding an online supplement for technical details.

reviews.assessment: Sees an important contribution but wants more technical detail on the polynomial chaos implementation and discussion of how uncertainty interpretations affect biological conclusions.
strengths: Figure 5c is an awesome presentation of global sensitivity results
time-resolved sensitivities offer an interesting way to think about transient dynamics

comments.issue: The paper lumps unknown parameter values and spatial heterogeneity under 'uncertainty' and distinguishes them with jargon, obscuring the key feature of heterogeneity.
comments.request: Motivate the method as representing both epistemic uncertainty and heterogeneous systems.
comments.quote: the paper lumps two concepts (unknown parameter values and heterogeneity) under the umbrella of uncertainty and then uses specialized jargon to distinguish them

comments.issue: The biological interpretation of the resulting distributions differs between epistemic uncertainty and heterogeneity but is not distinguished.
comments.request: Discuss how interpretations of results differ between the two cases.
comments.quote: I think it would be useful to discuss how these models can be used to represent both processes and how the interpretation of the results would differ between the two cases

comments.issue: The specific basis functions and quadrature points used for each method are not described, nor whether the basis choice depends on parameter distributions.
comments.request: Describe the basis functions and quadrature points and their dependence on the parameter distributions.
comments.quote: The paper included some description of the specific basis function and quadrature points used for each method and how/if the choice of basis function changes depending on the distribution of the unknown parameters.

comments.issue: It is not explained how multidimensional basis functions were constructed, how terms were selected, or how the number of terms scales with the number of random parameters.
comments.request: Explain the construction and scaling of multidimensional basis functions.
comments.quote: There was some discussion of how multidimensional basis function were constructed. How were the terms included in these representations chosen?

comments.issue: The choice of approximation order and its effect on accuracy and computational efficiency is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss how the approximation order was chosen and how it affects accuracy and efficiency.
comments.quote: Finally, the paper should discuss how the order of the approximations was chosen and how this choice effects the accuracy of the approximation and the computational efficiency.

comments.issue: The description of how the algorithm scales treats the number of basis functions as a constant and hides how it is chosen.

comments.issue: In the S16 equation B incorrectly appears as a coefficient as well as in the expectation.

reviews.assessment: Clear, organized and useful demonstration of the method; supports publication with suggestions on method contrasts, interpretation and one figure.

comments.issue: The comparison of UQ methods is not detailed enough regarding efficiency, implementation and robustness.

comments.quote: It would be very useful to spend a bit more time contrasting the methods in terms of efficiency, implementation and robustness.

comments.issue: The 'quantification' aspect of UQ and the interpretation of measures such as skewness are not brought forward clearly.

comments.quote: to explain to the ecological audience how to interpret the measures such as skewness etc. in experimental of control settings would be helpful

comments.issue: It is not discussed how quantities of interest that are not proportional to state variables (e.g. total biomass) can be handled in PC.

comments.issue: Figure 5C is hard to interpret: the text says most sensitivities are near zero, yet the P_0 sensitivity is always between 0.3 and 0.8.
comments.request: Clarify how to read Figure 5C and reconcile it with the text.

reviews.assessment: Well-written paper whose aims are clear; several technical corrections and clarifications are needed before publication.

comments.issue: A typo capitalises 'ARE' in the sentence on page 6, line 116.

comments.issue: Page 7, line 163 refers to a relationship without giving its exact equation number.

comments.issue: The number of samples and polynomial degree per method appear only in the figure caption, and the polynomials, quadrature rules and nonintrusive evaluation algorithm are not specified.
comments.request: Report these numerical details in the main text.

comments.issue: The number of samples M and the quadrature rule used for the test on page 17, line 343 are not stated.

comments.issue: The claim that gPC is rarely used in ecology and only in its intrusive form is contradicted by nonintrusive gPC applications in disease ecology.

editor_summary: Both reviewers appreciated the manuscript's overall nature and scope but identified a number of concerns and suggestions for improvement.

general and appropriate for Ecology Letters
well written abstract that pulled me in

comments.issue: Structure is poor; key components reappear across multiple sections, forcing readers to assemble the threads.

comments.quote: the structure of this manuscript could be improved. The various components of this manuscript (e.g., what the GRH is, what GRH models require, violations of assumptions related to nutrient limitation, etc.) seem to appear in multiple sections.

comments.issue: Terms (GRH/GRR, biological/ecological stoichiometry, assumption/breaker) are switched and used loosely.
