title: Seasonal patterns of dietary partitioning in vertebrates

study.system: five Tetrahymena ciliate species; microcosm dispersal assays

editor_summary: Both reviewers found the study highly interesting but raised design and interpretation concerns reaching the core: justify species choice, explain statistics, address phenotypic versus dispersal plasticity and maladaptive dispersal.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, well-written study; experimental and analytical details need clarification and justification.

comments.issue: Unclear to what extent species or genotypes evolved different degrees of dispersal plasticity and why.
comments.request: Clarify reasons to expect evolved differences among species and genotypes.
comments.quote: it is unclear to what extent the different species or genotypes may have evolved different degrees of dispersal plasticity and why

comments.issue: Explanation for frequent maladaptive dispersal away from high-fitness patches seems ad hoc.
comments.request: Provide a better-supported explanation for maladaptive dispersal.
comments.quote: The explanation regarding spatiotemporal variation seems a little ad hoc

comments.issue: Disputes the claim that predictable environmental fluctuations favour dispersal plasticity.
comments.request: Reconsider the claim about predictable environments and plasticity evolution.
comments.quote: I would disagree with the statement that dispersal plasticity is expected to evolve when environments fluctuate predictably

comments.issue: Rapid environmental change and reduced cue reliability should be considered for maladaptive dispersal.
comments.request: Consider these mechanisms when discussing maladaptive dispersal.
comments.quote: It seems like rapid environmental changes due to anthropogenic factors could result in maladaptive dispersal

comments.issue: Phenotypic plasticity is ignored as an alternative way of coping with environmental variation.
comments.request: Bring up phenotypic plasticity in the introduction and discuss its association with dispersal plasticity.
comments.quote: In addition to dispersal, another major way in which organisms cope with environmental variation is phenotypic plasticity, and this aspect has been largely ignored in this study.

comments.issue: Only three replicates per genotype-environment combination; sample size at that level is modest.
comments.request: Acknowledge and address the limited replication per genotype.
comments.quote: For each genotype and environmental factor combination, however, the sample size is very modest with just three replicates.

comments.issue: No a priori expectations for species differences; rationale for choosing these species is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the rationale for species choice based on ecological or evolutionary differences.
comments.quote: It is unclear, however, whether the authors held any a priori expectations regarding differences among species.

comments.issue: Species should be a random factor and genotype a nested factor in the models.
comments.request: Include species as a random factor and genotype nested within species.
comments.quote: Otherwise, ‘species’ should be included as a random factor in the models, as well as genotype, which should be included as a nested factor within species.

comments.issue: Homogeneous two-patch microcosms may not represent an appropriate measure of adaptive dispersal.
comments.request: Justify why this procedure measures adaptive dispersal or habitat choice.
comments.quote: If the two patches being offered in each assay were homogeneous, the authors should justify better why they consider that this procedure represents an appropriate measure of adaptive dispersal or habitat choice.

comments.issue: Sudden transfer from stock conditions may affect cells beyond triggering dispersal.
comments.request: Explain how the sudden environmental modification may have affected cells.
comments.quote: it would be important to explain how the authors think that a sudden modification of the environment

comments.issue: Differential mortality may bias dispersal estimates; survival is not incorporated into models.
comments.request: Report how mortality affected dispersal estimates and was modelled.
comments.quote: How did differential mortality affect the estimates of dispersal? How was that survival incorporated onto the models?

comments.issue: A supplementary figure depicting the experimental design would aid visualisation.
comments.request: Add a supplementary figure of the experimental design.
comments.quote: Perhaps a supplementary figure depicting the experimental design would help visualising it.

comments.issue: Dispersal patterns may reflect overall environmental effects on metabolic activity and motility.
comments.request: Test or discuss whether activity changes explain the dispersal results.
comments.quote: could it be that at warmer temperatures cells simply moved faster and more often?

reviews.assessment: Well-written with clear results; asks clarifications on statistics and the dispersal plasticity measure.

comments.issue: Signed slope may not measure dispersal plasticity magnitude; absolute values may be more appropriate.
comments.request: Consider using absolute slope values and clarify the F-statistic analysis.
comments.quote: would taking the absolute values of these slopes not be a more appropriate measure to identify whether more dispersal plasticity is found with higher fitness sensitivity?

comments.issue: Salinity levels are all above standard while other gradients span below and above, possibly driving results.
comments.request: Discuss whether gradient-level asymmetry explains the salinity results.
comments.quote: Both temperature and nutrient gradient seem to be one value below and above the standard conditions, while for salinity both values are above a standard condition.

comments.issue: Phrase when environmental gradients impact fitness more is vague about the comparison.
comments.request: Clarify more than what.
comments.quote: when environmental gradients impact fitness more”, more than what?

comments.issue: Unclear whether analyses were done per genotype or in a full model across species.
comments.request: Explain in detail how these analyses were performed.
comments.quote: For me it was unclear whether these analyses were done for each genotype separately, or by taking out the subcomponents from a full model taking all species into account.

comments.issue: Unclear whether expected fitness is observed growth rates or model-estimated growth rates.
comments.request: Define what expected fitness refers to.
comments.quote: Is the expected fitness the population growth rates that were calculated previously, or are it the estimated growth rates from a statistical model

comments.issue: How the variation of dispersal rate along expected fitness was evaluated is unclear.
comments.request: Explain how this analysis was performed.
comments.quote: Similarly, I was unsure how evaluating the variation of dispersal rate along expected fitness was done.

comments.issue: Environmental variability experienced during the species evolutionary history is not addressed.
comments.request: Provide information on past environmental variability to broaden the results.
comments.quote: Is there any information available on the environmental variability these species have experienced during their evolutionary history?

comments.issue: Dispersal ability linked to cell shape may explain species differences in dispersal plasticity.
comments.request: Consider cell morphology as an alternative driver of dispersal plasticity.
comments.quote: But is this not because dispersal ability of ciliates is often related to the cell shape, with more elongated individuals having a faster swimming speed and hence more dispersal ability?

comments.issue: Dispersal-rate response may be linked to changes in cell morphology.
comments.request: Assess how much of the response is linked to cell morphology.
comments.quote: I wonder how much of this response in dispersal rate is also linked with changes in cell morphology.

comments.issue: Viability-range differences between gradients may explain larger salinity differences.
comments.request: Assess whether viability-range variation explains the salinity results.
comments.quote: But I wonder if the viability range for temperature was larger than for salinity, and whether there was a higher variation in this viability range for salinity.

title: Dispersal plasticity driven by variation in fitness across species and environmental gradients

study.system: African barbets; continental song, morphology and environmental data

editor_summary: Editor says all three reviewers are excited but raise serious statistical and framing issues; new analyses, including path analysis and direct temperature/radiation variables, are needed before a major revision can be considered.

reviews.assessment: Sees high scientific merit but raises serious statistical concerns, especially proxy variables, model inconsistencies and predictor collinearity.
strengths: enormous data collection effort across Sub-Saharan Africa

comments.issue: Temperature and solar radiation were not tested directly; latitude and elevation are poor proxies with high spatial heterogeneity.
comments.request: Model temperature and radiation directly, since these data should be available.
comments.quote: Why authors did not test for these relationships directly? Rather than temperature/solar radiation, authors used indirect proxies for them – latitude and elevation.

comments.issue: Observer ID is a random effect for body size models but a fixed factor for beak size models.
comments.request: Justify or harmonise the treatment of observer ID across models.
comments.quote: Why was observer ID included as a cross random effect in models with body size as response variable (L183) but as a fixed factor in models with beak size as response variable (L194)?

comments.issue: Song pitch is modelled per species while morphology is modelled jointly with species as fixed factors, precluding species interactions.
comments.request: Use a single model including species by latitude/elevation/vegetation interactions.
comments.quote: Why did you run separate models for each species (Table 2) in analyses regarding song pitch but you included species as fixed factors (and ran a single model for all species together) in analyses regarding morphological traits (Table 1).

comments.issue: Vegetation variables (EVI, NDVI, LAI, VCF) are probably highly intercorrelated, risking spurious effect estimates.
comments.request: Select the most relevant variable, fit alternative models, or use PCA components.
comments.quote: I have suspicion that their mutual intercorrelation may be quite high and then you can get spurious effect estimates in your models.

comments.issue: The direct link between song pitch and body and beak size was not modelled.
comments.request: Model song pitch on morphological traits, potentially with path analyses.
comments.quote: But it is unclear to me why the authors did not model directly whether song pitch is correlated with body and beak size (either controlling or not controlling for effects of latitude/elevation/vegetation)?

comments.issue: Ratio variables such as beak-to-body size are problematic.
comments.request: Use beak size as the response with body size as a fixed predictor.
comments.quote: rather than using a ratio between beak and body size as a response variable, I would suggest using beak size as a response variable and body size as a fixed predictor to control for its confounding effects

comments.issue: It is unclear whether body size or song pitch were log-transformed, though log scales suit pitch perception.
comments.request: Report and justify the transformations used.
comments.quote: Was body size or song pitch log-transformed? For example, for song pitch, log-transformation is recommended because logarithmic (i.e., ratio) scales of song pitch conform to how animals perceive and modulate sound frequency

comments.issue: The abstract should say that Allen's rule applies to body and appendage size, not body size per se.
comments.request: Revise the abstract sentence to include appendage size.
comments.quote: Because Allen’s rule is not working with body size per se (although body size and appendage size might be correlated).

comments.issue: The abstract statement about Bergmann's rule effects is too general.
comments.request: State specifically what was found.
comments.quote: Can you be more specific what you have actually found, here?

comments.issue: The heat dissipation framing on lines 7-10 ignores metabolic sustainability.
comments.request: Acknowledge other physiological processes.
comments.quote: L7-10 – this is not exclusively about heat dissipation. This is also about sustainability of metabolic processes etc.

comments.issue: Several line-level copy edits (word choice, commas and phrasing).
comments.quote: L37 – I suggest deleting “important in ecology and evolution”.

comments.issue: The largest study linking body size and song pitch in passerines is not cited.
comments.request: Cite Mikula et al. 2021 Ecology Letters (also at line 281).
comments.quote: L48 – perhaps, it would be good to cite here also Mikula et al. (2021), Ecol. Lett.

comments.issue: The acoustic adaptation hypothesis is not explained.
comments.request: Briefly define the hypothesis and Mikula et al.'s habitat-song test.
comments.quote: it would be good at least briefly explaining what is acoustic adaptation hypothesis or that Mikula et al. study actually tested for association between habitat type and song pitch

comments.issue: How environmental variables were assigned to morphological and song data is not described.
comments.request: Explain georeferencing of recordings and environmental extraction.
comments.quote: Please, be more specific on how environmental variables were assigned to your morpho and song data. Was each song recording georeferenced?

comments.issue: It appears only PC1 was used in all analyses, but this is not stated.
comments.request: State explicitly how many principal components were used.
comments.quote: did you use only PC1 in all analyses? It seems so. Please, write this directly to the text.

comments.issue: The correlation among vegetation characteristics is unknown and may be high.
comments.request: Report the correlations between vegetation variables.
comments.quote: What is the level of correlation between these variables? I am a bit concerned that mutual intercorrelation between vegetation characteristics can be quite high.

comments.issue: The standardisation procedure for variables is not described.
comments.request: Describe how variables were standardised.
comments.quote: How were variables standardized? E.g. by scale function?

comments.issue: Collinearity was apparently checked only between latitude and other predictors.
comments.request: Report collinearity among all predictor variables.
comments.quote: can you provide details on collinearity between all predictor variables? It seems that you tested only for collinearity between latitude and other predictors.

comments.issue: A new package for partitioning R2 in GLMMs is available but unused.
comments.request: Consider partR2 for variance partitioning.
comments.quote: there was recently published a new R package that can partition R2 in GLMMs

comments.issue: How phylogenetic signal was estimated and whether uncertainty was quantified is unclear.
comments.request: Describe the estimation approach and any bootstrapping.
comments.quote: How was the phylogenetic signal estimated? Using species-specific values or did you use individual bird values?

comments.issue: Only one random phylogenetic tree appears to have been used.
comments.request: Download at least 50 BirdTree trees and build a consensus or maximum credibility tree.
comments.quote: Did you download just one random tree for this analysis? Which backbone – Hackett or Ericsson?

comments.issue: Lines 239-240 do not say which variable or relationship differs, in what direction, or where results are shown.
comments.request: Specify the differences and link the relevant figure or table.
comments.quote: differences in what variable/relationship? And in what direction? Where we can find these results (please, add link to figure or table)?

comments.issue: The name P. chrysopus is used inconsistently across the text.
comments.request: Use only P. chrysopus consistently (lines 243, 255 and beyond).
comments.quote: L255 – this information was already provided in methods. Please, use only P. chrysopus here and in the following text.

comments.issue: Bergmann's and Allen's rules concern morphology only and make no direct predictions for song pitch.
comments.request: Avoid phrasing results as contradicting or confirming rule predictions for song.
comments.quote: Both Bergman’s and Allen’s rules are exclusively focused on morphological traits variation and they do not propose direct predictions for song pitch.

comments.issue: The claim that the beak cannot act as a resonator is questioned, since a gap may exist between maxilla and mandible.
comments.request: Address the resonator possibility.
comments.quote: Isn’t there at least a small space between maxilla and mandible in singing tinkerbirds? If yes, then the beak can work as a resonator.

comments.issue: Differences from Mikula et al. may reflect their interspecific versus the paper's intraspecific focus.
comments.request: Compare the two studies' levels of variation in the discussion.
comments.quote: The main difference between the results of Mikula et al. and yours could be that Mikula et al. focused on INTERspecific variation in song pitch, whether you explored INTRAspecific variation in song pitch.

comments.issue: Only three species were effectively analysed, giving little power to detect phylogenetic signal.
comments.request: Acknowledge the low interspecific sample size.
comments.quote: Another reason may be that you had (effectively) only 3 species in your dataset. So, interspecific variation and effective sample size may be simply too low to detect any meaningful phylogenetic signal.

comments.issue: The abbreviation AAH is used without definition.
comments.request: Define AAH at first use or spell it out.
comments.quote: “AAH” – this abbreviation has not defined the text above.

comments.issue: The abbreviation “Lmg” in Tables 1-2 is not explained.
comments.request: Define Lmg.
comments.quote: Table 1-2 – “Lmg” - what does this abbreviation mean?

comments.issue: The HBW illustration credit in Fig. 2 is not correctly stated.
comments.request: Use the standard permission statement from Lynx Edicions.
comments.quote: a correct reference for illustration from HBW should be something like this “Illustrations reproduced by permission of Lynx Edicions”

comments.issue: Fig. 3 has wrong panel letters, and the same problem occurs in Fig. 4.
comments.request: Correct the panel labelling.
comments.quote: Fig. 3 – there are mistakes in letter labelling – there should be “k” and “l” labels instead of “m” and “n”.

comments.issue: It is unclear which method was used for the non-linear rightmost panel of Fig. 4.
comments.request: Report the method used and give more methods detail.
comments.quote: Which method (e.g. GAM) was used to model the relationship between song frequency and latitude in the rightmost panel?

comments.issue: Full model results are not provided in the supplemental methods.
comments.request: Provide the full model results.
comments.quote: 1. Supplemental methods – can, you, please, provide full models results here?

comments.issue: There is no data accessibility statement and primary data availability is unclear.
comments.request: Add a data accessibility statement and provide the primary data.
comments.quote: Will authors provide primary data which were used in analyses? I was looking for a data accessibility statement in the manuscript but I did not find it.

reviews.assessment: Enthusiastic with essentially no major complaints; requests PCA detail and more discussion of song identity and acoustic adaptation.
strengths: one of the most interesting papers read recently
excellent choice of study birds that do not learn songs

comments.issue: PCA diagnostics such as KMO and Bartlett's sphericity test are not reported.
comments.request: Add these values to Table S3.
comments.quote: I suggest adding more information about Principal Component Analyses. What was the KMO and Bartlett's sphericity test?

comments.issue: The R packages used to conduct the PCA are not stated, affecting repeatability.
comments.request: State which packages and versions were used for the PCA.
comments.quote: it would be great to add in which R packages did you conduct PCA as different packages gave slightly different results

comments.issue: The role of individual identity in songs and the densities of congeners are not discussed as drivers of song differences.
comments.request: Discuss whether congener and own-species densities shape song differentiation.
comments.quote: Do you think that differences between individuals could be potentially shaped not only because of the number of competing congeneric species but also by densities of the own and congeners?

comments.issue: General environmental variables may miss microhabitats, so Mikula et al.'s lack of AAH support should not be overinterpreted.
comments.request: Discuss the contribution to the acoustic adaptation hypothesis and compare learning with non-learning taxa.
comments.quote: One of the possible explanations is that having in analyses only a general information about the environment (like the EVI or NDVI) could be simply not enough to catch micro-habitats variation which could affect singing.

reviews.assessment: Finds the study an enjoyable, thorough contribution, with only minor fixes apart from inaccessible R code and incomplete vocal data.
strengths: good read and fascinating contribution to continent-level biogeography

comments.issue: The R code supposed to be on Dryad could not be accessed for review.
comments.request: Ensure the R code is accessible on Dryad.
comments.quote: with the major caveat that I was unable to find a way to access the R codes that are supposed to be on Dryad

comments.issue: Not all vocal data are on figshare and specimen and recording lists may not be included.
comments.request: Upload the remaining vocal data and complete lists of specimens and recordings.
comments.quote: it seems not all are. Is there a reason for not uploading the rest of the vocal data?

comments.issue: The NHM acronym is ambiguous and should be verified.
comments.request: Check whether NHMUK is the correct museum abbreviation.
comments.quote: Is this the British Natural History Museum or the Natural History Museum of the United Kingdom? Please verify the name, as I often see it listed as NHMUK in contemporary manuscripts.

comments.issue: Fig. S1 plots multiple species at top without making clear what is shown.
comments.request: Clarify what is being plotted.
comments.quote: Fig S1 shows multiple species at top; please make it more clear what exactly is being plotted.

comments.issue: Several line-level copy edits and formatting fixes throughout.
comments.quote: Table 1: Usually R in R^2 is italicized; check and see whether it should be.

comments.issue: Methods are not elaborated at line 116 even at a basic level.
comments.request: Elaborate on the methods there if length permits.
comments.quote: 116: If possible, elaborate on these methods a little here, even if just the basics.

comments.issue: No Macaulay recordings were used, without explanation.
comments.request: Explain why Macaulay recordings were excluded.
comments.quote: 127: No Macaulay recordings? Is there a reason for this?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether a table of all recordings exists and where it is referenced.
comments.request: Reference the table of recordings.
comments.quote: 130: is there a table of all recordings used? If so please reference here.

comments.issue: The name “chrysopus” is used as if de novo and inconsistently.
comments.request: Use consistent notation such as P. ‘chrysopus’ throughout (lines 142, 243, 255, 306).
comments.quote: 142: Is chrysopus a combination of the names? Clarify, to make it clear this isn't a de novo name

comments.issue: Environmental rasters may be overspecific relative to recording locations.
comments.request: Explain any steps taken to mitigate overspecifity.
comments.quote: 163: some of these rasters are extremely specific. Were any steps taken to mitigate overspecifity?

comments.issue: The percentages mentioned at line 313 are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify what the percentages refer to.
comments.quote: 313: What exactly are these percents? Unclear.

comments.issue: The abbreviation AAH is never defined.
comments.request: Define AAH at first use.
comments.quote: 377: AAH is never defined.

comments.issue: Figure 1 colours may not be suitable for colourblind readers.
comments.request: Use a colourblind-friendly scheme.
comments.quote: Figure 1: Please double check your color scheme and ensure this is suitable for all readers (e.g., suitable for colorblindness etc.).

comments.issue: Figure 2 uses red versus green points that are indistinguishable to some readers.
comments.request: Use a colourblind-friendly scheme with larger points and clearer background.
comments.quote: Figure 2: Please pick a colorblind friendly way to show the data; red vs. green points will be indistinguishable to some.

comments.issue: Figure 4 shows Loess fits although other analyses are linear.
comments.request: Explain why Loess fits were used.
comments.quote: Figure 4: Why are Loess fits shown here when everything else is linear?

title: Continent‐wide patterns of song variation predicted by classical rules of biogeography

study.system: freshwater phytoplankton communities; outdoor mesocosms and R* traits

editor_summary: Topic of wide interest, well executed and exceptionally well placed in context; reviewers provide clarifying points, especially that PCA is not suited for inferences about tradeoffs.

reviews.assessment: Excellent, well-framed study; asks to reconsider prediction 2, replace PCA for tradeoffs, and discuss grazing-defense tradeoffs.
strengths: rare test of R* theory with diverse natural communities
measures multiple traits on coexisting competitors

comments.issue: It is not clear that balanced N:P supply should select for opportunists rather than balanced nutrient competitors.
comments.request: Clarify or revise the rationale for prediction 2.
comments.quote: It’s not clear to me that balanced N:P supply (Redfield) should select for opportunists (prediciton #2).

comments.issue: PCA biplots only show two dimensions and are not suited to testing trait tradeoffs.
comments.request: Use partial correlations or similar analyses, and consider log-transforming traits.
comments.quote: PCA is a good analysis for visualizing the different trait measurements, but maybe not the best for testing tradeoffs.

comments.issue: Filtering out grazers may mean the species pool is dominated by well-defended, slow-growing species, hiding resource tradeoffs.
comments.request: Discuss the competition-defense tradeoff and grazing exclusion in the discussion.
comments.quote: I think the discussion would benefit from a bit more consideration of the effect of filtering out grazers < 100 µm.

reviews.assessment: Much to like, but the resource-limitation treatments and R* interpretation raise several methodological concerns.
strengths: thoughtful connections between theory and empirics

comments.issue: Treatment names such as N-Lim imply a single limiting resource, but actual limitation depends on species R* values.
comments.request: Rename or reframe treatments to reflect actual resource limitation.
comments.quote: Somehow the naming of the resource treatment levels (“N-Lim” etc.) implies that the balanced supply causes all resources to limit growth to a similar extent.

comments.issue: Adjusting resource concentrations weekly breaks the resource-consumption feedback that underpins R* theory.
comments.request: Justify or reconsider controlling concentrations rather than supply rates.
comments.quote: I’m worried that this feedback was broken, thus disturbing interactions within and between species, by adjusting resource levels in the system whilst the populations are growing.

comments.issue: The mesocosm dilution rate mentioned at L226-227 is not described, though it is needed to interpret the results.
comments.request: Report the dilution rate in the mesocosm methods.
comments.quote: I was not able to find this back in the section of the mesocosm experiment; I think it’s really important to have this info to permit a proper interpretation of the results.

comments.issue: R* for light differs from nutrient R* because light is not well mixed; whether the measured I* matches Huisman and Weissing's concept is unclear.
comments.request: Compare the I* measurement with Huisman and Weissing (1994) and justify the name.
comments.quote: I wonder how the measurement of I* in the present paper resembles the one proposed by Huisman and Weissing, and if it is the best approach to call it I* althogether.

comments.issue: Figure 4a is cited at L294 but does not appear to exist.
comments.request: Check and correct the Figure 4a reference.
comments.quote: L294: I don’t see a Fig4”a”. L279-299: Prediction 2 is explicitly about the balanced treatment.

comments.issue: Prediction 2 concerns the balanced treatment; the mumax-delta correlation is not evaluated in the limiting treatments.
comments.request: Evaluate the mumax-delta correlation in the other treatments.
comments.quote: Would it be possible to evaluate correlation between mumax and delta for these other treatments?

comments.issue: Why D. armatus would have a greater SGV than other species is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the expected species difference in SGV.
comments.quote: Why would this species have a greater SGV than the others?

comments.issue: Evenness also dropped in the balanced treatment, weakening its use to explain a particular result.
comments.request: Reconcile the evenness pattern with the interpretation.
comments.quote: Unless I’m mistaken I think that evenness also dropped in the balanced treatment.

comments.issue: The upper row of Figure 1 introduces concepts not used or explained in the manuscript.
comments.request: Consider removing the upper row of Figure 1.
comments.quote: Is the upper row really needed? I feel it introduces concepts that are not used in the manuscript, and which are not really explained either.

comments.issue: Figure 2 shows all four replicates without clear justification.
comments.request: Justify or reduce the replicate panels in Figure 2.
comments.quote: Fig2: Why show all 4 replicates? SI, section D (Monod curves): Some of these curves are not the best fit to the data.

comments.issue: Some Monod curves in SI section D fit poorly; sensitivity to dropping these data is unknown.
comments.request: Test sensitivity of results to dropping poorly fitted points or strains.
comments.quote: Some of these curves are not the best fit to the data. How sensitive are the results to dropping those data points/strains?

title: Ecology and evolution of competitive trait variation in natural phytoplankton communities under selection

study.system: farmland biodiversity; 123 landscapes with structural equation models

editor_summary: Importance and novelty recognized, but methodological and analytical concerns need attention, and citation practices should be more equitable (redundant citations, credit for R packages).

reviews.assessment: Well-designed and well-written study with an important message; mostly needs more detail on explanatory variables.

comments.issue: Details of explanatory variables are sparse; which variables were used and how composition/configuration were computed is unclear.
comments.request: Describe explanatory variables, metrics and software.
comments.quote: the manuscript is quite light on the details of the data for the explanatory variables, and therefore it is necessary to dig into the supplementary information to get an idea of data sources/spatial information etc.

comments.issue: The manuscript contains many long paragraphs.
comments.request: Break up long paragraphs.
comments.quote: the manuscript contains a lot of long paragraphs, which I would suggest the authors take a look at and break down

comments.issue: The exact source of figures on the website is unclear.
comments.request: Specify the data source location.
comments.quote: It is not clear where on the site (www.agrarbericht.ch) the figures come from - need to be more specific.

comments.issue: The L109 data lacks description of resolution and content.
comments.request: Describe the data's resolution and content.
comments.quote: L109: More information needed about this data - spatial resolution, what it is measuring etc.

comments.issue: The multi-stage unequal probability selection is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the selection procedure.
comments.quote: L118: Explain the multi-stage unequal probability selection

comments.issue: The time point and randomness of selection at L119 are unclear.
comments.request: Specify the time point and selection.
comments.quote: L119: At which time point? Was this randomly selected? If so, how.

comments.issue: Species categorization needs documentation, including which species fall in each category.
comments.request: Document species categories and list them in a supplement.
comments.quote: Need more information about how species were categorised

comments.issue: The link at L150 is broken.
comments.request: Fix the link.
comments.quote: L150: This link is broken.

comments.issue: Line-level wording edits (L154 'birds'; L212 increase vs change composition/configuration; L275 'prove').
comments.quote: L212: I'm not sure you can necessarily increase landscape composition or configuration.

comments.issue: Figure 1 could indicate which explanatory variables are considered.
comments.request: Add explanatory variables to Figure 1.
comments.quote: I wonder if at this stage you can add in a little more about the explanatory variables (e.g. which abiotic conditions, which land-use/EFA types, measures of land-use intensity)?

reviews.assessment: Nicely written and relevant, but the SEM design does not support the main conclusions about EFA and biodiversity.

comments.issue: The SEM only measures abiotic-factor effects; EFA is a mediator, so EFA-biodiversity conclusions are not supported.
comments.request: Rebuild SEM with EFA uptake as exogenous.
comments.quote: The causal pathway has been built in a way that it only measures the direct and indirect effects of abiotic factors. Any conclusion linking EFA and biodiversity are irrelevant in this context

comments.issue: The LUI-to-composition causation is questionable: same dataset and unknown direction.
comments.request: Reconsider the causal direction or label as correlation.
comments.quote: some drivers, in terms of causation, are questionable. For example, the causation between mean LUI at the landscape scale and landscape composition.

comments.issue: Gámez-Virués et al. 2015 is not about beta-diversity and is an inappropriate reference.
comments.request: Use an appropriate reference.
comments.quote: the study from Gámez-Virués et al. 2015 is not about beta-diversity but focusses on the effect of local management and landscape heterogeneity on alpha diversity in grasslands

comments.issue: 'Traits act as filters' confuses the ecological filtering concept; the environment filters species by traits.
comments.request: Correct the ecological filtering concept.
comments.quote: I think the authors made a confusion with what ecological filtering is about. The environment can filter species based on their traits

comments.issue: The EFA example does not well illustrate contrasting alpha and gamma responses.
comments.request: Explain the mechanisms for contrasting alpha/gamma responses.
comments.quote: I’m not sure the example of EFA has been well handled to illustrate a potential negative effect of management on gamma diversity while increasing alpha diversity

comments.issue: Line-level wording edits (L172 'wherefore' is dated; L344 needs rewording).
comments.quote: L 172: “wherefore” is a bit dated

comments.issue: Spillover from non-farmland to farmland should be detectable since non-farmland types were included.
comments.request: Clarify the spillover interpretation.
comments.quote: Wouldn’t you detect such a spillover effect from non-farmland to farmland, since the vegetation types included all non-farmland vegetation types too?

reviews.assessment: Nice dataset with new insights on direct and indirect effects, but several major clarifications on causation, context and diversity definitions.
strengths: new insights from revealing direct and indirect effects

comments.issue: Negative correlations with favourable abiotic conditions are described as effects; they should be framed as correlations.
comments.request: Present as correlation and discuss causes.
comments.quote: Could we just call it a negative correlation and discuss the causes?

comments.issue: EFA conservation strategies parallel earlier mosaic strategies that are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss parallels with earlier mosaic strategies.
comments.quote: The proposed conservation methods using diverse EFAs are in parallel with earlier proposed strategies for conservation such as “management mosaics” and “inter-cropping mosaics” in agriculture practice

comments.issue: Evenness is not analysed despite abundance data being available.
comments.request: Analyse evenness alongside richness.
comments.quote: since you have the abundance data, could you also measure evenness and discussed the results in conjunction with richness

comments.issue: Assignment of the three diversity levels is scale dependent and beta-diversity is barely addressed.
comments.request: Justify the scale definition and report beta-diversity values.
comments.quote: A related issue is how to define the three levels of diversity as assigning the three levels of diversity itself is scale dependent.

comments.issue: The Introduction's long paragraphs contain too many general statements.
comments.request: Cut general statements from the Introduction.
comments.quote: The Introduction especially those long paragraphs could be shortened by removing some very general statements

comments.issue: No local historical data on farmland biodiversity decline are shown.
comments.request: Add local historical diversity data.
comments.quote: Any actual data showing the decline in farmland biodiversity in the study area?

comments.issue: Invasive or exotic species in the study area are not considered.
comments.request: Report invasive/exotic species.
comments.quote: Any invasive or exotic species in the study area especially under intensive land use?

comments.issue: Cross-taxon richness relationships at each diversity level are not reported.
comments.request: Report cross-taxon richness relationships.
comments.quote: How were plant, butterfly and bird species richness measures related to each other at each diversity level?

comments.issue: The meaning of 'values' at page 158 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify what 'values' means.
comments.quote: P. 158, what “values” – richness?

title: Disentangling direct and indirect drivers of farmland biodiversity at landscape scale

study.system: 351 empirical food webs; human disturbance gradients

editor_summary: Both reviewers pointed out the study's importance but raised major concerns preventing publication; new analyses, such as R1's Comment 10 simulation suggestion, may strengthen the study.

reviews.assessment: Well-written with impressive spatial coverage, but the transposition of network theory to food webs rests on unsupported assumptions.
strengths: impressive spatial coverage of food webs

comments.issue: Assumption that undisturbed food webs are scale-free contradicts published findings.
comments.request: Better justify and support this assumption.
comments.quote: this assumption is far to be proven, studies rather demonstrated that the degree distribution of food webs do not fulfil the characteristics of random (Dunne et al. 2002) or scale-free networks

comments.issue: Assumption that random and targeted disturbances never co-occur cannot be validated by the disturbance metric.
comments.request: Validate this assumption or discuss the consequences.
comments.quote: the method used to assess the level of disturbances a given food web is experiencing does not allow to validate this assumption

comments.issue: Assumption that high-intensity human disturbances target the most connected species lacks literature support.
comments.request: Provide references supporting this assumption.
comments.quote: this assumption is not supported by sufficient references to the literature that indeed show that high-levels disturbances do not affect all species in a similar way but mainly highly connected species

comments.issue: Resolution and aggregation level of the empirical food webs are not described.
comments.request: Report richness, link density, connectance and taxonomic resolution.
comments.quote: Please provide information on the resolution of the empirical food webs.

comments.issue: Binning data to maximise fit between topology distance and human pressure may guarantee a significant relationship.
comments.request: Show the unaggregated relationship with regression statistics.
comments.quote: It seems that using this method will necessarily lead to a significant relationship between two variables.

comments.issue: Number of food webs per bin varies and is not reported.
comments.request: Add a supplementary table with bin counts.
comments.quote: It would be useful to provide a Supplementary Table with the number of food webs within the bins displayed in Figure 3.

comments.issue: Average degree and distances to pure distributions per food web and ecosystem are not reported.
comments.request: Add a supplementary table with these values.
comments.quote: It would also be useful to provide a Supplementary Table with the average degree, the distances between pure uniform, random and scale free degree distributions for each food web

comments.issue: Diverse human activities are classified as targeted disturbances without justification.
comments.request: Justify why these disturbances are targeted rather than affecting all species.
comments.quote: it is hard to see why the authors think these disturbances can be defined as targeted disturbances, that would impact specific species rather than all species

comments.issue: Definitions of degree distributions, especially the arbitrary uniform distribution, lack references; only three topologies are assumed.
comments.request: Provide references and acknowledge other degree distributions.
comments.quote: please provide references to the definitions of the degree distributions you use, especially for the definition of uniform distributions, which seem quite arbitrary

comments.issue: Inequations on p. 10, l. 8 did not display correctly.
comments.request: Fix the equation formatting.
comments.quote: p. 10, l.8: the inequations did not display correctly.

comments.issue: Distance to pure topology exceeds 1 (1.25) in Figure 3, which should be impossible.
comments.request: Explain or correct the distance metric.
comments.quote: the distance to pure topology (x-axis) goes beyond 1 with value of 1.25, how is it possible according to the methodology?

comments.issue: Scale-free webs require highly connected generalists, not specialists, so the specialist sentence misstates the theory.
comments.request: Correct this interpretation.
comments.quote: Food webs must have few highly connected species to be scale-free (i.e. keystone generalists), not specialists.

comments.issue: Disturbance types are inferred from impact metrics rather than simulated random or targeted removals.
comments.request: Simulate random and targeted disturbances on empirical webs and compare with Fig. 3.
comments.quote: the authors could additionally test Albert et al. (2000) results using simulations of disturbances rather than using metrics of disturbance impact

reviews.assessment: Well-designed and well-written study with clearly stated hypotheses and no major flaws; a few contextual and methodological points remain.
strengths: novel use of 351 empirical food webs
potential to inspire new theoretical work

comments.issue: Previous work suggests skewed degree distributions fit exponential better than power law, but this choice is not justified.
comments.request: Justify the use of a power law rather than an exponential distribution.
comments.quote: It may strengthen the paper to explicitly justify why they use a power law instead of an exponential distribution in their analysis

comments.issue: Last introduction paragraph is technical and introduces too many things.
comments.request: Move some of this material to the methods.
comments.quote: The last paragraph of the introduction is quite technical and introduces a lot of different things, maybe some of it could be moved to the methods section.

comments.issue: Food web sampling is biased towards Europe and North America, potentially affecting interpretation.
comments.request: Discuss how this regional heterogeneity impacts the results.
comments.quote: there is still a bias towards certain regions (and thus biomes, and possibly type of human impact)

comments.issue: The uniform distribution appears in the methods without hypotheses about how it emerges.
comments.request: Add hypotheses for the uniform distribution in the introduction.
comments.quote: There are hypotheses about how power law and random distributions could be selected by respectively random and targeted disturbances but none about how uniform distributions could emerge.

comments.issue: Two in-text equations on p. 10 render only as squared symbols.
comments.request: Fix the equation rendering.
comments.quote: I was not able to see the 2 in-text equations, only squared symbol

comments.issue: Distance to uniform topology may classify diverse distributions (e.g. bimodal) as uniform, hiding variation.
comments.request: Discuss this limitation of the metric.
comments.quote: based on the way the distance to pure topology is calculated, there are more ways to be “uniform” than to be Gaussian or scale free

comments.issue: Discussion does not engage with literature on degree distribution and resilience to extinctions.
comments.request: Build hypotheses about mechanisms from this literature.
comments.quote: the link between degree distribution and resilience to extinctions. There have been many papers investigating the dynamical consequences of targeted VS random removal on food web persistence and topology.

comments.issue: Discussion ignores how sampling methods and node aggregation may generate topological patterns.
comments.request: Discuss the link between sampling methods and degree distribution.
comments.quote: the link between food web sampling methods and degree distribution, because it is possible that certain sampling methods or assembly choices (aggregation of nodes for example) could generate particular topological patterns

comments.issue: Covariance among food web topology descriptors is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss descriptor covariance, citing Vermaat, Dunne and Gilbert 2009.
comments.quote: the covariance between descriptors of food web topology, as we now that many of these descriptors co-vary (see, for example, Vermaat, Dunne and Gilbert, 2009)

comments.issue: Human disturbance data come from different sources for terrestrial and marine systems, potentially biasing results.
comments.request: Discuss this heterogeneity.
comments.quote: I would also like to see a discussion about the heterogeneity of human disturbance data as they come from distinct sources for terrestrial and marine ecosystems.

title: Human disturbances affect the topology of food webs

study.system: freshwater organisms; warming and stressor experiment database

editor_summary: All three reviewers shared the editor's positive view but raised similar concerns about missing detail in the introduction, methods, results and discussion; the revision will require substantial effort.

reviews.assessment: Well-written, relevant synthesis, but the treatment of stressor asymmetry is too simplistic and context-dependencies are underexplored.
strengths: shows the additive null model is rarely most accurate

comments.issue: Stressor asymmetry is treated as binary via a 50% cutoff, so the degree of asymmetry is never investigated.
comments.request: Model asymmetry as a continuous scale or explore different cutoff values.
comments.quote: The stressors are either asymmetric or not, based on a cutoff value of one stressor exerting effects 50% larger than the other, but the degree of asymmetry is not investigated.

comments.issue: Context-dependencies such as organism type and taxonomy are not analysed despite their importance.
comments.request: Analyse responses by organism type and other available contexts.
comments.quote: It would be valuable to investigate how different organism types respond to the stressor treatments. This was shown to have notable effects in the previous meta-analysis

comments.issue: The expectation that stressors cause synergisms is wrong; antagonisms are expected to be more prevalent.
comments.request: Correct the stated expectation about synergisms.
comments.quote: however it seems that the expectation is actually that antagonisms will be more prevalent.

comments.issue: The IPCC sentence is written out unnecessarily fully.
comments.request: Shorten the IPCC sentence.
comments.quote: There is no need to write this out in full

comments.issue: Stressor magnitude should be focused on more explicitly throughout.
comments.request: Foreground stressor magnitude more explicitly.
comments.quote: Since stressor magnitude is important, it should be more explicity focused on throughout.

comments.issue: Results are not compared with similar studies in other ecosystem types.
comments.request: Compare with similar papers from other ecotypes in the discussion.
comments.quote: Can these results be compared to similar papers in other ecotypes in the discussion section?

comments.issue: 'Degree of asymmetry' is claimed but asymmetry is only a binary cutoff.
comments.request: Align the wording with the actual asymmetry measure.
comments.quote: “degree of asymmetry” is mentioned but asymmetry is just determined by a cutoff point.

comments.issue: Why the additive model is expected to yield this result is not stated or referenced.
comments.request: State why this expectation arises and cite its source.
comments.quote: State why you expect this and/or where this expectation came from.

comments.issue: The text says four main hypotheses but only three are presented.
comments.request: Fix the hypothesis count.
comments.quote: You have only three main hypotheses presented.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether both models are expected to perform best at the community level or whether it depends on community features.
comments.request: Clarify the H3 prediction.
comments.quote: Do you expect that both will perform best or that it will depend on some community feature?

comments.issue: 'Interacting' implies direct stressor interactions, which is not necessarily the case for co-occurring stressors.
comments.request: Replace 'interacting' with 'co-occurring'.
comments.quote: Replace “interacting” with “co-occurring” (or something similar) as interacting implies direct stressor interactions, which is not necessarily the case.

comments.issue: Food quantity appears to be a subset of nutrient level in the stressor typology.
comments.request: Clarify the stressor category definitions.
comments.quote: Food quantity is a subset of nutrient level, I would argue.

comments.issue: Salinity and salinisation are used inconsistently.
comments.request: Use consistent stressor terminology.
comments.quote: Inconsistent stressor terminology with salinity vs salinisation.

comments.issue: It is doubtful that response variables cannot be negative, since condition, growth and decomposition can be.
comments.request: Clarify the justification for the response-variable constraint.
comments.quote: I don’t think that any of the responses used should be able to be less than zero? How can condition, growth, or decomposition be negative?

comments.issue: Stressor types could be grouped by similarities in their results.
comments.request: Group similar stressor types, potentially in Figure 3.
comments.quote: Are there any broad groupings of stressor type that show similarities in their results?

comments.issue: Organism type and other factors such as organism size and community type are not taken into account.
comments.request: Include organism type and other context factors in the analyses.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to also take organism type and other important factors into account (organism size, population/community size, type of community, etc.).

comments.issue: The explanation of effect-size inversion is long and hard to follow.
comments.request: Shorten and clarify the explanation.
comments.quote: I find this explanation is a bit long and hard to follow.

comments.issue: Other models are grouped when reporting their 23% accuracy.
comments.request: Report each other model's percentage individually.
comments.quote: Ungroup other models and state their percentages individually.

comments.issue: More could be done to capture the uncaptured context-dependencies.
comments.request: Explore the context-dependencies further with the available data.
comments.quote: Is there more you can do to capture these context-dependencies?

comments.issue: 'Dominant' is used loosely where it does not mean statistical dominance.
comments.request: Avoid 'dominant' when not referring to 'dominance'.
comments.quote: “Dominant” is a word to avoid when it does not specifically refer to “dominance”.

comments.issue: Jackson et al. 2016 is reused as support although it shares much of the same data.
comments.request: Use a different or additional reference.
comments.quote: It would be better to use a different/additional reference here, as this paper uses much of the same data as Jackson et al. 2016.

comments.issue: The context-dependency paragraph does not exploit the data available to probe these effects.
comments.request: Probe the context-dependencies with the available data.
comments.quote: This paragraph discusses extensively context-dependencies which could likely be somewhat looked into with the data available.

comments.issue: Thirteen line-level copy edits across writing and equations (wording, hyphenation, italics, notation).
comments.quote: P4 L3: “Frequently used nulls”: Hyphenate “Frequently-used”.

comments.issue: The equation syntax does not match Schäfer and Piggot 2018, and the comparison to the control is not explained.
comments.request: Explain in the main text how the control comparison works for each null model.
comments.quote: I would appreciate a better explanation in the main text of how the comparison to the control works for each null model.

comments.issue: The 'within range' row of Table 1 is in the wrong position.
comments.request: Move the 'within range' row between 'Larger' and 'Smaller'.
comments.quote: Put the “within range” row between “Larger” and “Smaller” rows.

comments.issue: Table 1 is dense and might work better as a figure.
comments.request: Consider converting Table 1 into a figure.
comments.quote: Table 1 may be better as a figure, there is lots to digest that could work better visually.

comments.issue: Some text in Figure 1 overflows its containers.
comments.request: Fix the overflowing text in Figure 1.
comments.quote: There is some text that goes outside their containers in places

comments.issue: Figure 1 subplot labels b and c are ordered by column instead of row.
comments.request: Switch subplot labels b and c.
comments.quote: Typically subplot numbering goes by row rather than by column, so labels b and c should be switched.

comments.issue: Black letters are used in the Figure 1 vertical bars.
comments.request: Use white lettering in the vertical bars.
comments.quote: No need for black letters in the vertical bars, white lettering works well throughout.

comments.issue: S_A and S_B are not subscripted in Figure 1.
comments.request: Add subscripts for S_A and S_B in all Figure 1 subplots.
comments.quote: Subscript needed for $S_A$ and $S_B$ in all subplots of Figure 1.

comments.issue: Figure 1 mixes three conceptual panels with one empirical panel.
comments.request: Consider splitting Figure 1.
comments.quote: It is confusing to have a figure comprised of three parts example of how the null models work (a-c) and one part empirical results (d) - could it be split?

comments.issue: Effect sizes outside the null model range are not labelled as antagonisms or synergisms in the legends.
comments.request: Add antagonism/synergism terminology to the figure legends.
comments.quote: Effect sizes below/above the null models could be termed antagonisms/synergisms, which would be good to include in the figure legends.

comments.issue: Figures 2-4 split subplots a and b unnecessarily.
comments.request: Combine subplots a and b and add frequencies above the error bars.
comments.quote: Subplots a and b could be combined, including the frequency as numbers/percentages above the error bars.

comments.issue: Figure 3 does not include all secondary stressor types.
comments.request: Include all secondary stressor types in Figure 3.
comments.quote: Why does this not include all secondary stressor types?

comments.issue: The Figure 3b labels 'stressor_X asymmetric' and 'temperature asymmetric' are confusing because asymmetry is symmetric.
comments.request: Use clearer wording such as 'prevailing' or 'most intense'.
comments.quote: I suggest avoiding “dominant” so perhaps use “prevailing” or “most intense” or something similar.

comments.issue: Figure 4 omits populations within communities as a fourth category.
comments.request: Plot populations within communities as a fourth category.
comments.quote: A fourth category could be plotted, showing individual populations within a community (i.e. affected by heterospecifics).

reviews.assessment: Well-written and valuable synthesis, but the dominance model's distinctness and the pooling of undefined response variables raise doubts.
strengths: nice attempt to analyse multiple stressors

comments.issue: It is unclear what the dominance model means and how it differs from log response ratios and factorial models.
comments.request: Explain how the dominance model differs from established approaches.
comments.quote: So I’m unsure what is meant here by the dominance model. I see how the authors define it from Figure 1, but wouldn’t it be the same as telling you a single additive factor is what’s causing change?

comments.issue: Response variables are poorly defined and it is unclear whether they can all be placed on the same scale.
comments.request: Define the response variables and justify pooling them.
comments.quote: the response variables are not really well defined at all, and none of the figures really describe them

comments.issue: Response variable types are lumped together and never examined or mentioned in the figures.
comments.request: Analyse how different response variable types respond to the stressors.
comments.quote: Examining how different types of response variables respond to these stressors, and if certain ones categorize into different types of null models is really interesting.

comments.issue: The biological meaning of the three models is not interpreted before the results.
comments.request: Add biological interpretation of what the models mean.
comments.quote: I would like more biological interpretation of what the additive, multiplicative and dominance models mean in the lead up to the results.

comments.issue: The link between asymmetry and the null models is lost between introduction and results.
comments.request: Explain early on how the models predict asymmetry.
comments.quote: I think there needs to be more attention paid to the relationship between asymmetry and the different null models early on

comments.issue: Stressor asymmetry is not defined.
comments.request: Define stressor asymmetry.
comments.quote: Please define stressor asymmetry. It’s not clear from the current version what you mean by that.

reviews.assessment: Potentially great paper, but the message oscillates between null-model assessment and warming effects, and the asymmetry rationale risks circularity.
strengths: addresses two topics of high interest

comments.issue: The focus alternates between null models and warming effects, diluting the main message, title and discussion.
comments.request: Emphasise one focus and streamline the narrative.
comments.quote: Currently, the focus on null models or warming effects varies depending on the section, which sometimes result confusing and dilutes the main message.

comments.issue: Null models depicting modes of stressor action are mixed with net cumulative effect types.
comments.request: Explain how null model predictions relate to cumulative effect types.
comments.quote: I feel that there is a mixture between null models depicting different mode of stressor action and net cumulative effects

comments.issue: Whether the three null models yield different patterns of cumulative effects is not evaluated.
comments.request: Add a results section comparing cumulative effects across null models.
comments.quote: it would be very useful to have a result section where authors evaluate if the three null models give rise to different (or similar) patterns of cumulative effects

comments.issue: The expectation that asymmetry determines multiple stressor effects seems trivial and is not well justified.
comments.request: Better justify the asymmetry expectation (H1).
comments.quote: There is a need to better justify this expectation (H1), which currently seems too forced and trivial.

comments.issue: The title is not informative and 'asymmetry' is too broad out of context.
comments.request: Revise the title to be more informative.
comments.quote: authors should try to revisit the title to make it more informative. “Asymmetry” is a bit broad and unspecific when read without a context.

comments.issue: The superiority of the dominance null model is oversold given the similar performance of all models.
comments.request: Communicate and discuss the model differences more cautiously.
comments.quote: I think that authors perhaps oversell a bit the fact that the dominance null model tends outperforms the multiplicative and additive ones.

comments.issue: Results on net cumulative effects of warming plus a second stressor are scattered and buried.
comments.request: Give these results a clearer focus, for example with a summary figure.
comments.quote: I feel that the results regarding net cumulative effects of warming and the second stressor are scattered and sometimes “buried”.

comments.issue: The list of primary-data articles is missing, denying credit and transparency.
comments.request: List and cite the articles providing primary data.
comments.quote: I did not find the list of articles from which authors extracted primary data. I think this is a critical aspect of any review or meta-analysis to give credit to those that generated empirical evidence

comments.issue: Data and R code are not shared, limiting transparency and replicability.
comments.request: Share the data and the R code used for the analyses.
comments.quote: It would be really great if authors can share their data (observed and predicted interaction effects plus associated metadata) and R code

comments.issue: The opening sentence of P4 L3 is unclear.
comments.request: Reword the sentence.
comments.quote: The first bit of the sentence seems to be a bit unclear

comments.issue: 'Interacting' should be 'combined' since whether stressors interact is not relevant to the design.
comments.request: Replace 'interacting' with 'combined'.
comments.quote: I would change “interacting” by “combined” in this sentence

comments.issue: 'Strongly' is used inconsistently where 'asymmetric' was defined before.
comments.request: Revise 'strongly' for consistency.
comments.quote: authors should revise the use of “strongly” here for the sake of consistency

comments.issue: P10 L29-39 mixes methodological and ecological aspects, and the term 'popular opinion' should be replaced.
comments.request: Separate the two aspects and reword the claim.
comments.quote: These lines are a bit confusing. There is a mixture between the explanation of null model performance (methodological) and resulting combined effects (ecological).

comments.issue: The rationale for expecting the smallest combined impact to be most accurate is missing.
comments.request: Explain the theoretical rationale for this expectation.
comments.quote: I don’t understand why the smallest combined impact should be the most accurate. Which is the theoretical rationale for this expectation?

comments.issue: 'Birks et al 2020' is not in the bibliography and 'spatial process' is too broad.
comments.request: Check the reference and detail the spatial process.
comments.quote: I did not find ‘Birks et al 2020’ in the Bibliography - please, check and revise accordingly.

comments.issue: Which processes are meant on P11 L25 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify which processes are meant.
comments.quote: P11, L25: Which processes? Please, clarify.

comments.issue: A sentence on P11 L25-29 lacks a supporting citation.
comments.request: Add a supporting citation.
comments.quote: This sentence needs a supporting citation; Jackson et al (2016) showed that antagonisms are prevalent at the individual and community levels.

comments.issue: The justification for greater dominance-model accuracy at the community level is not accepted.
comments.request: Revise the justification for community-level dominance.
comments.quote: I don’t agree with the way in which authors try to justify the greater accuracy of the dominant null model at the community level.

comments.issue: The land-use intensification claim on P11 L55 is not explicit enough.
comments.request: State the claim more explicitly.
comments.quote: I suggest to say it more explicitly (“land-use intensification impacts are likely to become increasingly dominant”)

comments.issue: The phrase 'erode strongly antagonistic interactions' is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify what 'erode' means here.
comments.quote: What authors mean by “erode strongly antagonistic interactions”?

comments.issue: Evidence does not clearly show non-additive effects are more common than additive or dominant effects.
comments.request: Temper the claim about non-additive effects.
comments.quote: I don’t think that current evidence clearly indicates that non-additive effects are more common that additive or dominant effects.

comments.issue: A claim on P13 L27 overstates the evidence.
comments.request: Tone down or reword the claim.
comments.quote: This claim should be toned down or reworded. Please, see comment to P12, L13-14.

comments.issue: The sentence on P13 L38-41 is hard to follow.
comments.request: Split or simplify the sentence.
comments.quote: this sentence is a bit hard to follow. I suggest splitting or trying to use a simpler wording.

title: Local stressors mask the effects of warming in freshwater ecosystems

study.system: amphibians; comparative species-level reproductive traits and egg attendance

editor_summary: Concurs that the manuscript merits revision and encourages the authors to address each of the recommended changes from Reviewers 2 and 3 with a thorough point-by-point response.

reviews.assessment: Calls the paper publication-ready, praising sound assumptions, appropriate methods and appropriately cautious conclusions.
strengths: assumptions sound, data and methods appropriate
does not overreach in its conclusions
worthy contribution that should be published

reviews.assessment: Likes the comprehensive dataset and question but found the narrative inconsistent and key trait data and inferences insufficiently explained.
strengths: interesting questions on the origins of care
significant implications of interest to a broad readership
builds on recent work by these authors

comments.issue: The opening sentence could be reworded to say we know little about conditions promoting initial evolution of care.
comments.request: Consider the suggested rewording of the line 21-22 sentence.
comments.quote: How about “ However, we know little about the ecological conditions that promote the initial evolution of parental care”?

comments.issue: Framing amphibian systems as an 'alternative approach' misrepresents them as the key approach.
comments.request: Reframe this as identifying tractable systems being the approach.
comments.quote: I am not sure that an alternative appraoch is the right way to frame this.

comments.issue: The paragraph should incorporate the points about parent-offspring interaction and the lability of egg attendance.
comments.request: Bring these points into this paragraph.
comments.quote: I think you could probably bring these two points up in this paragraph and then highlight the fact that it is common (and labile) across taxa

comments.issue: The paragraph jumps between previous work on amphibians and introducing amphibians as model systems.
comments.request: Move this text to the end of the paragraph introducing amphibians.
comments.quote: I would move this to the end of the paragraph where you introduce amphibians and instead here talk about the function of egg attendance across taxa.

comments.issue: The logic behind the prediction that terrestrial deposition leads to egg attendance is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify whether the additional terrestrial challenges select for care.
comments.quote: I was not quite clear on the logic in setting up the hypothesis regarding the prediction that terrestrial deposition should lead to egg attendance.

comments.issue: The attendance-hiding predictions seem force-fitted when alternative causal links are equally likely.
comments.request: Keep the discussion of links broader and leave nuance to the discussion.
comments.quote: they both seem a little force fitted to a particular direction when alterative causal links may be just as likely

comments.issue: Functionality of egg attendance varies among species and the data cannot distinguish functions, limiting tests of causal mechanisms.
comments.request: Be more circumspect in developing directional predictions.
comments.quote: your data collection, as far as I can tell, does not allow you to distinguish between these different functions – so your ability to test some of your suggested causal mechanisms for the emergence of egg attendance across transitions is a little limited

comments.issue: The text implies data on egg deposition location were not collected, making other eggs seem assumed aquatic.
comments.request: State that egg deposition location data were collected and describe the traits collected.
comments.quote: you presumably collected data on egg deposition location (e.g., whether they were aquatic or terrestrial). Mentioning only terrestrial eggs makes it sound a little like all other eggs were assumed to be aquatic

comments.issue: Sex-specific differences in parental care evolution are not introduced, so later sex differences lack context.
comments.request: Introduce sex-specific expectations earlier in the manuscript.
comments.quote: The potential for sex specific differences in the evolution of parental care is not really introduced anywhere and thus when it comes up it is a little unclear what the contexts or expectations are with respect to this.

comments.issue: How trait data were acquired, their sources and the criteria used are not described.
comments.request: Describe the data sources and criteria for each trait.
comments.quote: There is no information on how this data was acquired. Where did this data come from? What were the sources?

comments.issue: The model tests attendance against three predictors but not co-variation or collinearity among predictors.
comments.request: Test the associations among predictor traits.
comments.quote: The model you outline seems to explore the relationship between egg attendance and all three predictor variables – but does not explore the relationship between any of the other three predictor variables.

comments.issue: Very few species have female attendance with exposed eggs, questioning robust inference of gains and losses.
comments.request: Assess whether this supports robust gain/loss inference.
comments.quote: It seems to me that there is an extremely low number of species where females both attend eggs and who lay exposed eggs.

comments.issue: The phrase 'what ecological factors promote' is vague; reproductive ecology is the actual focus.
comments.request: Keep the discussion focused on reproductive ecology.
comments.quote: I think you are probably best off keeping this focussed on reproductive ecology as those are the traits that you focus on – ecology is a little vague as a result.

comments.issue: Repeated terms make the results description heavy and hard to follow.
comments.request: Use more direct language when describing the results.
comments.quote: There is a lot of different terms utilised repeatedly throughout and I often found myself re-reading paragraphs to ensure I understood them.

comments.issue: The key argument in the discussion is unclear, and it is not explained why egg investment prevails over predation.
comments.request: Clarify the argument and why it overrides alternatives.
comments.quote: It was not totally clear what your key argument is here.

comments.issue: It is not explained why male and female egg attendance follow such different evolutionary pathways.
comments.request: Explain the sex-specific pathways and expectations.
comments.quote: Why are there such different evolutionary pathways between the evolution of male and female egg attendance?

comments.issue: It is unclear why no association with males was found, given the reproductive value of direct-developing eggs.
comments.request: Explain the absence of a male association.
comments.quote: Why did you not find an association with males. Presumably the increased reproductive value of direct developing eggs is also relevant to male investment in care?

comments.issue: The co-evolutionary dynamic with egg size is not formally explored; effects may be mediated by egg size.
comments.request: Include egg size in models to see whether effects are maintained.
comments.quote: could this be explored more formally by including egg size to these models to explore whether the effects of terrestrial deposition and direct development are maintained even when you control for differences in egg size

reviews.assessment: Impressed by the dataset and methods, but flags semantic framing issues, non-independence of the sexes and confounds from unstated data subsets.
strengths: builds on an excellent array of previous work
large sample size and complex statistical techniques

comments.issue: Species traits are mislabelled as ecological drivers, conflating traits with the ecological conditions that select for care.
comments.request: Reframe the terminology away from ecological drivers.
comments.quote: I would not class traits belonging to the species as ecological drivers. To me, these are traits that influence the ecology of the species, but are not aspects of the ecology that select for egg attendance.

comments.issue: Terrestrial egg-laying species do not share the same ecological conditions; ecological factors may covary with terrestrial laying.
comments.request: Reframe statements accordingly and consider covariation.
comments.quote: all terrestrial egg laying species do not experience the same ecological conditions

comments.issue: Male and female egg attendance evolve non-independently, yet the sexes are analysed separately without addressing this.
comments.request: Analyse attendance by any sex and then subset, reporting species counts per sex.
comments.quote: The evolution of female and male egg attendance are therefore non-independent.

comments.issue: Subsequent adaptations following egg attendance could confound the drivers; restricting to attendance-only and no-care species may be a truer test.
comments.request: Restrict data to species with only egg attendance and no care.
comments.quote: Would restricting the data to only these species and species that exhibit no parental care behaviour be the truest test of the drivers of the evolution of egg attendance?

comments.issue: It is unclear which data enter each analysis, especially for hidden eggs and aquatic species.
comments.request: Report which species and data go into each analysis.
comments.quote: Having more information about which data go into each analysis would allow the reader to better understand the results, as currently many of these traits are correlated/highly dependent on other traits.

comments.issue: Statements that care evolution is poorly understood do a disservice to decades of prior work.
comments.request: Soften these statements to acknowledge prior work.

comments.request: Increase sampling or temper the partitioning of trait variation.

comments.issue: Text implies strong universal skeletal and morphological change despite few significant results (9 of 45).

comments.quote: Skeletal and morphology traits are particularly poorly differentiated (9 significant effect sizes out of 45) but the text makes it seem as if changes in this category were strong and universal.

comments.issue: Conclusions should be more cautious given minimal sample sizes; 'acute unidirectional changes' rest on few colonies.
comments.request: Temper the conclusions.
comments.quote: These sample size issues suggest the authors might be more cautious about the conclusions – this seems like the minimal data set to show the patterns they are highlighting.

comments.issue: Intraspecific variation sources (acclimation, genetics, symbionts, cryptic species) and local symbiont pools are barely discussed.
comments.request: Discuss alternative sources of intraspecific variation.
comments.quote: One last issue is that intraspecific variation can come from many sources – acclimation, differential host genetics, different symbionts, undiscovered cryptic species.

reviews.assessment: Exciting, broadly interesting intraspecific trait study, but fixed versus plastic effects cannot be disentangled and language must be tempered.

comments.issue: Fixed and plastic effects cannot be disentangled; observational data cannot support mechanistic conclusions.

comments.issue: Abstract, discussion and conclusion attribute genetic filtering or plasticity without distinguishing the mechanisms.

comments.quote: In the abstract, we cannot reliably say "indicating strong environmental filtering" (which suggests genetic components) or "physiological tissue traits were flexible within species" (which suggests plasticity).

comments.issue: Potential sources of trait differentiation are not outlined in the introduction.
