comments.quote: I would suggest that the authors outline potential sources of trait differentiation (genetic and plastic) in the introduction, but then avoid attributing one or the other to their own observations without appropriate caveats.

title: Inferring spatially varying animal movement characteristics using a hierarchical continuous‐time velocity model

study.system: spatially explicit eco-evolutionary metacommunity model; mutualistic and antagonistic networks

editor_summary: All reviewers found the topic timely, but the editor asks for a much fuller model explanation, justification and robustness testing of assumptions, clearer contribution relative to existing literature, and more intuition for readers.

reviews.assessment: Ambitious and valuable framework whose main results are compelling, but their robustness to the model's assumptions remains hard to evaluate.
strengths: ambitious integration of ecology, evolution and habitat loss
end results on traits and diversity are compelling and important

comments.issue: Robustness of the main results to the modelling assumptions is unclear.
comments.request: Test or discuss sensitivity of outcomes to key assumptions.
comments.quote: But what I find hard to evaluate is how robust those outcomes are to the assumptions made along the way.

comments.issue: A single matching trait is assumed to govern all interaction types without justification.
comments.request: Justify where this holds or narrow the model's scope.
comments.quote: I think it is a huge assumption that trait matching of a single trait Z\_j for species j is what determines these dynamics between all species i and j.

comments.issue: Equation 2 bundles many assumptions and lacks gradual build-up and unpacking.
comments.request: Explain Eq. 2 step by step and unpack its implications.
comments.quote: This has an enormous amount of infromation and important assumptions packed into it, and I think it would really benefit from more gradual build-up

comments.issue: I_ij is not expressed in terms of the underlying traits.
comments.request: Write the selected phenotype I_ij in terms of the traits.
comments.quote: Can I write this phenotype in terms of the traits?

comments.issue: q_ij and I_ij are not clearly distinguished.
comments.request: Explain how q_ij differs from I_ij.
comments.quote: I did not fully understand how to distinguish this from I\_ij. Both appear in identical way in some parts of Eq 2, but not others.

comments.issue: Unclear whether the interaction network is fixed externally or determined by traits, and how it is chosen.
comments.request: Clarify how a_ij is set and how it affects results.
comments.quote: In short, it was not clear whether the network of interactions was fixed externally, or itself determined by trait values.

comments.issue: The evolutionary component is not validated against established models of evolving interactions.
comments.request: Compare model outputs with previous models to show sensible behaviour.
comments.quote: Can the authors make a comparison of these kinds of quantities just to show that their evolutionary model works well and produces sensible results in isolation of the spatial features of the unified model?

comments.issue: No comparison with metacommunity theory when evolution is switched off.
comments.request: Check whether the model reproduces known metacommunity outcomes.
comments.quote: Does the current model have similar outcomes in the limit of interaction strengths being fixed in time, and unable to evolve?

comments.issue: No baseline for judging the magnitude of diversity changes under habitat loss.
comments.request: Compare diversity changes with neutral or literature baselines.
comments.quote: it would help to compare with other baselines from the literature. E.g. neutral models like Chisholm et al EL (2018) give some kind of baseline with which to evaluate how big the observed changes are

reviews.assessment: Interesting approach and important topic, but the depth of analysis and interpretation is insufficient and some results may be artifacts of model implementation.
strengths: habitat destruction is an important addition to eco-evolutionary metacommunity knowledge
showing results from the Web of Life

comments.issue: The Discussion largely repeats the Results and does not clearly present the study's contribution.
comments.request: Restructure the Discussion around the contribution and relevant literature.
comments.quote: The Discussion section is too repetitive of the Results section, or rather reads as an extension of the Results section focusing on the supplementary material section

comments.issue: Introduction and Discussion do not synthesise prior work on eco-evolutionary dynamics under habitat destruction, including very close recent papers.
comments.request: Review this literature and clarify the novelty and importance of results.
comments.quote: The manuscript (Introduction and Discussion) should review the literature on evolution in metacommunities in a way that clearly outline known/expected eco-evo dynamics under habitat destruction

comments.issue: Results read as a repository of findings without clear links to the questions raised.
comments.request: Restructure the Results around the key questions.
comments.quote: I feel the Results section could be better structured around key questions.

comments.issue: The main (co)evolution result is unsurprising and the divergent antagonistic response remains unresolved.
comments.request: Explain what drives the variability in antagonistic networks.
comments.quote: This result is not entirely surprising and other potentially important results, such as divergent roles of co-evolution in antagonistic networks, are not sufficiently resolved

comments.issue: High variability in antagonistic networks may be an artifact of the reinforcing trait divergence-convergence mechanism.
comments.request: Test whether this reinforcing mechanism drives the variability.
comments.quote: the fact that antagonistic networks evolve from trait divergence and trait convergence at the resource and consumer levels introduces a strong reinforcing mechanism that could explain the high variability in these networks to habitat destruction

comments.issue: Independent consumer colonization may artifactually inflate the net extinction rate.
comments.request: Test this implementation artifact against the observed extinction rates.
comments.quote: The implementation of consumer colonization as independent from resources also introduces some artifacts because colonization is, in the model, a different process from simple movement of individuals

comments.issue: Spatial dynamics are barely analysed and local processes are not controlled for.
comments.request: Run mean-field simulations to assess local colonization and extinction.
comments.quote: I did not see simulations controlling for these local processes. I would have expected some mean-field simulations to control the importance of nearest-neighbor colonization and extinction.

comments.issue: Results from a single species network may not represent variation across networks.
comments.request: Report mean and variance metrics across all networks per interaction type.
comments.quote: I really don’t see the advantage of showing results from a single species network. The variations shown in supplementary material seem substantial

comments.issue: The study does not systematically control network and spatial properties needed to explain the main results.
comments.request: Add simulations that systematically vary network and spatial properties.
comments.quote: systematically controlling for properties of networks and of spatial dynamics would be essential here

comments.issue: Two sentences in P4L28-36 duplicate a later explanation.
comments.request: Remove the redundant sentences.
comments.quote: These 2 sentences are redundant because this is explained more clearly and succinctly late in the same paragraph

comments.issue: The term 'partner' wrongly implies a positive interaction for consumers.
comments.request: Remove the term 'partner'.
comments.quote: ‘partner’ would normally imply a positive interaction; I would simply remove that term

comments.issue: Reflective boundary conditions may introduce stronger finite-size effects.
comments.request: Justify or reconsider the reflective boundary conditions.
comments.quote: The choice of reflective boundary conditions is surprising. Wouldn't you expect stronger finite size effects with this choice of boundary condition?

comments.issue: Unclear whether consumer and resource colonize jointly via consumer movement.
comments.request: Clarify whether colonization is a joint event.
comments.quote: is this a joint colonization event (both the consumer and resource colonize via movement of the consumer?)

comments.issue: Colonization implementation assumes establishment is independent of consumer presence.
comments.request: Justify or revise this assumption and its consequences.
comments.quote: the dynamics is instead implementing colonization, which thus assumes successful establishment of a population is independent from the presence of its consumers

comments.issue: Quantity I_ij has no formal definition and is described inconsistently.
comments.request: Define I_ij formally and give a general expression.
comments.quote: There must be a clearer way of defining I\_ij. I cannot be a phenotype unles it is a continuous variable.

comments.issue: Selection strength and genetic variance are treated as multiplicative, and genetic load on fitness is ignored.
comments.request: Justify the treatment of genetic variance and its missing effect on fitness.
comments.quote: aren't selection strength and genetic variance 2 different components that are expected to have multiplicative effects on trait dynamics?

comments.issue: Equation 2 terms and structure are not explained and its assumptions are unclear.
comments.request: Explain each term and the rationale for the equation's structure.
comments.quote: I think it would help the reader to interpret each (sub)term of the equation, which would make the explanation of each parameter and variable clearer and shorter

comments.issue: Co-evolution strength is assumed independent of partner identity.
comments.quote: This assumes the strength of co-evolution m\_i on species i is not modulated by the identity of species j as long as a\_ij=1.

comments.issue: The meaning of 'sequential update' is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the update scheme.
comments.quote: I assume ‘sequential update’ means synchronous update with a temporary buffer to avoid artifacts imposed by the fixed update sequence?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether steady state is the only possible regime.
comments.request: Clarify whether the model was parameterized to reach steady state.
comments.quote: is steady state the only regime possible or was the model parameterized to limit dynamics to steady state?

comments.issue: Dependence of outcomes on initial conditions is unknown.
comments.request: Assess sensitivity to initial conditions.
comments.quote: any dependence on initial conditions? If communities were seeded from data (single initial condition), does it mean this dependence is unknown?

comments.issue: The software implementation is not described.
comments.request: State whether a Julia package or custom code was used.
comments.quote: Was any Julia package used, or was the code built from scratch?

comments.issue: The metric NODF is not defined.
comments.request: Define NODF.
comments.quote: P8L47 – What is NODF?

comments.issue: Spatial aggregation is not measured, leaving the spatially explicit model unjustified.
comments.request: Add spatial aggregation metrics to the analysis.
comments.quote: Surprising to see no measure of spatial aggregation given the model is spatially explicit. It is hard to justify the complexity of the model without integrating the spatial component in the analysis

comments.issue: Components of variability tracked in the analysis are not defined.
comments.request: Define these variability components in the Methods.
comments.quote: Please define components of variability that are tracked. This could be done in the Methods section (unless I missed it).

comments.issue: It is unclear how trait variability measures a coevolutionary trajectory.
comments.request: Clarify the link between trait variability and coevolutionary trajectories.
comments.quote: How is (spatial?) trait variability a measure of coevolutionary trajectory?

comments.issue: The phrase 'become' as a function of fragmentation is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the wording.
comments.quote: P9L58 – ‘become’ as a function of fragmentation?

comments.issue: Null expectations are needed when controlling for components of evolutionary dynamics.
comments.request: Establish null expectations for these control scenarios.
comments.quote: This is a good example for the need to establish some null expectations when controlling for components of evolutionary dynamics.

comments.issue: 'Abundances of interactions' is not defined or justified as a metric.
comments.request: Define and justify this metric.
comments.quote: not sure 'abundances of interactions' was clearly defined in the Methods section and justified as an appropriate metric

comments.issue: The trait-matching effect may arise from independent resource colonization rather than matching.
comments.request: Test whether this assumption explains the trait-matching effect.
comments.quote: could the effect of trait matching be a result of resource colonization being independent from consumers?

comments.issue: Results are not structured around take-home messages.
comments.request: Restructure so key results do not need four figures.
comments.quote: The end of the Results section illustrates the need to structure results around main take-home messages.

comments.issue: The referent of 'these changes' is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify what 'these changes' refers to.
comments.quote: P13L13 - I lost what 'these changes' refer to.

comments.issue: The conservation recommendation does not follow from the results.
comments.request: Justify or temper the conservation recommendation.
comments.quote: Not sure I see how the result leads to this recommendation for conservation.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether habitat destruction directly changes optimal traits.
comments.request: Clarify whether optimal traits change only through co-evolution.
comments.quote: Maybe clarify (if this is the case) that optimal traits vary only in relation to co-evolution (species interaction) and no change in optimal trait occurs as a direct consequence of habitat destruction

comments.issue: The explanation of what drives variability in antagonistic networks is missing.
comments.request: Provide specific insights into the drivers of this variability.
comments.quote: This is a repeat of the Results section and remains unsatisfying as to what drives that variability.

comments.issue: The consumer/resource dichotomy limits extrapolation to systems where species are both.
comments.request: Discuss applicability to systems without a clear consumer/resource divide.
comments.quote: This divergence consumer/resource dichotomy in trait matching is also hard to extrapolate to systems where many species are both resources and consumers.

comments.issue: Fig. 2 is ambiguous given the many components of variability.
comments.request: Make the figure explicit about which variability is shown.
comments.quote: Be more explicit given there are many components of 'variability' in the study

comments.issue: Figure 6 predictions are not framed against expectations set at the start.
comments.request: Frame these predictions as expectations in the Introduction.
comments.quote: It would be nice to set some of these predictions as a part of some null expectations at the beginning of the manuscript

reviews.assessment: Clearly written and highly interesting study; comments mainly concern model details and the presentation of some results.

comments.issue: Environmental optima (Theta) do not affect fitness, so their role and necessity are unclear.
comments.request: Justify the Theta parameters or remove this model component.
comments.quote: these probabilities are not affected by how close a species' trait Z\_i is to its environmental optimum

comments.issue: Critical mismatch uses trait difference rather than trait matching and applies only to resources.
comments.request: Explain this formulation and its counter-intuitive consequences.
comments.quote: Why does the critical mismatch between the traits of antagonistic consumer and resource species, epsilon, (page 4, line 38) depend on the absolute difference of the traits

comments.issue: The label 'evolution' is misleading for a scenario with static traits.

comments.issue: The abstract statement about altered coevolutionary outcomes is vague.

comments.issue: 'Non-interacting' species cannot impose reciprocal evolutionary changes.

comments.issue: Typo in the Eq. 2 sum subscripts.

comments.issue: The critical threshold is not indicated in Table S2.

comments.issue: Generic novelty statement adds no information.

comments.quote: this generic novelty statement is not very informative and might be removed

comments.issue: The reduction in abundance is claimed but not shown directly.

comments.issue: Argument about limited adaptation conflicts with the model's assumption of unlimited adaptive potential.
comments.request: Remove or revise this argument.

comments.issue: The 'evolution' scenario is again misnamed as it involves no evolution.

comments.quote: as pointed out above (comment 3), the so-called evolution scenario does not involve any evolution

title: Effects of habitat destruction on coevolving metacommunities

study.system: temperate semi-arid grassland; N and P addition experiment with drought

editor_summary: Editor requires major revisions: clarify resilience and functional stability, structure results and discussion around the three hypotheses, consider N×P interactions, and sharpen mechanistic interpretation.

reviews.assessment: Well-written, clearly structured study worth publishing after fixing concerns about data choice, interactions and mechanistic interpretation.
strengths: well-conducted experiment and appropriate data processing

comments.issue: Plant cover data are less accurate than the available biomass data for quantifying stability.
comments.request: Re-analyse using the harvested biomass data.
comments.quote: using the biomass data to quantify the nutrient addition effect on ecosystem stability is a better option

comments.issue: Functional-group and abundance effects, and common versus rare species stability, are not analysed.
comments.request: Analyse functional groups and compare common versus rare species.
comments.quote: it would be interesting to examine the effects of nutrient addition on ecosystem stability of plant species from different functional groups

comments.issue: Nitrogen-phosphorus interactions are considered too lightly.
comments.request: Consider N × P interactions more fully.
comments.quote: the authors found that there were interactions effects between nitrogen addition and phosphorous addition on community biomass and functional stability. However, the consideration of the interactions is a bit light in the paper.

comments.issue: The inconsistency with Xu et al. on resilience is attributed to N addition timing without explanation.
comments.request: Explain why addition timing changes stability responses.
comments.quote: why did the different timing of nitrogen addition affect ecosystem stability differently?

comments.issue: The small richness gradient explanation for the missing diversity effect is not convincing.
comments.request: Reconsider the interpretation of the missing diversity effect.
comments.quote: I think that in small gradient community, the changes in species richness is more important

comments.issue: Two 'in more diverse communities' occur in one sentence.
comments.request: Remove the duplication.

comments.issue: Figure 2c labels resistance where resilience is meant.
comments.request: Correct the label.
comments.quote: In Figure 2c, resistance should be resilience.

comments.issue: A blue dot in Figure 3b is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain or remove the blue dot.
comments.quote: In Figure 3b, there was a blue dot in it. I do not know what the blue dot means.

comments.issue: The Tukey HSD letters in Figure S4f appear wrong.

comments.quote: In Figure S4f, I think the letters that indicate the results of post hoc Tukey’s HSD test was wrong.

reviews.assessment: Novel and interesting theme, but questions the functional stability metric and resilience calculation and wants reorganization and extra analyses.

comments.issue: Plant cover may not quantify ecosystem function, so 'functional stability' is the wrong label.

comments.issue: The paper is hard to follow because it is not organized around the three hypotheses.

comments.issue: Many long sentences harm the flow of arguments.

comments.issue: The insurance hypothesis is not mentioned in the introduction.

comments.issue: Figure 2c labels resistance where resilience is meant.

comments.issue: A paragraph at lines 294-306 duplicates content of a later section.

title: Nitrogen enrichment alters multiple dimensions of grassland functional stability via changing compositional stability

study.system: seagrass; multiple stressor fluctuation experiment

editor_summary: Two highly qualified reviewers conclude this is a timely study presented compellingly; revision should address the reviewer points including an updated version of the statistics and discussion.

reviews.assessment: Exciting, timely and well-framed study; wants clearer terminology, better-justified statistical models and a restructured discussion.

comments.issue: Referring to stressor 'timing' suggests sequential application and confuses readers; the L36 example also mismatches its sentence.
comments.request: Stick to 'synchronicity' or 'synchrony' throughout and align the example.
comments.quote: One thing that got me really confused is that you refer to the stressor timing quite often (e.g., L29, L332, L334) which initially made me think that the main stressor is applied to the system before the other one.

comments.issue: It may be unpredictability rather than fluctuation itself that makes dynamics stressful; seasonal cycles are tolerated.
comments.request: Add a few sentences comparing predictability of environmental dynamics.
comments.quote: It seems to me that fluctuations become a stressor the moment they become hard to predict for species/communities.

comments.issue: It is unclear how the stressor intensity component differs from the Light level and Herbicide level variables.
comments.request: Clarify the distinction between intensity and the stressor levels.
comments.quote: If so, to what extent the intensity component is different from the Light level and the Herbicide level?

comments.issue: The design may not have enough observations to estimate more than two variables plus random effects.
comments.request: Consider model averaging (Knape & de Valpine 2011; Johnson & Omland 2004) or simplify the models.
comments.quote: I don't think you have enough observations to properly estimate the effect of more than two variables (and you already have the random effects), except for Eq. 1 where you have temporal data

comments.issue: The ID random variable is not included in Eq. 1.
comments.request: Explain why ID is not included in Eq. 1.
comments.quote: In addition, why not include the ID random variable in Eq. 1 ?

editor_summary: Editor notes reviewers appreciate the topic but raise major concerns, some requiring substantial rethinking and restructuring of the manuscript, its focus and communication to a broad readership.

title: Contemporary tree growth shows altered climate memory

study.system: simulated population dynamics models; two empirical time series

editor_summary: All reviewers very positive; editor emphasizes testing methods with shorter, noisier series and stochastic simulations, clarifying correlations and sensitivity interpretation, validating LSTM ranking and discussing scope of use.

reviews.assessment: Supportive of the approach and clear writing; asks for tests on shorter/noisier series and discussion of scaling and related work.
strengths: well written and clear, even for non-mathematical readers
nice combination of simulations and empirical data

comments.issue: Methods were tested only on long, clean time series; sensitivity to shorter, noisier series, including the machine-learning approach, is unknown.
comments.request: Test performance on reduced-length and noisier simulated and empirical time series.
comments.quote: What I think is critical is to see how sensitive these approaches are to shorted and noisier time series before making sweeping generalisations about how they could be used in real-world systems.

comments.issue: How the methods scale with species number and interaction number/strength is unknown, as only simple systems were analysed.
comments.request: Add a short discussion of scaling with community complexity.
comments.quote: I also wonder how these methods scale with number of species in the system, or number/strength of interactions between nodes (given both the systems you analyse are relatively very simple).

comments.issue: A recently archived paper on dominant eigenvalue as a warning signal conceptually overlaps and is not considered.
comments.request: Consider the implications of that archived paper for these findings.
comments.quote: I believe there is some conceptual overlap between these two papers (although I don’t believe that the archived paper undermines the potential impact of this work)

reviews.assessment: Likes the idea and finds the article clear; wants a sharper ranking metric and clarity on sensitivity versus vulnerability.
strengths: glad the supplementary information and equations are included

comments.issue: Spearman's rho equates distinct rankings, obscuring differences in the performance of the ranking approaches.
comments.request: Use a permutation-based rank metric that distinguishes all possible rankings.
comments.quote: The authors are trying to understand the performance of these ranking approaches, so I’d recommend using a metric that can actually distinguish between all the possible different rankings rather than equating different rankings.

comments.issue: Small sensitivity differences are treated as meaningful rankings; the tolerance below which species have 'the same' sensitivity is not addressed.
comments.request: Explore a sensitivity margin below which species are treated as equivalent.
comments.quote: giving some idea of at what sensitivity margin one should just treat species as having ‘the same’ sensitivity seems important to me, rather than just talking always about ranks.

comments.issue: Data and code will only be archived on GitHub upon acceptance, without a permanent identifier.
comments.request: Archive data and code now and get a DOI via Zenodo or figshare.
comments.quote: They could already be archived and available. I’d also recommend getting a doi on something like zenodo / figshare so there is a permanent fixed record

comments.issue: Sensitivity is conflated with vulnerability; sensitivity can reflect increasing or decreasing abundance.
comments.request: Do not claim the definition is better at identifying endangered species.
comments.quote: the authors’ definition of sensitivity is not the same as vulnerable, so I wouldn’t be seen to claim that the definition is ‘better’ at identifying endangered species.

comments.issue: The phrase 'constant threat' is inaccurate and wrongly frames all perturbations as threats.
comments.request: Rephrase to 'are subject to external perturbations which are increasing in magnitude'.
comments.quote: This is pedantic of me, but ‘constant threat’ is a colloquial phrase that isn’t right here. The perturbations are not constant and I suspect the probability is not constant either.

comments.issue: The choice of this specific sensitivity definition is not justified; its 'instantaneous' nature and relation to Lyapunov exponents are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify and justify the definition, including its relation to Lyapunov exponents.
comments.quote: First, this sensitivity is a kind of ‘instantaneous sensitivity’, which makes sense with the authors’ aims, but I’d clarify that. Why did the authors choose this specific definition of sensitivity?

comments.issue: The time interval k is set to 1 without justification, and different k values could change the order of sensitivities.
comments.request: Justify the choice of k and check whether rankings depend on it.
comments.quote: In the 3-species example given, the authors use k=1 but don’t specify why this is chosen. For different values of k, couldn’t you get a different order of sensitivities?

comments.issue: The normalisation term's properties (non-negativity, boundedness) and whether abundances are normalised are not specified.
comments.request: Specify the bounds of the normalisation term and whether abundances are normalised.
comments.quote: Maybe specify that is always greater than or equal to 0 - and is not bounded? Can one make numerator arbitrarily big and denominator arbitrarily small?

comments.issue: How the definition applies at equilibrium and why it is the best definition among alternatives are not clarified.
comments.request: Clarify behaviour at equilibrium and justify the definition against alternatives.
comments.quote: This is just to point out that ‘sensitivity’ is a fuzzy word that means different things to different people, so it could be worth clarifying why the authors’ definition is the best one

comments.issue: The assumption that perturbation p(t) has mean zero is not justified and appears inconsistent with the Fig. 1 example.
comments.request: Explain why p(t) can be assumed to have mean zero.
comments.quote: why can one assume that p(t) follows a distribution with mean zero – because it is normalised abundances and everything must cancel out? I don’t understand because in the Fig 1 example, p(t) was [7,7,7].

comments.issue: Only one division of the data into training and test sets is used.
comments.request: Try splitting the data temporally, e.g. recent 70% training and oldest 30% test.
comments.quote: It would be interesting (for example) to use the more recent 70% as a training set and the oldest 30% as the test set. This should work?

comments.issue: Most sensitive species can increase in abundance, so sensitivity is not vulnerability and the least sensitive could be most endangered.
comments.request: Make clear that sensitivity and vulnerability are not equivalent.
comments.quote: By the authors’ definition, the most sensitive species can be one that becomes much more abundant after a perturbation. This is the opposite of vulnerable.

comments.issue: Figure 1 layout: food web diagram placement, mismatched y-axis scales, and inconsistent species labels.
comments.request: Move or remove the food web diagram, match y-axis scales, and use consistent labels.
comments.quote: I would put the food web diagram at the top, rather than as part of panel A, or remove it. It might be helpful to make the abundance y-axis in A and B the same scale.

comments.issue: Figure 2 panels C and D do not show temporal ordering, so whether values flip through intermediates is unclear.
comments.request: Connect points in time with lines in panels C and D.
comments.quote: In panel C and D, it would be interesting to connect the points in time with a line. It’s not clear whether the behaviour jumps around randomly or whether there are patterns of ‘flipping’

comments.issue: Expected-sensitivity differences are not visible from the point colouring in Figure 4A.
comments.request: Plot the four species' expected sensitivities over time for the test set.
comments.quote: I really can’t tell any difference in expected sensitivity from the colouring of points in A, sorry. Is it possible to instead have a plot of the four species’ expected sensitivities over time for the test set?

comments.issue: Some barnacle measurements around 1992 look wrong, and whether variables should sum to 100% is unclear.
comments.request: Check the suspicious measurements and explain the variables for non-specialist readers.
comments.quote: in ~1992 there are some strange barnacle measurements that look wrong? And a few other places. Which variables should sum to 100%?

reviews.assessment: Fascinated by the approach and finds it novel; raises stochasticity and LSTM-validation concerns and wants guidance on where the method applies.
strengths: well written manuscript and supplementary files

comments.issue: Simulations are deterministic; performance may collapse with stochasticity because the Jacobian must be estimated well.
comments.request: Test how the sensitivity measures perform when stochasticity is added.
comments.quote: I would be afraid that the performance would become very low, because the proposed measures are based on a good estimation of the Jacobian matrix.

comments.issue: The assumption that LSTM forecasting errors reflect species sensitivity was never validated.
comments.request: Calculate LSTM rankings on synthetic time series to validate the assumption.
comments.quote: the authors did not test this assumption. I would suggest to calculate the LSTM ranking in the synthetic timeseries generated with the population dynamic models as well, to validate this assumption.

comments.issue: Empirical results are weak and it is unclear for which ecosystems and data the method is useful.
comments.request: Add a discussion paragraph on utilization and what the ranking tells us.
comments.quote: I think it would be helpful if the authors include a paragraph in the discussion on utilization. For which type of ecosystem and data would this method be useful, and what does the ranking exactly tell us?

title: Ranking species based on sensitivity to perturbations under non‐equilibrium community dynamics

study.system: herbaceous productivity, western US rangelands; statistical and climate model projections

editor_summary: All reviewers find components novel but share substantial reservations about broad reach/fit for Ecology Letters; letter format may be insufficient; re-submission possible if narrative and supplementary address modelling-choice issues.

reviews.assessment: Well executed and novel uncertainty analysis, but headline messages may not fit Ecology Letters' readership.
strengths: impressive amount of data and sophisticated analysis

comments.issue: The claim about past climate change rates at P3 L41-44 is inaccurate; the PETM and Younger Dryas had similar magnitudes and rates.
comments.request: Qualify the sentence about past climate change.
comments.quote: P3 L41-44 - this sentence needs more qualification. Both the PETM and the Younger Dryas appear to have periods of climate change with not just similar magnitudes but rates to modern climate change.

comments.issue: The terms "minimal acclimation" and "rapid acclimation" are not intuitive, especially since rapid acclimation includes slow compositional changes.
comments.request: Use more intuitive terminology for the acclimation scenarios.
comments.quote: I just did not find the terms “minimal acclimation” vs “rapid acclimation” to be intuitive.

comments.issue: The remotely-sensed dataset is not specified; it is a LANDSAT-derived NPP estimate.
comments.request: Name the LANDSAT-derived dataset up front.
comments.quote: can you be more specific than a “remotely-sensed dataset”. I eventually worked out this was a LANDSAT-derived estimate of NPP.

comments.issue: 2 line-level edits: weather vs climate wording (P6 L32) and a missing "2)" (P6 L48).
comments.quote: P6 L32 - I believe you mean weather data rather than climate data? P6 L48 - the “2)” is missing

comments.issue: Moisture stress and heat stress are substantially the same thing; the labels do not match the temperature and precipitation variables.
comments.request: Call these temperature and precipitation stress instead.
comments.quote: I did not understand the terms moisture stress and heat stress as these are substantially the same thing.

comments.issue: The notation at P8 L3742 is unclear, with subscripts dropped from Pbar and deltaP.
comments.request: Clarify the subscripts and the space-time variation of deltaP.
comments.quote: First why are the subscripts dropped on Pbar (should still have an i subscript, no) and deltaP should still have a t and an i subscript, no?)

comments.issue: It is unclear whether temperature x precipitation interaction terms were included.
comments.request: Include the statistical interaction term if no physiological proxy is used.
comments.quote: not clear to me what if any interaction terms for temperature X precipitation were included

comments.issue: The headline messages about prediction error may not interest Ecology Letters readers and may fit an applied journal better.
comments.request: Strengthen the broad significance or reconsider the target journal.
comments.quote: I'm just not sure the headline messages about sources of prediction error is a focus of Ecology Letters readers or if this is a better fit for a more applied ecological journal.

reviews.assessment: Novel but frustrating; distributional assumptions and absent model assessment undermine the modelling.
strengths: ingenious decomposition of climate into spatial and temporal components

comments.issue: Figure S2, integral to the decomposition approach, is relegated to the supplement.
comments.request: Move Figure S2 into the main manuscript.
comments.quote: I think you do a disservice to the work to demote S2 to the supplementary materials and would strongly encourage you to include this figure in the main

comments.issue: A strictly non-negative, censored/truncated response is modelled as Gaussian without justification, producing nonsense extrapolations.
comments.request: Justify the Gaussian assumption or use a suitable distribution.
comments.quote: Productivity is a non-negative random variable. I would go further and suggest that your data is either censored or truncated at the lower end

comments.issue: Model assessment is almost absent; a single linear-correlation GOF measure is insufficient and unjustified.
comments.request: Add prior and posterior predictive checks.
comments.quote: Model assessment is (almost) entirely absent from the manuscript. It is insufficient to boil model evaluation down to a single goodness-of-fit (GOF) measure (linear correlation (!))

comments.issue: The manuscript lacks line numbers, making specific locations hard to reference.
comments.request: Include line numbers in the manuscript.
comments.quote: it would have been very helpful to this reviewer if you had included line numbers in your manuscript

comments.issue: "Capacity" should be plural "capacities" in the abstract if multiple ecosystems are meant.
comments.request: Correct the abstract wording.
comments.quote: Abstract L1: are you referring to multiple ecosystems and their capacities here? As written it seems “capacity” -> “capacities” is needed.

comments.issue: "Project" may not be the most intuitive word in the abstract.
comments.request: Consider "predict" or "forecast" instead.
comments.quote: is “project” the typically used word here? I would prefer “predict” but “forecast” would also seem more immediately intuitive.

comments.issue: The "critical gaps" in palaeo data are not specified or supported by citations.
comments.request: Expand on the gaps or cite supporting work.
comments.quote: what “critical gaps” do you perceive in the palaeo data? As a palaeoecologist myself I am interested in this. please expand or cite something to justify this comment.

comments.issue: Aggregated daily values over long periods are described as "weather", a term usually reserved for short-term realisations.
comments.request: Reconsider describing these anomalies as weather.
comments.quote: it is a stretch to describe these temporal anomalies as “weather”, which I take to mean the very short term, hour-to-hour and day-to-day realisations

comments.issue: Sequential removal of outliers beyond 3SD is not explained or justified.
comments.request: Explain and justify the outlier removal.
comments.quote: “sequentially removed outliers” why? Please explain and justify this. Outliers that are beyond 3SD of the mean are perfectly reasonable values

comments.issue: How the data were aggregated to 6.9 km (means, weighted means) is not stated.
comments.request: Describe the aggregation method.
comments.quote: P7 “which we aggregated to 6.9 km” aggregated how? means, weighted means?

comments.issue: Selecting model variables based on fits to the same observed data is double dipping.
comments.request: Avoid data-driven variable selection based on observed fits.
comments.quote: choosing what to include in your model on the basis of fits to your observed data is double dipping and very problematic from a modelling point of view

comments.issue: Justification is lacking for summed precipitation and averaged temperature as the appropriate community features.
comments.request: Justify the chosen features; consider extrema and growing season length.
comments.quote: justify why these are the appropriate features for these communities/ecosystems.

comments.issue: "This model" should be "these models" for consistency at P8.
comments.request: Correct the singular/plural inconsistency.
comments.quote: P8 last line “and then used this model” -> “and then used these models” as you refer earlier in the sentence to “models”

comments.issue: Bayesian ridge regression uses the data to define a prior, which is problematic.
comments.request: Use an alternative shrinkage prior such as a horseshoe prior.
comments.quote: You are using your data to define a prior which is scandalous behaviour in the extreme! What benefit does this process afford you that you wouldn't have been able to achieve using something like a horseshoe prior

comments.issue: Sums-of-squares is used as a variation measure although the response is not conditionally Gaussian.
comments.request: Justify or replace the variation measure.
comments.quote: P13 “First, we took a sums-of-squares” justify this as your measure of variation when your response variable is not conditionally Gaussian

comments.issue: The sensitivity analysis may compare non-equivalent changes: 1 cm precipitation versus 1 degree C.
comments.request: Clarify whether the sensitivity comparison is proportional and fair.
comments.quote: Is a 1cm change in precip equivalent in proportional terms to a 1 degree C change in temperature? I'm wondering if the sensitivity analysis is comparing apples with apples or with oranges here.

comments.issue: The claim that palaeo data cannot provide sub-century resolution is not justified; superposition may circumvent age uncertainty.
comments.request: Expand and justify the palaeo resolution claim.
comments.quote: can you expand on this and justify why palaeo can't provide the relevant resolution. We might not have great control on ages of samples, but superposition of those samples would circumvent that.

title: Climate disequilibrium dominates uncertainty in long‐term projections of primary productivity

study.system: Trinidadian killifish; field transplant experiment with mark-recapture

editor_summary: Editor notes mixed but largely positive reviews; low replication of the transplant experiment is a concern but the novelty warrants revision, especially to balance interpretation of environmental novelty versus predation or density.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, unusual study of brain size across environments, with clarifying comments on framing, design and discussion.
strengths: highly unusual and understudied aspect of brain size
should inspire similar studies across taxa

comments.issue: It is not certain that the pattern reflects evolution rather than plasticity.
comments.request: Rephrase and remove 'with the evolution of'.
comments.quote: Can you be certain it is ‘evolution’ and not plasticity? I suggest rephrasing and removing ‘with the evolution of’ just in case.

comments.issue: The ending sentence is weak.
comments.request: Write a more potent ending sentence.
comments.quote: I suggest you try to write a more potent ending sentence instead of just about what ‘such’ results might mean.

comments.issue: The rarity of translocation experiments like this is not highlighted.
comments.request: Emphasise in the introduction how rare such experiments are.
comments.quote: Is it worth highlighting that translocation experiments such as this are extremely rare?

comments.issue: Trade-offs and energy requirements of larger brains are not addressed.
comments.request: Discuss these trade-offs in the introduction.
comments.quote: there are also important trade-offs to consider for brains of different sizes given their different energy requirements

comments.issue: The different levels of the predator community are not explained.
comments.request: Clarify what the predator community levels mean.
comments.quote: l. 132. Please clarify further what the different levels of the predator community mean.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the translocation was properly replicated or only a single swap between two sites.
comments.request: Clarify the replication and add a figure of the translocation design.
comments.quote: it is unclear if this is a properly replicated translocation experiment or not

comments.issue: The key interaction effect in Fig 3 is buried by earlier results.
comments.request: Consider presenting the Fig 3 interaction first.
comments.quote: I wonder if the super cool interaction effect in Fig 3 should come first?

comments.issue: The discussion is too killifish-specific and lacks examples from other taxa.
comments.request: Add references to costs of larger brains from other species and taxa.
comments.quote: it gets very killifish specific, can the authors add also other references from other species and maybe taxa in this section?

reviews.assessment: Important merits in the design, but the cognitive-flexibility assumption, brain-size measure and over-emphasis on predation need clarification and reconsideration.
strengths: part of a large successful research program on life history responses to predation

comments.issue: The premise that brain size enhances behavioural flexibility is assumed without evidence, and the relevance of measuring immature brains is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the evidence linking brain size to cognitive performance.
comments.quote: The main assumption of the study is that brain size is associated with enhanced behavioral flexibility. However, no evidence is provided.

comments.issue: Absolute brain size may merely reflect allometry, which would remove the need for adaptive explanations.
comments.request: Compare static allometric coefficients of OT and the rest of the brain.
comments.quote: The use of absolute brain size is also problematic because it may be merely driven by allometry

comments.issue: Relative and absolute brain size measures are mixed across analyses without a clear logic.
comments.request: Clearly distinguish and justify when each measure is analysed.
comments.quote: the authors also use relative measures of brain size for some analyses but not for others, making it difficult to follow the logic

comments.issue: The cognitive buffer hypothesis discussion is too speculative for the current section.
comments.request: Move it to the discussion section.
comments.quote: Shifting the focus does not deny the possibility to discuss the cognitive buffer hypothesis, but this would be more speculative and should go to the discussion section

comments.issue: Optic tectum size may not measure overall brain size, and other brain areas may drive the pattern.
comments.request: Focus on the optic tectum itself and integrate the eye size results.
comments.quote: However, this can be problematic because other brain areas may also be strongly associated with brain size, perhaps associated with allometric effects of body size.

comments.issue: Measuring the optic tectum volume from a single linear measure is questionable.
comments.request: Justify or revise the measurement of the TO.
comments.quote: the way the TO is measured can also be criticized, as it implies measuring a volume based on a single linear measure

comments.issue: The eye size results are little integrated into the general story.
comments.request: Integrate the eye size results with the brain size story.
comments.quote: This would better fit with the results for eye size, which currently seem to be little integrated into the general story

comments.issue: The role of predation is over-estimated; K-selection from increased intraspecific competition is an alternative driver.
comments.request: Consider the K-selection alternative in the interpretation.
comments.quote: The role of predation as driver of evolutionary changes seems to be over-estimated. The alternative that changes in life history and brain size are driven by K-selection associated with increased intra-specific competition.

comments.issue: Results are only marginally significant and validated in models containing non-significant interactions, so they may be spurious.
comments.request: Simplify models and check that results are not spurious.
comments.quote: First, they are marginally significant. Second, the significance is validated in models that include interactions that are not significant, which can be problematic.

comments.issue: Stabilizing selection in the original populations was not tested directly.
comments.request: Add a quadratic term and report within- versus across-population variation.
comments.quote: why do not directly test whether stabilizing selection is in play. Adding a quadratic term could be useful for this purpose

comments.issue: The focus on predation neglects density as an alternative explanation.
comments.request: Consider density as an alternative driver.
comments.quote: The focus on predation neglects the importance of alternative explanations, including the possibility that is density what matters.

comments.issue: The section title is uninformative and potentially confusing.
comments.request: Use a title that states the section concerns selection in ancestral populations.
comments.quote: This tittle is little informative and may confound; it would be better a title that informs that the section is about selection on the ancestral populations.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether 11 days are long enough to measure selection.
comments.request: Justify the 11-day duration for measuring selection.
comments.quote: L109: Are 11 days long enough to measure selection?

comments.issue: How fish were sexed is not explained.
comments.request: Describe how fish were sexed.
comments.quote: How were they sexed? We cannot assume that all readers will be familiar with the biology of the species.

comments.issue: The number of marked fish is not reported.
comments.request: Mention how many fish were marked.
comments.quote: L116: You should mention how many fish were marked.

comments.issue: The sentence is confusing because the sampling protocol was already explained.
comments.request: Rewrite or remove this sentence.
comments.quote: This sentence is a bit confusing. You already explained the sampling protocol.

comments.issue: It is unclear why brains were not measured once fully grown.
comments.request: Justify the timing of brain measurements.
comments.quote: L125: Should not the brain be measured when has achieved its maximum size and hence is fully operative?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the supporting information is shown in the supplement.
comments.request: Show this information in the supplementary material.
comments.quote: L126-127: Is this shown in the supplementary?

comments.issue: Using residuals assumes a strong brain-body size correlation, which is not demonstrated.
comments.request: Report the brain-body size correlation.
comments.quote: The use of residuals requires a strong correlation between brain and body size. Is this the case for the present study?

comments.issue: 'Community' is used where 'population' is meant.
comments.request: Replace 'community' with 'population'.
comments.quote: You mean “population” not “community”, right? Community in ecology has a different meaning.

comments.issue: The growth model assumes linear growth and omits initial body size as a covariate.
comments.request: Check non-linear growth and include initial body size as a covariate.
comments.quote: This assumes that growth increases linearly over time. However, what if growth rate is non-linear and decreases as the individuals reaches it maximum size? Should not initial body size be included as co-variate?

comments.issue: 'Brain size' is used where relative brain size is meant, without clarification.
comments.request: Clarify that 'brain size' means relative brain size throughout.
comments.quote: you need to have previously clarified that throughout the text “brain size” is used to describe “relative brain size”

comments.issue: The types of models tested are not introduced in advance.
comments.request: Advance the type of models tested so readers can follow.
comments.quote: It would be useful to advance the type of models tested, so the reader knows what you are talking about.

comments.issue: The section on CJS models is confusing and breaks the flow of ideas.
comments.request: Summarise it in one line and move details to the supplement.
comments.quote: Reading this section I got confused, as I know that CJS models allow to include co-variates. Moreover, the section breaks the flow of ideas.

comments.issue: The transplant design is not explained upfront, including why transplants went only one direction.
comments.request: Explain the design and sampling protocol in the first sentence.
comments.quote: The design of the transplant experiment should be briefly explained in the first sentence, so the reader has a general idea of what you did.

comments.issue: Abbreviations and full words are mixed inconsistently.
comments.request: Use abbreviations consistently.
comments.quote: Decide whether use or not abbreviations, but better do not mix both.

comments.issue: The description of the design is unnecessarily complex.
comments.request: Explain simply the two types of control at translocation sites.
comments.quote: I think the description of the design is unnecessarily complex. Why do not explain simply that you used two types of control in each site where HP fish were translocated?

comments.issue: The sampling protocol changed and the reason is not given.
comments.request: Explain why the sampling protocol changed.
comments.quote: So the sampling protocol is not like before. Why has now changed?

comments.issue: The term relative brain size and its explanation appear too late.
comments.request: Introduce the term and explanation earlier.
comments.quote: Why now the term relative brain size is used? And why this explanation here and not before?

comments.issue: It is unclear how differences between translocated and resident individuals were tested.
comments.request: Show the model testing this comparison.
comments.quote: How did you test for differences between translocated and resident individuals? I cannot see this is the model.

comments.issue: Outliers were removed without a non-biological justification.
comments.request: Justify outlier removal, e.g. by measurement error.
comments.quote: Outliers cannot merely be removed from the analyses because they depart from the rest; the removal should be supported by a non-biological justification

comments.issue: Mortality rates in the translocation experiment were not assessed.
comments.request: Assess mortality rates in the translocation experiment.
comments.quote: L219: Why do not assess mortality rates in the translocation experiment?

comments.issue: Establishment success may reflect trap avoidance rather than survival of non-recaptured fish.
comments.request: Explain the logic linking recapture to establishment success.
comments.quote: Is not establishment success the result of surviving the study period? The individuals that were not recaptured may have simply avoided the traps better.

comments.issue: The section lacks a sentence anticipating its main result.
comments.request: Add a sentence anticipating the main result of the section.
comments.quote: In addition, a sentence anticipating the main result of the section would be useful.

comments.issue: The sentence on line 259 is unclear.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence on line 259.
comments.quote: L259: rather than predation regimes, the interest was not in translocated and not translocated individuals?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether selection is described as weak or absent on line 267.
comments.request: Clarify whether selection was weak or absent.
comments.quote: L267: Weak or absent?

comments.issue: The phrase 'As a result, our results' on line 280 is awkward.
comments.request: Reword the phrase on line 280.
comments.quote: L280: “As a result, our results”?

comments.issue: It is surprising that the pattern was not found in the transplanted fish.
comments.request: Explain this discrepancy.
comments.quote: L303: It is also surprising that you did not find a similar pattern in the transplanted fish.

comments.issue: The section on lines 307-317 belongs in the results.
comments.request: Move this section to the results.
comments.quote: L307-317: This section should go to results.

comments.issue: Main effects are assessed in models retaining non-significant interactions.
comments.request: Remove non-significant interactions before assessing main effects.
comments.quote: If interactions are non-significant, they should be removed from the model. Assessing main effects with interaction in the model is not recommended.

reviews.assessment: Novel and exciting transplant result, but the manuscript is hard to follow and the environmental-novelty interpretation ignores more relevant hypotheses.
strengths: well-designed study with robust established metrics
elegant two-part comparative and transplant design
novel, convincing and exciting transplant findings

comments.issue: The wording about mortality and selection in HP versus RO sites is counterintuitive.
comments.request: Clarify the description of previous research on fitness.
comments.quote: The wording implies that mortality is higher in HP vs RO sites, but that selection is stronger in RO vs HP sites which seems counterintuitive (Lines 74-77)

comments.issue: The Cognitive Buffer Hypothesis is not related back to the predictions at the end of the introduction.
comments.request: Clearly state how predictions follow from the hypotheses.
comments.quote: The authors do mention the Cognitive Buffer Hypothesis, but they do not directly relate/reiterate this hypothesis at the end of the Introduction which makes the predictions seem isolated

comments.issue: The choice of relative brain size measures and of including only certain fish sizes needs explanation.
comments.request: Explain these methodological choices.
comments.quote: Some parts of the Methods with regards to the choice of relative brain size measures and the choice of including only fish of a certain size needed more explanation

comments.issue: The link between the system and predictions of the Brain Size-Environmental Change Hypothesis is missing.
comments.request: Explain why RO sites represent greater environmental change.
comments.quote: do RO sites experience greater environmental change? How do the previous results lead to the author’s decision to use this system to test predictions of the Cognitive Buffer/Brain Size-Environmental Change Hypothesis?

comments.issue: Energetic constraints offer a null hypothesis: relaxed predation allows more foraging, enlarging brains regardless of original size.
comments.request: Discuss this alternative null hypothesis.
comments.quote: a null hypothesis to the idea that larger brains are adaptive in RO fish is that, freed from predation risks the fish are able to spend more time foraging and thus have larger brains as a result of investment in foraging vs hiding

comments.issue: The life-history filter hypothesis for brain size evolution is not considered.
comments.request: Consider van Schaik's (2012) life-history filter hypothesis.
comments.quote: I highly recommend the authors consider van Schaik’s (2012) hypothesis of a life-history filter on brain size evolution

comments.issue: RO pools are probably not evolutionarily novel; competition, not novelty, is the more plausible driver.
comments.request: Refocus the interpretation on high intraspecific competition.
comments.quote: I am not convinced that the RO pools represent evolutionary novel environments. This is my largest concern with the manuscript.

comments.issue: The Social Intelligence Hypothesis is more relevant but not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the Social Intelligence and ecological intelligence hypotheses.
comments.quote: A more relevant hypothesis here (in addition the life-history cut-off hypothesis) is the Social Intelligence Hypothesis, which posits that social complexity/larger groups favored the evolution of larger brains

comments.issue: The brain-size growth-rate relationships are extremely weak and their interpretation borders on over-interpretation.
comments.request: Avoid interpreting positive or negative trends in these plots.
comments.quote: I found Discussion of the brain-size growth-rate links bordering on over-interpretation. The relationship was extremely weak for both the comparative study and the RO transplants.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the stated main selective forces (competition in RO, predation mortality in HP) were replicated.
comments.request: Discuss whether these selective forces were replicated.
comments.quote: In addition, the authors mentioned in the Introduction that the main selective forces are competition in RO streams and mortality from predation in HP streams- was that result not replicated here?

comments.issue: The abstract is confusing without context and does not explain how results support the hypothesis.
comments.request: Clarify transplant direction and the fitness proxy in the abstract.
comments.quote: Without context, on first read-through, the Abstract was confusing and difficult to interpret. Transplanted in which direction?

comments.issue: The phrase 'and thus population persistence' dangles at the end of a long sentence.
comments.request: Rework the sentence on line 65.
comments.quote: Line 65: ‘and thus population persistence’ dangles at the end of this long sentence.

comments.issue: The sentence on lines 67-68 is unnecessary as the results already state the relationships are correlational.
comments.request: Remove or revise this sentence.
comments.quote: I am not also not sure this sentence is necessary, the above results already state that the relationships are correlational.

title: Evolutionary double suicide in symbiotic systems

study.system: house mice; three-generation semi-natural food-quality experiment with transcriptomics

editor_summary: Two positive reviews; editor asks for broader literature connections, discussion of lab-condition skepticism, justification of food quality manipulation, and reformatting to Ecology Letters style.

reviews.assessment: Broad-interest, well-designed plasticity study; asks for reorganized results, more literature links and deeper interpretation.
strengths: likely to be of broad interest
quality of experimental design and data
examines phenotypic plasticity generating trait covariances

comments.issue: The results are organized unintuitively: pattern and mechanism analyses should be presented in sequence.
comments.request: Present observed patterns first, then the analyses addressing their mechanism.
comments.quote: I found the organization of the results to be unintuitive.

comments.issue: Connections to the broader literature on food availability, phenotypic plasticity, POLS evidence and resource acquisition are missing.
comments.request: Cite and discuss this literature.
comments.quote: There is quite a big literature on how food availability affects age at first reproduction and fecundity (via phenotypic plasticity). These should be cited.

comments.issue: The dramatic F1 behavioural change may reflect the shift from cages to an open enclosure rather than the diet signal.
comments.request: Address the potential enclosure confound.
comments.quote: If this is due to a shift from being held in cages to being in an open environment, this might suggest this might make the diet signal hard to tease out from the larger effect of the enclosure.

comments.issue: Why female fecundity plasticity changes over different timescales than male fecundity is not explained.
comments.request: Explain this sex difference.
comments.quote: why would plasticity for fecundity in females change over different timescales compared to fecundity rates for males?

comments.issue: Traits diverging across different generations suggest transgenerational inheritance or covarying conditions rather than pure plasticity.
comments.request: Discuss transgenerational inheritance and alternative covarying conditions.
comments.quote: Why would some traits diverge in F1, but other require multiple generations? This is a bit surprising if the mechanism underlying the shifts in trait expression is plasticity, isn't it?

comments.issue: What the results mean for the POLS framework, and whether plastic covariances still count, is not addressed.
comments.request: Discuss the implications for POLS.
comments.quote: I was left wondering what your results mean for our understanding of POLS.

comments.issue: POLS and risk-taking in the title are redundant.
comments.request: Remove the redundancy.
comments.quote: POLS and risk-taking in title are redundant: risk-taking is part of the pace-of-life syndrome

comments.issue: 'Slightly informative inverse Wishart' is vague and not reproducible; the prior specification or code is not provided.
comments.request: Provide the prior specification in the text or share the analysis code.
comments.quote: “slightly informative inverse Wishart” is very vague and not reproducible. Please provide the prior specification in the text, or better yet, make the full code required to reproduce the analyses available.

comments.issue: The discussion passage claims a distinction from phenotypic studies, but the data are still phenotypic, just partitioned among individuals.
comments.request: Rephrase to clarify the distinction.
comments.quote: this is still the phenotypic level (as is your data) – it’s simply that the phenotypic data is partitioned to the among individual level.

comments.issue: Table 1 would be clearer as a matrix of correlation plots.
comments.request: Consider presenting Table 1 as correlation plots.
comments.quote: Table 1 could better be represented as a matrix of correlation plots.

reviews.assessment: Novel, high-quality multi-generational experiment; asks for stronger justification of food quality and fuller discussion of lab limitations.
strengths: rates high on novelty and originality
very high scientific quality with state-of-the-art analyses
combination of experiment and gene expression quantification

comments.issue: It is not justified why food quality rather than food availability should affect POLS; only low-quality animals show the assumed trade-off.
comments.request: Justify the choice of food quality and engage with density-variation theory.
comments.quote: I still miss some more justification why variation in food quality, and not food availability, should affect POLS.

comments.issue: The potential for more general conclusions from the novel findings is not fully explored.
comments.request: Draw broader conclusions at the end of the discussion.
comments.quote: the novel findings of this study could give rise to some more general conclusions at the end of the discussion but this potential is not fully explored in the current version of the manuscript

comments.issue: Key natural selection pressures (parasites, diseases, predators) are absent in the semi-natural setting, and the caveats of laboratory studies are not thoroughly addressed.
comments.request: Discuss the implications of the laboratory setting for adaptive inferences.
comments.quote: important natural selection pressures, such as parasites, diseases and predators, are absent under these semi-natural conditions

comments.issue: The abstract lacks sample sizes and the number of generations.
comments.request: Add sample sizes and generation number to the abstract.
comments.quote: Add sample sizes and the number of generations studied.

comments.issue: The scientific species name is not given in the abstract.
comments.request: Add the scientific species name.
comments.quote: Please consider adding the scientific species name.

comments.issue: The individuals are descendants of wild-caught mice, but the number of generations is not specified.
comments.request: State how many generations separate the study animals from wild-caught ancestors.
comments.quote: The individuals used in this study are not directly wild-caught but decedents of wild-caught individuals (after how many generations). Please be specific.

comments.issue: Model details are insufficient; prior robustness and the calculation of among-individual correlations are unclear.
comments.request: Provide more model detail.
comments.quote: Please provide some more detail on the models. How robust are the findings to different priors? How did you calculate the among-individual correlations?

comments.issue: The results section is unclear about whether there was differential expression between treatment groups.
comments.request: Detail the differential expression results.
comments.quote: This results part is not very clear. Please detail whether there was differential expression between treatment groups, as the sub-title suggests.

comments.issue: The conclusion that no genetic differentiation occurred is not supported by non-coding microsatellite data.
comments.request: Explain how microsatellites inform functional genetic differentiation.
comments.quote: Population genetic differentiation analyses are entirely based on microsats, which are non-coding. How can genetic differentiation based on this marker type be informative for judgement of functional genetic differentiation?

comments.issue: The reference list needs serious proof-reading (italics, page numbers, journal names).
comments.request: Proof-read and fix the reference list.
comments.quote: The reference list needs serious proof-reading (species names in italic, missing page numbers, missing journal names, etc.).

comments.issue: Figures are not aligned in design and use inconsistent colour-coding between Fig. 2 and Fig. 5.
comments.request: Improve and align the figure design.
comments.quote: The figures can still be improved and aligned in design to each other. For example, please use comparable colour-coding in Fig. 2 to Fig. 5.

title: Fast adjustment of pace‐of‐life and risk‐taking to changes in food quality by altered gene expression in house mice

study.system: threespine stickleback and prickly sculpin; lake populations

editor_summary: Editor and reviewers were unanimously positive; recommends minor revision, particularly regarding the statistical treatment.

reviews.assessment: Much improved and exciting manuscript, well framed with interesting results, and only extremely few comments remaining.

comments.issue: The authors downplay the abiotic variation among lakes that their own data reveal.
comments.request: Acknowledge the abiotic variation more directly in the supporting information.
comments.quote: the authors seem to slightly downplay the abiotic variation among lakes compared to what their data reveal

comments.issue: The PC2 result, where sympatric lakes differ from both allopatric types, is never discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the PC2 differentiation of sympatric lakes.
comments.quote: The latter result for PC2 is never really discussed as far as I can tell.

comments.issue: The models on line 435 include the abiotic PCs separately rather than together.
comments.request: Redo the models including both abiotic PCs simultaneously.
comments.quote: I think the analyses should be re-done to include both PCs within the models, simultaneously testing for all the potentially important effects of abiotic and biotic factors.

comments.issue: Figs. 2, 4 and 5 could better convey allopatric versus sympatric differences with different symbol colours.
comments.request: Use distinguishing colours or symbols for the two site types.
comments.quote: I wonder if the authors should consider a slight alteration in Figs. 2, 4, and 5 simply to help visually convey the differences between allopatric and sympatric sites by using different symbol colors.

comments.issue: Four line-level edits (typo 'coastal', a missing figure reference, a confusing phrase, an extraneous legend symbol).
comments.quote: I think the authors forgot to state which figure they were referring to.

title: Species divergence under competition and shared predation

study.system: host-parasite interactions; 154 studies, 582 effect sizes

editor_summary: All three reviews favourable; the one substantive request is to explore the random-effects structure, add detail on variance partitioning, and compare models with species-level and phylogenetic random effects (or show it is unnecessary).

reviews.assessment: Interesting, well-conducted analysis filling an important niche; praises it, with a good number of style and wording recommendations only.
strengths: discussion functions as an effective review

comments.issue: The title is uninformative and wishy-washy rather than active and informative of the results.
comments.request: Retitle to be active and informative, e.g. 'Parasitism has a wide range of negative and positive effects...'.
comments.quote: Needs retitling to be active and informative of the results: the title is uninformative and a bit wishy-washy currently, and gives the appearance of attempting to titillate.

comments.issue: The phrasing about individuals hosting parasites implies some host zero parasites, which is arguably impossible.
comments.request: Rephrase as 'a minority of individuals hosting the great majority of parasites'.
comments.quote: I would rephrase this as “with a minority of individuals hosting the great majority of parasites”, as the odds of any individuals hosting zero parasites of any species is infinitesimal and arguably impossible

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the definitive host is never the consumer in the trophic transmission classification.
comments.request: Clarify the definition of definitive host used.
comments.quote: 122: Is the definitive host never the one doing the consumption?

comments.issue: Relevant literature on predation suppression by trophically transmitted parasites is not cited.
comments.request: Consider the suggested paper on predation suppression.
comments.quote: 126: I thought you might be interested in predation suppression by trophically transmitted parasites: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1600-0706.2011.19585.x

comments.issue: Cannibalism is within-species, so lumping it with predation may be inconsistent with the intra/interspecific competition treatment.
comments.request: Clarify how cannibalism is classified relative to predation.
comments.quote: cannibalism is inherently between individuals of the same species; could that just be lumped in with predation in the same way that intra- and interspecific competition was?
101: very repetitive; I would suggest rephrasing to make it clearer that this paragraph is about to delve into the specifics rather than making a general point about the possibility.

reviews.assessment: Articulate, robust meta-analysis with appropriate methods; outstanding questions concern random-effects structure, variance component identifiability, and model reporting.
strengths: appropriate literature search, inclusion criteria and random effects
accounts for host, parasite and interaction phylogeny
sufficient power for complex rma.mv models

comments.issue: Pseudo-replication by host and parasite species; species-level random effects are needed alongside phylogenetic ones to avoid biased fixed effects.
comments.request: Consider alternative random effects structures and compare them formally (e.g. REML).
comments.quote: models with a phylogenetic effect but not an additional species-level effect can produce biased estimates. Arguably, including both phylogenetic and species-level random effects for both hosts and parasites would likely be a more robust model to fit.

comments.issue: Variance components of the complex random effects may not be identifiable.
comments.request: Check identifiability with likelihood profile plots.
comments.quote: it would also be helpful to check whether the variance components for the random effects are identifiable. This can be done with likelihood profile plots for each random effect (as a sanity check on possible overfitting).

comments.issue: I2 variance partitioning is used in Table 1 but never described in the Methods.
comments.request: Briefly describe I2 in the Methods.
comments.quote: it was helpful to see variance partitioned through I2 in Table 1, but the authors should also briefly describe I2 in the Methods.

comments.issue: The fixed effects included in each model are unclear, including whether models were univariate, how interactions were chosen, and whether sampling variance weighting was used.
comments.request: Clarify the fixed-effect structure, interaction choices and weighting.
comments.quote: the details of what factors were included as fixed effects in each model were somewhat unclear. L271-272 notes the 5 fixed effects (species interaction, fitness component, parasite evolutionary strategy, agent parasitized, habitat)

comments.issue: The degree to which each model explains variation in the effect sizes is not reported.
comments.request: Provide pseudo-R2 values for the rma.mv models.
comments.quote: One missing detail in the presentation of model results (alongside the QM statistics that are reported) is the degree to which each model explains variation in both effect size measures (mean and variance).

reviews.assessment: Novel and important meta-analysis with clear figures and a good discussion of variance; line-level clarifications requested on wording and result statements.
strengths: important results worthy of a broad audience
good discussion of the high variance

comments.issue: The stated goal of studying species interactions within food webs does not match the discussion, which barely mentions food webs.
comments.request: Reframe the goal as species interactions, dropping the food-web context.
comments.quote: This sentence states that the goal was to study species interactions within food webs, but the discussion has very little mention of food webs.

comments.issue: Superlative descriptors of responses (severely, strongly, large, severe) are arbitrary and overstated.
comments.request: Remove or tone down superlatives and use consistent defined language.
