comments.quote: I think that you could remove or tone down the superlative words describing the responses throughout, for example; ‘severely’ (394), ‘strongly’ (396), ‘large’ (410), and ‘severe’ (411).

comments.issue: The summary statement suggests a bimodal response rather than the continuous negative-to-positive response.
comments.request: Clarify the summary statement.
comments.quote: I am a bit confused by this summary statement. From this description I would expect a bimodal response, not the continuous response from negative to positive.

comments.issue: The section at lines 531-553 contains too much content and reads like a list of options.
comments.request: Restructure this section.
comments.quote: I think this section could use some restructuring – a lot of content is in this paragraph and it comes across feeling a bit like a list of options.

comments.issue: It is unclear which results the sentences at lines 557-560 refer to, and whether trophically-transmitted parasites are only in intermediate hosts.
comments.request: Clarify the results referred to, including the fitness breakdown.
comments.quote: I am a bit confused by these sentences and what results they are referring to. Do you mean ‘fitness’ here? I don’t see results where fitness is broken down by trophically-transmitted parasites.

comments.issue: The habitat pattern may be driven by parasite type composition, but no supplementary figure or table shows this.
comments.request: Add a supplemental figure/table of parasite type distributions across habitats.
comments.quote: it might make sense to have a supplemental figure/table that shows how parasite types (e.g. nematode, acanthocephalan, etc) are distributed between the habitat types.

comments.issue: The mean response referred to at line 1036 is ambiguous.
comments.request: Clarify what mean response is meant (e.g. host mean response).
comments.quote: Line 1036 – effects of parasites on what mean response? Host mean response?

title: Resetting our expectations for parasites and their effects on species interactions: a meta‐analysis

study.system: Drosophila melanogaster; three-generation experimental evolution of diet preference

editor_summary: Editor finds the work interesting but flags major concerns: sexual selection was not excluded, the fecundity drop at generation zero is puzzling, the ancestral population was not dimorphic, and the sex-by-treatment interaction was not tested.

reviews.assessment: Fascinating and significant topic, but the design cannot separate resource competition from sexual selection and some analyses are unclear.
strengths: clearly explains the novelty and significance
topic of interest to many researchers
highlights resource competition as a cause of sexual dimorphism

comments.issue: Sexual selection operated during the experiment, so resource competition cannot be isolated as the cause of dimorphism.
comments.request: Limit opportunities for sexual selection or temper the causal claim.
comments.quote: I do not think the design goes far enough to disentangle the effects of resource competition and sexual selection

comments.issue: Fecundity dropped sharply at generation zero and never recovered, so calling the evolution adaptive is questionable.
comments.request: Explain the low fecundity and justify or temper the adaptive-evolution claim.
comments.quote: Is claiming that evolution was adaptive during the experiment (line 238, figure 2A) misleading as fecundity of generation zero females was abnormally low

comments.issue: The Statistical Analysis section is unclear and inconsistent with the results (mixed vs linear model, vague weighting).
comments.request: Rewrite the Statistical Analysis section to describe the approach clearly.
comments.quote: I found the quality of the writing to be weaker compared to the rest of the manuscript. Consequently, I’m not sure I fully understand approach taken.

comments.issue: The key sex-by-treatment interaction was not tested and the statistical-power justification is unconvincing.
comments.request: Fit and report the sex-by-treatment interaction model.
comments.quote: I was surprised when I read that the author avoided using a model that tested whether there was an interaction effect between sex and the treatment

comments.issue: Figure 3a lacks replicate labels and error bars, and the axis units may be wrong (micrograms vs microliters).
comments.request: Label replicate populations, show errors and fix the axis units.
comments.quote: I think it would good if the open circles had indicators as to what replicate population that they are from

comments.issue: Figure 3b does not identify which points belong to which food treatment.
comments.request: Indicate the treatment membership of points in Figure 3b.
comments.quote: figure 3b could be improved by indicating which points belong to low food treatment and which points to the high food treatment

comments.issue: The mortality assays are not described in the methods.
comments.request: Describe the mortality assays in the methods.
comments.quote: The mortality assays don’t seem to be described in the methods.

comments.issue: Degrees of freedom differ between tests and do not match the stated sample size.
comments.request: Explain why the degrees of freedom differ from the stated n.
comments.quote: It is not explained why the degrees of freedom for each test is different (1,236 and 1,195) and why neither reflect the methods

comments.issue: Mean fitness is actually female fitness divided by two; male fitness is not estimable from this design.
comments.request: Relabel the fitness measure and clarify what it represents.
comments.quote: Estimates of mean fitness (figure 2a, line 238) is really a measure of female fitness divided by 2.

comments.issue: Reference style at line 90 should be revised.
comments.quote: Line 90, revise referencing style for “prompted Dawin (Dawin 1871)”

reviews.assessment: Praises the elegant experiment but argues the diet shifts may reflect reproductive roles rather than intersexual resource competition.

comments.issue: Any competition acting through sex-specific reproductive roles would generate the observed pattern, not intersexual competition specifically.
comments.request: Reconsider the causal interpretation of the diet shifts.
comments.quote: any form of competition, whether between females, between females and males, or between females and another species, would generate the observed result

comments.issue: The Discussion should weigh reproductive-role and intersexual-competition mechanisms and the open question between them.
comments.request: Emphasise both mechanisms and the remaining question in the Discussion.
comments.quote: we still need to know whether competition for the same type of resources alone can drive sexual dimorphisms

comments.issue: Line-level text edits: 'fitnesses', 'our' to 'my', and adjacent numbers that are hard to read.
comments.quote: in many places, sentences contain two numbers in succession (lines 143, 148, 164-5, for example)

comments.issue: Figure 1 axes numbers are too small and the legend does not label the sexes.
comments.request: Enlarge the axes numbers and label female (blue) and male (red) in the legend.
comments.quote: axes numbers need to be larger. Legend should indicate female (blue) and male (red).

reviews.assessment: Interesting experimental evolution study, but several design details are unclear and the artificial assay raises relevance concerns.

comments.issue: Density is ambiguous: 16 flies in total or 16 of each sex.
comments.request: Clarify the density used.
comments.quote: was the density 16 flies in total, or 16 flies of each sex? Clarify

comments.issue: The paragraph at lines 179-182 is confusing.
comments.request: Clarify that paragraph.
comments.quote: 179-182:This paragraph is confusing – please clarify

comments.issue: Unclear whether high-food vials also ran out of food, which would create competition at the end.
comments.request: Report whether capillary tubes were empty in the high treatment.
comments.quote: I am assuming that in 48hours with capillary tubes, the low competition groups finished all the food from each capillary tube.

comments.issue: High evaporation and artificial CAFE assays undermine the ecological relevance of the treatments.
comments.request: Test humidity effects and discuss the assay's limitations.
comments.quote: the treatments that you are imposing are not ecologically relevant either

comments.issue: The ancestral population lacked a known sexual dimorphism, contradicting the literature and hinting at methodological problems.
comments.request: Explain why the starting population was not dimorphic for diet.
comments.quote: Why do you think your starting population showed no sexual dimorphism for diet consumption? This trait is known to be sexually dimorphic.

title: Rapid evolution of ecological sexual dimorphism driven by resource competition

study.system: within-host parasite dynamics; food-web loop analysis models

editor_summary: Editor: sharpen the paper's focus and goals, justify the modeling approach, expand coverage of prior loop analysis, highlight novelty, and connect more to real host-pathogen systems and Lafferty et al. 2015.

reviews.assessment: Enjoys the comprehensive analyses and logical points, but questions the paper's broad interest, its main aim and the relevance of deterministic stability models.

comments.issue: The main aim of the work is never clear; the intro opens with a diverse overview and a vague question.
comments.request: Articulate the key question of the paper clearly at the start.
comments.quote: My first issue was that it was never quite clear what the main aim of the work was – the opening paragraph of the Intro provided a rather diverse overview of different outcomes of various different systems

comments.issue: The framework relies on deterministic local stability analyses, ignoring transients, stochasticity and time delays relevant to infection.
comments.request: Justify the deterministic stability approach or extend analyses to these factors.
comments.quote: this approach relies on local stability analyses of deterministic ODE-based models, with associated assumptions about system equilibria, irrelevance of stochastic effects and time delays etc.

comments.issue: Holt & Dobson (2006) is not cited as an early application of community modules to disease ecology.
comments.request: Cite Holt & Dobson (2006).
comments.quote: the chapter by Holt & Dobson (2006, in ‘Disease Ecology: community structure and pathogen dynamics’, Eds Collinge et al) should be cited

comments.issue: The comparison between within-host and community ecology scenarios is not novel or helpful and becomes a distraction.
comments.request: Cut the repeated community ecology comparisons and focus on within-host dynamics.
comments.quote: I don’t see the comparison between within-host dynamic scenarios and community ecology scenarios to be hugely novel or helpful.

comments.issue: Lines 111-129 are a weighty summary of key findings.
comments.request: Trim this summary and make it more accessible.
comments.quote: Lines 111-129 is quite weighty as a general summary of the key findings – any way to trim this down and make it more accessible would really help

comments.issue: 3 line-level copy edits
comments.quote: Line 227 – I’m not sure “spread” is the right word here. “show”?

comments.issue: The abbreviation 'ab' is not defined in the main text.
comments.request: Define 'ab' at first use.
comments.quote: Line 166 – “ab” isn’t defined in the main text – we can probably infer what it means from the surrounding text, but it would be preferable to define it clearly at first use.

comments.issue: The stable and oscillation regions in Fig. 4 legend look pink rather than orange.
comments.request: Check the colours in the Fig. 4 legend and plot.
comments.quote: Line 239 etc and Fig 4 legend – probably just my computer or my eyes, but the stable and oscillation regions in Fig 4 look pink to me, not orange

comments.issue: The abbreviation 'alt SS' is unnecessary.
comments.request: Write 'alternative stable states' in full.
comments.quote: Line 498 onwards – I don’t think the abbreviation “alt SS” is necessary – I think fine to just write “alternative stable states” in full.

title: Niche theory for within‐host parasite dynamics: Analogies to food web modules via feedback loops

study.system: log response ratio meta-analysis; simulation study of missing SDs

editor_summary: Editor sees merit but agrees with R3 that presentation needs work: systematically compare approaches with multiple imputation, guide when shortcuts suffice, improve method names and Fig. 1, and use MI in the case study.

reviews.assessment: Values the method's importance for ecology but is confused about central aspects of weighting and heterogeneity, and about the final recommendation of Method 1A.
strengths: well reasoned and supported from accepted previous work

comments.issue: The significance of the method as more than a minor technical advance is understated.
comments.request: Argue more forcefully why estimating missing SDs for lnRR matters.
comments.quote: The authors could make this point of why a method for the estimation of missing SDs for LnRRs is more than a minor technical advance more forcefully

comments.issue: The paper does not explain why weighting and heterogeneity estimation are central, or why unweighted GLMs are insufficient.
comments.request: Discuss why weighting matters and why unweighted GLMs are inadequate.
comments.quote: this bears more discussion, and perhaps some convincing argument as to why unweighted generalized linear models are insufficient for meta-analysis

comments.issue: Unclear why averaged CVs fully express inverse-precision weighting; the constancy assumption seems to negate weighting's purpose.
comments.request: Explain the weighting rationale clearly, including for readers with less statistical background.
comments.quote: I was unclear as to why averaged values fully express the usefulness of weighting by the inverse of precision

comments.issue: The simulated range of sample sizes may not represent real ecological meta-analyses.
comments.request: Justify or widen the simulated range of sample sizes.
comments.quote: Was the range in sample sizes sufficient to represent the very wide range in actual ecological (or other) meta-analyses?

comments.issue: Sample sizes used in the simulations are not reported.
comments.request: Report the n's used in the simulations.
comments.quote: Please report the sample sizes (n’s) actually used in the simulations.

comments.issue: If CVs are homogeneous, why weighting is needed at all, or why an unweighted analysis is insufficient, is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain why unweighted analysis is insufficient when CVs are homogeneous.
comments.quote: If the CV values are fairly homogeneous across studies, why is any of this necessary?

comments.issue: How the random-effects component (tau^2) was estimated in the simulations is not described.
comments.request: Describe how tau^2 was estimated.
comments.quote: How was the random effect component estimated in the simulations?

comments.issue: Equation 7 appears to be missing a plus sign at the end of line 147.
comments.request: Add the missing plus sign.
comments.quote: In Eq 7, shouldn’t there be a "+" at the end of line 147

comments.issue: Equation 8 should be credited to Hedges and Olkin (1985).
comments.request: Cite Hedges and Olkin (1985) for Eq 8.
comments.quote: Eq 8 was, I believe, first suggested by Hedges and Olkin in their 1985 textbook, and if I am remembering that correctly, that should be cited here

comments.issue: Treatment of non-independence is unexplained and should be separated from the missingness discussion.
comments.request: Explain the non-independence treatment in detail, separately from missingness.
comments.quote: I don’t understand the way non-independence was treated; since this is a substantive and substantial issue, this should be explained in more detail

comments.issue: Results do not contrast the one-effect-size-per-study case with non-independent cases or give practical guidance.
comments.request: Highlight both cases in the results and advise analysts working with non-independent data.
comments.quote: The results should also highlight the outcome for the one-effect size per study case vs. the other cases with non-independent outcomes

comments.issue: Simulations omit very large sample sizes, which are common in real meta-analyses.
comments.request: Simulate some very large sample sizes.
comments.quote: simulating a collection of studies with some very large samples would be useful

comments.issue: 'Abundance data' at line 351 is undefined (biomass? proportions?).
comments.request: Clarify what abundance data means.
comments.quote: Line 351: What exactly is meant by abundance data? Is this biomass? Proportions?

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 378-380 is unclear and ungrammatical.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence clearly.
comments.quote: was not clear (and not really a grammatical sentence); please clarify

comments.issue: The recommendation of Method 1A despite Method 1B performing better is confusing.
comments.request: Explain in more detail why Method 1A is recommended.
comments.quote: I don’t understand the recommendation to use Method 1A, if Method 1B performed better

reviews.assessment: Strongly positive; praises the contribution, code and writing, with only minor comments on clarity and figures.
strengths: great contribution to handling missing data
code and case studies provided in R

comments.issue: Early in the manuscript, how cross-study CVs substitute for missing SDs is unclear.
comments.request: Add a clarification around lines 151-152.
comments.quote: it was not clear early on in the MS how weighted cross-study CVs can substitute the missing SDs

comments.issue: No rationale is given for stopping missing-SD levels at 55%.
comments.request: Explain why missingness levels stop at 55%.
comments.quote: I am curious of why the levels for the missing SDs stopped at 55%

comments.issue: No rationale is given for the chosen K levels (12, 30, 100).
comments.request: Explain the choice of K levels.
comments.quote: Was there a specific reason for the choice of K levels 12, 30, and 100?

comments.issue: Trends at lines 320-322 are hard to see because differences are tiny.
comments.request: Quantify the differences or use a clearer visualization than violin plots.
comments.quote: The “trends” that are mentioned are hard to see, the differences are very small

comments.issue: The claim about overestimating heterogeneity is hard to verify from Fig 3A.
comments.request: Show this result more clearly.
comments.quote: It is hard for me to confirm this statement while looking at Fig 3A, perhaps the violin plot is not helpful to showcase this point?

comments.issue: 'All including analysis' wording is confusing.
comments.request: Change to 'all simulations including analysis'.
comments.quote: consider changing “all including analysis” (sounds confusing)

comments.issue: Figure references at lines 330-338 may point to the wrong figure.
comments.request: Check that in-text figure references match the correct figures.
comments.quote: I think it should be Fig 4 in the rest of the paragraph; please double-check if the references in the text match the correct figures

comments.issue: Line-level copy edits: 'Implimentation' (L339), missing 'BY' (L368-369), 'oneS' (L417), 'Meths' in Fig 2.
comments.quote: Lines 417. I think it needs to say “are not the first oneS to use”

comments.issue: Figures may not be color blind friendly.
comments.request: Use color blind-friendly palettes in all figures.
comments.quote: I am not sure if they are color blind friendly; if they are not, I recommend switching to color blind-friendly palettes in all figures

comments.issue: X-axis labels are too small.
comments.request: Increase the size of x-axis labels.
comments.quote: I think increasing the size of x-axis labels, if possible, will also be helpful

comments.issue: Figure 1 legend should distinguish new methods and cite the existing one.
comments.request: Tag new methods and cite the non-new method.
comments.quote: Since the legend highlights that 3 of the methods are new, perhaps the title of each method in the Figure could have a “NEW” tag and the citation for the one that is not new

comments.issue: Color should also highlight the variance column so differences between methods stand out.
comments.request: Extend the color coding to the variance column.
comments.quote: if you were to add that same color to the column of the variance, to highlight the changes regarding each of the previous methods

comments.issue: Panel A should be rotated to compare coverage across panels.
comments.request: Rotate panel A so scales align across panels.
comments.quote: I suggest rotating panel A so that we can visually compare the coverage across all panels since the scale used is the same

comments.issue: Method labels 1.1/1.2 are confusing; use 1A/1B consistently.
comments.request: Use the 1A/1B letters as in the text.
comments.quote: Is method 1.1 equivalent to 1A and 1.2 equivalent to 1B? If so, I would use the letters like in the rest of the text

comments.issue: X-axis levels are hard to interpret; use high/low heterogeneity labels.
comments.request: Simplify the x-axis and put details in the caption.
comments.quote: Maybe instead of the current levels in the x-axis, it could be simplified to “high heterogeneity” versus “low heterogeneity” and have the details in the figure caption?

comments.issue: Coverage differences with sample size are not shown.
comments.request: Add a panel showing coverage by sample size.
comments.quote: Were there any differences in coverage with sample size? Could that be another in another panel?

comments.issue: Figure 4 caption says 'Results on coverage' but should refer to bias in heterogeneity.
comments.request: Correct the Figure 4 caption.
comments.quote: I believe the caption should refer to bias in heterogeneity, and currently starts as “Results on coverage”, same as in Figure 3

comments.issue: Figure 4 x-axis labels should be simplified like Figure 3.
comments.request: Use low/high heterogeneity labels on the x-axis.
comments.quote: The same comment as in figure 3, it will look cleaner and easier to understand if having “low heterogeneity” and “high heterogeneity” on the x-axis

comments.issue: Panel D shows only Method 1B, unlike other figures; label methods directly in panels.
comments.request: Keep methods consistent across figures and label panel D.
comments.quote: Why only method 1B appears on panel D given that in the other figures Method 1A was compared to Method 1B? I think consistency across figures is helpful

comments.issue: Supplementary figure captions wrongly refer to multi-level models instead of random-effect models.
comments.request: Correct the supplementary figure captions.
comments.quote: Based on the main text, it seems that the supplementary figures should be showing the results of the random-effect meta-analytic models

reviews.assessment: Has mixed feelings: the methods are interesting but unpolished, with key assumptions relegated to the discussion and practical guidance missing.

comments.issue: Manuscript lacks the polish expected for Ecology Letters.
comments.request: Improve organization and presentation.
comments.quote: it lacks the polish expected from an Ecol. Letters paper

comments.issue: Vague method labels (1A, M1A) are impossible to keep track of in results and discussion.
comments.request: Use clearer, memorable method names.
comments.quote: Many interesting approaches are introduced, yet they are vaguely referred to Method 1A, M1A, etc. I couldn’t remember for the life of me what these were

comments.issue: Table 1 is hard to navigate and does not directly report needed information.
comments.request: Redesign Table 1 to report the needed information simply.
comments.quote: Table 1 just had me hop-scotching around the find information rather than simply reporting what I need to know

comments.issue: Key assumptions of the methods are relegated to the discussion instead of the methods.
comments.request: Integrate assumptions and trade-offs of each method into the methods.
comments.quote: all assumptions need to be integrated with methods, so the reader knows right away what challenges and issues exist when implementing these tools

comments.issue: The risk when CV homogeneity assumptions fail, and how to evaluate them, is not addressed.
comments.request: Explain the risks and how to check the homogeneity assumptions.
comments.quote: if you assume the CVs between the contrast pairs are homogeneous, and further also homogeneous across studies, then what is the risk if they are not, and how can you evaluate these assumptions

comments.issue: Why the methods are limited to lnRR rather than SMD is not addressed.
comments.request: Explain or extend the methods to SMD.
comments.quote: Other issues I would like to see addressed is why these methods are limited to lnRR? Why not implement these with SMD?

comments.issue: Results for different missingness levels, the most practical information, are absent.
comments.request: Report results across missingness levels.
comments.quote: where are the results about various levels of missingness – these seem important as they offer the most practical information on when imputing lots of information fails

comments.issue: No guidance on how ecologists should report meta-analyses using imputed SDs.
comments.request: Provide reporting guidance, including minimum information and conflicting results.
comments.quote: how should ecologists report applications? Should they contrast between imputed and non-imputed syntheses?

title: A robust and readily implementable method for the meta‐analysis of response ratios with and without missing standard deviations

study.system: habitat fragmentation; reanalysis of Chase et al. patch datasets

editor_summary: Positive reviews; editor asks to tap fragmentation-scaling literature, temper applied conclusions, explain Fig. 1 ellipses and Fig. 3 legend, and fix the appendix title.

reviews.assessment: Important contribution to landscape ecology with an extensive dataset, but explanatory power and some framing issues need attention.

comments.issue: Marginal r2 values are very low and random factors explain most variance; conditional r2 values are missing.
comments.request: Discuss low explanatory power and report conditional r2.
comments.quote: many of the the marginal r2 values presented in the statistical tables are very low

comments.issue: The claim that Chase et al.'s findings are widely misapplied is not convincingly demonstrated.
comments.request: Substantiate the misuse claim with per-study details.
comments.quote: I am not convinced by what is presented that the problem is as widespread as they suggest

comments.issue: The dataset is not described in this paper.
comments.request: Add a paragraph describing the dataset.
comments.quote: a paragraph summarizing the data set and relevant details about how it was compiled would remove the need for readers to go back to Chase et al.

comments.issue: How landscapes were assigned to matrix quality levels is unclear.
comments.request: Describe the matrix-quality categorization.
comments.quote: how were individual landscape or regions assigned to one of the three level of matrix quality?

comments.issue: Generalist/specialist taxa were assigned from relative abundance rather than attributes, with no stated limitations.
comments.request: Justify the assignment and its limitations.
comments.quote: The assignment of taxa as generalist vs. specialist also concerns me because this was done based on the relative abundance of different taxa

comments.issue: Dispersal ability and patch connectivity are not explored despite being central to landscape-scale patterns.
comments.request: Address dispersal ability and patch connectivity.
comments.quote: the lack of attention that is paid to a key element of landscapes that can dictate population dynamics and community structure, which is patch connectivity

comments.issue: Fragmentation is rarely observed without habitat loss, questioning the applied relevance of the argument.
comments.request: Discuss how the argument applies to real fragmented landscapes.
comments.quote: But in real landscapes, how often does fragmentation proceed without habitat loss?

comments.issue: The discussion text on lines 134-149 adds little value.
comments.request: Cut this text and add concrete examples.
comments.quote: I didn’t find a lot of value in the text on lines 134 – 149

comments.issue: The logic for choosing reference treatments in the models is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the choice of reference treatments.
comments.quote: how are reference treatments chosen in the models? Is there some logic to this?

reviews.assessment: Important, close-to-decisive contribution to the SLOSS debate; mostly needs clarification of complex methods and predictions.
strengths: important contribution to the SLOSS debate

comments.issue: Predictions 1 and 2 are not explained enough for the paper to stand alone without reading Chase et al.
comments.request: Explain the two predictions in enough detail to stand alone.
comments.quote: I think more space is needed on explaining prediction 1 and prediction 2 in the introduction or methods.

comments.issue: The methods for testing Prediction 1 (lines 235-251) are too dense to understand.
comments.request: Clarify the Prediction 1 methods.
comments.quote: the methods behind testing Prediction 1 are very complex. Lines 235-251 are very dense

comments.issue: The resampling approach is phrased as a generic statement rather than what was done.
comments.request: Rephrase as a declarative statement.
comments.quote: Took me a while to figure out this was a declarative statement of what you did.

comments.issue: Whether there are one or two 0-1 indices is confusing.
comments.request: Explain the indices.
comments.quote: What I found most confusing is there 1 or 2 indices ranging from 0-1.

comments.issue: What a single data point in Fig. 3a represents is not clear from methods or legend.
comments.request: Clarify the resampling design and figure legend.
comments.quote: Understanding what a single data point in figure 3a is is a little mind bending and essential.

comments.issue: Averaging pairwise beta diversity misses higher-order interactions.
comments.request: Provide more detail on the beta-diversity calculation.
comments.quote: I'm not a fan of averaging pairwise beta diversity - it misses higher order interactions such as species that show up in 2 fragments

comments.issue: The IUCN species result lacks its own data figure.
comments.request: Add a figure for the IUCN result.
comments.quote: The result on IUCN listed species is really important and neat. It needs its own data figure.

comments.issue: The paper's ordering (methods last) weakens the logical connections.
comments.request: Reorder the paper to improve logical flow.
comments.quote: I hope the authors will take the opportunity from reordering the paper to improve the logical connections and explanation

comments.issue: The term 'Lands. complementation' in Figure 1 is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the term in the legend.
comments.quote: not obvious what “Lands. compelementation” is. It needs explanation in the legend.

reviews.assessment: Extremely compelling in concept, methods and results, with concerns about motivation framing, nearest-neighbor confounding and CI interpretation.
strengths: extremely compelling concept, methods and results

comments.issue: The motivation is framed around citation misuse rather than the scientific question.
comments.request: Reframe the motivation beyond citation misuse.
comments.quote: I believe some reframing of the motivation for this study is necessary, so as not to suggest that the only reason for conducting this study is that some authors have (potentially) misquoted Chase et al. (2020).

comments.issue: Appendix 1.1 quotes appear taken out of context and miscategorized into black/white bins.
comments.request: Re-examine and recategorize the Appendix 1.1 quotes.
comments.quote: I feel that several quotes have been taken out of context and potentially miscategorized.

comments.issue: Differing nearest-neighbor distances among resampled patch sets could inflate richness and confound results.
comments.request: Describe or account for nearest-neighbor distances.
comments.quote: comparing sets of resampled patches that differ in nearest-neighbor distance across orders of magnitude could artificially inflate species richness due to species turnover across far away patches

comments.issue: Relationships are called 'strong' although confidence intervals include zero.
comments.request: Consider CI width and overlap with zero.
comments.quote: some relationships are referred to as ‘strong’ when the estimate is relatively large, yet the CI includes zero

comments.issue: 'Equivalent' is the wrong characterization; 'analogous' is better.
comments.request: Use 'analogous' instead of 'equivalent'.
comments.quote: Line 10: I’m not sure I would characterize these patterns as ‘equivalent’, but perhaps ‘analogous’.

comments.issue: Suggested edits to the abstract sentence would improve clarity.
comments.request: Apply the suggested edits.
comments.quote: I believe the following edits to this sentence will improve clarity.

comments.issue: The SLOSS debate is not cited.
comments.request: Cite the SLOSS debate.
comments.quote: Line 31-33: I think the SLOSS debate should be cited here.

comments.issue: The extrapolation referred to at lines 46-47 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the extrapolation referred to.
comments.quote: Line 46-47: What extrapolation is being referred to here?

comments.issue: The statement about misquoting comes across harshly.
comments.request: Soften this statement.
comments.quote: As written, this may come across quite harshly. The act of misquoting a publication does not threaten biodiversity.

comments.issue: The paragraph at lines 78-85 belongs in the discussion.
comments.request: Move the paragraph to the discussion.
comments.quote: Line 78-85: This paragraph seems more suited to the discussion.

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 91-94 is complex and its model numbering is unclear.
comments.request: Break up the sentence and clarify model numbers.
comments.quote: Please consider breaking up the sentence for clarity. In addition, is this sentence referring to models 1-6 or 7-11?

comments.issue: The negative relationship does not always hold, but exceptions are not discussed.
comments.request: Note and discuss the exceptions.
comments.quote: The negative relationship does not always hold (as this sentence as written suggests), so it may be interesting to note and discuss those cases.

comments.issue: The IUCN richness sentence does not acknowledge that the CI includes zero.
comments.request: Acknowledge the CI includes zero.
comments.quote: Line 103: I think this sentence should include an acknowledgment that the CI includes 0 for the IUCN richness analyses.

comments.issue: Counter-scenarios where small patch sets do not include more declining species are not acknowledged.
comments.request: Acknowledge counter-scenarios.
comments.quote: But the CI included zero. Sets of small patches can include more declining species, yet it seems there are also scenarios (perhaps fewer) where this is not true.

comments.issue: More information from model 21 on mean patch size versus total area is needed in the main text.
comments.request: Report model 21's relative importance results.
comments.quote: I think providing more information from model 21 in the main text is warranted to describe the relative importance of mean patch size vs total habitat area.

comments.issue: Calling Model 2 'stronger' ignores that its CI overlaps zero, indicating more variation.
comments.request: Describe the variation, not just magnitude.
comments.quote: Yes, the magnitude of the estimate is larger in Model 2 than 1, however, the CI overlaps zero in Model 2

comments.issue: A double negative makes the sentence hard to follow and the finding is absent from the results.
comments.request: Rewrite and report the finding in results.
comments.quote: The double negative in this sentence makes it hard to follow. In addition, this finding is not mentioned or implied by the text in the results section

comments.issue: Repeated long descriptions of patch-set types hurt readability.
comments.request: Use abbreviations for patch-set types.
comments.quote: I wonder whether abbreviations for sets of ‘several small patches’ and ‘few large patches’ can be used throughout the MS to improve readability.

comments.issue: Vague qualifiers ('especially higher') are used instead of magnitudes, and matrix/time patterns are unexplained.
comments.request: Give magnitudes and explain the matrix/time patterns.
comments.quote: Can magnitudes be given rather than ‘especially higher’?

comments.issue: 'In other words' is repeated seven times.
comments.request: Reduce repetition of 'in other words'.
comments.quote: The phrase ‘in other words’ is used 7 times in the manuscript.

comments.issue: The scenario sets lack descriptive metrics beyond mean patch size.
comments.request: Report additional descriptive metrics for the scenarios.
comments.quote: can you give some more descriptive metrics [mean, SD] for the sets of few large patches vs sets of many small patches (i.e., beyond mean patch size)?

comments.issue: Whether the 425 scenarios are evenly distributed across the 71 datasets is unknown.
comments.request: Report the scenario distribution across datasets.
comments.quote: Line 261-263: Were the 425 scenarios fairly evenly distributed across the 71 datasets?

title: Landscape‐scale habitat fragmentation is positively related to biodiversity, despite patch‐scale ecosystem decay

study.system: 28 urban community gardens, California; 5 years of ecosystem service data

editor_summary: Reviewers generally positive about the dataset and topic but execution is below journal standard: analysis inadequate and likely Type I errors, explanations are just-so stories, and a multiple-comparison correction, meta-analysis and hypothesis-driven reanalysis are needed.

reviews.assessment: Interesting synthesis of a valuable dataset, but the many pairwise correlations may be false positives and key results are under-discussed.
strengths: idea of synthesizing a huge and valuable dataset

comments.issue: About half of the 24 significant correlations out of 264 comparisons are expected by chance; no correction for multiple comparisons.
comments.request: Correct for multiple comparisons and address false-positive risk.
comments.quote: given the number of comparisons made, at alpha of 0.05 one should expect ~13 significant values, about half of the number that were found, to occur just by chance as potential false positives

comments.issue: The surprisingly few significant relationships, especially the decoupling within pest suppression and pollination categories, are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss why related metrics are decoupled.
comments.quote: I was also surprised that there were no significant relationships between the various metrics within the pest suppression and pollination categories.

comments.issue: Fig. 2 shows only significant relationships, hiding the overall pattern and effect sizes.
comments.request: Show all relationships in Fig. 2, for example as a heat map.
comments.quote: I think Fig 2 should show all the relationships and not just the significant ones. That way the reader can see the overall pattern (would look like a heat map)

comments.issue: No meta-analytic synthesis of correlation coefficients is attempted.
comments.request: Use a meta-analytic approach with weighted mean correlations.
comments.quote: You could also use a meta-analytic approach and ask what is the weighted mean correlation coefficient, aggregated at the group level or overall.

comments.issue: The discussion of food production versus biodiversity lacks nuance and Fig. 2 excludes biodiversity measures.
comments.request: Add nuance about land-use change and biodiversity comparisons.
comments.quote: I think some more nuance could be added to the discussion of whether food production is at odds with biodiversity.

comments.issue: The definition of the intermediate landscape complexity hypothesis at L107 is confusing.
comments.request: Describe the hypothesis more simply.
comments.quote: maybe this is subjective, but I got lost in the definition of the intermediate landscape complexity hypothesis is the best framework for this study

comments.issue: The predictions at L157 are unnecessary and not justified.
comments.request: Consider removing the predictions.
comments.quote: In some ways the predictions here are not needed, since the objectives/questions are stated above and seem to cover it. The predictions aren't really justified in detail so if it were me I would simply skip them.

comments.issue: A cited study at L195 is still in preparation and cannot be verified.
comments.request: Avoid relying on in-prep work.
comments.quote: 195 Hard to verify something that is still in prep

comments.issue: No citation is given for the study assessing gardener-reported food production (L201).
comments.request: Add the citation.
comments.quote: 201 citation for the study assessing gardener-reported food production?

comments.issue: The definition at L227 could be moved to the introduction for clarity.
comments.request: Consider defining the term earlier.
comments.quote: could consider putting this definition in the intro so it is defined clearly from the outset. Although it works nicely here too

comments.issue: Using conditional rather than full model averaging inflates the apparent importance of rare variables.
comments.request: Use full model averaging or justify the conditional average.
comments.quote: Why is the conditional average used instead of the full average? My understanding is the conditional average can inflate the perceived importance of variables

comments.issue: Correlation is conflated with causation, and directionality could be reversed or relationships spurious (L319).
comments.request: Take more care to separate correlation from causation and consider directionality.
comments.quote: I think more care could be taken here to avoid conflating correlation with causation. In some cases there is a clear predictor and response, but in others the directionality could be reversed or the relationships could be spurious.

comments.issue: The L362 statement depends on the p<0.05 filtering of correlations.
comments.request: Report what the statement looks like without significance filtering.
comments.quote: I would be interested to know what this statement might look like if the correlations in Fig 2 were not filtered by p<0.05 as per my comment above.

comments.issue: The well-being and mulching relationship at L410 could be reversed: high well-being may allow more mulching.
comments.request: Consider the reverse direction of this relationship.
comments.quote: Isn't it also possible that people who would report high well-being have more time and energy to mulch their gardens thoroughly?

comments.issue: The statement at L421 is speculative.
comments.request: Temper or support the speculation.
comments.quote: 421 This seems quite speculative

comments.issue: The claim at L488 that this is the only study examining local management effects on multiple ecosystem services is questionable.
comments.request: Support or soften the uniqueness claim.
comments.quote: 488 This is the only study that has examined effects of local management on multiple ecosystem services?

comments.issue: Fig. 3 is confusing: bars sometimes span both directions although points indicating effects were expected.
comments.request: Redesign Fig. 3 for clarity.
comments.quote: I feel like I shouldn't have been confused here, but if it threw me for a loop it will probably do something similar to other readers as well.

reviews.assessment: Very well written study with appropriate methods; urban agriculture importance may be overstated and the small geographic scope needs acknowledgement.
strengths: rationale and conceptual framework explained well

comments.issue: The importance of urban agriculture to food security is supported only by one non-scientific citation and may be overstated.
comments.request: Provide better evidence for the food-security importance of urban agriculture.
comments.quote: Can you please provide better evidence for the importance of urban agriculture to food security. You have only included one general non-scientific citation (L 132).

comments.issue: The supplemental methods would be clearer as a table, which should be prioritised over the conceptual figure.
comments.request: Transform the supplemental methods into a table.
comments.quote: I am hoping that the authors may be able to transform the supplemental methods supporting information into a table as this will increase understanding of how the study was undertaken

comments.issue: The dataset covers a small area of the Californian coast, but the language is definitive and limits to other urban contexts are not acknowledged.
comments.request: Add nuance and report details enabling comparisons with other cities.
comments.quote: This needs to be acknowledged more as different, more densely urbanised landscapes or countries with less natural habitat may have different results but the language within the paper is pretty definitive.

comments.issue: Line-level copy edits: L74 should read urban community gardens, and spaces are missing between numbers and units (L179, L180).
comments.quote: L 179, 180 Space between a number and its unit needed. Please correct this throughout the manuscript

comments.issue: It is unclear whether L125 refers to the intermediate landscape-complexity hypothesis or resource dilution theory.
comments.request: Clarify with consistent wording.
comments.quote: Are you referring to the intermediate landscape-complexity hypothesis here or another ecological theory focussing on resource dilution ? Please clarify perhaps by using consistent wording.

comments.issue: The % natural cover of the sites and its range are not reported.
comments.request: Report % natural cover in the paper or supplement.
comments.quote: The % natural cover for the sites needs to be reported somewhere in the paper or supplementary material and the range here to enable comparisons in different landscapes / countries

comments.issue: The L382 pattern presumably applies to larger scales in non-urban settings, which is not acknowledged.
comments.request: Acknowledge the scale and setting dependence.
comments.quote: yes but this is presumably at larger scales in non-urban settings - something which needs to be acknowledged here

comments.issue: The statement about water conservation regulations as the reason for mulching is incorrect (L408).
comments.request: Remove or correct this statement.
comments.quote: Remove "Because urban areas often face water conservation regulations" as this is not the primary reason why gardners use mulch.

comments.issue: The claim that community gardens support animal biodiversity in the landscape is not demonstrated by the study design (L523).
comments.request: Reword to avoid claiming landscape-level biodiversity support.
comments.quote: I don't see how you have demonstrated that the community gardens support animal biodiversity in the landscape as your study was not designed to do this. Reword to avoid any confusion

comments.issue: Figure 1 is nice but unnecessary given journal space limits.
comments.request: Consider removing Figure 1.
comments.quote: While it is a nice figure I do not think it is needed if there are journal space considerations

comments.issue: Figure 2 does not explain what circle size represents or link it to significance ranges.
comments.request: Add a legend linking circle size to correlation strength.
comments.quote: The size of the circle indicates the strength of the correlation but there is nowhere telling the author what this is as Table S1 is a list of the data source.

comments.issue: Figure 3's y-axis term "studies" is misleading, as gardens/models rather than publications are meant.
comments.request: Rename the y-axis term.
comments.quote: Is the use of the term studies on the y axis potentially misleading - you are not referring to multiple publications but different gardens / models aren't you?

reviews.assessment: Interesting study on an impressive dataset, but text clarity, questionable well-being indicators and multiple-testing inflation are concerns.

comments.issue: The introduction and methods are very hard to follow, so the validity of the argumentation cannot be judged.
comments.request: Critically rephrase these sections for clarity.
comments.quote: I found some parts of this manuscript very hard to follow, and could not always follow the logic even after re-reading sections several times.

comments.issue: It is unclear why well-being indicators such as social relations or freedom of choice were included, and whether theory predicts links to ecological services.
comments.request: Justify the inclusion of each well-being indicator with hypotheses.
comments.quote: I wondered why they are included in the study: simply because the data is available, or because there are also some theory-driven expectations on why they should relate positively or negatively to the other ecosystem services?

comments.issue: The many statistical tests (e.g. 276 raw correlations) risk Type I errors, and no multiple-testing correction is applied (also L376-378).
comments.request: Apply a correction such as Bonferroni across these and other analyses.
comments.quote: Therefore, I strongly recommend to perform some count of correction (e.g. bonferroni) correction for these and other (e.g. those underlying fig 3 and 4, and the supplementary results) analyses, to minimize the likelihood of type I errors.

comments.issue: Line-level copy edit: L99 should say positive and negative correlations instead of "+/- correlations".
comments.quote: L99: I would prefer 'positive and negative correlations, respectively' instead of '+/- correlations'

comments.issue: "Simple habitat" at L108-109 is undefined.
comments.request: Define simple habitat.
comments.quote: L108-109: what is a 'simple habitat'?

comments.issue: Habitat complexity, natural habitat cover and herbaceous plant richness are conflated, and the claim that complexity supports biodiversity is circular (L104-117).
comments.request: Use consistent terminology close to what is measured in the field.
comments.quote: I found this text very hard to follow, as several terms seem to be used for the same concept.

comments.issue: The meaning of L142-145 is unclear.
comments.request: Rephrase these lines.
comments.quote: L142-145: I am not sure what is meant here so I would suggest rephrazing

comments.issue: The model description at L258-261 mentions only two predictors, but the VIF statement implies many more were used.
comments.request: Clarify the full set of predictors.
comments.quote: I assume that in reality, more variables are analysed? Especially the statement 'we then calculated a variance inflation factor (VIF) for each model set' suggests that a much larger range of predictors were used

comments.issue: It remains unclear how the analyses at L291-298 quantify synergies and trade-offs.
comments.request: Rewrite this section so most readers can follow it.
comments.quote: it is still not clear for me how these analyses address the quantification of synergies / trade-offs, so I really think this section (or the statistical analyses in general) need some major rewriting

comments.issue: The L308-312 numbers are confusing: food has 8 synergies with ecosystem services but only two when providers are combined.
comments.request: Clarify this inconsistency.
comments.quote: this is quite confusing: food has 8 synergies with ecosystem services, but only two synergies with ecosystem services and ecosystem service providers combined?

comments.issue: The conclusion that food production is not at odds with biodiversity is contradicted by Fig. 3, where trade-offs are ignored (L376-379).
comments.request: Add balance to the discussion of management trade-offs.
comments.quote: However, looking at fig. 3 (which focuses more on management driven trade-offs/synergies), I could come at quite different conclusions, as some management promoting food (e.g. natural habitat cover) mostly negatively affects natural enemies

comments.issue: Opposite responses of pest control and natural enemies may reflect bottom-up rather than top-down regulation (L504-508).
comments.request: Consider and discuss the bottom-up alternative explanation.
comments.quote: a perhaps more straightforward explanation for the often opposite responses of pest control and natural enemies to garden size, tree abundance and mulch cover, is that these trophic interactions are mostly bottom-up, rather than top-down regulated

comments.issue: "Positive or negative concentration effect" at L571-572 is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the concentration effect.
comments.quote: I found this sentence hard to understand: what is a positive or negative concentration effect?

comments.issue: Fig. 1D took 20 minutes to understand.
comments.request: Improve Fig. 1D.
comments.quote: I think this figure can be improved, as I had to study it for 20 minutes before I finally understood it.

comments.issue: Fig. 3's y-axis "proportion of studies" is misleading because this is not a meta-analysis.
comments.request: Rename the y-axis.
comments.quote: what is meant with 'proportion of studies'? Since this is not a meta-analysis, only one study is done, right?

comments.issue: It is unclear why several ecosystem service indicators show exactly the same response in Fig. 4.
comments.request: Explain the identical responses of these indicators.
comments.quote: what I don't understand from this figure, is why some ecosystem service indicators, such aphid removal, egg removal and larvae removal show exactly the same response to local/landscape complexity.

title: Multiple ecosystem service synergies and landscape mediation of biodiversity within urban agroecosystems

study.system: ectotherm temperature acclimation; quantitative synthesis of plasticity rates

editor_summary: Editor: both reviewers find the framework interesting and creative; address clarity and meta-analysis method concerns and supply annotated R code and data.

reviews.assessment: Nicely written and widely interesting; primary concerns are the informal meta-analytic approach and missing covariates, plus review-methodology gaps.
strengths: addresses important questions of wide interest
nicely written and enjoyable to read

comments.issue: The approach is informal rather than formal meta-analysis; slope SEs and phylogenetic information were not used.
comments.request: Justify the approach or run a formal meta-analysis.
comments.quote: My primary comment concerns the informal rather than formal meta-analytical approach taken by the authors. Did the authors consider a formal meta-analysis, and if so, why did they take the approach they did?

comments.issue: The literature review is not exhaustive, does not follow PRISMA, and the sampling approach is not justified.
comments.request: Explain the sampling approach and its limitations.
comments.quote: the literature review was not exhaustive and does not follow the Prisma guidelines for reviews and syntheses

comments.issue: Publication bias from the sampling approach was not assessed.
comments.request: Assess or discuss potential publication bias.
comments.quote: Did the sampling approach to data collection result in any publication bias and were any estimates of publication bias performed?

comments.issue: Life stage tested and tolerance measurement type are unconsidered covariates that may drive taxon differences.
comments.request: Include these covariates or report them in the supplement.
comments.quote: have you considered other possible covariates for your models that may explain variation in plasticity rate in thermal tolerance?

comments.issue: The claim that variable environments favour greater plasticity lacks citations.
comments.request: Add supporting citations.
comments.quote: citations would be useful here for “For example, it has been proposed that organisms inhabiting more variable environments should evolve greater plasticity capacities”

reviews.assessment: Exciting and ambitious but needs major revision: weighted meta-analysis, better search reporting, and clearer rate-of-plasticity terminology.
strengths: ambitious analysis of an understudied question

comments.issue: 'Rate of plasticity' is confusable with the reaction norm slope; the paper should state it means the rate at which the slope changes.
comments.request: Add explicit statements and a conceptual figure clarifying the concept.
comments.quote: I would suggest the authors have a 1-2 sentences after L48 that explicitly state that ‘rate of plasticity’ is the rate at which the slope of a reaction norm changes.

comments.issue: 'Plastic responses' at L70 can also be confused with the reaction norm slope.
comments.request: Clarify that this means the rate of acclimation.
comments.quote: the use of “plastic responses” can be confused with the slope of the reaction norm

comments.issue: Relevant prior work (Seebacher et al. 2015; Pottier et al. 2022) is not cited or contrasted.
comments.request: Cite and contrast these studies.
comments.quote: I’m actually surprised to not see this cited here, even if it’s not quite addressing what the authors are.

comments.issue: Claiming a lack of empirical interest is wrong and weakens the rationale for a general journal.
comments.request: Remove the claim and position the study against past work.
comments.quote: I don’t think it’s a lack of empirical interest (see studies above), and I’d suggest the authors avoid stating this in any case.

comments.issue: Search and inclusion/exclusion reporting is insufficient to reproduce; no PRISMA diagram.
comments.request: Add a PRISMA diagram with dates and exclusion reasons.
comments.quote: I would like to see the authors present a PRISMA diagram detailing this section, the dates searched, how many were excluded at each step and why

comments.issue: Only means were extracted; variance or SE around the mean could improve precision.
comments.request: Extract and use the variance or SE around means.
comments.quote: Did the authors only extract the mean? Why not the variance/sd/se around the mean?

comments.issue: Incomplete acclimation is expected to bias the SE of lambdaE, but no weighted model is used.
comments.request: Use a weighted meta-analytic model accounting for SE.
comments.quote: a weighted meta-analytic model that accounts for the SE of lambdaE has the potential to correct such biased as each lambdaE estimated is weighted by lambdaE

comments.issue: No R code is provided for review.
comments.request: Provide the annotated analysis code.
comments.quote: It is very unfortunate the authors do not provide any R code for review.

comments.issue: The unweighted analysis gives all studies equal weight, leaving publication bias, incomplete acclimation and low power unaddressed.
comments.request: Re-analyse with a weighted meta-analytic model (e.g., metafor).
comments.quote: Using an unweighted analysis, as the authors appear to be doing, won’t necessarily bias point estimates, but it will mean that all studies get equal weight in the calculation of overall means

comments.issue: Taxonomic differences may partly reflect incomplete acclimation rather than real taxon effects.
comments.request: Check whether incomplete acclimation explains the taxonomic pattern.
comments.quote: I wonder how much of the taxonomic difference you observed could be the result of incomplete acclimation discussed in the methods and supplement?

comments.issue: Phylogenetic signal was not estimated explicitly with a phylogeny.
comments.request: Estimate phylogenetic signal to support the claim.
comments.quote: I’d be curious to see if there is a phylogenetic signal in these data estimating it explicitly with the phylogeny as this might support the statement made here.

comments.issue: Packages and versions used for the analysis are not reported.
comments.request: Report packages and versions.
comments.quote: L194. Using what packages and versions?

comments.issue: 'This discrepancy' at L57 is not explicit.
comments.request: State what 'this' refers to.
comments.quote: L57: “this discrepancy”. Be explicit about what ‘this’ means.

comments.issue: Heterogeneity is reported without a clear reference and could better use ICC and prediction intervals.
comments.request: Use ICC and report prediction intervals.
comments.quote: Relative to what? ICC would be better here and you can generate prediction intervals from these data which would be much better!

comments.issue: Table 2 lacks confidence intervals and uncertainty for the species random effect; phylogeny and residual variance are not reported.
comments.request: Add CIs, phylogeny partitioning and residual variance.
comments.quote: Table 2 - Provide 95% confidence intervals. What about uncertainty on species random effect variance?

comments.issue: Fig S6 axes are labelled with R object names.
comments.request: Label axes properly.
comments.quote: Fig S6. Label axes properly. Don’t use object names in R.

comments.issue: Colour schemes differ across figures.
comments.request: Make the colour scheme consistent.
comments.quote: I suggest the authors consider the colour scheme more carefully across the figures. Make them the same

title: Divergence in rates of phenotypic plasticity among ectotherms

study.system: animal site fidelity; agent-based random-walk simulations

editor_summary: Editor supports the cautionary message but says practical utility must be demonstrated: provide a usable workflow, respond to R2 on return probabilities, and engage mathematical theory instead of only agent-based simulations.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and worthwhile framework, but the mathematical grounding, terminology, model description and generality all need substantial work.
strengths: random walks are relevant nulls in movement ecology

comments.issue: Previous uses of random walks as null models in movement applications are not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention previous uses of random walks as nulls in movement research.
comments.quote: random walks have been used as nulls in many movement-related applications (which could be mentioned)

comments.issue: A large mathematical literature on random-walk return times that explains some results is not engaged.
comments.request: Ground the results in the mathematical literature on random-walk return times.
comments.quote: There is a large body of mathematical literature that considers return times in random walks that seem directly relevant to what is being considered here and explains some of the results.

comments.issue: Key terms such as memory (path memory vs. mental maps) and perception are left undefined.
comments.request: Define memory, perception and related terms explicitly.
comments.quote: You need to explain what is meant by terms such as memory (short-term path memory vs. persistent mental maps, for example), perception, etc.

comments.issue: The operational definition of site fidelity ignores time spent at a site.
comments.request: Clarify whether site fidelity requires residence time at a site.
comments.quote: Surely, however, fidelity implies some length of time spent at a site. For example, if the same bird traverses the same location each day or week or during a seasonal migration is that site fidelity?

comments.issue: Pattern- versus process-oriented definitions are treated as a sharper dichotomy than warranted.
comments.request: Revise the claimed binary distinction between pattern- and process-oriented definitions.
comments.quote: I am also not convinced that the distinction between pattern- and process-oriented definitions are as binary as is implied.

comments.issue: Model description omits key information, e.g. how synthetic landscapes were generated.
comments.request: Describe the ABM following established protocols such as ODD.
comments.quote: The model description is lacking important information (e.g., about the generation of the synthetic landscapes)

comments.issue: Model is parameterised from one species; applicability to other movement syndromes is unproven.
comments.request: Show whether the approach works for animals with periodic movement syndromes.
comments.quote: but is this really as generalisable as stated (line 144)? Can the approach be used for animals that show different movement syndromes such as highly periodic movement

comments.issue: The abstract's random-walk return result is already well established theoretically.
comments.quote: Line 8-9 – Isn’t this outcome well-established theoretically?

comments.issue: Details of the literature search, at least its date, are missing.
comments.request: Report the search date and details.
comments.quote: Line 27 – You need to provide some more information on the search (at least the date)

comments.issue: Statements labelled as definitions actually concern inferred causality, not definitions.
comments.request: Reconsider what is labelled a definition.
comments.quote: I am not sure these are really definitions; you define site fidelity in line 17

comments.issue: Scale is central to the arguments and deserves fuller treatment.
comments.quote: Line 39 – The arguments about scale are central to much of this.

comments.issue: Unclear whether territoriality and central-place foraging fall under site fidelity.
comments.request: Clarify whether such behaviours count as site fidelity.
comments.quote: Line 41-42 – Would behaviours such as territoriality and central-place foraging count as site fidelity?

comments.issue: Items listed as mechanisms are actually outcomes of informed behaviours.
comments.request: Reclassify these as outcomes rather than mechanisms.
comments.quote: Lines 52-58 – These are not mechanisms – they are outcomes of informed behaviours that led to site fidelity.

comments.issue: Imperfect memory or an intrinsic value unmeasurable by observers may equally produce the pattern.
comments.quote: Line 60 – It may equally occur because memory is imperfect or the intrinsic value is hard to measure (by the observer).

comments.issue: Memory and spatial familiarity are not distinguished.
comments.request: Explain the difference between memory and spatial familiarity.
comments.quote: Line 95 – What is the difference between memory and spatial familiarity?

comments.issue: Infinite returns in 1D and 2D simple random walks are well-established theory.
comments.request: Reference the theoretical literature on random-walk return times.
comments.quote: Line 120-121 – As noted above this is very well-established (it will occur infinitely many times in 1D and 2D for a simple RW)

comments.issue: CRW tends to a simple RW under aggregation, so the distinction is scale-dependent.
comments.request: Address the scale dependence of CRW versus RW behaviour.
comments.quote: Line 124 – True, but under aggregation, a CRW will tend to a simple RW as well so this is affected by scale.

comments.issue: Biological barriers such as home ranges and territories are not considered.
comments.request: Consider adding home ranges and territories to the models.
comments.quote: Line 125 – What about biological barriers such as home ranges and territories?

comments.issue: The 4-hour step interval and six-steps-per-day schedule are not justified.
comments.request: Justify the temporal sampling scheme.
comments.quote: Line 147 - Why 4-hours? And is this continual through each day (so six steps per day)?

comments.issue: Variable step lengths and the Weibull distribution are used without justification.
comments.request: Justify the variable step length and Weibull choice.
comments.quote: Line 154 (and elsewhere) – Why did you use a variable step length?

comments.issue: A pure random walk has a fixed unit step length, unlike the model used.
comments.request: Clarify why unit steps were not used.
comments.quote: Line 156 – A pure random walk has a fixed unit step length.

comments.issue: No reference is given for the CCRW.
comments.request: Cite a reference for the CCRW.
comments.quote: Line 159 – Is there a reference for the CCRW?

comments.issue: The r values seem small for an organism with a 200 m mean step length.
comments.request: Justify the r values and cross-reference Table 1.
comments.quote: Line 160 – Cross-reference to Table 1 in SM so the reader knows what r you used? And the values seem small for an organism with a mean step length of 200 m?

comments.issue: The ×10 scaling factor is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the ×10 factor.
comments.quote: Line 170 – Why ×10?

comments.issue: Landscape generation is under-described and heterogeneity/contagion values are unclear.
comments.request: Provide details of landscape generation and parameter values.
comments.quote: Line 182 – You need to provide more detail here. How did you generate the landscapes (there are many ways to do this)?

comments.issue: Symbol k is used for both step length and contagion.
comments.request: Use a different symbol for contagion.
comments.quote: Line 183 – Given you use k for step length, could you use a different symbol for contagion to avoid confusion.

comments.issue: The fully factorial simulation design may be inelegant.
comments.request: Consider a more elegant design layout.
comments.quote: Line 192 – This (Table 1 in the SM) looks like you have done a fully factorial design – aren’t there more elegant ways to lay this design out?

comments.issue: The 50% return criterion is arbitrary and robustness to it is untested.
comments.request: Run sensitivity analyses across return thresholds.
comments.quote: Line 197 – Why 50%? How robust are the outcomes to this parametrisation?

comments.issue: No persistence element: merely traversing a location may not equal site fidelity.
comments.request: Clarify whether time spent in an area is required.
comments.quote: Line 198 – As noted above, is there no persistence element here? Is site fidelity simply traversing through a location?

comments.issue: The result follows almost by definition.
comments.quote: Line 227 – This result is (almost) by definition.

comments.issue: A 1 × 1 km domain seems too small for 200 m steps and a ~600 m 95% range.
comments.request: Reconsider the simulation domain size.
comments.quote: Line 237 – A 1 × 1 km area seems very small for an organism with a mean step length of 200 m and a 95% of nearly 600 m?

comments.issue: Results show returns can occur without memory, not corroboration of reported site fidelity.
comments.request: Restate what the results actually corroborate.
comments.quote: Lines 285-286 – I don’t see how the results corroborate reports of site fidelity – didn’t we know that? What they show is that this return can occur in the absence of a ‘memory’ mechanism, which is not the same.

comments.issue: The conclusion depends on scale and on what counts as site fidelity.
comments.request: Discuss scale and elephant seal behaviour during residential periods.
comments.quote: Lines 314-315 – Doesn’t this depend on scale (and also what constitutes site fidelity)? What is the movement behaviour of the elephant seals during their residential periods?

comments.issue: Other restricted domains, including semi-permeable barriers, are not considered.
comments.request: Explore behavioural domains and semi-permeable barriers.
comments.quote: Lines 319 – There are other forms of restricted domains that it would be informative to consider, some of which are behavioural. It would also be interesting to see what the effect of semi-permeable barriers was.

comments.issue: Return driven by habitat-dependent tortuosity may not be meaningful site fidelity.
comments.request: Discuss whether such returns count as site fidelity.
comments.quote: Lines 338-339 – Isn’t this outcome inherent in the way habitat use is represented in the models, especially if habitat is limiting? If tortuosity is a function of habitat is return to a site really ‘site fidelity’ in a meaningful sense?

comments.issue: The argument assumes perception and memory are independent cognitive processes.
comments.request: Acknowledge that perception may be influenced by memory.
comments.quote: Line 348 – This argument seems to presuppose that perception and memory are somewhat independent cognitive processes.

comments.issue: The individual-level argument may not hold for flocking or herding animals.
comments.request: Consider group-living species.
comments.quote: Lines 355-356 – As individuals maybe but many animals operate in flocks or herds, which certainly can!

comments.issue: Temporal predictability central to long-lag fidelity is not treated.
comments.request: Address temporal predictability in the fidelity concept.
comments.quote: Line 378 – Isn’t this temporal predictability central to the long lag (e.g., seasonal or annual) fidelity that you mention?

comments.issue: Only time-to-return is included; lacking a residence-time perspective may inflate fidelity.
comments.request: Clarify whether models over-estimate site fidelity.
comments.quote: I think you only include one temporal component of site fidelity time to return); without any temporal perspective as to what fidelity means (in the sense of staying at a point for some period of time) do your models potentially over-estimate site fidelity?

comments.issue: The discussion section reads like an introduction and should be tightened.
comments.request: Condense the discussion.
comments.quote: Lines 398-448 – I think this section could be tightened. Much of it reads more like an Introduction than a Discussion of the results presented here.

reviews.assessment: Very pleased with the thought-provoking paper, but asks how the null-model workflow could actually be implemented in practice.
strengths: valuable note of caution on interpreting foraging site fidelity
clear theoretical route to null expectations

comments.issue: Parameters estimated from movement data implicitly contain memory effects, making the memory-free null circular.
comments.request: Explain how movement properties can be estimated without memory contamination.
comments.quote: any null movement model would need to be parameterised in such a way that memory had no effect, yet parameters estimated from movement data would implicitly include any effects of memory

comments.issue: The proposed workflow is never illustrated on real data.
comments.request: Illustrate the workflow with a real example.
comments.quote: the paper would be stronger still if the proposed workflow were illustrated using a real example

comments.issue: Null site fidelity in more complex systems, such as central-place foragers and social information transfer, is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss estimation of null site fidelity in complex systems.
comments.quote: it would have been nice for the Discussion to touch upon how null site fidelity might be estimated in more complex systems

comments.issue: The framework appears to allow only positive habitat quantities; avoidance may need accommodating.
comments.request: Clarify whether habitat avoidance can be represented.
comments.quote: L118 – This implies that habitat has only positive quantities. Presumably, habitat avoidance could also be accommodated in this framework?

comments.issue: The quantifier 'many' is too weak; all animals presumably do this.
comments.request: Correct the quantifier.
comments.quote: L127 – “Many”? Surely, all animals do this.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the metric is the probability of at least one return, and return frequency is not reported.
comments.request: Clarify the metric and report return frequency.
comments.quote: So this is the probability of at least one return within that period? Is that correct? Wouldn’t it also be useful to know how frequently animals returned?

comments.issue: With a biologically sized grid, the definition cannot distinguish visiting-and-returning from simply staying in an area.
comments.request: Refine the definition so that staying versus returning is distinguished.
comments.quote: this definition of site fidelity seems problematic, because it does not distinguish between an animal visiting an area, leaving that it and then returning and an animal simply staying in the same area

comments.issue: How parameters would be estimated from species-specific empirical data is not explained.
comments.request: Expand on how parameterisation would work in practice.
comments.quote: Could you expand on how that would be achieved in practice.

reviews.assessment: Likes the paper and its message, but finds the focus on return frequency too simplistic and asks for other metrics.
strengths: paper is needed and shows returns need not be due to memory
introduction and writing are clear and easy to follow
simulation methods are clear and results easy to understand

comments.issue: Memory may reduce return rates below the memory-free baseline, so frequency alone cannot indicate memory.
comments.request: Acknowledge that memory can lower return rates.
comments.quote: processes involving memory could result in return rates below the expected frequency under a memory-free process

comments.issue: The spatial and temporal distribution of returns differs under memory, not just their frequency.
comments.request: Consider metrics based on the distribution of returns.
comments.quote: the frequency need not always be higher but the distribution over space and time will be different when memory is involved

comments.issue: Alternation between seasonal ranges in trajectories could also reveal memory.
comments.request: Consider seasonal-range alternation as an additional expectation.
comments.quote: how they alternate between e.g. summer and winter range will also show if memory is involved or not

comments.issue: A plateau in the number of revisited locations may distinguish memory from baseline models.
comments.request: Test the plateau expectation against the baseline models.
comments.quote: With memory involved, wouldn’t you expect that the number of locations revisited will reach a plateau quite quickly

comments.issue: The discussion is lengthy and could be shortened.
comments.request: Shorten the discussion at places.
comments.quote: Just in general I think the discussion is a bit lengthy and could be shortened at places.

comments.issue: The 50% threshold used to define a return is arbitrary and lacks sensitivity analysis.
comments.request: Test sensitivity to return thresholds such as 50%, 40% and 30%.
comments.quote: Did you do a sensitivity analysis where you for instance would use 50%, 40%, 30% percentile

comments.issue: Pooling the probability of return per step over all animals is not explained and may not be sensible.
comments.request: Clarify the computation and consider per-animal proportions.
comments.quote: why you calculated the probability of return per step over all animals - each replicate by definition is independent from all others?
