comments.issue: The purpose of the constrained CRW model is explained only after the results.
comments.request: Introduce the model's purpose where the models are introduced.
comments.quote: Again, I wasn’t sure what we learn from the constrained correlated random walk model before it was explained.

comments.issue: It is not only about baseline frequency; spatial distribution of returns differs with memory.
comments.request: Broaden the inference beyond return frequency.
comments.quote: Is it really just about the baseline frequency? I think the frequency need not always be higher but the distribution over space will be different when memory is involved.

comments.issue: The reason for using a spatial constraint is explained too late.
comments.request: Explain the constraint rationale at the outset.
comments.quote: I think the reasoning why a constraint was used should be elaborated already at the beginning, otherwise this is not clear, see comment above.

comments.issue: Example references are needed for this point.
comments.request: Provide example references.
comments.quote: 453 I think here you need to provide some example references

comments.issue: The univariate return-frequency approach is too simplistic.
comments.quote: 458 Again, this univariate approach seems much too simplistic to me

title: Defining null expectations for animal site fidelity

study.system: Northern Hemisphere forests; tree-ring isotopes and CMIP6 simulations

editor_summary: Editor: the manuscript has many strengths and is potentially suitable for publication as long as the reviewer comments can be adequately addressed.

reviews.assessment: Enjoys the sound study and recommends publication after more methodological detail and code availability.
strengths: reliable new framework for carbon source-sink interactions

comments.issue: The statistical analyses are valid but need more detail.
comments.request: Provide more details of the statistical analyses.
comments.quote: The statistical analyses are valid, but more details need to be provided

comments.issue: Computer code availability is not stated.
comments.request: Make the computer code available.
comments.quote: I encourage the authors to make the computer code available

comments.issue: Post-eruption responses are not compared across latitudinal bands.
comments.request: Compare iWUE and tree-ring density across latitude bands.
comments.quote: It would be interesting to see some comparison of superposed post-eruption iWUE, and tree-ring density under various latitudes

comments.issue: The difference between carbon source and sink regulation of woody growth is not explained at lines 46-48.
comments.request: Explain source versus sink control of woody growth.
comments.quote: Please give some explanation about the difference between C source and sink in regulating woody growth in this part.

comments.issue: The arguments at lines 107-109 are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify these arguments.
comments.quote: Line 107-109: Unclear arguments, please clarify.

comments.issue: Line 162 should refer to gradients of temperature and climatic water deficit.
comments.request: Revise the wording.
comments.quote: Line 162: --> associated with gradients of temperature and climatic water deficit.

comments.issue: The detrending with 50% frequency cutoff splines lacks detail and references.
comments.request: Describe this detrending method and provide references.
comments.quote: Please provide some details about the method of detrending with 50% frequency cutoff splines, and provide the references.

comments.issue: Variable order in Fig. 1B differs from Figs. 2 and S7.
comments.request: Reorder variables to corrected iWUE, MAT and MACWD.
comments.quote: It would be better to change the order of variables to corrected iWUE, MAT, and MACWD; like Fig. 2. and Fig. S7.

reviews.assessment: Well-written and important study; wants the fate of the extra carbon discussed, assumptions clarified and data archiving fixed.
strengths: well-written, concise and to the point
cautions against interpreting photosynthesis increases as carbon sink increases

comments.issue: The discussion does not say where the extra assimilated carbon is allocated, and the autotrophic respiration evidence is unclear.
comments.request: Discuss where the extra carbon goes and compare effect sizes.
comments.quote: In my opinion what is missing is the discussion of where is the extra C allocated.

comments.issue: The assumption that ring width is a proxy of NPP is imprecise; detrended ring widths proxy detrended NPP only.
comments.request: State this detail in the text at line 204.
comments.quote: is the assumption that ring width was a proxy of NPP, but that may have been an inaccurate formulation

comments.issue: ESM grid cells of 100 km may have small forested fractions, so they may not match the sampled tree-ring sites.
comments.request: Filter model grid cells to those represented by the sampled trees.
comments.quote: I would suggest authors filter the model gridcells and analyze only the ones that could be represented by the trees sampled at the tree ring sites

comments.issue: The paper does not comply with the journal's data archiving guidelines; the data statement only points to previously published sources.
comments.request: Archive analysed data, metadata and annotated code in a public repository.
comments.quote: Data statement in the manuscript only directs the reader to the previously published sources cited in the text.

comments.issue: Tree rings record individual tree productivity, not forest productivity.
comments.request: Correct this statement.
comments.quote: L75: tree rings do not record forest productivity, rather individual tree productivity.

comments.issue: Wood growth is not decoupled from photosynthesis; it is the changes in the two processes that are decoupled.
comments.request: Reword the decoupling statement.
comments.quote: if there is no photosynthesis, there cannot be wood growth, so I would argue that wood growth is not decoupled from photosynthesis

comments.issue: 2 line-level word edits at L107 and L114.
comments.quote:
L107: “lasted”
L114: “drives”

comments.issue: The reasoning behind the statement at L187-189 is not elaborated.
comments.request: Explain the reasoning for this statement.
comments.quote: L187-189: Could you please elaborate more on the reasoning for this statement?

comments.issue: Model formulation, diagnostics, results and code are not included for transparency.
comments.request: Include model formulation, diagnostics, results and code for reproducibility.
comments.quote: I suggest including model formulation, diagnostics, results, and code to increase transparency and reproducibility of the results.

comments.issue: The 'dashed lines' and their purpose at L458 need checking.
comments.request: Correct and justify the dashed lines.
comments.quote: L458: I think you meant “dashed lines”, and why are they needed?

comments.issue: The goodness of the mixed models at L465-472 is not reported.
comments.request: Report mixed model diagnostics.
comments.quote: L465-472: How good were the mixed models?

comments.issue: The Fig. 3B y-axis label may say 'variation' instead of 'deviation' (also Fig. 4).
comments.request: Correct the axis label.
comments.quote: Fig. 3 B: was the y-axis label supposed to say “deviation”, not “variation”?

comments.issue: The distribution underlying the RW z-scores is not stated.
comments.request: State the distribution used for the RW z-scores (also Fig. 4).
comments.quote: what underlying distribution was used for the RW z-scores? (same questions/issues for Fig 4)

title: Large volcanic eruptions elucidate physiological controls of tree growth and photosynthesis

study.system: tropical rainforest caterpillars and parasitoids; CTmax and food webs

editor_summary: Not publishable as is: justify hypotheses, improve narrative, show results support conclusions and title, address network completeness and adult-larval differences; single-tree sampling, season comparisons and canopy-ground food web definition also questioned.

reviews.assessment: Likes the study but says the title, abstract and introduction overstate what was tested, with further questions on food-web assembly and analysis.

comments.issue: The study does not directly measure changes in interactions or food web structure because heat responses were measured on adults in isolation.
comments.request: Clarify that only species sensitivity to heat is tested.
comments.quote: I am not convinced that this is what this study offers as the response to heat is measured for adult individuals in separation only.

comments.issue: The title, abstract and introduction do not reflect what was actually tested.
comments.request: Change title, abstract and introduction to match the analyses.
comments.quote: However, I would change the title, abstract and introduction to make clear what has actually been tested.

comments.issue: The English grammar is sometimes slightly off.
comments.request: Edit the English.
comments.quote: The English could do with editing as sometimes the grammar is slightly off.

comments.issue: The abstract implies that species interactions were tested under warming.
comments.request: Rewrite the abstract sentence about species interactions.
comments.quote: this reads if you tested how species interactions are changed by warming, I would suggest rewriting this part.

comments.issue: Herbivore control rather than the current wording may be the main vulnerable process.
comments.request: Frame herbivore control (parasitism) as the main vulnerable process.
comments.quote: maybe rather herbivore control (parasitism) as the main vulnerable process here?

comments.issue: How external thermal experience differs from intrinsic thermal sensitivity, and whether effects are plastic or population-level, is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the external versus intrinsic distinction and the level at which it acts.
comments.quote: can you explain this in more detail how external thermal experience is expected to change thermal sensitivity that is different from what you call intrinsic

comments.issue: Two line-level copy edits: 'for' at line 27 and 'were entirely' at line 295.
comments.quote: Line 27 “for” ecosystem processes

comments.issue: 'Less studied' would be more precise, given existing pollination network and parasitoid studies.
comments.request: Soften the claim and acknowledge existing studies.
comments.quote: maybe “less studied” would be more precise here, I am aware of a other studies looking into pollination networks

comments.issue: The expectation about parasitoids contradicts hypothesis 2 and is not justified.
comments.request: Justify or revise the parasitoid expectation.
comments.quote: parasitoids: why would you expect that? Especially as this contradicts hypothesis 2

comments.issue: Only adults were measured although most lepidopterans live as caterpillars.
comments.request: Discuss why only adults were studied and its implications.
comments.quote: I was wondering why you only focussed on adults, as most lepidopterans spend most of their live as caterpillars.

comments.issue: The replication unit is unclear: tree identity may need to be a random factor or each level treated as one food web.
comments.request: Clarify the replication unit and include tree identity if appropriate.
comments.quote: Should tree identity be included as random factor into the model, or are you treating the whole canopy/ground level as one food web each?

comments.issue: How parasitoid hosts were identified and food webs assembled is not described.
comments.request: Describe host identification and food-web assembly.
comments.quote: sorry if I have missed that, but how did you identify the hosts of parasitoids? Was that possible with the remains? Can you describe how you assembled the food webs?

comments.issue: Using only bottom-up extinction pathways likely underestimates secondary extinctions.
comments.request: Include top-down extinction pathways or justify their omission.
comments.quote: only using bottom -up extinction pathways is very likely to underestimate secondary extinctions, e.g. Saterberg et al.

comments.issue: The sentence at line 242 is hard to follow.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence, possibly splitting it in two.
comments.quote: I would suggest to rewrite, maybe split into two sentences this is hard to follow.

reviews.assessment: Finds the study interesting and generally well written, but the narrative is narrow, hypotheses weakly motivated and analyses poorly linked to them.

comments.issue: The narrative focuses only on maximum temperatures and ignores physiological effects at less extreme temperatures.
comments.request: Expand introduction and discussion to cover sub-lethal temperature effects.
comments.quote: I think that your general narrative is too single-edged. In addition to maximum temperatures and associated effects, changes/increases in temperature will certainly already affect physiological processes under less extreme values.

comments.issue: Why the canopy is warmer and more variable than the understory is never explained.
comments.request: Explain mechanistically why the canopy is warmer and more variable.
comments.quote: While I do not question this, you never actually explain why.

comments.issue: Hypotheses 3-4 are only weakly motivated and the expectations are unclear.
comments.request: Motivate hypotheses 3-4 and explain the explicit predictions.
comments.quote: Hypotheses 3-4 are only weakly motivated from the introduction. Your expectations are partly unclear (except for a specialized reader familiar with the topic), and the reader is left wondering why you make such explicit predictions.

comments.issue: Analyses are disconnected from the hypotheses, and the discussion structure does not follow them.
comments.request: Link hypotheses and analyses explicitly throughout, including the discussion.
comments.quote: it is difficult to follow why a specific analysis was done, as the analyses are disconnected from the hypotheses

comments.issue: The rationale given for studying only ectotherms also applies to endotherms.
comments.request: Justify why only ectotherms are considered.
comments.quote: Why only ectotherms? The same rationale can likewise apply to endotherms.

comments.issue: The abstract writing is vague and superficial.
comments.request: Make the abstract more specific and explicit.
comments.quote: I find the writing a bit vague and superficial. Readers would appreciate if you could be more specific and explicit.

comments.issue: Five line-level copy edits including precipitation units (mm not ml) and spacing between numbers and units.
comments.quote: L65 (and elsewhere): The unit of precipitation is mm not ml.

comments.issue: Humidity conditions and rearing success rates are not reported directly in the methods.
comments.request: Report humidity conditions and rearing success for canopy and understory.
comments.quote: Was the humidity regime also comparable to ambient conditions? My experience with rearing experiments is that low humidity due to air-conditioning impedes rearing success

comments.issue: The phylogeny's coverage and geography are not described.
comments.request: Add a sentence describing the phylogeny.
comments.quote: Maybe one additional sentence describing the phylogeny (e.g. coverage, geography) would be helpful.

comments.issue: Herbivore and parasitoid phylogenies differ in resolution, making results hard to compare.
comments.request: Add a supplemental analysis restricting the caterpillar phylogeny to family level.
comments.quote: it would be good to add a supplemental analysis in which the caterpillar phylogeny is restricted to family level as well

comments.issue: Citations for the R packages used are missing.
comments.request: Add citations for the R packages.
comments.quote: L 156ff: Citations for r-packages are missing.

comments.issue: Mean temperatures are not informative for a CTmax rationale.
comments.request: Report maximum temperatures and their variation instead.
comments.quote: For your rationale on CTmax, the mean temperatures are not informative. Better report maximum temperatures and variation therein.

comments.issue: Incomplete species coverage, especially for rare parasitoids, will influence the extinction simulation.
comments.request: Address the incomplete coverage limitation in the text.
comments.quote: One issue with your extinction simulation is the incomplete species coverage, especially for parasitoids.

comments.issue: Strata differences may themselves induce microclimate differences, reversing the implied causal direction.
comments.request: Reconsider the causal direction between strata and microclimate.
comments.quote: Well, isn’t it more the differences in strata that then induce differences in microclimate?

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 281-282 is unclear.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence at lines 281-282.
comments.quote: Please rewrite this sentence. There is something amiss.

comments.issue: Body-size effects on heating rate and water loss offer an alternative explanation to the physiological one.
comments.request: Consider the body-size alternative explanation.
comments.quote: Larger individuals have a smaller surface in regard to volume. Thus, their bodies will take longer to heat up completely in the experimental setup.

comments.issue: 'Hibernate' is the wrong term for insects; 'diapause' is more appropriate.
comments.request: Replace 'hibernate' with 'diapause'.
comments.quote: Maybe ‘diapause’ is the more appropriate term instead of ‘hibernate’.

comments.issue: The paragraph at lines 305-309 is vague and adds no content.
comments.request: Delete the paragraph at lines 305-309.
comments.quote: This paragraph is vague and weak. Could be deleted without loosing any content.

comments.issue: Critical reanalyses of the Lister & Garcia study are not acknowledged.
comments.request: Acknowledge the critical reanalyses of Lister & Garcia.
comments.quote: please note the critical reanalyzes (also published in PNAS) that identified many issues with the study

comments.issue: Staab et al. 2016 is relevant to microclimate tolerance of parasitoids.
comments.request: Consider Staab et al. 2016 in the discussion.
comments.quote: Maybe have a look at Staab et al. (2016, Proc R Soc B 283: 20160275).

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 321-322 is disconnected from the surrounding text.
comments.request: Integrate or remove the disconnected sentence.
comments.quote: This sentence is disconnected from the remaining text.

comments.issue: Dormann et al. 2009 does not fit because it does not cover lake food webs.
comments.request: Remove or replace the Dormann et al. 2009 citation.
comments.quote: I don’t think Dormann et al. 2009 does fit here (nothing on lake food webs in this study).

comments.issue: The single-site design is the most important missing limitation, and generality to other forests is unaddressed.
comments.request: Discuss the single-site limitation and generality to other ecosystem types.
comments.quote: The most important limitation is probably missing: You only investigated a single site!

comments.issue: The density curve legend omits null model specification details.
comments.request: Add the null model information to the legend.
comments.quote: The information behind the density curves (null model specification etc

comments.issue: Figure 2 lacks regression splines per sampling type.
comments.request: Add regression splines for canopy, ground hot and ground cool.
comments.quote: It would be very interesting for readers to add the regression splines per sampling type (canopy, ground hot, ground cool).

comments.issue: It is not tested whether the body-size pattern interacts with sampling type.
comments.request: Test for interaction effects between type and body size.
comments.quote: Have you tested for potential interaction effects between type and body size?

reviews.assessment: Finds the study well-written and interesting but raises major concerns about larval versus adult stages, network completeness, extinction simulations and modelling.

comments.issue: CTmax was measured on adults although the interaction occurs at the larval stage, so conclusions may be misleading.
comments.request: Elucidate larval versus adult CTmax and its consequences.
comments.quote: The interaction between parasitoids and herbivores occur during the herbivore larval stage but you did measure the thermal metrics only for the adults.

comments.issue: Parasitoid sampling coverage is about 50% and rearing success about 60%, lowering network completeness.
comments.request: Report differential mortality and be cautious about the canopy versus ground effect.
comments.quote: The sampling coverage of herbivores was initially very good while for parasitoids was around 50%.

comments.issue: Extinction cascades are simulated using CTmax rather than the more appropriate TSM.
comments.request: Use TSM for climate-change extinction simulations.
comments.quote: It is not clear why the authors simulate extinction cascades using CTmax and not TSM.

comments.issue: Rearing temperatures are much lower than canopy hot-season temperatures shown in Figure 1, and the choice is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain why such low rearing temperatures were selected.
comments.quote: Why did you select such low temperature for the rearing?

comments.issue: Model diagnostics are missing, including residual plots and handling of singletons in the unbalanced design.
comments.request: Show residuals with species as random factor and handle singletons.
comments.quote: I would like to see the residuals of the models including species as random factor.

comments.issue: The trophic-level effect could simply reflect body size.
comments.request: Test the overall body-size effect irrespective of taxon.
comments.quote: The strong effect of trophic level could be simply the effect of body size.

comments.issue: How the experimental temperatures were selected is not explained.
comments.request: Explain how the experimental temperatures were selected.
comments.quote: Please explain how you selected these temperatures.

comments.issue: How temperature was averaged across space and time to compute TSM is unclear.
comments.request: Describe how TSM was computed from temperature data.
comments.quote: Please provide more details on how you averaged the temperature across space and time to compute TSM.

comments.issue: Figure S4 shows very little variability in maximum CTmax for the canopy in the hot season.
comments.request: Explain the low variability in Figure S4.
comments.quote: In figure S4 there is very little variability in Maximum CTmax for canopy in the hot season. Why is that?

comments.issue: Mortality patterns of the rearing, including which individuals died, are not reported.
comments.request: Add a section reporting mortality by habitat and season.
comments.quote: We need to know who were the dead individuals and if the mortality differed between habitats and seasons.

comments.issue: How the analysis at lines 281-283 was performed is not described.
comments.request: Provide more details on the test used.
comments.quote: How did you test that? More details are needed.

comments.issue: The statement at lines 325-328 is not supported by the results.
comments.request: Remove the unsupported statement.
comments.quote: This statement is not supported by the results. Remove it.

comments.issue: The proportions at lines 349-350 are wrong; only individuals completing development matter.
comments.request: Recalculate proportions using individuals that completed development.
comments.quote: These proportion are wrong. The ones that matter are those that completed development.

title: Heat tolerance variation reveals vulnerability of tropical herbivore–parasitoid interactions to climate change

study.system: riverine fish; range-size and population synchrony data

editor_summary: Both reviewers see value in the rich database and analyses, but require: discussion oversold (especially generalization), excess conservation emphasis, rewriting and less jargon, better description of synchrony data, and fuller discussion of mechanisms.

reviews.assessment: Interesting idea and rich data, but the presentation must improve, synchrony mechanisms need deeper treatment, and the results section is too short.
strengths: great data linking synchrony, range size and body size

comments.issue: Spatial synchrony background is thin; known synchrony mechanisms and their effects on extinction risk are not covered.
comments.request: Review the mechanisms generating synchrony and how they affect extinction probability.
comments.quote: I found surprisingly little information about spatial synchrony, which I find essential to include in a paper which uses it to highlight extinction risks.

comments.issue: Ecological mechanisms driving the different processes are described superficially and without structure.
comments.request: Extend and structure the description of the ecological mechanisms.
comments.quote: I generally found that the descriptions and discussions surrounding the ecological mechanisms driving different processes were not deep or diverse enough, and should be extended considering the standards of this journal.

comments.issue: Writing is wordy with many grammatical errors, terminology inconsistencies and line-level edits throughout.
comments.quote: I found it very wordy at times, and I found a great deal of grammatical errors and terminology inconsistencies throughout the text.

comments.issue: The results section is too short, does not present synchrony results separately and omits Figure 3.
comments.request: Expand the results section and cover the synchrony results and Figure 3.
comments.quote: The results sections is very short. Doesn’t cover the spatial synchrony results independently, and doesn’t mention figure 3.

comments.issue: No exact definition is given of what the authors mean by geographic range size.
comments.request: Define geographic range size explicitly.
comments.quote: 81 – For clearness, I recommend you write exactly what you mean with geographic range size.

comments.issue: The reason why species with smaller ranges face higher extinction risk is not explained.
comments.request: Explain why small ranges imply higher extinction risk.
comments.quote: 83 – Why are species occupying a smaller range associated with a higher extinction risk?

comments.issue: Why range size is the most used criterion is not explained and lacks a supporting reference.
comments.request: Explain and reference why range size is the most used criterion.
comments.quote: I think it would be important to explain the reason as to why it is the most used criterion, and include a reference that back that up.

comments.issue: The two parts of a sentence do not complement each other.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence so its two parts are consistent.
comments.quote: The first part of the sentence doesn’t complement the second.

comments.issue: Four different terms are used for the same concept (extinction risk, species vulnerability, likelihood of extinction, extinction vulnerability).
comments.request: Choose one term and use it consistently throughout.
comments.quote: I might have misunderstood something, but I think that up to this point you have used “extinction risk”, “species vulnerability”, “likelihood of extinction” and “extinction vulnerability” to refer to the same thing.

comments.issue: The energetic-constraint argument is built incorrectly.
comments.request: Rewrite the argument linking energetic constraints, density and range size.
comments.quote: The energetic constraints don’t cause large species to have large ranges to compensate for their population density.

comments.issue: A boundary defined only by the extent of the study area carries no ecological meaning.
comments.request: Clarify what the boundary represents ecologically.
comments.quote: If the boundary is simply defined by the extent of the study area, then it carries no ecological meaningfulness.

comments.issue: A reference is missing.
comments.request: Add the missing reference.
comments.quote: 126 – Reference needed

comments.issue: The 'well-recognized implications' for extinction probability are not specified; the point could be stated directly.
comments.request: Specify the implications or state the point directly at the start.
comments.quote: 129 - What “well-recognized implications” for extinction probability do you refer to?

comments.issue: 'Rescue' in quotation marks is unclear; its meaning should be stated explicitly.
comments.request: Write explicitly what rescue means, e.g. rescue through migration.
comments.quote: 138 – Instead of writing “rescue” in quotation marks, I advise you write clearly what you mean for clarity.

comments.issue: The term 'portfolio effect' is used without a brief description.
comments.request: Briefly describe the portfolio effect.
comments.quote: 140 – I believe that the term “portfolio effect” deserves a brief description.

comments.issue: The sentence on asynchrony is inaccurate: asynchrony reduces rather than prevents extinctions and does not imply divergence.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence to clarify what compensatory mechanisms mean.
comments.quote: asynchrony does not prevent extinctions or local declines, it reduces the probability of extinctions.

comments.issue: The wording of the minimum viable range size definition is ambiguous (range that can maintain a species vs range a species could maintain).
comments.request: Use wording describing a range size that can maintain a species.
comments.quote: 149 – Maybe you mean to say that its the “minimum viable range size that can maintain a species”, not that that it’s the “minimum viable range size that a species could maintain”?

comments.issue: The claim that the synchrony-based MVRS can be estimated for a variety of species is wrong; it can be estimated for one species at a time.
comments.request: Remove 'for a variety of species with different body sizes'.
comments.quote: 152 – The synchrony-based MVRS, as you define it up to this point, can be estimate it for just one species.

comments.issue: Exclusion of lake species is not justified.
comments.request: Explain why lake species were excluded.
comments.quote: 184:186 – Why did the authors exclude lake species?

comments.issue: 'Size classes' and 'selecting a set' are vague and unclear on first reading.
comments.request: Specify what size classes mean and how they were selected.
comments.quote: It is not intuitive to understand what “size classes” you refer to when reading it first time.

comments.issue: It is unclear which points the regression line was fitted through and why; results appear only for the lower boundary.
comments.request: Clarify which points were used and give the rationale.
comments.quote: Which “them”? All upper and lower points? Combined? Separately? The results only show for the lower?

comments.issue: The methods paragraph reads as if all world species and all three biogeographic regions were analysed.
comments.request: Clarify which species sets were actually analysed.
comments.quote: 196:198 - This reads weird/wrong. As if you worked 1st with all the species in the world and also all the species in the 3 biogeographic regions.

comments.issue: The actual size ranges of the classes are not reported, and log transformation may conflict with 'equal' class sizes.
comments.request: Report class size ranges and clarify the transformation used.
comments.quote: 199 – I think that the authors should include the actual size ranges of the classes.

comments.issue: The description of varying body-size class widths is unclear.
comments.request: Rewrite the description of how body-size classes were defined.
comments.quote: 203 – I don’t understand what this means

comments.issue: The rationale for integrating major reproductive and movement events, and its expected effect, is missing.
comments.request: Explain why these events were integrated and the expected effects.
comments.quote: 219 – Why integrate major reproductive and movement events? What effect do the authors expect it to have on the results?

comments.issue: The assumption that occurrences are non-intersecting points is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify how occurrences and their intersections were defined.
comments.quote: 221 – I assume an “occurrence” is a point, and points do not intersect.

comments.issue: Assignment of occurrence status based on the closest river is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the closest-river assignment procedure.
comments.quote: 222:223 – What do you mean assigned status based on closest river?

comments.issue: The reason why Tedesco's method was not used for all cases is not explained.
comments.request: Explain why only some cases used Tedesco's method.
comments.quote: 223 – In what other cases? Why not use Tedesco’s way for all?

comments.issue: 'Common years' is not defined.
comments.request: Define what 'common years' means.
comments.quote: 229 – What is “common years”?

comments.issue: The abundance-threshold exclusion may remove rare and vulnerable species that are central to the study's aims.
comments.request: Justify the exclusion threshold and its consequences for rare species.
comments.quote: Also, couldn't this exclude rare and vulnerable species, which would be perhaps most relevant for a study aiming to assess risks and best management practices for those species?

comments.issue: The '20% included' threshold explanation is unclear and alternative thresholds are not examined.
comments.request: Describe the inclusion threshold more informatively.
comments.quote: 235:236 – I don’t understand the “20% included” part.

comments.issue: The relationship between the x-intercept and the scale of synchrony is unclear, and plots with multiple intercepts add confusion.
comments.request: Explain the difference between x-intercept and scale of synchrony.
comments.quote: 240 & 247 – Isn’t the “x-intercept” the same as the “scale of synchrony”? If not what is the difference?

comments.issue: Centering the correlogram to the region-wide average is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the centering procedure.
comments.quote: 249 – Could you please explain the last bit about centering the correlogram to the region-wide average?

comments.issue: The occurrence-based polygon is not described; geographic range estimation should be explained earlier.
comments.request: Describe how geographic ranges were estimated.
comments.quote: 254:255 – occurrence-based polygon is not described anywhere else in the text, so including it here as in brackets provides little help.

comments.issue: Calling the threshold 'the minimum geographical range area for persistence' overstates it; persistence is not guaranteed beyond that range.
comments.request: Use a more descriptive, cautious definition of the threshold.
comments.quote: I don’t think it is right to write “the minimum geographical range area for persistence”, because it implies too much too soon.

comments.issue: The implied directionality of sampling effects on the scale of synchrony is unsupported.
comments.request: Explain the basis for this directionality or remove it.
comments.quote: The "respectively" at the end infers that widespread sampling could have increased the scale of synchrony, and more sampling size would have reduced it.

comments.issue: The phrasing about the lower boundary is questionable; it may not demonstrate larger ranges for larger species if the upper boundary is horizontal.
comments.request: Rephrase the inference about the lower boundary.
comments.quote: 282 – I'm not sure about the phrasing here. The lower boundary does not demonstrate that larger species have larger rages if the upper boundary of the triangle is horizontal, right?

comments.issue: The text refers to Table S3, which only shows regression lines, not a triangular distribution of points.
comments.request: Correct the reference or the claim.
comments.quote: 291:292 – The sentence refers to the Table S3, which only shows the regression lines and not a triangular distribution of points.

comments.issue: 'Related traits' are not exemplified.
comments.request: Provide examples of the related traits.
comments.quote: 304 - What other “related traits”? please provide examples

comments.issue: The dispersal-based mechanism is weak; small species can disperse well and large ones poorly.
comments.request: Broaden the mechanistic discussion beyond dispersal capacity.
comments.quote: Small bodied species can also present high dispersal capacities and large ones can present low dispersal, depending for example on morphology or foraging strategies.

comments.issue: The claim that high dispersal protects populations contradicts the earlier rescue argument; wording should be corrected.
comments.request: Reword to say that high dispersal stabilizes local dynamics.
comments.quote: Yet, here the authors say high dispersal protects. I think a more accurate wording would be that high dispersal “stabilizes local dynamics”

comments.issue: Writing that large ranges could 'avoid synchronizing dynamics' is misleading.
comments.request: Rephrase: large ranges prevent full synchronization, not synchronization itself.
comments.quote: I find misleading to write that occupying large geographic ranges could “avoid synchronizing dynamics”.

comments.issue: The climate-synchrony reference is confusing because synchrony mechanisms are never established in the introduction.
comments.request: Establish the mechanisms before referring to climate-synchrony.
comments.quote: Since the authors never established the mechanisms driving synchrony in the introduction, this reference to “climate-synchrony” might be very confusing to many readers.

comments.issue: The argument that large species in different niches would not be synchronized is not understood.
comments.request: Clarify or revise this mechanistic argument.
comments.quote: If large species live in different environmental niches, where the populations can fluctuate independently, then they would not be synchronized, right?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the 'alternative challenges' are attributed to small or to large species.
comments.request: Clarify which species face these challenges.
comments.quote: But isn’t this the challenges that large species have? Am I missing something?

comments.issue: How the listed traits reduce local extinction probability is not explained, and it conflicts with the dispersal protection statement.
comments.request: Explain how these traits reduce the probability of local extinction.
comments.quote: Could the authors also explain how the listed traits (highly-abundant populations, short life histories and low dispersal capacities) reduce the probability of local extinction?

comments.issue: The link between space requirements and synchrony area is asserted without basis.
comments.request: Support the link to synchrony area or remove it.
comments.quote: I am fairly confident that the link they try to make to “synchrony area” is without base.

comments.issue: The relevance of the slope being approximately 1 is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the importance of the slope estimate.
comments.quote: 343:361 – Could the authors explain the relevance of the finding that the slope of the relationships is ~1?

comments.issue: No comparison between the proposed range limits and the limits already used by the IUCN.
comments.request: Discuss how the estimated limits compare with IUCN criteria.
comments.quote: 363:365 – The IUCN already uses certain geographic range limits to assess species (as you mentioned), perhaps this would be a great moment to discuss how yours would compare.

comments.issue: The assumption that body size and range data exist for the target species is not stated.
comments.request: State the data assumptions explicitly.
comments.quote: 373:375 Assuming that there is at least data on their body size and geographic range size, right?

comments.issue: A completely new result is introduced at the end of the discussion rather than in the results.
comments.request: Move the new result to the results section.
comments.quote: You may not introduce a completely new result at the end of the discussion. This should have been covered in the results.

comments.issue: 'Small number of locations' is not a valid example of severely fragmented distributions.
comments.request: Replace it with an appropriate example.
comments.quote: 387 – “small number” of locations is not an example of severely fragmented distributions.

comments.issue: The phrasing about evolutionary-time forces is wordy and hard to read, and those links are never mentioned in the text.
comments.request: Rewrite the passage more clearly and concisely.
comments.quote: I find this phrasing very wordy, unnecessary and much harder to read.

comments.issue: The regional examples are limited and appear to refer only to temperate regions.
comments.request: Include other regions or state clearly which regions are meant.
comments.quote: Any other regions you can include as examples? I feel like you actually just mean to refer to temperate regions, especially considering how you then talk about tropical regions.

comments.issue: The statement about small-range species' climatic niches and dispersal in other regions is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the intended point.
comments.quote: Are you trying to make the point that small-range species do not have narrow climatic niches and poor dispersal in other regions? Sounds like that.

comments.issue: Figure 1 has unexplained connecting lines, inconsistent units, redundant label text and a possibly wrong y-axis label in panel (b).
comments.request: Revise Figure 1 labels and explain the connecting lines.
comments.quote: The way it has been explain throughout is that “scale of synchrony ” = distance, and synchrony-based MVRS = area.

comments.issue: Blue points defining the distribution-based MVRS should be distinguished, and realms should have different shapes.
comments.request: Differentiate defining points and realm shapes in Figure 2.
comments.quote: I would like differentiate the blue points that actually define the distribution-based MVRS from the rest of blue points.

comments.issue: Table 1 duplicates information already shown in a figure.
comments.request: Consider removing the redundant table.
comments.quote: TABLE 1 – I find redundant including the same information as a figure and as a table.

comments.issue: Key graphs illustrating the spline correlation approach are relegated to the supplementary material.
comments.request: Show some of the Figure S2 graphs in the main text.
comments.quote: I believe that at least some of these graphs could be shown in the main text to illustrate the spline correlation approach used.

comments.issue: Units are missing in Figures S3 and S4.
comments.request: Add units to Figures S3 and S4.
comments.quote: FIGURE S3 – Units missing. FIGURE S4 – Units missing.

reviews.assessment: Well-written, robust and novel, but the conservation-oriented discussion and generalization from 21 species are exaggerated.
strengths: novel and interesting contribution to ecological theory

comments.issue: Generalizing from 21 species to about 15,000 freshwater fishes is not justified.
comments.request: Restrict the generalization or justify it with more species.
comments.quote: The test is performed on 21 species, but the authors propose a generalization to about 15K species of freshwater fishes.

comments.issue: The conservation and Red List discussion is exaggerated; predictions are only usable for initial screening.
comments.request: Tone down the conservation discussion and clarify it cannot be used for assessments.
comments.quote: Second, the predictions are not applicable in a Red List context, if not for simple initial screening (among other existing approaches) for prioritization of new assessments and reassessments.

comments.issue: The link between threatened species and the range-body relationship stems from Red List classification bias (criterion B), not independent evidence.
comments.request: Acknowledge the classification bias when interpreting this support.
comments.quote: This is because, as the authors correctly explain, the majority of these species were classified under crit. B. However, this stems from a classification bias in the Red List.

comments.issue: The reference Diniz-Filho et al. 2005 on the range-size pattern in carnivorans is missing.
comments.request: Cite Diniz-Filho et al. 2005.
comments.quote: A reference missing is Diniz-Filho et al. 2005, which tested the range-size pattern on mammalian carnivorans and highlight the relevance for conservation assessments.

comments.issue: Range size is not used directly for criterion B; it estimates the EOO used under B1.
comments.request: Correct the description of how range size feeds into criterion B.
comments.quote: the range size is not used directly for criterion B, but can be used to estimate the EOO, which is then used to assess species under B1

comments.issue: The claim linking small ranges to higher extinction risk only holds if range proxies population size; criterion B EOO is independent of density.
comments.request: Qualify the claim about range size and extinction risk.
comments.quote: the Red List criterion B on EOO is used as a proxy of risk spread, which is independent on the population density of the species

comments.issue: The binned approach is sensitive to the definition of bins; quantile regression is suggested instead.
comments.request: Consider quantile regression instead of binning.
comments.quote: This approach risks to be sensitive to the definition of the bins, why not a simple quantile regression instead?

comments.issue: The dispersal mechanism is supported by citations that do not concern fishes, whose dispersal is mostly passive.
comments.request: Support the mechanism with fish-specific evidence or revise it.
comments.quote: Is this also true in fishes? The citations provided do not refer to fishes. Fishes's dispersal is in most cases passive AFAIK, so this mechanism may not apply to your case study.

comments.issue: Unclear whether the mechanisms are meant to explain this study's results or patterns found in other taxa.
comments.request: State explicitly which results the mechanisms explain.
comments.quote: In general, it is unclear if the mechanisms that you describe are supposed to explain your results, or similar patterns found in other studies on different taxa.

comments.issue: Density-synchrony and life-history effects on synchrony are only hinted at and not clearly explained.
comments.request: Explain more clearly how density and life history shape synchrony.
comments.quote: Large species live at lower population densities, which implies that range size must be larger at equal minimum population size.

comments.issue: Evidence for the pattern and slope in fishes is not given.
comments.request: Provide fish evidence and compare slopes with other groups.
comments.quote: Is there any evidence of this pattern in fishes? If so, is the slope similar to other groups?

title: Scale of population synchrony confirms macroecological estimates of minimum viable range size

study.system: Terrestrial and freshwater communities; dispersal, speciation, selection and drift under human impacts

editor_summary: Editor advises a clearer focus on the four community processes, suggests dropping Figure 1, finds Figure 2's heatmap unclear, and praises Figure 3 and Table 1.

reviews.assessment: Appreciative of the synthesis and framework; asks for stronger motivation and caveats when comparing the two ecosystem types.
strengths: synthesizes general perspectives based on the metacommunity concept
directive for future research in global ecology and biogeography

comments.issue: The motivation for treating terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems together is weak given scale dependence and heterogeneity.
comments.request: Strengthen the motivation and emphasize the benefits.
comments.quote: More explanations were required for the motivation considering terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems together.

comments.issue: Statements about ecosystem differences in Table 1 ignore life-history context and need caveats.
comments.request: Add cautions and limitations to temper the statements.
comments.quote: Alternatively, some cautions/limitations can be added to lower the tone (as reminder messages), and therefore relieve the feeling due to this concern.

comments.issue: The island-like nature of lakes and ponds is linked to metaecosystem ideas that are not cited.
comments.request: Connect this point to the metaecosystem literature.
comments.quote: This was an interesting point that lakes/ponds were island-like habitats.

comments.issue: Tube fishway technology for overcoming dam fragmentation is not mentioned.
comments.request: Add this technology to the dispersal discussion.
comments.quote: This may be an interesting point for discussing habitat fragmentation-related dispersal.

comments.issue: Recent experimental studies quantifying drift directly are missing.
comments.request: Cite these drift studies.
comments.quote: Drift was indeed rarely quantified directly. A few recent studies showed some advances in this aspect using filed or laboratory experiments

comments.issue: 6 line-level copy edits (sentence revisions and typos).
comments.quote: Line 344: Correct 'naïvete' (as well as in Table 1).

reviews.assessment: Strongly positive about the synthesis and figures but wants a clearer focus and more balanced terrestrial counterparts.
strengths: Table 1 and Figure 3 really well done
impressed by how the concepts were tied together

comments.issue: The main focus is confused between comparing the four processes and linking the three columns of Figure 1.
comments.request: Clarify and focus on the community processes.
comments.quote: I feel like there’s confusion between if they are trying to focus on the differences in the 4 community processes in terrestrial and fresh water systems

reviews.assessment: Enjoys the paper but says re-analysis and rewriting are needed to address survey, detection, and scope concerns.
strengths: enjoyed a paper on density-dependent habitat selection in an elk herd
very cool idea that DDHS drives population distribution

comments.issue: Aerial surveys are one-winter snapshots; morning timing and December versus March months bias habitat selection.

comments.issue: Discussion is narrow and a poor fit for Ecology Letters, focusing on Yellowstone elk instead of broader systems.

comments.quote: the discussion focused narrowly in on elk habitat selection instead of expanding to other species in other systems, which would highlight the ecological insights you found in this paper.

comments.issue: Eulerian versus Lagrangian data discussion does not reconcile results with past tracking-based research.
comments.request: Discuss which methodology better captures DDHS and why results differ.
comments.quote: which methodology provides a better understanding of DDHS? Would it be fine-scale habitat associations provided by tracking data, or a snapshot in time provided by the aerial counts?

comments.issue: Expansion of the winter range definition is unexplained.
comments.request: Clarify why the winter range definition was expanded.
comments.quote: Line 68 – Why did you expand the definition of the winter range in Yellowstone? Some clarification would be helpful for readers used to the more common definition.

comments.issue: Copy edit: Moll et al. 2017 is cited twice at line 138.
comments.quote: Line 138 – “Moll et al. 2017” was repeated twice.

comments.issue: The composite safety variable is ambiguously described and its combination with covariates unclear.

comments.issue: Rationale for using RSS to interpret the food/safety-density interaction should be stated.

comments.issue: Effect-size summary statistics are missing; Open:log(Dens) overlaps zero yet is treated as important.

comments.issue: Very low mean pseudo-R2 raises doubts about what the results say about habitat selection.

comments.issue: Predator-prey interaction implications of DDHS-driven redistribution deserve a dedicated paragraph.

comments.quote: What are the outcomes of DDSH affecting elk population distribution for predator-prey interactions in Yellowstone, for example?

comments.issue: The paragraph ending at lines 337-338 reads oddly and engages poorly with the cited literature.
comments.request: Rework this paragraph and broaden the papers discussed.
comments.quote: Either way, I think that it comes across as strange to end the paragraph like this, and maybe focusing on other, non-related elk/red deer papers would be useful here

comments.issue: The statement about not identifying the redistribution mechanism seems to contradict the paper's own density-driven argument.
comments.request: Clarify this statement and discuss the redistribution mechanism.
comments.quote: Maybe I’m interpreting this incorrectly, but aren’t you arguing in the paper that the change in density changed the habitat selection of elk to focus more on safety and less on food?

comments.issue: Figure 6 could move to supplementary material as it adds little.

reviews.assessment: Thoroughly impressed; sees a rare major finding warranting publication, with only supportive minor comments.

shows predator density and type shape DDHS

comments.issue: The alternative conceptualisation of high-density scrambling as habitat generalization is not discussed.

title: Density‐dependent habitat selection alters drivers of population distribution in northern Yellowstone elk

study.system: model communities; Lotka-Volterra trait-based competition and ESS simulations

editor_summary: Editor notes all reviewers find the study robust and timely, but the symmetry assumption, lack of environmental variability, unclear terms and weak links to empirical reality require major revision.

reviews.assessment: Well-written contribution, but key methods are underdescribed, terms unexplained, and the unrealistic interaction and static-environment assumptions limit the message.

comments.issue: ESS methodology is only briefly summarized although it is the evolutionary benchmark of the comparison.
comments.request: Describe the ESS method more clearly and completely.
comments.quote: Most notably, the description of the ESS methodology is briefly summarized.

comments.issue: Technical terms (ESS, competitive exclusion, limiting similarity, trait distribution) are used without explanation; traits and organisms never specified.
comments.request: Explain the technical terms and specify the traits and organisms.
comments.quote: Too much technical terms are used without a clear explanation.

comments.issue: Reference usage is unclear (Levine et al. 2017; Chase 2003; Fukami and Nakajima 2011); links to the model are not explained.

comments.quote: the strength of conspecific density dependence, the intraspecific interactions, are equal to 1 for all species (line 73). This is very unrealistic as hundreds of study have shown empirically.

reviews.assessment: Well-written and reasonable theoretical contribution; the key concern is that symmetric interaction matrices may bias the ecological versus ESS diversity comparison.

provides working hypotheses for natural communities

comments.issue: Discussion needs more nuance and positioning within the ecological assembly and diversity distribution literature.

comments.quote: the discussion should be made a bit more nuanced, in order to place their new results within the broader field of ecological assembly and diversity distributions

comments.issue: Symmetry assumption is unrealistic; asymmetric gLV matrices allow unfeasible stable states and complex dynamics that symmetric matrices cannot produce.
comments.request: Run a numerical exercise showing how symmetry affects ecological versus ESS diversity.
comments.quote: I think their approach would be better off if they make a small exercise to show how the critical (and completely unrealistic) assumption of symmetry impacts on the relationship between ecological vs. ESS diversity distributions.

comments.issue: Discussion in lines 326-340 is hard for less technical readers without numerical or graphical results.

title: Maximal ecological diversity exceeds evolutionary diversity in model ecosystems

strengths: fundamental contribution to the evolutionary theory of reproductive skew
shows why different kinds of skewness naturally emerge
clear arguments based on constrained fitness maximization

comments.issue: The relatedness value 0.81 is given without context.
comments.request: Give context for the number or simply say “high”.
comments.quote: So a number like 0.81 must be accompanied by a little context! Or, you can just say "high"

comments.issue: Two line-level edits: the economic term “budget constraint” and a garbled citation.
comments.quote: Line 35, the term "budget constraint" is better written as "energy budget constraint" or, indeed can be left out of the sentence. Ecologists rarely use the term.

comments.issue: “Earlier” at line 226 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify what earlier refers to.

reviews.assessment: Appreciates good theory but is not convinced that reducing social evolution to production and food acquisition provides real insight into animal social systems.

comments.issue: The case that production, reduced to food acquisition, is an overlooked and important driver of social-system evolution is not convincing.

comments.quote: the authors do not make a convincing case that we can understand the evolution of animal social systems (including classic eusociality) through this particular framework. In part, this stems from this being a rather unique take on the subject.

comments.issue: The theory is not grounded in concrete examples or compared against prevailing theory.

comments.quote: the strongest theoretical papers often do use specific examples in which the theory is applied. Comparisons against the prevailing theory then add strength to the case made.

title: Reproduction and production in a social context: Group size, reproductive skew and increasing returns

study.system: plant-pollinator communities; greenhouse warming experiment

reviews.assessment: Strong, novel simultaneous warming experiment with clear writing, but asks for clearer hypotheses, replication details and statistical alternatives.
strengths: novel simultaneous warming of plants and pollinators

comments.issue: Predictions about mismatches and bee preference lability lack rationale.
comments.request: Explain the rationale for the predictions.
comments.quote: Predictions could be better contextualized in the introduction. You predict that flowering and bee emergence would mismatch with species-specific responses that reflect evolutionary history.

comments.issue: The study's life-stage framing is unclear because warming only covers adult bee and reproductive plant stages.
comments.request: Clarify which life stages the warming treatment covers.
comments.quote: I think in the framing of the study it should be clarified that warming refers primarily to increased temperatures during adult bee foraging and when plants are already in the reproductive state.

comments.issue: The focus on nectar rather than pollen is not justified.
comments.request: Justify focusing on nectar over pollen.
comments.quote: Why is there a focus on nectar rather than pollen as a factor limiting optimal foraging and bee reproductive success?

comments.issue: The true unit of replication (arena or greenhouse) is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the replication unit and greenhouse layout.
comments.quote: it is unclear whether the true unit of replication is the mesh arena, or the greenhouse. Was there only one greenhouse per treatment?

comments.issue: Whether multiple greenhouses per treatment require a nested random effect is unclear.
comments.request: Account for greenhouse structure in the random effects.
comments.quote: It is unclear whether the mesh arenas were subdivided into multiple greenhouses per treatment, or whether each warming treatment was housed in the same greenhouse.

comments.issue: Survival analysis would better model flowering and emergence timing.

comments.quote: A survival analysis would be more appropriate to evaluate the likelihood of flowering/bee emergence over time.

comments.issue: Nectar concentration is inappropriately modelled with Gaussian errors.

comments.quote: For nectar concentration, it would be more appropriate to model using a beta distribution.

comments.issue: Sex-specific bee effects are tested without stated expectations.

comments.quote: You test for bee sex-specific effects but don’t explain why you would expect male and female bees to respond differently.

comments.issue: Treatment and visitation rate are correlated in the same model, risking type 1 error.

comments.issue: Bee reproductive output could be assessed via cocoon weight or number per nest.

comments.quote: Could you test for an effect on the weight or number of cocoons per nest as a way to evaluate effects on bee reproductive output?

comments.issue: The logic of the 5-month overwintering statement is unclear.

comments.quote: I don’t follow the logic here. Is 5 months a longer overwintering period than is typical of this species?

comments.issue: The term 'bee nesting success' is confusing.
comments.request: Define what nesting success means here.
comments.quote: I am confused by how the term “bee nesting success” is being used here – does it mean whether eggs were laid at all?

reviews.assessment: Clear, well-designed experiment with appropriate analyses and thorough discussion of limitations; only minor suggestions.
strengths: appropriate experiment design and sample sizes

comments.issue: The bee-release setup at lines 136-138 is hard to visualize.
comments.request: Describe the tube setup and bee release timing.
comments.quote: Consider improving this description, I was having a hard time visualizing the setup. Was the tube blocking the bee exit?

comments.issue: The term 'straw' appears without prior introduction.

comments.quote: the word "straw" is not in the previous section when bee setup is mentioned, maybe use it there as well

comments.issue: Figure 1 species order does not match the text order.

comments.quote: consider changing the order of the species so the bee is at the end. This way, the order of the species will match the order in which they are mentioned in the text.

comments.issue: Apparent sex-specific responses to warming are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the sex-specific responses (Figure S6).
comments.quote: Consider discussing the apparent sex-specific responses to warming (Figure S6).

comments.issue: The order-of-magnitude difference in bee reproduction between treatments is understated.
comments.request: Acknowledge the difference in wording.
comments.quote: Bee reproduction output seems to follow an unexpected pattern with higher reproductive success (11 cocoons) under warmer conditions than under ambient conditions (1 cocoon).

reviews.assessment: Admires the experiment but sees several statistical issues and two major caveats that must be resolved before publication.
strengths: interesting findings, e.g., reduced mismatch but lower seed production
important contribution to understanding climate-change impacts

comments.issue: Results from a reduced, arbitrary species set are hard to extrapolate to nature.
comments.request: Frame this extrapolation caveat clearly in the Discussion.
comments.quote: the results are from an experiment with an isolated, reduced and somewhat arbitrary set of species; so it is thus difficult to extrapolate too much to what will happen in nature

comments.issue: Resource limitation cannot be ruled out without hand-pollination experiments.
comments.request: Acknowledge that resource limitation cannot be excluded.
comments.quote: the authors did not conduct hand-pollination experiments to distinguish between resource and pollen limitation in terms of reproduction

comments.issue: Model assumptions are never assessed, especially dispersion for binomial/Poisson GLMMs.
comments.request: Check assumptions with DHARMa and use negative binomial/beta-binomial if needed.
comments.quote: Throughout the analysis section, I do not see any reference to assessing the models to see if they meet basic assumptions.

comments.issue: LMM error distributions for bounded concentration and positive volume may be inappropriate.
comments.request: Consider beta errors for concentration and gamma for volume.
comments.quote: concentration is a percentage variable that is continuous, but also bound between 0 and 100

comments.issue: Including day of year and its square is questionable and their effects are inconsistently interpreted.

title: Warming of experimental plant–pollinator communities advances phenologies, alters traits, reduces interactions and depresses reproduction

study.system: Amazonian bird community; 97-ha plot resampled after 36 years

reviews.assessment: Well written and methodologically clear, but lacks environmental data and the stability result may reflect weak statistical sensitivity.
strengths: methodological details sufficiently described and clear

comments.issue: Single-site case studies cannot support generalisations about Amazonian bird communities.
comments.quote: All three bird papers are narrow case studies and thus do not allow for generalizations.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether observed stability exceeds expectations from an ecological drift model.
comments.request: Compare observed stability with drift or Brownian motion model expectations.
comments.quote: I wondered whether the observed stability is higher or lower than expected from an ecological drift model.

comments.issue: The lack of data on environmental changes makes the discussion of causes speculative.
comments.request: Add environmental change data or temper the causal discussion.
comments.quote: The major shortcoming of this study is the lack of data on environmental changes (or lack of change).

comments.issue: Wide bootstrap confidence limits may make different SAD shapes undetectable, and the 1% error band method is unclear.
comments.request: Compare goodness-of-fit metrics using bootstrap samples.
comments.quote: Bootstrapped confidence limits might be very wide and different SAD shapes might become undetectable.

comments.issue: The rank order correlation between 1982 and 2018 is not reported, and Table 1 correlations hold only after excluding outliers.
comments.request: Report rank order correlations and reconsider outlier exclusion.
comments.quote: In my feeling high stability would imply a rank order correlation of > 0.9.

comments.issue: The same data could be presented as ongoing compositional restructuring rather than stability.
comments.request: Consider presenting the data as compositional restructuring.
comments.quote: In other words, the data might also have been presented as an example of ongoing compositional restructuring.

reviews.assessment: Happy to see this repeat of a classic study with analytical advances, but several important concerns about drivers, methods and the similarity claim.

comments.issue: Two snapshots from one plot give no sense of year-to-year variation.
comments.request: Discuss the limits of two snapshots without year-to-year variation.
comments.quote: Unfortunately, it does end up as two snapshots on one plot. We don’t get any sense for how year-to-year variation might be involved

comments.issue: A plot near the river may not represent the wider Amazon region.
comments.request: Address how representative the river-adjacent plot is.
comments.quote: what might be expected 5km away from the river (which would probably be more representative of that part of the Amazon)

comments.issue: Reserve scale is identified as the driver although other studies were also in undisturbed areas and climate has been stable.
comments.request: Consider alternative drivers rather than reserve scale.
comments.quote: How can this being a large-scale reserve be identified as the driver? It isn't like the other studies that are being compared are in the middle of disturbed areas.

comments.issue: The sampling designs of the compared studies (replicate plots, plot networks) are not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention the designs of the compared studies.
comments.quote: It is probably worth mentioning that the Blake and Loiselle study included two replicate plots, and the Stouffer et al. study was a network of plots over a greater spatial extent.

comments.issue: The tree papers cited may not be the most up to date on structural changes across Amazonia.
comments.request: Update the tree-paper citations or discuss structural changes.
comments.quote: Are these the most up-to-date tree papers? Maybe you don't want to introduce the structural changes identified across Amazonian plots?

comments.issue: A relevant paper on flock gatherings as evidence of stability is not cited.
comments.request: Cite this paper as evidence of stability.
comments.quote: I’d say the first author’s paper on flock gatherings in French Guiana qualifies as evidence of stability.

comments.issue: The minimum sample size for kernel estimates is not reported until much later.
comments.request: Report minimum sample sizes earlier in the methods.
comments.quote: What was the minimum sample size for this? For how many species could it be applied?

comments.issue: Handling of species whose territories extend outside the plot is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the handling of territories extending outside the plot.
comments.quote: Also, could you explain what happens with species whose territories extend out of the plot?

comments.issue: Lek counts might be a better measure for some hummingbirds.
comments.request: Consider lek counts for hummingbirds.
comments.quote: It seems lek counts would be a better measure for some hummingbirds.

comments.issue: Parrot density estimates from such studies are questionable.
comments.quote: I remain highly skeptical of parrot density in studies like this.

comments.issue: The Piculus sentence is unclear and seems inconsistent with the table.
comments.request: Clarify the Piculus sentence and align it with the table.
comments.quote: I don’t understand this sentence. Does this mean that e.g. multiple species of Piculus weren’t detected during spot mapping, but only during flock observations?

comments.issue: Changes in rare species may not be evaluated by the analysis.
comments.request: Ensure rare-species changes are evaluated.
comments.quote: This worries me that rare species becoming slightly more rare (or slightly more common, for that matter) won’t be evaluated.

comments.issue: The claim of strong similarity in almost all species is not supported; effect sizes seem ignored in favour of p values.
comments.request: Support the similarity claim with effect sizes, not just p values.
comments.quote: I can’t see how ‘strong similarity in almost all species in 1982 and 2018’ is supported.

comments.issue: Survey error for difficult canopy birds is not addressed.
comments.request: Discuss survey error for canopy birds.
comments.quote: some of these canopy birds can be really difficult to survey, so I wonder about the associated error

comments.issue: The interpretation for the riverine species P. cayennensis and Nasica seems inconsistent with their increase.
comments.request: Check the interpretation for these riverine species.
comments.quote: when I saw the increase in P. cayennensis and Nasica I would have though these riverine species had increased

comments.issue: The language implies Manu is pristine in contrast to trashed landscapes sampled elsewhere.
comments.request: Revise the comparison language about other sites.
comments.quote: The language you used is likely to conjure Manu as pristine, in stark contrast to trashed landscapes sampled elsewhere. That’s not accurate.

comments.issue: The body size and territory considerations are not aligned with work on thermal or hygric niches.
comments.request: Relate findings to thermal and hygric niche work.
comments.quote: How do they align with work from Panama and elsewhere on thermal or maybe hygric niches?

comments.issue: Supplemental figure axes are not equally scaled, so the expected line is not at 45 degrees.
comments.request: Use equal axis scaling.
comments.quote: I suggest scaling the x and y axes the same so the expected line is at 45 degrees.

reviews.assessment: Supportive of the rare resampling dataset, but the analyses are under-described and likely need redesign.
strengths: excellent opportunity to study 36-year community change

comments.issue: The analyses are not described in enough detail to be understood, and likely need redesign.
comments.request: Describe the analyses in detail and redesign where needed.
comments.quote: the analyses were not presented in enough detail for me to understand what was done

comments.issue: A binomial GLMM modelling counts with overdispersion and phylogenetic correlations is not used.
comments.request: Use a binomial GLMM accounting for overdispersion and phylogeny.
comments.quote: A relatively simple approach would be to use a binomial GLMM in which a "success" is a count in 1982 and a "failure" is a count in 2018.

comments.issue: Sensitivity of the analyses to phylogenetic uncertainty is not tested.
comments.request: Repeat analyses across several phylogenies.
comments.quote: A simple approach would be to perform the analyses with several phylogenies to see if the overall conclusions are affected.

comments.issue: Subsets are analysed separately instead of all data together with guild and body size terms.
comments.request: Analyze all data together with guild and body size terms.
comments.quote: I would analyze the data all together, including categorical variables for feeding guides.

comments.issue: A zero intercept in the regression analyses makes a positive relationship inevitable.
comments.request: Remove the zero-intercept constraint.
comments.quote: An intercept of zero should never be used in the regression analyses. A zero intercept makes a positive relationship inevitable.

comments.issue: Whether the SAD confidence intervals are 95% is not stated.
comments.request: State whether the SAD confidence intervals are 95%.
comments.quote: The authors don't state whether there CIs for the SADs are 95%.

comments.issue: If outliers are expected by chance, the outlier designation is questionable.

comments.quote: If outliers are expected to occur by chance, doesn't this mean that they are not outliers?

comments.issue: Local and regional are used too loosely, conflating climatic with other processes.

comments.quote: I didn't understand how the authors could draw any conclusions about “local” versus “regional” processes, and I suspect that this is because the authors “local” and “regional” too loosely.

comments.issue: The results are hyped as surprising although they are expected given little human impact.
comments.request: Tone down the surprise framing.
comments.quote: I found the apparent hyping of the results as a “surprise” unnecessary.

comments.issue: The manuscript contains many vague and inaccurate statements.

comments.issue: Table 1 says 'No relationship' for guilds that the text reports as declining.

comments.quote: Nectarivores and bamboo specialists are characterized as having “No relationship” in Table 1, although the authors state in the text that they have declined.

title: The structure and organisation of an Amazonian bird community remains little changed after nearly four decades in Manu National Park

study.system: optimal foraging theory; stochastic dynamic programming models

reviews.assessment: Interesting idea, but the method promises more than it delivers for experimentalists and does not improve on existing SDP approaches.

comments.issue: The method is claimed to identify optimal behavior in multidimensional settings, but key parameters cannot be measured experimentally, so optimal GUDs remain unknowable.
comments.request: Temper the claims about experimental determination of optimal GUDs.
comments.quote: The authors seem to be claiming that their method will allow determination of the optimal behavior under a multidimensional setting. I don’t see this.

comments.issue: The strategy map ignores that animals near strategy borders must track state constantly, and information value depends on environmental variability, which learning theory already covers.
comments.request: Address border behavior and the role of environmental variability.
comments.quote: First, as stated above, small changes in state may not change the optimal behavior. However, this is only true if the animal is not on the border of where the optimal strategy changes.

comments.issue: The computational advantage is illusory: adding the states back would make the models as complex as existing SDPs.

comments.issue: The discrete diet-change assumption contradicts the partial preferences seen in all experimental evidence.

reviews.assessment: Sees an elegant, valuable theoretical contribution but asks for clearer explanation of the framework and its applications for a broad audience.

comments.issue: The domains of application of existing approaches versus the new framework are not made clear.

comments.issue: The complex method is not explained accessibly for a broad ecological readership.
