comments.issue: Lines 170-173 begin with 'after the searches' but appear to describe another search.
comments.request: Clarify this section.
comments.quote: I don't follow this little section -this para begins with 'after the searches' but here it seems to be about another search?

comments.issue: More inclusion criteria appear at line 175 than at line 145; link to the preregistration is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the modified question and criteria.
comments.quote: you defined some inclusion criteria already on line 145 so it's a bit of a surprise to see more inclusion criteria defined here

comments.issue: Clutch size is excluded from the reproductive success measure without justification.
comments.request: Explain included outcomes and the trade-offs of interest.
comments.quote: I am a bit surprised you didn't include variables like clutch size in your measure of reproductive success.

comments.issue: Which observational studies were included and their causal-inference implications could be clearer.
comments.request: Clarify the inclusion of multi-site observational studies.
comments.quote: This is implied by your last sentence here, but could be clearer since this has implications for the strength of causal inferences you can make.

comments.issue: Source of the habitat type classifications is not given.
comments.request: Explain where habitat types came from.
comments.quote: and from where did you get these habitat types? A global land cover map? Google Earth?

comments.issue: Rows and columns of the matrix at lines 240-251 are unclear, as is data lost to missing combinations.
comments.request: Explain the matrix and lost data.
comments.quote: I have read this para a few times now and I am still unclear what are on the rows and columns of this matrix.

comments.issue: Line 252 does not state which effect sizes are computed.
comments.request: State the effect sizes being calculated.
comments.quote: Start with a sentence making clear what effect sizes you are calculating

comments.issue: Line 275 seems to mean coefficient rather than matrix.
comments.request: Clarify coefficient versus matrix.
comments.quote: I think you mean coefficient instead of matrix. If it is a matrix, what is on the rows and columns?

comments.issue: Difference between variables and indicator variables at lines 278-281 is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the two variable sets.
comments.quote: What is the difference between the variables in the first sentence and the indicator variables in the second sentence?

comments.issue: I2 is not explained for non-specialists.
comments.request: Explain what I2 measures.
comments.quote: It worth explaining what I2 measures, for those not doing meta-analysis.

comments.issue: Publication bias is tested per pairwise comparison instead of across the standardised dataset.
comments.request: Test publication bias across all studies.
comments.quote: Why are you assessing publication bias at the level of each pair-wise comparison.

comments.issue: Heterogeneity is computed per pairwise combination rather than across all standardised effect sizes.
comments.request: Estimate heterogeneity across all studies.
comments.quote: Why is heterogeneity being calculated separately for each pairwise combination and not across all datasets when the effect sizes have been standardized?

comments.issue: No goodness-of-fit checks are reported.
comments.request: Report goodness-of-fit checks.
comments.quote: Line 306 - Any goodness of fit checks?

comments.issue: Multiple effect sizes per study require a study-level random intercept.
comments.request: Add study as a random intercept.
comments.quote: since you sometimes had multiple effect sizes from the same study, strictly speaking, 'study' should have been included as a random intercept

comments.issue: Q tests appear in results but not in the methods.
comments.request: Describe the Q tests in the methods.
comments.quote: you don't mention Q tests in your method section

comments.issue: A value of 1.1 contradicts effect sizes standardised to correlation coefficients.
comments.request: Clarify the standardisation of effect sizes.
comments.quote: I thought all the effect size were standardized to correlation coefficient, but here we have a value of 1.1

comments.issue: 'Best indicator' at line 375 is ambiguous between strongest and most consistent.
comments.request: Define what 'best indicator' means.
comments.quote: I am not sure what this means - that food availability was best indicated by insect population suppression.

comments.issue: The claim that nest success is the best indicator needs clarification.
comments.request: Explain what 'best indicator' means here.
comments.quote: is it quite correct to say nest success is the best indicator for reproductive success?

comments.issue: Existing meta-analyses of food supplementation are overlooked at line 389.
comments.request: Cite the food supplementation meta-analyses.
comments.quote: I am not sure that this is quite true. There have been a number of meta-analysis of food supplementation studies

comments.issue: Line 439 ignores that weaker supplementation effects may reflect confounding in observational studies.
comments.request: Discuss this alternative explanation and infer causality cautiously.
comments.quote: the alternative explanation here is the difference between experimental and observation studies and the potential for confounding factors

reviews.assessment: Strongly enthusiastic: calls it a timely, tutorial-quality meta-analysis of impressive scale, offering only a nutritional-value discussion point and minor editing.
strengths: timely and important addition on consequences of insect declines
tutorial-level methods and meticulous attention to detail

comments.issue: Poor nutritional value of mealworm larvae (low carotenoids) is a possible explanation not discussed.

comments.issue: Typos and punctuation errors are scattered through the manuscript.

comments.quote: There are typos and punctuation errors scattered throughout the manuscript, all of which are easily fixed with minor editing.

title: The effect of insect food availability on songbird reproductive success and chick body condition: Evidence from a systematic review and meta‐analysis

study.system: green swordtail fish; female mate choice experiments

editor_summary: All three reviewers liked the work very much; most comments are straightforward, but a few require thinking and work; two reviewers want to see the revised version.

reviews.assessment: Enthusiastic; no major revisions, but suggests framing the work in mate-choice decision-rule theory and clarifying several points.
strengths: valuable contribution to the mate choice literature

comments.issue: Introduction zeroes in on sensory biology instead of the broader mate-choice decision-rule framework.
comments.request: Allude to the decision-rule framework earlier and cite Real 1990 and Moore & Moore 1988.
comments.quote: I think it would be helpful if the paper at least alluded to this framework in the introduction, rather than immediately zeroing in on the sensory biology aspect of the study

comments.issue: Abstract refers to 'implications' without stating what they are.
comments.request: Spell out the implications in the abstract.
comments.quote: please don’t refer to “implications” without spelling out what those implications are

comments.issue: The significance of first demonstrating proportional processing in a visual rather than auditory modality is not explained.
comments.request: Explain why the sensory modality matters.
comments.quote: the emphasis on its first discovery in a visual, as opposed to auditory, signal doesn’t make it clear why that is important

comments.issue: Whether proportional processing is a byproduct of sensory construction or adaptive is discussed too late.
comments.request: Consider this question earlier in the paper.
comments.quote: Is this a kind of byproduct of the way the brain/sense organs are constructed, or is it an adaptive component of how animals evaluate signals?

comments.issue: Why females prefer greater signal magnitude, and whether they ever prefer smaller signals, is unaddressed.
comments.request: Discuss the function of preferring larger signals.
comments.quote: I wonder why females do indeed often prefer signals with greater magnitude in the first place

comments.issue: Group housing and paired testing raise issues of copying and olfactory cues affecting choices.
comments.request: Address social information and olfactory cue effects.
comments.quote: what about the two members of a pair copying each other, or gaining information from other group members?

reviews.assessment: Important demonstration, but the signal-versus-cue framing and the limits of behavioural discrimination measures need discussion.
strengths: detecting the pattern in swordtails is important for understanding selection
system provides an excellent opportunity to study preference for male size

comments.issue: Study is placed in a true-signal framework, but sensory bias or cue responses could also follow Weber's law.
comments.request: Frame the results in terms of signaler quality versus sensory bias and cues.
comments.quote: the results presented in this study do not necessarily rely on this type of true communication (benefits to signalers and receivers)

comments.issue: Behavioural assays estimate discrimination performance, not perceptual capacity; this limitation is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the limits of behavioural discrimination measures.
comments.quote: Animals might perceive differences between the available options but distribute their visits more evenly between the alternatives, regardless of expected value.

comments.issue: The word 'something' at line 39 is too vague given the information-theory context.
comments.request: Use 'information' or reword more generally.
comments.quote: The word “something” here seems too vague.

comments.issue: Line 74 is the place to note that benefits of preferring larger males are unknown and sensory bias is possible.
comments.request: Introduce the sensory-bias possibility here.
comments.quote: This would be the place to introduce the idea that we do not really know the benefits of preferring larger males

comments.issue: Adding 'quality' at line 92 is not justified; size may be meant instead.
comments.request: Use 'size' rather than 'quality' and shorten the sentence.
comments.quote: I think adding in quality is not a good idea, as it is unclear if larger males are higher “quality” mates in some respect

comments.issue: The claim of the first demonstration of proportional processing of a visual signal appears false.
comments.request: Correct the claim and cite prior visual examples.
comments.quote: This statement (“Our results are the first demonstration of proportional processing of a visual signal”) does not appear to be true.

comments.issue: Testing order and possible habituation effects on preference strength are not reported or analysed.
comments.request: Report testing order and analyse its influence.
comments.quote: What was the order in which females were tested, and did this influenced your results?

reviews.assessment: Elegant, sound study; only asks to address whether absolute size, not perceptual limits, explains the pattern.

comments.issue: Preference may break down above a certain absolute size rather than reflecting perceptual limits; 'cannot' and 'don't care' are not separable in this setup.
comments.request: Address whether absolute size explains the pattern.
comments.quote: Can the authors really claim that their results are due to limits of perceptual processing instead of preference breaking down once a certain size is reached?

comments.issue: Weber's law is not spelled out explicitly.
comments.request: Explain Weber's law more explicitly.
comments.quote: Consider spelling out what Weber’s law is more explicitly.

comments.issue: Figure 1 does not make clear which fish are being compared.

comments.quote: I suggest inserting a bit of white space between left and right fish columns to make that crystal clear also for the tired reader

title: Proportional processing of a visual mate choice signal in the green swordtail, Xiphophorus hellerii

study.system: shallow lake macrophytes; adaptive dynamics model of trait evolution

editor_summary: All reviewers find the problem important, the approach novel and the presentation clear; requests: broader appeal, robustness of results to evolutionary settings, and justification of depth as a continuous trait.

reviews.assessment: Positive and constructive; praises clarity and the mathematical framework, but wants a broader justification, biological grounding of depth, and discussion of fixed nutrients.
strengths: clear thematic connection with Scheffer et al. 2003

comments.issue: The justification of why the emergence of bistability matters is not strong enough for the broad Ecology Letters readership.
comments.request: Strengthen the broad justification, e.g. by moving conclusion content into the introduction.
comments.quote: the justification of why it matters to explore the emergence of bistability should be done much better

comments.issue: The biological meaning of depth as a continuous trait (e.g. z=7) is unclear and unjustified.
comments.request: Add a note or box justifying depth as a biologically meaningful continuous trait.
comments.quote: It is less clear though what a macrophyte with z=7 (for example) would entail in a biological sense

comments.issue: Using a fixed nutrient concentration as external input may be inadequate for evolutionary dynamics and positive feedback.
comments.request: Justify the fixed nutrient input and discuss it in the limitations.
comments.quote: The use of fixed nutrient concentration as an external input needs to be justified in more clarity and detail

comments.issue: 'Exploiter' and 'Exploited' are used without being defined.
comments.request: Define both terms.
comments.quote: Page 3, line 6-7. Need to define “Exploiter” and “Exploited”

comments.issue: The derivation of equation 2 is not shown.
comments.request: Explain how equation 2 is derived.
comments.quote: Page 4. How is equation 2 derived?

comments.issue: It is unclear why the initial population starts at z = 1 given the 0-10 m range, and Figure 3 suggests varying starting depths.
comments.request: Explain the choice of initial population depth.
comments.quote: Why start the initial population from z = 1 when z is from 0 to 10m?

comments.issue: Whether the 10e-4 mutation rate separates ecological from evolutionary time scales is unclear.
comments.request: Justify the mutation rate relative to the two time scales.
comments.quote: Is 10e-4 of mutation rate enough to separate ecological time scale with evolutionary time scale?

comments.issue: The initial density of 10e-2 g/L is not put in context relative to the resident population density.
comments.request: Report the initial density relative to the resident population density.
comments.quote: It is helpful to know how much an initial density of 10e-2 g/L accounts for relative to the resident population density

reviews.assessment: Highly praises originality and tractability; one concern that the diverging lineages remain too similar, plus many minor comments on presentation and notation.

comments.issue: The diverging lineages remain too similar, blurring the floating/submersed distinction and the link to clear/turbid states.
comments.request: Show that greater divergence is possible and robust, e.g. by altering Eqs. (8)-(11).
comments.quote: Their similarity means that the traditional distinction between floating and submersed strategies is blurred

comments.issue: The 'Because of' link between positive feedback and hysteresis is not justified, since positive feedbacks can occur without hysteresis.
comments.request: Revise or remove the causal claim.
comments.quote: But I don’t think they follow from each other: positive feedbacks are possible without hysteresis in principle

comments.issue: Working with per capita growth rates would make the model clearer from the outset.
comments.request: Introduce per capita growth rates right after Eq. (1).
comments.quote: It might help to start working with per capita growth rates instead of the full dM/dt equation right from the outset

comments.issue: Whether r is an intrinsic growth rate or an intrinsic birth rate is ambiguous given the explicit death rate l.
comments.request: Clarify r and, if a birth rate, fix Table 1.
comments.quote: Is r an intrinsic growth rate or an intrinsic birth rate (given that l is an explicit intrinsic death rate)?

comments.issue: Seven line-level notation and wording edits (p.4 l.57, Eq. 8, p.8 l.33, p.8 l.43, p.9 l.30, p.9 l.35, p.16 l.43).
comments.quote: I would change the * to \times or \cdot (like in the x-axis of the left panels of Figure 3)

comments.issue: N and z_b are missing from Table 1.
comments.request: Add N and z_b to Table 1.
comments.quote: N and z\_b are missing from the table - it would be good to add them

comments.issue: Too many abbreviations are introduced, which obfuscates the text.
comments.request: Drop BP and CSS, and consider dropping ES and PIP.
comments.quote: I think there are too many abbreviations introduced here (and elsewhere)

comments.issue: The final statement about the possibility of mathematical analysis may be unjustified.
comments.request: Drop or rephrase the statement.
comments.quote: Is such a final statement about the possibility of mathematical analysis justified here?

comments.issue: The text says simulations are time discrete, but only mutation events are; the differential equations are integrated between them.
comments.request: Rewrite the text to describe the integration between mutation events.
comments.quote: If I understand correctly, only the mutation events are time-discrete, and the differential equations are properly integrated between two mutation events

comments.issue: The phrasing about perturbation and response time scales is awkward.
comments.request: State clearly that perturbation and response are faster than mutation events.
comments.quote: I think what the Authors wanted to express is the assumption that the environmental perturbation and the system’s response to it are on a time scale faster than that of the mutation events

reviews.assessment: Strongly supportive: finds the question important, the modelling correct and the paper well written, requesting only minor revisions.

comments.issue: Figure 1 is too small for its details to be seen.
comments.request: Enlarge Figure 1 into a column-style, vertically stacked three-panel figure.
comments.quote: I would suggest enlarging the figure (to a column style with three panels put vertically), so that readers could see the details clearly

comments.issue: Figure 1 looks like scribbles, and axis labels in panel c need improvement.
comments.request: Improve the figure quality and axis labels.
comments.quote: Also consider improving the figure (they look quite scribbles to me. e.g. the axes labels in panel c)

comments.issue: The equations in the adaptive dynamics section lack intuitive explanations.
comments.request: Add concise intuitive explanations of the equations.
comments.quote: Consider providing concise (intuitive) explanations to the equations in Section 'Evolutionary analysis using adaptive dynamics'

comments.issue: British and American English styles are mixed.
comments.quote: There are some mixed uses of British and American English style

title: Evolutionary emergence of alternative stable states in shallow lakes

study.system: Daphnia magna populations; factorial harvest and food-stochasticity experiment

editor_summary: Editor: both reviewers are positive about the paper; one reviewer raises a number of concerns that all need to be addressed in revision.

reviews.assessment: Well-conducted and well-presented experimental study, with minor questions about EDM assumptions and reporting.
strengths: interesting and fills an empirical knowledge gap
important combination of harvest and stochasticity

comments.issue: The Hsieh et al. assumption that replicate dynamics are similar is not checked, and chaos is not excluded.
comments.request: Add a state-space embedding check and rule out chaotic dynamics.
comments.quote: It would be great to check that dynamics of replicates look similar with a state-space plot using the embeddings of the time series as a sanity check.

comments.issue: The effect of first differencing on system dimensionality and nonlinearity is not addressed.
comments.request: Address what first differencing does to these analyses.
comments.quote: What would first differencing do to the dimensionality of a dynamical system?

comments.issue: Possible synergistic effects of harvesting and stochasticity on nonlinearity are not discussed.
comments.request: Add discussion of this proposed synergy.
comments.quote: It has been suggested that harvesting and stochasticity may have synergistic effects in terms of nonlinearity. Some discussion is needed here.

comments.issue: rho and MAE can disagree for short time series.
comments.request: Report both rho and MAE.
comments.quote: Sometimes rho and MAE give different results for short time series. I would report both.

reviews.assessment: Important experimental contribution, but critical concerns about the mechanism interpretation and the model-fitting analysis.
strengths: well-designed factorial experiment with sufficient replicates
extremely useful information for testing hypotheses

comments.issue: The key mechanism that stochasticity acts through process error in growth rates is overlooked throughout the manuscript.
comments.request: Discuss this mechanism and whether the experiments rule it out.
comments.quote: This is a critical potential mechanism that seems to be overlooked throughout the manuscript.

comments.issue: The manuscript conflates the two hypotheses with their interaction and misstates the difference from Anderson et al.
comments.request: Clarify these differences and revise the explanation accordingly.
comments.quote: I feel, it is a good opportunity for the authors to clarify these differences, instead of creating more confusion (as the manuscript is written now)

comments.issue: Fitting the model to chaotic time series biases parameters towards limit cycles, so the model exercise is unreliable.
comments.request: Add caveats about this pitfall or remove the exercise.
comments.quote: The model fitting exercise suffers from the mathematical pitfall that if the time series exhibits chaotic dynamics, the fitted parameters tend to fall in the space of limit-cycle

comments.issue: Evaluating eigenvalues at equilibrium contradicts the study's own finding of nonlinear, nonequilibrium dynamics.
comments.request: Remove the return-time estimation section.
comments.quote: if the system exhibits nonlinear dynamics (not equilibrium), what is the point of evaluating the eigen-value at equilibrium?

comments.issue: Simulated series are used to compute CV but not nonlinearity.
comments.request: Estimate nonlinearity from simulated series as well.
comments.quote: The authors should do the same for estimating the nonlinearity.

comments.issue: The t-4 lag of density dependence in equation 1 is not justified.
comments.request: Explain why the lag is four time steps.
comments.quote: Please explain why the lagged density-dependent effect operates at t-4 in equation 1.

comments.issue: Simulation details such as initial conditions and process error are missing.
comments.request: Describe the initial conditions and how process error operates.
comments.quote: Please explain more details of the simulation, e.g., what is the initial condition?

comments.issue: Stability is inferred from a model lacking size truncation; EDM-based local Lyapunov stability is an alternative.
comments.request: Use EDM local Lyapunov stability without assuming a mechanistic model.
comments.quote: Given time series data, it is possible to estimate the eigen-value using EDM, known as local Lyapunov stability, following (Rogers et al. 2022).

comments.issue: The abstract reports the model-fitted slower recovery rates as if experimentally obtained.
comments.request: Remove the recovery-rate conclusion from the abstract and improve precision.
comments.quote: In addition, the conclusion of slower recovery rates is not obtained through experimental observations but is from model fitting.

comments.issue: Four line-level edits: L203, L223, L239 and L304 wording.
comments.quote: Line 304: Should be "empirical dynamic modeling"

comments.issue: The Results section does not explicitly present the three hypothesis-testing contrasts.
comments.request: State the Control-Fishing, Control-Stochasticity and Fishing-Fishing+Stochasticity contrasts.
comments.quote: In Results section, the authors should clearly point out the contrast of

comments.issue: The Discussion does not address the major concerns about mechanism interpretation.
comments.request: Rewrite the Discussion accordingly.
comments.quote: Discussion should be completely re-written to address my concerns in my major comments.

comments.issue: The first Discussion paragraph repeats the Introduction.
comments.request: Delete this paragraph.
comments.quote: The first paragraph of Discussion simply repeats what have been said in Introduction and can be deleted.

title: Experimental evidence of size‐selective harvest and environmental stochasticity effects on population demography, fluctuations and non‐linearity

study.system: savanna–forest ecotone; 41-yr fire frequency experiment, 89 species

editor_summary: Reviewers are positive and find the paper clear and rigorous, but trait selection and methodological details (for example, the regression model) need fuller explanation, and the redundant conclusion should be replaced with a novelty statement.

reviews.assessment: Well written, sound methods and interesting results; requests clarifications of sampling and trait collection, more references and numerous line-level and figure improvements.
strengths: well written and easy to follow

comments.issue: The number of plots per unit and how traits were sampled within plots/points are unclear, as is how CWMs were calculated.
comments.request: Clarify plot and point layout and whether CWMs use point or plot covers.
comments.quote: It is not clear to me how many plots you had per unit, and how the traits were sampled in the plots/points.

comments.issue: Calculating CWMs from the plot average instead of all 24 points reduces statistical power.
comments.request: Use all 24 points per plot for CWMs and include plot as a random effect.
comments.quote: I would suggest using all 24 points within one plot to calculated CWMs which would strongly increase the power of your statistical tests.

comments.issue: Ontogeny could confound fire-regime effects if juveniles were sampled or if fire occurred shortly before sampling.
comments.request: Report when the last fire occurred and confirm whether sampled individuals were adults.
comments.quote: And there is new literature out there saying that juvenile individuals have different traits than adult individuals, hence enough time to develop is needed

comments.issue: The study is not clearly placed in the broader literature, especially on intraspecific trait variability.
comments.request: Add text linking the findings to the broader intraspecific variability literature.
comments.quote: The paper could be improved by more clearly placing your study in the overarching literature.

comments.issue: Keywords duplicate words already used in the title or abstract, limiting findability.
comments.request: Update keywords with terms not used in the title or abstract.
comments.quote: you should also update your key words to words not used in the title or abstract for maximizing your findability when people search for papers

comments.issue: References supporting SLA as a light-capture investment indicator and N% as correlated with photosynthetic capacity are missing.
comments.request: Add references for these claims at lines 35-39.
comments.quote: Provide some references that SLA is an indicator of relative investment in light capture, and that N % is correlated with photosynthetic capacity.

editor_summary: Reviewers and editor appreciated the larger goals but felt the execution needed work; one reviewer suggested the piece might be better served as a letter after revision.

reviews.assessment: Likes the introduction's perspective but struggles with the model's utility, which repeats known patterns and does not address information rejection.
strengths: valuable perspective on social information use

comments.issue: The model illustrates patterns already described and adds no mechanistic insight.

comments.quote: The introduction places much emphasis on information rejection, but the model does not address this, and the remainder of the paper gets away from this theme

comments.quote: Figures 3 and 4 are difficult to extract meaningful information from

title: Ecological and evolutionary consequences of selective interspecific information use

study.system: terrestrial trophic interactions; phenological mismatch; 20 studies

editor_summary: Editor asks to address the three referees' insightful concerns and will consider a resubmission of an adequately improved version.

reviews.assessment: Timely and statistically strong, but the conceptual framework regresses by ignoring earlier reviews, especially Renner & Zohner 2018.

comments.issue: The conceptual framework disregards insights from earlier reviews of phenological mismatch.
comments.request: Engage with earlier reviews, especially Renner & Zohner 2018.
comments.quote: the conceptual framework is insufficiently developed and a step backward because it disregards insights in earlier reviews of this topic

comments.issue: Asynchrony need not lower fitness: in antagonistic interactions mismatch benefits at least one species, unlike mutualistic systems.
comments.request: Distinguish antagonistic and mutualistic mismatch predictions.
comments.quote: in all antagonistic interactions, mismatch increases the fitness of a least one of the interacting species, which is able to reproduce more successfully because it wasn’t consumed

comments.issue: Finding only two insect studies is implausible given the large literature on agricultural pest phenology.
comments.request: Check search coverage for insects.
comments.quote: only 2 were found here, perhaps because of more stringent criteria – but this is hard to believe because there is so much work on the phenology of agricultural pest

comments.issue: Calling Renner & Zohner 2018 findings inconsistent misrepresents that review.
comments.request: Correct the characterization of this review.
comments.quote: To claim that findings of Renner and Zohner 2018 have been ‘inconsistent’ is simply wrong.

comments.issue: The major review by Renner & Zohner (2018) is not cited.
comments.request: Cite Renner & Zohner 2018.
comments.quote: The MAJOR recent review is: Renner, S. S., and C. M. Zohner. 2018. Climate change and phenological mismatch in trophic interactions among plants, insects, and vertebrates.

reviews.assessment: Quantitatively strong conclusion of broad interest, but inadequate justification of analysis choices may bias results and overstate the message.
strengths: likely of broad interest to readers

comments.issue: The relative-timing metric may use consumer event timing rather than asynchrony relative to peak consumer demand as in Figure 1, biasing the analyses.
comments.request: Redo analyses using asynchrony relative to peak demand.
comments.quote: if the relative phenology metric used here is not in relation to the peak consumer demand (as explained in figure 1) then I think the analyses should be redone with this metric

comments.issue: If most studies cannot test mismatch, the data cannot support the claim that mismatch is unlikely to be widespread.
comments.request: Soften the conclusion to 'does not find strong evidence'.
comments.quote: if the latter is correct then the data are inadequate to support the former statement

comments.issue: The review claims to cover all terrestrial systems but is dominated by birds (73%).
comments.request: Acknowledge the bird bias and temper generality.
comments.quote: The study is framed as a review of mismatch across all terrestrial systems, but it is predominantly a review of mismatch in birds (73% of studies).

comments.issue: Fitness metrics with different distributions (Gaussian, Poisson, binomial) are pooled without discussion of the problem.
comments.request: Acknowledge and discuss this distributional issue.
comments.quote: The different fitness metrics used in different studies are likely to have very different distributions, some may be Gaussian, but others (eg., recruitment) will be better modelled as Poisson, binomial etc.

comments.issue: The preference for individual over population fitness is unjustified and lacks a year random intercept per interaction.
comments.request: Justify the fitness metric or add year random intercepts.
comments.quote: If the decision is to retain individual fitness in the models, then there are many observations per year and a year random intercept term specific to each interaction should be included in the model.

comments.issue: 'Species fitness' should be rephrased for clarity.
comments.request: Rephrase 'species fitness'.
comments.quote: Suggest rephrasing “species fitness” to “fitness of members of one or more of the interacting species”

comments.issue: Line 32 is ambiguous between system types prone to mismatch and timing of mismatch.
comments.request: Be more specific.
comments.quote: You could be a bit more specific here – I think you mean the types of systems prone to mismatch but it could also be taken as predicting when mismatch would occur in a system.

comments.issue: 'Their' on line 64 has an unclear referent.
comments.request: Clarify the referent.
comments.quote: Slightly unclear what ‘their’ refers to.

comments.issue: Search coverage relative to Samplonius et al. 2021 is unclear.
comments.request: Report search coverage.
comments.quote: Did your search capture all the studies in Samplonius et al. 2021? I.e. how good did the coverage of your search seem to be?

comments.issue: The assumption that mismatch impacts are equivalent in space and time is not explicit.
comments.request: State this assumption explicitly.
comments.quote: Suggest that you are explicit that you assume that impacts of mismatch are equivalent in space and time.

comments.issue: The taxonomic criterion was not applied consistently (e.g. frass resolved only to order).
comments.request: Clarify the taxonomic criterion.
comments.quote: I don’t think this taxonomic criterion was used in all cases, e.g., frass is at the order level at best.

comments.issue: 'Interaction' on line 115 may be confused with statistical interaction.

comments.issue: Key findings and suggestions should be presented as hypotheses to be tested.
comments.request: Present findings and suggestions as hypotheses.
comments.quote: Presenting the key findings as hypotheses to be tested seems appropriate and would work well.

comments.issue: Statements on LN43 and LN225 are too strong for the evidence presented.

comments.quote: I am not sure the evidence presented in the paper warrants this strong a statement.

comments.issue: The assumptions of Cushing's hypothesis should be clearly enumerated.

comments.quote: Given the importance of the assumptions of Cushing’s hypothesis, I think it would be good to very clearly outline the assumptions.

comments.issue: More information, including assumptions, is needed on LN110-113.

comments.quote: I would like to know more about this, including its assumptions.

comments.issue: The reasoning behind pooled versus unpooled intercepts needs clear upfront justification.
comments.request: Justify the analysis approach at the start of the section.
comments.quote: I do think that the authors could prevent this from happening with a clear justification of this analysis approach

comments.issue: The Bayesian framework should be pointed out explicitly for clarity.
comments.request: State that analyses are Bayesian.
comments.quote: It seems that it would be useful to briefly point out that this is all in a Bayesian framework for clarity.

comments.issue: The EPLD difference of 2.6 means the two models cannot really be distinguished.
comments.request: Reconsider what these model comparisons mean.
comments.quote: the EPLD difference between the models is 2.6, which means we really cannot distinguish the two models—they both have similar performance

comments.issue: The statement on LN184-185 is too strong given the available data.
comments.request: Temper the wording.
comments.quote: Upon reading this statement, I thought this was a bit too strong given the available data.

comments.issue: The LN197 claim would be better framed as a hypothesis, with trophic versus species specialists explained.
comments.request: Reframe as a hypothesis and explain specialist concepts.
comments.quote: Given the availability and bias in the data, I think this would be better framed as a hypothesis to be tested.

comments.issue: The LN213-214 point needs more setup and unpacking.
comments.request: Expand this point, possibly using Iler et al. 2021.
comments.quote: This is a very important point, but I think this needs a little more setup, and would probably benefit from some more unpacking.

comments.issue: Panel labelling is inconsistent across plots (a, A).
comments.request: Make panel labels consistent.
comments.quote: Easy fix, but panel labeling is inconsistent across plots

comments.issue: Figure 1 panel d is awkward as a lone central panel.
comments.request: Reconsider panel d and label match/mismatch on panel e.
comments.quote: Is panel “d” necessary? Might it be better to just put “match” and “mismatch” on panel e, or something like that?

comments.issue: Figure 2 could highlight only panels supporting the hypotheses, and axes placement is confusing.
comments.request: Colour supporting panels and swap images with axes.
comments.quote: might it be useful to only color the panels that have evidence in support of the hypotheses?

comments.issue: Figure 3 is easily misinterpreted; per-interaction shapes add complexity and the two fits look equally convincing.
comments.request: Simplify Figure 3 and visually distinguish the model fits.
comments.quote: it doesn’t seem to add much to have each interaction labeled with a different shape—if anything, this just makes the figure much more complicated

comments.issue: Figure 4's yes/no grey bars are not intuitive and questions sit in the caption.
comments.request: Widen the grey bars and put questions above panels.
comments.quote: in panel a, for trophic specialist, it isn’t very clear what is “yes” and what is “no/unclear”

title: Lack of evidence for the match‐mismatch hypothesis across terrestrial trophic interactions

study.system: phenotypic trait variation; PROCEED database meta-analysis

editor_summary: Generally supportive; reviewers identify places where further analyses and explanation are needed and the editor asks that all be carefully addressed in revision.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and timely for a niche audience, but the framing, narrow references and hidden variation need work to engage a broad readership.
strengths: acknowledges limitations and highlights illustrative case studies

comments.issue: The opening abstract sentences are vague and obscure the point.
comments.request: Rewrite the abstract opening for clarity.
comments.quote: The first sentences of the abstract are so vague they actually confuse the point of the next sentences.

comments.issue: Figure 1 reviews the topic broadly instead of focusing on mechanisms generating trait variation.
comments.request: Refocus Figure 1 on the specific mechanisms of trait variation.
comments.quote: This is on my mind as I look at Figure 1, which reviews the topic more broadly but doesn’t focus on mechanisms generating variation in traits with populations specifically.

comments.issue: References are narrow and mostly the authors' own work, ignoring harvest- and disease-driven eco-evo feedbacks.
comments.request: Broaden the reference base, e.g. Brunner et al. 2019.
comments.quote: the references, which are quite narrow, primarily representing prior work by the present manuscript’s authors, but ignoring, for example, relevant work on eco-evo feedbacks driven by harvest (fishing) or disease

comments.issue: lnVR is used but never defined, and the choice of lnCVR over alternatives is not justified.
comments.request: Define lnVR and justify the effect-size decisions.
comments.quote: the use of lnCVR rather than lnVR is mentioned as an aside but the latter is never defined - I am left guessing that lnVR refers to the variance ratio.

comments.issue: The term 'moderators' and the grouping of heterogeneous variables are unfamiliar and unexplained.
comments.request: Explain moderators for a broad readership.
comments.quote: the use of the term “moderators” is not as familiar to me in this context. They appear to be covariates (factors), but also are apples and oranges

comments.issue: lnCVR changes are nearly symmetrical around zero, so the approach hides interesting variation.
comments.request: Highlight this limitation and use it to motivate further investigation.
comments.quote: This suggests that the approach here actually hides a lot of the interesting variation, much as simply comparing means does.

reviews.assessment: Important, timely and well written, with relatively minor comments on framing, analyses and figure clarity.
strengths: very important and largely neglected question

comments.issue: Genotype-environment interactions, plasticity and environmental stress as sources of phenotypic variance are not discussed.
comments.request: Add plasticity and stress to the sources of variance and discuss in context.
comments.quote: In this section it would be good to refer to genotype-environment interactions / environmentally induced phenotypic plasticity as one source of phenotypic variance (on which selection can act) – as well as environmental stress.

comments.issue: Trait changes are not analysed against estimated strength of selection.
comments.request: Analyse mean and variance change versus selection strength where data allow.
comments.quote: Would it be possible from the existing PROCEED database to analyse also trait changes in mean and variance in relation to estimated strength of selection?

comments.issue: Trait change is not analysed against environmental heterogeneity.
comments.request: Consider analyses using environmental variance instead of disturbance type.
comments.quote: Likewise, analyses of trait change in relation to environmental heterogeneity (rather than “type of human disturbance) might be informative (though such data on environmental variance is likely sparse)

comments.issue: Human-induced change feels like an add-on; its implications for population responses and feedbacks are underdeveloped.
comments.request: Strengthen and better integrate the human-disturbance framing and implications.
comments.quote: Perhaps the strength of inferences in relation to human induced changes (given that is the data used) could be stronger at places (especially in the discussion) as it seems a bit of an “add on” in the introduction

comments.issue: The key take-home message is unclear, including how phenotypic variation monitoring could be implemented.
comments.request: State the message clearly and how monitoring could be done in practice.
comments.quote: The key take home message is perhaps not clear (see above and below), but the authors call – rightly in my mind – for the need to monitor phenotypic variation and not only genetic variation.

comments.issue: A lack of average change combines increases and decreases; this implication should be highlighted more.
comments.request: Emphasise that statistical no-change is not absence of change.
comments.quote: I also found it an important point to highlight that whilst variance does not change, on average, this reflects in fact a combination of increase and decreases – so statistical lack of change should not be considered “no change”.

comments.issue: PROCEED(S) is never spelled out for unfamiliar readers.
comments.request: Clarify what PROCEED stands for.
comments.quote: It would be useful for those not familiar with the data base to some way clarify what PROCEEDS stands for

comments.issue: The abstract closing sentence lacks prior key findings and implications.
comments.request: State key findings and implications before the closing sentence.
comments.quote: 1/27 – it would be useful to shortly state the key findings and main implications before the closing sentence

comments.issue: Whether eco-to-evo is meant as 'dynamic' or as one pathway of eco-evolutionary dynamics is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the eco-to-evo terminology.
comments.quote: is eco-to-evo (= primarily evolution by natural selection) explicitly “dynamic” or is here intended to refer to eco-evolutionary dynamics under which eco-to-evo is one of the causal pathways?

comments.issue: The link to human-relevant effects at 2/17-21 is poorly stated.
comments.request: Improve the link to human relevance.
comments.quote: 2/17-21 – the link to the relevance of the human relevant effects is somewhat poorly stated

comments.issue: Section 3/8-36 would fit better earlier for logical structure.
comments.request: Reorder the introduction.
comments.quote: when reading the introduction it seemed to me that this section (or parts of it) would be good to state earlier for a somewhat more logical structure

comments.issue: Human relevance at 4/6-10 again reads as an add-on.
comments.request: Link the human relevance more explicitly.
comments.quote: here the statement about relevance to humans seem (again, see above) a bit of an “add on” and could be better linked / be more explicitly stated

comments.issue: Question 2 at 4/36 needs rephrasing.
comments.request: Rephrase question 2 about disturbance types and trait variance.
comments.quote: “Do different types of human disturbances differ in their effects on trait variance?

comments.issue: The last sentence at 4/43-47 is too vague.
comments.request: Make the sentence more explicit.
comments.quote: the last sentence is a bit too vague to be useful. Could this be rather made more explicit ?

comments.issue: At 5/20 it is unclear which data set the noteworthy changes are compared to.
comments.request: Clarify the comparison.
comments.quote: 5/20 – noteworthy changes compared to which data set ? clarify text

comments.issue: Wording at 5/26 is odd.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence about heritable variation entries.
comments.quote: 5/26 – suggest rephrasing – wording is a bit odd as stands.

comments.issue: The two key variables are described after the statistical analyses at 5/42.
comments.request: Describe the key variables before the analyses.
comments.quote: for easier read, the description of these 2 key variables would be preferably be before the statistical analyses are described

comments.issue: lnVR at 6/25 is not defined.
comments.request: State what lnVR stands for.
comments.quote: 6/25 – what does lnVR stand for?

comments.issue: The statistical model type is not stated at 6/28-29.
comments.request: State the model type explicitly.
comments.quote: 6/28-29 state explicitly the type of statistical models that were used. Reading I infer mixed models but this should be stated

comments.issue: 'Moderators' at 6/50 is not explained.
comments.request: Define moderators.
comments.quote: 6/50 – what is meant by moderators?

comments.issue: The AIC difference threshold for model comparison is not stated.
comments.request: State the AIC difference criterion.
comments.quote: 7/10 – what was the level of difference in AIC between models that was considered ? (usually > 2 is used but this should also be stated)

comments.issue: Highlighted empirical cases are not marked in the figures.
comments.request: Indicate these cases in the figures where possible.
comments.quote: For the specific empirical cases that are highlighted in the discussion, it may be useful to indicate them explicitly in the figures (Where possible) as this would help visualizing the patterns described

comments.issue: Wording at 8/54 should state increases or decreases.
comments.quote: increases or decreases were found

comments.issue: An example of ecological consequences with references is missing at 9/43.
comments.request: Add an ecological-consequence example with references.
comments.quote: 9/43 – here an example of ecological consequences (with reference(s) would be good to add.

comments.issue: Wording at 10/23 should be 'either moment'.
comments.quote: 10/23 – rephrase to ..”either moment”

comments.issue: Kurtosis and the potential outlier are not evident in Fig 2.
comments.request: Make these patterns visible in the figure.
comments.quote: it is hard from Fig 2 to see the degree of kurtosis – also the potential outlier point is not evident (at least to me) from this figure

comments.issue: It is unclear from Fig 3 how the outliers are striking.
comments.request: Link the figure to the described outliers.
comments.quote: I can not see from Fig 3 how the outliers are striking. Having some link in the figure text would be useful.

comments.issue: The text at 11/19-38 is not linked to the manuscript's actual results.
comments.request: Point to where the evidence appears.
comments.quote: linking this to actual results from the manuscript would be useful (i.e. where is the evidence to be seen in the ms? (Figure?)

comments.issue: The section on non-significant +/-50% differences is too long.
comments.request: Condense this section.
comments.quote: I think this section of non-significant ± 50% differences could be condensed.

comments.issue: The use of response traits at 13/11 is unclear.
comments.request: Specify response traits in the methods.
comments.quote: 13/11 – the use of response traits is unclear. These should be specified in the methods section

comments.issue: The heading at 13/40 wrongly implies phenotypic studies tried and failed to establish heritability.
comments.request: Rephrase the heading to distinguish heritable-basis and phenotypic-only studies.
comments.quote: rephrase title to “Do studies establishing a heritable basis for trait change show a different pattern than phenotypic studies” ?

comments.issue: The countergenetic versus environmental contrast at 13/45 is overdrawn since responses combine both.
comments.request: Reduce the dichotomy.
comments.quote: 13 /45 – reduce the counter genetic vs environmental effects as the responses typically consist of both (and plasticity can have a genetic basis)

comments.issue: The implications section lacks a clear take-home message.
comments.request: Add a clear take-home message.
comments.quote: 16 – implications – I am missing a clear take home message (in terms of what the current study showed) in this section

comments.issue: Figure 1 does not match the text; plasticity is not among the listed sources of variance.
comments.request: Align the figure with the text.
comments.quote: this is a nice figure but does not fully match the text – for example, plasticity was not explicitly stated when these different sources of variance were listed

comments.issue: Figure 2 circle styles and x axis are unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the plotting symbols and axis.
comments.quote: Figure 2 – What is meant here by the circles vs bold circles? I can only see one type of circles. What is the x axis (precision?) – is this explained anywhere in the methods?

comments.issue: Figure 3 does not let readers infer outliers and the 'absolute value of lnRR' label is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the outlier display and axis label.
comments.quote: Figure 3- relating to earlier point (above) it is not clear how we infer outliers from this figure. It is also not clear what is meant by absolute value of lnRR (llnRRI?) on the left.

reviews.assessment: Enjoyed the work and finds the extreme-case framing valuable, with main comments on reporting random effects and figure design.
strengths: good reasons put forth for patterns

comments.issue: The relative contributions of random effects (study, effect size, system, species, phylogeny) are never reported.
comments.request: Report and briefly discuss the random-effect contributions.
comments.quote: but the relative contribution of any of these are not reported in the manuscript or the supplementary information.

comments.issue: The final model output is not reported in table form, and random effects are omitted from the orchard plots.
comments.request: Add a supplementary table with the full model output including random effects.
comments.quote: the random effects are omitted from these and therefore I think a table with the model output including the random structure results should be included as supplementary information

comments.issue: Figure 1 is underused in the text and its framework lacks supporting references and depth.
comments.request: Add key references for each direction of variation and discuss higher-level processes.
comments.quote: could be amplified by provided key references for each direction of variation for the different components in the processes and causes side, perhaps as supplementary information.

comments.issue: Figure S1 is more informative than Figure 2, which hides sample sizes and distributions.
comments.request: Replace Figure 2 with Figure S1.
comments.quote: I find Figure S1 far more informative than Figure 2 as too much information is lost in the simplification.

comments.issue: Figure 3 has ambiguous axis names, an inverted y axis and omits the discussed outliers.
comments.request: Resolve the axis ambiguity and show the extreme cases.
comments.quote: the y axis on Fig. 3A is ~ -6 to 2 and the caption states these values are residuals from the meta-analytical model, but the panel B uses the same axis name and a totally different range of values.

comments.issue: The discussion does not maintain the eco-to-evo and evo-to-eco terminology prominent in the introduction.
comments.request: Use the terms consistently or reduce emphasis in the introduction.
comments.quote: The discussion does not seem to follow the same use of eco-to-evo and evo-to-eco that was very prominent in the introduction

comments.issue: The opening example at Page 4 L29-34 is too non-specific.
comments.request: Elaborate the link between ecotypes and ecosystem function.
comments.quote: This example in the opening paragraph is rather non-specific, even for a high-level ‘setting the scene’ example. What it is that links the ecotypes to significant effects on ecosystem function?

comments.issue: The example at Page 5 L17-24 adds little without elaboration.
comments.request: Elaborate or reposition the example sentence.
comments.quote: As above, this example does not really add much without a bit more elaboration. The reference presents a good example of the overall statement, but the example itself could be written as a sentence before or after this overall sentiment.

comments.issue: The logic assigning 'large' changes to eco-to-evo and 'important' changes to evo-to-eco is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify these definitions and distinctions.
comments.quote: I do not follow the logic for why ‘large’ changes are assigned to be eco-to-evo and ‘important’ changes to evo-to-eco for trait variation.

comments.issue: Text refers to taxonomic lineages, but Table S1 has no taxonomic breakdown.
comments.request: Provide the taxonomic breakdown.
comments.quote: this sentence refers to 1431 systems, 177 species, and 8 taxonomic lineages (Table S1) – but Table S1 has no taxonomic breakdown at all.

comments.issue: Supplementary tables are mislabelled: two Table S1 and no Table S3.
comments.request: Fix the supplementary table labels.
comments.quote: Check labels for Tables in supplementary information – there are currently two Table S1 and no Table S3.

title: Contemporary changes in phenotypic variation, and the potential consequences for eco‐evolutionary dynamics

study.system: beech, oak and spruce; masting and weather time series

editor_summary: Editor notes three reviewers find the approach very interesting but question novelty of hypotheses and robustness of analyses; a resubmission must address suggestions and clarify novelty relative to similar recent studies using very similar datasets.

reviews.assessment: Interesting study linking the Moran effect and population-specific weather cueing, but possible spurious correlations, missing pollen coupling and unclear details are concerns.
strengths: interesting and relevant question for tree ecology
appealing combination of Moran effect and weather cueing

comments.issue: Weather-seed correlations may be spurious because high masting variability makes sensitivity to specific windows hard to detect.
comments.request: Test whether peak frequency or CV explains the cueing patterns.
comments.quote: Therefore, there is a possibility that some correlations highlighted in Figure 4 might be due to stochasticity and not due to a biological process.

comments.issue: Pollen coupling, one of the main theories explaining masting synchrony, is never mentioned.
comments.request: Discuss pollen coupling and its relevance to the results.
comments.quote: In this manuscript you don’t mention the pollen coupling hypothesis which is one of the main theories explaining masting synchrony, why?

comments.issue: A suggested reference on gene flow and adaptation is missing.
comments.request: Add the Kremer et al. 2012 reference.
comments.quote: L59- L61: You can also add “enhance gene flow promoting adaptation (Kremer et al. 2012)”.

comments.issue: The Moran effect and its fundamental difference from weather cueing are not defined.
comments.request: Define the Moran effect and distinguish it from weather cueing.
comments.quote: L64: Can you define the Moran effect here and the fundamental difference with the whether cue mentioned in the next sentence (L66-67)

comments.issue: 'Intraspecific' should read 'interspecific'.
comments.request: Correct the term to interspecific.
comments.quote: L74: In the following sentence: “and this intraspecific variation remains unexplained” it seems that you want to say interspecific and not intraspecific here.

comments.issue: Temperature periods and year lags are not associated with species, including in the Figure 3 description.
comments.request: Specify species-specific cue periods and lags and add them to Figure 3.
comments.quote: L 137: You need to associate the temperature periods with the species and specify the year lags.

comments.issue: The sentence is unclear about what is taken 'from'.
comments.request: Clarify the sentence.
comments.quote: L286: “from” what?

comments.issue: Unclear whether the summer mean max temperature cue was used only for beech.
comments.request: Clarify which species used this cue.
comments.quote: L298: The “summer mean max temperature” mentioned here is only used for beech and not for Norway Spruce, isn’t it?

comments.issue: Unclear whether both population-specific cues or only one were used in the analysis.
comments.request: State which cue (lag 1 or lag 2) was selected.
comments.quote: L332-337: In the previous analysis you highlight two population specific cues correlated with seed production for beech and Norway spruce at lag 1 and 2 but in this paragraph you don’t mention whether you took both or only one.

comments.issue: The dotted lines in Figure 1 are unexplained.
comments.request: Explain what the dotted lines represent.
comments.quote: Figure 1: What are the dotted lines used for here?

comments.issue: The rationale for the 1500 km distance limit is not given.
comments.request: Justify the 1500 km threshold.
comments.quote: Figure 2: The distances between pops are higher than 1500 km, why did you choose 1500 km as the limit in your analysis (Figure 3 and 5)?

comments.issue: The reason for different distance-synchrony patterns in Figures 3 and 5 is unclear, and time series are not described.
comments.request: Explain the difference and add the time series description to Figure 3.
comments.quote: Figure 3 and Figure 5: It is not clear why the pattern of the spatial Masting synchrony with distance is different between Fig 3 and Fig 5.

comments.issue: Figure S2 sorts populations by Tmax although Tmean is the cue used for spruce and oaks.
comments.request: Sort sites by mean annual Tmean for spruce and oaks.
comments.quote: Figure S2: Why did you order the population by “mean annual Tmax '' here and not the “mean annual Tmean ''?

reviews.assessment: Very original and convincing work, strongly support publication; only presentation and referencing suggestions.
strengths: very original approach to masting mechanisms
very well written with very well done analyses

comments.issue: The introduction presents synchrony itself as the key issue; it should be framed as a means to reveal mechanisms.
comments.request: Reframe the introduction around mechanisms revealed by synchrony analysis.
comments.quote: I wonder then if the introduction could be revisited to emphasise that the analysis of the degree of synchronisation between populations is an original and powerful approach to revealing key mechanisms

comments.issue: Figure 5 is redundant with Figure 3 and less relevant; direct correlations between spatial coefficients would be better.
comments.request: Replace Figure 5 with correlations among the spatial correlation coefficients.
comments.quote: Figure 5 is perhaps not the most relevant to present the major result of the paper because it is loaded with information already seen in figure 3.

comments.issue: A step is missing in the reasoning on phenological responses: budburst phenology is inspiring but summer phenology is unknown.
comments.request: State this gap and develop perspectives on summer phenology.
comments.quote: It seems to me that there is a missing brick in the reasoning to fully expose the proposal centred on the variability between species of phenological responses.

comments.issue: Recurrent misuse of 'intraspecific' plus small wording edits (remove 'that' L113, remove 'role' L29).
comments.request: Check the whole document for these wording issues.
comments.quote: I had difficulties with the recurrent use of the term intraspecific

comments.issue: Figure 1 is not obtained from the analysed data; consider removing it or moving it to an appendix.
comments.request: Remove Figure 1 or place it in an appendix.
comments.quote: I am not sure of the usefulness of this figure which is not obtained with the data analysed in the study. Should it be removed or put in an appendix?

comments.issue: The meaning of the vertical line lengths in Figure 4 is unclear and redundant with colour intensity.
comments.request: Revise Figure 4 to avoid the redundancy.
comments.quote: fig 4 : I don't understand the sense of length of the vertical lines (redundancy with the intensity of the colouring which captures the strength of the link between weather and fruiting).

reviews.assessment: Interesting question but parts are not novel; the two-process pattern, weak weather relationships and low species replication complicate the story.
strengths: interesting question on the distance-decay of synchrony

comments.issue: Parts of the study are not novel; distance-decay variation and synchrony in these species were already studied.
comments.request: Clarify the novel contribution relative to prior work.
comments.quote: I thought this study was interesting. Some parts of the study are not exceptionally novel.

comments.issue: Alternative explanation: weather may explain seed production poorly, so low synchrony and little distance-decay arise regardless of cueing.
comments.request: Address the possibility that weak weather relationships drive the result.
comments.quote: I imagine an alternate hypothesis might be that weather just does not account for variation in seed production particularly well in a species even at relatively small spatial scales.

comments.issue: Oak and spruce show two processes (less decay and lower local synchrony), making the pattern more complex than described.
comments.request: Acknowledge and discuss the two-process pattern.
comments.quote: (2) a lower ‘y-intercept’ of synchrony at very small spatial scales in oak and spruce than beech.

comments.issue: Critical information on the weather-seed production relationship is buried in the manuscript.
comments.request: Move key information to more prominent places.
comments.quote: I found some of the critical information on the weather-seed production relationship to be buried in the manuscript.

comments.issue: Low species replication limits generality, although more species data appear available in Figure 1.
comments.request: Use additional species or temper the generality claims.
comments.quote: Another issue with interpretation is the low replication of species, which makes it a bit difficult to understand the generality of this pattern.

comments.issue: Key hypotheses are hard to understand on first reading; sentence structure and grammar need work.
comments.request: Improve sentence structure and clarify the hypotheses.
comments.quote: The layout of the paper was fairly clear, though I struggled to understand the key hypotheses on first read. The sentence structure / grammar of the paper could use quite a bit of work.

title: Mechanisms driving interspecific variation in regional synchrony of trees reproduction

study.system: Tropical montane birds; nest predation and camera-trap predator communities, Andes

editor_summary: Editor notes considerable enthusiasm for the paper and its dataset, but both reviewers feel the paper needs significant work and provide many suggestions.

reviews.assessment: Enthusiastic about the phenomenal dataset but wants the goals directly tested, null models for superpredators and improved figures.
strengths: real data on a topic where data are sparse

comments.issue: The shape of the predation-elevation relationship is unresolved, with Figure 1 suggesting a linear decline while Figure 3 suggests a hump shape.
comments.request: Resolve the shape discrepancy and clarify model flexibility.
comments.quote: But then in Figure 3 the authors report a hump shaped pattern of successful nests - what explains this discrepancy?

comments.issue: The leading goal of linking predator communities to bird turnover is never directly tested.
comments.request: Test this hypothesis directly or refocus the study.
comments.quote: As is, this is the leading goal of the study and the subject of the first paragraph in the Introduction. Yet it is never directly tested.

comments.issue: The superpredator claim lacks a null expectation for the distribution of predation events among predators.
comments.request: Use a null model to test for superpredators.
comments.quote: I think the authors should choose some reasonable null model (or models), and then evaluate whether there is evidence that there are indeed “superpredators” in this system

comments.issue: No map of the study gradient and sites is provided.
comments.request: Add a map figure with the study sites.
comments.quote: A map figure showing the study gradient with study sites would be helpful.

comments.issue: Figure 1's three panels dilute the take-home message and hide the y-axis difference.
comments.request: Reconsider the panel layout.
comments.quote: Having three panels makes it harder for the reader to get the take-home message.

comments.issue: Only model outputs are shown; actual data and sample distribution are not visualized.
comments.request: Add a plot of the raw data with a loess fit or boxplot.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to provide a plot that shows actual data and communicates the large sample sizes and distribution of the data along the elevational gradient.

comments.issue: Figure 2 is incomprehensible as presented.
comments.request: Redo Figure 2.
comments.quote: I stared at this figure at length on multiple occasions and still don’t understand what is going on at all. This figure needs to be redone.

comments.issue: Video stills identifying the main predators are not used.
comments.request: Add predator identity images from the videos.
comments.quote: it would be a really good idea to use good quality stills from the videos as images in a figure showing the identity of the main predators.

comments.issue: Figure 3 contains too many panels and non-identical y-axis scales.
comments.request: Focus on the main predators with identical y-axes.
comments.quote: I would prefer focusing on the main predators (i.e. 3 or 4 panels). The y axis scales should be identical between panels

comments.issue: No figure shows the actual data for predator identity.
comments.request: Add a mosaic plot of predator identity by elevational zone.
comments.quote: I would also appreciate a figure showing the actual data for predator identity.

comments.issue: Two recent meta-analyses on nest predation gradients are not cited.
comments.request: Cite these recent meta-analyses.
comments.quote: (meta-analysis about latitudinal gradients in nest predation, but also presents evidence for a general decline in nest predation rates with elevation)

reviews.assessment: Praises the unique dataset but finds the paper unclear, the interpretation biased against the camera-trap evidence, and the elevation treatment problematic.

comments.issue: The paper is hard to follow due to terminology, incomplete variable descriptions and unclear method distinctions.
comments.request: Improve clarity and distinguish methods throughout.
comments.quote: The first is easily addressed and it refers to the clarity of the paper, which is often hard to follow

comments.issue: The interpretation seems biased: the most robust camera-trap data do not clearly support higher predation at higher altitude.
comments.request: Present camera-trap predation rates and weigh them more heavily.
comments.quote: the most robust data, the camera traps, do not seem to support higher predation at higher altitudes

comments.issue: Elevation is modelled as continuous despite three discrete sites, violating linear-model assumptions.
comments.request: Treat elevation appropriately and acknowledge n=1 site per level.
comments.quote: I imagine the distribution of the actual nest elevations is strongly trimodal, breaking a key assumption of linear models

comments.issue: The discussion is not written clearly.
comments.request: Rewrite the discussion for clarity.
comments.quote: I think the discussion could be written more clearly.

comments.issue: The abstract lacks a strong concluding sentence.
comments.request: Strengthen the abstract's ending.
comments.quote: Abstract could be stronger and needs an exciting concluding sentence.

comments.issue: Methods may differ by elevation or species and were apparently not controlled for.
comments.request: Control for monitoring method in the analyses.
comments.quote: Did the way these were used differ according to a) elevation or b) species or type of species? If so, this could bias the results.

comments.issue: It is unclear how thermocouple nest sensors were used to interpret predation.
comments.request: Explain the role of thermocouple sensors.
comments.quote: I don’t recall seeing how thermocouple nest sensors were used to interpret predation patterns.

comments.issue: Classifying nests as depredated only if destroyed is questionable for birds and snakes.
comments.request: Justify this criterion and acknowledge the limitation.
comments.quote: What’s the justification for this assumption? It would seem you should acknowledge the limitation here.

comments.issue: 'Information about the elevation' is vague; categorical or continuous is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify what information about elevation means.
comments.quote: what do you mean by “information about the elevation”? Vague.

comments.issue: Splitting exposure days between egg and nestling stages may pseudoreplicate nests without a random effect.

comments.issue: The exposure-days sentence is unclear.

comments.issue: The fixed effects included in this analysis are not listed.

comments.quote: 5,19: what fixed effects were included in this analysis?

comments.issue: The exclusion of still-active nests lacks logic and the number excluded is not given.

comments.issue: It is unsubstantiated that predators at 412 m represent lowland predator communities.

comments.quote: Can you give a reference that substantiates this important assumption?

comments.issue: The incomplete-sampling indicators are not elaborated.

comments.quote: Elaborate a little. Is it that the greater the number of species represented by one and two, the more incomplete the sampling is?

comments.issue: The meaning at 5, 52-53 is unclear.
comments.request: Rephrase this passage.
comments.quote: 5, 52-53: meaning unclear. Rephrase.

comments.issue: The distinction between nest-success and daily-predation approaches is unclear.

comments.quote: The distinction could be clearer if this is indeed the issue.

comments.issue: Figure 1 legend omits confidence intervals and the list of methods.
comments.request: Expand the Figure 1 legend.
comments.quote: Fig 1 legend. Mention confidence intervals, what they are precisely. Mention also that includes data for each of the three methods, and list them.

comments.issue: It is not stated that the min and max are per year.
comments.request: Indicate the min and max are per year.
comments.quote: 6, 17-18: indicate min and max are per year.

comments.issue: Figure citations do not identify specific panels.

comments.issue: No figure shows overall predation rate as Figure 1 does.

comments.issue: The claimed pattern is not visible in the figure.

comments.issue: The successful and predated plots differ from Figure 1 without explanation in the heading.

comments.issue: No predation-rate equivalent is provided at 7, 29.

comments.quote: 7, 29: why not give predation rate equivalent?

comments.issue: Figure 2a is hard to read and species names are invisible.

comments.quote: I found it difficult to see any pattern in Figure 2a. I think it would be much clearer if you make it stacked to a total proportion of 1, as done for b-d.

comments.issue: The logic of the sentence at 7, 41-43 does not connect.
comments.request: Rewrite this sentence.
comments.quote: logic of first part of sentence doesn’t explain second part?

comments.issue: The 'Overall' conclusion depends on method weighting and the representativeness of three sites.
comments.request: Qualify this conclusion accordingly.
comments.quote: it’s equally the case that this is dependent on the relative weight you give to camera traps and other methods, and how representative your n=3 sites are of different elevations

comments.issue: The argument in the paragraph at 7, 49 is unclear and disjointed.
comments.request: Clarify the point of this paragraph.
comments.quote: the argument in this paragraph is not clear. What’s the point?

comments.issue: The Badyaev study supporting longer incubation at high elevations is not cited.

comments.issue: Low-altitude birds may desert nests that are then secondarily predated, a confound undetectable in the overall data.
