comments.quote: Was the per female reproductive output comparable between treatments?

comments.issue: If time stationary is equal but flatwings moved more, they may simply move faster, which should be discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the moving-faster alternative.
comments.quote: If the crickets spent the same amount of time stationary, but flatwings moved more, would this not mean that the time spent moving was also the same, but they simply moved faster?

comments.issue: Why singing does not elicit phonotaxis in normal-winged crickets is unexplained, undermining the movement interpretation.
comments.request: Explain why phonotaxis appears not to operate.
comments.quote: Why would singing not influence movement of other crickets, i.e., elicit phonotaxis in the normal-winged crickets?

comments.issue: The discussion needs to acknowledge alternative explanations; direct evidence that movement alone causes reproductive output is missing.
comments.request: Carefully phrase the discussion and discuss alternatives.
comments.quote: Correlation does not necessarily mean causation and I am missing the direct evidence that increased movement alone explained the reproductive output of flatwinged crickets.

comments.issue: Calling did not affect movement as assumed, which is crucial for the calling-versus-silent comparison.
comments.request: Discuss why phonotaxis seemingly plays no role and how this affects interpretation.
comments.quote: calling did not affect movement as originally assumed, which is crucial for the comparison

comments.issue: Increased movement may be an evolved mate-finding adaptation or simply a consequence of lacking an acoustic target.
comments.request: Distinguish adaptation from passive consequence and cite relevant studies.
comments.quote: Is increased movement of silent flatwings here actually an evolved adaptation to find mates or simply the consequence of having no acoustic target to move to?

comments.issue: Lower female mate acceptance in flatwing populations could explain equal offspring output with fewer encounters.
comments.request: Discuss mate acceptance differences and present any related data.
comments.quote: Do flatwing and singing populations differ in female mate acceptance (i.e., being less choosy)?

comments.issue: Whether crickets can see and orient towards each other at 6 LUX, and how this compares with natural conditions, is unclear.
comments.request: Justify the light conditions.
comments.quote: Can crickets see in 6 LUX LED light, i.e., can they see each other and orient toward and find each other this way?

comments.issue: 'Indirect fitness costs' has a different established meaning (fitness of relatives).
comments.request: Reword the phrase.
comments.quote: ‘Indirect fitness costs’ has another meaning, i.e., indirect fitness is the fitness of related organisms.

comments.issue: The context for females growing heavier ovaries at lines 73-74 is unclear.
comments.request: Specify the context.
comments.quote: In which context do females grow heavier ovaries?

reviews.assessment: Novel and compelling study; suggests incorporating male genetic background evidence and fixing presentation details.
strengths: fairly realistic simulation of the natural environment

comments.issue: The discussion of male genetic background is incomplete; sperm competition could be an additional compensatory mechanism.
comments.request: Include Heinen-Kay et al. 2019 and unpack male genetic background effects.
comments.quote: I think the current discussion doesn’t sufficiently unpack what features of male genetic background could, in addition to the behavioral differences observed, explain the results.

comments.issue: The Results section reads as a non-sequitur and its first paragraph belongs in earlier sections.
comments.request: Restructure the opening of the Results.
comments.quote: The whole first paragraph of Results also felt like it belonged in one of the earlier sections – it contained information about the background and design.

comments.issue: Heinen-Kay et al. 2019 JEB found females reared with the flatwing genotype invested less in reproductive tissue.
comments.request: Cite and discuss this finding at lines 73-74.
comments.quote: found that females reared in with the flatwing genotype invested less in reproductive tissue (but still managed to produce an equivalent number of offspring)

comments.issue: Target densities were taken from Big Island conditions although the crickets are from Kauai.
comments.request: Justify the choice of target densities.
comments.quote: I’m curious why the target densities were set at the population conditions on the Big Island, since the cricket surveys were done across all three islands

comments.issue: The relationship between increasing female mass and decreasing or zero reproduction at lines 252-253 is unexplained and absent from the discussion.
comments.request: Discuss the cause of this relationship.
comments.quote: To what do the authors attribute this effect of increasing female mass being related to decreasing or zero reproduction?

title: Behavioural plasticity compensates for adaptive loss of cricket song

study.system: Drosophila; latitudinal cline; thermal fitness surfaces

reviews.assessment: Well-written and neat study, but scope, fitness proxies, modelling assumptions and missing fecundity undermine the conclusions.
strengths: very well written and pleasing to read
neat combination of thermal modelling and local adaptation
in silico transplant experiments are a good idea

comments.issue: Scope is unclear: the study is about thermal gradients but framed in generic terms of environmental gradients.
comments.request: Narrow and clarify the scope from the abstract onwards.
comments.quote: Environmental gradients are much more diverse that latudinal or thermal gradients.

comments.issue: Viability is a non-standard composite of survival and development time (h^-1).
comments.request: Motivate this metric or analyse the two components separately.
comments.quote: Viability is here calculated as something mroe complicated that one would generally expect.

comments.issue: The exact viability calculation and the treatment of dead individuals are not given.
comments.request: Provide a formula or reference.
comments.quote: A formula is needed to make this precise to the reader.

comments.issue: Performance prediction methods involve many unjustified choices and assumptions.
comments.request: Spell out and justify the modelling choices.
comments.quote: methods to plot performance predictions are overall quite complex, with many choices and assumptions that are not always well spelled oud or justified

comments.issue: Alternative thermal curve models were not compared; poor fits in Fig. S1 could bias predictions.
comments.request: Fit alternative models and use model selection.
comments.quote: Did the authors try alternative models? It is becoming common practice to comapre several models and seleect the best ones based on statsitical criteria.

comments.issue: It is unclear how multi-day lab viability can be integrated hourly, and what adding proportions divided by development time means.
comments.request: Explain the temporal integration approach.
comments.quote: What is the basing for doing the calculation every hour, when viability at fixed temperature was measured in the lab over several days (up to 60)?

comments.issue: Averaging days over years may mix out-of-phase years instead of computing per-year fitness and averaging afterwards.
comments.request: Justify or change the averaging approach.
comments.quote: why average days over years (when different years can be significantly out of phase on a calendar perspective), rathre than perform the computation per year and then do a arithemetic or geometric mean of fitness metrics across years?

comments.issue: Fecundity, a major fitness component, is excluded from the fitness surface.
comments.request: Measure or motivate the exclusion of fecundity.
comments.quote: Fitness predictions can never be complete, but it seems strage in this case to ignore such an important component, as conclusions could be overturned by it.

comments.issue: Results focus on methodology and thermal biology while the adaptive conclusions are compressed and rushed.
comments.request: Expand the adaptive conclusions and rebalance the paper.
comments.quote: I found the results were a bit too much oriented on the methodological aspects or the purely thermal biology aspects, whereas the main topic is supposed to be local adaptation.

comments.issue: The first abstract sentence about diversity patterns along environmental gradients is unclear.
comments.request: Be more specific about what remains unclear.
comments.quote: I found the first of the sentence of the abstract unclear. What ‘diversity patterns’?

comments.issue: Three line-level copy edits (ARE, caGes, missing space).
comments.quote: L41 : ARE predicted

comments.issue: The abstract does not clearly state that the novelty is in silico transplant experiments.
comments.request: Make the original contribution explicit in the abstract.
comments.quote: It would be good to be more explicit that what you propose as original is to perfom in silico transplant experiments, based on a thermal development model, to alleviate the experimental burden real expeeriments would represent.

comments.issue: Different sampling dates across latitudes could confound the results given rapid genetic change.
comments.request: Discuss the sampling window and its implications.
comments.quote: were the sampling dates in accordance with latitude? I mean, were flies sampled at similar ‘thermal dates’ across latitudes?

comments.issue: A 12:12 photoperiod may not match the Austral summer conditions where flies were sampled.
comments.request: Justify the photoperiod choice.
comments.quote: Why a 12:12 LD photoperiod? For populations that were sampled in Austral summer, where I presume days are much longer?

comments.issue: Figure 1A legend does not explain the temperature histogram or the circles.
comments.request: Explain what the histogram and circles show.
comments.quote: Could you explain, in the legend of (A) what the histogram of temperature show exactly? (daily, hourly, winter-to-winter?

comments.issue: The blue/red gradient is not visual and is inaccessible to colourblind readers.
comments.request: Use a more appropriate 8-colour ramp.
comments.quote: the blue/red gradient is not very visual. And completely useless to colorblind people. Pelase choose a more appropriate ramp of 8 colors.

comments.issue: Figure 2B appears to label viability wrongly or reflect the integration method.
comments.request: Check and fix the figure.
comments.quote: vibility is here eggs, not eggs. t-1. Is it a typo, or a consequence of the itnegration method

comments.issue: Figure 3D is conceptual and belongs in the discussion.
comments.request: Move it to a separate Figure 4.
comments.quote: Figure 3D really is strictly a conceptual panel, not a result panel. It is only used in the Discussion.

comments.issue: Only three main figures, with little biological result content.
comments.request: Bring material from Figures S1-S3 into the main figures.
comments.quote: I would suggest the uahtor to bring back material from Figures S1 and S2, and especially from Figure S3, into the main Figures.

reviews.assessment: Nice data and models but not clearly explaining mechanisms, less novel than claimed, and missing key literatures.
strengths: combination of lab measures and transplant modelling

comments.issue: Behaviour and thermal plasticity, key to local adaptation, are not acknowledged.
comments.request: Acknowledge these aspects somewhere.
comments.quote: They are super difficult to capture or measure but this needs to AT LEAST be acknowledged somewhere.

comments.issue: No field validation of the transplant predictions is provided.
comments.request: Add field validation or discuss the transplant and local adaptation literature.
comments.quote: There is also some field validation that is needed for this paper if it is going to land in a high-quality journal like Ecology Letters.

comments.issue: The premise that local adaptation along latitudinal clines is unclear is misleading.
comments.request: Recognise existing work, including on D. subobscura.
comments.quote: Philosophically, I find the premise of the paper a bit misleading- is it really unclear how local adaptation operates along latitudinal clines?

comments.issue: The tally of plant versus non-plant transplant studies is presented without discussing their quantity or quality.
comments.request: Discuss the transplant literature more carefully.
comments.quote: The idea that plants over-represent transplant experiments is a strange way of tallying in my opinion.

comments.issue: Non-overlapping maintenance and a fixed 12:12 photoperiod ignore natural overlap and photoperiod clines.
comments.request: Acknowledge these limitations and their fitness implications.
comments.quote: photoperiod is an important part of a latitudinal cline and likewise has fitness implications, yet there is a decision (I assume based in practicalities) to maintain them at 12:12 L:D

comments.issue: The paper is framed as the first model of fitness as a function of temperature although related models exist.
comments.request: Discuss pros and cons of this model relative to rate-of-increase approaches.
comments.quote: The tone of the paper is that they are first ever to come up with a model of fitness/population growth as a function of temperature.

comments.issue: Large fitness differences are implied although measures are relativized.
comments.request: Discuss this limitation, especially for climate change implications.
comments.quote: there is an implication that these are large differences in fitness but these are relativized measures

comments.issue: It is unclear whether bootstrapping was used when fitting the curves.
comments.request: Bootstrap the curves and report mean and standard error.
comments.quote: Given how variable 20 vials can be, a boot strapping approach to these curves (figure 1B and figure S1) is important.

comments.issue: The paper does not explain the mechanisms of local adaptation and misses entire literatures.
comments.request: Properly explain and contextualise the results.
comments.quote: Overall, this paper is doing some nice things but I am not sure it is explaining mechanisms of local adaptation

comments.issue: The statement on line 98 depends on the method of dispersal.
comments.request: Add this caveat.
comments.quote: Line 98: this does not have to be true; it depends on the method of dispersal.

comments.issue: Three line-level copy edits (unfeasible, missing e, starting with And).
comments.quote: Line 100: infeasible rather than unfeasible.

comments.issue: A supplemental table referenced on line 203 is missing from the SM.
comments.request: Locate or add the table.
comments.quote: Where is this supplemental table? It is not with the rest of the SM

comments.issue: Citations on line 340 are inadequate.
comments.request: Improve the citations.
comments.quote: Line 340: These citations leave much to be desired

comments.issue: Line 389 oversells the findings.
comments.request: Tone down the statement.
comments.quote: Line 389: This is overselling

comments.issue: The point of line 408 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the argument.
comments.quote: 408: where are you going with this?

comments.issue: Parameters in Eqn 1 are not all defined.
comments.request: Define all parameters.
comments.quote: Eqn1: please define all parameters

comments.issue: Attached papers are provided as supporting documents without explanation.
comments.request: Clarify their role.
comments.quote: What are these other attached papers as supporting documents?

title: Fitness surfaces and local thermal adaptation in Drosophila along a latitudinal gradient

study.system: duckweed; experimental range expansion along temperature gradients

editor_summary: Editor says the reviews are mixed but critical on novelty, speculation about mechanisms, missing limitation discussion and the model system's generality; rejection with possibility to resubmit after reworking the study.

reviews.assessment: Positive on writing, replication and statistics, but flags speculative mechanisms, differing starting conditions and the clonal model system's special priority effects.
strengths: overall well written and framed within the existing literature

comments.issue: Priority effects and directional selection remain speculative because genotype-trait associations and temporal dynamics were not demonstrated.
comments.request: Demonstrate the proposed mechanisms or present them explicitly as untested.
comments.quote: These mechanisms remain speculative as they were not demonstrated by the genotype-trait associations, and nor were these dynamics followed in time.

comments.issue: Starting temperatures differed between treatments, so initial selection may confound the slowed expansion along the gradient.
comments.request: Provide data on starting conditions and disentangle initial selection.
comments.quote: Hence, the starting conditions differ already between the two treatments, and this initial selection may strongly contribute to the observed slowed down dynamics along the gradient. Ideally, such data should be provided.

comments.issue: Duckweed monopolises space clonally, making the priority effects a special case with shadowing that may not generalise.
comments.request: Describe this special attribute of the model system and interpret the results accordingly.
comments.quote: As an experimental system, I would like this special attribute of the model system described and results accordingly interpreted.

reviews.assessment: Finds the study clear and interesting but questions how spatial priority effects are inferred and how among-replicate variability is quantified.
strengths: interesting research questions with a great description of experiments and results

comments.issue: It is unclear how spatial priority effects can be observed from these results or whether they are only an additional explanation.
comments.request: Test whether replicates with the dominant front genotype differ from those without it.
comments.quote: My main question to this manuscript would relate to the spatial priority effects which were only mentioned in the discussion. I wasn’t sure how this could be observed from these results

comments.issue: How range-boundary steepness is quantified from the first three percent-cover estimates is unclear.
comments.request: Explain how steepness is calculated.
comments.quote: I wasn’t entirely sure how exactly the steepness is quantified. What is meant with “the first three estimates of percent cover at the range front”?

comments.issue: Bench ID is treated as a fixed covariate without justification.
comments.request: Explain why bench ID is fixed rather than random.
comments.quote: Is there a reason why bench ID was included as a fixed covariate and not a random covariate?

comments.issue: The among-replicate variability metric cannot distinguish balanced spread from one distant replicate.
comments.request: Justify the metric and correct for unequal replicate numbers per treatment.
comments.quote: I was not entirely convinced about how among-replicate variability was quantified. Because I think that you can get the same result when all replicates have an equal distance around the mean versus everyone the same and one very distant replicate.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether “pooled genotypes” refers to abundances or genotype IDs and why replacement sampling was needed.
comments.request: Clarify the pooled-genotype procedure.
comments.quote: With ‘pooled genotypes’ do you mean the genotype abundances or rather genotype IDs?

comments.issue: It is unknown whether both putative species persisted equally at the end of the experiment.
comments.request: Report the genotypic composition of each putative species at the end.
comments.quote: do you see if the genotypic composition at the end of the experiment has genotypes of each “species”, or is one of the “species” more abundant?

reviews.assessment: Sees an interesting, well-written study but raises concerns about predictability terminology, two-species confounding, CV metric and significance overreach.
strengths: takes analyses a step further with more complicated environments and variability comparisons

comments.issue: “Predictability” is used synonymously with variability although they are distinct concepts.
comments.request: Use “variability” to avoid confusion.
comments.quote: I was a bit confused by the use of the term predictability. Predictability to me means an a priori prediction, whereas here it seems to be used synonymously with variability.

comments.issue: Two species are used, so it is unclear whether results are ecological or genetic.
comments.request: Analyse the results as two species to test whether genetics is necessary.
comments.quote: Given that two species are used, it’s unclear if what we see is purely ecological in nature or also is genetic.

comments.issue: CV confounds variability with the mean, which differed between treatments.
comments.request: Also examine variability without dividing by the mean.
comments.quote: However, with CV, both variability and the mean contribute to differences in the metric. I would look at variability without being divided by the mean as well, since we know that the means differed between treatments.

comments.issue: Increased variability could reflect dispersal-phenotype evolution rather than spatial priority effects.
comments.request: Measure a dispersal trait as an alternative explanation.
comments.quote: I’m wondering if the increase in variability could be linked to the differential emergence of dispersal phenotypes.

comments.issue: Late genetics were used although the temporal dynamics analysis used an earlier time point.
comments.request: Use the earlier genetics to match the temporal decision.
comments.quote: It's not clear why the earlier genetics (L 406) were not the main test for the results that were being compared and instead, the late genetics were used.

comments.issue: Non-significant trait differences are discussed as if they were significant.
comments.request: Do not discuss non-significant patterns as results.
comments.quote: For example, the traits were not significantly different between treatments, yet a paragraph in the discussion is devoted to how these traits impart higher fitness on the thermal gradient.

comments.issue: The introduction considers only abiotic drivers, ignoring biotic ones.
comments.request: Make the framing more general to include biotic drivers.
comments.quote: L 82-4, why just abiotic? Also, could be biotic – make this more general?

comments.issue: Asymmetric maladaptive gene flow is not mentioned.
comments.request: Include the potential for asymmetric maladaptive gene flow.
comments.quote: L 85-6, but also the potential for asymmetric maladaptive gene flow.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether conditions are simply not conducive or something prevents the process.
comments.request: Clarify the mechanism.
comments.quote: L 128 -9, because the conditions are not conducive, or is it prevented somehow?

comments.issue: The uniform environment appears to have been decreasing, contrary to the text.
comments.request: Correct the description of the uniform environment.
comments.quote: L 171, wasn’t the uniform environment actually decreasing?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the steepness analysis is a rate or slope, and why an exponential rather than logistic model was fitted.
comments.request: Clarify the analysis and model choice.
comments.quote: Is it a rate through time or a slope? If the response was a percent, then how was an exponential distribution fitted to it, when I would have expected a logistic.

comments.issue: Plasticity could alternatively be evaluated as adaptive plasticity with phenotypes modelled as a slope across temperature.
comments.request: Examine phenotypes as a slope across temperature.
comments.quote: the other way to evaluate plasticity would be to evaluate adaptive plasticity and examine phenotypes as a slope across temperature.

comments.issue: A non-significant result is discussed as if significant at lines 349-50.
comments.request: Do not present this as a significant result.
comments.quote: L 349-50, If this was not significant, then do not discuss it as if it was significant.

comments.issue: The traits on lines 415-429 were not significant but are discussed as patterns.
comments.request: Remove or reframe discussion of these non-significant traits.
comments.quote: L 415-429, These traits were not significant, so do not discuss them like they are.

title: Range expansion is both slower and more variable with rapid evolution across a spatial gradient in temperature

study.system: goldenrod gall flies and enemies; urban field survey, 84 sites

editor_summary: Editor says all three thoughtful reviews were positive with suggestions for improvement, and asks authors to address all points in revision.

reviews.assessment: Praises the clear writing and simple design; one major concern about tree cover as the only environmental factor.
strengths: first link between socio-economy and natural selection

comments.issue: Bird predation differences may reflect tree cover, pesticides or insect predator densities rather than socioeconomic effects.
comments.request: Discuss these alternative explanations and check whether gall densities correlate with socioeconomic variables.
comments.quote: the relative importance of bird predation can be due to positive effects of more tree cover on bird population density or due to negative factors that affect a lower population densities of insect predators/parasitoids in the higher income areas

comments.issue: Several line-level copy edits: extra word at L226 and missing words at L227 and L281.
comments.quote: Line 226: there seems to be an extra, unrelated word (“based”)

comments.issue: How selection gradient differences were assessed statistically is not clearly stated.
comments.request: Describe the model structure and whether population was a factor in the GLM.
comments.quote: It is not clear how (statistically) differences in selection gradients were assessed. Was population simply included as an independent factor in the GLM?

comments.issue: The data could alternatively be interpreted as lower income communities being better insect habitats.
comments.request: Consider this alternative interpretation.
comments.quote: Based on the alternative hypothesis stated above, the data could also be interpreted as lower income communities being better habitats for insects.

comments.issue: “Positive selection on gall flies” conflates selection on the fly with selection on gall size.
comments.request: Clarify that selection acts on gall size.
comments.quote: doesn’t make sense to me. I think, what you mean here is selection on “gall size”. Please clarify.

comments.issue: What the reported positive selection acts on (larger galls?) is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify what trait is under positive selection.
comments.quote: Line 275-276: Please also clarify what the positive selection is on here? Are the wasps also selecting for larger galls, increasingly with minority proportions increasing?

comments.issue: “Especially” at line 288 implies tree cover was the strongest of many measured correlates.
comments.request: Rephrase to avoid implying comparison with unmeasured variables.
comments.quote: Line 288: Tree cover is the only thing you measured. The “especially” makes it sound as if this was the strongest correlate out of a large number of variables measured.

comments.issue: “Goldenrod gall” is too broad because only Eurosta makes the ball galls studied.
comments.request: Call them “Eurosta galls” instead.
comments.quote: I would argue it would be more appropriate to not call it “goldenrod gall” but instead call it “Eurosta gall”.

reviews.assessment: Thoughtful, relevant study, but the convenience sample and SEM error correlations temper the causal language used.

comments.issue: A convenience sample undermines describing the study as a “test”.
comments.request: Replace “test” with “examine” or “model” at lines 24 and 223.
comments.quote: Since this paper uses a convenience sample, to claim that the study is a “test” is somewhat undermined. Far better to say, “we examine” or “we model”

comments.issue: Sampling located goldenrod populations rather than pre-selecting SES areas, which affects how the work should be described.
comments.request: Describe the sampling approach honestly and its implications.
comments.quote: It seems that the sampling was conducted by locating populations of goldenrod, rather than by starting with a selection of areas of the city with defined differences in SES.

comments.issue: A blanket prediction overgeneralizes beyond the Greater Toronto Area and similar cities.
comments.request: Restrict the prediction to the study region and similar metropolises.
comments.quote: you might say on line 132, “We predict that in the Greater Toronto Area and metropolises with similar structure

comments.issue: piecewiseSEM does not adjust for endogenous error correlations, so significant ones indicate bias in estimates.
comments.request: Address the error correlation issue, e.g. with covariance-based SEM packages.
comments.quote: one technical issue with your SEM is that you specified error correlations in piecewiseSEM without (I assume) recognizing that that package does not actually adjust for endogenous error correlations

comments.issue: “Hypothesized” at line 259 needs “final” inserted or clarification.
comments.request: Insert “final” before “hypothesized” or explain.
comments.quote: Line 259 – Insert “final” in front of “hypothesized”, unless you mean to imply that no changes were made from the first model evaluated

comments.issue: No references are given for the assumptions of the SEM/d-separation methodology.
comments.request: Cite the assumptions underlying the methodology.
comments.quote: You cite a software package and Shipley’s d-sep test, but provide no references regarding the assumptions of the methodology, which are much more fundamental to interpretations than are statistical assumptions.

comments.issue: Causal language at lines 285 and 298 is not justified by the sampling design or SEM assumptions.
comments.request: Say “suggest” instead of “show” and discuss causal assumptions.
comments.quote: Best to say “suggest” instead of “show”. You have not provided a sufficient discussion of causal assumptions to avoid criticism for implying that fitting an SEM (especially using piecewiseSEM) automatically qualifies results supporting causal language (“influences”).

comments.issue: Interpretations rest on mechanistic knowledge rather than the design or SEM methodology, which should be acknowledged.
comments.request: Report the assumptions and use example reporting language from Grace and Irvine.
comments.quote: your ability to draw the interpretations you do come from our mechanistic knowledge of the systems under investigation, not from the sampling design nor from the SEM analysis methodology

comments.issue: A complementary urban landscape paper is not cited.
comments.request: Consider citing Matteson et al. (2013).
comments.quote: One paper I know of that is in some ways complementary to this manuscript is Matteson et al. (2013).

comments.issue: The claim that everything is unique at line 57 is unhelpful.
comments.request: Rephrase, e.g. “Cities create atypical and complex environments”.
comments.quote: At some level everything is unique, so typically better to say something like, “Cities create atypical and complex environments

comments.issue: Wrong figure cross-reference at line 217.
comments.request: Change the reference to Figure 4.
comments.quote: Line 217 – Should be Figure 4, should it not?

title: Urban socioeconomic variation influences the ecology and evolution of trophic interactions

study.system: Mediterranean woody plants; plant-soil feedback seedling experiment

editor_summary: All reviewers find study interesting and novel but request clarity and raise methods concerns, including an error in the stabilization formula that could affect main results; careful revision needed.

reviews.assessment: Mixed; well-written and interesting, but formula errors and insufficient justification of the network analysis undermine confidence.
strengths: integrates recent PSF theory with a network perspective

comments.issue: The stabilization formula is wrong: intraspecific terms should be numerators, with interspecific terms in denominators; the same error appears in Fig. 3.
comments.request: Correct the SD formula and re-run the analysis.
comments.quote: the authors seem to have used the wrong formula for calculating the strength of (de)stabilization

comments.issue: Fig. 2, Fig. 3 and Table S11 disagree about whether any pair has stabilization >1.
comments.request: Recheck the analysis, figure drawing and table column names.
comments.quote: according to Fig 3 there should be one species pair with a mean stabilization value > 1 (furthest right pie-chart), yet according to Fig 2 the largest absolute effect size of stabilization is < 1

comments.issue: The validity of the multispecies network analysis is not justified, especially given that the Bever model breaks down in multispecies extensions.
comments.request: Demonstrate the network approach avoids the problems raised by Miller et al. 2022.
comments.quote: the authors need to demonstrate that the network analysis does not fall victim to the same problems highlighted by Miller et al when extending from the classic PSF model to multispecies systems

comments.issue: 3 line-level edits (L50 wording; L83 typo "stablished"; L206 ISE/Os naming).
comments.quote: I recommend replacing “is widely recognized” with “being widely recognized”

comments.issue: Claiming a lack of experiments limits PSF understanding is unfair; hundreds of species pairs have been studied.
comments.request: Revise the claim about missing experiments.
comments.quote: I don't think it's fair to say that a lack of experiments per se is what limits understanding of PSF effects on plant coexistence

comments.issue: L98-99 conflates single-species feedback with negative pairwise PSF, and misstates Kardol et al.'s result.
comments.request: Distinguish single-species and pairwise PSF and correct the wording.
comments.quote: in both of these cases, it seems like the “PSF” being referred to here is a single-species feedback

comments.issue: The design cannot distinguish PSFs mediated by soil biota from physicochemical soil changes.
comments.request: Remove the soil biota wording at L109.
comments.quote: the experimental design of this paper does nothing to distinguish between PSFs mediated by soil biota vs. changes to the physiochemical properties of the soil

comments.issue: Kandlikar et al. 2019 is a conceptual model paper; the 2021 paper may fit better at L136.
comments.request: Change the citation.
comments.quote: Kandlikar et al. 2019 was a conceptual model paper; Kandlikar et al 2021 may be more appropriate citation here.

comments.issue: Germination data were collected but not used or reported.
comments.request: Provide the germination data as a supplement.
comments.quote: Providing germination data in different contexts at least as a supplement would increase the value of this paper.

comments.issue: Averaging across soil sources discards design information; random effects on non-averaged data would be better.
comments.request: Model seed and soil sources as random effects instead of averaging.
comments.quote: I am puzzled as to why the authors would average across the soil sources for each seed source

comments.issue: The "unconditioned soils" statement at L288-292 conflicts with the reference-soil description.
comments.request: Clarify the reference soil used for fitness differences.
comments.quote: so please clarify what “we used unconditioned soils” means

comments.issue: Species are described as having positive or negative PSFs with all partners although most values are not significantly different from zero.
comments.request: Temper the claims at L379-380.
comments.quote: In most of the cases the values referred to here are not statistically different from zero, so saying they are positive or negative PSF seems a stretch.

comments.issue: "Pairwise PSF" is used inconsistently (one species' performance vs SD/FD-based pairs).
comments.request: Use the term pairwise PSF consistently.
comments.quote: In some cases, the authors seem to consider “plant species A affects growth of species B seeds” to be a “pairwise” PSF

reviews.assessment: Positive; excellent, well-designed contribution, but coexistence claims are overstated and the network analysis needs dynamism.

title: Intransitivity in plant–soil feedbacks is rare but is associated with multispecies coexistence

editor_summary: Theoretical contribution valued, but EL rarely publishes purely theoretical work; the empirical food-web comparison is weak, 'balanced' is undefined, and the theory is not tested against data; revision needs stronger empirical links.

title: Crop and landscape heterogeneity increase biodiversity in agricultural landscapes: A global review and meta‐analysis

study.system: complex ecological communities; random interaction networks and multistability

editor_summary: All reviewers enthusiastic and find it well written; concerns on the Allee effect, biological justification for separating cooperation/competition matrices, empirical applicability of the classification, figures, and introduction context.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, clearly presented framework, but two of the four regimes look like simulation artefacts and the Allee effect's role needs clarification.
strengths: complex matter presented in a pleasing and understandable way

comments.issue: Mutual exclusion and global bistability regimes are deemed unrealistic simulation artefacts; realistic abrupt changes are not located.
comments.request: Show where realistic abrupt changes occur or extend the model.
comments.quote: I would claim that both mutual exclusion states and global bi-stability are largely un-realistic, i.e. artefacts from the simulation

comments.issue: The Allee effect is assumed for all species; its necessity for the four regimes is unclear.
comments.request: Test how essential the Allee effect is to the results.
comments.quote: what if Allee effects are rare, do these patterns then disappear?

comments.issue: No practical way is given to identify which regime a natural community occupies.
