reviews.assessment: Elegant, well-written combination of theory and experiment, but the claim of a wholly novel competitive mechanism is not convincingly justified.
strengths: elegant combination of theory, field analysis and inference

comments.issue: Necessary and sufficient criteria for competition for time are not clearly defined, including whether it requires abrupt responses.
comments.request: Define the mechanism clearly and state the criteria and required assumptions.
comments.quote: I think it would be helpful to be more clear about what the necessary/sufficient criteria are for competition for time

comments.issue: The mechanism may just be resource competition with an abrupt physiological response, so the claim of a novel form of competition is not justified.
comments.request: Justify the claimed new distinction or reframe it as a unique functional response.
comments.quote: We're still talking resource competition, with the dynamics mediated by the physiology of the species. How is this not just a different functional response curve on the consumption vector?

comments.issue: Important earlier work on competition for time (Schoener, Abrams, Carothers) is overlooked.
comments.request: Place the work in the broader context of previous research on competition for time.
comments.quote: it would be useful to place this work in the broader context of previous work in this area rather than present it as something fundamentally new

comments.issue: Near-zero growing-length observations may reflect failed germination or establishment rather than competition during growth.
comments.request: Justify including these observations or treat them separately.
comments.quote: Firstly, does it make sense to even include these here? That is, is it clear that they died due to competition per se vs. lack of germination or establishment?

comments.issue: The data are near zero-inflated but this is not addressed in the modelling.
comments.request: Account for zero inflation in the models.
comments.quote: Secondly, from a statistical perspective, these would all be (nearly) zero-inflated distributions, but nowhere is this discussed in the text

comments.issue: Fig. 3 would benefit from showing dynamics of species off the trade-off line to illustrate extinction.
comments.request: Show dynamics for species not exactly on the trade-off line.
comments.quote: Would it be possible to show the dynamics (even in Supplemental) for some species not exactly on the trade-off line?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the centre figure in Fig. 6 is an actual SEM/path analysis.
comments.request: Clarify and add weights if it is an SEM.
comments.quote: Is the centre figure an actual SEM / path analysis? Or are these colours just highlighting the general strength (slope) of the relationships?

comments.issue: A section reference is missing at the top of Supplemental page 44.
comments.request: Add the missing section reference.
comments.quote: Top of Supplemental pg 44 -- there's a missing section reference.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and worthwhile theory, but under-contextualised and the empirical evidence is not compelling due to design limits and weak species differences.
strengths: theory around competition for time worthwhile for study
alignment with a specific ecophysiological mechanism

comments.issue: The mechanism is not placed in the context of other coexistence and diversity-maintenance mechanisms such as R*.
comments.request: Contextualise competition for time among established coexistence mechanisms.
comments.quote: what I find lacking is an effort to place this mechanism in the context of other coexistence and diversity maintenance mechanisms

comments.issue: The mechanism is strongly analogous to the competition-colonization trade-off and this analogy is not addressed.
comments.request: Address the analogy and draw on insights from the competition-colonization literature.
comments.quote: While this is not a problem or a failing of this model, I think the analogy is strong enough that the authors should address it

comments.issue: The model assumes a perfect competitive hierarchy that is likely unrealistic, as in the competition-colonization trade-off.
comments.request: Explore consequences of breaking the hierarchy assumption, including intraspecific variability and plasticity.
comments.quote: A broader exploration of the consequences of breaking that assumption (which has been done in the C-C context) would be very valuable

comments.issue: The experiment is insufficient to show that season length is set by water dropping below species-specific critical levels.
comments.request: Add data or redesign to test species-specific water thresholds.
comments.quote: I worry that the experimental design to test growing season length is inappropriate, or perhaps insufficient, to assess the particular mechanism you are proposing

comments.issue: Growing season length is used to estimate growth rate, so the growth-rate patterns may be partly circular.
comments.request: Test whether growth-rate patterns are driven by biomass or by season length.
comments.quote: especially when growing season length itself is one of the parameters used in estimating growth rate

comments.issue: Species responses are counter to expectation: the shortest-season species shows no density relationship while a long-season species has the strongest negative slope.
comments.request: Reconcile these patterns with the theoretical expectation.
comments.quote: I also find it interesting and counter to expectation that the species with the shortest growing season (FEMI) had no relationship with competitor density

comments.issue: Fig. 7 shows no significant differences in critical water content, so competition for time is not a strong coexistence candidate for these species.
comments.request: Acknowledge this weakness and its implications for the coexistence claim.
comments.quote: competition for time does not seem like a strong candidate for a mechanism that supports coexistence of these species or helps maintain high diversity

comments.issue: The claim that competition is the dominant process structuring systems is not generally accepted.
comments.request: Soften the wording and acknowledge environmental filtering and dispersal.
comments.quote: I am not sure competition is generally accepted as the dominant process structuring systems

comments.issue: The examples could equally be read as resource depletion slowing growth rather than constraining growth time.
comments.request: Clarify why the examples demonstrate a time constraint.
comments.quote: it seems like one could as easily think about it as the reduction of resources would make growth slower after a given point in time, but growth could continue nonetheless

comments.issue: The population-level pattern and its equivalence to the community-level pattern are unclear.
comments.request: Explain the population-level pattern and the equivalence.
comments.quote: Not clear exactly what you mean here. Explain the population level pattern you refer to and the equivalence to the community level pattern

comments.issue: It is unclear whether species would segregate growth periods or all compete for the earliest period, and whether this is behavioural or evolutionary.
comments.request: Clarify the expected temporal niche dynamics and their time scale.
comments.quote: Perhaps (in analogy to resource competition and R*) all species would attempt to take the earliest time period and grow to the point that they could exclude other species.

comments.issue: The theory section is functionally analogous to the competition-colonization trade-off in its coexistence implications.
comments.request: Note this analogy in the relevant section.
comments.quote: While described differently this seems functionally analogous to the competition-colonization tradeoff, at least in it's coexistence implications.

comments.issue: The word 'seeds' appears to be missing at line 352, leaving the measured propagule ambiguous.
comments.request: State explicitly which propagule weight is used.
comments.quote: Line 352: I think you mean to say “seeds” here but it is missing.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether plots contained a mix of all species or also focal-species monocultures.
comments.request: Clarify the plot composition.
comments.quote: Lines 358-360: Does this mean the plots were a mix of all species or also monocultures (but of just the focal species)?

comments.issue: Uncertainties around the trade-off line are too large to support the claim that species fall along it.
comments.request: Temper the trade-off claim or account for the uncertainty.
comments.quote: While some of the species do fall along this tradeoff line, the uncertainties are so large that I think it is inappropriate to make this claim.

reviews.assessment: High-quality, compelling study that needs clearer justification of its theoretical novelty for the Perspective format and more theory on coexistence and extinctions.
strengths: evidence for competition for time quite compelling
opens new avenues for wider ecological communities

comments.issue: The modelling approach was already introduced in Levine et al. (2022), so the theoretical novelty of the Perspective is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify how the modelling approach is new relative to Levine et al. (2022).
comments.quote: The authors should clarify how their modeling approach is new to this contribution, and how does it depart from the approach followed by Levine et al (2022).

comments.issue: It is not explained theoretically why the growth-longevity trade-off should promote coexistence.
comments.request: Provide a mathematical discussion of why the trade-off promotes coexistence.
comments.quote: the authors do not explain why this trade-off should promote coexistence, from a theoretical point of view

comments.issue: Whether the trade-off and coexistence result hold for a larger species pool is unknown.
comments.request: Test whether the trade-off is preserved with more competing species.
comments.quote: it would be interesting to see how these results could be altered when the number of species that compete in experiments is larger, to check whether the trade-off is preserved for a larger species pool

comments.issue: The exponential growth-longevity trade-off is assumed, but other functional forms such as power laws may change coexistence patterns.
comments.request: Explore alternative trade-off functions, including power laws.
comments.quote: The authors assume an exponential dependence between growth and longevity, but other functions may lead to different coexistence patterns.

comments.issue: Figures 3 (left panels) and 7 would be clearer on logarithmic scales.
comments.request: Plot figures 3 (left panels) and 7 on logarithmic scales.
comments.quote: In particular, figures 3 (left panels) and 7 should be plotted using logarithmic scales.

comments.issue: A possible theoretical relationship between equilibrium abundance and longevity is not explored.
comments.request: Test whether equilibrium abundance relates to longevity.
comments.quote: is there a relationship (at least, theoretical) between species abundance at equilibrium and longevity?

comments.issue: The framework predicts feasibility and stability for all species, ignoring extinctions that could occur in natural communities.
comments.request: Expand the model or discussion to include the role of extinctions.
comments.quote: The theoretical framework predict feasibility and stability for all species at equilibrium. This is unrealistic, because some species could be displaced in natural communities due to this new competitive mechanism.

comments.issue: The linear relationship in the left panel of Fig. 1 contradicts the non-linear model depicted on the right.
comments.request: Use a concave-up dependence as in the model.
comments.quote: The usage of a linear relationship here is misleading, given that the growth-mediated competition is depicted (conceptually) by a non-linear function in the right panel.

comments.issue: Fig. 3 has flipped axes, a vertical scale that should reach 0.3, and unclear units for critical water content.
comments.request: Fix the axes, scale and units in Fig. 3.
comments.quote: Why axes are flipped in left panels? Also, The vertical scale of panel B (left) should span up to the value 0.3.

title: Competition for time: Evidence for an overlooked, diversity‐maintaining competitive mechanism

study.system: forest litter decomposition; invertebrates; 476 case studies, 93 sites

editor_summary: Editor asks for PRISMA workflows and exclusion reporting, assessment of invertebrates in water bodies (the 31% claim is too broad), and quantitative modelling of excluding invertebrate decomposition.

reviews.assessment: Broadly interesting and timely, but the hypotheses and methods lack clarity and detail for a synthesis paper.

comments.issue: Hypotheses and methods lack clarity and detail.
comments.request: Clarify hypotheses and the variables in the models.
comments.quote: the lack of clarity/certainty in both the presentation of hypotheses (perhaps these would be better presented as questions, given the nature of the study?) and explanation of methods

comments.issue: 'Mass loss' and 'decomposition rate' need definition and standardization details.
comments.request: Clarify the metrics and litter-bag standardization.
comments.quote: Clarity in “mass loss” and “decomposition rate” (presumably of litter bags - but are these all standardized/identical across studies) as described in the methods is needed.

comments.issue: Use of unpublished termite diversity data is vague.
comments.request: Clarify how the data were used.
comments.quote: The reference to an unpublished study on “termite diversity” is vague and this study would benefit from clarity on just how those data were used in the current study.

comments.issue: Temperate/tropical distinction is vague; warm temperate and subtropical impacts are omitted.
comments.request: Clarify the zones and discuss the broader climatic breadth.
comments.quote: the distinction between “temperate” and “tropical” is also somewhat vague and warrants further clarity and mention in the Methods and Discussion

comments.issue: Subheadings are inconsistent across sections.
comments.request: Add matching subheadings.
comments.quote: The manuscript may also benefit from additional use of subheadings (as in the Discussion) matching the Intro, Methods, and Results

reviews.assessment: Well-written and interesting, but biome definitions are imprecise and the modelling and climate-change claims need stronger support.

comments.issue: Latitude/longitude descriptors are flawed; biomes would be more precise.
comments.request: Remove latitude/longitude descriptors.
comments.quote: My suggestion is to remove latitude/longitude as a descriptor because it is flawed.

comments.issue: Forest-only results are extrapolated to tropical land mass.
comments.request: Clarify the scope of inference.
comments.quote: The authors limit the study to forests, but then talk about the land mass of the tropics

comments.issue: Biome classification is undefined and inconsistent (tropical vs subtropical).
comments.request: Define biomes explicitly.
comments.quote: I would take the space to describe how you defined biome, especially since with some metrics forests that would by some definitions be subtropical because of the high temperatures, are considered tropical by others because they experience no frost.

comments.issue: Dry and wet tropical forests are grouped despite different controls.
comments.request: Group similar sites or justify the grouping.
comments.quote: I don't think that the dry tropical forests should be grouped with the wet tropical forests.

comments.issue: No modelling showing that excluding invertebrates biases global models.
comments.request: Run models with and without invertebrate decomposition.
comments.quote: the authors don't actually make an argument or do any modeling to demonstrate that excluding them actually influences our ability to accurately model

comments.issue: Climate-change argument lacks supporting citations.
comments.request: Cite experiments linking climate to invertebrate communities.
comments.quote: I think that this is a valid point, but I think this is where citing some experiments or studies that show that this will influence the invertebrate community will matter.

title: Global contribution of invertebrates to forest litter decomposition

study.system: coral reef fish; Great Barrier Reef abundance time series

editor_summary: The most uniformly positive reviews the editor has received, with reviewers apologising for having only minor comments; congratulates the authors on an outstanding paper.

reviews.assessment: One of the best community ecology papers in a decade; suggests better positioning and small presentation changes to widen its impact.
strengths: one of the best papers in community ecology in the last decade
deep knowledge of dynamical processes combined with advanced statistics
careful use of simulation to avoid flaws

comments.issue: The manuscript targets a narrow audience; it is not related to a more general ecological problem and the Loreau literature is not cited.
comments.request: Relate the approach to a general problem and cite the relevant Loreau papers.
comments.quote: Relate the approach to a more general problem in ecology, e.g. the stability-diversity interaction.

comments.issue: The multivariate Gompertz model and the stationarity assumption are not justified.
comments.request: Justify the Gompertz model and include the stationarity assumption.
comments.quote: The use of the mulitvariate Gompertz model is fundamental and should be justified

comments.issue: The interesting limited variability among reefs is buried in Fig S6 with little discussion.
comments.request: Move Fig S6 to the main text and extend its explanation.
comments.quote: I think that the authors should consider moving Fig S6 into the main text and extend the explanation of these effects in the discussion

reviews.assessment: One of the most polished papers the reviewer has reviewed; only minor suggestions to emphasise the simulation tests and consider multi-patch covariance.
strengths: one of the most polished and carefully thought-through papers reviewed
positive, interesting and important addition to community ecology

comments.issue: The simulation test that distinguishes among scenarios is not emphasised early enough.
comments.request: Emphasise the simulation test in the abstract and/or introduction.
comments.quote: My only minor comment would be to suggest that you emphasise this test more explicitly in the abstract and/or introduction

comments.issue: Why only systems where a subset of species have interactions were tested is not explained in the main text.
comments.request: Explain the choice of systems with a subset of interactions.
comments.quote: Perhaps also mention why you test only systems where a subset of species have interactions

comments.issue: Multi-patch impacts of environmental fluctuations and covariance of species responses are not considered.
comments.request: Consider multi-patch covariance of species responses in future work.
comments.quote: suggest that you think about multi-patch impacts of environmental fluctuations – e.g. including covariance of species responses within a patch, as well as between patches

comments.issue: The working definition of 'mechanistic' is missing and contested, since interactions are modelled phenomenologically.
comments.request: Include a working definition of 'mechanistic'.
comments.quote: Can you include your working definition of “mechanistic” here? I know many people who would dispute this point

comments.issue: A single two-species plant study is a poor justification for the horseshoe prior.
comments.request: Drop or replace the weak justification sentence.
comments.quote: The fact that a regularised horseshoe prior has been used in a single plant study of two species seems like a very poor justification of applying the method in your case

comments.issue: It is unclear why an 'other' distribution implies a Gaussian prior for species interactions.
comments.request: Cite examples supporting a Gaussian prior for interactions.
comments.quote: I don’t entirely understand why “other” distribution immediately implies “Gaussian”. I would suggest that you cite some examples of papers that support the use of a Gaussian prior for species interactions

comments.issue: The effect of modelling only part of the community on interaction-coefficient estimates is untested.
comments.request: Comment on or simulate the effect of modelling a partial community.
comments.quote: Can you comment briefly (or better yet, test by simulation) what the effect of modelling only part of the community might be on your ability to quantify unbiased estimates of species interaction coefficients?

comments.issue: Observation error might drive the reported effect and is not addressed.
comments.request: Comment on whether observation error is likely to be an issue.
comments.quote: Is there any chance that some of this effect is driven by observation error? Can you comment briefly on this, and explain why or why not it’s likely to be an issue?

comments.issue: The statement that time-series analysis precludes the discussed biases is unsupported.
comments.request: Remove the statement and acknowledge it as a challenge for future work.
comments.quote: I would suggest removing this statement – time-series analysis alone does not preclude the biases discussed by Detto, Hülsmann et al.

title: High response diversity and conspecific density‐dependence, not species interactions, drive dynamics of coral reef fish communities

study.system: 18 plant species; competition networks; nitrogen and fungicide

editor_summary: Both reviewers saw potential and were excited about the framing, but got lost amid the multiple network metrics; strengthen links between metrics, predictions, results and biology for a broad audience.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, important questions and a huge amount of work, but the link between network metrics and plant competition and the novelty beyond known N-pathogen effects are unclear.

comments.issue: The paper is hard to follow and lacks a clear link between network metrics and plant competition.
comments.request: Lay out the link between the network metrics and plant competition more carefully.
comments.quote: In general, I found the paper lacked a clear link between its two major facets (network metrics and plant competition).

comments.issue: The main takeaway has been demonstrated before and the novelty of the approach remains cryptic.
comments.request: Make the extra nuance and novelty of the results clearer.
comments.quote: The main thing I took away from the paper is that nitrogen and pathogens affect plant competition, in a way that depends on the growth strategy of the plant. This is certainly important, but it has been demonstrated before.

comments.issue: The referent of 'their' in line 30 is ambiguous.
comments.request: Change 'their structure' to 'network structure'.
comments.quote: unclear whether “their” refers to the plants or the networks

comments.issue: The introduction paragraph does not make clear the problem with current network approaches or the proposed solution.
comments.request: Clarify the problem, the significance of the solution and its implementation.
comments.quote: I’m unsure what the problem is with current network approaches, the significance of the proposed solutions or how they can/should be implemented

comments.issue: The need to understand multiple network metrics and their benefit is not justified.
comments.request: Explain the benefit of multiple metrics, e.g. via a Table 1 column.
comments.quote: Why do we need to understand multiple metrics of network structure?

comments.issue: 'Some aspects' in line 58 is vague.
comments.request: Give an example of these aspects.
comments.quote: In line 58, “some aspects” is quite vague, an example here would be helpful.

comments.issue: The link between per-capita effects and demographic consequences is unclear and per-capita measures seem unnecessary.
comments.request: Clarify what per-capita measures add.
comments.quote: The link between per-capita effects and demographic consequences is not clear (lines 63-64) – I don’t think you necessarily need per-capita measures to describe abundance shifts or local extinction

comments.issue: Two line-level copy edits: delete 'they' (line 95) and 'we' (line 110).
comments.quote: Line 95: delete “they” Line 110: delete “we”?

comments.issue: Table 1 needs verbal descriptions linking indices to ecological meaning and to the predictions.
comments.request: Add verbal descriptions and clarify how indices map to predictions.
comments.quote: At the risk of making this table massive, I think that the networks need some verbal description.

comments.issue: Table 1 predictions for diagonal dominance and modularity appear contradictory and hard to link to network layouts.
comments.request: Reconcile and explain the conflicting predictions.
comments.quote: Overall I’m just finding it really hard to link the network indices (and their values, whether they will be positive or negative etc, see previous comment) with the network layouts and then with the community predictions.

comments.issue: Phytometer sampling dates, destructive sampling and biomass drying details are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify phytometer sampling, drying and biomass measurement.
comments.quote: I assume they were destructively sampled (as you use biomass in dry weight), but you also say they were measured in June 2020

comments.issue: It is unclear how intraspecific and pairwise interspecific effects were separated in the models.
comments.request: Explain how the effects were estimated.
comments.quote: how can you separate out intra and interspecific effects? Or do you mean that each individual neighbour species was its own independent variable in these models?

comments.issue: 'Predict' should be 'estimate' in line 258.
comments.request: Replace 'predict' with 'estimate'.
comments.quote: Line 258: I think you mean ‘estimate’ rather than ‘predict’ here?

comments.issue: Only SLA has error bars in Figure 3.
comments.request: Explain or add error bars for the other effects.
comments.quote: Figure 3: Why does SLA have error bars but no other effect does?

comments.issue: Ecological interpretations of the metrics are missing from earlier in the manuscript and Box 1 is not ecologically focused.
comments.request: Integrate ecological interpretations into Table 1 or Box 1.
comments.quote: I feel like this sort of information (e.g. i.e. the ecological interpretation of high diagonal dominance, the ecological interpretation of high asymmetry, etc) is missing from earlier in the manuscript, and would really help make sense of all the predictions.

comments.issue: The claimed advance is inexact, as growth strategies are quantified by SLA alone, as in previous trait-based approaches.
comments.request: Clarify how this differs from previous trait-based approaches.
comments.quote: So how is this different to the previous approaches that have focused on trait differences to predict competition?

reviews.assessment: Well written and valuable integration of nutrients, consumers, traits and plant interactions, but terminology and new concepts make the many predictions and results hard to follow.
strengths: growth strategies help identify patterns in complex systems

comments.issue: Writing revisions are needed to clarify the many predictions and results.
comments.request: Revise the writing to improve clarity of predictions and results.
comments.quote: I do feel that some revision in writing would help clarify the many predictions and results that were a bit hard to follow by the end of the discussion.

comments.issue: Table 1 is hard to connect to the introduction; Box 1 is not cited and metrics are not tied to concepts.
comments.request: Tie metrics to concepts and cite Box 1, or reduce Table 1 text.
comments.quote: it can be a bit difficult to connect the setup and predictions in the main body of the introduction to Table 1 given the interchangeable language between the various metrics

comments.issue: The discussion introduces the concept of competitive effects and responses without introducing it earlier.
comments.request: Describe how to interpret these metrics in the introduction or methods.
comments.quote: One example is the idea of “competitive effects and responses” that are mentioned multiple times in the discussion but not any time before that.

comments.issue: The claim that slow species are better competitors under nitrogen or fungicide is not evident from the figures or results.
comments.request: Point readers to results supporting these patterns.
comments.quote: you state multiple times that you observe slow species (low SLA) being better competitors under nitrogen addition or fungicide addition but from the figures and results section I see no clear indication of this

comments.issue: The emphasised positive/negative interactions and per-capita rates are never introduced or used again.
comments.request: Explain why these aspects are key and describe per-capita rates.
comments.quote: The importance of focusing on both positive and negative interactions is not a central focus of this study and is not elaborated on ever again in the study.

comments.issue: The final introduction sentence omits pathogens, fungi and consumers, underselling the study's novelty.
comments.request: Mention consumers in the sentence to highlight novelty.
comments.quote: You don’t mention pathogens or fungi or consumers in this final sentence which is not giving enough novelty to your study of how consumers influence plant-plant interactions across varying plant growth strategies.

comments.issue: It is unclear how per capita effects were measured.
comments.request: Explain how per capita effects were measured.
comments.quote: Here you mention per capita effects but it is unclear at all how this is measured.

comments.issue: 'Four combinations of nitrogen and fungicide treatment' is ambiguous.
comments.request: Specify the four treatment combinations explicitly.
comments.quote: “four combinations of nitrogen and fungicide treatment” could be interpreted in many ways and it would be good to be clearer that you mean individual nitrogen, individual fungicide treatment, a combined treatment, and a control.

comments.issue: Trends for Achillea and Rumex are hard to discern from the matrices.
comments.request: Consider adding histograms of interaction strengths.
comments.quote: I wonder if a histogram showing the distribution of interaction strengths for each species would help illustrate this point.

comments.issue: Figure 2 is hard to interpret and the significance of prediction slopes is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the figure and whether slopes differ from zero.
comments.quote: In general this figure was a bit hard to interpret. Are all the slopes of the prediction lines significant from 0?

comments.issue: The different point colours in Figure 3 are unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the colour coding.
comments.quote: Figure 3: It is unclear why the points are different colors (light red versus dark red or brown?).

comments.issue: Interchangeable use of metric names and biological terms may confuse readers.
comments.request: Use consistent terminology for metrics and the biology they represent.
comments.quote: I assume that when referring to dominance of intraspecific interactions this is the diagonal dominance metric.

comments.issue: Citing Table 1 for results is confusing; the relevant theoretical works should be cited instead.
comments.request: Cite the theoretical works the results do not align with.
comments.quote: The reference to Table 1 is a bit confusing as you are referencing your results but then the Table 1 is your predictions.

comments.issue: 'Response-effect asymmetry' appears to be a new term for the same Table 1 metric, and the logic is hard to follow.
comments.request: Define the term and introduce it earlier.
comments.quote: The “response-effect asymmetry” described here is a new term but I assume it is another way of saying the same metric you describe in Table 1?

comments.issue: Slow species being better competitors under nitrogen contradicts the cited resource competition theory.
comments.request: Explain the discrepancy with Tilman (1982) and theory.
comments.quote: The idea of slow species being more competitive under nitrogen addition is counter to resource competition theory you cite such as Tilman 1982.

comments.issue: Statements about traits and competition are hard to connect to the figures; the reason fast species are poor competitors with foliar fungi is unclear.
comments.request: Remind readers why fast species are poor competitors with foliar fungi.
comments.quote: Can you remind the reader why you think fast growing species are poor competitors in the context of foliar fungi?

comments.issue: Competitive effects versus responses are only introduced in the discussion.
comments.request: Introduce the concept in the introduction.
comments.quote: you bring up the idea of competitive effects versus responses which tells me that this should be brought up in the introduction to help guide the reader

comments.issue: No statistics confirm that SLA shifts under nitrogen versus control.
comments.request: Report statistics for the SLA shift.
comments.quote: Can you report some statistics to confirm that SLA is shifting with nitrogen treatment compared to control?

comments.issue: The focus on early plant growth and phytometers is not mentioned in the introduction.
comments.request: Mention the early-growth focus in the introduction or discuss it more.
comments.quote: It would be nice to potentially mention this focus on early plant growth (and use of phytometers) in the introduction.

title: Fast–slow traits predict competition network structure and its response to resources and enemies

study.system: three-species Lotka-Volterra competition; mathematical analysis

editor_summary: Editor notes reviewers agree the work is important progress, clearly explained and of broad interest, but technical issues must be addressed; R3's suggested real-world application is welcome but not required.

reviews.assessment: Appreciates the beautiful, clear figures and the useful message that pairwise intuition fails for three species, with one technical caveat about recentering.
strengths: important message that two-species intuition does not translate to three species
clear writing given the technical nature

comments.issue: The long history of classifying three-species GLV and replicator dynamics, notably Bomze's classification, is not acknowledged.
comments.request: Acknowledge Bomze (1983, 1995).
comments.quote: The Authors might want to acknowledge the heroic efforts of Immanuel Bomze (1983, corrected by the same author in 1995)

comments.issue: The analysis stops at three species, although four species are the minimum needed to observe chaos.
comments.request: Consider extending the efforts to four species.
comments.quote: One could argue that maybe our efforts should extend to four species, which is the minimum needed to observe chaos in a competitive setting.

comments.issue: The promised Mathematica workbook was not accessible to reviewers.
comments.request: Make the Mathematica workbook available.
comments.quote: It is unfortunate that the promised Mathematica workbook was not accessible to reviewers.

comments.issue: Recentering in Eq. 11 effectively uses different time units per equation, so limit-cycle results and the reported simplex areas may be distorted.
comments.request: Use a consistent time scale across equations or discuss the distortion.
comments.quote: When the Authors attempt recentering in Eq. 11, they are practically measuring the time in each equation in a different way

comments.issue: The introduction does not note that a feasible equilibrium is necessary for coexistence in GLV.
comments.request: Mention this necessary condition at line 88.
comments.quote: It might be worth mentioning here that the existence of a feasible equilibrium in GLV is a necessary condition for coexistence.

comments.issue: Two line-level corrections: a wrong index in Eq 8 and 'inverse' instead of 'reciprocal' at l185.
comments.quote: Eq 8 l178 In the lhs, A13 should be A23

reviews.assessment: Exciting and thorough synthesis, but the metric's identification with intransitivity is questionable and the terminology and methods need much more precise explication.
strengths: incredibly thorough presentation of diverse competitive outcomes
of considerable interest to theoretical ecologists

comments.issue: The metric based on the geometric mean of interspecific competition coefficients is not consistent with conventional ecological or strict mathematical definitions of intransitivity.
comments.request: Reconsider whether the metric should be called intransitivity.
comments.quote: what the authors interpret as intransitivity based on the geometric mean of the interspecific competition coefficients is not wholly consistent with conventional ecological interpretations of intransitivity or indeed a strict mathematical definition based on binary relations

comments.issue: The metric may be better named as a potential for intransitivity rather than intransitivity itself.
comments.request: Consider renaming the metric.
comments.quote: Perhaps it might be better termed as something along the lines of the 'potential' for intransitivity?

comments.issue: Alternative definitions of intransitivity are introduced too late; the conventional definition appears only in the third paragraph.
comments.request: Disambiguate the alternative perspectives on intransitivity early in the introduction or methods.
comments.quote: If the authors are confident they can defend their terminology, then I think it would be enormously helpful to disambiguate these alternative perspectives on intransitivity comprehensively in the introduction or early as possible in the methods.

comments.issue: The paragraph on the missing parameter encoded in the three relative fitness differences (lines 168-174) is hard to follow.
comments.request: Rewrite that paragraph more clearly.
comments.quote: I indeed found the logic in the paragraph describing the "missing parameter encoded in the three relative fitness differences" hard to follow

comments.issue: It is not acknowledged early that niche differences, like fitness differences, are meaningful only in the context of pairs.
comments.request: Briefly acknowledge this for niche differences at lines 57-63.
comments.quote: it may be helpful to briefly acknowledge that this issue also holds for the niche differences (i.e. meaningful only in the context of pairs)

comments.issue: Introducing intransitivity via rock-paper-scissors primes readers to assume the metric captures that classic pattern.
comments.request: Add a qualifier at lines 76-78.
comments.quote: the first mention of intransitivity is with respect to the classic example of rock-paper-scissors, which primes the reader to assume that is what the metric of intransitivity captures

comments.issue: Heteroclinic cycles are used without definition.
comments.request: Define heteroclinic cycles.
comments.quote: Define heteroclinic cycles (not a term in wide usage outside of dynamical systems theory).

comments.issue: The claim that stable limit cycles are less common than heteroclinic cycles needs support and context from the literature.
comments.request: Clarify whether this is always the case and cite relevant work.
comments.quote: This sentence seems to suggest that stable limit cycles are not as commonly observed as heteroclinic cycles, which is something I was unaware of.

comments.issue: It is unclear why competitive asymmetry can only have a quantitative effect on pairwise competition outcomes.
comments.request: Explain why qualitative outcomes cannot change.
comments.quote: I don’t understand why it can be said that competitive asymmetry only has a quantitative effect on the outcome of pairwise competition?

comments.issue: Appendix B only shows the non-dimensionalisation for the three-species system.
comments.request: Also show the two-species non-dimensionalisation.
comments.quote: Appendix B only shows the non-dimensionalisation for the three species system.

comments.issue: The reminder that rho < 1 corresponds to alternative stable states, the key distinction, is missing.
comments.request: Remind the reader that rho < 1 translates to alternative stable states.
comments.quote: it would be helpful to remind the reader that rho < 1 translates to alternative stable states, and that is the key distinction (I think) that is being highlighted

comments.issue: The stated conditions may be necessary but not sufficient, as they would seem to include all rock-paper-scissors systems.
comments.request: Clarify the sufficiency of the conditions at line 216.
comments.quote: Necessary but not sufficient conditions (?) as this would seem to equate to all rock-paper-scissors systems even without heteroclinic cycles?

comments.issue: The text does not clarify that the heteroclinic cycle would in reality collapse to a single-species monoculture.
comments.request: Clarify the biological outcome at line 287.
comments.quote: Maybe clarify that in reality the heteroclinic cycle should collapse to a single species monoculture.

comments.issue: The limit-cycle parameter space is barely visible in the plot.
comments.request: Refer explicitly to the thin white band surrounding the heteroclinic cycles.
comments.quote: The parameter space corresponding to the limit cycle is barely visible in the plot so you could make explicit reference here to the thin white band surrounding the heteroclinic cycles.

title: The three‐species problem: Incorporating competitive asymmetry and intransitivity in modern coexistence theory

study.system: TreeDivNet forests; bird and arthropod predation on plasticine caterpillars

editor_summary: Editor reports all four reviewers appreciated the question, multi-site design and presentation, but all asked to include covariates such as species composition, bird avoidance, sampling interval, stand age and latitude to test robustness.

reviews.assessment: Praises the impressive multi-site study but raises clarifications on the response variable, tree species identity and climate gradients.

comments.issue: The statement that these groups exert strong top-down control should acknowledge that they can also be bottom-up controlled.
comments.request: Soften the statement and give examples of weak top-down control.
comments.quote: the two taxonomic groups may also be bottom-up controlled, I assume, so the authors may want to soften their statement by acknowledging this

comments.issue: The percentage of unknown predators is not reported in the Results.
comments.request: Report the percentage of unknown predators alongside other predator types.
comments.quote: the authors should also report the percentage of “unknown” predator in Results, as they have done with the other types of predators

comments.issue: It is unclear how the response variable (proportion of predation attempts by caterpillar days) was computed per tree, plot and survey.
comments.request: Clarify how the response variable was calculated.
comments.quote: what is the response variable (proportion of predation attempts by caterpillar days) composed of?

comments.issue: Tree species identity likely affects predation risk but is not accounted for, risking confounding of richness effects.
comments.request: Discuss this limitation and possibly examine broadleaf versus conifer effects.
comments.quote: tree species identity will surely influence predation risk in addition to effects of tree species richness

comments.issue: It is doubtful whether climate and richness gradients were sufficient to detect interactions, since richness gradients covary with climate and site setup.
comments.request: Discuss the confounding of richness gradients with climate across sites.
comments.quote: do the authors think that there were sufficient gradients in climate crossed with sufficient gradients in tree species richness to detect possible interactive effects?

reviews.assessment: Interesting study, but the methods lack detail and the statistics need improvement before the results can be judged solid.

comments.issue: Experiment age and canopy development are not reported or modelled, though they affect animal numbers.
comments.request: Report setup years and include age as a fixed factor if it varies widely.
comments.quote: It’s important to show which year the experiment set up, as the age and canopy situation can largely affect the numbers of different animals.

comments.issue: Using 1979-2013 climate data rather than study-year data, and the choice of MAP and MAT, are not justified.
comments.request: Justify the climate data period and the choice of MAP and MAT.
comments.quote: Here needs a justification why used the historical data, but not data from the studied years.

comments.issue: Sampling intervals and survey times vary greatly across sites without explanation.
comments.request: Explain the variation in sampling intervals and times.
comments.quote: From Table S1, the sampling intervals and survey times are largely different, is there a reason to have this variation or just due to the labor limitation.

comments.issue: The number of tree species per site is inconsistent (three versus two) and diversity gradients are unclear.
comments.request: Report the tree species numbers per site and plot.
comments.quote: It is not clear how many tree species were included in each site or plots.

comments.issue: Figure 2 axes are too brief and the scale should span the full range, as in panels c-f.
comments.request: Set axes from the lowest to the highest values.
comments.quote: The x-axis is very brief. The scale should set from the lowest to the highest. The same for Figure c-f.

comments.issue: Predicted lines in Figure 2 differ greatly from raw lines in Figure S2, suggesting model problems.
comments.request: Check the model given the mismatch between predicted and raw values.
comments.quote: If there are big difference between the predicted and raw ones, you have to check the model again.

comments.issue: Block as a random factor is missing from the text and Table S1 and its definition is unclear.
comments.request: Describe how blocks were defined and sized.
comments.quote: in line 236, it shows sites and blocks are the random factors. But this information is missing from the text and Table S1.

comments.issue: Year or stand age is not included in the model as a random or fixed factor.
comments.request: Include year or age as a random factor, or fixed if its range is large.
comments.quote: I would suggest to put year or age also as a random factor if they don’t have a large range.

comments.issue: Tree species composition is not included as a random factor despite differing among sites.
comments.request: Add species or composition to the random factors.
comments.quote: I would add species or composition into the random factors.

comments.issue: Basic information on local arthropod and bird diversity is missing.
comments.request: Report local animal diversity and whether results depend on it.
comments.quote: there is no detailed information in either method or introduction, the basic information of the diversity of arthropod and birds in the local area

reviews.assessment: Impressed by the global experiment and data, but flags spatial autocorrelation and the limited climate gradient.

comments.issue: Spatial autocorrelation across the 14 worldwide sites is not considered in the model.
comments.request: Include spatial autocorrelation (latitude and longitude) in the model.
comments.quote: when your research puts 14 sites worldwide into one model, you may have to consider the issue of spatial autocorrelation (latitude and longitude)

comments.issue: The precipitation gradient is a small segment of the global range, so consistency across climates may not generalise.
comments.request: Be more cautious and report this limitation in the Discussion.
comments.quote: The precipitation in this study, in particular, has a small range and is likely to be a very small segment of the complete global precipitation gradient.

comments.issue: Figures 1 and 2 are too concise and could carry more site and climate information.
comments.request: Consider adding climate statistics, a biome diagram and site colours.
comments.quote: Figure 1 and Figure 2 are so concise, you can try to modify them to make them better (including more useful information).

comments.issue: The abstract ends with significance only and gives no meaningful suggestion.
comments.request: Add a meaningful suggestion based on the results to the abstract.
comments.quote: The authors should try to elevate this study by making a meaningful suggestion based on the results.

comments.issue: The claim that birds respond more strongly to tree diversity lacks specificity about bird traits.
comments.request: Specify which aspects of birds drive the response.
comments.quote: Birds are more likely to exhibit stronger responses to changes in tree diversity compared to predatory arthropods. What are the specific aspects of the birds?

comments.issue: Climate variables were not log-transformed, unlike species richness, and this is untested.
comments.request: Test whether log-transforming climate variables changes the results.
comments.quote: You have log-transformed the species richness of the predictor variables. Would log-transforming the climate variables change the results?

comments.issue: The Climate Data section lacks detail.
comments.request: Add more details about the climate data.
comments.quote: Please add more details about Climate Data

comments.issue: The statistical methods, including how predicted log-odds values were obtained, are not detailed.
comments.request: Describe how predicted predation values were calculated.
comments.quote: Please add more detailed statistical analyses, such as how to get predicted values of predation (Log-Odds)

comments.issue: The outlook sentence at lines 273-276 belongs at the end of the Discussion, not the first paragraph.
comments.request: Move the sentence to the end of the Discussion.
comments.quote: This sentence is not appropriate in the first paragraph of the Discussion. It is more like a research outlook as summarized at the end of the discussion.

comments.issue: The Discussion relies on 'functional traits', a concept not introduced earlier in the text.
comments.request: Introduce functional traits earlier or revise the discussion to stay on topic.
comments.quote: I noticed that “functional traits” was not mentioned at all in the text before the Discussion

reviews.assessment: Excellent topic, but the hypothesis logic is unconvincing and bird avoidance confounds the predation measure.

comments.issue: The hypotheses are not supported by solid evidence in the Introduction.
comments.request: Provide evidence supporting the statements when developing the hypotheses.
comments.quote: the logic of developing the hypotheses is not convincing. I would suggest the authors provide solid evidence to support their statements in the Introduction when developing the hypotheses.

comments.issue: Bird avoidance of model caterpillars confounds the predation measure.
comments.request: Separate or control the bird avoidance effect.
comments.quote: the authors should separate or control the confounding effect of bird avoidance on model caterpillars

comments.issue: The claim that arthropods cannot track resources like birds is not supported by the cited references.
comments.request: Provide evidence for the comparison or revise the claim.
comments.quote: I also checked the cited references of Arribas et al. 2021 and Perry et al. 2021, and didn't find clear evidence of this comparison between predatory arthropods and insectivorous birds.

comments.issue: The statements that arthropods respond more to temperature and birds more to tree diversity contradict each other if the drivers are correlated.
comments.request: Resolve the contradiction in the hypotheses.
comments.quote: If tree diversity and temperature are correlated, these statements are contradictory.

comments.issue: The causal link between climate and tree diversity in the hypotheses is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the causation between climate and tree diversity.
comments.quote: However, the causation between them could be clearer.

comments.issue: The claim that birds track resources better than arthropods lacks experimental evidence.
comments.request: Show experimental evidence or revise the statement.
comments.quote: please show the experimental evidence that supports insectivorous birds have better abilities to track resources than arthropods

comments.issue: The hypothesis that birds are more affected than arthropods lacks evidence, given birds' sensitivity to temperature and precipitation.
comments.request: Provide evidence for this hypothesis.
comments.quote: again, do you have evidence to support this hypothesis? Birds (an endotherm) are very sensitive to changes in temperature and precipitation as well.

comments.issue: Caterpillar colour composition may shift toward non-green caterpillars in July.
comments.request: Check whether colour composition changes from May to July.
comments.quote: are the most caterpillars occurring from May to July in green, especially when closing to July? There may be more non-green caterpillars coming out in July.

comments.issue: The number of caterpillars per plot is not constant and the reason is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain why caterpillar numbers vary.
comments.quote: why is the number of caterpillars not constant?

comments.issue: Long sampling intervals let birds learn to avoid model caterpillars, biasing predation rates at those sites.
comments.request: Check sites with intervals over 7 days and use first attempts only.
comments.quote: the authors need to check the data for sites with sampling intervals > 7 days since birds can avoid model caterpillars after the first attempts

comments.issue: Longer caterpillar-day totals do not necessarily mean longer sampling periods because of bird learning.
comments.request: Account for bird learning when interpreting caterpillar days.
comments.quote: please also be aware that longer caterpillar days don't mean a more extended sampling period

comments.issue: Some predation marks may come from slugs rather than birds or arthropods.
comments.request: Check whether slugs contribute to predation marks.
comments.quote: maybe some of these makes come from slugs?

comments.issue: The marginal association may change significance after correcting for bird avoidance.
comments.request: Re-test the association after correcting for bird avoidance.
comments.quote: the association is marginal (close to 0.05), given the sampling size. If the authors correct the effect of bird avoidance on the model caterpillars, is the effect of this association more significant or not?

comments.issue: Splitting arthropods into finer groups (hornets, ants, others) might reveal associations.
comments.request: Analyse finer arthropod groups separately.
comments.quote: if the authors separate the arthropods into finer groups, e.g., hornets, ants, and others, can we find any significant associations between them?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether 'relationship' or 'association' is meant at L280.
comments.request: Use the appropriate term at L280.
comments.quote: L280: do you mean 'relationship' or 'association'?

comments.issue: Dietary specialization, mobility and resource tracking ability were never actually examined.
comments.request: Acknowledge that these traits were not tested.
comments.quote: but actually, the authors haven't examined the effects of 'dietary specialization, mobility, and resource tracking ability' on the predation rates

comments.issue: The acknowledged limitations are central to the hypotheses, so the conclusions remain weak.
comments.request: Weigh the limitations when drawing conclusions.
comments.quote: I appreciate that the authors acknowledged the weakness of this study while these limitations are key to addressing the hypotheses the authors developed

title: Tree diversity enhances predation by birds but not by arthropods across climate gradients

study.system: herbivorous mites on wheat plants; population experiment

editor_summary: Editor notes divergent reviews, sees potential but says considerable work is needed to convince the referees, particularly reviewer #1.

reviews.assessment: Excited by the novel application of coexistence theory to temporal interactions but asks for simulation validation and clearer framing of the method.
strengths: novel application of coexistence theory to temporal interactions
clear and succinct explanation of the method
timely contribution on dynamic species interactions

comments.issue: The method's ability to recover known interactions is not validated across interaction contexts.
comments.request: Use simulated interaction data to demonstrate reliable recovery of interactions.
comments.quote: I hoped to see a validation showing that the method does in fact reliably recover the correct interactions between species under a wide variety of interaction contexts

comments.issue: Framing the method as coexistence analysis obscures how this application differs and confuses the borrowed niche and fitness terms.
comments.request: Reframe around temporal interaction dynamics and announce the differences explicitly.
comments.quote: I recommend that the Authors more strongly frame their study around what it actually delivers very nicely: a tool for inferring the temporal dynamics of complex species interactions

comments.issue: Plant thinning from destructive harvesting may have driven the regime shifts rather than mite interactions.
comments.request: Comment on how much the design forced temporal variation and what to expect in nature.
comments.quote: it seems possible that this was responsible for the ‘regime shifts’ in N and F (Fig. 4) rather than something intrinsic to the mite interaction

comments.issue: 'Best adapted' is tautological and obscures the underlying mechanism.
comments.request: Rephrase as species that most efficiently convert resources to offspring.
comments.quote: “best adapted” is tautological and obscures the underlying mechanism

comments.issue: 'Coexistence status' implies a coexistence outcome.
comments.request: Replace with 'experimental condition' or 'competitive scenario'.
comments.quote: I suggest replacing “coexistence status” with “experimental condition”, “competitive scenario”, or a similar phrase

comments.issue: Paragraph is hard to follow; unclear how the interpretation follows from the results.
comments.request: Explain the logic and consider stating the interpretation first.
comments.quote: This paragraph was difficult for me to understand. I would benefit from more explanation of how the interpretation (sentence 3) follows from the two results (sentences 1-2).

comments.issue: Parenthetical text about Ni>1 is unintelligible.
comments.request: Rephrase the parenthetical text.
comments.quote: I don’t understand the text in the parentheses

comments.issue: Implied link from inferred interactions to underlying mechanisms is overly general.
comments.request: State which specific mechanisms are plausible or can be ruled out.
comments.quote: the connection between the inferred species interaction and underlying mechanism seems overly general

comments.issue: Meaning of 'exhaust a map' and its link to multiple mechanisms is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the term and its implication.
comments.quote: What does it mean to “exhaust” a map, and how does this suggest that there are many mechanism underlying the species’ interaction?

comments.issue: 'Ongoing colonization' is undefined and its relation to the design unclear.
comments.request: Define the term and relate it to the experimental design.
comments.quote: I don’t understand what “ongoing colonization” means, nor how it relates to the experimental design.

comments.issue: Figure 5 lacks time labels for cross-referencing the two N-F maps.
comments.request: Add small time labels every five time points.
comments.quote: I suggest adding small time labels, perhaps every 5 time points, to help the reader cross-reference between the two N-F maps.

comments.issue: Line-level copy edits (preposition fix; delete an unnecessary word).
comments.quote: P14 L52: Change “to interpolate to” to “interpolation of”.

reviews.assessment: Cannot understand the motivation or results and sees no direct support for the biotic-resource claim, though the topic is timely.

comments.issue: Motivation for applying coexistence-theory niche and fitness differences to temporal interactions is confusing.
comments.request: Explain the motivation carefully or use Lotka-Volterra coefficients or empirical dynamic modelling instead.
comments.quote: Coexistence theory is to understand how multiple species coexist despite the competitive exclusion principle. However, the authors seem not interested in the question.

comments.issue: Claim that biotic resources drive complex niche and fitness dynamics lacks direct support.
comments.request: Model abiotic versus biotic resources, or apply the method to existing datasets.
comments.quote: the authors proposed that biotic resources (here wheat) produced the complex dynamics of niche and fitness differences, but there seems no direct support for this argument

comments.issue: Results are not compared with Pastore et al.'s theoretical findings on time-varying niche and fitness differences.
comments.request: Compare with this theoretical study and discuss the implications.
comments.quote: The authors need to carefully compare their results to this theoretical study and discuss the implications.

comments.issue: No line numbers, making specific comments difficult.
comments.request: Add line numbers.
comments.quote: Please add line numbers. It is hard to make specific comments without them.

comments.issue: Title does not clearly convey how niche and fitness differences explain higher-order interactions.
comments.request: Clarify the title.
comments.quote: Title: How do niche and fitness differences explain higher-order interactions? It would be great to clarify it more.

comments.issue: Claim that biodiversity is driven by coexistence ability is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the statement.
comments.quote: L2: How is biodiversity driven by the ability of species to coexist? Please clarify it.

comments.issue: 'MCT explains this' is vague.
comments.request: Clarify what is meant.
comments.quote: L2-3: "MCT explains this" is very vague and it is hard to understand what the authors mean. Please clarify it more.

comments.issue: How consumption rates change over time is not explained.
comments.request: Explain what drives the temporal change in consumption.
comments.quote: It would be great to clarify how consumption rates change over time.

comments.issue: Non-standard niche and fitness differences borrowed from one author are not flagged.
comments.request: State that these definitions are non-standard.
comments.quote: It may be better to mention that the authors considered (non-standard) niche and fitness differences recently proposed by one of the authors.

comments.issue: Whether facilitation can be considered in coexistence theory is not explained.
comments.request: Add explanations about facilitation in coexistence theory.
comments.quote: I guess most readers wonder whether it is possible to consider facilitation in the context of coexistence theory. It would be great to add more explanations.

comments.issue: Paper does not clarify that MCT is used for dynamic interactions, not coexistence mechanisms.
comments.request: Clarify the purpose of using MCT here.
comments.quote: Again, it would be great to clarify that MCT is used not for understanding coexistence mechanisms, but for understanding dynamic interspecific interactions here.

comments.issue: Sutherland et al. (2013) is an applied conservation paper, inappropriate here.
comments.request: Reconsider the citation.
comments.quote: Why did the authors cite Sutherland et al. (2013)? It is a paper for applied ecology (conservation), not for basic ecology (coexistence theory).

comments.issue: Claim that the topic is 200 years old seems wrong.
comments.request: Justify or revise the 200-year statement.
comments.quote: Why 200 years? The topic is not so old.

comments.issue: 'Differences in adaptation' is vague.

comments.quote: L17: "Differences in adaptation" sounds very vague. Please clarify it more.

comments.issue: Terry et al. (2021) studied apparent competition, which should be stated.
comments.request: Clarify that the cited study considered apparent competition.
comments.quote: Please clarify that Terry et al. (2021) considered apparent competition.

comments.issue: Definition of basal species and why bacteria and yeasts are excluded is missing.
comments.request: Define basal species and justify the exclusions.
comments.quote: It may be better to clarify the definition of basal species and why bacteria and yeasts are not basal species.

comments.issue: Focus is limited to MCT; classic competition studies are not engaged.
comments.request: Apply MCT to classic datasets or justify the narrow focus.
comments.quote: For example, the classical paper on competition and coexistence (Rothhaupt 1988 Nature) considered competition of rotifers on algae.

comments.issue: HSS hypothesis and recent defence-coexistence theory are not cited.

comments.quote: What about citing the paper on HSS hypothesis? In the context of HSS hypothesis, the world is green and there is no resource competition between herbivores?

comments.issue: Mechanism behind the result is not explained carefully.
comments.request: Explain the mechanism more carefully.
comments.quote: Please explain the mechanism behind it more carefully.

comments.issue: Higher-order interaction paragraph distracts from the focus.
comments.request: Move this paragraph to the Discussion.
comments.quote: I guess this paragraph on higher-order interactions can be moved to Discussion to clarify the focus of this manuscript.

comments.issue: Relationship between invasibility and stable coexistence is not explained.
comments.request: Add explanations of this relationship.
comments.quote: It would be great to add more explanations on the relationship between invasibility and stable coexistence.

comments.issue: Point about MCT and coexistence is absent from the Abstract.
comments.request: Explain this point in the Abstract as well.
comments.quote: This point should be explained in Abstract as well.

comments.issue: First research question is unclear, including what failure to apply MCT means.
comments.request: Clarify the question and its criteria.
comments.quote: The first question is not clear. What is the difficulty? When can we say we failed to apply the methods of MCT?

comments.issue: Spaak & De Laender (2020) niche and fitness differences differ from standard definitions, which is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the non-standard definitions and how widely they are used.
comments.quote: The authors need to explain that niche and fitness differences defined by Spaak & De Laender (2020) are different from the original and standard definition.

comments.issue: Obligatory mutualism and relation to Johnson (2019) are not explained.
comments.request: Add explanations and clarify the relationship to Johnson (2019).

comments.issue: Box 1 is not mentioned where relevant.
comments.request: Mention Box 1 around this point.
comments.quote: It may be better to mention Box 1 around here.

comments.issue: Fitness differences defined via interspecific interactions seem to conflict with single-species negative growth rate.

comments.issue: Notation r and mu conflicts with earlier use.
comments.request: Use different notation.
comments.quote: r and mu are used in the previous section. What about using different notations?

comments.issue: Possible typo; Fig. 2 is not a semi-log plot.
comments.request: Check the typo and correct the figure description.
comments.quote: Typo? And Fig. 2 is not a semi-log plot, right?

comments.issue: Part of the text distracts from the focus.
comments.request: Move this part to the Discussion.
comments.quote: This part may be moved to Discussion.

comments.issue: 'Mal-adapted' is undefined.
comments.request: Explain the term.
comments.quote: What does "mal-adapted" mean?

comments.issue: Objective definition of the three phases is missing; 'Therefore' is unclear.

comments.issue: Section is hard to follow; non-standard niche and fitness differences should be replaced by competition coefficients.

comments.issue: Definitions of N and F are missing here.

comments.issue: 'Previously qualitatively observed mechanism' and the meaning of mechanism are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the reference and the definition of mechanism.

comments.issue: Letten & Stouffer (2019) and Spaak et al. (2023) are not explained.
comments.request: Add explanations of these studies.

comments.issue: Recent theoretical studies showing this are not cited.

comments.issue: This part is inconsistent and hard to understand.

comments.issue: Box 1 is never mentioned in the main text.

comments.issue: Coexistence region is missing from Figure 5, which is mentioned only once.

strengths: novel hypothesis on an evolutionary driver of bleaching
addressed points from the previous review

comments.issue: Sections 2 and 6 should be combined into one methods section.

comments.issue: Claims about symbiont shifts to heat-tolerant types contradict each other across sections.

editor_summary: Both reviewers share enthusiasm for the premise but raise substantial intellectual and methodological concerns; neither is convinced the results address the title question, and statistical improvements are needed.

comments.issue: Local/novel, coevolved/distant and geographic distance are conflated into a single axis.

comments.issue: The time dimension linking local, coevolved, novel and distant is missing.

comments.quote: Further, a key dimension that may help to explain their linkages – time – is largely missing from the manuscript.

comments.issue: Species, populations and sites are used interchangeably.

comments.issue: Fig. 1A is not worthwhile unless contrasted with 1B.

title: Are novel or locally adapted pathogens more devastating and why? Resolving opposing hypotheses

study.system: plant-soil feedback; theoretical community model of HOIs and germination timing

editor_summary: Editor notes reviewers appreciated integrating higher-order interactions and priority effects but raised serious conceptual and methodological concerns: empirical grounding, assumption generality and robustness, model consistency, hard vs soft HOIs, and coexistence effects.

reviews.assessment: Finds the topic interesting but sees little practical benefit in the modelling approach and found the aims and model structure hard to follow.
strengths: interesting subject with relevance to a broad audience

comments.issue: No practical benefit: the HOI framework has resisted empirical fitting for decades and may be doomed.
comments.request: Discuss how these interactions could actually be measured.
comments.quote: One of the main concerns I have with the paper is not any of it's technical aspects, but rather that I do not see practical benefit.

comments.issue: The aims and the links between the three models are unclear until the results.
comments.request: Explain the research idea and model links early.
comments.quote: It was not until having read the results that I understood what you actually did, which I think should be clear from the method section already.

comments.issue: Priority effects and multispecies community are interpreted differently: species all arrive together but germinate at different times.
comments.request: State your interpretation of these terms in the introduction.
comments.quote: I think of priority effects when the arrival time of species affects the community composition. Conversely, in your paper all species "arrived" at the same time in the community.

comments.issue: The introduction jumps between priority effects and higher-order interactions.
comments.request: Introduce one concept, then the other, then combine them.
comments.quote: The introduction jumps often between the concept of priority effects and the concept of higher order interactions.

comments.issue: Many model assumptions are complex and insufficiently justified; their necessity is unclear.
comments.request: Justify assumptions and show effects of changing them.
comments.quote: many of these were too complex assumptions for me to see their effects and they were often not justified enough for me to directly agree

comments.issue: 'Overlooked' at L19 sounds too harsh.
comments.request: Soften the wording.
comments.quote: To me overlooked sounds a bit harsh, as if this was an obvious mistake.

comments.issue: Equation at L83 should be folded into equation 1.
comments.request: Put it directly into equation 1.
comments.quote: I' put this directly into equation 1, not as a separate eqauation

comments.issue: No reason given for including only one HOI effect at L89 while others appear later.
comments.request: Justify this modelling choice.
comments.quote: I saw no real reason why you only included this HOI effect, especially because later you included the others as well

comments.issue: L126 introduces another unjustified assumption.
comments.request: Justify this assumption.
comments.quote: L126: This is another of these assumptions (see point 5 from above)

comments.issue: d_x is used before definition and S_x is defined only much later.
comments.request: Define symbols before use.
comments.quote: d_x does not occur before, so not clear what you are referring to. Conversely, S_x is only defined quite a few lines below

comments.issue: Equation 5 may need a minus sign before the sum, as it represents microbial mortality.
comments.request: Check the sign in equation 5.
comments.quote: Shouldn't it be a minus infront of the sum symbol? After all it's mortality by the soil microbiotes?

comments.issue: Subscripts change between equations 5-6 and earlier equations without explanation.
comments.request: Use consistent subscripts.
comments.quote: Why did you change to different subscripts compared to the previous equations?

comments.issue: Unclear whether equation 7 is within-year and equation 8 between-years, and why the within-year model is discrete.
comments.request: Clarify the temporal structure of equations 7-8.
comments.quote: Am I correct in understanding that equation 7 is for within a year and quation 8 is for between years? If so, why is the within year a discrete model and not continuous?

comments.issue: Line 154 introduces another unjustified assumption.
comments.request: Justify this assumption.
comments.quote: Line 154: This is another of these assumptions (see point 5 from above)

comments.issue: Microbiomes differ but plants are barely affected; the reason is unclear.
comments.request: Explain this model behaviour.
comments.quote: The microbiome behaves different, but I'd argue that the plants are barely affected by the different microbiomes. Why is that so?

comments.issue: Overlap between microbiomes seems to have almost no effect; arrival time drives interaction strength.

comments.quote: I'd again argure that the overlap has almost no effect but it's only the arrival time which affects the interaction strength

reviews.assessment: Likes the novel idea of time-dependent HOIs and finds results sound, but wants soft HOIs considered and the modelling validated or made more robust.
strengths: very novel and interesting idea that HOIs produce temporal changes in species interactions
nice integration of priority effects with HOIs
results sound, well presented and discussed

comments.issue: Only hard HOIs are modelled; soft HOIs are ignored without theoretical or statistical justification.
comments.request: Justify the restriction or include soft HOIs.
comments.quote: they only model one type of HOIs, those considered as hard HOIs in the literature, while the authors completely ignore the importance of soft HOIs

comments.issue: No validation against real data; the chosen parameter range is not justified.
comments.request: Add empirical evidence or test a broader parameter range.
comments.quote: there no validation of the modelling approach with "real" data from an experiment or a survey or a mesocoms study

comments.issue: Figures and Table 1 do not show whether HOI strength is comparable to pairwise interactions.

comments.issue: Modelling restricts HOIs to competitive interactions although facilitation is possible.

comments.issue: The reference on line 96 is wrong.
