comments.issue: Observations are not weighted by sampling variance or sample size, contrary to established practice.
comments.request: Justify the lack of weighting or weight the observations.
comments.quote: I am curious why there is no consideration about weighing observations based on sampling variances or sample sizes.

comments.issue: Within-study sampling variance is used as a random factor, but it may belong as observation weighting.
comments.request: Reconsider whether sampling variance should weight observations.
comments.quote: I do not understand why within-study sampling variance was used as a random factor. Shall it be used as weighting for observations?

comments.issue: How the optimal random-effects structure was selected using AIC is not described.
comments.request: Describe the random-effects model selection procedure.
comments.quote: I would like to see more description about how the optimal random effects structure was based on AIC.

comments.issue: What 'individual effect size' means and whether it is numerical is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the individual effect size variable.
comments.quote: L195, individual effect size? Is it numerical?

comments.issue: Uni-moderator models risk collinearity and confounding, e.g. lifespan with Poaceae versus non-Poaceae.
comments.request: Address collinearity among moderators.
comments.quote: there are high probabilities of collinearity in meta-data or confounding among other predictors. For example, the lifespan effect can be confounded with Poaceae vs. non-Poaceae.

comments.issue: The full model used for model selection is not reported.
comments.request: Report the full model.
comments.quote: while model selection is applaudable for meta-analysis, I missed what the full model was.

comments.issue: Too many appendix items make the analysis hard to navigate.
comments.request: Reduce the number of appendix items to no more than 10.
comments.quote: there are so many for me or future readers to navigate, making it so difficult. I would recommend no more than 10 to be allowed.

comments.issue: Only mean estimates are reported for some key results; confidence intervals are missing.
comments.request: Include 95% confidence intervals for key estimates.
comments.quote: L231ff, Mean estimates are reported. Shall 95%CI be included for some key estimates?

comments.issue: The time effect may apply only to supplement experiments; experiments and natural variation are not separated.
comments.request: Separate experiments from natural variation for the time effect.
comments.quote: The time effect is mentioned here. Is it for supplement experiments only? I do not see the separation between experiments and natural variation.

comments.issue: A cause-effect hypothesis (higher Si means stronger effect) is expected instead of correlation analysis.
comments.request: Include silicon levels as a predictor in the model.
comments.quote: I would expect a specific hypothesis that higher Si would have a greater effect on herbivore performance, that is, a cause-effect relationship.

comments.issue: The statistical model is not described explicitly in terms of predictors and interactions.
comments.request: Describe the statistical model(s) explicitly.
comments.quote: I missed a detailed description of the statistical model(s), which shall be explicit in terms of predictors and possible interactions.

comments.issue: Numerous appendix items and exclusive referral to the Appendix in Results reduce readability.
comments.request: Reduce reliance on the Appendix in the Results.
comments.quote: it is very difficult with so many appendix items. Moreover, referring Appendix almost exclusively in Results reduces readability.

comments.issue: The full and reduced AIC models with all predictors and weighted observations are not shown.
comments.request: Show full and reduced models with weighted effect sizes.
comments.quote: I would like to see the full model and reduced model based on AIC to show hypothesized effects -- including all predictors effect sizes with observations weighted.

comments.issue: Figures lack variation; interaction plots are missing.
comments.request: Add interaction plots.
comments.quote: Figures are nice, but I would expect some variations. Particularly, I would like to see interaction plots.

reviews.assessment: Recommends acceptance; finds the meta-analysis offers a general pattern of silicon-mediated defence with only a few revision points.
strengths: offers a general pattern of silicon-mediated plant defense
addresses remaining controversy about silicon's role in plants

comments.issue: The statements that fluid-feeders were mostly unaffected and that silicon impacts herbivores regardless of diet breadth seem contradictory.
comments.request: Clarify the apparent contradiction.
comments.quote: silicon negatively impacted herbivores regardless of diet breath’ seems somewhat contradictory.

comments.issue: Figure 1 is not easy to understand; panel labels and label ordering could be improved.
comments.request: Add panel labels and reorder the labelling in Figure 1.
comments.quote: Figure 1 is not easy to understand. It may read easily if ‘Silicon defence on herbivore performance’ is added in panel A

title: Plant Silicon Defences Suppress Herbivore Performance, but Mode of Feeding Is Key

study.system: global coastlines; larval dispersal ocean model

editor_summary: Three expert reviews see a strong contribution with modification; follow their suggestions, especially reviewer 2's points on multiple spawning and spawning frequency.

reviews.assessment: Good and useful paper; main concern is that the PLD conclusion reflects assumptions that ignore longevity and spawning frequency.
strengths: goal of testing sensitivity rather than exact prediction

comments.issue: PLD's dominance may be an artefact of assuming discrete semelparous generations and ignoring adult longevity.
comments.request: Analyse how spawning frequency and longevity interact with currents.
comments.quote: One of the main conclusions is that PLD is the most influential life-history trait, but this seems to be because the physical adversity metric is, as far as I can tell, for a discrete generation semelparous organism

comments.issue: 'Resistance to invasion' misnames a metric that only measures persistence after arrival.
comments.request: Reframe the study around population persistence rather than invasion.
comments.quote: I found the phrasing ‘resistance to invasion’ a bit odd. To me, invasion implies a process of getting to a new site, then persisting once there, but the metric analyzed here is just the persistence part.

comments.issue: Correlation evidence is buried in large tables and significance is trivial with huge samples.
comments.request: Plot the coefficients across variables of interest.
comments.quote: The section in the results on “Relative influence on ln(RC)” is interesting, but the evidence is buried in a huge list of tables containing correlation coefficients.

comments.issue: Depth and season sensitivity comparison is not visualized.
comments.request: Add a scatter plot of depth versus season sensitivity.
comments.quote: A scatter plot of depth vs season sensitivity might help here too

comments.issue: Model likely misrepresents dynamics very near the coast; applicable species are not clearly delimited.
comments.request: State the model's near-shore limitations and target species.
comments.quote: The model is described as applying to species living within 10 km - 18km of the coastline (depending on latitude), but it probably doesn’t represent dynamics well very near the coast

comments.issue: The Ldiff statement holds only when Ladv exceeds zero.
comments.request: Correct or qualify the statement.
comments.quote: This is only true when Ladv > 0, and assuming symmetrical gaussian distribution, right? With Ladv=0, increased Ldiff moves more larvae away from the point of introduction?

comments.issue: The '1m' label should not appear in the Figure 3 legend.
comments.request: Remove '1m' from the Figure 3 legend.
comments.quote: I think the “1m” needs to be removed from the legend in Figure 3.

comments.issue: Author comments remain in the supplement file.
comments.request: Clean the supplement before resubmission.
comments.quote: Note that the supplement file still has author comments in it.

reviews.assessment: Well-justified model study, but lacks validation and omits coastal geometry and seasonal realism, limiting its conclusions.

comments.issue: Model outputs are not validated against field data.
comments.request: Provide field data from at least two map locations for validation.
comments.quote: The study is not validated by field data and hence we cannot say much if whether the model outputs reflect some aspect of the real process of invasion.

comments.issue: Results are not cross-validated against other dispersal or metapopulation models.
comments.request: Compare model outputs with other models of larval dispersal.
comments.quote: it will be useful if the output of their specific model was compared and validated (at the model level) with the output of other models about larval dispersal and/or metapopulation dynamics.

comments.issue: Coastal geometry and current-speed variation such as tides are ignored and could invalidate the results.
comments.request: Include these effects in a single longer paper.
comments.quote: A critical point is the lack of consideration of coastal geometry and areas varying in current speed for example due to tides.

comments.issue: An April simulation is not meaningful for the southern hemisphere's spring.
comments.request: Simulate by season to reflect natural seasonality and larval phenology.
comments.quote: the simulation of April is not very useful for the southern hemisphere if what is meant is a simulation of spring; this suggest a prevalence of thinking about human made calendar based on the North hemisphere.

comments.issue: The assumed 30-day life cycle restricts the results to short-lived taxa.
comments.request: Justify or relax the 30-day life-cycle assumption.
comments.quote: This case may apply to animals like ascidians or bryozoans characterised by short life cycles. If this is correct, the domain of application of results is rather restricted

comments.issue: Methods section is not detailed enough and is placed after the references.
comments.request: Expand the methods and place them after the introduction.
comments.quote: the section of methods should be much more detailed, and it should be placed after the introduction. At least at this stage, the materials and methods is the most important section of the paper.

reviews.assessment: Laudable and impressive approach, but the manuscript is hard to follow and several assumptions need clarification.
strengths: interesting approach building on prior work
clearly laid out challenges and assumptions

comments.issue: Manuscript is hard to read, with unclear phrasing, definitions and missing details.
comments.request: Improve clarity throughout.
comments.quote: I did find the manuscript quite hard to get through and found myself re-reading sections numerous times.

comments.issue: The statement that larval dispersal does not vary over a single generation is undefined.
comments.request: Explain what this statement means.
comments.quote: They state that they have focused on open coastlines where “the dispersal of larvae does not vary significantly over the distance of a single generation of dispersal” (L86-87). What exactly does this mean?

comments.issue: How rapidly varying alongshore currents were assessed and excluded is unexplained.
comments.request: Describe the threshold and treatment of excluded areas.
comments.quote: How has this been assessed and have they applied some threshold of velocity variance (speed over a fixed distance) to justify excluding particular areas of coastline?

comments.issue: The claim that alongshore dispersal statistics are the same everywhere is unclear.
comments.request: Explain what this assumption means.
comments.quote: They later go on to say “We examine the simple case where the statistics of alongshore dispersal rates are the same everywhere” (L102-103) but it is unclear what this means.

comments.issue: 'Suitable habitat' and how F_R is determined are not clear.
comments.request: Define suitable habitat and explain the F_R calculation.
comments.quote: What is least clear to me is what is being considered as “suitable habitat” (e.g. L112), and how this has been implemented within the model.

comments.issue: Using mean distance for Ladv is questionable given the kurtosis of dispersal kernels.
comments.request: Justify or revise the mean-distance approach.
comments.quote: although dispersal kernels are well known to exhibit significant kurtosis – therefore is the use of mean distance for Ladv a sensible/defensible decision?

comments.issue: Ladv units, Euclidean versus seaway distance, and self-recruitment treatment are unspecified.
comments.request: Report units and clarify these definitions.
comments.quote: Also, is Ladv calculated as a Euclidean (as the ‘crow flies’) distance or a seaway distance, which can be markedly different. What are the units of Ladv?

comments.issue: FR is described as a fraction rather than a proportion.
comments.request: Consider using 'proportion' and noting its 0-1 bounds.
comments.quote: Is describing FR as a ‘fraction’ the best phrasing, or would proportion be a better option?

comments.issue: The claim that Ladv and Ldiff are usually equal in magnitude is questionable.
comments.request: Clarify or substantiate this claim.
comments.quote: But could you clarify the statement in L122-123 where you suggest Ladv and Ldiff are usually equal in magnitude. Is this really true?

comments.issue: The variable depth simulation's placement and vertical diffusivity parameterisation are unclear.
comments.request: Explain where the depth analysis is reported and how diffusivity was set.
comments.quote: You introduce the variable depth simulation (L193-194) but it is not clear where this analysis is included? If included, you need to explain the vertical diffusivity parameterisation.

comments.issue: Which parameters implement the 10% larval mortality reduction in the example is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the parameters modified in the example.
comments.quote: In the provided example in L161-164, if ‘larval mortality’ is reduced by 10%, given your derivation of R, which parameter(s) are being modified to result in this mortality

comments.issue: The expectation that a smaller Rc increases population growth faster is a major, unjustified assumption.
comments.request: Justify the relationship between Rc and population growth.
comments.quote: This is quite a major assumption – why would we expect a smaller Rc to increase its population more quickly?

comments.issue: Definition and justification of the seasons are missing.
comments.request: Explain how seasons were defined.
comments.quote: How have you defined the ‘seasons’ – are there particular phenomena that justify this classification or is it arbitrary?

comments.issue: The correlation approach at L227 is not described in the methods.
comments.request: Explain how the correlation ratio is derived.
comments.quote: L227 – The correlation approach is not explained in the methods.

comments.issue: The focus on April-June, 1m release and 30-day PLD is not justified.
comments.request: Justify the choice of focal scenario.
comments.quote: In the results, you have chosen to largely focus on the April-June spawning period, surface (1m) release and a PLD of 30 days. Why focus on this scenario?

comments.issue: The RA value of 400 seems low relative to known invertebrate fecundities.
comments.request: Reconsider or justify the RA value.
comments.quote: Is a value of 400 especially high? Numerous intertidal species including invaders like the Pacific oyster have very high fecundities

comments.issue: The Case Studies section appears without introduction and is verbose.
comments.request: Introduce the section and discuss representativeness.
comments.quote: The Case Studies section comes a little bit out of the blue with no introduction, as well as being quite verbose in comparison to other sections.

comments.issue: Whether Ekman layers are modelled effectively and consistently is doubtful.
comments.request: Clarify the treatment and predictability of Ekman layers.
comments.quote: Ekman layers – are these modelled effectively/predictable and consistent as suggested?

comments.issue: Statements at L366 and L377 are too strong.
comments.request: Soften 'will' to 'might shift' and 'invasion' to 'expansion'.
comments.quote: L366 & 377 – I suggest softening from “will” to “might shift”, and “invasion” to “expansion”.

comments.issue: Expected circulation changes at L368 lack reference support.
comments.request: Provide references for expected circulation changes.
comments.quote: L368 – Do the authors expect significant change in circulation patterns, and if so, can they provide some reference support?

comments.issue: The term 'non-upwelling adapted species' does not fit the study context.
comments.request: Clarify or replace the term.
comments.quote: L375 – What is a “non-upwelling adapted species”? In the context of this study, that doesn’t seem quite right to me.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the mechanism is reduced mortality or increased recruitment.
comments.request: Clarify the process referred to.
comments.quote: L376 – Is it really reduced mortality, or increased recruitment?

comments.issue: The last sentence of L385-387 seems disjunct.
comments.request: Clarify the sentence and the alternative mode.
comments.quote: L385-387. This last sentence seems disjunct to me, and if not planktonic, what mode?

comments.issue: Passive vertical depth variation by larvae is doubtful given weak vertical mixing.
comments.request: Justify or revise the passive depth assumption.
comments.quote: L393 – Do larvae really vary their depth passively? Lots of evidence to suggest otherwise as vertical mixing often quite weak in comparison to horizontal advection.

comments.issue: Claim that current-pattern similarity is the main determinant ignores other abiotic filters.
comments.request: Consider additional environmental filters or soften the claim.
comments.quote: I am not quite sold on the suggestion that similarity of current patterns is the main determinant of success, without consideration of other environmental (abiotic) filters of suitability.

title: Variation in Oceanographic Resistance of the World's Coastlines to Invasion by Species With Planktonic Dispersal

study.system: North American birds; seasonal functional diversity from eBird and AVONET

editor_summary: Editor notes three constructive and quite positive reviews; concerns focus on elements of the analysis and interpretation and on improving clarity for readers.

reviews.assessment: Excited and impressed by the study, with a main concern that land and water birds should be analysed separately and several clarity points.
strengths: great use of eBird and AVONET

comments.issue: Patterns may be driven by the replacement of waterfowl with songbirds; land and water birds were pooled.
comments.request: Re-run the models treating land birds and water birds separately.
comments.quote: What I would love to see is some re-runs of the models treating land birds and water birds separately.

comments.issue: The extent to which functional turnover is driven by phylogenetic turnover is not tested.
comments.request: Assess whether functional turnover is driven by phylogenetic turnover.
comments.quote: A related question would be: to what extent is functional turnover driven by phylogenetic turnover?

comments.issue: Precipitation is not included although precipitation seasonality matters in some regions.
comments.request: Consider including precipitation.
comments.quote: I was very surprised to not see precipitation included. Seasonality in precipitation can be very important in some areas, such as the monsoons of the southwest.

comments.issue: The concept of predictability of seasonality is not fully explained.
comments.request: Explain what unpredictable seasonality would be.
comments.quote: Predictability of seasonality is a key component of this study but I don’t think the concept is really explained fully here or in the methods.

comments.issue: The SI is often not referenced in the main text and is redundant, reading like an unabridged methods version.
comments.request: Reference the SI and streamline it.
comments.quote: There were many instances throughout the Methods where more information is available in the Supplementary Information but the SI is not referred to in the main text.

comments.issue: Line 171: 'unreliable' is not defined.
comments.request: Explain in what sense it is unreliable.
comments.quote: L171: Unreliable in what sense?

comments.issue: Lines 175-178 are unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the passage.
comments.quote: L175-178: I’m not sure what this means exactly?

comments.issue: The density of trait space is introduced but never analysed formally.
comments.request: Analyse this metric formally or explain why not.
comments.quote: The density of trait space doesn’t get much mention after this point; is there a reason this metric isn’t analyzed more formally?

comments.issue: The metric on lines 211-214 is not explained precisely.
comments.request: Explain what the metric measures, e.g. overlap proportion.
comments.quote: Can I get a more explicit sense of what this metric measures? Is it like (1 minus) the proportion of overlap in niche space between seasons?

comments.issue: Lines 255-258 need conceptual explanation and examples.
comments.request: Explain and give examples of predictable environments.
comments.quote: Explain what this means conceptually? What would be examples of more or less predictable environments?

comments.issue: The Central Valley pattern is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain why the Central Valley stands out.
comments.quote: I wonder why the Central Valley pops out? All the wintering shorebirds and waterfowl?

comments.issue: Lines 325-326 combining higher latitudes and southerly regions is confusing.
comments.request: Clarify the statement.
comments.quote: L325-326: Higher latitudes AND southerly regions?

comments.issue: Covariate terms in Figure 4A are not explained in the caption.
comments.request: Explain the covariate terms in the caption.
comments.quote: L344: Can the covariate terms in Fig. 4A be explained in the caption.

comments.issue: The statement that turnover was lowest in the most productive regions seems to contradict line 349.
comments.request: Resolve the contradiction.
comments.quote: The statement here that turnover was lowest in the most productive regions seems to contradict L349?

comments.issue: Lines 374-375 should reference Figure 5.
comments.request: Fix the figure reference.
comments.quote: L374-375: I think these should be referencing Fig. 5.

comments.issue: The axis on lines 393-394 is hard to interpret.
comments.request: Clarify the axis meaning.
comments.quote: L393-394: It’s kind of a strange axis; I’m trying to imagine what these short-tailed long-billed species are vs the long-tailed short-billed.

reviews.assessment: Well-written and clearly answered study that can be recommended once the clarity and originality comments are addressed.

comments.issue: The abstract sentence about niche packing in productive regions does not match the manuscript's emphasis.
comments.request: Use the proposed reformulation.
comments.quote: I propose the following reformulation “seasonal shifts in bird species richness were largely due to niche packing but niche expansion increased in regions with higher seasonality”.

comments.issue: The key term 'seasonality' is not defined in the introduction.
comments.request: Add a definition.
comments.quote: As “seasonality” is the key word of this study, I suggest adding its definition in the introduction.

comments.issue: Figure 1A is cited at the end of the sentence rather than after 'greatly across space'.
comments.request: Move the citation.
comments.quote: I suggest calling the Fig1A after “greatly across space” L96 and not at the end of the sentence.

comments.issue: 'Richness' mixes functional and taxonomic richness; 'species richness' and 'species turnover' should be used.
comments.request: Use the precise terms throughout.
comments.quote: in the introduction, I suggest talking about “species richness” (and “species turnover”) and not only “richness” as you are mixing both functional and taxonomic richness in your manuscript

comments.issue: Figure 1B is cited before functional diversity has been introduced.
comments.request: Remove the early citation.
comments.quote: I suggest not calling the Fig1B there, as this figure is also about functional diversity which has not been introduced yet.

comments.issue: References on seasonal diversity responses are missing.
comments.request: Add references on richness and turnover responses.
comments.quote: Add references about studies on seasonal-diversity responses focused on species richness and turnover.

comments.issue: The phrase 'roles that species occupy within an ecosystem' is incomplete.
comments.request: Complete the phrase.
comments.quote: I suggest completing “roles that species occupy within an ecosystem”.

comments.issue: Functional diversity is called a metric although it is a component of diversity; 'more precise' should be removed.
comments.request: Rephrase as proposed.
comments.quote: I don’t think that functional diversity is a metric (but a component of diversity - while functional richness is a metric)

comments.issue: The claim that the taxonomic-functional diversity link is unclear is not well supported; temporal patterns are the overlooked aspect.
comments.request: Refocus the originality on temporal patterns.
comments.quote: I think that you can highlight even more the originality of your study by focusing here on the fact that TD and FD spatial patterns have been studied a lot, while their temporal patterns are overlooked

comments.issue: Lines 151 and 154 should specify 'seasonal changes'.
comments.request: Precise the wording.
comments.quote: L151, 154: Precise “seasonal changes”

comments.issue: The rationale for the three hypotheses is not elaborated, and niche packing is defined within a hypothesis.
comments.request: Elaborate why each hypothesis is expected.
comments.quote: You could elaborate the explanation of your three hypotheses: why do you expect seasonal beta diversity to be greater in more predictably seasonal ecosystems

comments.issue: Figure 1B is hard to understand: dot and circle colours lack a legend and the 'entirely' packing case is inconsistent.
comments.request: Add a colour legend and reorganise the figure by seasonal beta diversity.
comments.quote: First, I think that the colors of dots and circles should be a legend of the picture.

comments.issue: Why the selected traits were considered is not explained.
comments.request: Add a short explanation.
comments.quote: L187: I suggest adding a short explanation on why these traits were considered.

comments.issue: Line 189 should use the term 'functional trait space'.
comments.request: Use the clearer term.
comments.quote: L189: I suggest using “functional trait space”, so the sentence is easier to understand.

comments.issue: Lines 217-219: expansion should presumably increase functional richness, which is not consistent with the metric's description.
comments.request: Reconcile the metric with the expansion concept.
comments.quote: I agree for packing but for expansion don’t you expect functional richness values to increase if you have an expansion?

comments.issue: The sentence on lines 224-226 is misplaced relative to the preceding explanation.
comments.request: Move the sentence.
comments.quote: I don’t think this sentence is at the right place because it has little to do with the previous explanation

comments.issue: Environmental predictability is not expected to affect packing, yet it is not tested in the model.
comments.request: Test predictability in the model.
comments.quote: If you expected that environmental predictability does not play a role on niche packing, why don’t you test it and add it to the model?

comments.issue: Line 331: 'changes in' is redundant with seasonal beta diversity.
comments.request: Remove the redundant words.
comments.quote: L331: I suggest removing “changes in” as seasonal beta diversity is already reflecting the change between seasons, right?

comments.issue: Lines 355 and 377-381 are discussion material placed in the results.
comments.request: Remove them from the results section.
comments.quote: These parts of sentences or sentences are more discussions than results, they should be removed from the results section.

comments.issue: Figure captions interpret the graphs rather than only describing them.
comments.request: Move interpretation to the main text.
comments.quote: In the figure captions you should only describe what represents the graph and not how to interpret it, this part should go in the main text.

comments.issue: Y-axis labels in Figures 4A and 5 need clarity.
comments.request: Modify the labels.
comments.quote: Figure 4A, 5: Modify the labels on the y-axis to enhance clarity.

comments.issue: Line-level copy edits (L67 comma, L185 wording, L713 completion, L714 comma).
comments.quote: L185: I would change “capture” by “are”

reviews.assessment: Interesting and well-presented study, but the expansion/packing categorisation may always favour a deterministic conclusion and should be revisited.
strengths: adds seasonal resolution to previous work

comments.issue: Pellissier et al. (2018), which has similar findings, is only mentioned cursorily in the discussion instead of framing the problem.
comments.request: Engage with this study when articulating the problem, especially at L110.
comments.quote: It is curious that Pellissier et al.’s study is not missed, but is only mentioned cursorily in the Discussion section, while it should be of greater relevance for articulating the study’s problem

comments.issue: The expansion/packing procedure is binary and deterministic, so it always favours deterministic conclusions; thresholds and an opposing removal strategy are needed.
comments.request: Set statistical thresholds and estimate packing by removing similar species iteratively.
comments.quote: This results in a binary (expansion/packing) categorisation; therefore, all traits are putatively related to a deterministic process (either expansion or packing) and never to stochastic dynamics.

comments.issue: The sentence on lines 90-91 is self-evident.
comments.request: Remove or revise the sentence.
comments.quote: L 90-91. This sentence is self-evident.

comments.issue: Line 99 wording could be confounded with the general effect of seasonality on diversity.
comments.request: Use 'temporal diversity and seasonal turnover'.
comments.quote: To follow Tonkin et al.'s reasoning closely, this should be ‘temporal diversity and seasonal turnover’.

comments.issue: The reference community is called A2 on L229 and A1 on L237.
comments.request: Clarify the inconsistency.
comments.quote: In L 229, the authors mention that A2 stands for the ‘reference community’ while in L 237 the reference community is A1. Please clarify.

title: Seasonality Structures Avian Functional Diversity and Niche Packing Across North America

study.system: predator-prey interactions; sensory information constraints, functional responses

editor_summary: Interesting to editor and referees; needs clarity on how the approach is more novel than Hein & Martin 2020, more precise equation derivations, grammar check, and toned-down claims.

reviews.assessment: Excited by the novel framework and promising results, but wants more discussion of validation needs, model limitations and system scope.
strengths: novel model framework incorporating sensory information constraints

comments.issue: With only six datasets and limited prey-density ranges, declaring the model's performance is preemptive.
comments.request: Discuss what additional validation is needed and what caution applies.
comments.quote: The lack of datasets testing an adequate range of prey densities resulted in IFR definitively being the best supported model for only one datasets.

comments.issue: Datasets cover only insects/invertebrates, and chemical information transfer may not follow the assumed noise-detection relationship.
comments.request: Discuss whether the IFR applies to other taxa and chemical signalling systems.
comments.quote: the datasets here comprise only a limited range of taxonomic groups (i.e., all insects/invertebrates) and may not account for differences in other model systems

comments.issue: Prey behaviour, defenses beyond body size and non-lethal effects are not considered and may limit the model.
comments.request: Discuss whether such factors could invalidate the model's application.
comments.quote: How are the model results effected by prey behavior or other defenses beyond relative body size? How may their application be limited by assuming an absence of non-lethal effects?

comments.issue: Line-level copy edits: 'recently' L94, quantify/quantifies L219, tense/words L262-264, who/they L270, figure reference L317, rephrasing L573-575.
comments.quote: Line 94 – would suggest removing the word recently from the start of the sentence or moving it to the start of the next sentence

comments.issue: It is unclear what is incomparable at line 119.
comments.request: Specify the incomparability at line 119.
comments.quote: Line 119 – the incomparability of what?

comments.issue: Environmental noise conditions for datasets D1-D6 are not described.
comments.request: Provide detail on environmental noise conditions for D1-D6.
comments.quote: could you provide some additional detail about the environmental noise conditions for D1-D6?

comments.issue: Introductory information at line 278 repeats the methods.
comments.request: Reduce the repetition or move details to the methods.
comments.quote: much of this introductory information to the results of applying the IFR to published datasets is repeated from the methods and could be reduced

comments.issue: The phrase 'the experiments were set on purpose' at line 441 is unclear.
comments.request: Rephrase the phrase at line 441.
comments.quote: Line 441 – not clear what you mean here by “the experiments were set on purpose”

comments.issue: Table 1 bolding only ranges of 0, which conflicts with the text calling some models supported.
comments.request: Make the table formatting consistent with the text.
comments.quote: it is a little counter intuitive that all cases where the text of the results section states a model was supported are bolded except for the IFR values for D6

reviews.assessment: Very enthusiastic and finds the IFR model a valuable contribution; asks only for better acknowledgment of prior functional-response literature.
strengths: IFR model is a valuable contribution to the functional response literature

comments.issue: The broader literature on functional response models and drivers of sigmoidal responses is underacknowledged.
comments.request: Acknowledge prior literature and show how the IFR builds on it.
comments.quote: the manuscript would benefit from better acknowledging the broader existing literature on functional response models and the ecological factors that contribute to sigmoidal functional responses in particular

title: Decoding Information Flow and Sensory Pollution: A Systematic Framework for Understanding Species Interactions

study.system: C3 plants; phylogenetic comparative analysis of photosynthetic capacity and diversification

editor_summary: Editor concurs the research is innovative and significant but requires the authors to address the study's limitations and concerns about the reliability of the Vcmax and Jmax curves.

reviews.assessment: Interesting subject, but strong methodological biases (missing ferns, apparent Vcmax/Jmax) mean no clear conclusion can be derived from the data.

comments.issue: Ferns are excluded from the diversification analysis although sufficient data exist.
comments.request: Include ferns in the analysis and justify taxon sampling.
comments.quote: but for sure FERNS should have been included, especially because there are quite data enough in the literature for all the parameters included in this study.

comments.issue: TRY Vcmax/Jmax values come from A-Ci curves and are only 'apparent' values, unreliable for phylogenetic comparison.
comments.request: Account for mesophyll conductance or use A-Cc based values.
comments.quote: The problem of using TRY data as for Vcmax and Jmax data is that most of them if not all are based on A-Ci curves and not A-Cc curves. Then, they should be termed 'apparent' Vcmax and Jmax.

comments.issue: Because of these two biases, no clear conclusion can be derived from the presented data.
comments.request: Revise the conclusions in light of these biases.
comments.quote: Considering these two strong biases I do not think that any clear conclusion can be derived from the data presented.

comments.issue: Different dispersion and the 'shadow' in the blue lines of figures 1a and 1b are unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the dispersion and the meaning of the shaded areas.
comments.quote: An additional minor concern is that I cannot find anywhere explained why the atmospheric CO2 trends in figures 1a and 1b present so much different dispersion

title: Significant Links Between Photosynthetic Capacity, Atmospheric CO 2 and the Diversification of C 3 Plants During the Last 80 Million Years

study.system: Argentina anserina flowers; elevation gradient, time-lapse and plasticity study

editor_summary: Both reviewers found the work very interesting and elegant; the text needs further elaboration and clarity; resubmission with a point-by-point response letter.

reviews.assessment: Elegant, interesting study with only a few suggestions about context, thermal terminology and specific lines.

comments.issue: The paper would gain broad interest by discussing plant and flower behaviour more generally before thermoregulation.
comments.request: Broaden the context to other adaptive floral movements.
comments.quote: I think the general interest in this paper would be increased by broadening the context somewhat, e.g. by discussing plant/flower behavior more generally before delving into behavioral thermoregulation.

comments.issue: 'Ambient temperature' is used confusingly; operative and environmental temperatures are not distinguished.
comments.request: Define thermal terms and adopt operative temperature (see Bakken).
comments.quote: A source of confusion is the use of “ambient temperature” (lines 61, 113, 443, etc.). I suggest define thermal terms in use, including also operative and environmental temperatures.

comments.issue: Claiming evidence for behavioural thermoregulation is lacking overstates the case given work on solar tracking.
comments.request: Soften to limited understanding of its ecology and evolution.
comments.quote: I think that “but evidence for behavioral thermoregulation is lacking” is a bit if an overstatement.

comments.issue: 'More closely tracked ambient temperature' is ambiguous at line 61.
comments.request: Clarify whether operative floral temperature correlates with air temperature.
comments.quote: I find “more closely tracked ambient temperature” confusing. You mean operative floral temperature was tightly correlated with air temperature?

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 94-96 implies the thermal environment alters organism temperature.
comments.request: Replace 'that' with 'which' and rewrite.
comments.quote: Replace “that” with “which” and/or rewrite.

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 99-101 is awkward.
comments.request: Revise the awkward sentence.
comments.quote: Lines 99-101. Awkward sentence: revise.

comments.issue: Bee and moth temperature-dependence literature is not cited.
comments.request: Cite additional bee or moth thermoregulation literature.
comments.quote: additional bee or moth temperature-dependence/thermoregulation literature could be cited, especially with respect to operative temperature

comments.issue: Circadian floral reorientation examples are missing from the introduction.
comments.request: Mention circadian reorientation such as Nicotiana (Haverkamp et al. 2019).
comments.quote: Circadian reorientation of flowers has also been demonstrated where Nicotiana flowers face upward at night promoting moth pollination

comments.issue: Creux et al. 2021 is not cited in the introduction or discussion.
comments.request: Cite Creux et al. 2021 in the introduction and discussion.
comments.quote: N.M. Creux et al., New Phytologist 2021, might be cited in this part of the Introduction

comments.issue: It is unclear what 'optimum' at line 182 refers to.
comments.request: Specify that the optimum is for pollen germination.
comments.quote: Line 182. You mean optimum for pollen germination?

comments.issue: Day of Year as a covariate assumes a linear sun-angle relationship that only holds on one side of the solstice.
comments.request: Use absolute deviation from the solstice and report field dates.
comments.quote: Using “Day Of Year” as a covariate assumes a roughly linear relationship with sun angle.

comments.issue: It is not stated at the start of the section that lines 389 ff. are growth-chamber/common-garden results.
comments.request: Indicate the growth-chamber or common-garden setting up front.
comments.quote: I assume these are growth-chamber / common garden results, but this should be indicated at the beginning of this section.

reviews.assessment: Neat, novel study that should be published, but the introduction and results sections need reworking.

comments.issue: Introduction does not cover previous work on floral trait plasticity under temperature.
comments.request: Discuss previous floral plasticity studies (e.g. Plantago, Arabidopsis).
comments.quote: I think there needs to be some discussion on the floral traits that have previously been reported to show plasticity under different temperatures as was briefly touched on in the discussion with the Plantago example.

comments.issue: Figures and tables are not cited in order; Fig 1D and Table S1 are never referenced.
comments.request: Reorder figures, refer to Fig 1D and Table S1, and re-evaluate what is needed.
comments.quote: In particular figure 1D and Table S1 do not appear to be referred to at all in the text.

comments.issue: The section on putative thermoregulatory traits is a shallow dive and does not fully describe the results.
comments.request: Lay out and fully describe the results in this section.
comments.quote: spending some time on the section “Putative floral thermoregulatory traits differ between low and high elevation populations”, laying out and fully describing the results

comments.issue: The discussion does not mention thermal patterning of flowers and its effect on pollinators.
comments.request: Add discussion of thermal patterning and pollinator visits.
comments.quote: I also wondered if in the discussion there should be some mention of thermal patterning of flowers and how that might influence pollinator visits.

comments.issue: The Atamian et al. citation misrepresents sunflower heliotropism, which stops once flowering.
comments.request: Remove this citation and correct the sunflower example.
comments.quote: This is not an appropriate citation. Sunflowers do not heliotrope when in bloom and only heliotrope as juveniles.

comments.issue: The statement at lines 145-147 about why population-level differences matter is not well reasoned.
comments.request: Rephrase to focus on within-population variation.
comments.quote: I would say that since many plant species have independently evolved different floral thermoregulatory responses to temperature in different plant species is a good indicator that this trait has the capacity to evolve.

comments.issue: The native range of silverweed cinquefoil is not given for non-US readers.
comments.request: State the native range in the introduction.
comments.quote: I think it would be valuable for readers not from the US or familiar with this plant to state what the native range is in the introduction.

comments.issue: 'Interiors warmed' at line 153 does not make clear the previous work was on the same species.
comments.request: Insert 'of this species' between 'interiors' and 'warmed'.
comments.quote: I think it would add clarity to insert the words “of this species” between “interiors” and “warmed”

comments.issue: Average summer high and low temperatures for the two study regions are not reported.
comments.request: Give the average summer temperatures, here or in Table S1.
comments.quote: If possible, I think it would be helpful to give the average summer high and low temperatures for the two study regions, perhaps here or in table S1?

comments.issue: It is unclear what time counts as 'late afternoon' given measurements ran 11:00-14:00.
comments.request: Indicate what time is classified as late afternoon.
comments.quote: given the measurements were taken from 11:00 to 14:00 I think it would be helpful here to indicate what time classifies as late afternoon.

comments.issue: How petal angle was measured (field or images) is not described.
comments.request: State how and where petal angle was measured.
comments.quote: what was used to measure the petal angle? Was this done in the field or on images after the fact?

comments.issue: How floral height was measured, and with what equipment, is not described.
comments.request: Describe how floral height was measured.
comments.quote: again, was this done in the field? With what type of equipment? Or was it measured from images later?

comments.issue: Thermal patterning and its influence on pollinator choice (Harrap et al. 2017) are not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention thermal patterning here, in the introduction or discussion.
comments.quote: It might be worth mentioning thermal patterning somewhere? Here or the introduction or the discussion?

comments.issue: The assumption that day 1 flowers offer more resources ignores prior visitation and overnight rewards.
comments.request: Discuss whether day 1 flowers were visited and how rewards accumulate.
comments.quote: Why would this assumption be made? Would it not depend on if the day 1 flowers had been visited or not before and how many resources are left?

comments.issue: Figure order makes results hard to follow; Fig 2D could be integrated into Figure 1.
comments.request: Reorder the figures and incorporate Fig 2D after Fig 1C.
comments.quote: I suggest that it would be easier to follow the results if the figures were reordered. Perhaps Fig. 2D could be incorporated into Figure 1 maybe after Fig. 1C.

comments.issue: The first graph in Figure 2 is missing the bottom x-axis line; other figures also have missing axis lines.
comments.request: Check and fix missing axis lines in all figures.
comments.quote: In figure 2 the first graph is missing the bottom line for the x-axis.

comments.issue: Numerous line-level style and copy edits (L61, L94-95, L100, L107, L121, L149, L151, L264, L302).
comments.quote: Line 264: “Both treatments following” you can probably delete the word “following”

title: Behavioural Thermoregulation of Flowers via Petal Movement

study.system: migratory songbirds; 52-yr territory maps, 10-ha forest plot

editor_summary: Unique, substantial dataset; reviewers disagreed about whether the paper should proceed in Ecology Letters; authors encouraged to address concerns; likely the same three reviewers.

reviews.assessment: Praises the unique 52-year dataset but doubts the across-year patterns can distinguish ideal free from ideal despotic; within-year fitness data are needed.
strengths: unique depth of territoriality data for birds
territory mapping as precise as possible

comments.issue: Across-year territory-size changes with density are consistent with both IFD and IDD, so they cannot test between the two models.
comments.request: Explain how the analyses discriminate IFD from IDD.
comments.quote: My main concern is that I am struggling to see how these data allow us to test between the ideal free versus ideal despotic distributions.

comments.issue: IFD requires equal fitness within years; density-driven territory-size changes across years do not demonstrate this.
comments.request: Show within-year fitness does not vary with territory size or habitat quality, or reframe.
comments.quote: a clear test of the IFD requires showing that individual fitness does not vary with territory size or quality, and this needs to be done within years, not with comparisons across years.

comments.issue: Demographic data (fledglings, nest predation/parasitism) that could test within-year fitness are not used.
comments.request: Use these data to test whether fitness varies with territory size or preferred habitat.
comments.quote: I also wonder if the authors might have additional data that could assess the within year patterns and see if there are fitness patterns.

comments.issue: Across-year predictions are unclear and not a critical test; within-year variation is the key test.
comments.request: Clarify the predictions and base tests on within-year variation.
comments.quote: the predictions about across-year patterns are not all that clear; the fact that mean territory size changes is not a critical test of either theory.

comments.issue: It is not stated whether birds were colour-banded, so individual identification across time is unclear.
comments.request: State banding status and how individuals were linked to locations over time.
comments.quote: Are the birds color-banded? This would seem necessary to be able to get a territory size and should be mentioned.

comments.issue: The rationale for controlling for the abundance-territory size relationship is unclear; it seems a result, not a covariate.
comments.request: Explain why abundance was controlled for in the analysis.
comments.quote: I was a bit confused by needing to control for the relation between abundance and territory size. Isn't this a result rather than something that needs to be controlled.

comments.issue: Where the P variable comes from is not shown, though it is central to the study.
comments.request: Clarify how P was derived and used.
comments.quote: I read the results twice and I am not seeing where you get the P variable from. This is a critical part of the study so this needs to be clearer.

comments.issue: The IDD prediction tested is asymmetric and weak; failing to find it does not reject IDD.
comments.request: Justify the prediction and temper the rejection of IDD.
comments.quote: The expectation that dominants will not change territory size in the best quality habitat is a very specific prediction of ideal despotic, and it seems to me that it is an asymmetric prediction.

comments.issue: Why the absence of a habitat-preference effect supports IFD is unclear given expected preference-territory size links.
comments.request: Explain the logic and define what preference means here.
comments.quote: I am not sure I understand why the observed lack of effect on territory size of habitat preference supports the ideal free distribution.

comments.issue: Habitat saturation and floaters affect the expected density-territory size relationship and are unaddressed; floaters would reject strict IFD.
comments.request: Report habitat saturation and floater status, and consider their effects.
comments.quote: These two factors, degree of habitat saturation and existence of floater males, will affect the expected relationship between population density and territory size.

comments.issue: It is unclear how IDD predicts across-year changes, or whether Fretwell made this prediction.
comments.request: Clarify the theoretical basis for the across-year IDD prediction.
comments.quote: I do not see how why the ideal despotic makes this prediction for the across-year changes. Hopefully the authors can make this clearer in revision.

comments.issue: Territory size may track food while habitat preference reflects nest predation/parasitism risk; fitness consequences are untested.
comments.request: Test whether nest survival and fledgling number vary with habitat and territory size.
comments.quote: Is it possible that territory size is connected to something like food, while habitat preference is based on risk of nest predation

comments.issue: If larger territories confer fitness benefits, IFD is violated, yet the discussion assumes quality/age relates to territory size.
comments.request: Reconcile the discussion with the equal-fitness requirement of IFD.
comments.quote: if there are fitness benefits to having a larger territory, and there is variation in territory size, then birds are not distributed according to the deal fee distribution.

comments.issue: Optimal and evolutionarily stable territory sizes may differ; high-density birds may not attain optimal size.
comments.request: Consider discussing optimal versus ESS territory size.
comments.quote: One thing the authors might consider is the difference between optimal territorial size and stable territory size (ESS, or evolutionarily stable).

reviews.assessment: Commends the unique dataset and important question, but raises concerns about alternative explanations, statistical independence, and what mapped territories represent.

comments.issue: 'Dramatically' is subjective and the surprising level of variation is unexplained; quantitative examples are lacking.
comments.request: Use quantitative examples such as coefficients of variation.
comments.quote: the term “dramatically” is a bit subjective – especially for a general ecological audience. A better approach would be to give quantitative examples with, say, coefficients of variation.

comments.issue: The abstract's last sentence, especially on the efficacy of singing, lacks context and clarity.
comments.request: Add context and clarify the abstract's final sentence.
comments.quote: The last sentence of the abstract needs more context and clarity – especially the remark about the efficacy of singing in songbirds.

comments.issue: The introduction does not address floaters, which may influence territory holders' behavior.
comments.request: Discuss floaters and their influence in the introduction.
comments.quote: Somewhere in the introduction, the issue of floaters and territoriality needs to be addressed as these individuals are likely to influence the behavior of territory holders.

comments.issue: The term territory is undefined; several territory types exist and foraging exclusivity is implied but unstated.
comments.request: Define territory for this system and clarify whether birds forage only within mapped territories.
comments.quote: there are different types of territories with animals (A, B, etc.), so define what you mean by term in the context of your system and focal species.

comments.issue: Agonistic behavior may serve paternity assurance rather than defense of space and food.
comments.quote: Agonistic behavior between male songbirds can have a lot to do with assurance of paternity rather than defense of resources such as space and food.

comments.issue: Floaters are an alternative strategy to settling in poor habitat and are not considered.
comments.request: Address floaters as an alternative to settling for low-quality habitat.
comments.quote: again, the issue of floaters is important as an alternative strategy to simply settling for less-than-optimal habitat.

comments.issue: Individual identification (banding) and whether singing males could be unmated are not reported.
comments.request: State banding status and whether singing males were mated.
comments.quote: Were your birds banded for individual identification? Critically, could any of your singing males be unmated?

comments.issue: The section on long-term studies is dismissive of existing knowledge.
comments.request: Revise the section to acknowledge prior long-term work fairly.
comments.quote: a lot of studies you cite are long-term. This section seems a bit dismissive of what is known.

comments.issue: The data come from only a 10-ha plot, limiting the generality of the conclusions.
comments.request: Address the 10-ha limitation when framing generality.
comments.quote: Yes, your study is extraordinarily long-term, but you are vulnerable to the concern that the data are from only 10 ha.

comments.issue: Territories defined by singing males may not cover breeding birds' foraging areas, as shown for Ovenbirds.
comments.request: Support the assumption that territories are the only places breeding birds go.
comments.quote: Another study on one of your focal species (Ovenbirds) found that foraging areas were not exclusive and much larger than territories as defined by singing males

comments.issue: The assumptions behind the habitat-quality index need clarification.
comments.request: Clarify how the habitat-quality index was derived.
comments.quote: Your assumptions leading to the index of habitat quality need clarification.

comments.issue: No ancillary evidence supports the assumed fitness consequences of choosing one area over another.
comments.request: Provide data on reproductive success, foraging rates or resources supporting this assumption.
comments.quote: Do you have any ancillary information on reproductive success, foraging rates, resource availability, etc. that would support the assumption that there are fitness consequences to choosing one area over another?

comments.issue: The assumption that birds reassess habitat quality annually lacks support.
comments.request: Provide support for annual reassessment of habitat quality.
comments.quote: You are assuming that the birds are reassessing habitat quality every year – can you provide some level of support for this assumption?

comments.issue: Information on the temporal pattern of settling, including whether hot spots were occupied first, is missing.
comments.request: Report the temporal sequence of territory occupation.
comments.quote: again, some information on the temporal pattern of settling would be helpful.

comments.issue: Treating each territory-year as independent ignores site fidelity and temporal autocorrelation by the same males.
comments.request: Account for temporal autocorrelation and reconsider the replication definition.
comments.quote: your definition of an independent statistical replication as a territory in each year is problematic. In many cases, the same males undoubtably demonstrate site fidelity and occupy/defend the same territory over, say, a 2–3-year period.

comments.issue: Large sample sizes inflate p-values' utility; effect sizes would be more informative.
comments.request: Focus more on effect sizes than p-values.
comments.quote: Owing to your definition of a replicate, the sample sizes presented are quite large, and this diminishes the utility of p-values. Consider more focus on effect sizes over p-values.

comments.issue: Too much space goes to comparative and descriptive details peripheral to the main thesis.
comments.request: Condense material not relevant to the main thesis.
comments.quote: a lot of bandwidth is devoted to comparative analyses and descriptive details that are of interest to avian ecologists (e.g., the paragraph beginning on line 339) but perhaps less appreciated by a general ecological readership.

comments.issue: Resource-availability estimates are not integrated, leaving food as an untested driver of territory size variation.
comments.request: Integrate resource-availability estimates into analyses of temporal territory size variation.
comments.quote: you mention estimates of resource availability for some of the years in this study (line 492); is there any way to integrate these estimates into the analyses of temporal variation in territory size?

comments.issue: Insect abundances could help explain what differentiates hot spots from cold spots.
comments.request: Consider insect abundance data for hot versus cold spots.
comments.quote: Consideration of insect abundances might also shed light on what differentiates hot spots and cold spots.

comments.issue: The statement at line 403 is over-speculative without annual breeding productivity data.
comments.request: Elaborate how the findings identify processes promoting persistence of small populations.
comments.quote: without direct information on annual breeding productivity/success this statement is over-speculative.

comments.issue: Possible predation risks of singing are ignored.
comments.quote: you seem to be ignoring possible risks of singing with respect to probability of detection by predators.

comments.issue: The discussion could be condensed with little loss of content.
comments.request: Condense the discussion.
comments.quote: Overall, the discussion could be condensed with little loss of content.

comments.issue: The discussion assumes breeding pairs forage only within mapped territories; this needs more foundation.
comments.request: Provide stronger support that pairs forage only within mapped territories.
comments.quote: Again, much of the discussion rests on the assumption that a breeding pair only forages within the territory as mapped via singing males. This assumption needs far more foundation.

title: Territory Sizes and Patterns of Habitat Use by Forest Birds Over Five Decades: Ideal Free or Ideal Despotic?

study.system: Nearctic migratory birds; 88,965 arrival dates; 222 species

editor_summary: Both reviewers recognise the study's importance and novelty; add more on eco-evolutionary dynamics and demographic, ecological and evolutionary consequences.

reviews.assessment: Excellent, clearly written analysis with only small suggestions on references, clarifications and discussion.
strengths: excellent analysis of a good set of datasets

comments.issue: The statement about limited long time-series data is not balanced with existing examples.
comments.request: Signpost examples of long arrival-date time series.
comments.quote: It would be good for a more balanced statement here that signpost a few examples of long time series of arrival data that have been used for this kind of work

comments.issue: A new similar study on European spring arrival (Border et al.) is not cited.
comments.request: Cite Border et al. in the relevant discussion sections.
comments.quote: It might be also worth including reference to this new paper within relevant sections of the discussion.

comments.issue: The cited studies are old; recent carry-over effect work is missing.
comments.request: Add recent studies on winter conditions, NDVI and NAO.
comments.quote: it would be good to include some more recent studies on this topic including perhaps some of the more recent carry-over effect papers that consider winter conditions, NVDI, NAO etc.

comments.issue: Coastline cells may have higher detection probability as busier flyways, affecting arrival estimates.
comments.request: Discuss whether and how this detection bias affects the estimates.
comments.quote: might the probability of detection be higher in these as these are busier migration flyways?

comments.issue: A switch in units occurs at one distance threshold.
comments.request: Use consistent thresholds such as <0.5km and 0.5-1km.
comments.quote: a switch in units, should it be <0.5km, 0.5-1km to avoid that.

comments.issue: A statement on Line 173 lacks supporting citation.
comments.request: Provide a citation for the statement.
comments.quote: is there a citation that can support this statement?

comments.issue: The meaning of 'usual' on Line 340 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify whether 'usual' means greater than average.
comments.quote: by ''usual' do you mean greater than average?

comments.issue: A study showing survival costs of early arrival (Lerche-Jorgensen et al. 2018) is not cited.
comments.request: Cite the early-arrival survival cost study.
comments.quote: there is also a study showing negative effects on survival of early arrival

comments.issue: The weak rain effect may reflect balanced negative and positive effects of rain.
comments.request: Consider positive effects such as faster greening and food availability.
comments.quote: Might the weaker effect of rain be partly because the negative effects of it may be balanced to some extent by positive effects of rain

title: Spatial Nonstationarity in Phenological Responses of Nearctic Birds to Climate Variability

study.system: 95 tropical forest trees, Panama; wind mortality risk

reviews.assessment: Interesting, valuable and well-written study; methods details and some interpretations need clarification.
strengths: interesting to a large group of potential readers

comments.issue: Sensor setup unclear: purpose of horizontal sensor, orientation, whether only vertical tension data were used.
comments.request: Explain the sensor setup and data used, and consider including compression data.
comments.quote: You mentioned that you installed two sensors per tree. What was the reason for installing the horizontal one?

comments.issue: Wind speed-strain modelling step may be unnecessary; measured strain should be used directly.
comments.request: Use greatest measured strain relative to maximal strain instead of modelled values.
comments.quote: I think that linking strain and the risk could had been done without the unnecessary modelling step by simply using greatest strain during the 4-month period relative to maximal strain from earlier studies

comments.issue: Wind climate description too limited; directions, speed distributions and strongest winds are needed.
comments.request: Describe wind directions and speed distributions, focusing on strongest winds.
comments.quote: The wind climate could be described more in detail based on the Lutz tower.

comments.issue: Figure reference likely wrong: Fig 1c should be Fig 3c.
comments.request: Correct the figure reference.
comments.quote: Page 4 – Line 13 “Fig 1c” should probably be: Fig 3c.

comments.issue: Reduce their wind exposure is misleading; bending direction relative to the crown matters.
comments.request: Rephrase to reflect direction-dependent bending forces.
comments.quote: I believe that “reduce their wind exposure” is somewhat misleading

comments.issue: Stronger is vague; claim about tension and compression may be incorrect.
comments.request: Clarify and correct the statement about wood strength.
comments.quote: “stronger” is vague here. Does it mean stronger for a given carbohydrate investment both tension and compression?

comments.issue: Vague phrase about dramatic increase should state that it corresponds to the cube of diameter.
comments.request: Rephrase and cite Niklas's Plant Biomechanics.
comments.quote: “will increase dramatically with trunk diameter” could be replaced by: corresponds to the cube of diameter.

comments.issue: Contraction don't may be inappropriate for the journal.
comments.request: Avoid the contraction.
comments.quote: 5 – 12 Is “don’t” normal in this journal?

comments.issue: Abstract surprise at no exposure effect contradicts the acclimation-based reasoning in the text.
comments.request: Resolve the contradiction between the abstract and the text.
comments.quote: you wrote in the Abstract that you were surprised that wind exposure does not increase wind snap risk. There is some contradiction with these lines of thinking.

comments.issue: Risk to be minimal contradicts the abstract's surprise; minimal is also vague.
comments.request: Rephrase to avoid contradiction and vagueness.
comments.quote: “risk to be minimal” is again somewhat contradictory to the surprise mentioned in the Abstract

comments.issue: Site climate description insufficient; needs temperature, precipitation, dry-season definition and elevation.
comments.request: Add climate and elevation details for readers unfamiliar with the area.
comments.quote: is not enough for readers who have never been in the area. Maybe mean annual temperature and precipitation could be given.

comments.issue: Disturbance rate may be misread; clarify it refers to natural gap dynamics.
comments.request: Clarify the meaning of disturbance rate.
comments.quote: “disturbance rate” refers here to natural gap dynamics? Some readers may start thinking of people cutting down trees.

comments.issue: The word all is ambiguous in context.
comments.request: Clarify what all refers to.
comments.quote: 7 – 3 What is “all” here?

comments.issue: Wood specific gravity explanation is redundant with metric units and could be deleted.
comments.request: Delete this sentence.
comments.quote: Now with metric units “wood density” is more straightforward and is defined as any material density. Therefore, you could simply delete this sentence.

comments.issue: Breaking strain values (0.0017-0.0035) differ from Lavers (0.005-0.01); source and moisture content unclear.
comments.request: Explain the strain data source and use green wood max strain.
comments.quote: There is something strange in the Breaking strain values. They range from 0.0017 to 0.0035.

comments.issue: Figure 1 caption unclear whether tree height is measured from ground or water level.
comments.request: Clarify the height reference in the caption.
comments.quote: is unclear in the caption as tree height normally refers to the height from ground but here it is about height from the lake or sea?

comments.issue: Whether maximum value refers to tension or compression is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the strain type.
comments.quote: “maximum value”? Is this only about tension or also compression?

comments.issue: Assumption that wind moment scales with speed squared may not hold for streamlined trees.
comments.request: Reconsider the squared relationship and add support.
comments.quote: Because of streamlining the moment caused by the wind could be close to linear

comments.issue: Wind mortality risk should be distinguished from trunk breakage risk or justified.
comments.request: State the root-trunk balance assumption or rename the risk.
comments.quote: some readers might want to state (somewhere before this location) that roots and trunks are in balance and likelihood of uprooting and trunk snapping are about the same

comments.issue: Wording suggestion: use short instead of small.
comments.request: Change small to short.
comments.quote: I am not a native English speaker but would write short instead of “small”.

comments.issue: Description of the Lutz tower surroundings and distances is insufficient.
comments.request: Describe the site openness and distances.
comments.quote: You could be explicit about the distance and maybe explain how open the area around Lutz tower is.

comments.issue: Canopy surface height calculation needs explanation or a citation.
comments.request: Explain the method or give a citation.
comments.quote: Please explain more about the methods or at least give a citation.

comments.issue: Wind speeds should always be reported in m/s.
comments.request: Use m/s consistently.
comments.quote: 9 – 47 Better with winds speeds always in m/s.

comments.issue: Wind threshold of 10 km/h is too low; snapping-relevant winds exceed 20 m/s.
comments.request: Use an appropriate strong-wind threshold.
comments.quote: Important for trunks snapping (and probably for acclimation as well) here are winds over 20 m/s. This 10 km/hr is just 2.8 m/s.

comments.issue: Clustering of sampled trees around data loggers is unclear.
comments.request: Explain logger placement and tree clustering.
comments.quote: Did you mention in the Methods about clustering of sampled trees around loggers?

comments.issue: Well acclimated is vague; could mean low or optimal wind risk.
comments.request: Clarify the meaning.
comments.quote: “well acclimated” means here probably that they have low wind risk? This is vague as well acclimation could mean also that the wind risk is optimal

comments.issue: Crown size and density differences (e.g. Anacardium) could affect wind risk beyond wood density.
comments.request: Consider crown characteristics in the interpretation.
comments.quote: Yes, but Anacardium could have much larger or denser crowns.

title: Wind Shapes the Growth Strategies of Trees in a Tropical Forest

editor_summary: All three referees flag unclear model assumptions, limited empirical embedding and absent validation; editor also asks how the work advances the field and whether measurable population or community traits can be recommended.

interactions under stress finding really interesting

comments.issue: Labelling effects 'positive' is relative; directional language would be clearer.

comments.issue: Environmental stress is introduced too late and its expected effects are not set up.

comments.issue: Some definitions and the metric belong in the methods section.

comments.quote: Some of these definitions and the metric could go to M&M; section.

comments.issue: Intro questions are vaguely formulated and not clearly linked to the discussion.

comments.issue: Model section (L132-160) needs more detail, reiterating the earlier point.

L146: I understand that this is a feature of DEMENT

title: The Impact of Microbial Interactions on Ecosystem Function Intensifies Under Stress

study.system: soil microbial communities; DEMENT decomposition model simulation

reviews.assessment: Unique and exciting modeling contribution, but questions whether hundred-year simulations support claims about ecological timescales and asks for clarity on model and hypothesis details.
strengths: appreciates discussion of simultaneous mutation and dispersal
nice exploration of relative effect sizes

comments.issue: The justification for comparing mutation and dispersal magnitudes is not broadly introduced for non-specialist readers.
comments.request: Add a broader introduction to the research question and its justification.
comments.quote: I wonder if other readers would appreciate a more broad introduction to this research question and its justification.

comments.issue: The hypothesis wording is weak because 'change' in litter chemistry is not testable; 'declines' would be better.
comments.request: Strengthen the hypothesis wording, e.g. use 'declines'.

comments.issue: The conceptual basis for modeling dispersal and mutation, and how adaptation is quantified, are not explained enough.

comments.issue: It is unclear why mutation is the only adaptation mechanism considered; horizontal gene transfer could also explain new traits, and mutation seems to be shorthand for trait acquisition.

comments.issue: Hundred-year simulations span nearly a million bacterial generations, which challenges the claim that results apply on ecological timescales.

comments.quote: The methods (e.g. L155) says 100 years, but the results in Figure 3 are presented over 100 days.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the hypothesis holds at 10-20 years, the timescale of long-term field experiments, where mutation and dispersal effects look similar.
comments.request: Test the hypothesis over shorter, field-relevant timescales and report when mutation becomes significantly stronger.
comments.quote: Can your hypothesis still be accepted if the results are viewed after 10 or 20 years, which is closer to the time scales experienced at many field long-term climate experiments?

comments.issue: Confidence intervals for the mutation-dispersal comparison are not reported.
comments.request: Report confidence intervals.

comments.issue: It is unclear how well available cellulose represents litter quality, especially in a model without fungi.

comments.issue: Isolating mutation and dispersal may produce artefacts, e.g. complete diversity loss under short-range dispersal.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the stated parameter sensitivity concerns initialization only or also the genotype number and cellulase scalar tests.

comments.issue: How the results scale to the ecosystem level is not discussed enough.

comments.issue: The meaning of 'at the population level' at L105-107 is unclear and the sentence needs rewriting.

comments.issue: It is unclear how biomass reaches a threshold without reproduction at L122-123.

reviews.assessment: Strong, well-presented paper that convincingly argues mutation matters relative to dispersal, with only a request to soften 'reveal'.

editor_summary: Three reviews: value in aspects but falls short; reviewers 1 and 3 independently call questions 1-3 straw men, question 4 more interesting; analytical and structural problems; open to restructured resubmission.

comments.issue: Research question 3 has already been addressed in previously published studies.

reviews.assessment: Mixed; clearly written but the framing repeatedly argues straw-man hypotheses and lacks deeper theoretical development.

interesting overall question about spatial autocorrelation

comments.issue: The manuscript repeatedly argues straw-man hypotheses rather than addressing an open question.

comments.issue: Question 1 (species differ in trends) is trivially obvious.

comments.issue: Question 2 implies ecologists believe trends are spatially constant, for which there is no contemporary evidence.
comments.request: Reframe Question 2 away from the straw man.
comments.quote: This framing implies that both (1) ecologists typically believe population trends to be spatially nonvarying, and (2) the practice of modeling spatially constant trends is common. However, I don't see any contemporary evidence for either of these items.

comments.issue: Question 3 is not developed and its relevance to data aggregation is unclear.
comments.request: Develop the rationale for Question 3 or remove it.
comments.quote: Question 3 (the existence of year x treatment effects within studies) is not well developed in the introduction. Why does the answer to question 3 (yes or no?) matter?

comments.issue: The introduction provides only one paragraph of true framing, leaving the study on weak theoretical footing.
comments.request: Deepen the theoretical framing.
comments.quote: the lack of a deeper framing of the study (i.e., only 1 paragraph of true "introduction") signals that this study may not stand on particularly strong footing

comments.request: Acknowledge spatially-explicit monitoring practice.
comments.quote: Is this a commonly done practice? It is not common for, for example, the North American Breeding Bird Survey, which has, for many years, presented spatially-explicit population trajectories.

comments.issue: The detailed model structure description at line 172 is unnecessary.
comments.request: Cite the model formulation and give only effect details.
comments.quote: describing the specific model structure in great detail seems unnecessary; you can specify what model you used, cite that model formulation, and given fixed and random effect details.

comments.issue: Site-level random effects do not account for temporal autocorrelation, so trend coefficients are likely over-estimated.
comments.request: Model temporal autocorrelation explicitly.
comments.quote: While the site-level random effect (u) does account for dependence between years, it does not account for temporal autocorrelation, as it assumes that all years are randomly distributed

comments.issue: Observer effects, day of year and time of day are more important detectability factors than weather covariates.
