comments.quote: What about observer effects, day of year, or time of day? In bird surveys, those are generally more important for detectability than weather factors like temperature and cloud cover

comments.issue: The meaning of line 191 and the priors used are unclear.

comments.issue: How inference on Q1 was made is not stated.

comments.issue: The niche-distance metric assumes equal linear influence of all PCA axes.

comments.issue: Using the linear component of a model containing both linear and quadratic terms is not interpretable for Q4.

comments.issue: Discussing "significance" in Bayesian models mixes paradigms.

comments.quote: Since these are Bayesian models, it is generally ill-advised to 'mix paradigms' and discuss 'significance'.

comments.issue: It is doubtful that modelling constant trajectories across sites is common practice today.

title: Predicting and Prioritising Community Assembly: Learning Outcomes via Experiments

study.system: Soay sheep; individual-based IPM simulations across densities

reviews.assessment: Very positive; well-written study combining long-term empirical data with models, with only minor edits suggested in an attached file.

interesting explanation of density-dependent life-history shifts relevant to management

comments.issue: Only very minor edit suggestions are given, in an attached file rather than the report.
comments.quote: I really enjoyed reading the manuscript and do only have a few very minor suggestions to edits in the attached file.

reviews.assessment: Novel modelling approach, but the main trade-off patterns may be forced by model formulation rather than inferred from the data.
strengths: novel and interesting way to explore possible individual life histories
combines individual-based data with generated life-history strategies

comments.issue: The growth increment–juvenile survival trade-off is directly imposed by the model equations, not inferred from data.
comments.request: Prove that this pattern is not an artefact of the model formulation.
comments.quote: For me, it therefore seems that this is not an actual tradeoff caused by patterns in the data dependent parameters, but an outcome forced by the model formulation.

comments.issue: The juvenile–adult survival correlation arises because a long adult period adds non-zero survival classes to the average.

comments.issue: The juvenile survival–reproduction trade-off is forced by the equilibrium constraint that mean LRS equals one.

comments.quote: Looking at figure 3, it seems that the size of offspring slightly decreases with population density. This suggests that offspring condition decreases with population density.

comments.issue: The model's population structure, stages and size definitions are described inconsistently.

comments.issue: The derivative functions for survival and reproduction are presented but not used.

comments.quote: As far as I can tell, the derivative functions for survival and reproduction (page 7 line 33) are not used in the analysis and results described in the main text.

title: Density Dependence Shapes Life‐History Trade‐Offs in a Food‐Limited Population

comments.issue: Text says 'probability' while the figures say 'rate'; axes labels should be adjusted.

comments.issue: Fig. 6c shows increased variability, not an increase in pair-bond disruption, and the average increase is small.

comments.issue: The male widowhood slope is rather constant with sea ice, while the female slope is stronger.

comments.issue: It is unclear how foraging efficiency correlates more with sea ice in females while males forage at higher sea ice, and how this links to survival.

comments.issue: The scale of the divorce-rate increase should be mentioned explicitly.

comments.issue: The claim that successful breeders divorce more in heavy snow years is not shown in Figure 5b.

comments.issue: How intruders cause a forced divorce is not explained and was not introduced earlier.

comments.issue: The term 'pure partner change' is not defined.

comments.issue: No increase in breeding success of ND versus SB or reduction in survival is visible.

comments.issue: The number of missed breeding seasons is not quantified.

comments.issue: The statement about skipped breeding cannot be made without knowing the counterfactual, as poor condition might have reduced survival.

comments.issue: How the initiator of a divorce is identified is not explained.

comments.issue: The rates are not predicted to rise; only the chance of both high and low widowhood increases.

title: Climate Change Impacts Pair‐Bond Dynamics in a Long‐Lived Monogamous Species

study.system: rhesus macaques; simulated disease spread and social structure after a hurricane

reviews.assessment: Interesting simulation question with rigorous methods, but it is poorly linked to real infections and repeatedly overstates simulated risks.

comments.issue: The simulation nature of the study is only revealed late and is unclear in the abstract.
comments.request: State clearly up front and throughout that this is a simulation exercise.
comments.quote: It wasn't until late in the manuscript that I realized this was a simulation study.

comments.issue: No information on actual infectious diseases or their correlates (rank, sex) in this population.
comments.request: Link the simulations to real infection data or acknowledge the gap.
comments.quote: In the end, it is entirely a simulation – a sophisticated and rigorous approach mostly on the simulation side, but not well linked into actual infectious diseases in this population

comments.issue: p-values are nonsensical in a simulation study; conclusions appear based on them.
comments.request: Use fully Bayesian analysis with credible intervals or model averaging.
comments.quote: why use p-values in any of the statistical models? As one issue, they are nonsensical in a simulation study

comments.issue: Three-level categorical rank loses variation and uses arbitrary cutoffs.
comments.request: Use actual dominance percentages instead of rank categories.
comments.quote: Why use the 3-level categorical measure of rank, rather than the actual percentages of animals that an animal dominates? Why those cutoffs used?

comments.issue: Figure 1 colour coding for groups H, R, S and T is not explained in the legend.
comments.request: Note the pre/post sampling gaps in the legend.
comments.quote: Why no purple for panel A in groups H and R? and only purple in S and T?

comments.issue: Panel D describes a 10 percentage point increase (doubling), not a 10% increase.
comments.request: Correct the percentage wording.
comments.quote: I think it is a 10 percentage point increase (doubling), not 10% increase. Right?

comments.issue: Why the error is much smaller pre/post hurricane in panel D is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the smaller uncertainty.
comments.quote: And I didn't fully understand why the error on that was so much smaller on the pre/post hurricane.

comments.issue: Only within-group infection is modeled; inter-group transmission is ignored despite its importance.
comments.request: Discuss or model inter-group transmission, including male dispersal.
comments.quote: The focus is on infection within groups. What about effects of the hurricane on inter-group transmission?

comments.issue: Statements such as 'the macaques doubled their risk of infection' overstate what simulations show.
comments.request: Rephrase as risk of simulated infection.
comments.quote: Well, you don't actually have the infection data to show that, and it isn't even clear what pathogens they have that this would apply to.

comments.issue: It is unclear which pathogens the results apply to.
comments.request: Discuss which pathogens this could apply to in this population or primates generally.
comments.quote: it would be nice to know more about what pathogens specifically this might apply to, for this population or primates in general

title: A Natural Disaster Exacerbates and Redistributes Disease Risk Among Free‐Ranging Macaques by Altering Social Structure

study.system: coral reef fish communities; 27-year survey of 39 reefs

editor_summary: Reviewers like the study but want full methodological detail on community-dynamics parameters and SEMs, robustness checks for cryptic species, richness/evenness and observation error, a combined SEM figure, and broader implications.

welcome spatial analysis of coral reef fish stability

comments.issue: The chosen definition of stability is not justified against the many other definitions in the literature.
comments.request: Justify and discuss the authors' definition of stability.
comments.quote: The choice of the authors’ intuitively simple definition must be justified and discussed.

comments.issue: Cryptic species groups are excluded; their distribution across sites and number of species are not reported.
comments.request: Report how many cryptic species exist and whether they are evenly distributed across sites.

comments.issue: It is unclear which kinds of environmental stochasticity are modelled, especially the split between species-specific and common responses.
comments.request: Specify which environmental stochasticity components are considered in Eq 6 and 8.
comments.quote: Please specify which kinds of environmental stochasticity that are considered, especially in eqn. 8.

comments.issue: The advantages of the bivariate PLN are not justified and more general references on it are missing.
comments.request: Justify the bivariate PLN and cite Engen et al. 2011 and Solbu et al. 2022.

comments.issue: The discussion does not generalise the findings for a wider readership.
comments.request: Expand the discussion to generalise the results for a wider readership.
comments.quote: I would see the discussion expanded to generalize the results for a wider readership

comments.issue: Effects of spatial variation in overall abundance on density dependence and environmental response are not included.
comments.request: Include the effects of spatial variation in overall abundance.

reviews.assessment: Well written and well researched, but the CV-based results likely overestimate stochastic variability and the SEMs seem under-developed.
strengths: long-term Great Barrier Reef time series

comments.issue: CV is interpreted without accounting for observation error or deterministic fluctuations, likely overestimating stochastic variability.
comments.request: Estimate the potential upper limits of observation error and deterministic variability.
comments.quote: there is no attempt to account for effects of observation error (which is a major aspect of the Loreu & Mazancourt framework), nor to account for deterministic fluctuations in population dynamics

comments.issue: The SEMs are under-developed: causal structure, model assembly, confounding tests and functional forms are not described.
comments.request: Justify the SEM causal structure a priori and describe model assembly, confounding tests and functional forms.
comments.quote: any causal interpretations of SEMs need to be strongly justified based on a priori hypotheses about the underlying causal structure

reviews.assessment: Interesting topic and potentially important conclusions, but the statistics and modelling are presented too obscurely to check or reproduce.
strengths: conclusions would be very interesting if true

comments.issue: Statistics are presented too vaguely to check or reproduce; the writing discourages scrutiny of the analyses.
comments.request: Add sufficient statistical detail to reproduce all analyses, in the main text or SI.
comments.quote: all statistics should be presented transparently and in sufficient detail to straightforwardly check them

comments.issue: Skeptical that legitimate causal inferences can be drawn from SEMs with 38 data points and up to 8 variables.
comments.request: Justify that the SEMs support causal inference given the small sample size.
comments.quote: I am highly skeptical that legitimate and solid causal inferences with that many variables can be made based on 38 data points

comments.issue: The SEM process, assumptions and formal statistical models are not described.
comments.request: Add a detailed SI explaining each SEM, its assumptions and formal statistical models.
comments.quote: please add a DETAILED SI section explaining the entire process that was carried out and the assumptions made, tested, etc.

comments.issue: The Tsai et al. modelling framework and the authors' modifications cannot be understood from the manuscript.
comments.request: Provide a complete, linear description of the modelling from start to finish in a detailed SI.
comments.quote: a complete, linear description of the modelling as it pertains to this paper should be presented, from start to finish, in a long and detailed SI

comments.issue: Richness and evenness estimates may depend on arbitrary PLN assumptions; standard simple estimators are not compared.
comments.request: Recalculate all results with observed richness and evenness and report them in the SI.
comments.quote: I would like to see all results recalculated for standard, simple methods of calculating richness and evenness

comments.issue: The Zenodo code is a set of functions without a complete reproducible workflow.
comments.request: Provide a main.R script that reproduces all figures, tables and inline numbers.
comments.quote: I would like to see a complete workflow, i.e., include a script called main.R (or something like that)

comments.issue: Line-level copy edits: unclear antecedent for 'those' at L102-3 and typo 'crown-or-thorns' at L154.
comments.quote: Unclear antecedent for ‘those”. What does it refer to?

comments.issue: Figure 1 lacks a map showing where the Great Barrier Reef study area is.
comments.request: Add a map of Australia with a box indicating the panel a location.
comments.quote: Please include a map of Australia with a box on it indicating where the main scene in panel a is, to orient the reader

title: Environmental Gradients Linked to Human Impacts, Not Species Richness, Drive Regional Variation in Community Stability in Coral Reef Fishes

study.system: subtropical forest; termite and tree traits; coarse wood decomposition

editor_summary: Editor notes reviewers were hard to find and the paper is narrowly focused; agrees with the more critical reviewer that it does not meet Ecology Letters' threshold even substantially revised, being better suited to a specialised journal.

reviews.assessment: Impressive four-year study with novel results on termite-tree trait complementarity, needing clarity and wider context before publication.

expands understanding of termites in deadwood decay

comments.issue: WES is never defined and its interpretation must be inferred from figure legends.

comments.issue: Mixed model details, random factors and the abundance model output are not reported in the main methods.

comments.issue: The range of WES values across the 27 wood species is not given.

comments.issue: Substantial differences between sites in niche overlap, trait relations, volume loss and niche width are not addressed.

comments.issue: Whether the niche centre is significantly closer to autumn than summer is untested.

comments.issue: Species are hard to distinguish in supplementary figures because colour schemes vary.

comments.issue: Results may be driven by seasonal resource availability or wood quality rather than trait complementarity.

comments.issue: WES and 'high quality wood' are used without explanation on lines 100-101 and 132.

comments.issue: Seasonal temperature differences, the premise of the study, are not reported although precipitation is.

comments.issue: Criteria for choosing the 27 'important, representative' tree species are not explained.

comments.issue: Physical traits are referred to on line 203 without naming them.

title: Seasonally Changing Interactions of Species Traits of Termites and Trees Promote Complementarity in Coarse Wood Decomposition

study.system: six terrestrial and aquatic taxa; 20-year monitoring across Finland

editor_summary: Editor summarises R1's concerns about sampling uncertainty, correlated responses and shallow mechanism, and R2's view that prior natural-system DSR studies make the work insufficiently novel; reject with option to resubmit.

reviews.assessment: Clear, generally well-written study; methods details are missing and the introduction and discussion need better linking.
strengths: uses long-term data from multiple systems

comments.issue: No a priori expectations explain why taxonomic groups would differ in their responses.
comments.request: State a priori expectations for group differences.
comments.quote: Why would the different groups vary in their responses? If the authors establish some a priori expectations, it may be easier for the reader to follow the results/discussion.

comments.issue: Phylogenetic history and the very different taxonomic breadth of the groups are not considered.
comments.request: Consider phylogenetic diversity and taxonomic breadth.
comments.quote: Did you consider the phylogenetic history and/or diversity for each group? – the scales may be different.

comments.issue: Chi-square alone is too conservative; other fit indices should be reported.

comments.issue: How AIC was calculated and used for model comparison is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the AIC calculation.
comments.quote: How was AIC calculated? Indicate this is the metric you will use for model comparisons.

comments.issue: When phylogenetic distance can stand in for functional distance is unclear.

comments.issue: Line numbers restart after the methods, making specific comments hard.

comments.issue: Using phylogenetic distance as functional diversity is misleading in broad groups like bacteria.

reviews.assessment: DSR evidence from natural systems is already extensive; the novelty claims are inaccurate and the study does not advance the field enough for Ecology Letters.

comments.issue: The large existing literature on diversity-stability relationships in natural systems is not recognized.

comments.issue: The claim of being among the first to support diversity-begets-stability in natural communities is inaccurate.

comments.issue: It is unclear how the study advances the field beyond existing experiments and natural-system analyses.

comments.quote: it isn’t clear how the work presented in this manuscript advances the field in any substantial ways, provides unexpected or new insights, or addresses existing gaps

editor_summary: Major overhaul required, especially moving essential supplementary elements into a well-integrated main text; reviewer 1's presentation concerns must be addressed.

comments.issue: Acclimation hypothesis is only weakly supported; radish deviates and model generality is uncertain.

comments.issue: Comparisons with previous acclimation models are conclusive for only one of three parameters and the discussion is superficial.

comments.issue: Main text is not self-contained: equations, parameters and models are only understandable with the supplementary notes.

reviews.assessment: Elegantly designed and enjoyable experiment; asks to position the novelty, drop the straw-man hypothesis and explore Fig. 5 fully.

comments.issue: The straw-man hypothesis formulation adds unnecessary complexity and length.

comments.issue: The acclimation experiment (duration, procedure, separation from growth) is not described.

comments.issue: What differs between An' and An to improve prediction, and whether species acclimate differently, is not explored.

comments.issue: The paper should cut to the chase and make the Fig. 5 finding the take-home message.

comments.issue: The proposed mechanisms are not quantified in the plots.

comments.issue: 'Necessitates' is too strong a claim for the advocated transition to high-throughput traits.

comments.quote: “necessitates” feels like a very strong claim here.

comments.request: Add statistical fit information as an inset.

comments.issue: Strong novelty claims lack background on prior studies, leaving motivation, design choices and hypotheses unsupported.

comments.quote: The authors make strong claims of novelty in the introduction but don’t provide enough background on the state of the field and the previous studies that approached this question differently.

comments.issue: Methods lack sample sizes, information on which species were measured and where, and references for measurements.
comments.request: Add the missing methodological detail and references.
comments.quote: The methods are also lacking a lot of relevant information, including sample size, and additional information about the species that were measured for traits and where.

comments.quote: The categorization of PCA axes as “named functional axes” (i.e., hydraulic strategy) is done quite frequently, but I find it very uninformative and naïve.

comments.issue: 'Deeper' and 'more general' are undefined and no papers are cited.

comments.quote: This is not where the novelty of this study lies, but rather in the approach used to create these models and the ability to predict an actual probability of occurrence from climate and traits.

title: A Functional Basis for the Assembly of Australian Subtropical Rainforest Tree Communities

study.system: grassland leaf nitrogen; nutrient addition experiment across 26 sites

editor_summary: Editor notes reviewers are optimistic about impact but want data analysis and interpretation concerns addressed, and the novelty articulated within existing literature.

reviews.assessment: Well written and interesting, but novelty relative to Anderson et al. and generalizability to ESMs need discussion.
strengths: considers a wide range of drivers

comments.issue: The primary finding appears superficially the same as Anderson et al. 2018, so the study’s novelty is unclear.
comments.request: Discuss how these results are novel relative to the existing literature.
comments.quote: how does the primary finding of this study compare and contrast with Anderson et al 2018 Ecology?

comments.issue: No limitations section; representativeness, scaling of variable importance, and C3/C4 turnover need discussion.
comments.request: Add a limitations section discussing generalizability, especially to ESMs.
comments.quote: The manuscript also lacks a clear limitations section. While the manuscript does well to consider many factors know to influence nitrogen distributions, I was left with many questions about the generalizability of the results especially to ESMs.

comments.issue: Wording at line 51 could be softened.
comments.request: Consider “can improve” or “could inform”.
comments.quote: L51 – maybe “can improve” or “could inform” ?

comments.issue: Lines 83-84 need an edit and are unintelligible.
comments.request: Edit lines 83-84 for clarity.
comments.quote: L83-84 - needs and edit, I don’t know what this means

reviews.assessment: Interesting topic and well organised, but collinearity and scale mismatch need addressing and several interpretations are unconvincing.

comments.issue: Collinearity among climate, soil, trait and functional-group variables may distort interpretations.
comments.request: Report multicollinearity and test direct, indirect, independent and interactive effects.
comments.quote: These variables should have some collinearities among them, which could influence the result interpretations. Therefore, the authors should provide more details regarding the impacts of multi-collinearities among variables.

comments.issue: Species-level traits, community-level biomass and site-level climate create a scale mismatch.
comments.request: Analyse data at both species and community levels and compare.
comments.quote: The authors sampling the leaf traits at the species level but the aboveground biomass at the community level. In addition, all the climate variables are extracted from the site-level.

comments.issue: The nutrition allocation explanation for decoupled leaf nitrogen and biomass is speculative and unsupported.
comments.request: Be cautious and support the allocation interpretation with evidence.
comments.quote: This is totally speculative, lacking the direct evidence. The authors should be very cautious when deriving this conclusion.

comments.issue: The explanation for why phosphorus supply weakens the nitrogen response is ambiguous and unconvincing.

comments.issue: Missing definite articles at lines 43-44.

comments.issue: Relevant references are missing at lines 71-74.
comments.request: Add appropriate references.
comments.quote: Lines 71-74: The relevant references should be added as appropriate.

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 90-92 is confusing and hard to understand.
comments.request: Rewrite the sentence for clarity.
comments.quote: This sentence is very confusing and hard to understanding.

comments.issue: The Introduction is fragmentary with too many paragraphs.
comments.request: Merge paragraphs and make the section more concise.
comments.quote: The entire Introduction section looks like very fragmentary and has lots of paragraphs. The authors should pool some paragraph together, and make this section more concise.

comments.issue: It is unexplained why log-transformed response ratios were not used for the nitrogen response.

title: Soil Nitrogen Supply Exerts Largest Influence on Leaf Nitrogen in Environments with the Greatest Leaf Nitrogen Demand

study.system: Northern Hemisphere woody plants; occurrence, trait and climate data

strengths: ambitious study linking biotic and abiotic environments
maps stress tolerance strategies in space

comments.quote: on visual examination the new biome maps seem to mostly recapitulate existing major biomes

reviews.assessment: Praises the dataset and writing, with a main critique about the excluded low-intermediate tolerance cluster and a caveat about trait variation.

comments.issue: It is unknown how results would change if the low to intermediate tolerance cluster were retained.

comments.issue: The meaning of 'treatable' at line 465 is unclear.

title: Macroecology of Abiotic Stress Tolerance in Woody Plants of the Northern Hemisphere: Tolerance Biomes and Polytolerance Hotspots

study.system: marine fish; size-based bioenergetic model, North Sea

editor_summary: Reviewers found the extension interesting but raised important criticisms, especially reviewer #3's call for thorough sensitivity analysis of model assumptions; substantial revision required.

reviews.assessment: Interesting bioenergetic model, but output sensitivity to key assumptions is hard to assess and needs more self-critical analysis.

comments.issue: The empirical data used to test the model are not described in enough detail.
comments.request: Explain the empirical data used to evaluate the model in greater detail.
comments.quote: Additionally, the nature of the empirical data used to test the model could be explained in greater detail.

comments.issue: The assumption that active metabolic rate responds less strongly to temperature than maintenance rate lacks empirical support.
comments.request: Provide empirical support and test how these temperature dependencies affect predictions.
comments.quote: Here the authors assume that the temperature dependence of the “mobilized energy rate” or active metabolic rate is less strong than the “maintenance rate” or basal metabolic rate.

comments.issue: It is unclear how alternative ingestion functional-response forms, such as linear consumption scaling, would change model outputs.
comments.request: Test whether results differ under a linear consumption relationship.
comments.quote: the authors model ingestion rates based on functional response curves. This is a reasonable approach, but how might differences in this assumed relationship affect model outputs.

comments.issue: Justification and magnitude of higher early-stage mass-specific ingestion rates are unclear, as is why only this stage is adjusted.
comments.request: Report how much higher the rates are and justify the stage-specific adjustment.
comments.quote: max. mass-specific ingestion rates are set higher for early life stages to “to depict fish faster growth during this period”. But, how much higher and why the adjustment only at this life stage?

comments.issue: The term 'early life stages' is undefined; it is unclear whether eggs or yolk-sac larvae are included.
comments.request: Define which ages and stages are classified as early life stages.
comments.quote: I’m not clear what ages/stages qualify as “early life stages”. Do these include egg stages or larva with yolk sacs where food resources are provided?

comments.issue: Whether inter-individual variability within age groups affects model results is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify whether and how individual variability contributes to the results.
comments.quote: I’m also not clear if/how inter-individual variability among these age groups might contribute to the results.

comments.issue: The mechanistic link between early-stage hypoxia insensitivity and lower mass-specific ingestion at older stages is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the mechanism and state whether hypoxia also affects maintenance rates.
comments.quote: I’m not clear how/why lower sensitivity to hypoxia in early life stages is mechanistically linked to lower-mass-specific ingestion at older life stages (L. 47).

comments.issue: Whether adults' near-absence of food limitation depends on assumed body-mass scaling of consumption or growth is untested.
comments.request: Test how sensitive food-limitation patterns are to body-mass dependence assumptions.
comments.quote: To what extent does this depend on any body mass-dependence of consumption rate or growth rate?

comments.issue: A few line-level copy edits and word choices are suggested.
comments.quote: Aside from fixing the typo/awkward language quoted in the second paragraph of #2 above, I would suggest

comments.issue: A recent overview of bioenergetics models for temperature questions is not cited.
comments.request: Cite Rose et al. (2024) Marine Ecology Progress Series.
comments.quote: I would also suggest citing this recent paper that provides an overview of the use of bioenergetics models to address questions related to temperature.

reviews.assessment: Important, broadly appealing bioenergetic model with clear graphics, but parameter provenance, oxygen tolerance and generality need more attention.
strengths: practical analysis with potential for broad application

comments.issue: The lengthy defence of the aerobic scope argument makes the introduction cumbersome.
comments.quote: There was a lengthy defense of the aerobic scope argument (OCLTT), which was necessary although it made the introduction a little cumbersome.

comments.issue: It is not shown which species' physiological constraints came from data versus phylogenetic assumptions, particularly for oxygen.
comments.request: Provide species-level parameter provenance, e.g. in a small table or with asterisks.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to show more specific information about data informing the physiological thresholds, instead of having to refer to another paper.

comments.issue: The fundamental Topt appears to have been estimated from field data, which reflects the realized rather than the fundamental Topt.
comments.request: Clarify or correct the Topt estimation and its labelling.
comments.quote: it seems like the fundamental Topt was estimated from field data, but that should have been the realized Topt (ln 230).

comments.issue: Empirically estimated oxygen tolerances appear not to have been used despite available data.
comments.request: Use empirical oxygen tolerance data in the model.
comments.quote: it didn’t seem like empirically-estimated oxygen tolerances were used at all. I would assume there is quite a bit of data on that, so it seems strange that it was not used.

comments.issue: The oxygen tolerance text is confusing and jargon makes the abstract claim seem to contradict physiological sensitivity.
comments.request: Rewrite the oxygen tolerance passage and abstract claim more clearly.
comments.quote: That seems to contradict what I think you said which is that they physiologically more sensitive to hypoxia, it’s just that in the real world they are not exposed to low O environments

comments.issue: The model's predicted oxygen demand has not been checked against empirical oxygen tolerance data.
comments.request: Compare model-predicted oxygen demand with empirical measurements.
comments.quote: I did want to see more empirical work on O tolerances, and whether the model-predicted O demand is consistent with the data.

comments.issue: The discussion does not address how far results extend to other ecosystems or communities.
comments.request: Extend the discussion to other regions, species and phylogenetic patterns in hypoxia tolerance.
comments.quote: Generally there wasn’t much discussion of other ecosystems and how generally these results can be applied. This is a highly parameterized and very specific model for a particular ecosystem.

comments.issue: Acronyms such as HTLs make the writing harder to follow.
comments.request: Replace acronyms with full terms.
comments.quote: Another suggestion for the writing is to get rid of the acronyms like HTLs and others.

Fig 1 legend – define the light blue curve

title: Realised Thermal Niches in Marine Ectotherms Are Shaped by Ontogeny and Trophic Interactions

study.system: multivoltine butterflies; 27-year monitoring, 30 species

editor_summary: Reviewers find the topic relevant and interesting but raise important caveats: voltinism is inconsistently quantified, modelling issues make results hard to interpret, and methods, terminology and dataset description need substantial clarification.

reviews.assessment: Interested and sees reasonable, important conclusions, but found the methods and results so difficult to understand that many clarifications are needed.
strengths: tests the generality of the lost-generation hypothesis

comments.issue: Why winter severity was included alongside winter onset is never explained.

comments.quote: The reasoning behind the inclusion of this variable (along with timing of winter onset) is never explained—and in fact the authors present fall and winter temperature trends separately in their results (l. 279).

comments.issue: Spatial variation is treated as local adaptation, but it also includes plastic responses.
comments.request: Acknowledge plasticity within spatial variation.
comments.quote: spatial variation will encompass local adaptation AND plastic responses to local conditions (Ramirez-Parada et al. 2024)

comments.issue: The words adapt/adaptation imply genetic adaptation rather than adaptive responses.
comments.request: Use wording that does not suggest documented evolutionary change.
comments.quote: Maybe the authors could find wording that doesn’t suggest they’ve documented evolutionary change?

comments.issue: 'Lost generations' and 'missing generations' mean different things but sound confusingly similar.

comments.issue: The precise meaning of match/mismatch is unclear and could confuse readers.

comments.issue: Study sites are not described in enough detail.

comments.issue: Calling climate change a leading cause of insect declines is misleading.

comments.issue: The claim that added generations increase growth rates may not be causal.

comments.issue: N line-level copy edits (They->butterflies, Is->are, Predict->describe, 'species WITH poor', ellipses, emphasis).

comments.issue: Why late generations are doomed is not explained for readers unfamiliar with the hypothesis.

comments.issue: 'Increase voltinism' is not explained.
comments.request: Explain it as an increase in generations per year.

comments.issue: 'Overwinter demography' is undefined.

comments.quote: l. 113. What is “overwinter demography”?

comments.issue: 'Limited overlap' and 'adequate sample size' are not operationally defined.

comments.issue: Whether model fits and assumptions were checked is unclear.

comments.issue: Collinearity between winter onset and temperature is not addressed.

comments.quote: l. 149. Were winter onset and temperature not correlated with one another?

comments.issue: Clustering choices may bias results and are not shown to be repeatable.

comments.issue: 'Population index with the trapezoidal rule' is not explained.

comments.issue: 'Last generation size variability' is unclear and suggests body size.

comments.issue: The density-dependence predictor seems to measure interannual variability, not density dependence.

comments.issue: 'Annual variation in phenology scaled by site' is undefined.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether random effects were removed based on likelihood-ratio tests.

comments.issue: How annual variation was quantified remains unclear.
comments.request: Explain the quantification.
comments.quote: l. 225. Same question: how was annual variation quantified?

comments.issue: The effect size 0.60 lacks units per change in last generation size.

comments.issue: The numerators of the slope units are unclear.

comments.issue: An 'evolutionary trap that limits voltinism flexibility' is hard to imagine.

comments.issue: Why local adaptation would preclude adaptation to longer seasons is not explained.

comments.issue: 'These' has no clear referent.

comments.issue: The 30C threshold and panel C colours are unexplained.

comments.issue: Fig. 3 is not intuitive; 'response to phenology' values need explanation.

comments.issue: Fig. 5B quadrants are unlabelled and genus abbreviations are ambiguous.

comments.issue: Fig. S1 caption reverses the top and bottom row descriptions.

comments.issue: The key figure is only in the supplement.

reviews.assessment: Relevant and interesting topic, but the mixture model's fixed parameters clash with the voltinism premise, leaving key results difficult to interpret.

bootstrap approach for trends and traits seems sensible

comments.issue: Last generation size is used as a proxy for voltinism but does not capture variation in generation number.

reviews.assessment: Finds the modelling strong and results interesting, but asks for substantial reorganization and clearer links between last generation size and voltinism.
strengths: results organized in the same order as the methods

comments.issue: The introduction does not connect photoperiod to climate change variables strongly enough.
comments.request: Strengthen this connection and bring the lost generation hypothesis in earlier.
comments.quote: Overall, there needs to be a stronger connection between photoperiod and climate change variables relevant to this study.

comments.issue: If photoperiod is the main diapause cue, why voltinism should change with climate is unclear.
comments.request: Make the temperature-voltinism connection clearer.
comments.quote: If photoperiod is the main cue for initiating diapause, why would voltinism change with climate change at all? Make this connection clearer.

comments.issue: The expectation that voltinism increases with warming is not explained.
comments.request: State the expectations and their rationale.
comments.quote: Again, as written, it's not clear why voltinism would increase in response to warming.

comments.issue: Whether generations are 'lost' if they would not have happened otherwise is unclear.
comments.request: Bring in the lost generation hypothesis earlier as framing.
comments.quote: Line 95: Are these generations “lost” if they wouldn’t have happened otherwise?

comments.issue: Predictions are hard to follow because the variables are introduced after them.
comments.request: Present the variables before the predictions.
comments.quote: Your predictions would be easier to follow if the variables you’re planning to test come before your predictions.

comments.issue: How last generation population size indicates voltinism is not justified; brood number may matter more than brood size.
comments.request: Provide rationale for the voltinism proxy.
comments.quote: it’s not clear to me how last generation population size is indicative of voltinism. Wouldn’t the number of broods matter more than the size of broods?

comments.issue: The meaning of 'mismatch' in Fig. 1 is unclear.
comments.request: Define mismatch.
comments.quote: I’m also struggling with what you mean by “mismatch” in Fig 1.

comments.issue: Findings at the end of the introduction do not read like introduction material.
comments.request: Reconsider this ending.
comments.quote: Lines 111-114: Maybe Ecology Letters wants you to end the intro with findings but this doesn’t feel like intro material.

comments.issue: Model and likelihood-ratio-test results are not tabulated.
comments.request: Add a supplemental table with models and LRT results.
comments.quote: It also might be helpful to have a supplemental table with models/LRT results.

comments.issue: A map of the study sites is missing.
comments.request: Add a map of sites.
comments.quote: Really cool that you have a dataset this large to work with! A map of sites would be helpful here.

comments.issue: What counts as an adequate sample size is not defined.
comments.request: Define adequate sample size for the models.
comments.quote: Line 128: What did you define as adequate sample size for the models?

comments.issue: The threshold for too much generation overlap is not given.
comments.request: State the threshold and consider a visual.
comments.quote: Line 169: What was the threshold for too much generation overlap? A visual might be helpful here.

comments.issue: Rationale for using last generation size to quantify voltinism is still missing.
comments.request: Justify it or use number of generations as the continuous variable.
comments.quote: Again, need rationale for why last generation size was used to quantify voltinism. Why not use number of generations as the continuous variable?

comments.issue: What a mismatch means in this paper is unclear, and mismatches may not be examined.
comments.request: Define mismatch or remove the framing.
comments.quote: Line 213: What would you define as a mismatch for this paper? I don't think you're actually examining mismatches?

comments.issue: Voltinism traits are not defined before the focal trait is chosen.
comments.request: Define voltinism traits in the introduction and justify the focus.
comments.quote: Would be worth defining various voltinism traits in the introductions and then describing which voltinism trait you will focus on and why.

comments.issue: The lost generation hypothesis appears too late in the methods.
comments.request: Move it earlier in the methods or introduction.
comments.quote: Lines 266-268: If the lost generation hypothesis is at the center of this paper, this should come earlier in the methods (maybe even come in the intro).

comments.issue: Some results are written in present tense.
comments.request: Use past tense throughout the results.
comments.quote: Make sure results are written in past tense throughout--some places were present tense used.

comments.issue: 'Increasing last generation size' and 'decreasing voltinism' refer to the same variable.
comments.request: Use one phrasing throughout the results.
comments.quote: Comparing “increasing last generation size” to “decreasing voltinism” is confusing here. These are the same variables, correct? If correct, use one phrasing throughout the results.

comments.issue: A figure reference is missing for this result.
comments.request: Refer to the relevant figure.
comments.quote: Lines 322-323: Referring to a figure for this (Fig 4?) would be helpful.

comments.issue: The positive-consequence result does not come across in Fig. 3, and the term is undefined.
comments.request: Clarify what counts as a positive consequence.
comments.quote: This result doesn't come across when looking at Fig 3. My understanding of Fig 3 is that only three species are experiencing population growth

comments.issue: Whether a smaller last generation size equals a 'lost' generation is not explained.
comments.request: Clearly connect last generation size to lost generations in the discussion.
comments.quote: Is a smaller last generation size a “lost” generation? Or just a smaller generation?

comments.issue: The link between cold winters/early frosts and climate change trends is not developed.
comments.request: Make predictions based on climate trends.
comments.quote: Line 374: Negative effects tend to happen when last generations experience cold winters or early frosts--what's the general trend with climate change?

comments.issue: Poleward range limits appear without connection to voltinism.
comments.request: Connect them clearly or remove.
comments.quote: Lines 377: Poleward range limits come out of nowhere here--connect this more clearly to increases in voltinism or remove.

comments.issue: Species examples are not connected to the literature.
comments.request: Discuss declining or trap-caught species from the literature.
comments.quote: You mention some specific species as examples here--would it be useful to bring in examples in context of the literature?

comments.issue: How photoperiod relates to the tested overwinter conditions is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the connection.
comments.quote: Line 395: How does photoperiod connect (or not?) to the overwinter conditions you tested?

comments.issue: Pesticide use appears without context.
comments.request: Connect it to the argument or remove.
comments.quote: Line 414: Pesticide use comes out of nowhere here.

comments.issue: The rejection of the hypothesis' generalizability is overstated, as it still holds for some species.
comments.request: Qualify the conclusion.
comments.quote: Lines 430-431: Mostly reject the generalizability of the lost generation hypothesis? It's still true for some species, correct?

comments.issue: Other drivers of insect declines are not considered in the conclusion.
comments.request: Discuss what else may drive declines.
comments.quote: In the intro, you say there are many factors contributing to insect declines in Ohio. Does anyone think it's just the lost generation hypothesis?

comments.issue: Figure captions with tags below the figures are hard to follow.
comments.request: Reformat the caption tags.
comments.quote: I had trouble following figure captions with the tags (A, B) below the figures and after the relevant caption.

comments.issue: Fig. 1 is hard to follow and needs clearer voltinism definitions.
comments.request: Reorganize the intro and clarify voltinism traits and alignment.
comments.quote: Fig 1: I really had trouble following this--might be easier with a reorganization of the intro and/or clearer definitions of voltinism traits and “alignment.”

comments.issue: Misalignment is not visible in Fig. 2A, unlike the top panel of 2B.
comments.request: Add an arrow pointing to misaligned generations.
comments.quote: Fig 2A/B: An arrow pointing to misaligned generations. Misalignment is clear to me int he top panel of 2B, but not so much in 2A.

comments.issue: Peak counts in Fig. 2C are hard to see.
comments.request: Add fitted curves to the predicted counts.
comments.quote: Fig 2C: Those peak counts are hard to see since points aren't as dense--curves fit to these predicted counts would be helpful.

comments.issue: The Fig. 2D y-axis label does not match log-population growth rate.
comments.request: Fix the axis label.
comments.quote: Fig 2D: Y-axis label is not consistent with log-population growth rate.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether Fig. 5B point colours duplicate the y-axis information.
comments.request: Clarify or remove the colour coding.
comments.quote: Fig 5B: Do points need to be color-coded by population trend? Is this redundant with the y-axis? If not, make more clear what the difference is.

title: Voltinism Shifts in Response to Climate Warming Generally Benefit Populations of Multivoltine Butterflies

study.system: Amazonian everwet forest; 22-yr seed-trap and climate data

editor_summary: Both reviewers see promise, but one raises large methodological concerns about imputation and analyses that need thorough attention.

reviews.assessment: Prizes the long-term dataset but raises major concerns about imputation, collinear OLS models, figure model choice and species-aggregated analysis.
strengths: analysis results interesting and potentially informative

comments.issue: Data imputation may be untrustworthy if meteorological covariance changes over time, affecting results.
comments.request: Test sensitivity of results to imputation, e.g. restrict RH analysis to 2008–2017.
comments.quote: Data imputation might be untrustworthy in this case if the covariance structure of the meteorological variables changes over time.

comments.issue: Consistency of measurements between pre-2012 and post-2012 instruments is unknown.
comments.request: Report consistency and covariance structure across the two instruments.
comments.quote: Is there any data on the consistency in measurements (and associated covariance structures) between pre 2012 and post 2012 instruments?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether abnormal years are real or artifacts of gap filling.
comments.request: Check whether abnormal years reflect data or imputation artifacts.
comments.quote: are abnormal years truly abnormal or due to gap filling (e.g. in Fig. 3)

comments.issue: A maximum std. dev. of 0.96 on missing-data days suggests imputed values cluster near the mean; downstream impact is unclear.
comments.request: Assess whether this imputation diagnostic biases downstream analyses.
comments.quote: is a maximum std. dev. of 0.96 on missing data days a good metrics?

comments.issue: Separate OLS models for highly correlated climate variables risk collinearity-driven effects.
comments.request: Use a multivariate regression including all climate variables.
comments.quote: Why conduct OLS for each climate variables (Line 262-267) given many of them are highly correlated (e.g. RH and TMIN)?

comments.issue: Statistical signal may reflect decadal trends while interannual patterns tell a different story.
comments.request: Explain the inconsistency between decadal and interannual timescales.
comments.quote: most of the statistical signal might be attributed to decadal trend while inter-annual variations seem to suggest different stories

comments.issue: Figure 4 displays the most extreme-effect models rather than the highest-R² models, with narrow, hard-to-interpret windows.
comments.request: Explain the model choice and improve interpretability of windows.
comments.quote: In Fig.4, why pick the model with most extreme effect instead of the model with highest R2?

comments.issue: Community-mean analysis assumes all species respond identically; species-level patterns are not examined.
comments.request: Contrast species-level temporal patterns with PCA.
comments.quote: This implicitly assumes that the temporal patterns across species are the same and all species respond to climatic variables in the same way

comments.issue: The promised contrast between forest responses is not actually provided.
comments.request: Provide the contrast or revise the motivation.
comments.quote: no real contrast is provided (both conditions just describe changing forest dynamics with no indication of direction or magnitude)

comments.issue: The argument implies more thermal/water stress when air is wetter, and TMAX shows no effect despite the thermal-stress mechanism.
comments.request: Reconcile the RH mechanism with the absence of a TMAX effect.
comments.quote: the logic reads counter-intuitive to me, which basically says more thermal/water stress when the air was wetter

comments.issue: Lines 158-161 and 169-171 repeat information.
comments.request: Remove the repetition.
comments.quote: Line 158-161 and 169-171, repeat information.

comments.issue: The sentence about 10.5% of days without data reads confusingly.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence.
comments.quote: “No variable had data for 10.5% of the days” reads confusing, please rephrase.

comments.issue: The justification for using RH_ave is weak; RH_max and RH_min are not tested.
comments.request: Test RH_max and RH_min and compare their slopes.
comments.quote: Why not test different role of RH\_max and RH\_min and see whether they have similar slopes as RH\_ave?

comments.issue: The antecedent of 'Latter' at line 321 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the reference.
comments.quote: Line 321, Latter of what?

comments.issue: The flower-mediated hypothesis seems more plausible than the thermal-stress explanation.
comments.request: Consider emphasizing this alternative explanation.
comments.quote: Line 356-359, this is an interesting hypothesis, which seems to be more plausible than the thermal stress explanation above.

comments.issue: The meaning of I (irradiance?) in Figure 2 regression equations is not specified.
comments.request: Specify I in the Figure 2 caption.
comments.quote: Line 604 Fig 2, what does I mean in the regression equations in panel a, irradiance? Please specify in the caption.

comments.issue: The right Y-axis for Seed/Flower Production is missing from Figure 4 sub-panels.
comments.request: Add the right Y-axis as in Figure 2b.
comments.quote: Line 611 Fig 4, the right Y-axis for Seed/Flower Production is missing for the sub-panels.

comments.issue: RMSE is not defined in Fig. S7.
comments.request: Define RMSE as root mean squared error.
comments.quote: Fig S7 -RMSE is root mean squared error.

reviews.assessment: Strongly positive; finds the study excellent and the conclusions appropriately limited, suggesting only more discussion of next steps.
strengths: clear methods and sufficient supplementary material
conclusions limited to what was found

comments.issue: Next steps for evaluating the effects, particularly Tmin, are not articulated.
comments.request: Add future directions, especially for Tmin effects.
comments.quote: It would be interesting to articulate more at the end about the next steps in evaluating the effects found, particularly with Tmin, in the discussion or the conclusions as future directions.

title: Seed Production and 22 Years of Climatic Changes in an Everwet Neotropical Forest

study.system: global island avifauna; hand-wing index and species-area relationships

editor_summary: Editor: reviewers acknowledge the importance, novelty and dataset, but raise many concerns; the introduction and discussion lack clarity and conviction, the scale-dependency explanation is unclear, and methods issues need meticulous attention.

reviews.assessment: Impressive global dataset, but the conceptual justification for scale-dependence and the interpretation of community mean HWI are not convincing.
strengths: global coverage across all zoogeographical realms

comments.issue: Theoretical justification for expecting dispersal to affect SAR slopes more at small than large scales is unconvincing.
comments.request: Strengthen the theoretical justification for the scale-dependence prediction.
comments.quote: I was not fully convinced of the theoretical justification for why dispersal should have a greater impact on species-area slopes at small scales over large scales

comments.issue: Insights from nested SAR models do not transfer directly to the non-nested island SARs studied here.
comments.request: Justify using nested-SAR theory for non-nested island relationships.
comments.quote: it’s not clear to me that the logic and insights derived from theoretical models of *nested* species -area relationships

comments.issue: Claim that elevated dispersal steepens log-log SAR slopes holds only under unstated assumptions.
comments.request: State the assumptions under which dispersal steepens SAR slopes.
comments.quote: Elevated dispersal is expected to increase richness at all scales, and only under a very particular set of unstated assumptions would this be expected to increase a log-log slope

comments.issue: Unclear why the strength of the target effect should depend on dispersal rate.
comments.request: Explain the logic linking target effect and dispersal rate.
comments.quote: It’s not clear to me why the strength of the target effect should depend on dispersal rate

comments.issue: The diminishing-returns argument applied to large scales applies equally to small scales, contradicting the Figure 1 cartoon.
comments.request: Reconcile the argument and Figure 1 with this inconsistency.
comments.quote: This argument that the authors only apply to “large scales” also applies to “small scales”

comments.issue: Chave et al.'s scale-dependence arises at a single-individual limit and does not apply to the islands studied.
comments.request: Reconsider the relevance of Chave et al. to these scales.
comments.quote: the observed scale-dependence shown in this figure is due to defining “small spatial scale” at the limit of a single individual

comments.issue: Prior studies are misrepresented as having addressed scale-dependent dispersal effects on SARs.
comments.request: Correct the description of these prior studies.
comments.quote: I would not say that Finaly et al., Hillebrand et al., or Walentowitz et al. can be claimed to have addressed scale-dependent effects of dispersal ability on SARs

comments.issue: Wing shape and HWI reflect foraging mode and habitat constraints, not only dispersal ability.
comments.request: Acknowledge that HWI is not a pure dispersal measure.
comments.quote: wing shape reflects a variety of other evolutionary contraints as well based on habit (e.g. foraging mode) and habitat

comments.issue: HWI values are not comparable across orders, so averaging across orders is hard to interpret.
comments.request: Compare HWI within taxa or use percentile-based measures.
comments.quote: an HWI of 30 for A. poliogaster is only in the 28th percentile of HWI for all Accipitriformes meaning it’s a weak disperser for a bird with the various constraints of living like a hawk

comments.issue: Community mean HWI over realms may reflect taxonomic composition rather than dispersal ability.
comments.request: Control for taxonomic composition when interpreting community mean HWI.
comments.quote: the community mean could be lower simply because it contains a greater proportion of species with a lifestyle that is correlated with low HWI

comments.issue: Alternative analyses (within families/orders, or z-scored HWI) are proposed to isolate dispersal effects.
comments.request: Repeat analyses within families or orders and use percentile-based HWI.
comments.quote: Rather than calculating the mean of raw HWI scores, transform each species' HWI into a z-score or percentile based on the mean and standard deviation for its respective family or order

comments.issue: Skeptical that contrasting small versus large spatial scales is justified; a single cross-realm analysis may suffice.
comments.request: Justify the two-scale design or simplify to one analysis.
comments.quote: I am currently skeptical of the justification for contrasting “small” versus “large” spatial scales as used here

comments.issue: Terms 'within zoogeographic realms' and 'within and across zoogeographic realms' are misleading.
comments.request: Use clearer terms for the two spatial scales.
comments.quote: When I first read “across zoogeographic realms”, my interpretation was that it referred to lumping together islands from across different zoogeographic realms into a single species-area analysis

comments.issue: The actual spatial extents of the two scales are not quantified.
comments.request: Quantitatively describe the spatial extents of both scales.
comments.quote: it would be useful to more quantitatively describe these different scales

comments.issue: The Neighbor Index of terrestrial isolation is unexplained, including the 13 buffer distances.
comments.request: Explain the Neighbor Index and its buffer distances.
comments.quote: Can you provide more explanation about this Neighbor Index measure of terrestrial isolation?

comments.issue: Figure 2 is first cited after Figure 3.
comments.request: Cite figures in order.
comments.quote: Figure 2 is not referred to for the first time until after Figure 3.

comments.issue: Slope uncertainty is not shown or propagated; the uncertain Palearctic slope has high leverage.
comments.request: Show slope uncertainty and weight models by slope standard errors.
comments.quote: should the authors incorporate that error into the analyses, e.g. by inverse-weighting by standard error of slope estimates

comments.issue: Figure 3 points are not linked across panels or to other figures.
comments.request: Colour-code Figure 3 points by zoogeographic realm.
comments.quote: consider color-coding the data points by zoogeographic realm, which will help the reader link points between panels

reviews.assessment: Well written, globally comprehensive test of dispersal effects on SARs, with one concern about inflated island richness from range polygons.
strengths: unveils how dispersal limitation affects SARs

comments.issue: Intersecting range polygons with islands inflates richness and may bias SAR shape differently across realms.
comments.request: Include range size in the model and validate richness estimates.
comments.quote: these range polygons presumably encompass many islands on which species are not present, inflating species occupancy and richness

comments.issue: The negative or flat Palearctic SAR is hard to understand and may reflect species richness inflation.
comments.request: Explain why the Palearctic SAR is negative or flat.
comments.quote: Why do you find a negative (or even flat) SAR in the Palearctic?

comments.issue: Island groups used in the small-scale analysis are not described.
comments.request: Provide more detail on the island groups.
comments.quote: What are these island groups? More detail should be provided

comments.issue: The wording 'within and across zoogeographical realms' is confusing.
comments.request: Explain the scales early and use small/large scale terms.
comments.quote: the wording “within and across” zoogeographical realms is confusing

comments.issue: Estimated model coefficients are missing from the bracketed statistics.
comments.request: Include estimated model coefficients in brackets.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to also include the estimated model coefficients in the statistical information provided within brackets

comments.issue: Fig. 3A and 3B are switched in the text.
comments.request: Correct the panel references.
comments.quote: Note also that Fig. 3A and 3B are switched in the text.

comments.issue: The link between the competition-colonisation trade-off and area effects at macro-scales is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify or reconsider invoking the trade-off at macro-scales.
comments.quote: I find this paragraph confusing, as the link between the competition-colonisation trade-off and the effect of area on richness is not clear

comments.issue: The result on L468 may be an artifact of false species occurrences from range polygon intersection.
comments.request: Check this result against the richness inflation issue.
comments.quote: Is this a real result (a nice one by the way!), or could it be the result of false species occurrence resulting from the intersection of range polygons with islands

comments.issue: The seed dispersal example does not follow from the preceding idea; the transition is odd.
comments.request: Improve the transition or remove the example.
comments.quote: The seed dispersal example does not really follow from the previous idea. This transition is a bit odd

reviews.assessment: Timely, well-written and well-analysed, but the main concern is that different datasets are used at different scales, plus several methodological questions.

comments.issue: The common term ISAR (island species-area relationship) is not used.
comments.request: Use the term ISAR to follow common practice.
comments.quote: why not using the term ISAR for “islands-species area relationship” to stick with common practice in the field

comments.issue: The connection between island area and expected richness, and how low dispersal raises richness at large scales, is unclear.
comments.request: Reformulate the argument and explain the mechanism.
comments.quote: How low dispersal increase species richness at large scale? What will be the mechanism?

comments.issue: Lines 141-150 contain confusing method details that belong later.
comments.request: Remove method details from this section.
comments.quote: It might be helpful to lighten the text by removing details of the methods here

comments.issue: Slopes come from Matthews 2019 at one scale but from the new dataset at the other, risking inconsistency across scales.
comments.request: Recreate ISAR slopes at small scales from the new dataset for consistency.
comments.quote: why not recreate the slope for ISAR using the dataset recovered in the second part of the study?

comments.issue: The explanatory power of HWI relative to AreaScale, Gamma and isolation is not assessed.
comments.request: Run univariate regressions for each predictor.
comments.quote: I’ll be very curious to see how much variance the HWI captures relative to AreaScale, Gamma, or even isolation

comments.issue: CWM is an unweighted mean; weighting by species range could better represent communities.
comments.request: Consider weighting CWM by species distributional range.
comments.quote: Why not using species distributional range instead of abundance to weight CMW: species with large range will have more weight in the CMW than species with restricted distribution

comments.issue: The random effect on line 239 repeats the same CWM value and may not be needed.
comments.request: Justify or remove the random effect.
comments.quote: If for a realm, we have 3 SAR, then the same CMW value will be repeated 3 time, how a random effect the name of the realms repeated 3 time will be useful here

comments.issue: The source of the spatial polygons for prediction 2 is not stated.
comments.request: State the polygon data source.
comments.quote: For prediciton 2: Please can you mention the source? Is it Global Administrative Areas?

comments.issue: It is unclear what '9 minor islands as spatial polygons' means on line 251.
comments.request: Clarify what these islands are.
comments.quote: Line 251: Sorry I don’t get it what do you mean by 9 minor islands as spatial polygons?

comments.issue: 'Spatial regression models' on line 327 is undefined.
comments.request: Explain what the spatial regression models are.
comments.quote: Line 327: what do you mean by spatial regression models? Is it spatial autoregressive models?

comments.issue: The purpose of the step on line 330 is not clear.
comments.request: Explain the rationale for this step.
comments.quote: Line 330: the same problem. I don’t see the point to do that.

comments.issue: The collinearity check is presented after the modelling strategy.
comments.request: Move the collinearity check before the modelling strategy.
comments.quote: The fact that you checked collinearity should be explicated before you present the modeling strategy.

comments.issue: The refitting of a spatial regression on line 354 seems redundant; the section could be moved earlier.
comments.request: Reorganize this section.
comments.quote: why you need to refit again a spatial regression? Again, maybe this a question of origination, then you should move up this section

title: Avian Dispersal Ability Shapes Species–Area Relationships on Islands Worldwide

study.system: North American demersal fish; long-term occupancy data and phylogeny

editor_summary: Reviewers agree the question is important and the approach elegant; editor asks for a much improved version addressing methodological and technical issues, with a clear point-by-point response.

reviews.assessment: Loves the introduction and finds the topic exciting, but has five questions about the metapopulation-speciation link and finds the paper structurally stuck.
strengths: compelling summary of speciation and persistence research

comments.issue: Stable subsets of localities can sustain a metapopulation and allow speciation even while other localities blink in and out, possibly explaining the null result.
comments.request: Consider this source-sink-like dynamic in the interpretation.
comments.quote: so long as a subset of localities or subcompartments of the metapopulation are stable, the metapopulation will persist and speciation may be possible even if many other localities are blinking in and out

comments.issue: A large metapopulation for one 'species' may comprise several unrecognized incipient species that go extinct before recognition, biasing conclusions.
comments.request: Address this bias explicitly.
comments.quote: What if a large metapopulation for a "species" was actually composed of several small metapopulations for several unrecognized incipient species?

comments.issue: Different taxa may experience different disturbance magnitudes in surveyed areas, creating artificial differences in resilience.
comments.request: Control for or discuss environmentally driven differences in resilience.
comments.quote: what if different taxa just experience different magnitudes of disturbance in the areas where occupancy was surveyed?

comments.issue: Commonness is not biased by metapopulation size, so common and rare species may receive similar scores and the cartoon may mislead.
comments.request: Clarify the interpretation of commonness.
comments.quote: a common and rare species may have a similar 'commonness' score simply because proportionally c and e are similar

comments.issue: Metapopulation size correlates with environment range, gene flow and speciation-lottery tickets, so persistence cannot be isolated as the mechanism.
comments.request: Explain how persistence is isolated from these correlated factors.
comments.quote: How do we isolate persistence as the mechanism for any correlation?

comments.issue: The role of traits in the story is unclear and they could be cut unless integrated more strongly.
comments.request: State explicitly what traits add, or remove them.
comments.quote: I wasn't 100% sure how traits fit into the story.

comments.issue: The manuscript is stuck between a methods paper and an empirical paper and should be pushed in one direction.
comments.request: Decide whether this is a framework or empirical paper and structure it accordingly.
comments.quote: the manuscript is currently stuck somewhere awkwardly between a methods paper and a traditional empirical paper

comments.issue: The framework may quantify metapopulation dynamics at a scale irrelevant to speciation, limiting its applicability.
comments.request: Discuss the scale mismatch and its implications.
comments.quote: the metapopulation dynamics are quantified at a scale that doesn't capture the scale that is relevant for speciation

comments.issue: Arguments should be written more tangibly for a wider audience.
comments.request: Rewrite key arguments to be more accessible.
comments.quote: examples of places where arguments could be written more tangibly so their full importance could be understood by a wider audience

comments.issue: Context for Question 2 at line 120 is lost.
comments.request: Clarify whether clade-specific rates imply similar dynamics among close relatives.
comments.quote: Line 120: Question 2 I've lost context for.

comments.issue: Why the analysis is at species-region level, and whether range-spanning species are split, is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the species-region unit.
comments.quote: Line 248: Why species-region? Are there cases where a species is found in different regions, thus the metapopulation is analyzed separately in each region?

comments.issue: Epsilon and tau are used a section before they are defined.
comments.request: Define symbols before use.
comments.quote: I believe epsilon and tau are first used a whole section before they are defined

comments.issue: Much of the paper is written in statistical rather than biological language.
comments.request: Clarify statements for the intended biological audience.
comments.quote: In general I found a lot of the paper written in statistical rather than biological language, which could be remedied given the intended audience.

comments.issue: How the product at line 316 was calculated is not explained.
comments.request: Provide details of the calculation.
comments.quote: Line 316: Details on how the product was calculated would be helpful.

comments.issue: Analyses assume causation while all variables may influence each other; the assignment of dependent/independent variables affects interpretation.
comments.request: Justify the causal direction of the models.
comments.quote: Some of the analyses assume a causative relationship between variables, but arguments could be made that all variables impact each other.

comments.issue: In Figure 2B the medians and black crosses do not overlap the data, and the gray dashed lines are too light.
comments.request: Correct the figure and improve the line visibility.
comments.quote: Why in B are the medians and black crosses not overlapping the data?

comments.issue: Figure 3 shows branches shifting colours several times without explanation.
comments.request: Explain the colour reconstructions.
comments.quote: Also some branches shift colors several times (anagenically?)

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the raw or transformed scale is more meaningful; squishing may affect phylogenetic signal estimates.
comments.request: Justify the scale used.
comments.quote: Still a little unsure of whether it makes more biological sense to look at the raw or transformed scale - the transformed scale squishes everything, which I could see affecting estimates of phylogenetic signal.

reviews.assessment: Impressed by the effort and novel framing; asks to clarify how persistence can matter for diversification despite the null result.
strengths: important start on an important question

reviews.assessment: Excellent, well-written and methodologically rigorous paper; recommends acceptance with minor revisions.

comments.issue: The abbreviation KM2 is not explained.

comments.issue: The discussion at line 442 belongs in the main text, not the supplement.

comments.issue: One line-level copy edit ('that' instead of 'which' at line 526).

editor_summary: All three reviewers found it useful and high quality but had many comments; writing could be easier on the reader in style and presentation for a general readership.

title: Plant Species Better Adapted to Climate Change Need Agricultural Extensification to Persist

editor_summary: Two reviewers: one very positive with minor suggestions, one critical requiring significant revisions; the critical comments must be fully addressed before further consideration.

reviews.assessment: Strong, well-replicated study showing network-identified central taxa act as keystones in a manipulative experiment; ready to publish with minor additions.

powerful demonstration that network analyses predict experimental outcomes
