title: Wind Patterns Influence the Dispersal and Assembly of North American Soil Fungal Communities

study.system: UK woodland invertebrates; citizen-science occurrence records

editor_summary: Praises the study; all reviewers worried about the connectivity–cover correlation, which must be addressed; clarify novelty relative to previous studies and consider analysing change over time.

reviews.assessment: Impressive data-rich study, but the connectivity measure is spuriously collinear with cover and the analysis misses temporal and mediation aspects.
strengths: particularly nice, data-rich example for invertebrates

comments.issue: Novelty of configuration effects being stronger at low cover is limited.
comments.request: Emphasise the data-rich invertebrate example as the advance.
comments.quote: the concept of ‘configuration effects’ (such as isolation/connectivity) being more important at low levels of habitat cover is actually not very novel.

comments.issue: Connectivity metric is mathematically spuriously collinear with woodland cover.
comments.request: Use normalised or median current flow instead of cumulative.
comments.quote: cumulative Amps is going to be very strongly (actually spuriously) collinear with woodland cover.

comments.issue: Figure S1 correlation matrix is ambiguous about what is correlated with what.
comments.request: Clarify the variables and units in Figure S1.
comments.quote: in Figure S1, it would pay to clarify exactly what is being correlated with what.

comments.issue: Insensitivity to buffer and resistance settings indicates the connectivity measure is not meaningful.
comments.request: Recalculate connectivity to break the spurious cover correlation.
comments.quote: Again, the lack of any meaningful difference in buffer/resistance settings is a marker that cumulative current flow is a poor independent measure of connectivity.

comments.issue: Conifer resistance set equal to broadleaf is implausible; other resistance scenarios untested.
comments.request: Test alternative resistance assumptions in sensitivity analyses.
comments.quote: it seems very unlikely that setting conifer resistance to be the same as broadleaf woodland resistance is a ‘good’ choice.

comments.issue: Cover and connectivity are not independent; models omit indirect mediating pathways.
comments.request: Use a structural equation model partitioning direct, indirect and interactive effects.
comments.quote: Partitioning these direct, indirect and interactive effects would require a structural equation modelling approach.

comments.issue: Figure 3 mixes total woodland connectivity with broadleaf cover and blurs species-group labels.
comments.request: Clearly distinguish total versus broadleaf woodland in caption and text.
comments.quote: it turns out that this is because the y axis refers to connectivity of ‘Total’ woodland (broadleaf and conifer), whereas the x axis refers only to cover of broadleaf woodland.

comments.issue: Derivation of the connectivity opportunity space dashed line is not described; 'entire CI' undefined.
comments.request: Explain how the dashed line was derived and define 'entire CI'.
comments.quote: There is very little description in the text or figure caption about how the location of this dashed line was derived.

comments.issue: Claim that top-left cells gain occurrence with connectivity seems implausible and unproven.
comments.request: Provide evidence for increasing occurrence in the top-left region.
comments.quote: it seems impossible to believe that the cells in the top left of Fig 3a (which already have some of the highest occurrence probabilities and highest connectivity values), would show any significant increasing in occurrence within increasing connectivity?

comments.issue: Colour scales in Figure 3a and 3b are confusing; 0.6 baseline occurrence seems unlikely.
comments.request: Use one absolute occurrence-probability colour scale for both panels.
comments.quote: The third issue is the perplexing colour-shading scales in Fig3a vs 3b. Both apparently relate to occurrence of broadleaf woodland species, but it is hard to make head or tail of their meaning.

comments.issue: Fine-scale map in Figure 3c appears redundant and its practical message is unclear.
comments.request: Rethink the general message and use of Figure 3c.
comments.quote: Even if the connectivity measure can be properly un-linked from woodland cover, I think the authors would need to think carefully about what general message they want to convey with Fig3c.

comments.issue: No explicit test of how temporal change in cover and connectivity affects occurrence.
comments.request: Analyse time period as a fixed effect within the existing data.
comments.quote: This is not the same thing as being able to explicitly test the fixed effect of ‘time period’ and ask whether 1x1km grid cells with higher/lower connectivity in 2015 vs 1990 had higher/lower probability of occurrence.

comments.issue: Message implies planting woodland everywhere; conservation value of non-woodland areas ignored.
comments.request: Consider non-woodland conservation value and where woodland creation is acceptable.
comments.quote: Perhaps not all areas should be ‘available’ for woodland creation, and if not, then how is this factored into the analysis

comments.issue: Table 1 caption placement and low information content.
comments.request: Move the few values into the text.
comments.quote: Table 1 has the caption below the table, rather than above, and more generally the table has very low information content for the space it takes up.

comments.issue: Buffer radius units and 'block size' terminology are cryptic and unexplained.
comments.request: Explain units, blocks and Figure S1 buffer values.
comments.quote: In Fig. S1, yet another unit scale is given for buffer radius (20, 40, 80, 160) and there is no explanation given in the caption.

reviews.assessment: Well-done citizen-science study; asks to trim extraneous methods and move practical recommendations into the discussion.
strengths: great job explaining methods and implications

comments.issue: Extraneous climate and conifer material in methods distracts from the results.
comments.request: Remove or greatly reduce these sections.
comments.quote: The largest comment for the manuscript is that there is extraneous information in the methods that distract from the clear and concise results (and discussion) presented.

comments.issue: Discussion of where to create woodland is buried in the results section.
comments.request: Move lines 318-329 to the discussion.
comments.quote: The other major comment is that the discussion of where best places to create new woodland is buried in the results section in lines 318-329.

comments.issue: Introduction sets up a false dichotomy between fragmentation and connectivity.
comments.request: Clarify what the two frameworks are and how they relate.
comments.quote: The section on fragmentation versus connectivity in the second paragraph of the introduction sets up a false dichotomy between the two.

comments.issue: Nature of recording schemes and why taxa were separated is not explained.
comments.request: Explain what recording schemes are and why they were separated.
comments.quote: In the methods, the nature of the recording schemes is not immediately apparent. A little explanation of what these are and why they were separated would help explain the subsequent analyses.

comments.issue: Coniferous forest material appears in methods but is used only for connectivity.
comments.request: Reduce conifer information to the necessary minimum.
comments.quote: The inclusion of coniferous forests in multiple sections of the methods but then not using this data apart from the connectivity measurements makes it difficult to follow.

comments.issue: Inherent correlation between connectivity and forest cover is not mentioned.
comments.request: Acknowledge it, especially for new woodland creation.
comments.quote: the inherent correlation between connectivity and forest cover (as seen in figure s3, s5) should be mentioned, especially regarding the creation of new woodland which would necessarily increase connectivity to some degree or another.

comments.issue: 2 line-level copy edits (L25-27, L87-88)
comments.quote: “wood” used instead of woodland. This can probably be broader of a statement as well.

comments.issue: Connectivity and fragmentation need short descriptors where they are contrasted.
comments.request: Define the two terms in this context.
comments.quote: Need a short descriptor for connectivity and fragmentation in these contexts since they are contrasted here.

comments.issue: Unclear that recording schemes refer to how data were collected for different taxa.
comments.request: Clarify the meaning of recording schemes.
comments.quote: Unclear that the recording schemes are referencing the ways data were collected for different taxa.

comments.issue: Unnecessary references to non-broadleaf groups at two lines.
comments.request: Remove those references.
comments.quote: Line 242 & 249: Don’t need to reference non-broadleaf groups

comments.issue: Connectivity opportunity space terminology sounds too similar to an earlier term.
comments.request: Rename or drop this term.
comments.quote: This connectivity opportunity space is used more, and terminology is very similar sounding for both.

reviews.assessment: Exciting, influential study, but three substantive issues and an unconvincing prioritisation exercise need attention.
strengths: two time periods and climatic variables considered

comments.issue: Connectivity effect may be an artefact of forcing strictly linear cover effects.
comments.request: Fit alternative non-linear cover models without connectivity and compare via BIC.
comments.quote: Connectivity and cover are highly correlated, and the model formula forces them to have strictly linear effects on the link function.

comments.issue: Prioritisation exercise is an unconvincing afterthought adding little value.
comments.request: Drop or radically change the prioritisation exercise.
comments.quote: The ‘prioritisation’ exercise feels like an afterthought to the main analysis, and I’m not convinced it adds value to the paper.

comments.issue: Prioritisation ignores cover increases and omits conifer fixed effects.
comments.request: Account for cover effects and include coniferous woodland fixed effects.
comments.quote: Evaluating the ‘potential to increase connectivity’ without also considering the effects of increasing woodland cover per se doesn’t make much sense.

comments.issue: Prioritisation outputs are confusing and not usable by practitioners.
comments.request: Make the map actionable or remove the practitioner framing.
comments.quote: I personally would not feel comfortable presenting the map in fig. 3C to a practitioner and trying to explain what it means for them.

comments.issue: Methods behind Figure 3 (opportunity space, 'entire CI', thresholding) are missing.
comments.request: Describe how Figure 3 and the recommendation categories were produced.
comments.quote: All the methods behind Fig 3 are missing from the manuscript

comments.issue: Prioritisation exercise is hardly discussed in the discussion.
comments.request: Remove the prioritisation aspect or discuss it properly.
comments.quote: The prioritisation exercise is hardly discussed in the discussion (except for the sentence line 359 “we discuss” which is not followed up).

comments.issue: Grand-mean coefficients may not represent the average species; predictions should be averaged.
comments.request: Average occupancy predictions from all species across the 2D cover-connectivity space.
comments.quote: With these correlations, I think there is no guarantee that the relationships shown by taking the ‘grand mean’ of each coefficient, as shown in Table 1 and Fig. 2, represent the response of 'the average species’.

comments.issue: Figure symbols and elements are not explained in the legends.
comments.request: Explain all symbols and elements in the figure legends.
comments.quote: There are a number of symbols/elements on figures that are not explained in the legends.

comments.issue: Main result declared in the title is absent from the abstract.
comments.request: Report the title result in the abstract.
comments.quote: The main result declared in the title isn’t given in the abstract (different results are given instead)

comments.issue: '15 taxa' is uninformative out of context.
comments.request: Give numbers of orders or say 15 recording schemes.
comments.quote: “15 taxa” doesn’t mean much out of context, either give the no. of unique invertebrate orders or say “15 recording schemes”

comments.issue: 0.122 is reported without units in the abstract.
comments.request: Add units.
comments.quote: 11 0.122 without units means nothing

comments.issue: Number of significant positive main effects is uninterpretable without considering interactions.
comments.request: Interpret main effects together with the interactions.
comments.quote: talking about no. significant positive main effects without considering the presence of interactions is difficult to interpret

comments.issue: Introduction paragraph conflates connectivity and fragmentation and uses unclear terminology.
comments.request: Clarify the relationship and the terminology.
comments.quote: This paragraph is confused/confusing because if connectivity is conceptually the opposite of fragmentation, every study of one is a study of the other.

comments.issue: Supplementary methods need cross-references and subdivision.
comments.request: Insert cross-references and split into appendices.
comments.quote: Generally – cross-references need to be inserted to the supplementary methods. It may be better to subdivide the supplementary methods as Appendix A,B,C to aid this.

comments.issue: Land cover maps are mentioned before they are explained.
comments.request: Add a cross-reference to the later explanation.
comments.quote: land cover maps are mentioned before the section where they’re explained – give a cross-reference to later

comments.issue: Whether the 2020 revised LCM series was used is unclear.
comments.request: State the LCM version and warn about classification changes.
comments.quote: clarify whether you used the 2020 revised version of the LCM series that is suitable for change detection

comments.issue: CV is inappropriate for temperature, which can take values below zero.
comments.request: Clarify whether CV or variance was used.
comments.quote: CV does not make sense for a variable that can potentially take values below zero.

comments.issue: Native resolution and processing of soil moisture data are unclear.
comments.request: State the resolution and any interpolation or upscaling.
comments.quote: clarify the native resolution of the soil moisture data, and whether any interpolation or upscaling was done.

comments.issue: Whether only woodland cells receive connectivity values, and how NA cells are averaged, is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify connectivity values for non-woodland cells and 1-km averaging.
comments.quote: clarify whether this means that only woodland cells have a valid connectivity value (non-woodland cells would be NA). If so, how does this affect the averaging to 1 km squares?

comments.issue: Matern SPDE spatial autocorrelation is not stated.
comments.request: State that the Matern SPDE represents spatial autocorrelation.
comments.quote: state that the Matern SPDE model represents spatial autocorrelation

comments.issue: Second-order random walk effects are unexplained.
comments.request: Give a reference and explain the hierarchical unit and why they are random.
comments.quote: For example, how many degrees of freedom does each random effect soak up? What is actually the hierarchical unit that makes this effect ‘random’

comments.issue: Standardisation approach and use of identical variables across models should be noted.
comments.request: Mention that the same variables were kept for every model.
comments.quote: It’s worth mentioning that despite this, you kept the variables the same for every model (as I assume you did, otherwise the predictions would not be comparable).

comments.issue: Overlap between deciduous- and conifer-associated species and non-categorized models is unclear.
comments.request: Report overlap species and models outside the three categories.
comments.quote: clarify whether some species can be both deciduous-associated and coniferous associated; if so, how many species are in this overlap group.

comments.issue: Main-effect statement ignores that the credible interval only holds at mean cover.
comments.request: Clarify the main effect in the presence of interactions, also in the Fig. 1 legend.
comments.quote: clarify that this is a positive main effect in the presence of interactions; so the credible interval is valid for the slope at the mean levels of broadleaf and coniferous woodland cover.

comments.issue: Calling locations species-rich ignores extrapolation of species distributions.
comments.request: Soften the species-rich claim.
comments.quote: It’s not safe to say these locations are “species-rich”, because species’ real distributions will be extrapolated to other locations with similar explanatory variables

comments.issue: Unclear phrase at L356 and ambiguous phrase at L362.
comments.request: Rephrase both phrases.
comments.quote: “above the greater benefits” – unclear what you mean and potentially self-contradictory

comments.issue: Claim about nearly all taxa being negative was not shown in the results.
comments.request: Show coefficient boxplots or scatter plots of the three coefficients.
comments.quote: this wasn’t shown anywhere in the results, and I’d like to see it in a figure, e.g. boxplots of the raw coefficients, or better still, scatter plots of the 3 related coefficients

comments.issue: Spiders result is over-interpreted without a balanced prediction space.
comments.request: Compare balanced model predictions before interpreting.
comments.quote: I think this is over-interpretation of the results concerning spiders.

comments.issue: 'Most important' is imprecise and value-laden.
comments.request: Justify importance and comparisons.
comments.quote: “most important” is imprecise and value-laden. What makes you think it’s important? Compared to what?

comments.issue: 'Consistently seen' claim is not robustly shown across species.
comments.request: Demonstrate consistency robustly and clarify the conditional-benefits phrase.
comments.quote: I wouldn’t agree with “consistently seen” unless it was more robustly shown to be consistent across species.

comments.issue: Sentence at L418 misattributes what is considered unvarying.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence.
comments.quote: rephrase because it’s the woodland quality/features that are considered unvarying, not the cover and connectivity considered homogeneous.

comments.issue: Final claim about greatest benefits is untested against other actions.
comments.request: Soften the claim or test other actions.
comments.quote: The final claim “will have the greatest benefits for overall species occurrence” is not supported, because you haven’t attempted to test the benefits of other kinds of action

comments.issue: 4 line-level copy edits
comments.quote: think you mean all “explanatory” variables here; the response variables are also “spatial”

title: Connectivity Benefits Most Woodland Invertebrate Species but Only in Landscapes With Low Woodland Cover

study.system: woody plants; mycorrhizal types; global distributions and phylogeny

editor_summary: Editor thanks two specialist referees and rejects the current version to allow time to rework it, warmly encouraging a resubmission that addresses the referees' ideas.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, well-designed and appropriate study whose conclusions are supported; asks for data-coverage checks and consistent terminology.

comments.issue: Coverage of dual and EM genera is not reported and phylogenetic gaps are unassessed.
comments.request: Report the numbers explicitly and assess representation.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to report on these numbers explicitly and provide some context: are ECM/dual plant families/orders well represented or are there large phylogenetic gaps?

comments.issue: The impact of data incompleteness is not tested with sensitivity analyses.
comments.request: Test inclusion of 'potential' dual genera and resimulate data error.
comments.quote: Teste et al. list 200 ‘potential’ dual genera. What if you include these as dual in the analyses? Do you reach the same conclusion?

comments.issue: Geographic range, ecological niche, niche space, climatic range and climatic niche are used inconsistently.
comments.request: Use these terms consistently.
comments.quote: there is not a very consistent use of terms like geographic range, ecological niche, niche space, climatic range, and climatic niche

comments.issue: Phylogenetic relationships were not tested at the species level.
comments.request: Test phylogenetic influence at species level.
comments.quote: The influence of phylogenetic relationships was not tested on species level.

comments.issue: Goals are not listed in the same order as discussed in the methods.
comments.request: Align the goal list with the methods order.
comments.quote: it would be helpful to list the goals in the same order as they are discussed on the methods

comments.issue: The reasoning for using biomes as a proxy for ecological niche is missing.
comments.request: Explain why biomes proxy the niche.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to include the reasoning on why biomes are used as a proxy for ecological niche.

comments.issue: Whether shrubs are included and how the woody/tree terminology relates to them is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify shrub inclusion and use 'woody' terminology.
comments.quote: So does the analyses also includes those shrubs? If yes, it might be better to address the taxa as ‘woody’ rather than ‘trees’.

comments.issue: The claim that associations evolved independently is not supported; independent evolution can still show phylogenetic clustering.
comments.request: Revise the independence statement.
comments.quote: This statement is not supported by the analysis. Traits can evolve independently and still show high phylogenetic clustering/conservatism.

comments.issue: A test possible with the available data (following Wang et al. 2021) is not performed.
comments.request: Consider performing the suggested test.
comments.quote: In principle, with the data at hand this can be tested

comments.issue: 'Mycorrhizal group' is used alongside 'mycorrhizal type'.
comments.request: Consistently use 'mycorrhizal type'.
comments.quote: I would recommend to consistently use ‘mycorrhizal type’ throughout the manuscript (and not mycorrhizal group).

reviews.assessment: Generally well-written and valuable addition; suggests clarifying results, enlarging figures and condensing the discussion, plus many specific points.
strengths: showcases recent insights into mycorrhizal ecology

comments.issue: Text in Figures S2 and S3 is too small to read comfortably.

comments.quote: the text in Figures S2 and S3 appears too small to read comfortably

comments.issue: The Discussion repeats Results points and needs condensing.

comments.issue: The abiotic and biotic factors influencing AM and EM abundance and diversity are not mentioned.

comments.issue: Read (1991) should be supplemented with a more recent reference.

comments.issue: Priority effects and mycorrhizal turnover across tree life stages are not discussed.

comments.issue: 'Certain situations' at L66-67 is vague.

comments.issue: The possibility of inhibitory effects of dual mycorrhizal relationships is not mentioned.

comments.quote: it should be worth mentioning that dual-mycorrhizal relationships can result in an inhibitory effect too

comments.issue: Species with regionally varying mycorrhizal status and the number excluded are not addressed.

comments.issue: How bioclimatic variables were chosen and whether collinearity was tested is unclear.

comments.issue: L229 repeats methodology from line 85.

comments.issue: L249-250 may refer to the wrong Figure 2 panel.

comments.issue: Climatic envelope, extensive climatic range and climatic overlap are not distinguished.

comments.issue: MAP and MAT are defined too late and inconsistently.

comments.issue: The Discussion is not framed around the questions raised in the Introduction.

comments.issue: 'Productivity' at L307-308 is undefined.

comments.issue: 'Alternative strategies' at L313-315 is confusing.

comments.issue: L323-324 does not specify panels or bioclimatic variables for Figure S2.

comments.issue: The closing sentences at L333 and L354-355 are weak.

title: The Increased Environmental Niche of Dual‐Mycorrhizal Woody Species

study.system: subtropical forest wood decomposition; 12 tree species; throughfall exclusion

editor_summary: Editor: all reviewers found the study interesting but raised critical concerns about missing methodological detail, interpretation of phylogeny, wood density and fungal-bacterial drought sensitivity, and English quality.

reviews.assessment: Timely, original and significant with sound data, but several methods details and mechanistic explanations need clarification.
strengths: strong correlation between fungal K/r strategies and wood CO2 efflux identified

comments.issue: Microbial analysis and sequencing methods are overly detailed in the main text.
comments.request: Streamline them or move them to supplementary materials.
comments.quote: the microbial analysis and sequencing methods are overly detailed in the main text and could be streamlined or moved to supplementary materials

comments.issue: The method for measuring wood density and assessing its changes is not described in enough detail for a key conclusion.
comments.request: Provide a clear description of the wood density method.
comments.quote: More details should be provided about the method for measuring wood density. How did the authors assess changes in wood density?

comments.issue: The role of phylogeny in explaining variance is intriguing but not explored.
comments.request: Relate wood CO2 emissions, traits and microbial composition to the species' phylogeny.
comments.quote: it may be more interesting to explore how the wood CO2 emissions, wood traits, and microbial community composition data relate to the phylogenetic relationships among these species

comments.issue: It is not explained why wood density should be a reliable predictor of carbon release.
comments.request: Clarify the mechanisms or properties that make wood density predictive.
comments.quote: It would be useful to clarify why wood density serves as a reliable predictor for carbon release from wood residues.

comments.issue: The greater drought sensitivity of fungi, especially Basidiomycota, relative to bacteria is not mechanistically explained.
comments.request: Explain why fungi are more sensitive to drought than bacteria.
comments.quote: it would be helpful to explain in more detail why fungi, particularly Basidiomycota, are more sensitive to drought than bacteria

comments.issue: Language and presentation of the results need improvement.
comments.request: Improve the language and presentation of the results.
comments.quote: The language and presentation of the results should also be improved.

title: Microbial Life History Mediates the Drought‐Induced Decrease in Wood Decomposition in Subtropical Forests

study.system: parasitic decomposers across taxa; life-history model and literature synthesis

editor_summary: Editor says both reviewers found much to like but provided many criticisms and suggestions that must be carefully considered in a resubmission.

reviews.assessment: Fascinating and coherent synthesis, but presentation of the model needs work and the paper may need more substance for the journal.

comments.issue: Equations lack numbers, making them hard to refer to.
comments.request: Number the equations, starting at line 115.
comments.quote: I’d love some equation numbers on these, starting with line 115.

comments.issue: Equation terms are unfamiliar and hard to follow without labels.
comments.request: Add word labels under the equations.
comments.quote: The life history of sapronotic agents, etc., are not necessarily familiar to all readers. I had to mark up the equations a bit to follow everything.

comments.issue: Compartment flows are not shown in a single clear figure.
comments.request: Make a flow figure for the four compartments and improve panel A.
comments.quote: Have you considered making a figure with flow between the four compartments (Lu, Li, Du, Di)? A figure might have some color, too.

comments.issue: How parameters switch off flows and NGM parts is not shown clearly.
comments.request: Show how parameter changes knock out specific flows.
comments.quote: If I could have seen easily how certain parameters knocked out certain flows and hence parts of the next generation matrix in the R0 expression, I could have cruised through the paper more easily.

comments.issue: No summary table of parameters, variables and default values.
comments.request: Add a parameter summary table with explanations and values.
comments.quote: I’d have really benefited from a summary table of all parameters (and variables), their explanations, default values, etc.

comments.issue: Next-generation matrix calculations are not shown.
comments.request: Show the NGM calculation in an appendix, including decomposition.
comments.quote: I am sure the authors can calculate NGMs in their sleep. It would be nice to see it calculated – an appendix would be great.

comments.issue: Whether sub-cycle dynamics are NGM elements is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the sub-cycles’ relation to the NGM (see Diekmann et al. 2010).
comments.quote: Are “dynamics of sub-cycles within the overall life cycle” elements of the next generation matrix (K) by chance (sensu Diekmann et al. 2010 Royal Interface)? Just a bit more explanation for normies here would help.

comments.issue: The four sub-cycles are not presented where they are introduced.
comments.request: Present and explain the four sub-cycles on page 7.
comments.quote: Still here on page 7, I wondered if the four “sub-cycles” could be presented. I’d better recognize everything later if they were presented and explained a bit here.

comments.issue: Sub-R0s are hard to relate to which NGM parts parameters remove.
comments.request: Ease readers into each sub-R0 and its zeroed components.
comments.quote: I said a few points above that I’d have benefitted from easing each sub-R0 because then I could better understand why setting this or that parameter to zero nuked that part of the NGM.

comments.issue: R0 expressions are not explained after they are presented.
comments.request: Explain each R0 expression right after its equation.
comments.quote: I think readers like me would benefit from explanations of R0 expressions right after the equations are presented. Like line 161 (equation number needed!), we’d benefit from explanation of all of this.

comments.issue: Evolution of the strategies is not analysed with adaptive dynamics.
comments.request: Add an adaptive dynamics analysis of strategy evolution.
comments.quote: idea 1 – the authors already say it – why not show us evolution of this strategies using adaptive dynamics?

comments.issue: The model’s dynamics and behaviour are not explored beyond R0.
comments.request: Explore what the model’s dynamics can teach and its parameterization.
comments.quote: idea 2 – dynamics of the model – the authors on R0 expressions. What else can the model do?

comments.issue: It is unclear whether the synthesis provides enough substance for the journal.
comments.request: Consider whether the synthesis has enough content for Ecology Letters.
comments.quote: I’m wrestling with the question “is this enough” for Eco Letters? Is there enough out there to synthesize with the variations in the R0s, was so much space needed to do that, etc?

comments.issue: Model structure does not reflect detritus competition or parasite exploitation lifespan.
comments.request: Relate parasitism-saprotrophy differences to the model structure.
comments.quote: there was no competition for detritus among decomposers, and there wasn’t an exploitation-life span issue for parasites, was there?

comments.issue: Strategy names such as “opportunistic sapronotic agents” sound awkward.
comments.quote: “Opportunistic sapronotic agents” – that doesn’t exactly roll of the tongue, does it.

comments.issue: Author name typo at line 102.
comments.quote: Line 102: Typo alert on an author name here.

comments.issue: “Fitness” is used loosely where invasion fitness is meant.
comments.request: Remind readers that fitness means invasion fitness.
comments.quote: Line 159, elsewhere: Consider continually reminding us that “fitness” is “invasion fitness”.

comments.issue: The statement that living hosts do not contribute to opportunistic fitness is confusing.
comments.request: Clarify the R0^OS reasoning about living hosts and Du.
comments.quote: I find this confusing. R\_0^OS is proportion to Du, which upon invasion is connected to living hosts, isn’t it?

comments.issue: Parameter names and symbols are used inconsistently without word explanations.
comments.request: Use consistent labels and give words plus symbols for parameters.
comments.quote: I’d greatly benefit if the authors - here and throughout – would include word explanations and symbols and then only use certain labels (words) for those parameters, not synonyms

comments.issue: “Nosocomial” may be unfamiliar to readers.
comments.request: Define “nosocomial” for general readers.
comments.quote: Line 174: I don’t know if all readers know “nosocomial”.

comments.issue: The newly non-zero R0^LD component is not explained.
comments.request: Explain why this component appears and what it means.
comments.quote: We notice that now we have a non-zero value in the R\_0^LD slot. Tell us more about this, and why.

comments.issue: The eigenvalue expression is tedious and lacks biological interpretation.
comments.request: Rewrite it as ratios of gains to losses with explanation.
comments.quote: I think we’re just stuck with the tedious formula of calculating the eigenvalue from a 2 x 2 matrix, but I sure wish there was a biological explanation for the drawn out line 208.

comments.issue: The tradeoff explanation may belong in the associated figure.
comments.request: Show the speculated scenarios in the figure.
comments.quote: This tradeoff explanation – is this something that I should be seeing in the associated figure? That I should be seeing? The authors seem to be speculating about scenarios – can they show us?

comments.issue: The R0 at line 249 needs more explanation and clearer grouping.
comments.request: Explain and regroup this R0 into gains-to-losses ratios.
comments.quote: More explanation of this R0, more words, possible regrouping into ratios of gains to losses

comments.issue: Varying three NGM components inversely is operationally unclear and Figure 4 is hard to follow.
comments.request: Clarify the manipulation and improve Figure 4 and its caption.
comments.quote: I don’t know what you mean (operationally) when you vary three NGM components inversely with one. Even reading the very long caption, I don’t quite get it.

comments.issue: The authors did not use their model to address strategy evolution.
comments.request: Consider adding adaptive dynamics to answer the evolution question.
comments.quote: Given that the authors have created an R0 expression and have a full ODE, I’m wondering why they didn’t answer their own question about evolution of these strategies using adaptive dynamics?

comments.issue: Figure 1 lacks references to the relevant R0 equation numbers.
comments.request: Add equation references to the Figure 1 legend.
comments.quote: consider adding a reference to the equation number of the relevant R0 (once you add it to the text)

comments.issue: chi lacks its subscript in the Figure 1 legend.
comments.quote: chi is missing its subscript in the legend.

comments.issue: “Selection against parasitic ability” is hard to understand from the R0 structure.
comments.request: Explain this selection statement more clearly.
comments.quote: I struggled to understand about “selection against parasitic ability” given the structure of this R0.

comments.issue: Figure 2 (and 3) lacks a tradeoff panel; captions carry too much.
comments.request: Add tradeoff panels and explain the max function.
comments.quote: Consider adding a panel for the tradeoff (ditto fig 3). I think I’d ‘get it’ more easily.

comments.issue: chi_i described as cadaver exploitation rate reads more like a loss rate.
comments.request: Explain chi_i as a loss rate and its inverse as longevity.
comments.quote: I don’t understand chi\_i as “cadaver exploitation rate”. It seems just like a loss rate from dDi/dt.

reviews.assessment: Finds the approach informative and interesting but questions whether the categories and terminology add enough beyond what is already known.

comments.issue: So many categories and processes confuse readers outside the field.
comments.request: Simplify or better guide readers through the categories.
comments.quote: concerns did arise that there are so many categories and processes they rapidly become confusing for readers outside of the specific research area

comments.issue: The new terminology has little precedent and may not be widely adopted.
comments.request: Ground the terminology in existing ecological literature.
comments.quote: the names and terminology of each life history strategy have little precedent in the general ecological literature

comments.issue: Biological examples are obscure and the target audience is unclear.
comments.request: Use examples familiar to a broad readership and define the audience.
comments.quote: a number of the biological examples are rather obscure and probably not familiar to most readers (e.g., myiatic flies). What is the primary target audience for this paper?

comments.issue: Biological examples are not described alongside the theory for each strategy.
comments.request: Describe more biological examples in parallel with the models.
comments.quote: I suggest that the paper could be improved by having more biological examples described in parallel with the epidemiology and population dynamics of each life-history

comments.issue: New or rare strategy names (sapronotic, parasaprotrophs) add confusion.
comments.request: Use less confusing terminology.
comments.quote: some of the names for the life history strategies seem like new or rarely used words (e.g., sapronotic, parasaprotrophs) that contribute to the confusion

comments.issue: The saprotropic parasitoid category adds nothing beyond known parasitoids.
comments.request: Justify what this category adds beyond existing knowledge.
comments.quote: The third category (saprotropic parasitoids) does not clearly add anything beyond what we already know about parasitoids, whose infections invariably kill the host.

comments.issue: The first two life-history categories lack rich biological examples.
comments.request: Add more examples for the first two categories.
comments.quote: The rich array of biological examples was absent in the first two life history categories.

comments.issue: No table summarising the four life histories and their exemplars.
comments.request: Add a table of life histories, exemplar species, traits and outcomes.
comments.quote: it would be useful in a paper like this to have a table with the four life histories that would also contain a list of exemplar species and a synopsis of critical traits and outcomes that separate the categories.

comments.issue: Categories are not mutually exclusive, questioning their usefulness.
comments.request: Address why the categories should be used despite overlap.
comments.quote: the proposed categories are not mutually exclusive which raises the issue of why use them? (line 355)

comments.issue: Examples rest on atypical immunocompromised-host infections and read as exceptions.
comments.request: Use more representative natural examples.
comments.quote: Several biological examples seem stretched where some of the parasite/saprotroph abilities are based on the ability to infect immunocompromised patients, not a typical situation found in nature.

comments.issue: The synthesis may not be necessary given existing knowledge of these groups.
comments.request: Clarify what the classification adds beyond current knowledge.
comments.quote: However, at the same time I asked whether this is necessary? We already know a lot about saprophytes, parasites, parasitoids and other specialized groups of organisms.

comments.issue: The paper is organised theory-first, unlike the suggested biology-first structure.
comments.request: Front-load the biology, then classifications, then the equations.
comments.quote: My suggestion would be to front load the biology and descriptions of life histories closer to the start of the paper, then present the classifications and then finally present the epidemiological and population dynamic equations

comments.issue: Broader relevance is not well defined, so readers may stop reading.
comments.request: Define the broader relevance early in the paper.
comments.quote: Some readers might stop reading because the broader relevance is not well defined and the number of categories, terms, and exceptions raise the question of whether organismal evolution neatly fits our classifications.

comments.issue: The statement at lines 166-167 is questioned.
comments.request: Explain the statement at lines 166-167.
comments.quote: Line 166-167- why?

comments.issue: The claim that parasites arose from decomposers is flagged.
comments.request: Support the claim that parasites arose from decomposers.
comments.quote: 366 – idea that many parasitic organisms arose from decomposers.

comments.issue: Useful synthesising text at lines 373-385 comes too late.
comments.request: Move this synthesising material earlier.
comments.quote: this was useful text that ties together several threads, but it comes late in the paper.

comments.issue: Too much emphasis on finding a model system; difficulty may reflect category continuity.
comments.request: Trim the emphasis and discuss what the difficulty implies for category discreteness.
comments.quote: too much emphasis on “finding” a model system. If it is not easy, that could say something about the discreteness or continuous nature of the life-history categories.

title: Deadly Decomposers: Distinguishing Life History Strategies on the Parasitism‐Saprotrophy Spectrum

study.system: Alternanthera philoxeroides invasion; native plant richness; field survey and experiments

editor_summary: Editor: three essentially positive assessments; many comments to address in a major revision; key papers on the invasion paradox (Fridley et al. 2007, Rejmanek 1989, Stohlgren et al. 2006) should be discussed.

reviews.assessment: Interesting first integration of small- and large-scale approaches; recommendations are mostly presentational and hypothesis framing.
strengths: first integration of small- and large-scale approaches
experimental and correlative evidence for the same species

comments.issue: The text omits that other observational studies, usually at very large scales, found positive richness-invasion correlations.
comments.request: Add this nuance and describe the scales of those studies.
comments.quote: Line 67 – if accurate please add something like However, other observational studies, USUALLY AT VERY LARGE SCALES, have revealed positive correlationS.

comments.issue: Control details are in the introduction rather than the Methods.
comments.request: Move the control information to the Methods.
comments.quote: Line 102 – I suggest moving the bit on control to the Methods.

comments.issue: The hypotheses are not formalized and the scale question, the paper's key thesis, is absent from them.
comments.request: Formalize the hypotheses and include the scale question.
comments.quote: What I wrote for the hypothesis is a bit awkward, but the whole key thesis of the paper is the scale question, so this must be in at least one the hypotheses.

comments.issue: The phrase 'richness =2, 24 holes for each species' is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the experimental setup more clearly.
comments.quote: Line 197 – It is not clear what this means - “e.g., richness =2, 24 holes for each species”.

comments.issue: The hypothesis implies causation while the large-scale patterns are correlative; the results should be stated with this in mind.
comments.request: Emphasize the correlative nature of the large-scale results.
comments.quote: Your current hypothesis is “diverse native species communities will reduce the performance of A. philoxeroides”. This implies cause, and the large-scale patterns are correlative.

comments.issue: The important results at lines 345-347 are not emphasized in the Abstract and Discussion.
comments.request: Emphasize these results in the Abstract and Discussion.
comments.quote: Lines 345 to 347 – Very interesting and important. Please be sure this is emphasized in the Abstract and the Discussion.

comments.issue: The caveat 'if supported by field experiments' is unnecessary given the study includes field experiments.
comments.request: Remove the unnecessary caveat.
comments.quote: Line 359 – it seems that since your results are from field experiments you don’t have to say “if supported by field experiments”.

comments.issue: The section heading promises competition but competition is not mentioned in the section.

comments.quote: the section heading is Diversity-invasibility occurs primarily via competition in the field experiment, but competition is not mentioned in the section. I suggest changing the heading

comments.issue: The conclusion emphasizes manipulated versus natural settings instead of the paper's small- versus large-scale thesis.
comments.request: Emphasize similar findings at very small and very large scales.
comments.quote: Line 389 – shouldn’t this emphasize similar findings at very small and very large scales? And not manipulated and natural settings?

comments.issue: The claim that something is underestimated lacks references.
comments.request: Provide one or two references for the claim.
comments.quote: Line 413 – if you claim something is underestimated you should provide a reference or two.

comments.issue: The sentence should end at 'resistance' and the paragraph is wordy.
comments.request: End the sentence at 'resistance' and tighten the paragraph.
comments.quote: Line 436 – end sentence at “resistance”. Also, this paragraph is a little wordy, I would try to tighten it.

comments.issue: 'Invasional meltdown' could be mentioned at line 465.
comments.request: Consider mentioning invasional meltdown.
comments.quote: Line 465 – Consider mentioning “invasional meltdown here.

comments.issue: The Discussion is repetitive.
comments.request: Reduce repetitiveness in the Discussion.
comments.quote: I also suggest poring over the Discussion in an effort to reduce a modest amount of repetitiveness.
Line 391 – “resistance”.

reviews.assessment: Nice studies that could become publishable, but experimental setup and statistical treatment of richness need fixing.
strengths: three complementary studies testing Elton's hypothesis

comments.issue: The composition of the native assemblages is not described, so species representation and frequencies across richness levels are unknown.
comments.request: Report the assemblage compositions and species frequencies.
comments.quote: I appreciate that in the two experiments the different levels of native species richness were represented by multiple assemblages. However, there is no information on the composition of the actual assemblages.

comments.issue: Richness was modeled as a factor, so the models test differences among levels rather than a trend with increasing richness.
comments.request: Include species richness as a continuous variable.
comments.quote: native species richness was included as a factor in the statistical models. This means that the models tested whether there are differences among the native species richness levels, but not whether the effect increases (or decreases) with species richness.

comments.issue: With only a few years, year should be a fixed term with richness interactions to test whether richness effects differ among years.

title: Native Plant Diversity Provides Resistance to Invasion by an Alien Species in Natural and Experimental Settings

study.system: Human shield hypothesis; literature review of predator-prey interactions

editor_summary: Editor notes reviewers value the contribution but require major revisions on the systematic-review methodology, search terms, inclusion criteria and a clearer delineation of the human shield hypothesis.

reviews.assessment: Positive; sees a valuable clarification of a nebulous topic and asks for clearer HSH delineation and explanation of the Fig. 4 inference.
strengths: valuable contribution clarifying a nebulous topic

comments.issue: It is unclear whether any human-driven trophic cascade counts as a human shield or whether behavioural decision-making is required.
comments.request: State whether behavioural decision-making is required for a human shield.
comments.quote: any human caused tropic cascade that reduces dominate pressure on a subordinate should be considered a human shield or whether some perception of reduced risk and decision making on the part of the subordinate is required

comments.issue: The logic that support 'converged above 0.05' is confusing and invokes the alpha level in a non-intuitive way.
comments.request: Explain this inference and what Figure 4 shows.
comments.quote: the proportion of tests that were consistent with the HSH appeared to converge to a value above the standard significance level of 0.05, suggesting that support for the HSH was more than just statistical noise

comments.issue: The subordinate's direct response to human cues as a sign of low risk is missing from Table 1.
comments.request: Consider adding this factor to the framework.
comments.quote: I’m not sure whether there is evidence for subordinates learning to associate human cues with low risk conditions (independent of changes in actual risk from dominants), but if so, this would seem highly relevant

reviews.assessment: Very positive about the review but insists it should not be framed as a systematic review and should be trimmed.
strengths: superb job defining the HSH and its contexts

comments.issue: The review does not meet systematic-review guidelines and should not be labelled as one.
comments.request: Stop framing the review as a systematic review.
comments.quote: Just to be clear – I don’t think there is anything wrong with the review itself. It just shouldn’t be addressed as a systematic review.

comments.issue: The reported search term is ambiguous: 'human shield*' versus a phrase search yield different results.

comments.issue: Web of Science categories are misdescribed and the multidisciplinary sciences category was omitted, excluding major journals.
comments.request: Correct and broaden the database search coverage.

comments.issue: The review methods are buried in the supplement despite shaping the results.
comments.request: Move the gist of the methods into the main text.

comments.issue: The paper is too long, with a redundant final section.
comments.request: Trim the manuscript overall.

comments.issue: The meaning of the heat-map colours in Figure 1 is not explained.

comments.quote: I still think that the meaning of the colors in your heat maps (b and c) should be explained in the legend.

comments.issue: It is unclear what 'over time' refers to at Line 324.
comments.request: Clarify whether a chronological trend is meant.
comments.quote: When you write “over time”, what do you mean? Is there a chronological trend here?

comments.issue: Figure 5 is not intuitive and its takeaway is unclear.
comments.request: Simplify or replace Figure 5.
comments.quote: Figure 5 is very not intuitive. What is the main takeaway that the readers are supposed to have from the figure?

comments.issue: The percentage at Line 608 may be wrong.
comments.request: Check whether it should read 51%.
comments.quote: Line 608 – Do you mean 51% and not 31%?

title: The Human Shield Hypothesis: Does Predator Avoidance of Humans Create Refuges for Prey?

study.system: marine midge Clunio marinus; temporal-spatial niche coexistence; model

editor_summary: Editor: all agree on the relevant topic, but the paper must connect much more strongly to niche and coexistence theory (especially regulating factors) and clarify arbitrary model choices and structure.

reviews.assessment: Interesting, methodologically rich system, but poor organization and unclear novelty make the paper hard to assess.
strengths: laudable integration of field, lab and genomic methods
novel real-world example of temporal niche partitioning

comments.issue: The paper is poorly organised, leaving the questions tested and their links to methods unclear.
comments.request: Restructure so that each question, method and result is clearly linked.
comments.quote: First, the organization of the paper was quite poor. This resulted in a lack of clarity in the actual questions being tested, as well as how each of the methods was used to address it

comments.issue: 'Asymmetric dispersal' is central in the abstract but never mentioned again.
comments.request: Explain and engage with asymmetric dispersal throughout the paper.
comments.quote: while this idea is central to the abstract and framed as a key finding in the introduction, the term (and the idea) are not mentioned again in the rest of the paper

comments.issue: Methods and results jump between field and lab approaches without rationale or signposting.
comments.request: Give a clear rationale and consistently signpost each approach.
comments.quote: the methods and results jumped back and forth between different approaches (field, lab) without giving a clear rationale at the beginning for each or consistently signposting the approach for the method/result

comments.issue: The main novelty of the paper is unclear relative to what was already known.
comments.request: State and justify the novel contribution in the introduction.
comments.quote: it was not clear what the main novelty contribution of this paper was

comments.issue: It is not specified which parameters were manipulated in the simulations.
comments.request: Specify the manipulated parameters.
comments.quote: the simulations are not well specified. What parameters are being manipulated? This was not specified in the methods

comments.issue: How the collected data were incorporated into the model is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the link between data collection and model parameters.
comments.quote: how were the data they collected incorporated in the model? The link between specified parameters and data collection was not clear.

comments.issue: The invader-resident proportion metric and the setup for Figure 4 are never explained.
comments.request: Elaborate on the coexistence metric and Figure 4.
comments.quote: they calculated segregation from the simulations but they did not mention that they also calculate invader-resident proportions and use this as a metric for coexistence

comments.issue: Zone numbering is counter-intuitive and centred emergence windows are mentioned only later.
comments.request: Clarify the zone numbering and emergence window specification.
comments.quote: Zone numbering seems counter-intuitive to me. Emergence windows are not clear that they are centered (not mentioned until later).

comments.issue: The quadratic survival form is unjustified and uncited, and stage notation is confusing.
comments.request: Explain why a quadratic rather than exponential form is used and cite its source.
comments.quote: I’m curious about the reasoning behind the quadratic form in the survival equation. Why quadratic and not exponential? Also no citations for this equation.

comments.issue: The beta-distribution equations are unnecessary in the main text and the negative integral numerator is unclear.
comments.request: Simplify the equations, move forms to the supplement and clarify the numerator.
comments.quote: The numerator is a negative integral, leading to a negative proportion. I’m not sure why there is a numerator at all.

comments.issue: The 50-daughter assumption lacks justification and the equations are not specified for z=0 or z=6.
comments.request: Justify the offspring number and specify boundary cases mathematically.
comments.quote: Any data or explanation to back this up the assumption of 50 daughters? Citation? Should there be separate equations for when z=0 or z=6?

comments.issue: The introduction at line 67 is very specific without general context and lacks clear topic sentences.
comments.request: Revise the introduction around the big ideas.
comments.quote: This section is very specific, without having provided sufficient general context for the types of questions. Overall, the introduction would benefit from a revision focused on very clear topic sentences about the big ideas of the paper.

comments.issue: The paragraph at line 74 makes the paper seem a repeat of what is already known.
comments.request: Clarify what is new beyond the known strain segregation.
comments.quote: This paragraph made it seem as if much of the work subsequently presented in the paper was a repeat of what is already known

comments.issue: The methods and their rationale are not foreshadowed at line 88.
comments.request: Foreshadow the methods and rationale in the introduction.
comments.quote: It would be good to foreshadow the methods (and rationale for them) here

comments.issue: Larval lifespan and whether the strains overlap as larvae are not stated.
comments.request: Provide an overview of the midge life history.
comments.quote: It’s not clear how long the larvae live and if the two strains would overlap as larvae

comments.issue: The basis for the claim that adults always lay eggs at the water level is unclear.
comments.request: State whether this is prior knowledge or measured here.
comments.quote: Similarly, how is it known that adults always lay their eggs at the water level? Is this previous research, or measured here?

comments.issue: Confirming the natural history in the field is presented as known rather than as a study goal.
comments.request: Clarify that this confirmation is part of the study.
comments.quote: It was not clear that confirming the natural history of these strains in the field was a goal of this study. It was written like this was already known (detailed in intro and methods).

comments.issue: The claimed difference between field and lab circadian rhythms lacks statistics.
comments.request: Add statistics for the field-lab rhythm comparison.
comments.quote: It was not clear that comparison between field and lab circadian rhythms was a goal of this study. They are compared and claimed to be different without any statistics.

comments.issue: The unexpected topography results should partly move to the methods.
comments.request: Move part of the topography section to the methods.
comments.quote: Unexpected section of results on topography. Part of this should be moved up to methods.

comments.issue: Figure 1A lacks annotations of strains, emergence window, tides and key time points.
comments.request: Annotate FM, NM, the 9-day window, neap and spring tides, and t=8 and 22.
comments.quote: Fig1A - Would be nice to annotate FM and NM and the 9 day emergence window. Could also label neap tides and spring tides.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether Figure 2A shows the AM or PM low tide height.
comments.request: Specify which low tide is shown.
comments.quote: Fig2A - Low tide height at which time, the am one or the pm one?

comments.issue: The Figure 2C y-axis name does not match the grey triangles and its day numbering differs from Figure 1A.
comments.request: Fix the axis label and keep day numbering consistent.
comments.quote: Fig2C - Y axis name doesn’t make sense for the grey triangles. Why is x axis (day of lunar cycle) not matched with the x axis of fig1a?

comments.issue: Figure 2D moves the y-axis to the right unnecessarily and its lab data may not be needed.
comments.request: Keep a consistent axis and reconsider showing lab data.
comments.quote: Fig2D - Y axis change to right side seems strange. Could have kept same axis without repeating it too. Generally don’t know if showing lab data is necessary here.

comments.issue: Figure 3 may have x and y axes flipped and does not highlight the variability of intermediate zones.
comments.request: Check the axes and highlight intermediate-zone variability.
comments.quote: Fig3 - X and Y flip? Response = y, predictor =x.

comments.issue: Figure 4H-J lacks consistent units and the meaning of 0.2 mean abundance is unclear.
comments.request: Keep units consistent with panels d-f and clarify the abundance measure.
comments.quote: Fig4H-J - Would be good to keep units of d-f here. Hard to know if this difference is meaningful. Also what is 0.2 mean abundance?? Abundance across 6 zones?

reviews.assessment: Nice deep study, but the framing misrepresents when temporal niche segregation can maintain coexistence.
strengths: studies a coexistence situation deeply, both empirically and theoretically
demonstrates the complicated inner working of ecosystems and the possibility of clear understanding of the coexistence mechanism

comments.issue: The paper frames temporal niche segregation as ineffective, but temporal segregation can maintain coexistence and niche segregation is only a possibility, not an assurance.
comments.request: Reframe the argument to acknowledge effective temporal niche segregation.
comments.quote: Second, temporal niche segregation is a perfectly good way to maintain coexistence. Chesson’s models and the model by Barabás et al. provide good theoretical examples.

comments.issue: The coexistence argument should be framed in terms of regulating variables; in this model the regulating variable (larval concentration) is present throughout, so temporal segregation is weak.
comments.request: Frame the mechanism around regulating factors as in coexistence theory.
comments.quote: What are the regulating factors, or variables in the model described in the manuscript? The total larval concentration at each location and time step.

reviews.assessment: Interesting case study with robust mechanistic explanations, but it needs a broader discussion and clearer model parameter justification.
strengths: robust, mechanistic explanations of a coexistence pattern

comments.issue: Parameter values such as the six zones and female offspring number seem arbitrary or unexplained.
comments.request: Explain and justify these parameter choices.
comments.quote: some parameter values still seem a bit arbitrary, or at least need explanations. For instance, the authors do not explain why the model has six zones (line 203).

comments.issue: The 100-year stabilization cap is extremely long relative to the midge generation time.
comments.request: Explain why such a long stabilization cap is needed.
comments.quote: The authors mention that the cap for the model to stabilize is 100 years (line 220), which, considering the generation time of the midge, is extremely long and far from “realistic”.

comments.issue: There is no table of model parameters and values.
comments.request: Add a parameter table to the main text.
comments.quote: the main text could benefit greatly from a table of all parameters and their values

comments.issue: The discussion lacks broader implications and connections to coexistence and niche theory.
comments.request: Expand the discussion to other space-time systems, niche theory, priority effects and eco-evolutionary perspectives.
comments.quote: I feel that the discussion lacks some content on the broader implications of the results

comments.issue: Two typos (lines 210 and 407-408).
comments.quote: considering that each zone is considered

comments.issue: That mortality depends on both strains' densities is only discoverable from Equation 1.
comments.request: State this inter-strain competition clearly in the text.
comments.quote: It took me a bit to realize that the mortality is dependent on the densities of both strains.

comments.issue: The claim that strains emerge at roughly the same time lacks statistical support.
comments.request: Provide statistics for the emergence timing claim.
comments.quote: There should be statistics to support the claim that they emerge “roughly at the same time”

comments.issue: The terms time-matched and time-shifted are undefined.
comments.request: Define these terms.
comments.quote: Line 344-345: Not sure what time-matched and time-shifted mean.

title: How an Insect Converts Time Into Space: Temporal Niches Aid Coexistence via Modifying the Amount of Habitat Available for Reproduction

study.system: population dynamics models; evolution of dormancy and stability

editor_summary: Editor asks to integrate Box 1 into the main analysis, show simulation results for verbally described findings, explain J in equation 5 and the PIP boundaries, and sharpen terminology and proofs.

reviews.assessment: Suitable for a wide readership, but the edge-of-stability claim is overrated, terminology is conflated and several SI proofs need revision.
strengths: written suitably for a fairly wide readership
dormancy is stabilising and advantageous under intrinsic fluctuations

comments.issue: Evolution to the edge of stability requires zero dormancy mortality, an unrealistic assumption.
comments.request: Analyse the model with realistic dormancy mortality.
comments.quote: this is so only if dormant individuals (e.g. seeds) have no mortality at all, which is not a typical situation and will not explain why many natural systems appear to be weakly stable

comments.issue: No reason to expect only low-amplitude oscillations since cycle amplitude changes fast near the bifurcation.
comments.request: Reconsider the claim of only weak oscillations.
comments.quote: since the amplitude of population cycles changes fast near the bifurcation point, there is no reason to believe that the population would show only low amplitude oscillations (line 269)

comments.issue: Edge of stability and edge of chaos are conflated; the Lyapunov exponent changes sign at the edge of chaos, not stability.
comments.request: Use the correct terminology and remove the edge-of-chaos claim.
comments.quote: the text on page 14 conflates the edge of stability with the edge of chaos. The two are distinctly different. It is misleading to imply that the results show evolution to the edge of chaos (also among the keywords).

comments.issue: Only the claim that dormancy stabilises is proved, not that more dormancy means more stability.
comments.request: Avoid treating the 'more dormancy, more stability' claim as fact.
comments.quote: the text should be careful (e.g. in line 155 and on page 14) not to take the latter claim (more dormancy, more stability) to be a fact

comments.issue: SI A.1 proof needs revisions: g decreasing is unnecessary, the unique bifurcation assumption is fragile, and the derivative range (-1,0) is wrong.
comments.request: Revise the SI A.1 proof assumptions and derivative range.
comments.quote: These proofs I found correct but the proof in SI A.1 needs some revisions: (1) I do not understand why the function g needs to be decreasing.

comments.issue: The argument in lines 190-191 only holds if J is independent of m, which it is not.
comments.request: Correct the argument accounting for J's dependence on m.
comments.quote: The simple argument in lines 190-191 holds water only if J is independent of m but it is not.

comments.issue: SI.B proof is overcomplicated; a strict-inequality and continuity argument suffices.
comments.request: Simplify the SI.B proof.
comments.quote: The proof in SI.B that the logarithm of the invasion growth rate (log IGR) is positive for small m is complicated and is based on a technical result from another paper. I wonder if this is unnecessary.

comments.issue: Mutual invasion is sufficient but not necessary for coexistence; unprotected coexistence is possible.
comments.request: Acknowledge unprotected coexistence.
comments.quote: mutual invasion is sufficient for coexistence (assuming a unique attractor on each boundary) but not necessary: two types can coexist at an interior attractor even if there is also a boundary attractor (unprotected coexistence).

comments.issue: Invasibility of the ESS does not imply it is approached by gradual evolution; convergence stability is needed.
comments.request: Discuss convergence stability and cite Geritz et al. 1998.
comments.quote: The fact that the ESS value alpha* can invade other trait values

comments.issue: Box 1 adds little and should be removed or integrated.
comments.request: Remove Box 1, keeping only the useful numerical example.
comments.quote: Box 1 on pp 16-18 should be removed. It adds little to the paper except the one numerical example in Figure 5.

comments.issue: SI.C fast-dormancy derivation is wrong (missing 1/epsilon, indeterminate 0/0); with fast dynamics and m=0 dormancy has no effect.
comments.request: Correct the SI.C derivation and its conclusions.
comments.quote: With fast dormancy dynamics and m=0, dormancy has no effect on the invasion growth rate.

comments.issue: SI.C slow-dormancy derivation wrongly assumes the integral of A(t) governs matrix dynamics.
comments.request: Correct the matrix formulation in equations S30-S32.
comments.quote: This is well-known to be incorrect (it works with scalars but not with matrices).

comments.issue: Quadratic map is not positivity preserving and can predict negative population sizes.
comments.request: Use the truncated quadratic map.
comments.quote: this model is not positivity preserving, i.e., it readily predicts negative population sizes. A negative population size is not "extinction" but an impossibility that invalidates the model.

comments.issue: Notation f_r is used in the main text without definition.
comments.request: Define f_r.
comments.quote: the notation f_r is used in the main text without defining it

comments.issue: Fig 2B labels a region as chaos that contains periodic windows.
comments.request: Correct the chaos region in Fig 2B.
comments.quote: Fig 2B: the region shown as "chaos" contains non-chaotic windows of periodic attractors

comments.issue: Metz et al. (2009) offers another explanation of dormancy that is not cited.
comments.request: Cite and discuss Metz et al. (2009).
comments.quote: another explanation of dormancy is found in Metz et al (2009): A different model to explain delayed germination.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and mostly clearly written, but the analysis is limited, several results are shown only verbally, and Box 1 should be dropped.

comments.issue: 'Very generally' at L4 overstates the generality of a very simple model.
comments.request: Soften the generality claim.
comments.quote: I think "very generally" is a bit of an overstatement. It generally happens in the model studied here, but it is only a very simple model.

comments.issue: L125-126 point seems to be a general feature of logistic growth; the message is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the point being made.
comments.quote: Isn't this always the case even if self-limitation is weak? It's a general feature of logistic growth that total population growth is maximized for intermediate population size.

comments.issue: J at L185-191 is not given or referenced; using J risks confusion with the Jacobian.
comments.request: Refer to where J is explained in the supplement.
comments.quote: If you do not give J, please at least refer to where this is explained in the supplementary material.

comments.issue: L192-206 lacks a figure illustrating the text; Fig. S1 should move to the main text.
comments.request: Move Fig. S1 into the main text.
comments.quote: This is one place where I really miss a figure illustrating what the text is explaining; it is a bit hard to follow otherwise.

comments.issue: 'Moderate' and 'considerable' mortality both mean 0.05, which is very low relative to natural systems.
comments.request: Compare these mortality rates with natural dormant mortality.
comments.quote: these both refer to a mortality rate of 0.05, which I would still consider very low. How does this compare to mortality rates of dormant individuals in natural systems?

comments.issue: Fig. 3 panels should be shown side by side.
comments.request: Show both panels side by side.
comments.quote: Fig. 3: I'd just show both panels side by side.

comments.issue: IGR > 1 and log(IGR) > 0 are used inconsistently.
comments.request: Use one condition consistently.
comments.quote: the earlier condition was log(IGR) > 0. I'm aware that these are two ways of giving the same condition, but please be consistent.

comments.issue: L230-237 verbal description is hard to follow; a mutual invasibility plot would help.
comments.request: Add a figure, perhaps a mutual invasibility plot.
comments.quote: I think this would also benefit from a figure, because I find the verbal description hard to follow. Perhaps a mutual invasibility plot?

comments.issue: Phrasing at L238 seems off.
comments.request: Rephrase as suggested.
comments.quote: The phrasing seems a bit off here. I'd suggest "Evolution of dormancy drives dynamics to the edge of stability"

comments.issue: 'Edge of stability' and 'edge of chaos' are used interchangeably, but unstable dynamics need not be chaotic.
comments.request: Explain and distinguish the two terms.
comments.quote: Are "the edge of stability" and "the edge of chaos" the same thing? They appear to be used interchangeably throughout the manuscript; but dynamics can be unstable without being chaotic, so this is not clear to me.

comments.issue: Inducible offense and defense models are known to be stabilizing but are not connected to this work.
comments.request: Connect the results with inducible offense/defense studies.
comments.quote: Inducible offenses are known to be stabilizing, as shown e.g. by Yamamichi & Letten 2021 (in the supporting information) and van Velzen et al. 2022.

comments.issue: L302 prediction is opposite to inducible defense/offense experience; random induction is more stabilizing than adaptive induction.
comments.request: Investigate the random versus adaptive induction scenario.
comments.quote: Counterintuitive as it may seem, they tend to be most stabilizing when induction is random; the more adaptive it is, the less it stabilizes.

comments.issue: L332-335 relationship is not immediately clear.
comments.request: Give more explanation.
comments.quote: This relationship is not immediately clear to me, could you give a bit more explanation?

comments.issue: Reference at L349 is duplicated.
comments.request: Remove the duplicate reference.
comments.quote: L. 349: The reference is duplicated.

comments.issue: Box 1 feels tacked on and is the least convincing part; only one simulation supports it.
comments.request: Drop Box 1 and use the space for the discrete-time model.
comments.quote: To me it feels tacked on, especially as the only result shown is based on a single simulation, and the authors are limited to saying that they "hypothesize" that it holds generally.

comments.issue: In eq. (6) alpha changes meaning from fraction active to rate of becoming dormant.
comments.request: Use consistent notation for alpha.
comments.quote: in eq. (6), alpha is now the rate at which active individuals become dormant; previously it was the fraction of active (i.e. non-dormant) individuals. This is very confusing.

comments.issue: Eq. (6) seems to give mortality only to dormant individuals.
comments.request: Clarify mortality for active individuals.
comments.quote: eq. (6): only dormant individuals experience mortality? What about active individuals?

comments.issue: Eq. (6) notation is so general that the predator-prey nature is unclear and misleading.
comments.request: Be specific about the model type from the start.
comments.quote: The authors really need to be more specific from the start about what kind of model they are describing.

comments.issue: Eq. (6) describes a different scenario from eq. (1) regarding dormancy switching.
comments.request: Correct the comparison between the two models.
comments.quote: I disagree; eq. (6) describes a very different scenario from eq. (1). In eq. (1), all individuals start as dormant and can become active; in eq. (6) individuals can switch between these states.

comments.issue: Eq. (7) seems overcomplicated; two prey are used only to obtain chaos.
comments.request: Justify or simplify the two-prey model.
comments.quote: For a model meant only to illustrate the concept, this model seems overcomplicated. Why does it need two prey instead of one?

comments.issue: Fig. 5 uses extreme alpha/beta rates (100-fold asymmetry) without justification.
comments.request: Justify the parameter values.
comments.quote: I was astonished by the parameter values for alpha and beta. Active individuals become dormant at 100 times the rate of the reverse change?

title: Stabilisation of Fluctuating Population Dynamics via the Evolution of Dormancy

study.system: 320 eddy covariance sites; canopy structure and light use efficiency

editor_summary: Two reviewers suggested revisions, especially statistical improvements from reviewer two; respond to each comment individually.

reviews.assessment: Well-written, globally extensive study, but several significant concerns about within-biome variation, statistics and data choices preclude acceptance as is.
strengths: integrates over 300 flux tower datasets globally
biome-level scope unlike previous plant-level studies

comments.issue: Within-biome variation in maximum LUE is not investigated; the nonlinear relationship may not hold within biomes.
comments.request: Test the relationship within individual biomes and explore environmental drivers.
