title: Phylogenomic Evidence of Fire Regime Changes: The Case of a Resprouting Juniper

study.system: grassland biodiversity experiment; 25 years; CO2 and N

editor_summary: Both reviewers see considerable merit and provide thoughtful, constructive suggestions to improve the manuscript.

reviews.assessment: Well-structured and clearly written with apparently correct analyses, but several questions on design, related work and statistics remain.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether lost species were reseeded and how the design fits the temporal-stability framework.
comments.request: Clarify reseeding and position the design in the stability framework.
comments.quote: Does this mean that species were reseeded when lost from a plot at the end of a growing season? If so, this may be an important point to discuss.

comments.issue: Results are not compared with prior papers on global change and richness-productivity effects.
comments.request: Compare results with Hong, Steudel and Baert studies.
comments.quote: There exist quite some papers showing how global change drivers affect richness effects on productivity. It could be interesting to check to what extent the presented results confirm/refute some of their results.

comments.issue: No comparison with the cited Su et al. meta-analysis on global change and stability.
comments.request: Compare with Su et al.'s meta-analysis.
comments.quote: It would be nice to see a comparison between the results in that paper with the results in this study.

comments.issue: A very close preprint is not discussed, leaving the advance unclear.
comments.request: Explain how the analyses go beyond or complement the preprint.
comments.quote: Would be good to explain in what sense the presented analyses go beyond / complement this other manuscript.

comments.issue: The natural-log transformation is not justified and a GLMM might be preferable.
comments.request: Justify the log transformation or use a GLMM.
comments.quote: What is the justification for this transformation and wasn’t using glmm an option instead?

comments.issue: Temporal autocorrelation of residuals is not reported as checked.
comments.request: Check temporal autocorrelation of residuals.
comments.quote: P8, L53: Has temporal autocorrelation of residuals been checked?

comments.issue: The agreement between planted and realised richness results is not interpreted.
comments.request: Discuss what the agreement between planted and realised richness means.
comments.quote: Isn’t the comparison between planted and realised richness interesting for more than methodological reasons? What does it mean when both give the same results?

comments.issue: May 1974 concerns asymptotic rather than temporal stability, and Tilman 1996 is not a theoretical paper.
comments.request: Remove or replace the May 1974 and Tilman 1996 citations.
comments.quote: I don’t think May 1974 is relevant here, as this paper talks about asymptotic stability, while the submitted manuscript talks about temporal stability.

reviews.assessment: Nicely shows contrasting productivity and stability trends, but the statistical models need the recommended random terms and cross-checks.
strengths: unique 25-year biodiversity and global change experiment
remarkable that stability declines while productivity relationships do not

comments.issue: The productivity result is missing from the abstract.
comments.request: Add the productivity result to the abstract.
comments.quote: biodiversity-productivity relationships increase over time across control and three global-change treatments (this should be added to the Abstract)

comments.issue: Increased synchrony could arise from novel environments even without species loss or composition change.
comments.request: Consider synchronous environmental responses as an additional explanation.
comments.quote: I would add the possibility that the novel environments may increase synchronous responses to environmental variation between species even without species loss or changes in species compositions or abundance distributions

comments.issue: Year group terms and Year group by ring/plot interactions are not fitted as recommended random terms.
comments.request: Fit the recommended random terms and cross-check with lm analyses.
comments.quote: it is absolutely necessary to use Year group x ring interactions as errors for Year group x CO2 and Year group x plot interactions as errors for Year group x N

comments.issue: The changed season of burning is not discussed as a potential issue.
comments.request: Discuss whether the changed burn season could be an issue.
comments.quote: Changing the season of burning: briefly discuss if that could be an issue.

comments.issue: The CWM calculation inputs are not explained.
comments.request: Explain the CWM calculation inputs.
comments.quote: CWM calculation: explain if this was only done with realized species richness and if so whether abundances were taken from cover or biomass.

comments.issue: The exotic species are not identified.
comments.request: List the exotic species.
comments.quote: Which species are exotics? Poa pratensis?

comments.issue: The stated reason for weeding mischaracterises why biodiversity experiments weed.
comments.request: Correct the stated reason for weeding.
comments.quote: This is not the main reason for weeding. Biodiversity experiments simulate extinction and thus cannot allow for the re-evolution and invasion of species simulated to be extinct!

comments.issue: Using relative values divided by monoculture means may affect results.
comments.request: Discuss the effect of using relative values.
comments.quote: Please discuss the potential effect of working with relative values (dividing by monoculture means).

comments.issue: Several line-level wording edits (duration wording, plot count, redundant adjectives).
comments.quote: “36 of the 9 species” --> “36 of the 296 plots”.

title: Elevated CO 2 and N Gradually Weaken the Influence of Diversity on Ecosystem Stability

study.system: macroevolution and extinction risk; review of phylogenetic and conservation literature

editor_summary: Reviewers found the idea interesting but flagged a mismatch with existing literature, unvalidated assumptions, weak conceptualisation, missing recent literature, unexplained terms, and oversimplified concepts.

reviews.assessment: Unfocused and mischaracterises the literature: cited studies test links to known risk, not estimating risk from macroevolutionary metrics.
strengths: depth and clarity of the discussion starting on lines 359

comments.issue: Review is unfocused and lists clades rather than synthesising how mechanisms were empirically tested and how processes overlap.
comments.request: Focus on empirical tests of mechanisms and better synthesise overlapping processes.
comments.quote: The review of potential relationships between macroevolution and extinction risk is fairly thorough but a bit unfocused

comments.issue: Studies dealing with IUCN Red List imputation are generalised, so the extinction risk metric considered in each case is unclear.
comments.request: State which extinction risk metric each cited study uses.
comments.quote: this detail is generalized by the authors in a way that makes it unclear exactly what metric of “extinction risk” is being considered in each instance

comments.issue: Cited studies tested links between macroevolutionary indicators and known, assessed extinction risks, not estimating risk from phylogenies.
comments.request: Correct the characterisation of what these studies did.
comments.quote: They were not attempting to use diversification rates estimated from phylogenies to estimate extinction risk

comments.issue: Claim that the link might be invalid misconstrues the issue: if a link exists it cannot be invalid, and studies test the link itself.
comments.request: Reframe the premise around testing whether links exist.
comments.quote: For one, if there is a link, it can’t be invalid – it exists. That’s what most studies have tested.

comments.issue: Conceptual models presented in the figures are overly simplistic.
comments.request: Revise the figure models.
comments.quote: I also think that the models presented in the figures are overly simplistic

comments.issue: The 'intermediate assumptions' are well-known evolutionary theory, not a novel mystery, and are not established de novo by this review.
comments.request: Acknowledge that these assumptions are long-established.
comments.quote: The “intermediate assumptions” are generally well-known aspects of modern evolutionary theory

comments.issue: Table 1 misrepresents studies, such as Tietje and Rodel (2018), which link traits to extinction rather than using macroevolutionary indicators.
comments.request: Correct Table 1 and its supporting claims.
comments.quote: Nearly all of the studies cited in Table 1 were about linking traits to extinction, not using macroevolutionary indicators

comments.issue: Greenberg et al.'s Hypothesis 2 does not assume no phylogenetic signal, and the treatment of phylogenetic signal is oversimplified.
comments.request: Correct the description of Hypothesis 2 and phylogenetic signal.
comments.quote: The authors are also not quite correct that Greenberg et al.’s Hypothesis 2 assumes no phylogenetic signal

comments.issue: No one proposed net diversification rate as a direct proxy for extinction risk; it is used as a predictor.
comments.request: Distinguish proxy versus predictor uses.
comments.quote: I don’t think anyone has proposed directly using estimates of net diversification rate as a proxy for extinction risk

comments.issue: Tonini et al. (2016) is mischaracterised: it tested ED differences among assessed threat statuses, not ED as a risk predictor.
comments.request: Correct the Tonini et al. and ED characterisation.
comments.quote: Tonini et al. 2016 did not use evolutionary distinctness as a substitute for diversification rate

comments.issue: The review ignores the literature on comparing fossil-record extinction dynamics with present-day environments and their generalisability.
comments.request: Engage this literature and discuss the generalisability limitation.
comments.quote: There is a large literature on the difficulty of comparing historical extinction dynamics from the fossil record to the current environment

comments.issue: Conclusion about diversification rates in barrier-rich settings restates generally known characteristics.
comments.request: Remove or reframe the claim as already established.
comments.quote: But these characteristics are generally known! We aren’t estimating diversification rates for totally unknown species

comments.issue: The review interrogates a proposal not in use: metrics are only used alongside other process-based estimates, not as naked proxies.
comments.request: Re-situate the review around what practitioners actually do.
comments.quote: I think the authors are interrogating a proposal that isn’t really in use by anyone

comments.issue: Assertion that only past extinction rates are a good predictor is unsupported as a standalone conclusion.
comments.request: Support or soften the synthesis conclusion.
comments.quote: I don’t think any evidence supports that assertion as a standalone conclusion

comments.issue: Confusion about rates: a rate summarises trait evolution and cannot itself have effects on traits.
comments.request: Clarify what is meant by an effect of a rate on a trait.
comments.quote: Rates themselves are not entities that have effects on traits – quite the opposite

comments.issue: The review needs better conceptualisation of its aims and better situating in the field.
comments.request: Reframe the review's aims and context.
comments.quote: I think the authors need to better conceptualize what they are trying to review here

comments.issue: The review largely reiterates current best practices and basic macroevolution rather than adding synthesis value.
comments.request: Clarify the review's added value beyond existing practice.
comments.quote: In some ways, the authors are just reiterating current best practices

reviews.assessment: Compelling topic, but niche evolution is impractical and biased, terminology is undefined, and findings are overgeneralised.

comments.issue: Niche evolution arguments differ from diversification/extinction: it needs extra data, questioning its practicality as a predictive tool.
comments.request: Discuss the practicality and data demands of niche evolution indicators.
comments.quote: This limitation calls into question the practicality of niche evolution as a predictive tool

comments.issue: Using past niche evolution to infer current processes can be invalid; ancestral reconstruction may misrepresent ranges and specialisation dynamics.
comments.request: Address these reconstruction biases more explicitly.
comments.quote: the use of past niche evolution to infer current processes may not always be valid

comments.issue: Unexplained terminology makes the manuscript hard to follow for a broad audience.
comments.request: Define terms central to the discussion.
comments.quote: the manuscript can occasionally be difficult to follow due to the use of unexplained terminology

comments.issue: Engagement with relevant literature is incomplete.
comments.request: Engage more comprehensively with the literature.
comments.quote: the study could benefit from a more comprehensive engagement with relevant literature

comments.issue: Findings are overgeneralised without addressing variability across clades and geographic contexts.
comments.request: Address variation across clades and regions.
comments.quote: the manuscript overgeneralizes findings, without sufficiently addressing the variability that exists across different clades and geographic contexts

comments.issue: 'Rarely' implies studies exist but no citations are given at line 120.
comments.request: Provide citations or rephrase.
comments.quote: The word “rarely” implies studies exist, but no citations are provided

comments.issue: 'Internal drivers' is not clearly explained at line 132.
comments.request: Clarify what 'internal drivers' means.
comments.quote: The term “internal drivers” is not clearly explained

comments.issue: Examples of the 'correlates' mentioned at line 138 would improve clarity.
comments.request: Provide specific examples of the correlates.
comments.quote: The sentence would benefit from examples of these “correlates.”

comments.issue: A cited study contradicts the statement at lines 187-189, and supporting references are missing.
comments.request: Add supporting references and qualify the statement.
comments.quote: you cite a study that seems to contradict your statement

comments.issue: Line 190 contradicts the earlier statement (lines 74-75) that life-history effects are well established.
comments.request: Resolve the internal contradiction.
comments.quote: This seems to contradict the initial statement (Line 74-75) that life-history effects are well established

comments.issue: More recent literature on birds is missing at line 262.
comments.request: Include recent bird literature.
comments.quote: For bird species, more recent literature could be included to support the arguments made here

comments.issue: Claims at line 278 need supporting citations.
comments.request: Cite studies backing these claims.
comments.quote: Consider citing studies to back up your claims in this section

comments.issue: Line 294 contradicts the previous paragraph suggesting very low variability in niche traits.
comments.request: Resolve the contradiction.
comments.quote: This contradicts with the previous paragraph, which suggests that there is very low variability in niche traits

comments.issue: Line 297 contradicts the 'empirical support for Hypothesis 1' stated at line 292.
comments.request: Resolve the contradiction.
comments.quote: This statement seems to contradicts with a “empirical support for Hypothesis 1”

comments.issue: 'Phylogenetic diversity' and 'evolutionary distinctiveness' are used without definitions (lines 321-322).
comments.request: Briefly define both terms.
comments.quote: A brief definition of “phylogenetic diversity” and “evolutionary distinctiveness” would be helpful

comments.issue: 'And in mammals' is out of place at lines 331-333.
comments.request: Continue the list consistently.
comments.quote: The phrase “and in mammals” seems out of place

comments.issue: Conclusion at line 432 raises internal barriers that were only tangentially discussed in the section.
comments.request: Modify the conclusion or add a nuanced discussion of barriers.
comments.quote: Here the conclusion mentions the importance of internal barriers, which was only tangentially mentioned in the section

comments.issue: Context on why evolutionary potential matters for conservation is missing (lines 444-445).
comments.request: Explain the conservation relevance of evolutionary potential.
comments.quote: The authors could provide more context regarding why understanding evolutionary potential is important for conservation

comments.issue: Statement at line 536 is unsupported: only two studies are cited and one does not support the conclusion.
comments.request: Provide stronger evidence or remove the statement.
comments.quote: This statement does not seem to be supported by evidence

comments.issue: 'Horizon-scanning tools' is not defined at line 549.
comments.request: Briefly define the term.
comments.quote: It would help to briefly define “horizon-scanning tools” to ensure clarity for all readers

comments.issue: The statement 'We lack primary data (e.g., population trends)' is vague at line 43.
comments.request: Specify the types of missing primary data.
comments.quote: The statement “We lack primary data (e.g., population trends)” is somewhat vague

comments.issue: Lines 44-50 are repetitive and could be more concise.
comments.request: Revise this section to be more direct.
comments.quote: This section feels somewhat repetitive and could be made more concise

comments.issue: Line 53 does not explain why past extinction rates are reliable predictors.
comments.request: Explain the basis for the reliability claim.
comments.quote: You can explain why past extinction rates are reliable predictors

comments.issue: Lines 54-56 state context dependence generically without specifying it.
comments.request: Specify why these relationships are context-dependent.
comments.quote: Instead of a general statement, specify why these relationships are context-dependent

comments.issue: 'Intermediate assumptions' at line 57 is imprecise.
comments.request: Reword the phrase more precisely.
comments.quote: What do you mean by “intermediate assumptions”? Consider rewording it to something more precise

comments.issue: IUCN abbreviation is not introduced at line 68.
comments.request: Add the abbreviation on first use.
comments.quote: Maybe add the abbreviation here if this is used later in the text

comments.issue: Island settings where humans and invasive species arrive abruptly deserve emphasis (line 130).
comments.request: Add this nuance about island settings.
comments.quote: This might be especially true for island settings, where conditions change drastically when humans (and accompanied invasive species) arrive

comments.issue: Responses to change include more than evolution and dispersal, e.g. behavioural flexibility (line 172).
comments.request: Add other response types such as behavioural flexibility.
comments.quote: responses to changes include more than evolution and dispersal. For instance, behavioral flexibility can help to deal with immediate changes.

comments.issue: What 'positive relationship' means is unclear at line 218.
comments.request: Clarify the meaning of positive relationship.
comments.quote: The sentence would benefit from clarifying what a “positive relationship” means

comments.issue: 'Autocorrelation' may confuse readers at line 226.
comments.request: Define or rephrase autocorrelation.
comments.quote: The term “autocorrelation” might confuse some readers. Define or rephrase it.

comments.issue: 'Phylogenetic signal' is not explained at lines 270-271.
comments.request: Briefly explain or reword phylogenetic signal.
comments.quote: I suggest including a brief explanation or rewording regarding the phrase “phylogenetic signal”

comments.issue: Sentence at lines 277-280 could be clearer.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence for clarity.
comments.quote: This sentence could be made clearer. For example, “In clades that include both generalist species and adaptive radiations

comments.issue: Line 294 could end by noting that related species share similar extinction risks.
comments.request: Add the suggested closing phrase.
comments.quote: Consider ending with something like, “suggesting that related species tend to share similar extinction risks.”

comments.issue: Sentence at lines 317-319 could be clearer and more concise.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence more concisely.
comments.quote: This sentence could be clearer and more concise

title: Can Macroevolution Inform Contemporary Extinction Risk?

study.system: xenarthran insectivores; stable isotopes and camera-trap surveys, Brazil

editor_summary: Editor: address the reviewer doubting species-level differences and weak hypothesis tests; also consider predators, link factors to population regulation and coexistence, and redo statistics using residual diagnostics.

reviews.assessment: Supportive and finds the study sound, but wants a general objective, broader discussion, recent references, and a workflow figure.
strengths: accurate and useful figures and tables
correct methodology and results consistent with objectives

comments.issue: The paper lacks a general objective that would focus the narrative.
comments.request: Formulate an overarching objective to frame the study.
comments.quote: I miss the formulation of a general objective that would also focus the narrative and the possibility of carrying out a more open discussion.

comments.issue: Discussion is too specific; replication in other contexts or species is not considered.
comments.request: Add a more general discussion about replicating the study elsewhere.
comments.quote: But I miss a less opportunistic or specific, and a more general discussion, towards the possibility of replicating the study in other geographical contexts or with other similar species.

comments.issue: Introduction lacks a narrative reinforcing theoretical and analytical frameworks with recent references.
comments.request: Strengthen this section with recent theoretical and analytical references.
comments.quote: I miss a narrative more oriented to reinforce the theoretical and analytical frameworks for quantifying and classifying ecological niche differentiation with more recent references.

comments.issue: No figure shows the full analytical workflow.
comments.request: Provide a figure showing the full workflow.
comments.quote: I also encourage providing a figure showing the full workflow.

comments.issue: Discussion is balanced towards specific findings rather than broader implications.
comments.request: Add narrative on applying the framework elsewhere and biodiversity-loss consequences.
comments.quote: I recommend reinforcing this section with narrative that shows the need to implement frameworks like the one described in this study in other mixed places

comments.issue: "Significant knowledge gaps" on page 3 line 7 is not explicit.
comments.request: Explain more explicitly what is meant.
comments.quote: What do you mean by "significant knowledge gaps"? Please be more explicit.

comments.issue: It reads as if the two study areas are being compared.
comments.request: Clarify that the study areas are not being compared.
comments.quote: When you mention the two study areas, it seems that you are comparing them. If not, please make that clearer.

comments.issue: Intra- and interspecific competition is not discussed as a possible explanation.
comments.request: Mention competition processes hypothetically to justify findings.
comments.quote: I wonder if it is not appropriate to mention processes of intra- and interspecific competition to try to understand or justify (hypothetically) some of the findings.

comments.issue: Landscape dynamics are not fully addressed and limitations are not criticised.
comments.request: Add critical discussion of the unaddressed dynamic component.
comments.quote: The same is true when trying to consider the landscape dynamics, since this work does not fully address the dynamic component. Additional criticism is needed in this regard.

reviews.assessment: Sympathetic to the aim, but doubts that species-level differences address the introduction and that the methods strongly test the hypotheses.

comments.issue: Zenodo archive contains too many files, complicating reproduction.
comments.request: Consolidate files into distinct scripts or QMD files per figure.
comments.quote: suggest that the authors consolidate the numerous files, e.g. by creating distinct script or QMD files for the different figures in the manuscript.

comments.issue: Analyses require defining working directories, hindering reproduction.
comments.request: Share the material as an RStudio Project folder.
comments.quote: I also suggest that the authors they share the share the material as an RStudio Project folder so that the analyses can be reproduced without having to define working directories.

comments.issue: Jargon such as "cathemeral" is not accessible to a broad audience.
comments.request: Avoid or explain technical jargon.
comments.quote: I had to look up some jargon (eg 'cathemeral') which the authors could avoid if writing this for a broad audience.

comments.issue: Species-level differences are not sufficient to address the conceptual issues laid out in the introduction.
comments.request: Refocus the paper or temper the ambitions of its framing.
comments.quote: I am not sure that identifying species--level differences, the focus of this paper, is sufficient to address the issues laid out in the introduction.

comments.issue: Methods are not suited to strongly test the hypotheses presented in the introduction.
comments.request: Revise the analyses or reframe the hypotheses accordingly.
comments.quote: Another concern is that the methods aren't suited for strong tests of the hypotheses that the authors present in the Introduction.

comments.issue: H1's morphological and evolutionary predictors are never tested and H5 is never addressed.
comments.request: Test or explicitly drop these hypotheses.
comments.quote: nowhere are morphological / evolutionary history actually tested as predictors of diet niches. Hypothesis 5, once stated in the Introduction, is never addressed later in the manuscript.

comments.issue: Proportional data in Figure 2 are shown with silhouettes instead of a clearer format.
comments.request: Use a side-by-side bar chart for these proportions.
comments.quote: the silhouettes filed with blue/orange in Fig 2 are pretty, but such proportional data seems better suited to a side-by-side bar chart.

comments.issue: Isotopic niche size above 100% in Figure 3A is unexplained.
comments.request: Explain what a niche size above 100% means.
comments.quote: In Fig 3A, C. squamicaudis has an isotopic niche size bigger than 100%. What does this mean?

comments.issue: Figures are hard to read in black-and-white and potentially for colour-blind readers.
comments.request: Improve figure legibility for black-and-white and colour-blind readers.
comments.quote: Also the figures are very tough to read in black-and-white, and potentially for color-blind readers.

reviews.assessment: Impressive, well-written analysis with surprising convergences; most comments are minor line edits plus requests for interpretive context.

comments.issue: Readers need more biological context to interpret the significant findings.
comments.request: Provide more biological context around the significant findings.
comments.quote: it would help to provide readers (especially those not that familiar with the techniques being used) with more biological context about how to interpret the significant findings.

comments.issue: It is unclear what large-scale differences mean biologically, especially individual versus population-level effects.
comments.request: Clarify how to interpret differences found at large spatial scales.
comments.quote: particularly with the spatial scale analyses, I was unsure what to conclude about differences found at large scales (e.g., 2000, 2500 m).

comments.issue: Unclear whether the three dietary groups are truly distinct trophic tiers and how they are defined.
comments.request: Define each tier or present them as variation within one tier.
comments.quote: I was unclear whether are really three distinct tiers, or just variations within a single tier (as described in hypothesis 3, page 6).

comments.issue: The abstract should make clear that the focus is on xenarthrans.
comments.request: State the xenarthran focus explicitly.
comments.quote: There are lots of different kinds of mammalian insectivores. It should be made clear that the focus is on xenarthrans.

comments.issue: "Delicate" on page 3 line 23 is unclear.
comments.request: Delete or clarify "delicate".
comments.quote: Not clear what is meant by delicate. Delete?

comments.issue: Unclear whether bi-dimensional refers to carbon and nitrogen.
comments.request: Make clear what bi-dimensional refers to.
comments.quote: I assume bi-dimensional refers to carbon and nitrogen? This could be made clearer.

comments.issue: Five species are sampled only in the Cerrado and the giant armadillo only in the Pantanal, confounding site and species.
comments.request: Address the site-specific confound and missing Pantanal camera-trap data in the main text.
comments.quote: Ideally, one would like data from all six species at both locations in order to eliminate potential confounds due to site-specific influences

comments.issue: It is not made clear that three cameras were deployed at each sampling site.
comments.request: State the camera deployment design explicitly.
comments.quote: Make clear that, if I understand correctly, three cameras were deployed at each sampling site.

comments.issue: Page 8 lines 30-34 need context on what larger delta-X values mean biologically.
comments.request: Explain the biological meaning of larger delta-X values.
comments.quote: This is a place where some additional context would be helpful, i.e., what do larger values of δX mean biologically?

comments.issue: The calculations behind page 9 values, e.g. habitat percentages, are not explained.
comments.request: Explain fully what calculations were made.
comments.quote: Explain more fully what calculations were made. Are these percentages of each habitat type present or what?

comments.issue: Diet data rely on frequency of occurrence only, which may poorly represent diets across studies.
comments.request: Assure the measures are congruent and informative, or use better diet data.
comments.quote: The authors only use frequency of occurrence data to average across studies (line 46). Is this just presence/absence (i.e., the item was either found in the diet or not)?

comments.issue: The provenance of P. maximus data (camera traps, overlap, Figure 6, site) is never explained.
comments.request: Explain where P. maximus data come from and whether it was excluded.
comments.quote: It is not clear where the data for this species were obtained to allow calculation of overlap.

comments.issue: "Cathemeral" activity pattern is used without defining the hours involved.
comments.request: Define what is considered a cathemeral activity pattern.
comments.quote: a definition of what the authors consider to be a cathemeral activity pattern would be helpful (i.e., what hours are involved?).

comments.issue: It is unclear which page 13 values refer to carbon and which to nitrogen.
comments.request: Label the carbon and nitrogen values clearly.
comments.quote: Need to be clear which values are for carbon and which for nitrogen.

comments.issue: Page 15 line 36 is misleading because no samples were analysed in this study.
comments.request: State that results come from literature searches, not new samples.
comments.quote: This is a bit misleading because no samples were analyzed in this study. Rather, results were obtained from literature searches.

comments.issue: Page 16 lines 1-18 need reminders of what increasing or decreasing delta C and delta N mean.
comments.request: Remind readers of the biological meaning of these isotope values.
comments.quote: This is another place where it would be helpful to remind readers what decreasing or increasing delta C and delta N values mean biologically.

comments.issue: Figure 4 panel C shows a 2500 m scale never mentioned as evaluated in the Methods.
comments.request: Reconcile the 2500 m scale with the Methods.
comments.quote: Figure 4: panel C indicates a spatial scale of 2500 m yet this is never mentioned as being evaluated. See Methods Page 11, line 11.

comments.issue: Figure 5 includes a non-significant effect and panel F solely to depict all six species.
comments.request: Reconsider whether these Figure 5 panels are needed.
comments.quote: I am not sure the non-significant effect for T. tetradactyla needs to be included. No non-significant effects are shown for the other species, and I am not convinced panel F is necessary just to have all six species depicted.

comments.issue: The broader diet explanation for higher armadillo trophic level does not fit P. maximus's small isotopic niche.

comments.issue: The C3 diet explanation reverses cause and consequence with the shift in habitat use.

comments.quote: Not sure how individuals with mixed and strictly C3 diets explain the increase in habitat use with increased savanna cover. This would seem to be a consequence of the shift in habitat use not an explanation of it.

comments.issue: The point of noting that E. sexcinctus is the most roadkilled vertebrate is unclear.

comments.quote: Not sure what point is being made by noting the E. sexcinctus is the most roadkilled vertebrate in the region.

comments.issue: Camera trapping methods are confusing, as trapping occurred only in the Cerrado where no P. maximus burrows exist.
comments.request: Clarify the camera trapping methods substantially.
comments.quote: Confusing. Camera trapping was done in the Cerrado, so there would be no P. maximus burrows there. The camera trapping methods need to be clarified substantially.

comments.issue: Table S1 uses U.S. home range values for D. novemcinctus, unlike the consistent dietary tables.
comments.request: Delete the U.S. values or explain why they are needed.
comments.quote: The authors should be consistent and delete U.S. values, or explain why they are necessary

comments.issue: The paragraph at page 31 lines 162-176 largely repeats the Methods.
comments.request: Cut or condense this redundant paragraph.

title: Continental Patterns of Phenotypic Variation Along Replicated Urban Gradients: A Mega‐Analysis

study.system: community evenness and Hill numbers; global biodiversity datasets and simulations

editor_summary: Editor says three reviewers all recommended revision; the controversial topic suits Perspectives; reviewers ask for much clarification and reworking, and the author should give well-argued reasons for comments not addressed.

reviews.assessment: Thought-provoking but conflates the existence, measurability and interest of evenness, and many line-by-line arguments need reconsideration.

comments.issue: The paper conflates the existence of evenness with problems of definition, interest and measurement.
comments.request: Separate the conceptual question from measurement and interest arguments.
comments.quote: I think the paper repeatedly seems to conflate the “existence” of evenness, challenges in operationalizing a definition of evenness, questions about whether evenness is particularly interesting, and challenges in the measurement/estimation of evenness in community data.

comments.issue: Measurement issues should be separated from the deeper conceptual question; evenness exists as a numerical summary.
comments.request: Distinguish the measurement problem from conceptual claims.
comments.quote: I think it’s important to separate the measurement problem from any deeper conceptual issues.

comments.issue: The same criticisms could be levelled at species richness, so the special treatment of evenness is unjustified.
comments.request: Explain what is different about evenness relative to richness.
comments.quote: I also think it’s worth considering much of the criticism of evenness in this manuscript could just as well be leveled at “species richness”

comments.issue: Lines 85-95 mischaracterize the literature as treating evenness as a drop-in richness replacement.
comments.request: Correct the characterization of prior work.
comments.quote: Lines 85-95 appear to suggest that researchers view metrics of evenness as drop-in replacements for richness wherever richness is of interest. I don’t think this is an accurate characterization of the literature.

comments.issue: The argument at L160 is internally inconsistent about capturing commonest-species abundance.
comments.request: Reconcile the two opposing arguments about evenness indices.
comments.quote: captures the abundance of the commonest species seems irrelevant to whether or not it is a useful piece of information to partially capture in an index of evenness.

comments.issue: The L167 argument confounds estimator sampling behaviour with spatial variation in biodiversity.
comments.request: Separate sampling behaviour from spatial patterns.
comments.quote: This argument seems to confound questions about the sampling behavior of the evenness estimators under study with questions about whether and how biodiversity varies in space.

comments.issue: Evenness definitions are numerical properties of the empirical SAD and cannot be unrelated to its shape.
comments.request: Reconsider the claim that evenness is unrelated to SAD parameters.
comments.quote: All definitions of evenness under consideration here are numerical properties of the empirical SAD, and so cannot be unrelated to the shape of a (sufficiently) realistic distribution.

comments.issue: If communities randomly omitted or repeated species, an index detecting that would be valuable.
comments.request: Consider this scenario in the argument.
comments.quote: If communities in nature started randomly omitting or repeating species, might we not want an index capable of detecting it?

comments.issue: Calling Hill numbers’ latitudinal patterns obscured rather than different is a mischaracterization.
comments.request: Present the south-of-equator peaks as different trends worth studying.
comments.quote: Why do you say that higher-order hill numbers are obscuring latitudinal trends in species richness, rather than saying that they reveal interestingly different trends?

comments.issue: Hill numbers are numerical properties of the empirical SAD, not poorly fitting models.
comments.request: Treat Hill numbers as numerical properties in the reality argument.
comments.quote: The hill number associated with a community is a numerical property of the empirical species abundance distribution. It’s not a poorly fitting model (like MacArthur’s broken stick model).

comments.issue: The paper conflates ease of measurement with theoretical interest.
comments.request: Separate measurability from theoretical interest.
comments.quote: Some of the most interesting things in the world are very hard to measure, and some of the most boring are very easy to measure. I don’t think it’s useful to conflate ease of measurement with theoretical interest.

comments.issue: Instability of evenness could reflect poor sampling or estimators rather than a flaw of the metric.
comments.request: Consider better sampling and estimators before rejecting the metric.
comments.quote: I agree that it’s not great to have a metric that jumps around due to sampling variation, but note that this could simply be an argument for better sampling or better estimators from incomplete samples.

comments.issue: “Measure evenness on its own” at L304 contradicts the paper’s overall stance.
comments.request: Clarify this apparent inconsistency.
comments.quote: Here again I’m confused, because it sounds like you have a very clear notion of what evenness means and whether or not we are succeeding in measuring it, where as much of the rest of the paper seems to suggest the opposite?

comments.issue: The L309 point is only that SADs can be approximated by 1-3 parameter families.
comments.request: State the point about approximation more precisely.
comments.quote: Abundance distributions routinely have very large numbers of governing parameters (all of the parameters governing the time evolution of the abundances of every species in the community!).

comments.issue: Metrics capturing what 2-parameter approximations miss should be interesting if reliably measured.
comments.request: Reconsider the dismissal of such metrics.
comments.quote: Metrics that capture something about communities that are not well captured by 2-parameter approximations of the SAD should be very interesting, as long as they can be measured reliably.

comments.issue: Poor proxy status does not mean J and Hill ratios encode no information; reparameterization may link them.
comments.request: Acknowledge the information content of these indices.
comments.quote: The fact that J and hill ratios aren’t good proxies for shape parameters in SADs doesn’t mean that they don’t encode information about the distributions.

comments.issue: “Which distribution?” at L335 is unclear.
comments.request: Specify that the empirical SAD is meant.
comments.quote: L335: Which distribution? The empirical SAD!

comments.issue: Even a one-parameter SAD lets the parameter be recovered from summaries including evenness.
comments.request: Reconsider the argument at L366.
comments.quote: it is likely the case that the parameter value can be recovered from any of numerous numerical summaries of the SAD, including those we call “evenness”

comments.issue: Weak latitudinal relationships do not justify concluding there are no strong ecological signals.
comments.request: Acknowledge other possible ecological signals of evenness.
comments.quote: Just because evenness isn’t strongly related to latitudinal trends doesn’t justify the idea that there aren’t strong ecological signals. Evenness could signal something important about various aspects of ecosystem function, community dynamics.

comments.issue: It is logically inconsistent to call H and D both redundant with richness and misleading for differing.
comments.request: Resolve the contradiction at L374-376.
comments.quote: It is logically inconsistent to say that H and D tell the same story as richness and also that they are misleading

comments.issue: Principled richness estimation only matters if richness is the biological target.
comments.request: Match estimators to the aspect of the SAD of interest.
comments.quote: Deriving a principled estimate of species richness is a better idea if, but only if, the biological thing of interest is the species richness.

comments.issue: The paper never asks which ecological questions evenness can appropriately answer.
comments.request: Discuss what questions evenness has been used to answer and whether it succeeded.
comments.quote: what sorts of ecological questions are appropriately explored/answered through the lens of evenness?

reviews.assessment: Finds the arguments exaggerated and misleading, and corrects multiple confusions between Hill numbers and H/D and about sampling behaviour.
strengths: some worthwhile discussion on fitting distributions
interesting and novel results on scatter

comments.issue: The title is overly dramatic and inconsistent with the paper’s own use of the evenness concept.
comments.request: Reconsider the title.
comments.quote: The title “Does evenness even exist?” seems overly dramatic, since you yourself seem to recognize the existence of some kind of “evenness” concept throughout the article.

comments.issue: The arguments against Hill numbers are exaggerated and misleading, contradicted by Figure 6.
comments.request: Temper the claims against Hill numbers.
comments.quote: There is some worthwhile discussion here, but it is marred by exaggerated and misleading arguments against Hill numbers.

comments.issue: The claim that Hill numbers lack ecological significance ignores their links to model parameters.
comments.request: Engage with Hubbell 2001, Jost 2008 and Chao et al. 2015.
comments.quote: You must be aware that Hill numbers (and the similarity and differentiation measures which can be derived from them) have deep connections to the key parameters of some ecological, evolutionary, genetic, and biogeographic models

comments.issue: Connections between some Hill numbers and SAD shape parameters are omitted.
comments.request: Acknowledge these connections.
comments.quote: It is also known that some Hill numbers can be connected to the shape parameters of some species abundance distributions.

comments.issue: Hill numbers are nonlinear transformations of H and D, not H and D themselves; axes mislabel them.
comments.request: Use Hill numbers correctly and label axes as exp H and 1/D.
comments.quote: As you know, Hill numbers are not Shannon’s H and Simpson’s D, they are nonlinear transformations of them, introduced precisely because H and D lacked important properties expected of diversity measures

comments.issue: Hill numbers should be written with qD notation.
comments.request: Use the conventional qD symbols.
comments.quote: When you are talking about or graphing Hill numbers, you should use those symbols to prevent confusion.

comments.issue: The claim that Hill numbers vary highly in simulation is untrue except at pathologically low sample sizes.
comments.request: Re-examine this claim with adequate sample sizes.
comments.quote: This is not true except perhaps for pathologically low sample sizes; see below.

comments.issue: Same Hill number/H confusion at L74.
comments.request: Correct the terminology.
comments.quote: L74: No, see comment for L38.

comments.issue: Same confusion at L79: Hill numbers are the transformed values.
comments.request: Correct the description.
comments.quote: L79: Same confusion as L38 again. Hill numbers ARE the transformed numbers, not the numbers to be transformed as he describes.

comments.issue: The L88 recommendation is to compare S, exp(H) and 1/D on the same scale.
comments.request: Correct the citation interpretation.
comments.quote: Same confusion as in L38 yet again; the recommendation in the articles you cite is to compare S, exp (H), and 1/D; the conversions are essential so that all these measures have the same scale of units.

comments.issue: The known coverage-standardization solution to sample-size dependence (Jost 2010) is not mentioned.
comments.request: Discuss this solution to evenness sample-size dependence.
comments.quote: Why do you criticize the statistical properties of evenness measures without even mentioning this possible solution which you know so well?

comments.issue: H + ln D is claimed to be the most important Hill ratio but is not a valid evenness measure.
comments.request: Correct the claim about the Hill ratio.
comments.quote: Also, contrary to your claim that this is the most important Hill ratio, the actual Hill ratio is not a valid evenness measure (Jost 2010).

comments.issue: Sensitivity to the dominant species is meaningful because removing it changes all relative abundances.
comments.request: Reconsider the dominant-species removal critique.
comments.quote: Removing the dominant species often has a large effect on the relative abundances of all the other species, so the Hill numbers ought to change significantly.

comments.issue: Fitted distribution parameters may not reflect real processes, so non-parametric summaries remain useful.
comments.request: Acknowledge limits of the parametric approach for process inference.
comments.quote: The free parameters of a single distribution, when fitted to the data, may or may not reflect real processes, even if they accurately fit the dataset.

comments.issue: An expected mean abundance of 1 for 100 species is pathologically low sampling intensity.
comments.request: Use realistic sampling intensities in simulations.
comments.quote: This is a pathologically low sampling intensity.

comments.issue: The dominant-species distortion claim should be qualified to Hill numbers of order > 0.
comments.request: Restrict the statement to higher-order Hill numbers.
comments.quote: Note that the Hill number of order 0, species richness, does not show such an effect (since it does not depend on relative abundances), so you should qualify your statement to include only Hill numbers of order > 0, not all Hill numbers.

comments.issue: The bootstrap bias is not normal behaviour and likely reflects tiny sample sizes.
comments.request: Revisit the bootstrap analysis with adequate samples.
comments.quote: This is not normal behavior. Bootstrapping exp (H) and 1/D (which is what you are graphing, in spite of the misleading axis label) normally produces a tight symmetric spread of values

comments.issue: Scatter dependence on sample coverage is not examined.
comments.request: Test whether scatter depends on coverage level.
comments.quote: It would have been nice to see whether the amount of scatter depended on the coverage level of the sample.

comments.issue: Figures 6A-E show Hill numbers tracking the parametric curves, contrary to the paper’s claims.
comments.request: Revise the claim that Hill numbers flatten the data.
comments.quote: In spite of your claims here, Figs 6 A-E show that the Hill numbers of order 1 and 2 track almost exactly the patterns shown by your fitted parametric curves.

comments.issue: The “would they continue to be real?” question ignores use in economics and model links.
comments.request: Reconsider this rhetorical question.
comments.quote: What a weird question. For starters, they would still be used in other fields like economics even if there were no ecologists.

comments.issue: The sampling-bias criticism ignores an available coverage-based solution.
comments.request: Acknowledge the coverage-standardization solution.
comments.quote: You mention the susceptibility of S to under-sampling bias, but this criticism seems disingenuous.

comments.issue: The replicability section is wrong for any reasonable sample size; estimators converge rapidly.
comments.request: Re-analyse replicability with adequate samples and unbiased estimators.
comments.quote: This section seems wrong for any reasonable sample size. It seems so badly wrong to me that I wonder if I may have misunderstood something.

comments.issue: Evenness measures were not evaluated using coverage standardization to control sample variation in S.
comments.request: Apply the coverage-standardization method to evenness measures.
comments.quote: You have not seriously evaluated evenness measures using the method that both you and I have invented to control for sample variation in S.

comments.issue: Hill-number evenness does appear to proxy real processes and link to model parameters.
comments.request: Reconsider the claim that evenness is not a good process proxy.
comments.quote: The kind of evenness reflected by Hill numbers does appear to be a good proxy for real-world processes (see your Fig 6) and sometimes can even be expressed directly in terms of model parameters

comments.issue: Comparing Hill numbers does provide information about community structure.
comments.request: Acknowledge the information content of comparisons.
comments.quote: Comparing them for a given community obviously does provide information about community structure.

comments.issue: Cross-reference at L408-416 should point to the earlier comment.
comments.request: Fix the cross-reference.

comments.issue: The claim that evenness has no deep evolutionary history is unsupported and disproven by model derivations.
comments.request: Remove or revise the unsupported statement.
comments.quote: This is an unsupported statement, disproven by the derivation of expected Hill numbers of orders 1 and 2 from ecological or genetic models

comments.issue: Figure 5 is a semi-log plot without justification.
comments.request: Explain why a semi-log plot is used.
comments.quote: Fig 5 Why is this a semi-log plot?

reviews.assessment: Enormously controversial and highly citable piece; suggests framing as opinion and more argument for the perturbation tests and conservation relevance.

comments.issue: The conclusion that evenness is irrelevant to conservation is not convincing; evenness predicts ecosystem function well.
comments.request: Soften the “evenness doesn’t exist” conclusion and discuss conservation relevance.
comments.quote: I am less convinced than the author that evenness is irrelevant to conservation. I also believe evenness has been shown to be a good (as good as richness) predictor of ecosystem function.

comments.issue: The CEGS distribution will be unfamiliar to many readers.
comments.request: Add supplemental material explaining the CEGS distribution.
comments.quote: The author is certainly entitled to use the CEGS distribution (and it performs well), but it will be unfamiliar to many people.

comments.issue: More argument is needed that resampling and dominant-species removal are meaningful perturbations.
comments.request: Justify the perturbation tests.
comments.quote: I am convinced, but I think a little more argument is needed that resampling with replacement and removing the dominant species are meaningful perturbations to communities.

comments.issue: Hill number is used interchangeably with diversity metric.
comments.request: Make the distinction clearer.
comments.quote: The author seems to use Hill number anonymously with diversity metric (richness+evenness). This might be made more clear.

comments.issue: Work on how sampling distorts SAD shape is not cited.
comments.request: Cite Green & Plotkin 2007.
comments.quote: The author might usefully cite Green & Plotkin 2007 on how sampling distorts the shape of SADs

title: Does Evenness Even Exist?

study.system: grassland plant functional groups; 8-yr precipitation experiment and IPMs

reviews.assessment: Appreciates the novel approach but finds the ecological framing and links to observable field patterns underdeveloped.
strengths: novel combination of IPM modelling and pseudospectral analysis
effort to link community responses to water availability

comments.issue: The paper stays mathematical without linking transient instability to observable field patterns such as succession.
comments.request: Explain links to community-level dynamics like succession and interannual shifts.
comments.quote: as written the paper really focuses on the mathematical parts without linking it to observable field patterns

comments.issue: Why detecting facilitation and competition is relevant to stability estimation is not explained.
