comments.issue: Similar performance of different mechanism combinations could reflect species-specific mechanisms.
comments.request: Discuss this alternative explanation for the redundancy.
comments.quote: If different mechanisms govern the interactions of different species, could this explain why different combinations of mechanisms perform similarly in explaining overall community composition?

reviews.assessment: Ambitious and innovative modelling study, but major concerns about model construction, clarity, mechanism explanation and missing coexistence results.
strengths: addresses a central challenge in community ecology

comments.issue: Biomass loss only from superior competitors is unrealistic; identical R* species would not compete.
comments.request: Revise the competition term so identical R* species still compete.
comments.quote: In an extreme case when all species have identical R^\*, biomass loss due to compeition is zero according to equation at 219.

comments.issue: Overlap estimated from maximum height and root depth ignores seasonal growth and light competition asymmetry.
comments.request: Model asymmetric light competition and reconsider height overlap calculation.
comments.quote: Competition for light is asymmetric (higher plants shade shorter ones), while competition for soil N is not.

comments.issue: How soil N enters the model and the seed-to-adult biomass conversion are unclear and unjustified.
comments.request: Explain soil N dynamics and justify the biomass equations.
comments.quote: In addition, line 263 states that xi units of arriving seed biomass should result in roughly xi/fi new units of adult biomass, why?

comments.issue: Simulation length, stabilization criteria and the equilibrium-versus-year-6 comparison are unexplained.
comments.request: Explain stabilization criteria and justify the year-6 comparison.
comments.quote: The predicted biomass at stablizing equiblibrium is compared to observed biomass in 6th year, so how can we know species in experiments have reached their equilbrium?

comments.issue: Ten replicate simulations may be too few given stochasticity.
comments.request: Increase the number of replicates.
comments.quote: stochasticity may have great impact on average of 10 replicates. More replicates should be considered.

comments.issue: Figure 1 merely lists keywords; a process diagram of population dynamics is needed.
comments.request: Add a diagram of the major population dynamics processes.
comments.quote: The current Figure 1 is not helpful by simply listing the key words.

comments.issue: The main process equation should come before explanation of its details.
comments.request: Introduce the main equation first, then explain parameters.
comments.quote: I think it is better to introduce the equation for the major process first and then explain the details of equation.

comments.issue: Equations are not in an equation editor and are not numbered.
comments.request: Re-edit and number equations for citation.
comments.quote: the equations should be reedited in an equation editor and numbered for proper citation to improve the clarity and readibility.

comments.issue: Key methods information, including Table S1, is only in supporting information.
comments.request: Move essential methods details, such as the 11 attributes, into the main text.
comments.quote: the authors should specify the important information of the methods in the main text without referring to supporting information and even a R script

comments.issue: The four mechanisms are not explained in the introduction and their attribute grouping is unclear.
comments.request: Explain each mechanism and how the 11 attributes map to them.
comments.quote: The four mechanisms, named resource competition, spatiotemporal niche differentiation, dispersal and colonization, and population growth rates, are not explained introduction.

comments.issue: Coexistence is discussed but no results address it; results are only observed-predicted correlations.
comments.request: Analyse how many species persist and which mechanisms maintain coexistence.
comments.quote: species coexistence appears several times in the manuscript, but none of the results relate to species coexistence

title: Multiple Mechanisms Required to Predict Grass Community Composition

study.system: insect time series vs vertebrates; 4,500+ series from ~1,500 species

editor_summary: All reviewers see broad appeal; improve spatial modelling and dataset description, deepen discussion (density dependence). Editor also asks to consider detrending, sampling noise and state-space models, and seasonal variation.

reviews.assessment: Monumental, well-curated and polished study; the only gap is discussion of insect rarity and the data inclusion criterion.
strengths: attention to detail and adequate polish

comments.issue: The criterion of an interannual mean of 10 or more individuals excludes most rare insect taxa and affects estimates of mean and variance of D.
comments.request: Elaborate on the implications of this inclusion criterion for rare species.
comments.quote: The single aspect that I find that the authors gloss over is the fact that most insects are rare, and how that affects their data and estimates.

reviews.assessment: Impressive synthesis and largely sound analysis, but novelty is limited and spatial autocorrelation, outliers and measurement error need attention.
strengths: definitive demonstration that insect populations are more variable

comments.issue: Theory and earlier empirical work (e.g. Hanski 1990) already predict that fast-growing species are more variable, so the result is unsurprising.
comments.request: Better articulate what is novel beyond the larger dataset.
comments.quote: From theory you would expect species with higher intrinsic growth rates to have more variable populations and there have been empirical demonstrations of this previously e.g. Hanski 1990.

comments.issue: Spatial and phylogenetic autocorrelation are not accounted for, and the justification for omitting them is weak.
comments.request: Robustly account for spatial and phylogenetic autocorrelation.
comments.quote: Why not just account for the potential spatial autocorrelation or see if it is present in the residuals - I find the justification for not including this weak.

comments.issue: Outliers in Fig. 3c may have large leverage on the fit, possibly reversing the expected relationship.
comments.request: Check leverage with PSIS or transformations.
comments.quote: Based on figure 3c there seem to be some outliers that might have huge leverage on the fit - I think it's worth checking this using something like PSIS, or if doing some kind of transformation might change the relationship.

comments.issue: The negative time-series-length result is discussed too vaguely; whether it is real or an artifact is unresolved.
comments.request: Provide more discussion of this negative result and possible explanations.
comments.quote: If you take the result seriously it could e.g. be that having an unusually stable time-series is a prerequisite for having a long-period of observation

comments.issue: Measurement error and differences in survey techniques among taxa are not discussed as drivers of apparent variability.
comments.request: Consider and discuss whether survey techniques contribute to the results.
comments.quote: There's no discussion of the role of measurement error. Could be that monitoring insects is subject to more error because we use different techniques to measure their populations.

comments.issue: The discussion is thin on ecological interpretation, population dynamics and why results differ from previous studies.
comments.request: Deepen the ecological interpretation and comparison with earlier work.
comments.quote: I find the discussion a bit thin, there are some recommendations about how the results could influence monitoring efforts and some ecological interpretation of the results

title: Are Insect Populations Inherently More Variable? A Multi‐Taxa Approach to Characterising Interannual Fluctuations in Insect Time Series

study.system: African savanna trees; 26-yr herbivore exclosure/rewilding experiment

editor_summary: Three positive reviews all pointing to ways to strengthen the paper, e.g. improving framing and connections to theory to enhance conceptual novelty; revision encouraged.

reviews.assessment: Well-written, novel long-term experiment; minor revisions to language, framing and methodological clarity would strengthen the message.
strengths: exciting, well-designed and novel long-term dataset
broad interest to ecologists and conservation biologists

comments.issue: The paper is brief in places; some ideas need unpacking for less familiar readers.
comments.request: Expand and unpack ideas where noted to provide context.
comments.quote: The paper is a bit brief in places, which may be necessary due to the journal conventions, but I note below a few places where it would be helpful to see some ideas unpacked and expanded a bit

comments.issue: The role of fire in mediating tree-grass coexistence and recruitment is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss fire in the broader context of this savanna system.
comments.quote: Fire plays an important role in mediating tree-grass coexistence in savannas in tandem with herbivores, as fuel build-up in the absence of herbivory increases the intensity of fire to the point where it can influence recruitment.

comments.issue: 'Simulated extinction' and 'simulated rewilding' are not the appropriate terms; exclosure and reintroduction are.
comments.request: Use 'exclosure' and 'reintroduction' throughout, reserving 'rewilding' for implications.
comments.quote: While I understand the appeal of calling it “simulated extinction,” I’m not sure that it’s the appropriate language here, both because of the timeline but also because there’s a long history of literature on exclosure experiments.

comments.issue: LiDAR was used to extend the time series without an overlapping year to validate the extension.
comments.request: Compare LiDAR and field data in an overlapping year or cite supporting sources.
comments.quote: Later (Line 187-189) it becomes clear that LiDAR was used to extend the temporal duration of the field sampling, but there doesn’t appear to be a year of overlap to establish that this is a reasonable extension.

comments.issue: Large herbivore community information is relegated to the SI; comparability of rewilding treatments across plots is unclear.
comments.request: Front-load herbivore community information and report treatment densities, composition and functional groups.
comments.quote: I do think the large herbivore community information should be front-loaded in the paper, instead of in the SI (climate and soil makes sense, as it likely has less of an impact on this timescale).

comments.issue: No conceptual figure or table hypothesizes individualistic impacts of different megafauna.
comments.request: Add a conceptual figure or table of megafauna-specific impacts.
comments.quote: Some kind of conceptual figure or table hypothesizing the individualistic impacts of different megafauna would be really useful.

comments.issue: Hempson et al. (2015) on differential herbivory by body size and traits ('herbivomes') is not considered.
comments.request: Consider the herbivome framework of Hempson et al. 2015.
comments.quote: I’m thinking specifically about Hempson et al., 2015 (https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aac7978), which finds differential effects of herbivory based on body size and traits (“herbivomes”). That may be informative here.

comments.issue: Tree data are aggregated across size classes although responses may differ by life history stage.
comments.request: Analyse tree data by life history stage (seedling, sapling, adult).
comments.quote: One question I had was whether you considered analyzing your tree data by life history stages (seedling, sapling, adult)?

comments.issue: 'Decline' understates the problem; extinction should also be mentioned.
comments.request: Mention extinction alongside decline.
comments.quote: 46 I would also mention extinction. “Decline” implies population reduction, and the problem is more severe and widespread than that.

comments.issue: 'Desirable' is subjective and loaded.
comments.request: Replace with wording reflecting the research, e.g. 'restoring processes that promote resilience'.
comments.quote: 48 “Desirable” is subjective—suggest replacing with a less loaded phrase that reflects the research rather than personal preference, like “restoring processes that promote resilience.”

comments.issue: Six line-level copy edits (L50 comma, L59 BP shorthand, L104 phrasing, L156 unit spacing, L339 wording, L415 wording).
comments.quote: 415 Suggest “completely” rather than “perfectly” to avoid normative language.

comments.issue: The point that some experiments lack pre-rewilding baseline data should be added.
comments.request: Add the sentence about missing pre-rewilding baseline data.
comments.quote: 107 Another issue is that some unintentional and even some intentional experiments lack pre-rewilding baseline data, which has made evaluating rewilding impacts problematic.

comments.issue: Information on plasticity of inducible defenses and how fast life history traits change after herbivore return is lacking.
comments.request: Discuss plasticity and rates of change in defenses and growth forms.
comments.quote: Is there any information on the other end – i.e., how plastic inducible defenses are in these taxa? How quickly can these life history traits (chemical defenses, thorns, growth forms) change in response to herbivore reintroductions or additions?

comments.issue: The point should be reframed as 'Individualistically' (sensu Gleason) to draw on ecological theory.
comments.request: Reframe using the individualistic concept sensu Gleason.
comments.quote: 395 I’d consider reframing this as “Individualistically” (sensu Gleason), since that more directly draws on ecological theory.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether 'negative growth' means shorter trees or declines in growth rates, which are different processes.
comments.request: Distinguish negative growth from smaller size due to browsing.
comments.quote: 397 Negative growth (shorter trees), or declines in growth rates? Was it negative growth, or smaller size due to browsing?

comments.issue: More mechanistic discussion of the plasticity of this response and its persistence is needed.
comments.request: Add mechanistic discussion of response plasticity and duration.
comments.quote: 401 I do think this is a really important point, but would benefit from a bit more mechanistic discussion about the plasticity of this response in other studies, and how long this effect persists.

comments.issue: 'Vulnerability' is a strong word without a specific measured outcome.
comments.request: Use wording tied to measured outcomes.
comments.quote: 403 Vulnerability is a pretty strong word, without a specific measured outcome (aside from changes in growth/growth rates, or declines in biomass).

comments.issue: 'Property' implies something inherent and immutable; metric or variable is meant.
comments.request: Use 'metric' or 'variable' instead of property.
comments.quote: 405 I would use “metric” or “variable” rather than property; a property is something inherent and, in theory, immutable.

comments.issue: Whether the escape from browsing pressure is transient and how fire-herbivory interactions modulate it are not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss the transient nature and fire-herbivory interactions.
comments.quote: This is another place where some discussion of fire could be useful. Your study suggests that because the duration of the exclosure/simulated extinction was long enough to allow trees to reach the height where they escape browsing pressure

comments.issue: 'Extinction-driven' is a stretch at this timescale; response timescales differ among rewilding contexts.
comments.request: Contextualize the timescales of extinction-driven responses.
comments.quote: I think at this timescale that “extinction-driven” is a bit of a stretch. The timescales of responses between, say, Pleistocene rewilding and more recent or historic rewilding efforts (e.g., elephants or bison) may be quite different

reviews.assessment: Well-designed, clearly written study recommended for publication, pending inclusion of statistical results and figure improvements.
strengths: important results for savanna dynamics and rewilding
well written and generally very clear

comments.issue: Results of the statistical analysis are absent from the manuscript and supplement.
comments.request: Include the statistical results in at least the supplement.
comments.quote: The first is that the results of the statistical analysis are not included in the manuscript or supplementary material. These need to be included in at least the supplement to fully access this paper for publication.

comments.issue: Figures only highlight control-versus-treatment differences, not extinction-versus-rewilding contrasts, and do not show effect directionality or size.
comments.request: Rework figures, e.g. plot experimental-control differences and mark pre-exclusion versus exclusion periods.
comments.quote: One suggestion is to present the results of at least some of the variables measured as the difference between the experimental and control plots. This would allow the reader to better understand the directionality and size of the effects

reviews.assessment: Well-written and insightful; recommends caveats about exclosure limitations and balancing browsing-trap predictions with defense relaxation.

comments.issue: Exclosures are small, short-term and simulate complete extinction and full rewilding, so they only partially represent reality.
comments.request: Add clear caveats about these limitations to the conclusions.
comments.quote: it is important to recognize that they only partially represent reality. This limitation arises because such experiments are typically small in spatial scale and short in temporal duration.

comments.issue: The absence of a tree-density decline may reflect browsing suppressing growth and canopy development rather than mortality.
comments.request: Consider browsing suppression as an alternative explanation for stable density.
comments.quote: the majority of trees in this system are below 2.5 m in height (Figure 1), which falls well within the browsing range of the major large herbivores—elephants, giraffes, and elands.

comments.issue: The browsing-trap prediction ignores defense relaxation in the absence of herbivory.
comments.request: Balance the browsing-trap prediction with defense relaxation.
comments.quote: The authors’ prediction that trees may escape the browsing trap (lines 134–137) should therefore be balanced with the opposing mechanism of defense relaxation.

comments.issue: The vegetation description should cite Mutuku (2019).
comments.request: Cite Mutuku (2019) for the study-area vegetation.
comments.quote: • Lines 142–147: For a description of vegetation in the study area, I recommend citing Mutuku (2019): https://www.jstor.org/stable/26607462.

comments.issue: Line-level edits at lines 86 and 158.
comments.quote: • Line 158: Replace “given” with “marked with.”?

title: Responses of African Savanna Trees to Large Herbivore Extinction and Rewilding

study.system: Mediterranean butterfly-plant networks; 13-29 year monitoring data

editor_summary: Editor: all impressed by data/idea/message but problems remain: R1 flags circular reasoning in rare-species exclusion, insufficient plant dynamics, alternative drivers; R2 wants phylogeny; R3 effect sizes.

reviews.assessment: Praises the outstanding dataset and contribution, but wants phylogeny accounted for in trait analyses and more plant-perspective context.
strengths: solid, unique and interesting contribution on rewiring-turnover

comments.issue: The plant perspective is missing: plant richness trends and possible plant-mediated effects on the interaction networks are not assessed.
comments.request: Consider plant phenology/abundance effects somewhere.
comments.quote: the plants themselves form a kind of backdrop to the results as reported, rather than being centre stage

comments.issue: Phylogeny is not accounted for in the trait analyses, risking inflated significance of trait effects.
comments.request: Account for phylogenetic relatedness in these analyses.
comments.quote: phylogeny is not mentioned or tested in any of the analyses using species populations rather than networks as datapoints

comments.issue: The statement at line 305 about dispersal and RLQ axis 1 does not match the figure or Supplementary Table.
comments.request: Correct the statement.
comments.quote: Line 305 - you state that high dispersal is negatively associated with RLQ axis 1 – but that isn’t the case in the figure or Supplementary Table.

comments.issue: The Mediterranean decline references come from one group/region; wider evidence should be included.
comments.request: Cite a broader set of groups and regions.
comments.quote: You cite 5 references from the same broad research group, recording scheme and specific geographic region here – there are other relevant references and groups from the Mediterranean region

comments.issue: The equal contribution of turnover and rewiring by the end of the survey is not commented on.
comments.request: Discuss this pattern and whether turnover will exceed rewiring.
comments.quote: It is interesting (but you don’t comment at the moment in the text) that by the end of the survey period, because of the changes you document in rewiring and turnover, the two contribute equally to the overall turnover.

comments.issue: The 'structural constraints' at lines 389-390 are undefined.
comments.request: Define them and their link to phylogeny.
comments.quote: Lines 389-390 – what are the “structural constraints” referred to here? Could these be related to the phylogeny of the species present (butterflies and plants)?

comments.issue: 3 line-level copy edits (L55-56, L109, L204).
comments.quote: L55-56 – rephrase, e.g. replace “being” using “with”

comments.issue: 'Population' is not defined before line 141.
comments.request: Define it as a species-site combination earlier.
comments.quote: Line 141 – “82 populations excluded” – you later define a population on line 212 as a species-site combination, but I think you need to define before line 141

comments.issue: The threshold count defining the phenological curve length is unclear (lines 223-224).
comments.request: Specify the threshold.
comments.quote: Lines 223-224 – what is the threshold estimated count for the start and finish of the length of the phenological curve?

comments.issue: Figure 1 does not distinguish significant from non-significant decline sites, and site altitudes are not shown.
comments.request: Use solid/dashed lines and add altitudes or a map.
comments.quote: Please in Fig 1 can you differentiate between the 4 sites showing significant declines (e.g. show solid trend line) and the 3 not showing significant temporal trends

comments.issue: Mobility categories are defined inconsistently across text, Table S5 and Figure 2.
comments.request: Unify the terminology.
comments.quote: The four mobility categories defined on line 187 and in Table S5 are not defined in the same way as shown in the figure. The terms used need to be unified through all parts of the work.

comments.issue: Whether temperature variation in Figures 3 and 5 is standardised or in °C is unclear.
comments.request: Specify units in the legends/axes.
comments.quote: I interpret that Temperature Variation (x axis in Fig 3b) is standardised – but maybe it is variation in ºC. Please specify this in the legend and/or the axis label.

comments.issue: Figure S1's legend lacks detail on Chao 1 estimation and software.
comments.request: Expand the legend.
comments.quote: Figure S1 – maybe provide some more detail in the legend about the approach and software used to estimate Chao 1 and sampling completeness.

reviews.assessment: Praises the beautiful study and open data, but wants the rewiring narrative reframed and effect sizes contextualized with standardized measures.
strengths: beautiful study with impressive multi-decadal dataset

comments.issue: The discussion should acknowledge rewiring's dual role: declining proportionally yet remaining dominant and climate-responsive.
comments.request: Reframe the rewiring narrative.
comments.quote: Perhaps it is better to somewhat reframe the discussion to more explicitly acknowledge this dual role.

comments.issue: The drivers of plant turnover (warming/drying, land-use change) are not discussed.
comments.request: Expand the plant-turnover discussion.
comments.quote: The discussion could be expanded to deal further on the potential drivers of this turnover in the plant community.

comments.issue: Cumulative species losses (21.5% overall; 40-65% at sites) are not stated in the discussion.
comments.request: State the cumulative effects.
comments.quote: It would be beneficial for the authors to explicitly state these cumulative effects in the discussion to ensure the full impact of their findings is appreciated.

comments.issue: Standardized effect sizes (e.g. pseudo-R²) and biologically meaningful coefficient translations are not reported.
comments.request: Report standardized effect sizes and interpret coefficients.
comments.quote: the authors should consider calculating and reporting standardized effect sizes (e.g., pseudo-R² for GLMMs) and, more simply, translating the model coefficients into more intuitive, biologically meaningful terms

comments.issue: Why longer-proboscis butterflies are more generalist is not explained in the introduction.
comments.request: Explain this briefly.
comments.quote: it might be helpful to briefly state why this might be the case for butterflies (e.g., ability to access a wider range of corolla depths?) directly in the introduction

comments.issue: The number of species fully excluded by the visit threshold is not stated (line 141).
comments.request: Report the excluded species.
comments.quote: it would be useful to state how many species (in addition to the 82 populations) were completely excluded from the analysis as a result of this filtering

comments.issue: Figure 3b would benefit from a panel showing the fit against absolute temperature values.
comments.request: Add this panel.
comments.quote: perhaps adding a second panel showing the fit against the absolute values would make the connection to the statistical result even more direct

comments.issue: Figure 4c would be clearer as violin-plots.
comments.request: Use violin-plots.
comments.quote: I think it would help to show violin-plots in panel (c). The structure of variation is really more easy to see with this sort of visualizations.

reviews.assessment: Important novel finding but raises substantive issues: circular reasoning from rare-species exclusion, thin plant treatment, and undiscussed alternative drivers.
strengths: important contribution to network responses to global change

comments.issue: Excluding populations with <3 visits may circularly remove the rare specialists that drive the turnover result; sensitivity analyses are needed.
comments.request: Show exclusions per year and test alternative thresholds.
comments.quote: The exclusion of 82 populations with <3 flower visits (Lines 140-143) may create circular reasoning. These excluded populations are most likely the rare specialists whose progressive loss drives your central conclusions about species turnover.

comments.issue: Plants are treated superficially: no plant richness trends, trait shifts or phenology, and no limitation statement.
comments.request: Add plant trend analyses and interaction discussion.
comments.quote: Plants receive superficial treatment despite this being a plant-pollinator study.

comments.issue: Alternative drivers of decline (habitat loss, agriculture, fire, land use) are barely discussed despite site heterogeneity.
comments.request: Discuss their potential contributions.
comments.quote: Declines are attributed primarily to climate, but other well-known drivers of species decline, such as habitat loss/fragmentation, agricultural intensification, fire regimes, and land use, are barely discussed.

comments.issue: 'Early' at line 36 needs a timeframe.
comments.request: Specify the period.
comments.quote: Line 36: Specify "early" timeframe (e.g., "first decade" or "before 2010").

comments.issue: The hypothesis II prediction about rewiring is not linked to the observed rewiring decline.
comments.request: Link the results back to the hypothesis.
comments.quote: Hypothesis II predicts that interaction turnover will increase "driven by both rising species turnover and rewiring," but your results show rewiring actually declined over time

comments.issue: Whether the log transform at line 158 is natural or base-10 is unspecified.
comments.request: Specify the log base.
comments.quote: Line 158: Specify natural log vs. log₁₀.

comments.issue: Actual VIF values for directional versus absolute variation are not reported.
comments.request: Report the VIFs.
comments.quote: Lines 159-162: Report actual VIF values for directional vs. absolute variation—these are mathematically related.

comments.issue: Smoothing basis type and dimension are not reported (lines 219-231).
comments.request: Report the smoothing specification.
comments.quote: Lines 219-231: Add details on smoothing basis type and dimension (k).

comments.issue: The Gaussian-log choice for overdispersed counts lacks diagnostics and justification against negative binomial/zero-inflated models.
comments.request: Provide diagnostics and model justification.
comments.quote: Using Gaussian-log for count data because negative binomial showed overdispersion is problematic—negative binomial is designed for overdispersion.

comments.issue: What randtest permutes is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the permutation scheme.
comments.quote: Line 261: Clarify what randtest permutes (sites, years, or both).

comments.issue: How 'best fitted' models were selected and why link functions differ is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the model-selection procedure.
comments.quote: Lines 262-272: Clarify how "best fitted the data" was determined—AIC comparison? Diagnostics? Why do related turnover components need different distributions/link functions?

comments.issue: 'Most parsimonious within ΔAIC<2' is contradictory.
comments.request: Clarify the selection rule.
comments.quote: Lines 284-285: "Most parsimonious within ΔAIC<2" is contradictory—clarify selection procedure.

comments.issue: The simultaneous shift to low-dispersal and migratory species is contradictory and needs clarification.

comments.quote: Communities shift toward both "low dispersal" and "migratory" species—opposite strategies.

comments.issue: Whether butterfly and plant turnover rates differ statistically is untested.
comments.request: Formally test the rate difference.
comments.quote: Lines 321-324: You state butterfly and plant turnover increase at "similar" rates (+1.85% vs +1.75%/year), but confidence intervals are wide and overlapping. Please formally test whether these rates are statistically distinguishable.

comments.issue: The rate of rewiring decline is not quantified.
comments.request: Report the decline rate.
comments.quote: Line 325: You report that rewiring declined significantly but don't quantify the rate of decline.

comments.issue: Whether aridity or vegetation encroachment dominates the declines is unclear.
comments.request: Compare their relative importance.
comments.quote: Lines 362-364: You attribute declines to both aridity and vegetation encroachment—different drivers with different effects. Which dominates? Could their relative importance explain site heterogeneity?

comments.issue: The opposite proboscis-length pattern from bees is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the contrast.
comments.quote: Lines 403-414: Why opposite pattern from bees? Does length enable access to both shallow and deep flowers for butterflies?

comments.issue: Conservation and management implications are never discussed.
comments.request: Add management recommendations.
comments.quote: Your findings have clear management relevance, but this is never discussed. Consider adding some conservation implications and management recommendations.

title: Three Decades of Butterfly–Plant Interaction Turnover Explained by Climate and Species Loss

study.system: 11 Great Barrier Reef corals; 5-year demographics and IPM simulations

editor_summary: Reviewers found the paper well-written and praised the integration of empirical data, demography and coexistence theory, but model parameterization and structure issues question the main conclusion; SE's role may be understated, novelty needs articulation, and subcommunity presentation clarified.

reviews.assessment: Strong, publishable study; asks for transparency about the poor-performance dataset and to repeat survivorship robustness analyses.
strengths: excellent application of field data to a parameterized community simulation
compelling description of the relative forcing strengths
dedication to robustness testing and external validation

comments.issue: The expansion of the conclusions to other reef systems goes beyond the study's data.
comments.request: Restrict the extrapolation or better support it.
comments.quote: I balk somewhat on their expansion beyond their study’s data to suggest that storage effects are likely similarly unimportant in other reef systems.

comments.issue: The demographic data come from five years of overall decline (cyclones, thermal stress) and are extended to 1000-year simulations.
comments.request: Show that conclusions are robust to this unrepresentative period.
comments.quote: the time period over which the data were collected was shown to be a period of overall decline in both cover and diversity, characterized both by cyclone activity and repeated thermal stress events

comments.issue: The frequency of all-species extirpation in the simulations is not reported.
comments.request: Report the frequency of all-species extirpation.
comments.quote: no reporting on the frequency of all-species extirpation in their simulations

comments.issue: Baseline fitness (posterior distribution of species per capita growth rates) is not reported.
comments.request: Report the posterior distributions of per capita growth rates.
comments.quote: the lack of reporting on baseline “fitness” (e.g. a posterior pdf of per capita growth rate per species, given their demographic parameter distributions)

comments.issue: A minor taxon dominates the simulated community, which raises concerns about model realism.
comments.quote: the dominance of a minor taxon in the community in simulation

comments.issue: The authors acknowledge that the five years may not reveal between-taxon correlations but dismiss the concern too quickly without robustness checks.
comments.request: Acknowledge the limitation and show conclusions are robust to the foundational data.
comments.quote: if true, the authors should more transparently acknowledge this, and do a bit more to show that their conclusions are robust to the effects imposed by their foundational data

comments.issue: The rare jackpot year concern is only addressed for recruitment and wave-forcing mortality.
comments.request: Extend the robustness assessment to other processes.
comments.quote: they really only do so within two important, but not all encompassing, modalities – recruitment and wave-forcing specific mortality

comments.issue: Temporal variation in whole-colony and partial mortality across species is under-addressed, although adult survival is the most sensitive term.
comments.request: Repeat the fecundity perturbation for survivorship.
comments.quote: I believe that there are important temporal variations across species in whole-colony and partial mortality that may be under-addressed here.

comments.issue: Temporal variation in survivorship is restricted to wave forcing, ignoring other time-varying mortality sources.
comments.request: Broaden or justify the mortality model.
comments.quote: temporal variation in survivorship is restricted to wave forcing

comments.issue: DeltaSA and DeltaSL values are presented only for wave-forcing mortality, and survivorship is not perturbed as fecundity was.
comments.request: Present year-specific mortality effects and perturb survivorship.
comments.quote: they only present values for wave forcing dependent mortality (not the year-specific), nor do they perturb survivorship to increase variation and inter-species correlation in survivorship as they do fecundity

comments.issue: The overall performance of the taxa and overall fitness comparisons are not presented, even in an appendix.
comments.request: Be more transparent about the taxa's overall performance.
comments.quote: being more transparent about the overall performance of the taxa in hand, likely in an appendix

comments.issue: The discussion's three points apply only to fecundity fluctuations, so the abstract's breadth of conclusions is unsupported.
comments.request: Restrict the conclusions or extend the analyses.
comments.quote: The three points they highlight in the discussion only apply to fecundity fluctuations.

comments.issue: Equation A.6 has the mortality inequality backward; this is the primary model of temporal mortality variation.
comments.request: Correct the inequality and check the simulation implementation.
comments.quote: Assuming mortality of 1 means “dead”, I think you have that “<” backward. Please check your simulation implementations as well.

comments.issue: 'Intra-specific' should be added before competition at line 57 to capture the goby dynamic.
comments.request: Add 'intra-specific' before competition.
comments.quote: 57 consider adding “intra-specific” in front of competition to better capture the goby population dynamic

comments.issue: The reviewer is unconvinced that the stated constraint does not apply to this system as well.
comments.request: Justify why the constraint does not apply.
comments.quote: 113-115: I’m unconvinced that this constraint does not apply here as well.

comments.issue: The dataset conditions and the scales of temporal variability accessible in five years are not discussed as a caveat.
comments.request: Expand the discussion of dataset conditions and their limitations.
comments.quote: 154-165: Could use a more expansive discussion of the dataset conditions: i.e. need to discuss scales of temporal variability accessible in the 5-year dataset as a caveat for estimating the year-effects

comments.issue: Assuming non-wave survival is constant across years limits discussion of survivorship variation; the year-effect model deserves more focus.
comments.request: Give the year-effect model greater attention.
comments.quote: 199 Assuming all other survival (aside from wave dependent) “remains constant across years” greatly limits your ability to discuss temporal variation in survivorship.

comments.issue: The stock-recruitment relationship reverses at 1-10 km scales, and this spatial interaction may matter for storage effects.
comments.quote: the stock-recruitment relationship working at 1-10 km scales reverses this relationship (i.e. more coral = more recruits, Couch et al 2023)

comments.issue: 1000 years without immigration may contribute to the surprisingly low coexistence by excluding metacommunity and spatial heterogeneity.
comments.request: Discuss the no-immigration assumption and its consequences.
comments.quote: 269 – 1000 years of absolutely no immigration, may be partial source of surprisingly low coexistence as it again avoids meta-community/spatial heterogeneity.

comments.issue: What happens when all species are extirpated is not reported, nor is any method to maintain single-species communities.
comments.request: Report all-species extirpation outcomes.
comments.quote: What occurs when all species are extirpated? You don’t report any such cases, nor any artificial method to maintain single species communities.

comments.issue: A supplementary figure on overall performance or the posterior distribution of per capita growth rates would address whether rarity of coexistence relates to demographic rates.
comments.request: Add such a figure, faceted by year if possible.
comments.quote: A great place for a supplementary figure in overall performance, or posterior distribution (e.g. pdf) of species-specific per capita growth rates given parameter distributions

comments.issue: The yearly mortality run is mislabeled as excluding wave disturbance when all-cause mortality was allowed to vary.
comments.request: Rename and describe the run accurately.
comments.quote: you refer to it as “no wave disturbance” or “when we excluded wave-disturbance mortality”, when you’re just allowing all-cause mortality (including waves) to temporally vary

comments.issue: The yearly mortality run is barely discussed; its fine-scale MCT breakdown and the perturbation needed to make survivorship matter are unclear.
comments.request: Present more detail on this run.
comments.quote: I’d like to hear more about this run, especially on fine-scale MCT breakdown, and what perturbation it takes to make it matter (if any)

comments.issue: Figure A.1 should be replotted with a fixed y scale to allow comparison with Madin et al. 2014.
comments.request: Replot with a fixed y scale of about -2.5 to 8, dropping the outlier at 15.
comments.quote: Please replot these with a fixed y scale, say -2.5: 8 (dropping the one outlier at 15), to better compare to Madin et al 2014.

comments.issue: Excluding thermally induced mortality to avoid double-counting dodges a major driver of differential mortality, and the yearly-effects analyses are undersold.
comments.request: Present and strengthen the yearly-effects analyses.
comments.quote: As storage effects via thermally induced mortality are likely to change across the years, to avoid "double-counting" you’re dodging a major driver of species differential mortality.

comments.issue: Equation B.2 may need exp(Xi) because Xi is log-transformed area.
comments.request: Check and correct Equation B.2.
comments.quote: Equation B.2 I think you need exp(Xi) here? i.e. Xi is log transformed area?

comments.issue: Survivorship correlation is avoided in the B.5 diffuse analyses as well.
comments.request: Include survivorship correlations there too.
comments.quote: You avoid survivorship correlation here as well.

comments.issue: The paragraph at lines 907-913 repeats the previous one.
comments.request: Remove the repetition.
comments.quote: 907-913 This whole paragraph is a repeat of the one above it.

reviews.assessment: Exemplary study with well-handled uncertainty; asks to add within-species vital-rate correlations and fix demographic model issues.
strengths: exemplary work about coexistence in nature
handling of statistical and structural uncertainty
clear writing and presentation of evidence

comments.issue: Correlations between different vital rates within a species are not preserved in the model, which may misrepresent EC covariance.
comments.request: Model within-species vital-rate correlations and analyse the impacts of observed covariances and estimation errors.
comments.quote: correlations of individual vital rates between species are acknowledged in the model, but, if I get it right, correlations between different vital rates within a single species are not

comments.issue: There is one storage effect concept, not 'five storage effects', even if it occurs via different routes.
comments.request: Rename the five routes rather than calling them five storage effects.
comments.quote: The storage effect is one, ist a single concept, although it may occur via different routes or mechanisms.

comments.issue: The manuscript understates the role of the storage effect, which is the sole stabilizing process and doubles when coexistence occurs.
comments.request: Acknowledge the SE as the sole stabilizing process and its doubling in coexisting pairs.
comments.quote: I also believe that you are understating a bit the role of the SE.

comments.issue: The background mortality function has two parameters and asymptotes at 0 and 1, yet Figure A2 shows upper asymptotes different from 1.
comments.request: Clarify whether a third parameter is needed.
comments.quote: Nevertheless, in figure A2 upper asymptotes appear to be different from 1. Wouldn’t that imply the need for a third parameter (upper asymptote value)?

comments.issue: Mean growth rates of small individuals are negative, implying recruits would dwindle and vanish, which seems biologically implausible.
comments.request: Explain or correct the negative growth of small individuals.
comments.quote: mean growth rates of small individuals are negative (Figure A3). This means that recruits (unless really big o really lucky) would tend to dwindle and vanish. Does this make any biological sense?

comments.issue: The recruitment model only makes sense if Sum(N') is smaller than one, but N appears to be in cm2 rather than a proportion.
comments.request: Clarify the units and the recruitment equation.
comments.quote: Unless Sum(N’) is smaller than one, this makes no sense.

comments.issue: It is unclear why [i] appears in survival and fecundity betas and whether colony was a random factor; growth lacks it.
comments.request: Explain the random-factor structure of the regressions.
comments.quote: Why is an [i] in the survival and fecundity betas? Was the colony included in the regressions as a random factor? Why not in growth?

comments.issue: The claim at L59 is not entirely true because competition includes all resident species; increase-when-rare requires mainly intraspecific competition.
comments.request: Correct the statement about competition and rarity.
comments.quote: Not entirely true as competition takes into account all resident species in the community.

comments.issue: The wording at L68-63 is difficult to follow.
comments.request: Use different wording.
comments.quote: I suggest a different wording, the current one is somewhat difficult to follow.

comments.issue: The reference '#1' at L77 is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify the reference.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether R is a probability or a number of recruits.
comments.request: Define R clearly.
comments.quote: 9) L172: Is R really a probability, or rather a number of recruits?

comments.issue: The main text equation should be cited instead of Eq. A34.
comments.request: Refer to Eq. 2 rather than Eq. A34.
comments.quote: 10) L225: rather than citing Eq A34, refer to Eq 2, which seems to be the same and is already in the main text

comments.issue: The meaning of the vertical bar in the notation is not explained.
comments.request: Explain the vertical bar notation.
comments.quote: 11) L302. You should explain what the vertical bar (|) represents in this notation.

comments.issue: What the deltas correspond to biologically is not explained or named.
comments.request: Explain or name the biological meaning of the deltas.
comments.quote: 12) L311: I suggest that you explain, or at least name, what do these deltas correspond to biologically.

comments.issue: The symbols E_j and C_t are not explained.
comments.request: Explain or delete E_j and C_t.
comments.quote: 13) L313: Eplain or delete E_j and C_t.

comments.issue: The complex appendix procedures need a final round of copyediting.
comments.request: Copyedit the more complex procedures.
comments.quote: I suggest a last round of copyediting in the more complex procedures.

comments.issue: Lines 617-620 repeat the previous paragraph.
comments.request: Remove the repetition.
comments.quote: 15) L617-620: This seems to contain the same information as the previous paragraph.

comments.issue: Why B_j,R is maximal is worth explaining.
comments.request: Explain why B_j,R is maximal.
comments.quote: 16) L680: Maybe this is clear, but maybe it’s wort explaining why B_j,R is maximal.

comments.issue: It is unclear whether baseline survival and background mortality are the same; one consistent term should be used.
comments.request: Choose one term and use it consistently.
comments.quote: 17) L752: Is baseline survival the same as background mortality? Choose a term and use consistently

comments.issue: The problem at L112-1118 is hard to follow and may affect the SE estimates.
comments.request: Explain why the problem arises and whether it matters.
comments.quote: 18) L112-1118. I’m lost here, and I wonder whether this problem may affect your SE estimates.

comments.issue: Other second-order interactions may inevitably appear in the model and be wrongly labelled HOT.
comments.request: Clarify how second-order terms are treated.
comments.quote: I wonder whether other second grade interactions inevitably appear in the model (I believe they do inevitably in the second-order Taylor series approximation of Chesson).

comments.issue: The statement at P61, L21 is inaccurate: one species exists.
comments.request: Correct the statement.
comments.quote: 20) P61, L21: one species exists.

comments.issue: The reason for 20 iterations is not given.
comments.request: Explain why 20 iterations were used.
comments.quote: 21) P61, L32: Why these 20 iterations?

comments.issue: What 'all S-1 subcommunities' means at L1184 is unclear.
comments.request: Explain the subcommunity definition.
comments.quote: 22) L1184: all S-1 subcommunities? What do you mean here?

title: Environmental Fluctuations Are Insufficient to Explain High Coral Biodiversity: A Test of Five Storage Effect Pathways

study.system: Drosophila melanogaster; experimental evolution of population density

editor_summary: Editor asks the authors to consider all of the reviews, particularly those of Reviewer 3.

reviews.assessment: Interesting experimental evolution, but statistical results are minimally presented and the comparison of two very different experiments gives a false impression of strength.
strengths: evidence for density-elicited selection and genome-wide trade-offs

comments.issue: Statistical results are presented only minimally, especially given that one replicate cage behaved unexpectedly.
comments.request: Present statistical results in full, including effects and p-values per variable and interaction.
comments.quote: My main concern with the manuscript is the minimal presentation of statistical results, especially given that one of the four replicate cages did not “behave” as expected

comments.issue: Comparing two experiments with very different designs, conditions and genetic backgrounds creates a misleading win-win impression of strength.
comments.request: Temper the claims based on the cross-experiment comparison.
comments.quote: An additional, equally important concern is the attempt to compare two experiments that differ considerably in their design, abiotic conditions, genetic background of the D. melanogaster populations, etc.

comments.issue: It is unclear how non-overlapping generations were ensured and cohort or age effects controlled.
comments.request: Explain how non-overlapping generations and cohort effects were handled.
comments.quote: It is unclear from the main text how the authors ensured non-overlapping generations and consequently controlled for cohort- or age-effects.

comments.issue: Removing all food and water is treated as desiccation only, not also starvation.
comments.request: Explain survival times without food, water or both to separate the stresses.
comments.quote: Why is “removing all food and water from our replicate cages” considered only desiccation and not also starvation?

comments.issue: It is unclear which variables were included in the Fst statistical analysis.
comments.request: Add a table of effects on Fst for treatment, time, cage replicate and interactions with p-values.
comments.quote: It is unclear from the concise F & p-value details which variables were included in the statistical analysis.

comments.issue: The hypothesized bottlenecks are not tested.
comments.request: Test the bottleneck hypothesis directly.
comments.quote: L234-5: Is there a way to test the hypothesized bottlenecks?

comments.issue: Details of pseudo R-squared, N and p-values are missing.
comments.request: Report pseudo R-squared, N and p-values to convey explained variability.
comments.quote: Please provide details of “pseudo” R-squared, N and p-value, so that the reader can get a feeling of the explained variability.

comments.issue: The statement about absent parallelism does not specify the chromosomal arms or why it matters.
comments.request: Specify the chromosomal arms and discuss the lack of parallelism, or remove the sentence.
comments.quote: Please specify explicitly on which chromosomal arms parallelism was not evident, and discuss why? Otherwise, why is this sentence needed?

comments.issue: It is unclear which variables were included in the allele-frequency analysis.
comments.request: Add a table of effects on allele frequencies for treatment, time, cage replicate and interactions with p-values.
comments.quote: I want to see (in the main text) a table showing the effects on allele frequencies of expansion/truncation treatment, time/generation, cage replicate and their interactions as dependent variables, with p-values for each variable/interaction.

comments.issue: R-squared, N and p-values are missing for the significant negative correlations.
comments.request: Report R-squared, N and p-values for these correlations.
comments.quote: Please provide R-squared, N and p-value of the significant negative correlations.

comments.issue: Only previously selected SNPs were analysed, with no comparison to all or non-selected SNPs.
comments.request: Run the same frequency-shift analysis on all SNPs or the non-selected SNPs, or explain why not.
comments.quote: did the authors conduct the same analysis of average frequency shifts on all SNPs, or at least using those SNPs that were not selected previously?

comments.issue: No p-values are given for the systematic inversion shifts.
comments.request: Provide p-values for the inversion shift statement.
comments.quote: Please provide p-values for the statement “all inversions shifted systematically across replicates during expansion.”

comments.issue: Without statistics, the statements about greater-than-chance overlap and failed statistical overlap appear contradictory.
comments.request: Clarify the apparent contradiction with appropriate statistics.
comments.quote: Given the lack of any stats, I am somewhat confused when comparing the statements “we found far greater overlap in SNPs exhibiting signatures of selection during expansion in the indoor replicates and outdoor mesocosm than expected by chance”

comments.issue: The sentence at L456 wrongly implies the results necessarily contradict temperature speculations, which were not measured.
comments.request: Change the wording to 'shifting population densities can also drive'.
comments.quote: to avoid giving the reader the wrong impression that the results necessarily contradict the speculations about temperature

comments.issue: Minor fixes: missing Greek-letter statistic at L324 and the typo 'involve din' at L499.
comments.quote: L324: Looks like the Greek-letter statistics is missing.

reviews.assessment: Sound, well-presented experiments of broad interest; asks for clarifications on selection and drift, candidate-gene enrichment, and improved figure readability.
strengths: clearly of interest to broad readership

comments.issue: Combining hard and soft selection may prevent large-effect alleles from rising, so the experiment may not capture them.
comments.request: Test how many rising alleles were fixed and in how many replicate populations.
comments.quote: I am not sure that the selection experiment presented here can actually capture large effect loci given that the authors are basically combining hard and soft selection in their experiment

comments.issue: GLMs may be inappropriate because they are very sensitive to among-replicate differences such as fixation in a subset.
comments.request: Use statistical tools better suited to the replicate structure.
comments.quote: GLMs may not be the best tool to test for this since it is very sensitive to differences among replicates, i.e fixation in a subset of the experiments

comments.issue: The next expansion was not started from different cohorts of survivors, which would have emphasized fluctuating selection.
comments.request: Consider using different survivor cohorts in the next expansion round.
comments.quote: why the authors did not begin the subsequent round of expansion using from different cohorts of survivors, which would have further emphasized the action of fluctuating selection?

comments.issue: No candidate-gene enrichment analysis was performed for loci under selection.
comments.request: Test for enrichment of candidate genes affecting reproduction, starvation and desiccation resistance.
comments.quote: In particular candidate genes that both affect reproductive traits but also starvation and desiccation resistance are fairly well characterized in Drosophila and it would be simple to test for an enrichment of candidate genes under selection.

comments.issue: The bottleneck interpretation lacks supporting evidence.
comments.request: Check for an observed bottleneck and shifts in Tajima's D in the relevant replicate.
comments.quote: Did you observe a bottleneck during establishment of the experimental populations? Do you see a shift in Tajima’s D towards positive values particularly in this replicate that may confirm your interpretation?

comments.issue: At line 326 the colour description is misleading because both selection types are coloured.
comments.request: Refer specifically to the orange points.
comments.quote: This is a bit misleading since both selection types are colored. I would specifically refer to the orange ones.

comments.issue: The independence and haplotype organization of candidate SNPs are not visualised.
comments.request: Add Manhattan-type plots and show the synteny of orange and purple SNPs.
comments.quote: What about showing a Manhattan-type plot, which depicts the mean allele frequency shifts from the start to the end of the expansion phase (or better the slope) for all SNPs that rise in frequency in the truncation phase

comments.issue: Replicates are not separated by shape in Figure 3A.
comments.request: Use different shapes for replicates, especially in Figure 3A.
comments.quote: It may be useful to further separate the replicates by different shapes, in particular in Figure 3A, which is central to the manuscript.

comments.issue: Figure 1 does not show the replicate population constitution and it is unclear why two instead of four cages are shown.
comments.request: Show the replicate populations and explain the cage representation and grey separators.
comments.quote: The Figure should also Show the constitution of the replicate Populations. It is further unclear why two and not four cages are shown and what the grey separators (grey ovals in the cages mean).

comments.issue: Figure S2 lacks a legend.
comments.request: Add a legend to Figure S2.
comments.quote: Figure S2. Please add a legend

comments.issue: Minor fixes: 'Wrigh' should be 'Wright' (L217); Chi-symbols are not correctly rendered (L324).
comments.quote: Line 324, here and elsewhere, Chi-symbols are not correctly rendered

reviews.assessment: Well done and of high interest; asks for clearer justification of the expansion-truncation comparison, interpretation of reversed allele frequencies, and the role of inversions.
strengths: high interest to the ecological genetics community

comments.issue: Reversed allele frequencies in the truncation population may reflect costs of lab adaptation rather than fecundity-stress tolerance trade-offs.
comments.request: Consider alternative explanations for the genome-wide reversion.
comments.quote: The genome-wide reversion of allele frequencies observed in the truncation population could simply reflect alleles that underlie costs of lab adaptation, and might include a larger pool of potential factors rather than strict fecundity vs stress tolerance.

comments.issue: The boom-bust comparison contrasts generations of adaptation with survival hours after resource removal.
comments.request: Explain why this contrast is appropriate compared with a gradual reduction over paired generations.
comments.quote: I would appreciate the authors making it clearer in the manuscript how this contrast was appropriate compared to say, reducing the population dramatically over the course of similarly paired generations.

comments.issue: The discussion of inversions does not clearly add to the paper's major points.
comments.request: Justify the relevance of the inversion analysis or move it to the supplement.
comments.quote: I am unsure what the discussion of inversions genuinely adds to this paper. More guidance from the authors about the relevance of this piece would be appreciated

title: Pervasive Fitness Trade‐Offs Revealed by Rapid Adaptation to Shifting Population Densities in Large Experimental Populations of Drosophila melanogaster

study.system: ringed seals, polar bears and fish; Hudson Bay movement and foraging data

editor_summary: Editor says the work has promise but the models, their linkage, assumptions and limitations are unclear, and conclusions may be built into the model rather than emerging from it.

reviews.assessment: Finds the premise interesting but says the modelling is opaque, unassessable and over-reliant on 91 pages of supplementary material for an obvious conclusion.
strengths: interesting premise addressing a broad-scale question in an interesting system

comments.issue: The accuracy of the state-space modelled seal locations is unassessable and the Argos reporting interval is not given.
comments.request: Report the transmitter interval and quantify how well the state-space model corrected Argos error.
comments.quote: Therefore, some measure of accuracy of these model predictions are needed. How did the state-space model do at correcting Argos error?

comments.issue: Only 39 collared female polar bears were assumed to represent all predation risk.
comments.request: Report what percentage of the local bear population was collared and whether males were present.
comments.quote: However, it is unlikely that all polar bears in the region were collared (for instance, the collars only accounted for female bears). What percentage of the local bear population was collared? Were there males in the area?

comments.issue: The fish prey predictions lack stated temporal and spatial resolution, so their predictive power for seal behaviour is unclear.
comments.request: Report the temporal and spatial scales of the prey predictions.
comments.quote: What were the timescales of these predictions (temporal resolution)? Similarly, what was the spatial scale of these predictions (spatial resolution)?

comments.issue: Error propagation across the multiple combined models is not addressed, so the accuracy of comparisons cannot be determined.
comments.request: Quantify error propagation and the limitations of each model and their combination.
comments.quote: This study is based on comparisons of model results and it is not possible to determine the accuracy of any single model used here, much less the accuracy of comparisons and combinations that integrate multiple models.

comments.issue: The paper relies excessively on 91 pages of supplementary material for basic premises and results.
comments.request: Move essential details into the main text and reduce dependence on appendices.
comments.quote: The reliance on supplementary material is excessive (91 pages of supplementary material for this 18 page paper!).

comments.issue: The main conclusion that polar bears influence seal behaviour is obvious and does not justify the model complexity.
comments.request: Demonstrate that the modelling yields knowledge beyond the obvious conclusion.
comments.quote: The primary conclusion of all this modeling is that polar bears influence the behavior and space use of seals. That is an obvious conclusion that could be reached without the opaque modeling described here.

comments.issue: The discussion is speculative about energetic gain and what seals key into when choosing foraging areas.
comments.request: Restrict discussion to what the data can show or provide evidence for these claims.
comments.quote: Nothing in the current study provides information on energetic gain of seals or what seals are keying into when choosing foraging areas (prey diversity vs. prey abundance).

reviews.assessment: Supports publication with novel insights, raising mostly writing and messaging issues plus figure clarity.
strengths: worthy of publication in Ecology Letters with novel insights on marine mammal prey behaviour
smart choice of a well-sampled Hudson Bay study area
extensive data set on polar bear and ringed seal movements

comments.issue: The abstract's final sentences lack context and do not mention ringed seals or ice-associated organisms.
comments.request: Expand and contextualise the abstract's closing sentences.
comments.quote: I would like the abstract to be allowed more words to expand on the final few sentences and put things in better context.

comments.issue: The results description is hard to follow and “use” versus “habitat” is ambiguous for ringed seals.
comments.request: Rewrite the results more clearly, possibly using “presence” instead of “use”.
comments.quote: Is “use” the use of a habitat? Or region? And how does “habitat” vary for a ringed seal?

comments.issue: The discussion oversells that polar bear effects on ringed seals have been overlooked.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Multispecies Coexistence in Large Herbivores Based on Functional Traits and Dietary Data

editor_summary: Three reviews: one positive, two less positive. Main concerns are the fear-generalization framing (lab and field threats are not disparate), statistical treatment of repeated measures, and linking measures cautiously to concepts.

strengths: efforts to validate captive behavioral assays are needed
connecting captive metrics with wild ones could be fruitful

comments.request: Clarify the fear-generalization concept and tone down the claim.

comments.quote: the wider ecological framing of the paper seems ill suited to their research approach, but this could be fixed with some reframing of the introduction

title: Integrating Lab‐ and Field‐Based Approaches to Decipher Individuals' Response to Anthropogenic Change

study.system: Paramecium-Didinium microcosms; predator-prey stability selection experiment

editor_summary: Three reviews are supportive with minor changes, but one finds the paper fatally flawed; editor questions how unconnected subpopulations can yield trait evolution via stability selection.

reviews.assessment: Fully supports publication of this novel idea.

editor_summary: Editor requires count and binomial models, spatial/temporal structure, sensitivity analyses for tiny clusters, separation of environmental vs biotic effects, complete method details, and resolution of impossible data points.

strengths: Discussion brings the results together nicely

comments.issue: The spatial resolution of the environmental data is not stated.

comments.issue: How trait similarity was calculated on line 146 is not explained.

comments.issue: Lines 106-107 repeat earlier statements.

comments.request: Remove the tidyverse mention.

comments.issue: NODF is not spelled out at first occurrence.
comments.request: Spell out NODF.

comments.quote: Line 238. I recommend "the relationship was negative, but weakly

comments.issue: Lines 318-319 repeat that deer mice are the primary reservoir.

comments.quote: this sentence feels redundant given that deer mice are the primary reservoir for SVN. I recommend simply highlighting the threshold effect.

comments.issue: The risk statement on lines 353-355 seems inconsistent about focal host exclusion.

comments.issue: Lines 361 suggest environmental dependence is universal rather than context specific.

comments.issue: Suggested rewording for line 368.

study.system: ecological models; sensitivity, uncertainty analysis and calibration

editor_summary: Editor says all three reviews are positive but raise suggestions to clarify; recommends major revision for presentation and flow (see reviewer 3), and some sections need better referencing; an enjoyable read with potential.

reviews.assessment: Interesting and technically accurate review, but the structure, unsupported recommendations and missing examples need improvement.
strengths: authors clearly understand the nuances and explain technical details accurately
parts would be useful for students

comments.issue: The structure changes too much between sections, hindering comparison of the three main sections.
comments.request: Make the structure consistent across sections.
comments.quote: I found the structure chopped and changed between the sections too much. Consistency between the three main sections would help the reader to make comparisons.

comments.issue: Recommendations are presented as opinions without references, including the limitations and recommendations section.
comments.request: Ground recommendations in literature or worked examples.
comments.quote: Recommendations sections in the three modelling sections are devoid of references – where are these recommendations coming from? Are they grounded in literature?

comments.issue: The manuscript lacks examples of these processes done well or poorly.
comments.request: Add examples showing the impact and implications of the recommendations.
comments.quote: Throughout, it would have helped support the story to provide examples of these processes done very well and (potentially) examples of where they have been done poorly.

comments.issue: Potential errors are not highlighted consistently in the model introduction paragraph.
comments.request: Discuss errors such as model/functional form selection more consistently.
comments.quote: In the model introduction paragraph (107-122), it would be good to highlight the potential errors more consistently.

comments.issue: The abbreviations SA and UA add unnecessary cognitive load.
comments.request: Spell out sensitivity analysis and uncertainty analysis.
comments.quote: The use of “SA” and “UA” don’t seem worth the extra cognitive load on the reader versus just spelling out the words.

comments.issue: The text language for Figure 2 does not match the figure.
comments.request: Align the text with the figure terminology.
comments.quote: When discussing Fig 2, the language in the text does not match the language in the figure. E.g. “response surface”.

comments.issue: Curse of dimensionality and xAI appear as unexplained parenthetical statements.
comments.request: Define or remove these topics.
comments.quote: Important topics e.g. curse of dimensionality, xAI are included as unexplained parenthetical statements and then never defined or addressed.

comments.issue: The notion of sensitivity metrics is too vaguely explained.
comments.request: Explain sensitivity metrics more clearly.
comments.quote: The notion of “sensitivity metrics” is too vaguely explained, but is important for the sensitivity analysis section.

comments.issue: The section at lines 222-264 is muddled.
comments.request: Restructure this section.
comments.quote: Section from lines 222-264 is muddled and could use restructuring

comments.issue: The claim that only global SA is recommended is not cited and seems doubtful.
comments.request: Cite papers recommending global SA.
comments.quote: Line 266 can you cite the papers that recommend only using global SA? I would have said that local SA was more often used in ecological modelling

comments.issue: The Uncertainty Analysis section is structurally inconsistent with the Sensitivity Analysis section.
comments.request: Align the structure of the two sections.
comments.quote: Structurally, the Uncertainty Analysis section does not match the Sensitivity Analysis section.

comments.issue: The first half of the Model Inversion section is not grounded in cited literature.
comments.request: Support this section with references.
comments.quote: The first half of the Model Inversion section is not grounded in cited literature

comments.issue: Which errors are avoidable versus inherent in the system is only briefly addressed.
comments.request: Discuss this distinction more thoroughly.
comments.quote: I would have liked to see more thorough discussion of which errors in ecological modelling can be avoided and which are inherent in the system

comments.issue: Risk versus uncertainty is not integrated into the framework.
comments.request: Identify where risk fits into the structure.
comments.quote: Optional – the other idea that often gets muddled into these discussions is risk vs uncertainty. There is an opportunity here for the authors to identify where (and if) risk should fit into this structure

reviews.assessment: Comprehensive and valuable review in good shape for publication; one general point on identifiability and a few line comments.
strengths: systematic classification will be a useful resource for modellers

comments.issue: Fitting models to simulated data to learn about model and parameter identifiability is missing.
comments.request: Add a section on fitting models to simulated data for identifiability.
comments.quote: One aspect I was missing in the manuscript is fitting models to simulated data to learn about model or parameter identifiability.

comments.issue: The examples focus on global or regional scale models.
comments.request: Add more local models such as community or food-web models.
comments.quote: These examples focus on models with global / regional scale. I would consider adding more local models to the list, for instance community / foodweb models?

comments.issue: Infinitesimal deviation involves a formal derivative or automatic differentiation, which is not mentioned.
comments.request: Add this mathematical clarification.
comments.quote: It could be added that „infinitisemal deviation“ would involve a formal mathematical derivative or automatic differentiation.

comments.issue: 'Model emulation' is not defined.
comments.request: Define model emulation.
comments.quote: l. 285. Please define what is meant by „model emulation“ here.

comments.issue: How stratified sampling propagates uncertainty is unclear, as low-discrepancy sequences imply uniform input uncertainty.
comments.request: Specify how stratified sampling contributes to uncertainty propagation.
comments.quote: It is not 100% clear to me how stratified sampling schemes contribute to uncertainty propagation as it was defined here.

comments.issue: The sentence at lines 430-435 introduces absolute probability but gives a relative example.
comments.request: Rephrase the sentence.
comments.quote: This sentence intends to introduce absolute probability statements, but the example describes a relative statement (twice as likely under phi1 compared to phi2). Please rephrase.

comments.issue: 'Behavioral and non-behavioral model parametrization' is not specified.
comments.request: Define these parametrization types.
comments.quote: Please specify “behavioral and non-behavioral model parametrization”.

comments.issue: Prior predictive checks are not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention prior predictive checks and cite Wesner & Pomeranz 2021.
comments.quote: I would also mention prior predictive checks here (e.g. Wesner & Pomeranz 2021)

comments.issue: The higher computational cost of MCMC compared with local optimization is not noted.
comments.request: Note that MCMC requires orders of magnitude more function calls.
comments.quote: It should be noted that MCMC requires order(s) of magnitude more function calls than (local) optimization methods.

reviews.assessment: Strong, clear and novel synthesis that should be published; two strong optional recommendations on decision theory and high dimensionality.
strengths: strong case for novelty and value

comments.issue: The subfield of decision theory is ignored, so uncertainty is discussed without decision consequences, utility or value of information.
comments.request: Add decision-analytic framing, e.g. utility theory and adaptive management.
comments.quote: My first main comment is that the manuscript ignores the whole subfield of decision theory in applied ecological modelling.

comments.issue: Ecological management problems are used as motivation while the analyses stay in pure ecology.

comments.quote: I think this manuscript should not use ecological management problems as motivation if their analyses and discussions stay squarely in the real of pure ecology.

comments.issue: Visualisations and text suggest one or two dimensions of uncertainty while the examples involve dozens.
comments.request: Add a section on how higher-dimensional problems differ from 2D.
comments.quote: The authors’ visualisations and text strongly suggest that their models have only one or two dimensions of uncertainty (e.g., Fig. 5 “Posterior”). Yet almost all the examples they seem to have in mind would have dozens of uncertain parameters.

comments.issue: The 'in practice' caveat stems from models being more complex than the Figure 2 schematic.
comments.request: Explain this with examples such as individual-based models.
comments.quote: The “in practice” part here is often because the model is more complex than the schematic in Figure 2.

comments.issue: Sloppy modelling as a global method assessing model structure is not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention model sloppiness and cite Vollert et al. and Monsalve-Bravo et al.
comments.quote: Can you mention sloppy modelling as an approach here? I’m not sure about this, but I think they’re global methods since they assess the model structure itself.

comments.issue: A central assumption is introduced too late in the paper.
comments.request: State the assumption closer to the beginning.
comments.quote: Given the centrality of this assumption to the thinking throughout the paper, it should be stated closer to the beginning of the paper.

title: Calibration, Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis of Complex Ecological Models—A Review

study.system: temperate benthic communities; CO2 vent transplant experiment, ecosystem functions

editor_summary: Editor finds analyses suboptimal (models predict impossible negative biomass; >100% reductions), questions Weibull for absolute changes and suggests response ratios, wants sharper focus, shorter discussion paragraphs, plus line-level fixes.
