study.system: ecological communities; self-regulation loss metric; protist experiments

editor_summary: Editor: reviewers were uniformly impressed with the potential contribution but raised substantial presentation concerns that risk obscuring the findings; a thorough revision is essential.

reviews.assessment: Novel and sound science, but poorly defined terms and inaccessible mathematics make the paper confusing.

comments.issue: Key terms such as stability and disturbance are not defined in the introduction, leading to overly grand claims.
comments.request: Define the kind of stability and disturbances early and temper the claims.
comments.quote: certain key terms are not well defined in the introduction (what kind of stability, what kind of disturbances), which makes the paper confusing and also leads to some rather grand claims

comments.issue: The methods and mathematics are not accessible to ecologists; new terms and equations need more interpretation.
comments.request: Define terms, interpret each equation ecologically and remind readers of notation.
comments.quote: I think a bit more could be done to make the methods and mathematics more accessible to ecologists, quantitative or otherwise, and this would increase readership and hopefully uptake of their new metric

comments.issue: The introduction is mismatched with the paper: SL is species-specific, not a community-level metric.
comments.request: Better present the distinction between community and species stability.
comments.quote: SL is a species-specific metric which defines how a species responds to press and pulse disturbances – not how a whole community responds

comments.issue: The motivation is unclear from the abstract and introduction.
comments.request: Rewrite the intro and abstract, noting that previous methods need the full interaction matrix.
comments.quote: I also suggest rewriting the intro and abstract to clarify the motivation behind this paper. Maybe bring up that previous stability methods require the full interaction matrix in the intro?

comments.issue: References on the well-documented role of self-regulation in stability are missing, and the trait-based paragraph is irrelevant.
comments.request: Cite the self-regulation literature and remove or justify the trait-based digression.
comments.quote: Introduction is missing references to the literature and past research on role of self-regulation in stability, which is well-documented.

comments.issue: Species-level stability is undefined and has been well explored before; a clearer term is needed.
comments.request: Define the concept clearly early, perhaps as single-species response to disturbance.
comments.quote: What do the authors mean by exactly species-level stability? When reading the intro I understood it as stability in the abundance of a single species, but that is not really true when reading the rest of the text.

comments.issue: The ways perturbations can vary are never explained; press versus pulse should be specified in the introduction.
comments.request: Specify the perturbation types in the introduction.
comments.quote: There are several references made to features of perturbations and that perturbations can vary, but it is not explained in what way.

comments.issue: The problem is not set up and SL may just be intraspecific competition, leaving the added value unclear.
comments.request: Clarify what the paper adds beyond linking alpha_ii to relative yield.
comments.quote: I’m also anticipating the self-regulation loss metric to be equivalent to intraspecific competition, in which case I’m left wondering what does this paper add ?

comments.issue: The angled-bracket notation is unfamiliar to ecologists and poorly explained.
comments.request: Define the angled brackets where they first appear.
comments.quote: In Eq.3, please define what the angled brackets mean.

comments.issue: 'Species stability' in the abstract is undefined and open to many interpretations.
comments.request: Define species stability in the abstract and introduction.
comments.quote: the problem here lies with the term ‘species stability’, which is undefined in the abstract and intro, and can be interpreted in many different ways

comments.issue: Line numbers do not match the text and restart on each page.
comments.request: Add correct line numbers.
comments.quote: It would be helpful to have line numbers for the manuscript, as the numbers to the left added by the manuscript processing platform do not match up with the actual lines in the text, and restart at 1 for every page.

comments.issue: 'Intrinsic species response traits' is undefined.
comments.request: Define the term.
comments.quote: P3 Line 32 – define ‘intrinsic species response traits’

comments.issue: 'Species-specific stability' is undefined.
comments.request: Define the term.
comments.quote: P3 L44 – define ‘ species-specific stability’

comments.issue: The contrast between functional and community approaches is oversimplified.
comments.request: Explain more carefully how community ecology assumes species-level stability.
comments.quote: community ecology typically assumes stability at the species level by setting the diagonal of the interaction matrix

comments.issue: Species-level stability at P3 L51-61 remains unclear and the patterns referred to are undefined.
comments.request: Explain what species-level stability and the patterns mean.
comments.quote: I’m not entirely sure what you mean by species-level stability. Is it whether a species can reach a stable population in the absence of other species?

comments.issue: Most equations are not numbered.

comments.quote: The first equation is not numbered. In fact, quite a few of the equations are not numbered, is this a choice made by the authors?

title: Linking Biotic Interactions to Species Stability

study.system: insect herbivores; 246 papers; 18 global change stressors

editor_summary: Three largely very positive reviews; important issues should be carefully addressed in a revision before publication, which is where the paper is heading.

reviews.assessment: Ambitious and impressive meta-analysis with fascinating results, but attribution to specific stressors and three key limitations need fuller discussion.

comments.issue: Most global-change effects arise from interacting stressors, so decomposing them statistically and biologically is difficult.
comments.request: Discuss how interacting stressors limit attribution to individual stressors.
comments.quote: if most of the effects of global change arise from the interaction of multiple stressors, trying to decompose them could be difficult for both statistical and biological reasons

comments.issue: Direct/indirect separation, long-term equilibrium effects and non-linear effects are not discussed enough.
comments.request: Discuss the three key limitations more fully.
comments.quote: I don't think it weakens the impact of this paper at all to more fully discuss three key limitations

comments.issue: The degree to which multiple stressors interact in the real world is not described.
comments.request: Describe how multiple stressors interact in the real world.
comments.quote: It also seems worth describing the degree to which these multiple stressors are likely to interact in the real world.

comments.issue: It is unclear how top-down effects of warming are defined.
comments.request: Define what the top-down effects of warming means.
comments.quote: It might be useful to provide a definition for “the top down effects of warming”.

comments.issue: The framing leaves unclear whether herbivore declines are a result of environmental change, a driver or both.
comments.request: Clarify whether herbivores are victims, drivers or both.
comments.quote: Should we think of insect herbivore declines as the result of environmental change, a driver of environmental change or both?

comments.issue: The 18 stressors are not listed in the text and are split between Tables 1 and S1.
comments.request: List all 18 stressors in one main-text table.
comments.quote: It would probably be useful to list these 18 global change stressors here, rather than requiring the reader to find them in Tables 1 and S1.

comments.issue: Unclear which trophic-level combinations were included and whether unmeasured levels were absent.
comments.request: Clarify the trophic combinations included and unmeasured levels.
comments.quote: For the studies that were not tritrophic, can we assume that the other trophic level was absent, or could it have been present and not measured?

comments.issue: It is unclear which fitness measures were accepted.
comments.request: State which fitness measures were accepted.
comments.quote: What measures of fitness were allowed? For example, were measures of herbivore abundance allowed?

comments.issue: Different fitness metrics (counts, rates, relative scales) may not be comparable even after standardization.
comments.request: Justify pooling heterogeneous fitness metrics.
comments.quote: So were different responses variables compared directly? Even when standardized by standard deviation, it seems like these different fitness metrics could potentially behave pretty differently?

comments.issue: The small value constant is unexplained and its influence on effect sizes unknown.
comments.request: Justify the small value constant and test its effect.
comments.quote: How did you determine the small value constant? Did it have much effect on your effect sizes?

comments.issue: What the effect size ID represents is unclear.
comments.request: Explain what the effect size ID represents.
comments.quote: Can you explain “effect size ID (an unique identifier for each effect size value)” more? Was this ID unique to the numeric value or to the fitness metric type?

comments.issue: Case ID, case study and entry are not clearly distinguished.
comments.request: Clarify case ID versus case study and entry.
comments.quote: Is Case ID the same as “case studies” in Fig. 1? What is a case study vs an “entry”?

comments.issue: The total number of observations is only given later in the results.
comments.request: Report the total number of observations in the methods.
comments.quote: If a subset had n=1962 observations, how many observations were in the entire data set?

comments.issue: The moderator-level threshold is limited by number of papers rather than observations.
comments.request: Explain the threshold based on paper number.
comments.quote: If there were data from multiple species per paper, why was the threshold for reporting moderator levels limited by number of papers rather than observations?

comments.issue: The three extreme data points below -35,000 are unexplained.
comments.request: Explain the extreme effect sizes.
comments.quote: Please interpret “(3 data points < -35,000)”. Is this in units of standard deviations? Did these extreme values arise from extremely small pooled SDs?

comments.issue: The main figure does not allow mean effect sizes and their significance to be assessed.
comments.request: Show means and confidence intervals in the main figure.
comments.quote: it might actually be more informative to present means and confidence intervals in the main paper figure, and then present a version with the raw data distributions in the supplemental

comments.issue: It is unclear whether effect sizes combine all stressors, so habitat differences may reflect different stressors.
comments.request: Clarify whether effect sizes combine all stressors.
comments.quote: These effect sizes combine all possible stressors? So habitat differences could reflect different stressors happening in different habitats?

reviews.assessment: Interesting and important synthesis, with minor comments and two larger concerns about the results presentation and degrees of freedom.
strengths: interesting synthesis in the context of insect declines
Table 1 nicely sets up the motivation

comments.issue: Directionality imposed on effect sizes for stressors such as water decrease is unclear.
comments.request: Clarify whether directionality was imposed on effect sizes.
comments.quote: I don't think it is clear from the stressors listed in table one, if there was directionality imposed on the effect size

comments.issue: The results section is hard to follow and is not explicitly linked to Table 1.

comments.issue: The meaning of high and low Cij values is not explained.
comments.request: Explain what high and low Cij values represent.
comments.quote: Lines 275–276: Please clearly explain what high and low values of Cij represent.

comments.issue: The sentence on lines 326-327 is ambiguous about 'high co-occurrence'.
comments.request: Clarify whether this means increases over time or more species pairs.
comments.quote: This sentence is difficult to interpret. By “high co-occurrence,” do the authors mean an increase in Cij over time, or that Cij could be calculated for a larger number of species pairs?

comments.issue: The quantity referred to by '100' at line 365 is unclear.
comments.request: Specify the unit or quantity.
comments.quote: Line 365: Please specify the unit or quantity referred to by “100.”

comments.issue: Line 436 may cite the wrong figure.
comments.request: Check whether Figure 5 was meant.
comments.quote: Line 436: Is really this result in Figure 4? Did you mean Figure 5?

comments.issue: Family-level labels may be arbitrary and better replaced by lineages or clades.
comments.request: Use 'lineages' or 'clades' instead of 'families'.
comments.quote: Rather than “families,” it may be more appropriate to refer to “lineages” or “clades,” as the family level may be partly arbitrary.

comments.issue: Figure 1 does not make clear that each row represents a potential plot.
comments.request: Clarify this in the caption.
comments.quote: It was not immediately clear that each row in panels A–D represents a potential plot; this should be clarified in the caption.

comments.issue: Figure 2 appears to add no substantial information.
comments.request: Consider removing Figure 2.
comments.quote: I am not convinced that this figure is necessary, as it does not appear to add substantial information beyond what is presented elsewhere.

comments.issue: Figure 4 label does not match the terminology used elsewhere.
comments.request: Rename to 'Co-occurrence trends'.
comments.quote: Figure 4: Maybe better “Co-occurrence trends” to match the terminology presented above.

reviews.assessment: Important question and novel application, but index interpretation, drift conceptualization and the small within-clade fraction leave the assembly implications uncertain.

comments.issue: The inherent problems with interpreting co-occurrence indices are not remedied and may be amplified.
comments.request: Address the interpretability of the co-occurrence indices.
comments.quote: the inherent problems with interpreting the outcome of such indices is not remedied, and maybe even amplified, by the authors approach

comments.issue: Asymmetric competition can also arise from fitness differences, not only from relatedness.
comments.request: Consider fitness differences (Mayfield and Levine 2010).
comments.quote: But such asymmetric competition could also arise through fitness differences (see Mayfield and Levine 2010).

comments.issue: Prior manipulation of Jena plots means reassembly did not start from a common state.
comments.request: Consider this plot history, e.g. as a random factor in models.
comments.quote: all the plots have undergone manipulation of present species. Though that manipulation had stopped by the time the data used here was recorded, there certainly was not a common playing field for the reassembly to play out on.

comments.issue: The assumption that co-occurrence reflects encounters is untested, and environmental heterogeneity could cause patterns.
comments.request: Test or acknowledge this assumption and alternative drivers.
comments.quote: Yet, that is a strong assumption that remains untested. There is no guarantee that supposedly aggregated or segregated pairs of species in fact spatially aggregated or segregated

comments.issue: The neutral-theory framing of drift and immigration is incorrect; seeding is a one-time massive immigration event.
comments.request: Revise the conceptual framework for drift and immigration.
comments.quote: In neutral theory, immigration is not affecting drift directly, but rather masks or counteracts it. To my understanding, ecological drift occurs due to stochastic birth, death, and reproduction events.

comments.issue: Adding the same species to all plots increases co-occurrence by chance, even in delta C.
comments.request: Use a null model that accounts for increased occupancy.
comments.quote: Adding the same species to all of the plots should lead to an increase in co-occurrence just by chance. Using the change in co-occurrence does not remedy that

comments.issue: Phylogram distances are treated as the only option, though a chronogram could be as informative.
comments.request: Confirm the phylogram results with a chronogram.
comments.quote: the authors use phylogram distances as a proxy for some (unmeasured) functional divergence and I would argue that a chronogram, while clearly not containing the same kind of phylogenetic information, could be as informative as a phylogram for that purpose

comments.issue: Within-family pairs are only 13% of all possible pairs, so their impact on overall assembly is unclear.
comments.request: Quantify the expected impact on overall community assembly.
comments.quote: But that represents 13 % of all possible pairs in the 60 species pool. What kind of impact on overall community assembly can we expect from that relatively small percentage of within-clade species pair interactions?

comments.issue: It is unknown how excluding the focal families would affect the results.
comments.request: Run a model excluding these families' pairs.
comments.quote: Have you run a model where you exclude the pairs of these particular families?

title: Species Assembly Is Lineage Specific: Phylogenetic Divergent Species Aggregate in Some Lineages but Segregate in Others

study.system: habitat selection analyses; literature review, simulation, murre/gull/narwhal case studies

editor_summary: Both reviewers positive and find the paper well written and potentially important; one reviewer's valid points, mainly literature review scope and model presentation, need addressing.

reviews.assessment: Well-written paper with sound, well-presented results and useful methods; concerns and suggestions are relatively minor.
strengths: methods useful across many use cases

comments.issue: Restricting the literature review to use-availability designs may omit many studies using point process, MaxEnt and other estimation methods.
comments.request: Broaden the search or acknowledge this limitation.
comments.quote: limiting to only studies with models fit with use-availability designs could substantially limit your results here. A fair number of studies likely use the poisson approximation, maxent, etc to fit the same exponential RSF/SSF models.

comments.issue: Equations 2/3 could reinforce the misconception that RSFs are logistic regressions rather than exponential selection functions.
comments.request: State that the equations approximate an exponential RSF and add the general weighted-distribution or point process form.
comments.quote: equations 2/3 (and ones in the SI) -- these equations could be misleading and contribute to the unfortunately common misconception that RSFs are equivalent to a logistic regression model.

comments.issue: The mathematical distinction between RSFs and SSFs (fixed availability versus space-time movement kernel) is not made.
comments.request: Include the point process equation and point to the distinction between the models.
comments.quote: line 162 -- this is where if you had the (space-time) point process equation for RSFs/SSFs included somewhere, you could point to the mathematical distinction between them as well (i.e. availability function fixed in time vs space-time movement kernel).

comments.issue: Calling the model the 'new model' is not descriptive.
comments.request: Use a more descriptive name such as the 'fitness model'.
comments.quote: line 199 -- here and elsewhere, calling it the “new model” is not very descriptive. Perhaps the “fitness model” or something like that might be better.

comments.issue: It is not shown that 30 available points are enough for stable selection estimates.
comments.request: Test 50 or 100 available points to confirm the estimates stabilize.
comments.quote: It might be worth trying 50 or 100 available points to confirm that 30 is enough. Indeed, many early SSF papers used or recommended much fewer, but more recent ones suggest more

comments.issue: The point that mechanisms can change space use without changing selection is underemphasized.
comments.request: Emphasize the use-versus-selection distinction more.
comments.quote: I suggest you consider emphasizing this point a little more, as it is relatively uncommon for researches to assess both use and selection

comments.issue: Figure S4, which highlights the scarred-narwhal mechanism, is relegated to the supplement.
comments.request: Consider moving Figure S4 to the main text.
comments.quote: This is highlighted by figure s4, which may be worth trying to move to the main text (although I realize you already have 6 figures there).

comments.issue: Line-level edits: replace the word 'promote' and correct the SI citation to Avgar et al (2016).
comments.quote: line 105 -- suggest using a different word than “promote”

reviews.assessment: Extremely well written, conceptually clear and methodologically sound; no substantive issues requiring revision.
strengths: compelling evidence from review, simulations and case studies

title: Including Fitness and Health Proxies Can Alter Our Understanding of Habitat Selection

study.system: 84 empirical MCT studies; literature review of coexistence mechanisms

editor_summary: All reviewers find the paper well written and enjoyable, but question its novelty and coherence: it combines an underdeveloped literature review with perspectives, relies heavily on the authors' own work, and has detailed problems.

reviews.assessment: Excited by the review but finds it a poorly integrated mix of underdeveloped review and opinion-based recommendations.
strengths: interesting section on niche and fitness difference modeling

comments.issue: The paper reads as two underdeveloped pieces pushed together: a light literature review and a perspectives section.
comments.request: Integrate the two parts or choose one direction.
comments.quote: the paper itself felt like two things pushed together

comments.issue: Recommendations feel arbitrary and grounded in the authors' experiences, so presenting them as arising from a deep review is misleading.
comments.request: Ground the recommendations in the reviewed literature or reframe the paper.
comments.quote: the arguing that the path forward recommendations arise from a deep literature review feels misleading

comments.issue: The recommendations could conflict in practice (broadening systems versus paired validation experiments) and slow the field.
comments.request: Address conflicts among the recommendations.
comments.quote: the recommendations given, while each good individually, taken collectively in practice could be at odds with each other and slow the field

comments.issue: The trade-off between capturing variation and increasing certainty in estimates is not acknowledged.
comments.request: Discuss how to balance these needs.
comments.quote: some acknowledgement of the balance of tradeoffs between capturing variation and increasing certainty in our estimates would be reasonable

comments.issue: The restriction of empirical tests to pairwise competitive interactions and its consequences for understanding are not discussed.
comments.request: Review approaches that address this restriction.
comments.quote: A lot of empirical tests have had to restrict to pairwise and competitive interactions based on the models that work well with partitioning methods

comments.issue: Stabilizing niche versus equalizing fitness mechanisms should be added as a third key feature early on.
comments.request: Add niche versus fitness quantification as a key feature.
comments.quote: I would suggest adding stabilizing niche versus equalizing fitness mechanisms as a third key feature

comments.issue: 'Realized its potential' is arbitrary without a benchmark for what realizing potential would mean.
comments.request: Give criteria for realizing potential.
comments.quote: “Realized its potential” – a bit arbitrary, without a benchmark for what it would mean to have/have not realized its potential.

comments.issue: The review focuses on what has not been done and barely engages with the findings of the 20 temporal coexistence studies.
comments.request: Systematically review when variation is stabilizing and why.
comments.quote: At the moment, the focus is on all the things that have not been done (which certainly warrants discussion), but very little on has been done.

comments.issue: The uncertainty barrier reads as opinion rather than review engagement; how many studies used means versus distributions is unknown.
comments.request: Link the uncertainty point to the literature review.
comments.quote: I’m also a big proponent of including uncertainty estimates, but this barrier as described felt more like opinion than engagement with the literature review.

comments.issue: The criticism about bias in competition coefficients could apply to many fields and did not require a systematic review.
comments.request: Link it to the review or move it to a separate paper.
comments.quote: It is a criticism that could be leveled at many branches of ecology, and didn’t require a systematic review of the literature to identify.

comments.issue: The niche/fitness section format should also be applied to the fluctuation-dependent papers.
comments.request: Use the same idea-synthesis format for the temporal papers.
comments.quote: This section on applications of niche and fitness difference modeling was really interesting

comments.issue: Matching method to question is not novel, and the example confuses invasion growth rates with non-MCT metrics.
comments.request: Clarify how much this issue has actually been a problem.
comments.quote: as written, matching method to question does not seem particularly novel

comments.issue: Requiring model testing for every study is inefficient and ignores that research builds on itself in well-studied systems.
comments.request: Clarify when model testing is necessary.
comments.quote: Is it necessary to test all models for each study, or when first working in a new system?

comments.issue: The model selection section omits facilitation and higher-order interactions and does not review what models exist and their assumptions.
comments.request: Include emerging functional forms and their assumptions.
comments.quote: a large criticism of MCT is that the models to date do not incorporate facilitation well, and there are emerging studies developing new functional forms to address this

reviews.assessment: Timely retrospective with valuable recommendations, but premature, self-focused and covering ground already treated by earlier syntheses.
strengths: appreciation of emerging alternatives to the niche-fitness paradigm

comments.issue: Almost every example comes from the authors' own work, so independent and contrarian perspectives are missing.
comments.request: Acknowledge contrarian perspectives (e.g. Abrams, McPeek, Simha et al.).
comments.quote: almost every example in the text comes from their own work

comments.issue: Earlier syntheses already cover much of this ground and present many of the same recommendations.
comments.request: Outline generalities in the results rather than study design.
comments.quote: Earlier syntheses (e.g. Godwin et al. 2017; Buche et al. 2022; Terry & Armitage 2023; Hawlena et al. 2022) already cover much of this ground and present many of these authors' recommendations.

comments.issue: Predictions are not grounded in natural history to generate directional quantitative hypotheses.
comments.request: Encourage trait-based, a priori hypotheses and report whether reviewed studies did this.
comments.quote: One recommendation might therefore be to encourage practitioners to ground their predictions in the natural history of the system to make directional, quantitative hypotheses.

comments.issue: External validity is the most important barrier to adoption of empirical MCT, and the recommendation is not concrete.
comments.request: Give concrete advice, such as distributed experiments.
comments.quote: I think section 4.5 is the most important barrier to adoption of empirical MCT — skepticism about its external validity.

comments.issue: Pattern-to-process and process-to-pattern mismatches need reconciliation.
comments.request: Discuss how these mismatches can be reconciled.
comments.quote: How can these pattern-to-process and process-to-pattern mismatches be reconciled?

comments.issue: MCT tools could be used for abundance dynamics instead of binary coexistence outcomes.
comments.request: Consider applying partitioning tools to abundance dynamics.
comments.quote: Rather than continuing to focus on a binary “coexistence” outcome, could one area of progress use the same approaches to examine how environment and competition jointly shape abundance dynamics?

comments.issue: The Drosophila example was already done by Terry (2025); stronger validation pairs lab invasion growth rates with independent co-occurrence data.
comments.request: Cite Terry 2025 and discuss additional validation approaches.
comments.quote: This was already done by Terry (Ecology Letters 2025), who conducted a Drosophila coexistence experiment and validated it using MCT.

comments.issue: Counterfactual scenarios echo earlier null-model controversies whose progress is not discussed.
comments.request: Discuss what progress in that area has looked like.
comments.quote: The reliance on counterfactual scenarios in MCT echoes earlier controversies over null models, which faced similar critiques concerning interpretability and ecological realism.

comments.issue: Areas outside plant community ecology (e.g. cancer, economies) where MCT could apply are not identified.
comments.request: End with an outward-looking recommendation and needed data.
comments.quote: I was somewhat disappointed that the authors did not identify areas outside of the typical domain of plant community ecology in which empirical MCT could be applied.

comments.issue: The proportion of cases where exclusion or invasion failure was directly observed rather than inferred is not reported.
comments.request: Report this proportion from the literature review.
comments.quote: it would be interesting to know the proportion of cases where competitive exclusion or invasion failure was directly observed in trials rather than inferred from model coefficients

comments.issue: The difficulty of collecting spatial coexistence data is not discussed and no recommendations are offered.
comments.request: Discuss how to collect spatial data in practice.
comments.quote: The authors mention spatial coexistence mechanisms a number of times, but do not really discuss the realities of how difficult this data would be to collect for most species.

comments.issue: Adding parameters consumes degrees of freedom, creating a trade-off between model complexity and parameter precision.
comments.request: Point out this trade-off.
comments.quote: adding additional parameters also consumes degrees of freedom

comments.issue: The move of MCT ideas into random matrix theory is not mentioned.
comments.request: Mention this direction of theory and empirical work.
comments.quote: a lot of ideas from MCT are now being applied to disordered systems (random matrix) theory to study stabilisation in high-diversity systems

comments.issue: The trait-partitioning approach deserves more emphasis as a key empirical contribution.
comments.request: Put more emphasis on trait-partitioning.
comments.quote: I think more emphasis could be put on the mechanistic partitioning's “trait-partitioning” approach.

title: What Have We Learned From Empirical Applications of Modern Coexistence Theory?

study.system: animal movement; 3D step selection functions; Antarctic petrels

comments.issue: Prokopenko's use of an iSSA is not acknowledged.

comments.quote: L62: Prokopenko used an iSSA; see first comment.

comments.issue: The term 'attraction' is unclear.

comments.issue: Several line-level wording fixes are needed.
comments.quote: L129: “as we use are” — something is off.

reviews.assessment: Timely, well-written 3D SSF extension, but the paper needs stronger ecological justification and accessibility aids such as diagrams and tables.
